SQE2 Model Answers, Marking Grids and Explanations

Companion answer page for the Uprising Test Prep SQE2 Study Guide, covering all 70 written and 20 oral stations: the 35 written and 10 oral stations printed in the book, and the 35 written and 10 oral stations in the free digital station library. Each section below is numbered to match its own surface exactly. Attempt each station cold before reading its answer.

How it is graded Written, printed in the book Written, digital station library Oral, printed in the book Oral, digital station library Part 4, questions and answers

How SQE2 is graded

Each criterion is graded A to F by a trained assessor making one global professional judgment, then converted to marks. Skills and application of law are weighted equally across the assessment as a whole.

GradeMarksMeaning
A5Superior performance: well above the competency requirements of the assessment.
B4Clearly satisfactory: clearly meets the competency requirements of the assessment.
C3Marginal pass: on balance, just meets the competency requirements of the assessment.
D2Marginal fail: on balance, just fails to meet the competency requirements of the assessment.
E1Clearly unsatisfactory: clearly does not meet the competency requirements of the assessment.
F0Poor performance: well below the competency requirements of the assessment.

There is one overall pass mark for SQE2, not a separate oral pass mark and written pass mark, and it is scaled at each sitting under the SRA's Marking and Standard Setting Policy. No fixed pass percentage exists, and this guide does not state one.

Ethics and professional conduct are pervasive and are never flagged. Every station in this book contains a conduct issue you were expected to find without being told it was there. Each one is set out below under its own heading.

Written stations printed in this book (1-35)

These 35 written stations are printed in Part 2 of the book, numbered 1 to 35 in the order they appear there.

Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)

Written station 1: Police station no comment interview and the risk of adverse inferences on a dwelling burglary

Case and matter analysis  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO PRIYA RAVAL, PARTNER

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 14 September 2026

Re: Dean Whitmore, burglary of 4 Larch Rise, Kettleworth. First hearing 21 September 2026

1. Purpose

This report analyses the strength of the Crown's case, the adverse inference risk created by the no comment interview, and my advice on plea, venue and next steps. It also raises a conflict of interest that must be resolved before 21 September.

2. The offence the Crown must prove

The charge is burglary under section 9(1)(b) of the Theft Act 1968, or in the alternative section 9(1)(a). Against Mr Whitmore as a principal the Crown must prove that he entered 4 Larch Rise as a trespasser and stole property there, or that he entered as a trespasser with intent to steal. There is at present no evidence at all that he entered the house. Nobody places him inside, no forced entry is attributed to him, and no fingerprint, footwear or DNA evidence has been disclosed.

The realistic prosecution route is therefore secondary liability under section 8 of the Accessories and Abettors Act 1861, on the basis that he drove Mr Barrow to and from the address knowing what Mr Barrow intended to do. That requires proof of assistance or encouragement plus knowledge of the essential matters of the offence. Presence and driving alone are not enough. Alternatively the Crown may in due course substitute or add handling stolen goods, given the console in the boot.

3. Strength of the evidence

Points in the Crown's favour:

(a) A neighbour puts a dark blue Vauxhall estate on the corner of Larch Rise in the 20 minute window when the burglary occurred, with a partial registration matching the car Mr Whitmore was driving.

(b) He was stopped roughly 75 minutes later, four miles away, with a games console concealed in the boot under a blanket.

(c) Concealment under a blanket supports an inference of knowledge, although it is Mr Barrow who is said to have loaded the bag.

(d) His antecedents include a 2019 dwelling burglary, which the Crown may seek to adduce as propensity evidence.

Points in our favour:

(e) The neighbour identified a car, not a person. There is no identification of Mr Whitmore at the scene.

(f) The laptop and the cash have not been recovered from him or from the car.

(g) Our client's account, that he waited in the car while Mr Barrow said he was collecting money owed, is not inherently incredible and is not contradicted by anything so far disclosed.

(h) The Crown has disclosed nothing on forensics, which may mean nothing links him to the point of entry.

Overall the case against him as a principal looks weak. The case as a secondary party is arguable but presently thin, and turns on whether the jury or bench accepts he knew what Mr Barrow was doing. That is a knowledge question on which he is likely to have to give evidence.

4. Adverse inferences under section 34

He was cautioned, he was questioned before charge, and he now relies on facts he did not mention: that he stayed in the car, that Mr Barrow went off alone saying he was collecting a debt, and that Mr Barrow loaded the holdall. Those are facts he could reasonably have been expected to mention. Section 34 is therefore engaged and the court may be invited to draw a proper inference. The absence of a prepared statement matters a great deal. A prepared statement setting out those facts would have removed the inference risk while still allowing him to decline questions. Nothing was handed in, so we have no contemporaneous record of his account.

Two things reduce the risk. First, disclosure was genuinely thin: no forensic position was given, and the officer would not say whether the neighbour had described anyone. Legal advice to stay silent in the face of incomplete disclosure is capable of being reasonable, and the reasonableness of reliance on that advice is what the tribunal assesses. Second, he can explain that he was reluctant to implicate a co-accused held in the same custody suite. That is a human explanation a bench or jury may accept.

The price is that to run the legal advice explanation properly he will normally have to waive privilege and let the court hear why the advice was given. He must be advised of that now, not on the morning of trial, and he must be advised of a specific difficulty. Waiver opens up what he told Tom at the police station, and what he told Tom is not the account he now gives. Tom's note of 00:20 on 12 September records only that he had been driving around with Mr Barrow all evening, had lent the car to nobody, and that Mr Barrow put a bag in the boot at some point. It does not record the ten minute stop on Larch Rise, or Mr Barrow getting out to collect a debt, which are the facts the defence now turns on. His proof says in terms that he has since thought about it and wants to say what actually happened. If privilege is waived, the Crown will be able to show that the exculpatory account was withheld even from his own solicitor, which strengthens rather than answers the section 34 point and invites a recent fabrication attack. My advice is that we take a careful further statement on what he did and did not tell Tom before we advise on waiver at all, and that we do not assume the legal advice explanation is open to him.

5. Advice on plea and venue

I advise a not guilty plea. He denies entry and denies knowledge, and the Crown's case on knowledge is not currently made out.

On venue, this is an either way offence. Nothing in the papers takes it into the indictable only category in Schedule 1 to the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980: there is no violence or threat of violence to anyone in the dwelling, and he has one, not two, previous dwelling burglary convictions. So allocation applies. If the magistrates accept jurisdiction he then has the right to elect. My advice would be to elect Crown Court trial. The case turns on whether a tribunal accepts an innocent explanation for presence and for property in a boot, a jury is the better tribunal for that, and the disclosure regime in the Crown Court is stronger, which matters here because our defence depends on what the Crown has not revealed about forensics and about the neighbour. He should be advised of the counterweight, which is that the Crown Court has greater sentencing powers.

6. Next steps before 21 September

(a) Resolve the conflict at paragraph 7 immediately.

(b) Request the initial details of the prosecution case and press for the neighbour's statement, the partial registration, the CCTV or ANPR on the Bexton Road, and the forensic position on the point of entry and on the console.

(c) Take a full further proof once he has separate representation confirmed, and take instructions on waiver of privilege.

(d) Consider a written prepared statement served now, which does not cure section 34 but does fix his account before he sees the evidence.

(e) Check whether the bail condition not to contact Mr Barrow can be complied with, and confirm his community ties for any bail issue at court.

7. Conflict of interest

Tom advised both Mr Whitmore and Mr Barrow at the police station and neither has been told. Their accounts are not merely different, they are in direct conflict: Mr Whitmore says Mr Barrow left the car and returned with the holdall, and Mr Barrow says he was in the pub until 21:00 and knew nothing about the boot. Mr Whitmore's defence is now to put the burglary on Mr Barrow, and Mr Whitmore has expressly asked that Mr Barrow is not told. We cannot act for both. There is a conflict of interest and, separately, we hold confidential information from each which is material to the other and which we could not disclose.

The firm must cease to act for at least one client and, because we hold confidential information from both, in practice for both, unless one file can be closed cleanly and no material confidential information from that client has any bearing. My advice is that we cease acting for Mr Barrow, whom we saw first, only if that can be done without prejudicing him, and that we take a considered view that acting for neither may be the safest course. Whichever we do, both must be told promptly and in writing, both must be told to obtain independent representation in time for 21 September, and we must not disclose what either told us to the other. We should record the decision and the reasons on both files.

Trainee Solicitor

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The paralegal advised both arrested men at the police station and sat in both interviews, and neither has been told. Their accounts are in direct conflict: the client says the co-accused left the car and came back with the holdall, the co-accused says he was in the pub and knew nothing. The client also asks that the co-accused is not told what he has said. There is a conflict of interest between two current clients on the same matter, and the firm holds confidential information from each that is material to the other and cannot be passed on. A competent candidate spots this from the attendance note without being invited to, concludes the firm cannot act for both, advises ceasing to act, tells both clients promptly and in writing so each can get independent representation before 21 September, discloses nothing either said to the other, and records the decision. An information barrier is not an answer where the conflict is between two clients on the same matter.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsPulls out the facts that actually matter: no evidence of entry, the car and not the man identified, the console concealed in the boot but loaded by the co-accused, the 75 minute and four mile gap, the missing laptop and cash, the silence on forensics, the 2019 dwelling burglary, and the fact both suspects were advised by the same firm.Recites the chronology of the arrest without separating what the Crown can prove from what it merely asserts, or misses that no evidence places the client inside the building.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsGives the partner usable advice: not guilty, elect Crown Court and why, warn the client now about waiver of privilege, serve a statement to fix his account, and chase the specific disclosure the defence needs.Analyses the law but never states a plea or venue recommendation, or recommends venue without giving the client the sentencing counterweight.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA tight report to a partner with headings, short paragraphs and no padding, written in British English and finished inside two sides.Writes a letter to the client instead of a report to the partner, or produces undifferentiated prose in which the conflict point is buried.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly applies section 9 of the Theft Act 1968 and identifies that the realistic route is secondary liability requiring assistance or encouragement plus knowledge, and correctly applies section 34 to facts now relied on which were not mentioned.Treats the client as a principal burglar without noticing there is no evidence of entry, or states that silence itself proves guilt rather than that a proper inference may be drawn.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers the whole picture: elements, secondary liability, the alternative of handling, section 34 and the missing prepared statement, the legal advice explanation and waiver, allocation under section 17A and Schedule 1, the right to elect, and bail conditions.Deals with adverse inferences only and never reaches allocation and election, or asserts the case is indictable only because of the earlier dwelling burglary when two such convictions are required.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies the conflict of interest without prompting, explains that the accounts conflict directly and that the firm holds material confidential information from each, concludes the firm cannot continue to act for both, and sets out how to withdraw properly and in time for the hearing.Notices only that acting for two defendants is untidy, or proposes an information barrier between two fee earners, which cannot cure a conflict between two clients on the same matter.

Examiner notes

The pass line is whether the candidate sees that there is no evidence the client entered the building, so the case is really about secondary liability and knowledge, and then handles section 34 as a live but manageable risk rather than as a catastrophe. The trap is the missing prepared statement. Weak candidates either ignore it or announce the case is lost because of it. Strong candidates explain that the facts now relied on were not mentioned, that an inference may properly be drawn, that thin disclosure supports the reasonableness of the advice, and that running the legal advice explanation will normally require waiver of privilege, which the client must be warned about now. The second trap is allocation: the earlier dwelling burglary is one conviction, not two, so the offence is not indictable only and the client keeps the right to elect. The conflict of interest sits quietly in the attendance note and is the single most commonly missed point.

Written station 2: Prosecution disclosure of unused material in a self defence assault and criminal damage case

Case and matter analysis  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO HELEN IWOBI, PARTNER

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 8 June 2027

Re: Ryan Osei, section 47 assault and criminal damage. Brayton Crown Court, PTPH 22 June 2027

1. The charges

Count 1, assault occasioning actual bodily harm under section 47 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. The Crown must prove a battery, that it occasioned actual bodily harm, and that the client intended or was reckless as to the application of unlawful force. The fractured nasal bone plainly amounts to actual bodily harm. The client admits one punch. So the only live issue on count 1 is unlawfulness, that is, self defence.

Count 2, criminal damage under section 1(1) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971. The Crown must prove damage to property belonging to another, without lawful excuse, with intention or recklessness. The door is damaged and belongs to the licensee. The issue is the mental element. The client says he pushed the door hard to get out of a confined corridor and did not think it would break. Since R v G [2003] UKHL 50 recklessness here is subjective: the Crown must prove that he was himself aware of a risk that the door would be damaged and that, in the circumstances known to him, it was unreasonable to take that risk. His account is therefore a denial of the mental element and not merely mitigation. It remains a difficult point on the facts as we presently have them, because a door pushed hard enough to come off its hinges invites the inference that the risk must have occurred to him, and the corridor CCTV matters more to this count than to count 1.

2. Self defence

Self defence is raised on the facts. The burden of disproving it is on the Crown to the criminal standard. Under section 3(1) of the Criminal Law Act 1967 and section 76 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, the client is judged on the circumstances as he believed them to be, and the question is whether the force used was reasonable in those circumstances.

Strengths. He gave a full account in interview at the first opportunity and it has not changed. A single punch in response to a push and a drawn back arm is not obviously disproportionate, and section 76 recognises that a person cannot weigh to a nicety the exact measure of necessary action. There is no duty to retreat.

Weaknesses. The Crown alleges two punches. Two punches, particularly a second after the complainant is going down, is much harder to defend as reasonable force, and the client says only that he does not remember a second punch, which is weaker than a denial. Amy Gorrick did not see the start, which cuts both ways but leaves the Crown with the complainant's account of an unprovoked punch effectively uncontradicted unless we get more material.

The whole case therefore turns on who moved first and on how many blows were struck. That is exactly what unused material would show.

3. Disclosure

The prosecutor's duty under section 3 is to disclose material capable of undermining the Crown's case or assisting the defence, and under section 7A that duty is continuing and must be reconsidered specifically in light of the defence statement. The 4 June letter does not show that any such reconsideration has happened. It is a bare assertion that nothing meets the test, and on two items it is plainly wrong.

Item 1, bar area CCTV. This is the single most important item in the case. It would show who moved first and how many blows were struck. It is obviously capable of assisting the defence. The prosecutor now says it was not retained by the premises. That raises a different and more serious problem: under the Code of Practice the investigator must pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry and must retain relevant material. If footage covering the alleged assault existed and was allowed to be lost or overwritten, that is a failure to obtain and retain plainly relevant material. We need, in writing: when the officer first attended the premises, whether the footage was viewed, by whom and when, whether any request to preserve it was made and when, and what the retention period on the system was. If it was lost through police failure the point is not disclosure but the fairness of the trial, and depending on the answers we may have an application to stay or, more realistically, a strong direction to the jury about the missing evidence.

Item 2, corridor CCTV. The prosecutor says it shows nothing of relevance. It covers the fire door. It goes directly to count 2 and to how the client left. It must be disclosed or we must see it.

Item 4, PC Warrilow's pocket notebook first account from Amy Gorrick. A first account is retained precisely because it may differ from the later statement. Asserting that it is consistent is the prosecutor's conclusion, not a reason for withholding it. It is capable of assisting the defence if it differs in any respect about who moved first.

Item 5, the complainant's previous convictions. The reason given, that he is not a defendant, is wrong as a matter of law. Disclosure of a non defendant's antecedents is governed by the section 3 test, not by whether he is charged. If Mr Prendergast has convictions for violence, they are capable of assisting a defence that he was the aggressor, and we would then apply under section 100 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 for leave to adduce them as having substantial probative value on a matter of substantial importance, namely who started it. Our client says he is told there is an affray and an assault on a doorman.

Item 3, the incident log for the 22:53 and 22:55 calls. First descriptions and contemporaneous accounts of what callers said are frequently inconsistent with later statements. It should be disclosed.

The door supervisor. The client says a door supervisor saw the whole incident and he appears nowhere in the papers. Under the Code the investigator must pursue reasonable lines of enquiry. We should ask in writing whether the door supervisor was identified, whether an account was taken, and if so where it is scheduled. If he was never spoken to, that is a failure to investigate a plainly relevant witness, and we should also make our own enquiries of the licensee and the door supervisor's employer.

Recommended course:

(a) Write immediately, before the PTPH, setting out item by item why the material meets the section 3 test, requiring the prosecutor to comply with the section 7A continuing duty, and asking the specific questions about the loss of the bar CCTV and about the door supervisor. Give a short deadline.

(b) If there is no proper response, apply under section 8 of the 1996 Act. We are entitled to do so because we have served a defence statement and we reasonably believe material has been withheld. The application should be issued so that it can be listed at or shortly after the PTPH on 22 June rather than left to trial.

(c) Raise the whole disclosure position on the PTPH form so the judge sets a disclosure timetable.

4. Plea and next steps

I advise a not guilty plea on count 1. Self defence is properly arguable, the burden is on the Crown, and we should not plead before we know what the CCTV and the first account contain.

Count 2 is more difficult. He should be advised realistically that if the corridor footage shows him kicking the door, as the Crown alleges, the recklessness element is likely to be made out and an early plea to that count alone would attract credit and would allow him to fight count 1 with a jury seeing him as someone who admits what he did and disputes what he did not. That decision should wait for the corridor footage, but he must be told the arithmetic on credit for plea now, not later.

Before 22 June: send the disclosure letter, prepare the section 8 application, trace the door supervisor, obtain the client's own account of his injuries and any photographs from 14 March, and take a further proof on the second punch, which is the weakest part of his account.

5. Matter arising from the conference

After you left the room the client told me that his cousin had been to see Mr Prendergast and that Mr Prendergast "won't be turning up", that we should say nothing, and that at trial we should tell the judge the complainant had simply lost interest. He asked me not to tell you. I told him I could not keep it from you.

This has to be dealt with before anything else happens on the file. What he describes may be an attempt to pervert the course of justice or witness intimidation. We cannot take any step that furthers it and we cannot tell the court that the complainant lost interest when we have been told something different. Telling the court that would be misleading the court, which we must never do and must never allow the client to do through us.

What he told us is confidential and privileged, so we cannot report it to the police or to the Crown without his consent. Our duty of confidentiality is not displaced simply because the information is discreditable.

The right course is:

(a) You should see him, with a note taken, and advise him in the plainest terms that interference with a witness is a serious offence in its own right, that it carries a real risk of a custodial sentence separate from this case, that if it comes out he will almost certainly lose his unconditional bail, and that if Mr Prendergast does not attend because he has been frightened off, the Crown may well succeed in putting his statement before the jury as hearsay, in which case the client will have made his own position considerably worse because the statement cannot be cross examined.

(b) Advise him to make sure nothing further of that kind happens and that he says nothing more to his cousin about the case.

(c) Make clear that we will not advance any suggestion to the court that the complainant lost interest, and that we will not run a submission built on the absence of a witness we have been told was approached.

(d) If he maintains the instruction to put that account to the court, we are professionally embarrassed and must cease to act. We would tell the court only that we can no longer act, giving no reasons, because the reasons are privileged.

(e) Record all of this in an attendance note and confirm the advice to him in writing.

Trainee Solicitor

The conduct issue hidden in this station

At the end of the conference the client tells the trainee that his cousin has been to see the complainant and that the complainant will not attend, asks the firm to say nothing, and asks that at trial the court be told the complainant simply lost interest. He also asks that the partner is not told. The firm cannot mislead the court, so it cannot advance the lost interest explanation or build a submission on the complainant's absence knowing what it knows. The information is confidential and privileged, so it cannot be reported to the police or the Crown without consent, and the trainee cannot keep it from the supervising partner within the firm. A competent candidate advises the client that interference with a witness is a serious offence, that it puts his bail at risk and may cause the complainant's statement to go before the jury as hearsay with no cross examination, warns him to take no further step, records the advice in writing, and states that if he persists in the instruction the firm must cease to act, telling the court only that it can no longer act and giving no reasons.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsIsolates the facts that decide the case: the single punch admitted against two alleged, the push and the drawn back arm, the fractured nose, the unidentified door supervisor, the lost bar CCTV, the untested first account of the bar worker, and the complainant's reported convictions for violence.Narrates the incident and the disclosure correspondence without identifying that the only live issue on the assault is unlawfulness, or misses the door supervisor entirely.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsTells the partner what to do and in what order: a specific item by item disclosure letter with a deadline, a section 8 application timed to the PTPH, tracing the door supervisor, and a realistic split advice on the two counts with credit for plea explained now.Recommends generally that more disclosure be sought without saying which items, on what basis, or by when, or advises not guilty on both counts without confronting the weakness on the door.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA disciplined report to the partner, item by item on disclosure, honest about the second punch and about count 2, in British English and within a workable length.Produces an undifferentiated essay on the CPIA regime, or writes to the client rather than to the partner.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies section 47 correctly, so that the only issue is unlawfulness, applies section 1(1) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971 with recklessness as the live element, applies section 76 with the burden of disproof on the Crown and the belief judged on the circumstances as the client believed them, and applies the section 3 test rather than the prosecutor's own conclusions.Places the burden of proving self defence on the defendant, requires an intention to cause harm under section 47, or accepts the prosecutor's assertion that a non defendant's convictions are outside disclosure because he is not charged.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers everything: both counts, self defence, the section 7A continuing duty triggered by the defence statement, each scheduled item measured against the test, the section 8 route, the retention and reasonable lines of enquiry duties in relation to the lost CCTV and the unidentified door supervisor, and section 100 leave for the complainant's bad character.Deals with the CCTV alone and never reaches the first account, the incident log or the complainant's antecedents, or treats the loss of the bar footage purely as a disclosure question rather than as a failure to obtain and retain relevant material.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots that the client has effectively disclosed witness interference and has asked the firm to present a false explanation to the court, refuses to advance it, advises him fully on the criminal and practical consequences including hearsay admission of the statement, keeps the information confidential, and sets out withdrawal without giving reasons if he persists.Proposes to report the client to the police or to the Crown in breach of confidentiality, or treats the complainant's likely non attendance as a tactical advantage to be exploited at trial.

Examiner notes

The pass line is a disclosure analysis that engages item by item with the schedule rather than reciting the CPIA regime. Strong candidates notice three specific things: that the prosecutor's stated reason for withholding the complainant's antecedents is legally wrong, that a first account is retained precisely because it may differ from the later statement so consistency is not a reason to withhold it, and that the bar CCTV going missing raises retention and reasonable lines of enquiry rather than disclosure. The trap is to treat the 4 June letter as the end of the matter. It is a bare assertion and does not show that the continuing duty was reconsidered after the defence statement, which is what unlocks the section 8 application. A second trap is treating both counts identically. Self defence answers the assault, it does not answer the door, and a candidate who never advises the client on the realistic position on count 2 and on credit for plea has not given client focused advice. The ethics point arrives after the partner has left the room and is deliberately mixed with a request that the partner is not told.

Written station 3: Defence statement in a Crown Court burglary of a commercial unit

Legal drafting  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  45 minutes

Model answer

IN THE CROWN COURT AT WRENBURY Case No: T2026/0417

REGINA

-v-

DENHOLM REEVE

DEFENCE STATEMENT

served under section 5 of the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996

1. NATURE OF THE DEFENCE

1.1 The defendant denies count 1. He denies that he entered Unit 14, Ashfield Trading Estate, Bramwell as a trespasser on 11 or 12 August 2026, and he denies that he stole any property from that unit at any time.

1.2 The defence is one of denial and of mistaken attribution. The defendant says he was not the person who forced the shutter and removed the property, and that the prosecution evidence does no more than place his van on a public road he uses regularly and place his fingerprint on a crate which is his own and which he left in the unit on an earlier and lawful visit.

1.3 No defence of lawful excuse, consent or claim of right is advanced in respect of the property alleged to have been stolen, because the defendant says he did not take it.

2. MATTERS OF FACT ON WHICH ISSUE IS TAKEN WITH THE PROSECUTION

Issue is taken with the following matters of fact:

2.1 That the defendant entered Unit 14 on 11 or 12 August 2026.

2.2 That the defendant entered Unit 14 as a trespasser on any occasion.

2.3 That the defendant stole power tools, or any property, from Unit 14.

2.4 That the presence of the defendant's van on Ashfield Road at 22:41 and 23:26 on 11 August 2026 shows that the van or the defendant attended the trading estate.

2.5 That the fingerprint on the yellow plastic crate was left during, or in connection with, the entry alleged in count 1.

2.6 That the white van seen by Mrs Ruth Chidgey at about 23:00 on 11 August 2026 was the defendant's van.

The following matters are not in issue: that Unit 14 was secured at 17:30 on 11 August 2026; that the side shutter was found forced at 07:10 on 12 August 2026; that property was taken from the unit; that the fingerprint on the crate is the defendant's.

3. WHY ISSUE IS TAKEN ON EACH SUCH MATTER

3.1 As to paragraphs 2.1 to 2.3, the defendant was not present at the trading estate at any time on 11 or 12 August 2026 and did not take any property from the unit.

3.2 As to paragraph 2.4, Ashfield Road is a public through road which forms part of the defendant's ordinary working route between his yard at Netherby Lane and the metal recycling depot at Cranmoor. He drives that route several times each week, including in the evening. Passing the camera in each direction is consistent with a journey along that route and is not evidence of a stop at the estate. The camera records passage on the road and does not record entry to the trading estate.

3.3 As to paragraph 2.5, the yellow plastic crate is the defendant's own property. He left it inside Unit 14 on or about 28 July 2026, approximately two weeks before the date on the indictment, when he attended the unit with permission to collect scrap steel offcuts and cable. The crate had a split base and he abandoned it there. The fingerprint is therefore explained by lawful presence on an earlier date and is not probative of entry on 11 August 2026. It is noted that the prosecution accepts the crate does not belong to Kestrel Site Services Limited and that its origin is not known to the prosecution.

3.4 As to paragraph 2.6, Mrs Chidgey does not identify a registration number, does not describe any distinguishing feature of the van and does not describe any person. Her evidence is not capable of identifying the defendant's vehicle.

4. PARTICULARS OF THE MATTERS OF FACT ON WHICH THE DEFENDANT INTENDS TO RELY

4.1 The defendant is a self employed scrap metal dealer trading from a yard at Netherby Lane, Bramwell, and holds a scrap metal dealer's licence issued by Bramwell Borough Council.

4.2 On or about 28 July 2026 the defendant attended Unit 14 at the request of a man who introduced himself as Wes and who was working at the unit. He was asked to remove a pallet of scrap steel offcuts and a quantity of old cable. He loaded the material into his own yellow plastic crates, carried them to his van and left. He was inside the unit for about 20 minutes. He left behind one crate which had a split base. He believed he had permission to be there. He has not returned to the unit since that date. Nothing was put in writing.

4.3 On the evening of 11 August 2026 the defendant collected a load of cable from a demolition site at Pellow Street, Bramwell, at about 22:15. He then drove along Ashfield Road to his yard at Netherby Lane, unloaded the cable there, and drove home to 6 Tyndall Court, Bramwell, arriving at about 23:45. He did not stop at the Ashfield Trading Estate. He remained at home for the remainder of the night. He lives alone.

4.4 On the morning of 12 August 2026 the defendant tipped that load at the metal recycling depot at Cranmoor. The load consisted of cable. It did not include power tools.

4.5 The defendant's van, registration LV21 KHX, is fitted with a telematics tracker installed by his insurer, Ambergate Mutual. The defendant relies on the tracker record for 11 and 12 August 2026 as showing the route taken and that the van did not stop at or near the Ashfield Trading Estate.

4.6 The defendant does not know Mr Adeyemi Oyelaran and has never spoken to him.

5. POINTS OF LAW AND ADMISSIBILITY

5.1 The defendant will submit at the close of the prosecution case, if appropriate, that there is no case to answer, on the basis that the fingerprint evidence is equally consistent with the earlier lawful visit and that the remaining evidence does not identify the defendant as the person who entered the unit.

5.2 The defendant reserves the right to object to the admission of the evidence of Mrs Chidgey as to the van, or to invite the court to direct that it carries no identifying weight, on the basis that it does not identify any vehicle or person.

5.3 The defendant reserves the right to make an application in respect of the estate's CCTV. The unused material schedule records that the estate cameras were not recording between 3 and 19 August 2026. If it emerges that any recording did exist and has been lost or destroyed, the defendant will consider an application to stay the proceedings as an abuse of process, or an application to exclude evidence under section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984.

5.4 No other point of law is presently taken. No authority is presently relied on.

6. ALIBI

6.1 The defendant relies on an alibi. Particulars: on the evening of 11 August 2026 the defendant collected a load of cable from a demolition site at Pellow Street, Bramwell, at about 22:15; he then drove along Ashfield Road to his yard at Netherby Lane, Bramwell, where he unloaded the cable; he then drove to his home address at 6 Tyndall Court, Bramwell, arriving at about 23:45, and remained there for the remainder of the night. He was not at Unit 14, Ashfield Trading Estate at any time on 11 or 12 August 2026.

6.2 There is no witness whom the defendant believes is able to give evidence in support of the alibi, and no witness is therefore named under section 6A(2)(a) of the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996. The defendant lives alone. He holds no information falling within section 6A(2)(b).

7. REQUEST FOR FURTHER DISCLOSURE

The defendant requests disclosure of the following material, which by reference to the matters put in issue above is reasonably capable of undermining the prosecution case or assisting the defence:

7.1 The full automatic number plate recognition download for the Ashfield Road camera and for any other camera on the surrounding road network for the period 21:00 on 11 August 2026 to 02:00 on 12 August 2026, together with the camera siting details and field of view, in order to establish whether the recorded movements are consistent with a through journey (paragraph 2.4).

7.2 Any record of other vehicles recorded in the vicinity during that period (paragraph 2.6).

7.3 All records relating to the estate's closed circuit television system, including the maintenance and fault log, any record of when the system ceased and resumed recording, and the identity of the person who reported the fault (paragraph 5.3).

7.4 Any record of persons who had access to or worked at Unit 14 in July and August 2026, including agency or subcontractor records, and any record identifying a man known as Wes (paragraph 4.2).

7.5 Any record of legitimate removals of scrap material from Unit 14 in July 2026 (paragraph 4.2).

7.6 The full fingerprint examination record for Unit 14, including the number and location of marks lifted, any marks not identified as the defendant's, and any elimination prints taken (paragraph 2.5).

7.7 Any first description of the van given by Mrs Chidgey and any record of her original account, including any officer's notebook entry (paragraph 2.6).

Signed: Halberd Rowe Solicitors, solicitors for the defendant

Dated: 20 October 2026

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client instructs the firm to name his sister's partner as an alibi witness while telling the solicitor in terms that the man was not present and was at work. Drafting that alibi into a defence statement, which is deemed by section 6E(1) to be given with the authority of the accused and is served on the court and the prosecution, would be misleading the court and would involve setting up a false account, contrary to the SRA Principles on honesty and integrity and to paragraphs 1.4 and 2.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs. It would also expose the proposed witness to giving false evidence. The competent candidate drafts the statement on the client's truthful instructions only, names nobody as an alibi witness, gives particulars of the client's own account of his movements, and does not dress that account up as supported evidence. The client remains entitled to a defence and to put the prosecution to proof, so the retainer does not have to end; but if the client insists on the false alibi the firm cannot act on that instruction and would have to cease to act, telling the court only that it is professionally embarrassed. The solicitor may not disclose the client's admission to the court or the prosecution, because it is confidential.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsEach disputed matter is expressed as a short, self contained factual proposition that the prosecution can answer. The positive case is written in plain declarative sentences with dates, places and times. No rhetoric, no argument dressed up as fact, no padding, no em-dashes, and correct British spelling throughout.Writing a narrative essay or a bare denial such as "the defendant denies the offence and puts the prosecution to proof", which tells the prosecution nothing and satisfies none of section 6A(1)(b) to (ca).
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsThe precedent's headings are used in order and each is actually populated. Disputed matters are numbered, the reasons in section 3 map one to one onto the matters listed in section 2, and each disclosure request in section 7 is cross referenced back to the issue it serves.Collapsing sections 2, 3 and 4 into one block of prose so that the reader cannot tell what is disputed, why it is disputed and what the positive case is, or leaving the alibi heading blank rather than answering it, either by pleading the alibi with particulars or, where there truly is none, by saying so.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawThe statement complies with section 6A(1)(a) to (d). It is correctly headed as a section 5 statement in the Crown Court. Crucially it pleads the alibi that the client's truthful instructions do disclose, namely his own account of his movements, gives particulars of it under section 6A(2), and states expressly that there is no witness able to support it, so that no witness is named who cannot truthfully do so. The section 9(1)(b) burglary is correctly understood as entry as a trespasser plus theft, so the earlier permitted visit is pleaded as an answer to the fingerprint and not as an answer to the count.Failing to plead the alibi at all, or pleading it while naming the sister's partner as a witness to it, when the candidate has been told that account is false. The defence statement must set out the defendant's own alibi and give such particulars of it as are known, but must not put forward a witness the candidate knows would not tell the truth.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawEvery strand of the prosecution case is addressed: the ANPR, the fingerprint and crate, the eyewitness van sighting, and the absence of CCTV. The positive case includes the 28 July visit, the route, the Pellow Street collection, the weighbridge load and the insurer's tracker. Points of law are flagged, including a possible submission of no case and a reserved abuse of process or section 78 point on the missing CCTV. Disclosure requests are tied to issues so that a section 8 application could later be built on them.Omitting the fingerprint explanation or the ANPR explanation, so that at trial the defendant relies on a fact not mentioned in the statement and exposes himself to comment and adverse inference under section 11. Also making scattergun disclosure requests unconnected to any pleaded issue.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawThe candidate recognises that paragraph 8 of the attendance note is an instruction to put forward an alibi the client has expressly said is untrue. The statement sets out the defendant's own account of where he was, which is an alibi, and gives the particulars known, but does not name the proposed witness the candidate knows would give a false account. The candidate does not connive in the account and does not simply stay silent about it; the drafted document is one the solicitor can properly sign, and the point is left for the partner to take up with the client before service.Including the alibi because the client instructed it, or hedging by writing something like "the defendant may have been at the home of a family member", which is the same deception in softer words. Equally poor is refusing to draft anything at all, or lecturing the client inside the body of the defence statement itself.

Examiner notes

A pass turns on producing a document that actually performs the section 6A function and that does not carry the false alibi. Weak candidates treat the defence statement as a denial plus a demand for disclosure. Strong candidates realise that a defence statement is the defence's own pleading and that every disclosure request has to be earned by an issue already pleaded. The trap is the alibi. It is buried at paragraph 8 of an otherwise routine attendance note and is phrased as helpfulness, and many candidates will draft it in because the client asked for it and because the section 6A(2) heading in the precedent seems to invite a name. The second trap is the opposite overreaction: some candidates abandon the entire alibi topic and leave heading 6 blank. The correct answer is to plead the alibi the client truthfully gives, his own account of his movements, with particulars under section 6A(2), and to record that there is no witness able to support it. Candidates should not be led by the absence of a witness into asserting that no alibi is relied on: section 6A(3) defines an alibi by the accused's presence elsewhere, not by whether anyone can corroborate it, and a defendant who states at trial that he was at home while his statement said no alibi was relied on exposes himself to comment and inference under section 11.

Written station 4: Adverse inference from silence after legal advice in a criminal damage trial

Legal research  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

RESEARCH NOTE

To: Alwyn Prestcott, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 9 June 2026

Matter: R v Teodor Blaskiewicz, Cawthorne Magistrates' Court, trial 7 July 2026

Subject: Section 34 inference and the position on legal advice to remain silent

1. SUMMARY OF ADVICE

1.1 Section 34 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 is engaged in principle. The client relies at trial on a fact, namely that Rafe Fanshawe asked him to paint the shutter and that he believed he had permission, which he did not mention when questioned under caution before charge. The court may therefore draw such inference as appears proper.

1.2 The inference is not automatic. The prosecution must establish the six Argent conditions, and the court must then be satisfied that this was a fact the client could reasonably have been expected to mention in the circumstances existing at the time.

1.3 Our best point is the quality of the pre interview disclosure. The officer disclosed almost nothing and expressly refused to say whether there was CCTV. That is the paradigm circumstance in which Howell accepts that silence may be objectively justified. It is a strong argument on these facts but it is not a guaranteed answer.

1.4 If the client wants the court to give weight to the advice, he will have to say why the advice was given, and doing so waives privilege to that extent. He and, if called, the duty solicitor can then be cross examined about the instructions he gave her. That is the central tactical decision and it needs to be taken before 7 July 2026, not in the witness box.

1.5 There is one professional conduct point which needs your attention before trial and I deal with it at section 5.

2. QUESTION 1: IS AN ADVERSE INFERENCE AVAILABLE?

The statutory route

2.1 Section 34(1)(a) applies where, before charge, on being questioned under caution by a constable trying to discover whether or by whom the offence had been committed, the accused failed to mention a fact relied on in his defence, being a fact which in the circumstances existing at the time he could reasonably have been expected to mention. Where it applies, section 34(2)(d) permits the court, in determining guilt, to draw such inferences as appear proper, and section 34(2)(c) permits the same in deciding whether there is a case to answer.

2.2 The six conditions were set out by the Court of Appeal in R v Argent [1997] 2 Cr App R 27. Applying them here:

(a) There are proceedings for an offence. Satisfied.

(b) The failure occurred before charge. The interview was at 15:40 on 2 May 2026 and preceded charge. Satisfied.

(c) The failure occurred during questioning under caution by a constable. Satisfied.

(d) The questioning was directed to discovering whether or by whom the offence had been committed. Satisfied.

(e) The failure was to mention a fact relied on in his defence. This is satisfied. The permission given by Rafe Fanshawe is not a comment on the prosecution case; it is a positive fact which founds the defence of lawful excuse under section 5(2)(a) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971, namely an honest belief that a person whom the defendant believed to be entitled to consent to the damage had consented, or would have consented had he known of the damage and its circumstances. It does not matter that Rafe Fanshawe is the owner's son rather than the owner, nor whether the belief was reasonable: by section 5(3) an honest belief suffices whether or not it is justified. It is exactly the kind of fact section 34 is aimed at.

(f) The fact was one he could reasonably have been expected to mention. This is the only condition genuinely in dispute and it is dealt with at 2.4 to 2.8 below.

2.3 Section 34(2A) does not assist us. It disapplies the inference only where the suspect had not been allowed an opportunity to consult a solicitor before questioning. The client had a solicitor present throughout, and Code C paragraph 6.1 was complied with.

The reasonableness condition

2.4 Argent establishes that "the circumstances" are to be construed broadly and include the suspect's age, experience, mental capacity, health, tiredness, knowledge and legal advice. Lord Bingham CJ made clear that the question is one for the tribunal of fact applying its collective common sense. Argent also makes clear that the existence of legal advice is a relevant circumstance but is not conclusive, otherwise the section could be defeated in every case by a solicitor advising silence.

2.5 R v Howell [2003] EWCA Crim 1 requires soundly based objective reasons for silence, cogent enough to weigh against the public interest in a suspect giving an account. The Court expressly identified the absence of material disclosure, such that the solicitor cannot usefully advise, as capable of being such a reason.

2.6 That is our case on the facts. The pre interview disclosure recorded on the custody record was: "We have a report of criminal damage to a shop shutter in Bell Vue Parade in the early hours. We have a witness. That is all I am prepared to say at this stage." The officer gave no account of what the witness said, did not mention the paint tins, and refused on the recording to say whether there was CCTV. Code C paragraph 11.1A requires that, before a person is interviewed, he and his solicitor be given sufficient information to enable them to understand the nature of the offence and why he is suspected of committing it, although it does not require disclosure of details at a time which might prejudice the investigation. Note for Guidance 11ZA states that what is sufficient should normally include, as a minimum, a description of the facts relating to the suspected offence that are known to the officer, including the time and place in question. The disclosure recorded here gave the place and an approximate time but no description of the facts at all, and a solicitor who does not know whether her client is on camera cannot sensibly advise him whether to advance a consent account.

2.7 Against that, the prosecution will say the following, and you should expect it. The client did not need disclosure to say the single thing he now says. If Rafe Fanshawe genuinely asked him to paint the shutter for £40, he knew that on 2 May 2026 and could have said so in one sentence. He could have handed in a short prepared statement without exposing himself to questioning, and he did not. R v Beckles [2004] EWCA Crim 2766 makes clear that genuine reliance on advice is important but not determinative, and that an inference may properly be drawn if the court concludes he was silent because he had no satisfactory answer rather than because of the advice.

2.8 My assessment is that the disclosure point is a real and respectable argument on these facts, but that the failure to give even a short prepared statement is the weakness the prosecution will press, and the court is entitled to take that into account.

Limits on any inference

2.9 Even if an inference is available, it is constrained. Condron v United Kingdom (2001) 31 EHRR 1 holds that a conviction must not be based solely or mainly on silence, that particular caution is required, and that an inference may be drawn only if the tribunal of fact is satisfied that the silence can only sensibly be attributed to the defendant having no answer, or none that would stand up to questioning. In the magistrates' court the bench must direct itself accordingly, and we should invite the legal adviser to record that.

2.10 Section 34(1) is also expressly limited to facts relied on in the defence. Anything the client says at trial which merely challenges the prosecution evidence, for example that the identification is mistaken, is not a fact relied on for these purposes and no inference arises from failing to mention it.

3. QUESTION 2: RELYING ON THE ADVICE, AND PRIVILEGE

3.1 A bare statement that the client was advised to remain silent will get us very little. R v Condron [1997] 1 WLR 827 holds that the bare assertion of legal advice is not, without more, likely to be regarded as a sufficient reason for not mentioning matters relevant to the defence. If the client wants the court to attach weight to the advice, the reason for the advice must be given.

3.2 The consequence is a waiver of legal professional privilege to that extent. Once the client or the solicitor gives evidence of the reason for the advice, the prosecution may cross examine on the instructions given and the basis of the advice. In practice this means the client can be asked what he told Ms Cardrow in the consultation. If he told her about the permission from Rafe Fanshawe and she still advised silence, that helps the reasonableness argument but invites the question why nothing was put in a prepared statement. If he did not tell her about the permission at all, the cross examination is likely to be very damaging, because it suggests the account was constructed later.

3.3 Two practical steps follow. First, we must take a full and careful statement from the client now about exactly what he told the duty solicitor on 2 May 2026. Second, subject to his informed consent, we should write to Sable and Roan Solicitors for Ms Cardrow's police station attendance note and her record of the disclosure given, before deciding whether to run the point. We should not commit to waiving privilege until we have seen that note.

3.4 An alternative is to keep the advice out of it and to run the disclosure point on the objective record alone, that is, on the custody record entry and the interview recording of the officer refusing to say whether there was CCTV. That preserves privilege. It is weaker than a fully supported Condron approach but it carries no cross examination risk. The decision is the client's, on our advice.

4. SOURCES I HAVE NOT RELIED ON

4.1 Section 35 of the 1994 Act and R v Cowan [1996] QB 373 concern inferences from a failure to give evidence at trial. The client intends to give evidence, so section 35 does not arise. It should not be confused with section 34.

4.2 Cadder v Her Majesty's Advocate [2010] UKSC 43 is an appeal from the High Court of Justiciary and concerns detention and access to a solicitor under Scots procedure. It is not authority binding or applicable in these proceedings and the client had a solicitor in any event.

4.3 Section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 governs the exclusion of confessions. The client made no confession and nothing he said is relied on by the prosecution, so section 76 has no application.

4.4 Clause 4 of the Criminal Evidence (Interview Records) Bill 2026 would, if enacted and commenced, bar an inference where no written pre interview summary was given. It is not in force and no commencement regulations have been made. It cannot be relied on and should not be cited to the court.

5. QUESTION 3: WHAT I ADVISE YOU TO TELL THE CLIENT

5.1 Explain that his silence in interview is now in play, and that the court can hold it against him, but only within limits and only if it is sure his silence can only sensibly be explained by his having had no answer.

5.2 Explain the choice in plain terms. He can keep the reason for the advice private, in which case the argument rests on the poor disclosure alone. Or he can explain the advice, which is a stronger argument but opens him and possibly Ms Cardrow to questions about what he told her. Take his instructions on that, record them, and confirm the decision in writing.

5.3 Take a detailed statement now on the consultation with Ms Cardrow and on the arrangement with Rafe Fanshawe, including the date and place of the conversation, the £40, where the paint was bought, and any message, receipt or bank record. The consent defence under section 5(2)(a) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971 turns on his honest belief that Rafe Fanshawe was entitled to consent and had consented, and by section 5(3) that belief need not be a reasonable one, and contemporaneous material supporting the arrangement is worth more than argument about silence.

5.4 Serve a defence statement or a written notice of issues identifying the consent defence, and make a written request for the store CCTV. The unused schedule records it as viewed with no evidential value. Footage showing the shutter covered in graffiti in the preceding week supports his account and is capable of assisting the defence.

5.5 Warn him not to contact Rafe Fanshawe. Mr Fanshawe has given a statement to the prosecution denying the request and is a witness.

6. CONDUCT POINT REQUIRING YOUR DECISION

6.1 The defence we are preparing depends in part on criticising the advice given by Ms Cardrow, or at least on exploring it. The file note records that this firm's police station representative attended the same custody suite on 2 May 2026 but was not instructed in this matter, and that Ms Cardrow is of a different firm and has never been a member of ours. I have checked that specifically because if the advice under scrutiny had been our own, we would have an own interest conflict under paragraph 6.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors: our interest in defending the quality of our own advice would conflict with the client's interest in explaining or criticising it, and we could not act.

6.2 As matters stand there is no conflict, because the adviser was independent of this firm. Before we go further I would ask you to confirm that no one in this firm advised the client on 2 May 2026, so that the position is recorded on the file.

6.3 Separately, if we approach Ms Cardrow for her attendance note we must have the client's informed consent first, because the note is his privileged material and not ours to obtain at will.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The defence depends on explaining, and to a degree criticising, the advice to make no comment. If that advice had been given by this firm, the firm would have its own interest in showing the advice was sound, which conflicts with the client's interest in explaining or attacking it, and the firm could not act under paragraph 6.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors. The file note is drafted to look like housekeeping: it records that the firm's representative was in the same custody suite that day but was not instructed, and that the duty solicitor was from an unconnected firm. The competent candidate reads it as the conflict check it is, concludes that no conflict arises on these facts, and asks for the position to be confirmed and recorded before the defence is built. The second, quieter point is that the duty solicitor's attendance note and the content of the consultation are the client's privileged material. The firm may not approach the previous solicitor for the file, and may not deploy the reason for the advice at trial, without the client's informed consent, given after he understands that doing so waives privilege and exposes him to cross examination on what he told her.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsSection 34, Argent, Condron in both courts, Howell and Beckles are used, and the Code C material on pre interview disclosure is used to build the reasonableness argument. The decoys are identified and expressly put aside with a one line reason each: section 35 and Cowan (silence at trial, not applicable), Cadder (Scottish), section 76 PACE (no confession) and the 2026 Bill (not in force).Citing section 35 or Cowan as though they governed the interview, treating Cadder as English authority, or relying on clause 4 of the Bill, which would put a provision that is not in force before the court. Equally weak is using every source in the folder without discrimination.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsThe note answers the partner's three questions in order and reaches a view rather than surveying the law. It gives the client a real choice between running the point on the objective disclosure record and running it on the advice with a waiver, sets out the risk of each, and identifies concrete next steps: a statement about the consultation, a request for the duty solicitor's attendance note with consent, a CCTV request and a warning about contact with the witness.An academic essay on section 34 which never says whether the inference is likely on these facts, or which recites the waiver rule without telling the partner what the client should actually do about it.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsHeaded, numbered and written for a partner who will read the first page and act on it. Citations are given in full once and are accurate. British spelling, no em-dashes and no research trail.Narrating the search process, quoting long slabs of statute without applying them, or burying the conclusion at the end of an undifferentiated discussion.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawThe Argent conditions are applied one by one to these facts, with the correct conclusion that only the reasonableness condition is really in issue. The permission account is correctly identified as a fact relied on in the defence founding lawful excuse under section 5(2)(a) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971, and not as mere comment on the prosecution case. Section 34(2A) is correctly held not to apply because a solicitor was present.Asserting that no inference can be drawn simply because the client was advised to say nothing, which is the exact error Argent, Howell and Beckles all reject. Also treating section 34(2A) as engaged, or failing to see that the permission account is a positive defence fact.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawBoth sides of the reasonableness argument are worked through, including the prosecution's strongest point that a short prepared statement would have preserved the account without exposing the client to questioning. The Condron waiver consequence is spelled out with its practical effect on cross examination, and the Condron v United Kingdom limits on the weight of any inference are applied to the way the bench must direct itself.Giving only the defence side of the argument, missing the prepared statement point entirely, or dealing with waiver as a bare rule of law without working out what the client would actually be cross examined about.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawThe candidate spots that a defence built on criticising the police station advice creates an own interest conflict under paragraph 6.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors if the adviser was from this firm, checks the file note which records that she was not, and asks the partner to confirm and record the position. The candidate also recognises that the duty solicitor's attendance note is the client's privileged material and cannot be obtained without his informed consent.Missing the conflict point altogether because the file note reads like background, or spotting it and then advising that the firm can act anyway while defending its own advice. A further common failure is proposing to write to the duty solicitor for her file without addressing privilege or the client's consent.

Examiner notes

The pass point is understanding that legal advice to remain silent is a circumstance, not a defence to section 34. Candidates who write that no inference can be drawn because the client was following advice have got the law backwards and will fail on application. The strongest candidates go further and argue both sides of the reasonableness condition, because the file has been built with a good defence point (near total absence of pre interview disclosure, plus the officer refusing to say whether CCTV existed) and a bad one (no prepared statement, when a single sentence would have preserved the account). The folder is deliberately overfull. Four of the ten sources are decoys and each fails for a different reason: section 35 and Cowan are about silence at trial and the client is giving evidence, Cadder is Scottish, section 76 PACE needs a confession and there is none, and clause 4 of the 2026 Bill is not in force. Candidates who cite the Bill have done something worse than waste words; they have proposed relying on a provision with no legal effect. The last mark is on privilege. Waiver is easy to state and hard to advise on, and the good answer explains what the client will actually be asked in the witness box if the reason for the advice is put in evidence.

Written station 5: Admissibility of a defendant's previous convictions on a charge of assault

Legal research  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

RESEARCH NOTE

To: Rowena Achebe, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 15 September 2026

Matter: R v Okonjo, Crown Court trial 9 November 2026

Subject: Admissibility of the defendant's previous convictions

1. Summary of advice

1.1 The 2021 conviction for assault occasioning actual bodily harm and the 2019 conviction for assault by beating are both likely to be admitted through the gateway in section 101(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 as evidence of a propensity to commit offences of the kind charged. Our best argument is exclusion under section 101(3), and the strength of that argument depends on how weak the identification evidence is.

1.2 The 2022 theft conviction and the 2024 excess alcohol conviction should be resisted and are unlikely to be admitted. Neither shows a propensity to commit offences of this kind, and neither shows a propensity to be untruthful on the Hanson test.

1.3 There is a separate and urgent professional conduct problem on the file about the complainant's own record. It is dealt with at paragraph 6.

2. The statutory framework

2.1 The four convictions are evidence of the client's bad character within section 98 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003, because they are evidence of misconduct, defined by section 112(1) as the commission of an offence, which does not have to do with the alleged facts of the present offence. They are therefore admissible only through one of the gateways in section 101(1).

2.2 The prosecution relies on section 101(1)(d), evidence relevant to an important matter in issue between the defendant and the prosecution. By section 103(1)(a) those matters include whether the defendant has a propensity to commit offences of the kind charged, unless that propensity makes it no more likely that he is guilty.

2.3 Propensity may be established under section 103(2) by convictions for an offence of the same description or of the same category. The 2021 conviction is for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, which is an offence of the same description as the offence charged. The 2019 conviction for assault by beating is not of the same description, and there is no prescribed category of offences of violence under the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (Categories of Offences) Order 2004: the only relevant prescribed categories are theft and sexual offences against children. Section 103(2) is not, however, an exclusive route, and propensity may be proved by other means, so the 2019 conviction can still be relied on as an assault in a public place following a night out.

3. Applying R v Hanson

3.1 R v Hanson [2005] EWCA Crim 824 sets the three questions: does the history establish a propensity, does that propensity make it more likely that the defendant committed this offence, and is it unjust under section 103(3) or unfair under section 101(3) to admit it.

3.2 Convictions 1 and 2. Two convictions for public violence in 2019 and 2021, both arising from confrontations outside licensed premises at night, do establish a propensity to commit assaults of this kind. The circumstances are close to the present allegation. On the assumption of truth required by section 109, that propensity makes it more likely that the client threw the punches rather than separating others. I expect the judge to admit both.

3.3 Conviction 3, theft of a bicycle in 2022. Theft is not an offence of the same description or category as an offence of violence, so section 103(2) does not assist the prosecution. Hanson makes clear that a propensity to be untruthful under section 103(1)(b) is not the same as a propensity to be dishonest, and that previous convictions only show a propensity to be untruthful where the defendant pleaded not guilty and gave an account the tribunal must have disbelieved, or where the offence itself involved false representations. The prosecution has served nothing about how the 2022 matter was disposed of. It is for the prosecution to establish those conditions if it wishes to rely on this limb, and on the material before us it cannot: nothing shows a contested trial, and a theft of a bicycle involves no false representation. This conviction should be resisted and I expect it to be excluded.

3.4 Conviction 4, excess alcohol in 2024. This shows no propensity to commit offences of violence and no propensity to be untruthful. Its only realistic effect is prejudice, namely to suggest that the client drinks and offends. It should be resisted on the same basis, and in the alternative under section 101(3).

4. The exclusion argument under section 101(3)

4.1 Where the prosecution succeeds on gateway (d), the court must exclude the evidence on our application if its admission would have such an adverse effect on the fairness of the proceedings that it ought not to be admitted. Section 101(4) requires the court to have particular regard to the time between the earlier matters and the present offence. Section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 gives the same discretion in wider terms and is normally argued alongside it.

4.2 Our strongest point is the one Hanson identifies expressly. The judge must consider the strength of the prosecution case, and if there is little other evidence against the defendant it is unlikely to be just to admit his previous convictions whatever they are. Here the CCTV shows a scuffle involving four men and no clear blow. The prosecution case rests on two witnesses describing a man in a green jacket, and the client accepts he was present in a green jacket. That is thin. We should argue that the convictions are being used to fill an evidential gap rather than to prove a genuine issue.

4.3 We should also argue that the 2019 conviction is now over seven years old at the date of trial, that the 2022 and 2024 convictions have no similarity at all to the present allegation, and that admitting a list of four convictions invites the jury to reason from general bad character rather than from propensity.

4.4 We should not overstate the point about the 2021 plea. The client says he pleaded guilty only to secure release. Two different provisions bite at two different stages. For the purposes of the admissibility ruling, section 109 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 requires the judge to assess relevance and probative value on the assumption that the conviction is true, so the client's account of why he pleaded is not a reason for the judge to keep the conviction out. At trial, section 74(3) of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 provides that, the conviction being proved, he is taken to have committed the offence unless the contrary is proved. He may therefore invite the jury to find that he was not the aggressor, but he carries the burden of proving it on the balance of probabilities, and doing so means giving evidence about a previous conviction and being cross examined on it. That is a matter for weight and for tactics, and it carries obvious risks.

5. Sources I have not relied on

5.1 Section 114 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 concerns hearsay. No party seeks to put in a statement not made in oral evidence, so it does not arise. R v Turnbull [1977] QB 224 concerns identification warnings. Identification is not truly in issue because the client accepts he was present and wearing the green jacket. The issue is what he did, not who he was. The Sentencing Council guideline for assault occasioning actual bodily harm is relevant only if the client is convicted and is not relevant to admissibility.

6. Professional conduct

6.1 The file note of 12 September records that our paralegal has obtained a printout of the complainant's previous convictions from a civilian employee at the police station as a personal favour, outside the disclosure process. That material has been obtained without authority and in breach of the confidence owed to the complainant and to the police. Using it would breach the SRA Principles, in particular the obligation to act with integrity and in a way that upholds public trust in the profession, and paragraph 1.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits abuse of our position to take unfair advantage of others.

6.2 My advice is that we must not use the printout, must not put it before counsel or the court, must quarantine it on the file and must not act on its contents. We should make a proper written request to the prosecution for the complainant's antecedents under the disclosure regime, which is the route by which any bad character application against a non defendant under section 100 would have to be supported. You will need to consider reporting the paralegal's conduct internally to the firm's compliance officer, and whether the firm has any duty to notify the police that one of their civilian staff has released data improperly.

7. Advice to give the client on Thursday

7.1 Tell him plainly that his two previous assault convictions will very probably be heard by the jury, that we will argue to exclude them, and that we may succeed on the theft and drink driving matters but should not promise more than that.

7.2 Explain that if the convictions go in, the judge will direct the jury that a propensity to commit assaults does not prove that he committed this one, and that they must not convict wholly or mainly on his record.

7.3 Explain that he is not shut out from telling the jury that he was not the aggressor in 2021, but that by section 74(3) of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 it would be for him to prove that, not for the Crown to disprove it, and that seeking to do so carries a real risk of making his record look worse rather than better.

7.4 We should not tell him anything about the complainant's record obtained through the informal route, and he should be told that we are asking the prosecution for that information properly.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The trainee's file note records that the firm's paralegal obtained the complainant's previous convictions from a friend working as a civilian in the custody suite, outside the disclosure process. The material is confidential and was released without authority. A competent candidate spots this without prompting, advises that the printout must not be used, shown to counsel or put before the court, advises that it be quarantined and that the antecedents be requested properly from the prosecution, and raises the need to report the matter to the firm's compliance officer. The point engages the SRA Principles on integrity and public trust and paragraph 1.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors on not abusing one's position to take unfair advantage of others.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
