Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses sections 98, 101(1)(d), 101(3), 103 and 109 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003, R v Hanson, the Categories of Offences Order and section 78 of PACE 1984, cites them accurately, and states positively that section 114, R v Turnbull and the sentencing guideline are not relevant and why.Treats the whole bundle as relevant and works through the hearsay provisions or the Turnbull warning, or relies on general assertions about bad character without citing the gateway or Hanson at all.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsReaches a clear conviction by conviction conclusion, tells the partner what to say to the client on Thursday, and is realistic about the prospects of exclusion rather than promising a result.Produces an abstract essay on bad character with no conclusion on any of the four convictions and nothing the partner could actually say to the client.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured note with numbered paragraphs, a summary of advice at the front, and no research trail.Narrates the search process, quotes long passages of statute without applying them, or buries the conclusion at the end of unbroken prose.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly identifies gateway (d) with section 103(1)(a), correctly notes that assault occasioning actual bodily harm is an offence of the same description while assault by beating is not, and correctly states that no violence category is prescribed so section 103(2) does not carry the 2019 conviction.Asserts that all four convictions are of the same category, or applies section 103(1)(b) to the theft conviction as showing a propensity to be untruthful without applying the Hanson distinction between untruthfulness and dishonesty.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with each of the four convictions separately, runs the section 101(3) and section 78 exclusion argument on the weakness of the prosecution case as Hanson directs, and answers the client's wish to go behind the 2021 plea correctly, by explaining that section 109 requires the judge to assume the conviction is true when ruling on admissibility and that at trial section 74(3) of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 places the burden on the client to prove he did not commit that offence.Deals with the convictions as a single block, or omits the exclusion argument entirely so the note says the convictions come in and stops there.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots that the complainant's record was obtained improperly through a personal favour, refuses to use it, advises quarantining it, advises a proper disclosure request and raises reporting the paralegal internally.Treats the printout as a useful piece of ammunition and advises how to deploy it, or does not mention the file note at all.

Examiner notes

The pass turns on doing the analysis conviction by conviction rather than in a block, and on saying out loud which of the seven sources do not apply. The trap is the theft conviction: candidates see a dishonesty offence, reach for section 103(1)(b) and assert a propensity to be untruthful, which is exactly the reasoning Hanson forbids. Candidates should also notice that the papers do not say how the 2022 matter was pleaded, so a candidate who asserts that it followed a guilty plea has supplied a fact that is not there; the correct point is that the prosecution has produced nothing capable of satisfying the Hanson conditions. The second trap is missing the file note, which reads like background housekeeping and is in fact the ethics issue.

Written station 6: Letter to a client advising on allocation and election of trial venue

Legal writing  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  30 minutes

Model answer

Halloran Byrne Solicitors

17 Chancel Row

Aldergate

Mr Tobias Ellick

Flat 3

91 Denehurst Road

Aldergate

12 May 2026

Dear Mr Ellick

Your case: hearing at Aldergate Magistrates' Court on 26 May 2026

Thank you for coming in on 10 May. This letter explains what will happen at the hearing on 26 May and what choice you may have to make. Please read it before the hearing and telephone me if anything is not clear.

The charge

You are charged with burglary of the storeroom at Marlow and Vance Hardware on 2 April 2026. Burglary of a shop is what is called an either way offence. That means it can be dealt with either by the magistrates or by a judge and jury at the Crown Court. You have told me you did not do it and that you were at your sister's flat. Your plea will be not guilty.

What happens on 26 May

You will be asked to confirm that you plead not guilty. The magistrates will then decide which court is more suitable to try the case. This is called allocation. The prosecutor will tell the magistrates what is alleged and will tell them about your 2022 conviction for shop theft. I will make representations for you. The magistrates must consider whether their own sentencing powers would be enough if you were convicted, and they must follow the Sentencing Council allocation guideline, which says that either way cases should normally stay in the magistrates' court unless the case is unusually complex or the sentence is likely to be too high for them.

There are then two possible outcomes.

If the magistrates decide the case is more suitable for the Crown Court, that is the end of it. The case is sent to the Crown Court and you have no choice in the matter.

If the magistrates decide the case is suitable for them, you then have a choice. You can agree to be tried by the magistrates, or you can insist on a trial by jury at the Crown Court. That choice is yours alone and nobody can take it away from you.

What turns on the choice

Sentence if you were convicted. The magistrates can send you to prison for up to 12 months for a single offence of this kind. The Crown Court can impose up to 10 years. That difference sounds decisive but it is not the whole picture, because if you were tried and convicted by the magistrates they can still send you to the Crown Court to be sentenced if they think their powers are not enough. So staying in the magistrates' court reduces but does not remove the risk of a longer sentence.

How long it takes. A trial at Aldergate Magistrates' Court would be listed in about 4 to 6 months. A Crown Court trial would be listed in about 12 to 16 months. You told me your partner is due to give birth in September. If that matters to you, it points strongly towards staying in the magistrates' court.

Your chances. Nationally, contested trials in the Crown Court end in acquittal more often than contested trials before magistrates. A jury also hears the case with no knowledge of your previous conviction unless it is formally put before them. Against that, in the magistrates' court the same bench decides both the facts and the law.

Cost. If you are granted legal aid, representation in the magistrates' court costs you nothing. In the Crown Court legal aid may carry a contribution from your income, which is refunded if you are acquitted.

Giving evidence. In either court you would be entitled to give evidence about being at your sister's flat, and I would expect us to call your sister. You told me you cannot face a jury looking at you. That is a real consideration and I do not dismiss it, but a magistrates' trial is still a public hearing and you would still give evidence and be questioned.

My advice

On what I know at present I would advise you to agree to summary trial in the magistrates' court if the magistrates keep the case. My reasons are that this is a single allegation with no violence and no weapon, the property is valued at about 2,400 pounds, you have no previous burglary, the magistrates' powers are very likely to be adequate, and you would be tried far sooner and at no cost to you. The main point the other way is the higher acquittal rate before a jury. If you decide that matters more to you than the delay, that is a proper decision to take and I will support it. The decision is yours and I will follow your instructions.

The evidence

I should be clear that the case against you is not strong at this stage. The prosecution rely on a partial fingerprint on a window frame and a witness who describes a man of your build. You have told me you did casual work at those premises about five months earlier, which may explain the fingerprint. No identification procedure has been held. I will be pressing for one and for the full evidence to be served. My advice on venue is not affected by that, but you should know that we have real points to make whichever court hears the case.

Your cousin

You asked whether this firm could also act for your cousin, Danny Ellick, who is charged with handling the same power tools. I am afraid we cannot. His interests and yours are not the same. He is said to be going to say that the tools came from someone else, and anything he says about where the tools came from may affect your case, and anything you tell me may affect his. Acting for both of you would put us in a position where we could not properly protect either of you. He needs to instruct a separate firm and I can give him a list.

I must also say something plainly, and I say it as your solicitor and not as a criticism. You mentioned that the two of you have discussed what each of you is going to say. Please do not do that again. If it is suggested that you and your cousin have agreed an account between you, that would be used against you both and could lead to a further and much more serious allegation. Whatever you tell the court must be your own account of what actually happened.

Next steps

Please come to my office at 9.15am on 26 May so we can go through the hearing before it starts. The hearing itself is at 10.00am at Aldergate Magistrates' Court. If you cannot attend on that date, telephone me straight away.

Yours sincerely

Nadia Halloran

Partner

Halloran Byrne Solicitors

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client asks the firm to act for his cousin, who is charged with handling the same stolen property and who intends to give an account about the source of the goods. There is a clear conflict of interest between two clients with adverse interests in the same matter, contrary to paragraph 6.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, and a confidentiality problem under paragraphs 6.3 and 6.4. A competent candidate refuses to act for the cousin, explains the reason plainly to the client and offers to refer him elsewhere. The stronger candidate also picks up that the client says the two of them have discussed what each is going to say, warns him not to do it again and explains the risk that this is treated as a concocted account, without accusing the client of anything and without advising anything that would itself mislead the court.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the client's own facts: the single commercial burglary, the value, the 2022 conditional discharge, the partial fingerprint and the earlier casual work, the baby due in September, and the listing times and sentencing powers taken from the materials.Writes a generic explanation of allocation that could be sent to any client, with no reference to this client's conviction, timescale worry or evidence.
Use a logical structure.SkillsMoves in order: the charge, what happens on 26 May, the two possible outcomes, the factors that bear on the choice, the recommendation, and next steps, under clear headings.Mixes procedure, advice and the conflict point together so the client cannot see what his actual choice is.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsGives a definite recommendation with reasons, makes clear the election is the client's own decision, and answers his stated worries about delay, cost and facing a jury.Sets out the pros and cons and refuses to recommend anything, or recommends a venue without saying why, or ignores that the client said he cannot face a jury.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsPlain English throughout, short sentences, letter format with an address and a proper sign off, statutory language translated rather than quoted.Quotes sections 19 to 21 of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980, uses terms such as allocation, indictment and committal for sentence without explaining them, or writes in the register of a note to a partner.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the allocation procedure accurately, that the magistrates decide first and the defendant elects only if they accept jurisdiction, the 12 month summary maximum for a single either way offence, the 10 year maximum for non dwelling burglary, and the power to commit for sentence after summary conviction.Tells the client he can choose the Crown Court whatever the magistrates decide, or the reverse, that he can insist on staying in the magistrates' court, or states that a summary conviction removes all risk of a Crown Court sentence.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers sentencing exposure, timescale, acquittal rates, cost of representation and the committal for sentence risk, and notes that the prosecution will put the previous conviction before the magistrates at allocation.Reduces the advice to sentencing powers alone, or omits the committal for sentence risk, which is the point that most affects the value of choosing summary trial.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses the request to act for the cousin on conflict of interest grounds, explains why in terms the client understands, offers a referral, and deals firmly with the two of them having discussed their accounts.Agrees to act for both to save the client money, says nothing about the cousin at all, or notes the conflict but says nothing about the discussion of accounts.

Examiner notes

The pass turns on getting the allocation sequence right: the magistrates decide first, and the right to elect a jury arises only if they accept jurisdiction. Candidates who tell the client he can simply pick his court fail on application of law however well written the letter is. The trap is stopping at the comparison of sentencing powers and never mentioning that magistrates can still commit for sentence after a summary conviction, which is what makes the recommendation honest. The conflict of interest sits at the end of the attendance note and reads like a cost saving question, so it is easily missed.

Dispute Resolution

Written station 7: Late delivery of a bespoke production line and a disputed limitation of liability clause

Case and matter analysis  |  Dispute Resolution  |  60 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

REPORT TO ADAEZE OKONJO

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 14 September 2026

Client: Harlow Rise Bakery Limited (HRB)

Matter: Claim against Brennall Engineering Limited (Brennall)

1. SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATION

1.1 HRB has a strong case on breach. Brennall delivered eleven weeks late and its argument that time was not of the essence does not answer the claim, because HRB claims damages and not termination.

1.2 The real battleground is clause 12. HRB contracted on Brennall's written standard terms, so section 3 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 applies and Brennall must prove that clauses 12.2, 12.3 and 12.4 are reasonable. In my view the GBP 5,000 cap and the sole remedy clause are vulnerable. The exclusion of loss of profit is the hardest of the three to defeat.

1.3 On a full recovery basis the claim is worth in the region of GBP 296,000. Discounting for the risk on clause 12 and for a real mitigation argument, I value the claim at about GBP 120,000 to GBP 150,000.

1.4 I recommend rejecting the GBP 60,000 offer, but not by silence. HRB should make a Claimant's Part 36 offer at GBP 145,000 now, before proceedings, and propose a one day mediation in November. That figure is at the top of the realistic bracket, is one Devan has said he would accept, and it puts costs pressure on Brennall while giving HRB a settlement route that fits the December bank review.

2. RELEVANT FACTS

2.1 Order dated 6 October 2025 for a bespoke automated sourdough line at GBP 214,000 plus VAT. Delivery and commissioning agreed for 12 January 2026. HRB signed Brennall's order form and accepts Brennall's standard terms were incorporated.

2.2 Delivery took place on 30 March 2026 and commissioning on 2 April 2026, eleven weeks late. The cause was a sub supplier's failure. There is no force majeure clause in the extract we have and a sub supplier's default is not ordinarily an excuse.

2.3 Brennall knew what the machine was for. Devan told Ruth Callan on 29 September 2025 and by email that the line was for the Caldon Stores contract, that it was worth about GBP 40,000 a month, and that production had to start by the end of January. Ms Callan's reply, that this was why Brennall quoted a January install, is important and we should secure the email trail at once.

2.4 Caldon terminated on 9 February 2026 for failure to start supply by 1 February 2026. The agreement had a 24 month minimum term and a costed margin of GBP 11,500 per month.

2.5 On 20 January 2026 Brennall offered the free loan of a reconditioned divider said to give about 60 per cent of the required output from early February. Devan did not reply.

2.6 HRB hired substitute plant from Ledwyn Plant Hire at GBP 1,450 per week from 19 January to 4 April 2026, GBP 15,950 in total, and paid GBP 3,200 in engineers' overtime.

3. LIABILITY

3.1 The order fixed 12 January 2026 for delivery and commissioning. Clause 9.1 waters that down to reasonable endeavours and clause 9.2 says time is not of the essence. Clause 9.2 goes only to whether HRB could have treated the contract as at an end. It does not remove the right to damages for late performance. Clause 9.1 is a more serious obstacle to establishing breach on the face of the terms, but it is itself a term which restricts liability for the purposes of section 3(2)(b)(i), because it lets Brennall render a performance substantially different from the January delivery HRB reasonably expected. It therefore has to pass the reasonableness test in the same way as clause 12.

3.2 Even taken at face value, reasonable endeavours were not used. Brennall placed a single order with one Italian sub supplier and had no second source for a bespoke build with a fixed install date. We should ask for disclosure of the sub supplier correspondence at the pre action stage.

3.3 I assess the prospects of establishing breach at about 80 per cent.

4. CLAUSE 12 AND THE UNFAIR CONTRACT TERMS ACT 1977

4.1 HRB dealt on Brennall's written standard terms, so section 3 applies and each of clauses 12.2, 12.3 and 12.4 must satisfy the requirement of reasonableness under section 11. Under section 11(5) the burden is on Brennall.

4.2 Clause 12.4, the sole remedy clause. This is the weakest of the three. It reduces the whole remedy for late delivery of a GBP 214,000 bespoke machine to a refund of a delivery charge, which is a nominal sum. That is close to leaving HRB with no remedy at all for the very default that was most likely to occur. Applying the Schedule 2 guidelines, the goods were adapted to HRB's special order under guideline (e), and there is no suggestion HRB was given any inducement or an alternative set of terms under guideline (b). I rate the prospects of defeating clause 12.4 at about 75 per cent.

4.3 Clause 12.3, the GBP 5,000 cap. Under section 11(4) the court looks at the resources available to Brennall to meet the liability and how far Brennall could have insured. A cap of GBP 5,000 on a contract worth GBP 214,000 is about 2.3 per cent of the price. Brennall is a manufacturer which can be expected to carry product and contract liability cover. We should ask about its insurance in pre action correspondence. I rate the prospects of defeating the cap at about 65 per cent.

4.4 Clause 12.2, the exclusion of loss of profit and loss of contract. This is the clause most likely to survive. Exclusions of consequential loss between commercial parties of comparable sophistication are commonly upheld, and HRB is an established business with a GBP 4.1m turnover which could have read the reverse of the order form. The counter argument is that Brennall knew before contracting exactly which contract was at stake, so the clause operates to exclude the one loss both parties actually had in mind. I rate the prospects of defeating clause 12.2 at no better than 40 to 45 per cent. That is the single largest risk in the case and it is what makes settlement attractive.

5. HEADS OF LOSS AND QUANTUM

5.1 The measure is the sum which puts HRB in the position it would have been in had the line been delivered and commissioned on 12 January 2026, subject to remoteness and to the duty to mitigate.

5.2 Loss of the Caldon contract. Margin of GBP 11,500 per month over a 24 month minimum term is GBP 276,000 before any discount. This head is not too remote. It is loss which Brennall actually knew about because Devan told Ms Callan the purpose, the value and the deadline before the contract was made, so it falls within the second limb of the ordinary rule on remoteness in contract. Recovery depends entirely on clause 12.2 falling away. There should also be a discount for the chance that Caldon would have terminated or reduced volumes during the 24 months for other reasons. I would plead the full figure and value it internally at around GBP 200,000.

5.3 Hire of substitute plant, GBP 15,950. This is a direct loss caused by the delay and is not caught by the wording of clause 12.2, which is limited to profit, business, contract, anticipated saving and indirect or consequential loss. Hire of replacement equipment is a direct cost of the breach. This head is good, subject to clause 12.3.

5.4 Overtime, GBP 3,200. Same analysis as the hire charges. Recoverable in principle, subject to proof that it was incurred because of the delay.

5.5 Interest under section 35A of the Senior Courts Act 1981 should be claimed from the dates of loss.

5.6 Full recovery therefore stands at about GBP 296,000 plus interest. That figure is only achievable if the whole of clause 12 falls.

6. MITIGATION AND THE LOAN MACHINE

6.1 This is the most damaging fact in the file and Devan must understand it. HRB was required to take reasonable steps to mitigate its loss. It could not recover loss which such steps would have avoided.

6.2 Brennall offered a free loan machine on 20 January 2026 said to deliver about 60 per cent of the required output from early February. Devan did not reply at all. Caldon terminated on 9 February 2026 for failure to start supply by 1 February 2026. A court is likely to ask whether an offer of partial supply on 1 February, coupled with a request for a short extension, would have kept the Caldon contract alive.

6.3 The points in HRB's favour are that the standard is one of reasonableness and not perfection, that the burden of proving a failure to mitigate is on Brennall, and that HRB is not obliged to take a step which is uncertain or which risks its commercial reputation. Whether 60 per cent supply would have satisfied Caldon at all is unknown and we should obtain a witness statement from Caldon's buyer.

6.4 The points against are that Devan did not even reply, and that it was free. The failure to reply is the fact which will be put to him in cross examination. Realistically the mitigation argument alone justifies a discount of the order of 25 to 35 per cent on the Caldon head of loss.

7. SETTLEMENT STRATEGY

7.1 Valuation. Taking 80 per cent on breach, applying the differing prospects on each limb of clause 12 and a mitigation discount, my risk adjusted valuation of the claim is GBP 120,000 to GBP 150,000. The GBP 60,000 offer is materially below that bracket and should be rejected.

7.2 Option one, accept. Not advised. It represents about 20 per cent of the pleaded claim and about half the risk adjusted value. It would, however, remove all risk and all cost exposure before the December bank review, so Devan must be told what he is giving up if we reject.

7.3 Option two, reject and issue. Unattractive on its own. The Caldon head would need expert accountancy evidence and the clause 12 argument is fact heavy. On the multi track this would be a Part 7 claim with costs budgeting, a likely trial in late 2027 and irrecoverable management time. It also cuts across the bank review, which is the outcome Devan most wants to avoid.

7.4 Option three, recommended. Reject in a reasoned letter which attacks clause 12 on the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 ground and asks for Brennall's insurance position and its sub supplier correspondence, and at the same time make a Claimant's Part 36 offer of GBP 145,000 inclusive of interest, with a 21 day relevant period. A Part 36 offer can be made before proceedings are issued and still carries the costs consequences. If Brennall does not accept and HRB later obtains a judgment at least as advantageous as its own offer, the court will normally order interest at up to 10 per cent above base on the sum awarded, indemnity costs from the end of the relevant period, interest on those costs and an additional amount of 10 per cent of the sum awarded up to the prescribed limit. That is real pressure at modest cost to HRB.

7.5 Set the figure at GBP 145,000 rather than at Devan's GBP 150,000 walk away figure. It sits just inside the bracket a court would be likely to award if HRB wins on the cap and the sole remedy clause but loses on the exclusion of loss of profit, which is the most probable single outcome, so it is a figure HRB has a genuine prospect of beating at trial. An offer HRB cannot beat gives HRB no protection at all.

7.6 Propose mediation in November 2026 in the same letter. Both parties are obliged to consider alternative dispute resolution and an unreasonable refusal carries a costs sanction. Mediation also fits the December bank review timetable, which is what Devan is really buying.

7.7 Advise Devan expressly that if he wishes to accept GBP 60,000 for commercial reasons that is his decision to make and we will act on it, but our advice is that the offer undervalues the claim.

8. PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT

8.1 Devan has asked that the schedule of loss include about GBP 12,000 for a consultant, and has confirmed no consultant was engaged and no fee was incurred, on the basis that the other side 'will never check it'.

8.2 We cannot do this. Advancing a head of loss we know was never incurred would be misleading the other side and, once proceedings are issued and the schedule is verified by a statement of truth, misleading the court. It would breach the SRA Principles requiring us to act with honesty and with integrity and to uphold public trust in the profession, and the provisions of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors which prohibit misleading the court or another party, whether by act or omission, and which prohibit being complicit in another person doing so.

8.3 The way to resolve it is to explain to Devan, before anything is sent, why the figure cannot go in, that a claim is stronger and not weaker when every figure in it can be evidenced, and that a fabricated head would be exposed on disclosure and would damage his credibility on the heads that are genuine. If he insists, we must not include it, and we would have to consider whether we can continue to act.

8.4 There is no obligation to report this to anyone at this stage. It is a client who has been talked out of a bad idea, not a client who has done anything. I should record the advice and his response in a file note.

9. NEXT STEPS

9.1 Obtain from Devan the September 2025 email trail with Ruth Callan and the Caldon supply agreement and termination letter.

9.2 Approach Caldon's buyer for a witness statement on whether partial supply from 1 February would have been accepted. This is the key mitigation evidence.

9.3 Obtain the Ledwyn hire invoices and the payroll records for the overtime.

9.4 Send the reasoned rejection letter with the Part 36 offer at GBP 145,000 and the mediation proposal.

9.5 Diarise the end of the relevant period.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

At paragraph 9 of the attendance note the client asks for about GBP 12,000 to be put into the schedule of loss for a consultant who was never engaged and whose fee was never incurred, on the basis that the other side will never check. Nothing in the partner's email points at this. Including the figure would mislead Brennall and, once the schedule is verified by a statement of truth, would mislead the court, contrary to the SRA Principles on honesty, integrity and public trust and to the provisions of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors on not misleading the court or others and not being complicit in another person doing so. The competent candidate refuses to include it, explains to the client that a claim is stronger when every figure is evidenced and that a false head would be exposed on disclosure and would contaminate the genuine heads, records the advice on the file, and recognises that if the client insists the firm would have to consider ceasing to act. No report to the SRA or to any outside body is required at this stage, since the client is not a person the SRA regulates and nothing has yet been put before anyone. The candidate must, however, record the advice on the file and put the position to the supervising partner, who owns the decision whether the firm can continue to act if the client persists.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsPicks out and uses the facts that decide the case: the fixed 12 January date, that HRB signed and accepts Brennall's written standard terms, the pre contract conversation with Ruth Callan about Caldon's value and deadline, the unanswered loan machine offer of 20 January, the 9 February termination date and the GBP 11,500 monthly margin over 24 months. Distinguishes proved facts from those still to be evidenced and says how each will be obtained.Recites the chronology without connecting it to anything. Misses that Devan never replied to the loan offer, or treats the Caldon margin as agreed when it is only the client's figure.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsGives a clear recommendation with a number, explains what the client gives up by rejecting GBP 60,000, and ties the strategy to the December bank review and the client's stated wish to avoid trial. Presents accept, fight and offer as real options and picks one.Sets out options without recommending any, or recommends a course without addressing that the client wants speed and certainty. Simply says 'reject the offer' with no figure and no plan.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsWritten as a report to a partner, headed and numbered, with a summary at the front. Confident, concise, no padding and no hedging that fails to advise.Written as a letter to the client, or as unstructured prose with no headings, so the partner cannot find the advice. Overlong recitation of the attendance note.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly separates time not being of the essence from the right to damages, applies section 3 and section 11 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 to Brennall's written standard terms, puts the burden of proving reasonableness on Brennall under section 11(5), uses section 11(4) on the cap and the Schedule 2 guidelines, and applies the second limb of the remoteness rule to the Caldon loss using the known purpose.Treats clause 12 as simply valid because HRB signed, or treats the Act as automatically striking it down. Puts the burden of reasonableness on HRB. Says the Caldon loss is too remote despite the pre contract disclosure of the contract, its value and its deadline.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with all three limbs of clause 12 separately and gives each a different assessment, addresses clause 9.1 as itself a restriction caught by section 3(2)(b)(i), covers every head of loss including hire, overtime and interest, and gives sustained treatment to mitigation and the burden of proving it.Analyses clause 12 as a single undifferentiated clause. Ignores mitigation altogether, or mentions it in one line without quantifying the discount. Omits the hire and overtime as direct losses which clause 12.2 does not on its wording catch.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies unprompted that the GBP 12,000 consultant figure would be a fabricated head of loss, explains the breach of the SRA Principles and the prohibition on misleading the court or another party, resolves it by refusing to include it and advising the client why, and records the advice.Misses the point entirely, treats it as a matter of evidence to be sorted out later, or says the figure can go in provisionally and be withdrawn if challenged.

Examiner notes

The pass turns on three things: recognising that the burden of proving reasonableness under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 sits on Brennall and not on the client, grading the three limbs of clause 12 separately rather than as one clause, and giving an actual recommendation with a figure. The trap is the loan machine. Candidates who see it only as a fact about the other side's conduct miss that it is a mitigation problem for the client and that the client's silence, not his refusal, is what will be put to him. A second trap is valuing the claim at the full GBP 296,000 and recommending a Part 36 offer close to that figure. An offer the client has no realistic prospect of beating gives no costs protection at all, which is the point of the regime. Weak candidates also write a letter to the client rather than a report to the partner, and lose marks across three criteria at once for doing so.

Written station 8: Particulars of claim for supply of non conforming stone flooring

Legal drafting  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 minutes

Model answer

IN THE COUNTY COURT AT CHELMSFORD Claim No.

BETWEEN:

ASHVALE INTERIORS LIMITED

Claimant

and

KINGSMOOR STONE LIMITED

Defendant

PARTICULARS OF CLAIM

The Parties

1. The Claimant is a company incorporated in England and Wales which carries on business as a fit out contractor from Unit 6 Bardfield Way, Chelmsford.

2. The Defendant is a company incorporated in England and Wales which carries on business as a supplier of natural stone.

The Contract

3. By a contract in writing contained in or evidenced by the Claimant's email of 4 November 2025 (to which the finishes specification for the Marn Quay Hotel, Ipswich was attached) and the Defendant's order confirmation KS-11447 dated 7 November 2025, the Defendant agreed to sell and the Claimant agreed to buy 480 square metres of Portland Whitbed limestone for the price of GBP 38,400 plus value added tax (the Contract).

4. The Defendant's conditions of sale printed on the reverse of order confirmation KS-11447 were incorporated into the Contract.

5. It was an express term of the Contract, contained in order confirmation KS-11447, that the goods would be '480 sq m Portland Whitbed limestone, honed, to client specification, slip resistance 36+ wet'.

6. The Contract was a contract for the sale of goods by description within the meaning of section 13 of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 and the description was that set out in paragraph 5 above. Accordingly it was an implied condition of the Contract that the goods would correspond with that description.

7. The Defendant sold the goods in the course of a business. Accordingly it was an implied condition of the Contract, by section 14(2) of the Sale of Goods Act 1979, that the goods would be of satisfactory quality, aspects of which include their appearance and finish and their safety.

8. Before the Contract was made the Claimant made known to the Defendant, by its email of 4 November 2025 and the attached finishes specification, the particular purpose for which the goods were being bought, namely use as flooring to the ground floor public areas of a hotel where a wet slip resistance value of not less than 36 was required. Accordingly it was an implied condition of the Contract, by section 14(3) of the Sale of Goods Act 1979, that the goods would be reasonably fit for that purpose.

Performance

9. The Claimant paid the price in full, as to GBP 19,200 on 11 November 2025 and as to GBP 19,200 on 5 January 2026, together with value added tax.

10. On 12 January 2026 the Defendant delivered 480 square metres of Portland Whitbed limestone to the Marn Quay Hotel, Ipswich. The Claimant laid that stone between 19 and 30 January 2026.

11. On 2 February 2026 the floor was tested on behalf of the hotel. The stone delivered by the Defendant had a polished finish and not a honed finish, and its wet slip resistance value was 21.

Breach

12. In breach of the express term pleaded at paragraph 5 and of the implied conditions pleaded at paragraphs 6, 7 and 8 the Defendant delivered goods which did not comply with the Contract.

PARTICULARS OF BREACH

(a) The goods delivered had a polished finish and did not have a honed finish, contrary to the express term and contrary to the description.

(b) The goods delivered had a wet slip resistance value of 21 and did not have a wet slip resistance value of 36 or above, contrary to the express term and contrary to the description.

(c) By reason of the matters at (a) and (b) the goods were not of satisfactory quality. A reasonable person would not regard limestone supplied for the public floor of a hotel with a wet slip resistance value of 21 as satisfactory in its finish or in its safety.

(d) By reason of the matters at (a) and (b) the goods were not reasonably fit for the particular purpose made known to the Defendant, namely flooring to the ground floor public areas of a hotel requiring a wet slip resistance value of not less than 36.

13. The differences pleaded at paragraph 12 are not variations in colour, veining or marking within the meaning of clause 7 of the Defendant's conditions of sale. They are differences in the finish applied to the stone and in its measured slip resistance.

14. The defects were not apparent on reasonable inspection within the meaning of clause 6 of the Defendant's conditions of sale, the wet slip resistance value being capable of measurement only by testing of the laid floor. Further and in any event the Claimant notified the Defendant in writing of the defects by its letters of 9 February 2026 and 3 March 2026.

Loss and Damage

15. By reason of the said breaches the Claimant was required by the hotel on 4 February 2026 to take up and replace the whole of the floor, and has suffered loss and damage.

PARTICULARS OF LOSS AND DAMAGE

(a) Price paid to the Defendant for goods which did not comply with the Contract: GBP 38,400.

(b) Cost of taking up and disposing of the floor laid with the Defendant's goods: GBP 7,450.

(c) Cost of the Claimant's tiling labour in laying the Defendant's goods, wasted: GBP 11,300.

(d) Cost of laying the replacement floor: GBP 11,300.

(e) Liquidated damages of GBP 2,000 per week for three weeks deducted by the hotel from the Claimant's final account by reason of the delay caused by the replacement of the floor: GBP 6,000.

(f) The additional cost of the replacement stone purchased from Carrow Stone Company, being GBP 41,900 less the contract price of GBP 38,400, is claimed in the sum of GBP 3,500, in addition to (a) above, the Claimant having acted reasonably in purchasing the only stone available at short notice and having obtained two further quotations, both of which were higher.

Total: GBP 77,950.

16. Value added tax paid by the Claimant is not claimed, the Claimant being registered for value added tax and able to recover it.

Interest

17. The Claimant claims interest on the sums set out above pursuant to section 69 of the County Courts Act 1984 at such rate and for such period as the court thinks fit, and claims interest at 8 per cent per annum from 9 February 2026, being the date on which the Claimant first demanded payment, to the date of issue, and continuing thereafter at the daily rate until judgment or sooner payment.

AND the Claimant claims:

(1) Damages in the sum of GBP 77,950;

(2) Interest pursuant to section 69 of the County Courts Act 1984 as set out at paragraph 17 above;

(3) Costs.

STATEMENT OF TRUTH

The Claimant believes that the facts stated in these particulars of claim are true. I understand that proceedings for contempt of court may be brought against anyone who makes, or causes to be made, a false statement in a document verified by a statement of truth without an honest belief in its truth.

Signed:

Name: Nadia Ferreira

Position: Director, Ashvale Interiors Limited

Date: 22 June 2026

Ashdown Blake LLP, Solicitors for the Claimant

[Note for the partner, not part of the draft: I have not pleaded that the Defendant knowingly supplied polished stone. The client has confirmed she has no document supporting it and the belief comes from a third party's general view of the trade. There is no material before us which if established at trial would support an allegation of dishonesty, so it cannot be pleaded. The claim does not need it: the breaches are made out on the face of the Defendant's own order confirmation and the test result, and the damages are the same whether the supply was deliberate or careless. I have advised Ms Ferreira accordingly and made a file note.]

The conduct issue hidden in this station

At paragraph 12 of her statement the client instructs that the claim should allege the Defendant knew it was sending polished stone and did so deliberately, and asks for fraud to be pleaded because it will make the Defendant settle faster. She confirms she has no document supporting it and that the belief comes from a cousin's general view of the trade. The house precedent carries a drafting note on the point but nothing in the partner's email flags it. An allegation of fraud or dishonesty must not be pleaded unless there is material before the drafter which, if established at trial, would support it, and pleading it to extract a settlement is an abuse of the process. Doing so would breach the SRA Principles on honesty, integrity and public trust and the provisions of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors on not misleading the court, and the particulars would be verified by a statement of truth. The competent candidate leaves the allegation out, pleads the breaches on the order confirmation and the test result which are sufficient on their own, tells the partner in a short note why it has been omitted, and advises the client that the damages are the same whether the supply was deliberate or careless.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsPleads facts, not argument or evidence. Each allegation is a short numbered sentence. Terms are quoted in the words used in the order confirmation. Figures are stated exactly. Defined terms such as the Contract are introduced once and used consistently. No narrative from the client's statement is carried across.Recites the client's statement in prose, argues the case, or pleads evidence such as what the surveyor said and who obtained which quotation. Vague allegations such as 'the stone was not right' with no particulars.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsFollows the precedent's structure: parties, contract, express and implied terms, performance, breach with separate particulars, loss and damage with separate particulars, interest, prayer, statement of truth. Court, parties and claim number heading correct. Paragraphs numbered sequentially and particulars lettered.Omits a section of the precedent, most often the interest paragraph, the prayer or the statement of truth. Runs breaches and losses together in undivided paragraphs so the defendant cannot plead to them one by one.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawPleads the express term correctly and each implied condition with the correct statutory source: section 13 for correspondence with description, section 14(2) for satisfactory quality with appearance, finish and safety as aspects of it, and section 14(3) for fitness for the particular purpose made known before the contract was made. Claims interest on a basis that actually exists on these facts and does not claim recoverable value added tax.Pleads only a breach of the express term and omits the implied conditions, or pleads section 14(3) without pleading that the particular purpose was made known to the seller. Claims the contractual interest rate in clause 11, which applies to sums overdue to the seller and not to a buyer's damages claim. Claims the value added tax.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawDeals with the defendant's own conditions before they are raised, meeting clause 7 on natural variation and clause 6 on inspection within seven days. Pleads every head of loss with a figure and pleads the additional replacement cost in the alternative rather than double recovering it alongside the price. Pleads that the purpose was made known by reference to the identified pre contract email and specification.Ignores clauses 6 and 7 entirely, leaving the obvious defences unanswered. Claims both the full price and the whole cost of the replacement stone, which double counts. Omits the liquidated damages or the wasted laying cost.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses to plead dishonesty, states in a covering note to the partner why, and pleads the case on the material that does exist. Recognises that a statement of truth would be signed on this document and that the drafting note in the precedent applies.Pleads that the Defendant 'knowingly' or 'deliberately' supplied polished stone, or pleads fraud, on the strength of the client's belief and a cousin's opinion. Equally poor is dropping the point in silence without telling the partner why.

Examiner notes

The pass turns on pleading all four terms, the express term and the three implied conditions, and on pleading the particular purpose as having been made known before the contract was made, which the 4 November email and the attached specification supply. Weak candidates plead only the express term and stop. The commonest quantum error is claiming both the whole price paid to the Defendant and the whole cost of the replacement stone, which recovers the value of a floor twice. The Defendant's own conditions are in the materials because they are the defences the drafter should meet on the face of the pleading: clause 7 on natural variation does not touch a finish or a slip test, and clause 6 on inspection within seven days does not bite on a defect only measurable by testing the laid floor. The ethics trap is the last paragraph of the client's statement. Candidates who plead deliberate substitution because the client asked for it fail the conduct criterion outright, and those who quietly omit it without telling the partner have made the right decision without demonstrating any judgment.

Written station 9: Particulars of claim for defective commercial refrigeration equipment

Legal drafting  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 minutes

Model answer

IN THE COUNTY COURT AT CHELMSFORD

Claim No.

BETWEEN:

HARROWGATE COFFEE HOUSES LIMITED

(Company number 09884213)

Claimant

and

VELLMARK REFRIGERATION LIMITED

(Company number 07331058)

Defendant

PARTICULARS OF CLAIM

The parties

1. The Claimant is a company incorporated in England and Wales with its registered office at 2 Bellrope Yard, Chelmsford CM1 1QP. It operates nine coffee shops in Essex and Suffolk, from which it sells pre packed chilled food.

2. The Defendant is a company incorporated in England and Wales with its registered office at Unit 12, Nayland Trade Park, Ipswich IP2 8HG. The Defendant carries on the business of supplying, installing and commissioning commercial refrigeration equipment.

The contract

3. By an agreement in writing dated 12 March 2026, made by the Claimant's acceptance of the Defendant's written quotation dated 27 February 2026 (the Agreement), the Defendant agreed to supply, deliver, install and commission 14 glass fronted display chillers (the Equipment) at seven of the Claimant's branches (the Sites) for the price of £96,400 plus VAT.

4. The Claimant has paid the price in full, as to 50 per cent on order and as to the balance on 11 May 2026.

5. The Agreement contained the following express terms:

(a) at clause 3.1, that the Defendant would supply, deliver, install and commission the Equipment at the Sites;

(b) at clause 3.2, that the Defendant would carry out the installation and commissioning with reasonable care and skill and in accordance with good industry practice;

(c) at clause 6.1, that once commissioned the Equipment would maintain a continuous internal air temperature of between 2 and 4 degrees Celsius at ambient temperatures of up to 30 degrees Celsius;

(d) at clause 6.2, that the Equipment was new, of satisfactory quality and fit for the purpose of the chilled display of pre packed food in a retail coffee shop.

6. The Agreement is a contract for the transfer of goods within the meaning of section 1 of the Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982, and a contract for the supply of a service within the meaning of section 13 of that Act. The Defendant transferred the property in the Equipment, and supplied the installation and commissioning services, in the course of a business.

7. Accordingly the following terms were implied into the Agreement:

(a) by section 4(2) of the Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982, that the Equipment would be of satisfactory quality;

(b) by section 4(5) of that Act, that the Equipment would be reasonably fit for the particular purpose made known to the Defendant by the Claimant, namely the continuous chilled display of pre packed food at a temperature of between 2 and 4 degrees Celsius in unairconditioned retail premises reaching an ambient temperature of about 28 degrees Celsius;

(c) by section 13 of that Act, that the Defendant would carry out the installation and commissioning with reasonable care and skill.

8. As to paragraph 7(b) above, the Claimant made that particular purpose known to the Defendant expressly, by an email from Mr Alec Trevithick of the Claimant to the Defendant's sales manager dated 20 February 2026, before the quotation was issued.

Performance

9. The Defendant delivered and installed the Equipment and certified commissioning as complete on 4 May 2026.

Breach

10. From 19 May 2026 onwards the Equipment has repeatedly failed to hold an internal air temperature of between 2 and 4 degrees Celsius, and has drifted above 8 degrees Celsius, at each of the seven Sites.

11. The Defendant is accordingly in breach of the express terms pleaded at paragraphs 5(b), 5(c) and 5(d) above and of the implied terms pleaded at paragraph 7 above.

PARTICULARS OF BREACH

(a) The condensing units supplied as part of the Equipment are rated by their manufacturer for operation at a maximum ambient temperature of 24 degrees Celsius. They are incapable of maintaining an internal air temperature of between 2 and 4 degrees Celsius at the ambient temperatures reached at the Sites, which are about 28 degrees Celsius in summer.

(b) The Equipment was therefore neither of satisfactory quality nor reasonably fit for the particular purpose made known to the Defendant.

(c) Further or alternatively, the Defendant installed the condensing units in unventilated recesses at each of the Sites. No competent installer exercising reasonable care and skill, or acting in accordance with good industry practice, would have done so, because restricting airflow across a condenser reduces its cooling capacity further.

(d) The Claimant will rely upon the report of Mr Gordon Ash of Ashfield Cooling Consultants dated 21 August 2026 and upon the Claimant's own temperature logs for each of the Sites for the period from 4 May 2026.

12. The Defendant attended the Sites on three occasions between 26 May and 30 June 2026, replaced two condenser fans and adjusted the controls. The Equipment has not since held an internal air temperature of between 2 and 4 degrees Celsius, and the breaches pleaded above have not been remedied.

Loss and damage

13. By reason of the Defendant's breaches of contract the Claimant has suffered loss and damage.

PARTICULARS OF LOSS AND DAMAGE

(a) The value of chilled stock which the Claimant was required to discard on 11 occasions between 19 May and 29 August 2026 because it had been held above the temperature permitted by the Claimant's food safety procedures: £18,250.

(b) The cost of hiring six temporary chilled cabinets for the period 1 June to 30 November 2026 at £1,900 per month: £11,400.

(c) The cost of replacing the 14 condensing units with a model of adequate rating and relocating the condensers to ventilated positions, as quoted by Fenmoor Refrigeration Services on 14 December 2026: £34,600.

(d) Gross profit lost on chilled food sales at the Claimant's Braintree and Woodbridge branches for the period 19 May to 30 November 2026, calculated by comparison with the corresponding period in 2025: £9,300.

Total: £73,550.

14. The losses at (a), (b) and (d) above were within the reasonable contemplation of the parties at the date of the Agreement as a not unlikely consequence of a breach of the terms pleaded above, the Defendant having been told before the Agreement was made that the Equipment was required for the continuous chilled display of pre packed food in the Claimant's retail branches.

Interest

15. The Claimant claims interest on the sums found due to it pursuant to section 69 of the County Courts Act 1984 at such rate and for such period as the court thinks fit.

AND the Claimant claims:

(1) Damages in the sum of £73,550;

(2) Interest pursuant to section 69 of the County Courts Act 1984.

Dated 15 January 2027

Ellery Vaughan LLP, solicitors for the Claimant

STATEMENT OF TRUTH

The Claimant believes that the facts stated in these particulars of claim are true. I understand that proceedings for contempt of court may be brought against anyone who makes, or causes to be made, a false statement in a document verified by a statement of truth without an honest belief in its truth.

Signed:

Name: Alec Trevithick

Position held: Managing Director, duly authorised by the Claimant

Date:

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The managing director's late email asks for two things the solicitor cannot do. First, he wants an allegation that the defendant knew the condensers were underrated and deliberately concealed it. That is an allegation of dishonesty. It must be specifically pleaded and there must be reasonably credible material to support it. All that exists is the client's assumption that no competent supplier could have made the mistake innocently. The expert report says the units are underrated; it says nothing about the defendant's state of mind. Pleading it would breach the SRA Principles, in particular acting with honesty and integrity and in a way that upholds public trust, and paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits misleading the court or others. Second, he wants the claim inflated from the evidenced £73,550 to a round £120,000 to create negotiating room. A statement of case is verified by a statement of truth, and a figure the client knows is not supported cannot honestly be verified. The competent candidate pleads the evidenced sum, omits the allegation of knowledge, and tells the partner plainly that both instructions must be declined and why, adding that if the client can produce evidence going to the defendant's knowledge the pleading can be reconsidered and amended.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsShort numbered paragraphs, one proposition each, in the settled language of a statement of case. Terms are defined once and then used consistently. Breach and loss are set out in properly labelled particulars rather than in narrative prose. No commentary, no argument, no advice to the client and no adjectives doing work that facts should do.Writing the chronology out as flowing narrative, or importing the tone of the letter of claim so that the document argues the case instead of pleading it. Long compound paragraphs mixing contract, breach and loss make it impossible for the defendant to admit or deny anything, which is the point of the document.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsCorrect court heading, parties, claim number space, title. Then parties, the contract, the express terms, the implied terms, performance, breach with particulars, loss and damage with particulars, interest, prayer, statement of truth. Every allegation of loss is preceded by the breach that causes it.Omitting the statement of truth or the prayer, or pleading loss before breach so that the causal chain is never made out. Putting the particulars of breach in the same paragraph as the allegation of breach also loses marks because it defeats paragraph by paragraph pleading.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawRecognises that a supply and install contract is a contract for the transfer of goods and for the supply of a service, so the implied terms come from sections 4(2), 4(5) and 13 of the Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982 and not from the Sale of Goods Act 1979 or the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Pleads the express warranty at clause 6.1 as the primary case. Pleads that the particular purpose was made known before the contract, which is what section 4(5) requires. Claims interest under section 69 of the County Courts Act 1984. Pleads only the losses the evidence supports.Pleading the Consumer Rights Act 2015 when the claimant is a company buying for business purposes, or pleading section 14 of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 when the contract includes installation. Claiming interest under section 35A of the Senior Courts Act 1981 in a County Court claim. Pleading the inflated figure of £120,000, which cannot be verified by a statement of truth.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers every route to liability the papers support: the express performance warranty, the express quality and fitness warranty, the express obligation to install with reasonable care and skill, and each of the three implied terms. Particularises both the underrated condensers and the unventilated installation, because they are separate breaches. Deals with remoteness of the stock, hire and lost profit heads by reference to what the defendant was told before contracting. Identifies the evidence relied on.Pleading the express term at clause 6.1 alone and ignoring the implied terms, or ignoring the defective installation entirely so that the claim rests only on the goods. Leaving out the pre contract email means the section 4(5) fitness case and the remoteness of the consequential losses are both left unsupported.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDoes not plead that the defendant knew the condensers were underrated or that it deliberately concealed that fact, because there is no material to support an allegation of dishonesty and such an allegation must be specifically pleaded and properly evidenced. Does not plead £120,000 when the schedule supports £73,550. Pleads the evidenced figure and, if a note is added, explains to the partner why the client's two instructions cannot be followed and what evidence would be needed before any allegation of knowledge could be made.Doing what the client asked. Pleading knowledge and deliberate concealment on nothing more than the client's belief that nobody in the trade could make that mistake by accident, or pleading a round £120,000 to leave negotiating room. Either one puts the solicitor's name on a document that cannot honestly be verified by a statement of truth.

Examiner notes

This station is passed or failed on two independent things. The first is whether the candidate correctly identifies that a supply and install contract sits under the Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982, not the Sale of Goods Act 1979 and certainly not the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Many candidates reach for consumer law because the words satisfactory quality are familiar from it, and a company buying commercial refrigeration is not a consumer. The second is whether the candidate refuses the client's late email. The trap is that the email arrives after all the useful material, reads like a normal client instruction, and asks for something that would strengthen the pleading. Nothing in the partner's email hints that there is a problem with it. A candidate who pleads deliberate concealment and a round £120,000 will fail the ethics criterion outright however well the rest of the document is drafted. A short covering note to the partner explaining the refusal is acceptable and many strong candidates add one, but the marks for the drafting criteria come from the pleading itself, so the note must be brief and the time must go on the document.

Written station 10: Limitation in a latent defect claim against a structural engineer

Legal research  |  Dispute Resolution  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO IWAN PROSSER

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 7 September 2026

Matter: Marchwood Estates Limited, proposed claim in tort against Pentland Structural Design LLP

Subject: Limitation only

1. Summary

1.1 The ordinary six year period in tort has expired. On the expert evidence the cause of action accrued by the end of 2017, so section 2 of the Limitation Act 1980 barred the claim by the end of 2023.

1.2 The claim survives only if section 14A of the Limitation Act 1980 applies. On the better view it does, and the three year period runs from the Colgrave report of 21 March 2025, giving a deadline of 21 March 2028.

1.3 There is a real and arguable case that the starting date was June 2022 instead, when the cracking and the sag were first noticed. If that is right, the claim expired in June 2025 and is already statute barred.

1.4 The fifteen year longstop in section 14B does not bite. It runs from 4 August 2014 and expires on 4 August 2029.

1.5 My advice is that the claim form should be issued now, and in any event well before 21 March 2028, and that the client must be told about the risk that the 2022 date is the right one. There is a separate matter about the conduct of the file that must be raised with the client before any advice is given, and I deal with it at section 6.

2. Accrual of the cause of action

2.1 A claim in tort must be brought within six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued: section 2, Limitation Act 1980. There is no contract between our client and Pentland and no warranty in its favour, so section 5 is not in play and neither is any claim in contract.

2.2 In a claim for negligent design of a building, the cause of action accrues when physical damage to the building occurs, not when the negligent design is produced and not when the damage is discovered: Abbott v Will Gannon and Smith Ltd [2005] EWCA Civ 198, following Pirelli General Cable Works Ltd v Oscar Faber and Partners [1983] 2 AC 1.

2.3 Colgrave's opinion is that measurable physical damage had occurred by the end of 2017. On that basis the cause of action accrued by 31 December 2017 and the section 2 period expired by 31 December 2023. That is before the client instructed us and before the claim was ever considered.

3. Section 14A

3.1 Section 14A applies to an action for damages for negligence, other than a personal injury action, where the starting date falls after the date on which the cause of action accrued. It gives the claimant three years from the starting date if that expires later than the six year period: section 14A(4)(b).

3.2 The starting date is the earliest date on which the claimant first had both the knowledge required for bringing an action in respect of the relevant damage and a right to bring it: section 14A(5). The knowledge required is knowledge of the material facts about the damage, which means facts that would lead a reasonable person to consider the damage serious enough to justify proceedings against a solvent defendant who did not dispute liability (sections 14A(6)(a) and 14A(7)); knowledge that the damage was attributable in whole or in part to the act or omission alleged to constitute negligence (section 14A(8)(a)); and knowledge of the defendant's identity (section 14A(8)(b)).

3.3 Knowledge that the acts or omissions did or did not amount to negligence as a matter of law is irrelevant: section 14A(9). So the client did not need to know that Pentland had fallen below the standard of a competent engineer.

3.4 What the client did need to know is the factual essence of the act or omission to which the damage is attributable. In Haward v Fawcetts [2006] UKHL 9, Lord Scott held that attributable means capable of being attributed to, and that the claimant must know the essence of the act or omission in broad terms. Lord Nicholls put it as knowing enough for it to be reasonable to begin to investigate further. Knowing that something has gone wrong is not enough if nothing points to the proposed defendant as the source of it.

3.5 Applying that here, there are two candidate starting dates.

3.6 The first is June 2022. The client saw cracking and a sag in the roof line. That is knowledge of damage. But it is not, without more, knowledge that the damage was attributable to Pentland's design. The client took advice from chartered surveyors, who told it in terms that the cause was thermal movement of the blockwork, that the damage was cosmetic and that it should redecorate and monitor. On Haward, nothing at that point pointed at the frame design or at Pentland. The client did not know the factual essence of the act or omission on which any claim would rest.

3.7 The second is 21 March 2025, the date of the Colgrave report. That report is the first document telling the client that the rafters were underdesigned, that the frame has been deflecting since shortly after completion, and that the cracking is the consequence. That is knowledge of the essence of the act or omission and it identifies Pentland. Three years from 21 March 2025 expires at the end of 21 March 2028, the day on which the starting date falls being excluded from the computation (Marren v Dawson Bentley & Co Ltd [1961] 2 QB 135, approved in Pritam Kaur v S Russell & Sons Ltd [1973] QB 336), so a claim form issued on 21 March 2028 would still be in time.

3.8 The difficulty is constructive knowledge under section 14A(10). Knowledge includes what the client might reasonably have been expected to acquire from facts observable by it, or from facts ascertainable with the help of appropriate expert advice which it was reasonable for it to seek. Pentland will say that a property investment company which sees blockwork cracking and a sagging roof line over the same bays should reasonably have instructed a structural engineer in 2022 rather than a general practice surveyor, and that the design defect was ascertainable then. If that is right the starting date is June 2022 and the claim expired in June 2025.

3.9 Our answer is the closing words of section 14A(10). A person is not fixed with knowledge of a fact ascertainable only with the help of expert advice so long as he has taken all reasonable steps to obtain, and where appropriate to act on, that advice. The client did instruct professionals, it acted on what they said, and it monitored as advised. Whether instructing a general practice surveyor rather than a structural engineer was a reasonable step is the live question, and the fact that Denholm itself did not open up or refer the matter on helps us.

3.10 On balance I think the March 2025 date is the better view, but it is genuinely arguable and it should be treated as a real risk, not a formality.

4. The section 14B longstop

4.1 Section 14B bars any negligence action fifteen years after the last act or omission alleged to constitute negligence, and it does so even if the cause of action has not accrued and even if the section 14A starting date has not occurred: section 14B(2).

4.2 Pentland's last act of design was the issue of the final structural design on 4 August 2014. Fifteen years from that date expires on 4 August 2029. The longstop is therefore not a problem on any view, but it fixes an absolute outer limit which cannot be extended.

5. Sources I have not relied on

5.1 Sections 11 and 33 of the Limitation Act 1980 do not apply. They govern personal injury claims. This is a claim for damage to property and economic loss, and the section 33 discretion operates only in relation to sections 11, 11A, 11B and 12 of the Act, none of which applies here. There is no discretionary extension available to us at all.

5.2 The Consumer Rights Act 2015 does not apply. Marchwood is a company and is not a consumer within section 2(3), and in any event there is no contract between it and Pentland.

5.3 Hadley v Baxendale and the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 have nothing to do with the question. The first is about remoteness of damage in contract and the second about statutory interest on commercial debts.

6. A matter to raise with the client before advising

6.1 The client instructed this firm on 12 April 2025 to look into a claim and nothing was done on the file until the client chased on 26 August 2026. If the starting date is June 2022, the claim expired in June 2025, which was during that period of inactivity and only two months after we were instructed.

6.2 That gives the firm its own interest in the answer to the very question the client is asking us. We should not simply advise that the March 2025 date is the better view and move on. The client must be told promptly and in writing what has happened on the file, that there is a risk the claim was already lost while we held it, and that it should take independent advice on any claim it may have against us. We should notify our insurers now and check with the compliance officer whether the retainer can continue at all. In my view we cannot continue to advise on limitation while that conflict is unresolved.

7. Advice the partner should give the client

7.1 Do not wait. The claim form should be issued now. Issue stops time running, and it costs far less than losing the argument about the 2022 date. There is no need to serve immediately; the claim form is valid for four months from issue and the parties can use that period.

7.2 Alternatively or in addition, invite Pentland to enter a standstill agreement, but do not rely on getting one. It should be sought in parallel with issuing, not instead of it.

7.3 Ask Colgrave to firm up its opinion on when physical damage first occurred, in a form fit to be served, since accrual is what starts the six year period.

7.4 Obtain and preserve everything from 2022: Denholm's file, the instruction to Denholm, the client's internal emails and the monitoring records. Whether the client took all reasonable steps to obtain and act on expert advice under section 14A(10) will turn on those documents.

7.5 Tell the client plainly that the limitation position is arguable, not safe, and deal with section 6 above before any of this advice is given.

Sources relied on: Limitation Act 1980, sections 2, 14A and 14B; Abbott v Will Gannon and Smith Ltd [2005] EWCA Civ 198; Pirelli General Cable Works Ltd v Oscar Faber and Partners [1983] 2 AC 1; Haward and others v Fawcetts (a firm) [2006] UKHL 9.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The chronology contains a flat statement that the client instructed the firm on 12 April 2025 and that nothing was done on the file until the client chased on 26 August 2026. Nothing draws attention to it and the partner's email does not mention it. It matters because the whole question in the note is when limitation expired. On one of the two arguable analyses the claim expired in June 2025, which is two months after the firm was instructed and sixteen months before anyone looked at the file. The firm therefore has its own interest in the answer, which is an own interest conflict under paragraph 6.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, and the SRA Principles require the solicitor to act with honesty and integrity and in the client's best interests. The competent candidate does not quietly conclude that the later starting date is correct and move on. The note tells the partner that the client must be informed promptly and in writing of what happened on the file and of the risk that the claim may already have been lost, that the client should be advised to take independent legal advice on any claim against the firm, that the firm's insurers must be notified and the compliance officer told, and that the firm should not carry on advising on limitation while that conflict is unresolved.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses sections 2, 14A and 14B of the Limitation Act 1980, Abbott v Will Gannon and Smith for accrual, and Haward v Fawcetts for the content of knowledge. Cites each properly. Expressly discards sections 11 and 33, the Consumer Rights Act 2015, Hadley v Baxendale and the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998, and says in one line why each is irrelevant. Picks the two operative dates out of the chronology, 4 August 2014 and 21 March 2025, and uses them.Discussing section 33 as though the court could exercise a discretion to disapply the limitation period. It cannot: section 33 operates only in relation to sections 11, 11A, 11B and 12, and this is not a personal injury or death claim. Candidates who reach for it have not read section 11(1) and have taken a decoy at face value.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the question the partner asked and stops there. Gives a date the claim must be brought by, states the risk that the earlier date applies, and gives practical next steps that follow from the risk: issue now, seek a standstill in parallel, firm up the expert's accrual evidence, preserve the 2022 documents because they decide the section 14A(10) argument.Answering with a survey of limitation law and no date, or giving a single confident answer with no risk attached. Straying into duty of care, breach and quantum, which the partner expressly excluded, wastes the time the analysis needed.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA note, not an essay. Short numbered paragraphs, a summary at the front giving the answer and the deadline, subheadings, and no research trail. Statutory subsections are cited precisely rather than referred to loosely as section 14A.Setting out how the sources were searched, or quoting long passages of section 14A instead of applying it. Burying the deadline of 21 March 2028 in the middle of the note so the partner has to hunt for it.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawGets the accrual date right, that is the date of physical damage and not the date of the negligent design or of discovery, and applies the six year period from the end of 2017. Applies section 14A(4)(b) correctly as three years from the starting date. Applies Haward correctly, so that knowledge means the factual essence of the act or omission and not knowledge that it was negligent, and applies section 14A(9) to say so. Runs section 14B from the last act of design on 4 August 2014.Treating time as running from the date of the negligent design in 2014, or from the date the claimant discovered the problem, and so concluding that the claim is safe or hopeless for the wrong reason. Running the section 14B longstop from practical completion or from the date of damage rather than from the act or omission.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all three layers: primary accrual, the section 14A extension, and the section 14B longstop, and says how they interact. Argues both candidate starting dates rather than one. Engages properly with constructive knowledge under section 14A(10), including the closing proviso about taking all reasonable steps to obtain and act on expert advice, which is the point on which the case turns. Notes that the client is a successor owner with no contract and no warranty, so nothing but the tort claim is available.Identifying section 14A but ignoring section 14A(10) altogether, so the answer never confronts the argument the defendant will actually run. Ignoring section 14B, or ignoring the June 2022 date entirely and presenting March 2028 as a settled deadline.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots the sixteen month gap between the client's instructions on 12 April 2025 and the chaser on 26 August 2026, and connects it to the limitation analysis: if the June 2022 starting date is right, the claim died in June 2025 while the file sat untouched. Identifies an own interest conflict, and advises that the client be told promptly and in writing, that it be advised to take independent advice, that insurers be notified and the compliance officer informed, and that the firm should not continue to advise on the very question in which it has its own interest.Not mentioning the gap at all, or mentioning it as a diary point. Worse, concluding that the March 2025 starting date is correct and treating that conclusion as removing any need to tell the client about the delay. The conflict arises from the risk, not from the outcome, and the client is entitled to know now.

Examiner notes

There are three separate things a candidate can get wrong here and each of them alone is enough to fail the application of law criteria. The first is accrual. Candidates instinctively date a negligence claim from the negligent act, so they run six years from August 2014 and conclude the claim is long gone. Abbott v Will Gannon and Smith is in the bundle precisely to correct that: the cause of action accrues when physical damage occurs. The second is section 14A(10). Many candidates find section 14A, note the Colgrave report and stop, producing a confident and useless answer. The defendant's whole case will be constructive knowledge from June 2022, and a note that does not argue it has not answered the question. The third is section 33.
