It is a decoy and it is attractive because candidates remember a judicial discretion to extend limitation. It exists only for personal injury claims and there is no discretion available here at all. Beyond that, the discriminator is the file gap. It is one line in a chronology and it is the most important line in the papers.

Written station 11: Limitation and a defect found seven years after completion

Legal research  |  Dispute Resolution  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO PARTNER

To: Rhiannon Salter

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 18 January 2027

Matter: Fairhurst Provisions Limited (FPL) v Brackenhall Construction Limited (BCL), limitation

1. Summary of advice

1.1 On the ordinary rules the contract claim expired on 12 March 2025 and is statute barred. The contract was signed under hand and not executed as a deed, so the period is six years under section 5 of the Limitation Act 1980, not twelve under section 8.

1.2 A claim in negligence probably adds nothing. FPL's loss is the cost of putting right a defect in the building itself, which is pure economic loss and is not recoverable in the tort of negligence (Murphy v Brentwood DC [1991] 1 AC 398). An ordinary building contract does not, without more, carry a concurrent Hedley Byrne duty (Robinson v PE Jones (Contractors) Ltd [2011] EWCA Civ 9), so section 14A cannot be used to get round the expiry of the contractual period.

1.3 FPL's real route is section 32 of the 1980 Act. If the falsified inspection record was a deliberate concealment, or if the sub-base was deliberately built short in circumstances where that was unlikely to be discovered for some time, time did not begin to run until FPL discovered the concealment or could reasonably have discovered it. On the present evidence that date is 2 October 2025 at the earliest. The contract claim would then run to about 2 October 2031.

1.4 Section 32 is therefore the whole case on limitation. FPL should be advised in those terms, and warned that it carries a real evidential burden.

2. The contract claim

2.1 Time runs from the date of breach, not from the date the damage appears. BCL's breach was building the sub-base to about 100mm instead of the specified 250mm in June 2018, and its failure to deliver a slab built with reasonable skill and care under clause 21. At the very latest the cause of action accrued at practical completion on 12 March 2019.

2.2 The execution page at Document 4 shows signatures only. There is no attestation clause, no witness and no statement that the document is a deed. It is a simple contract, so section 5 applies and six years ran out on 12 March 2025. Please have the original checked before we advise finally, because if a deed were located section 8 would give until March 2031 and the concealment argument would become far less important.

3. Negligence and section 14A

3.1 Section 14A gives three years from the date of knowledge where that is later than six years from accrual, subject to the fifteen year longstop in section 14B. If it applied, FPL's knowledge date would be 2 October 2025, when Marchwood's interim report showed the shortfall in hardcore. Knowledge under section 14A(6) to (10) is knowledge of the material facts about the damage and that it is attributable to the defendant's act or omission; knowledge that the act was negligent in law is irrelevant (section 14A(9); Haward v Fawcetts [2006] UKHL 9). Three years from October 2025 runs to October 2028, and the section 14B longstop of fifteen years from June 2018 does not expire until 2033.

3.2 The difficulty is that there must first be a cause of action in negligence, and there probably is not. The loss claimed is the cost of replacing the defective slab and the consequences of its failure. Damage to the defective thing itself is pure economic loss, not damage to other property (Murphy v Brentwood). A concurrent duty in tort arises only where the defendant has assumed responsibility in the Hedley Byrne sense (Henderson v Merrett Syndicates Ltd [1995] 2 AC 145), and the Court of Appeal held in Robinson v PE Jones that a builder in an ordinary contractual relationship does not assume that responsibility. Nothing in this file suggests any advisory or design role by BCL beyond building to FPL's specification.

3.3 Pirelli General Cable Works Ltd v Oscar Faber & Partners [1983] 2 AC 1 should not be relied on to fix a later accrual date. It decides when a tortious cause of action accrues on physical damage, it predates sections 14A and 14B, and it does not answer the prior question whether a duty exists at all.

4. Section 32, the strongest argument

4.1 Section 32(1)(b) postpones the start of the limitation period where a fact relevant to the claimant's right of action has been deliberately concealed by the defendant, until the claimant discovers the concealment or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it. Section 32(2) treats the deliberate commission of a breach of duty in circumstances in which it is unlikely to be discovered for some time as deliberate concealment. Note also section 32(5): where section 32(1)(b) applies, sections 14A and 14B do not, so on the concealment case the fifteen year longstop discussed at 3.1 falls away and the period is the six years under section 2 running from discovery or reasonable discoverability.

4.2 Two routes are available on these facts.

(a) Section 32(1)(b). Record SB/07 states that 250mm of Type 1 fill was laid and inspected. Marchwood says the record cannot be contemporaneous, and the named clerk of works says in writing that he never attended. If BCL created a false record to give the appearance of compliance, that is a deliberate act of hiding a fact relevant to FPL's right of action. Following Canada Square Operations Ltd v Potter [2023] UKSC 41, concealment must be intentional; recklessness is not enough, so we will have to prove that the record was made deliberately rather than carelessly copied.

(b) Section 32(2). A sub-base is buried under a concrete slab as soon as it is laid. Building it to 100mm instead of 250mm is a breach that by its nature is unlikely to be discovered for years. If FPL can show BCL knew it was building short, section 32(2) applies without proof of any separate concealing act. Cave v Robinson Jarvis & Rolf [2002] UKHL 18 confirms that knowledge or intention is required and that mere negligence will not do.

4.3 The postponed period runs from discovery or reasonable discoverability. FPL had cracking and racking movement in autumn 2023 and asked about a surveyor. BCL will argue that reasonable diligence at that point would have revealed the shortfall, which would start time in late 2023 and still leave the claim in time until late 2029. Either way the claim is in time, but the 2023 correspondence is a point we should confront now rather than later.

5. What to advise Delia Fairhurst on Thursday

5.1 The claim is not hopeless but it is not straightforward. It depends on persuading a court that BCL deliberately concealed the shortfall in the sub-base. Without that, the claim is out of time.

5.2 Practical steps to recommend now:

(a) Preserve everything. Do not disturb the remaining trial pits, and keep the excavated material, the batching tickets and the original of record SB/07.

(b) Take a signed statement from the clerk of works while his recollection is fresh, and trace Craig Bethell.

(c) Instruct Marchwood to report specifically on whether the record could have been completed innocently.

(d) Check BCL's financial standing and whether it held contractors' all risks or public liability cover, because a paper judgment is worth nothing.

(e) Comply with the Pre-Action Protocol for Construction and Engineering Disputes. There is no immediate limitation emergency if section 32 is right, so there is no need to issue and stay, but a standstill agreement should be considered if BCL wants time to investigate. A standstill agreement cannot revive a claim already barred, so it must be drafted to preserve, not concede, the section 32 argument.

(f) On the police: reporting suspected forgery is FPL's decision, but it should be taken separately from the civil claim. We should not threaten a report in order to extract payment.

5.3 Materials that do not assist. The Defective Premises Act 1972 and the extended periods in section 135 of the Building Safety Act 2022 apply to dwellings; a cold store is not a dwelling. The Consumer Rights Act 2015 does not apply because FPL is a company and not a consumer under section 2(3). Sections 11 and 11A of the Limitation Act 1980 are irrelevant as there is no personal injury and no product liability claim.

6. A matter for you

6.1 The file shows that on 14 November 2023 Delia Fairhurst described movement in the cold store floor to Alaric Penn and asked whether there was any deadline for complaining to the builder. He told her it was a maintenance matter and advised her not to instruct a surveyor. No limitation advice was given. On the ordinary contractual analysis the claim was then still in time, and it expired on 12 March 2025 while that advice stood.

6.2 If the section 32 argument fails, FPL may have a claim against this firm. That is an own interest conflict under paragraph 6.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs, which admits of no exception. We should tell the client promptly and in writing that there may be a claim against us, advise her to take independent legal advice on it, notify our insurers under the reporting obligation in the policy, and consider whether we can properly continue to act on the claim against BCL. We must not simply present section 32 as a comfortable answer in order to avoid the conversation. Please let me know how you would like this handled before Thursday.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The file note records that in November 2023 a partner of the firm was told about movement in the cold store floor and was asked expressly about deadlines for complaining to the builder, and advised that there was nothing to worry about and that no surveyor was needed. The contract claim was still in time then and expired in March 2025 while that advice stood. The firm therefore has a potential own interest conflict under paragraph 6.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs, which admits of no exception, and a risk of being sued itself. A competent candidate spots this without prompting and resolves it by advising prompt written disclosure to the client, recommending independent advice on any claim against the firm, notifying the firm's insurers, and considering whether the firm can continue to act. A weaker candidate either misses it or quietly relies on section 32 to make the problem go away, which offends Principles 2, 5 and 7. There is a secondary point in the client's question about going to the police: the candidate should keep any report of suspected forgery separate from the civil claim and must not offer to use it as leverage for payment.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses sections 5, 8, 14A, 14B and 32 of the Limitation Act 1980 and the Murphy, Henderson, Robinson, Haward, Cave and Canada Square line of authority, cited accurately, and expressly discards the Defective Premises Act, Building Safety Act, Consumer Rights Act, section 11 and section 11A materials with a reason.Cites Pirelli or the Defective Premises Act as though it governs, or simply lists every source in the bundle without separating the relevant from the irrelevant.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the question the client actually asked, tells her plainly that the claim turns on proving deliberate concealment, and gives concrete next steps on evidence, the protocol, a standstill agreement and the defendant's solvency.Produces an abstract essay on limitation with no advice on what to tell the client and no practical steps.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured note with numbered headings, a summary at the front that a partner can read in a minute, and no research trail.Sets out a research trail, or buries the conclusion at the end of an undifferentiated block of text.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly fixes accrual at breach or practical completion, correctly reads the execution page as a simple contract giving six years under section 5, and correctly applies section 32(1)(b) and 32(2) to the falsified record and the buried sub-base.Treats the contract as a deed and gives twelve years, or dates accrual from discovery of the cracking in 2023, or asserts that section 14A saves the claim without first asking whether a duty in tort exists.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with both routes to section 32, addresses the discoverability argument arising from the 2023 cracking, notes the section 14B longstop, and identifies that a tort claim fails at the duty stage before limitation is reached.Mentions section 32(1)(b) but misses section 32(2), or ignores the reasonable diligence point raised by the 2023 cracking, or fails to notice the section 14B longstop.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies the firm's own potential negligence arising from the November 2023 advice as an own interest conflict, and resolves it by proposing prompt written disclosure to the client, independent advice, notification of insurers and a decision on whether the firm can continue to act.Says nothing about the November 2023 advice, or notices it but treats it as a mere file oddity rather than a conflict requiring disclosure to the client and notification of insurers.

Examiner notes

The pass or fail turns on reading the execution page and on reaching section 32. Weak candidates spend the hour on section 14A because it is the section that looks like it was written for late discovery, and never ask whether there is a tort claim at all. Murphy and Robinson v PE Jones are in the bundle precisely so that a strong candidate closes that door and moves to section 32, which is where the case actually lives. The Defective Premises Act and Building Safety Act extract is the most attractive decoy because 30 years sounds decisive; it applies only to dwellings and this is a warehouse. The Consumer Rights Act extract is defeated by the definition of consumer in section 2(3), and sections 11 and 11A have nothing to do with these facts. Candidates who cite the two together as though they helped lose marks on the first criterion. The final trap is the November 2023 email, which reads as background chronology and is in fact the ethics issue.

Written station 12: Replying to the other side on a rejected consignment

Legal writing  |  Dispute Resolution  |  30 minutes

Model answer

TRELAWNY BAIRD LLP

Solicitors

Ref: TB/HTL/2209

Wroxall Deane LLP

Your ref: WD/CJL/4021

24 March 2027

Dear Sirs

Hollingbourne Timber Limited and Castlebrook Joinery Limited

Our client: Hollingbourne Timber Limited

This letter is open and we shall refer to it on the question of costs if that becomes necessary.

We have your letter of 19 March. Our client's position is as follows.

1. The sums due

412 units were delivered in four consignments between 6 October and 21 November 2026 and were invoiced at £84,500 plus VAT on 30 day terms. The whole of that sum is overdue. Payment was not withheld under any complaint at the time. Your client simply did not pay, and did not answer our client's chasing emails of December and January.

2. Quality

Our client does not accept that the goods were other than of satisfactory quality when delivered. Our technical manager attended your client's yard on 14 February 2027 and inspected the 32 units then unfitted. Five showed measurable warping. The units were stored outdoors in an unheated, open sided yard through December and January, unwrapped. Clause 12 of our client's terms requires kiln dried goods to be stored flat, under cover, dry, ventilated and at a stable temperature. On the material available the warping is consistent with storage on your client's site rather than with any defect on delivery. Colour variation between batches of natural birch veneer is inherent in the material and was known to your client, which has bought the same product from our client since 2019.

3. The complaint was made late

Clause 9 of our client's standard terms, on which each of these deliveries was made, requires written notice of any defect apparent on reasonable inspection within 14 days of delivery, failing which the goods are deemed accepted. Your client's first complaint was made on 3 February 2027, between 74 and 120 days after the four deliveries, and after the invoices had fallen overdue. Our client relies on clause 9.

4. Rejection is not open to your client

Even leaving clause 9 aside, your client has accepted the goods within the meaning of section 35 of the Sale of Goods Act 1979. Its own site progress reports, of which our client holds copies, record that approximately 250 units were installed in kitchens for its own customers between November 2026 and January 2027, and that a further 40 were cut down on site to fit non standard runs. Installing and cutting the goods are acts inconsistent with our client's ownership under section 35(1)(b). Retaining the whole consignment for more than two months without intimating rejection is also acceptance under section 35(4). By section 11(4), your client is confined to a claim in damages and cannot reject the goods or treat the contract as at an end. The demand that our client collect 412 units, most of which are now fitted in third party kitchens, is not a serious one.

5. The counterclaim

The counterclaim as presently formulated is not sustainable. Clause 10 limits our client's liability for defective goods to replacement or a credit, and excludes loss of profit and indirect loss. The claim for the Selmesford Homes contract falls squarely within that exclusion. If your client contends that clause 10 does not satisfy the requirement of reasonableness under sections 3, 6(1A) and 11 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, please say so and set out the basis, so that the point can be addressed now rather than at trial. We note that the parties are both commercial contractors of comparable size and have dealt on these terms since 2019.

6. Documents

To move matters forward we ask your client to provide, within 14 days: photographs and moisture readings of the units said to be defective; the delivery, storage and installation records for each of the four consignments; the correspondence with Selmesford Homes and the two housebuilder customers referred to in your letter; and a schedule identifying by unit which of the 412 units is said to be defective and why.

7. Resolution

Our client would prefer to resolve this without proceedings. We propose a mediation before a mediator experienced in construction supply disputes, to take place within eight weeks, with the parties sharing the mediator's fees equally. We are content to consider any other form of alternative dispute resolution your client prefers. We make this proposal openly so that it may be drawn to the court's attention on costs. As you know, the Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols expects the parties to attempt settlement, and the court may take an unreasonable refusal to engage in ADR into account when making costs orders.

We look forward to your response within 14 days. If the debt is not paid and this matter is not resolved, our client reserves the right to issue proceedings for the sum due together with interest and costs.

Yours faithfully

Trainee Solicitor

for Trelawny Baird LLP

NOTE TO NADIA OKONJO, NOT FOR SENDING

Bella Hollingbourne's instructions of 23 March cannot be carried out and I have not included them.

We cannot threaten a winding up petition. The debt is disputed and, on the face of it, disputed on substantial grounds, so presenting or threatening a petition would be an abuse of process. Castlebrook could restrain presentation by injunction and would very likely obtain indemnity costs.

We cannot threaten to report Rufus Castlebrook to the police or to Trading Standards in order to obtain payment of a civil debt. Threatening criminal or regulatory action to gain an advantage in a civil matter is taking unfair advantage of another party contrary to paragraph 1.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, and offends Principles 2 and 5. If our client genuinely believes a criminal offence has been committed she is free to report it, but that must be kept entirely separate from the recovery of the debt and must never be offered or withheld as a bargaining counter. On the facts we have, an allegation of fraud is unsupportable in any event.

We cannot say that we will apply to freeze Castlebrook's bank account. We have no instructions or evidence supporting a freezing injunction and no such application is contemplated. Saying otherwise would be a statement we know to be untrue, contrary to paragraph 1.4.

We cannot tell Castlebrook that our client will inform merchants and housebuilders that it is insolvent. It is not insolvent so far as we know, the statement would be untrue and damaging, and the threat is designed only to apply improper pressure.

Finally, the letter must not be marked without prejudice. It contains our client's open position and a demand for payment, so the label would be wrong in substance, and a label cannot protect improper threats in any event.

I suggest you speak to Bella before this goes out. She should be told plainly that these steps would harm her own case, and that the strong points here are clause 9, acceptance under section 35 and clause 10, which are worth more than any threat.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client instructs the solicitor to threaten a winding up petition over a genuinely disputed debt, to threaten a report to the police and Trading Standards unless payment is made, to assert that a freezing injunction will be sought when none is contemplated, to threaten to tell the trade that the other company is insolvent, and to mark the whole letter without prejudice so that none of it can be seen by a judge. Each is improper. Threatening insolvency proceedings for a substantially disputed debt is an abuse of process. Threatening criminal or regulatory action to obtain an advantage in a civil dispute, and threatening publicity of a damaging untruth, are taking unfair advantage contrary to paragraph 1.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and offend Principles 2 and 5. Asserting an application that will not be made breaches paragraph 1.4. This is the territory of the SRA's warning notices on conduct in disputes and on improper threats. A competent candidate sends a letter containing none of them, explains to the partner why each was excluded, keeps any genuine criminal complaint entirely separate from debt recovery, and refuses to mislabel an open letter as without prejudice.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsDeploys the delivery dates and total, the 3 February first complaint, the 250 installed and 40 cut units, the 14 February inspection finding 5 of 32 warped, and the open sided yard storage, and ties each to a legal consequence.Answers the allegations in general terms without using the installation and storage evidence, which is the whole strength of the case.
Use a logical structure.SkillsNumbered letter that moves from the sum due, to quality, to late notice, to rejection, to the counterclaim, to documents requested, to a proposal for resolution, followed by a separate internal paragraph to the partner.One continuous argument with the payment demand and the ADR proposal buried inside it, or omits the internal paragraph the partner asked for.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsFirm but professional to a fellow solicitor, invites the reasonableness argument to be articulated now, asks for specific documents, and makes a workable mediation proposal rather than a rhetorical one.Writes to the other side's solicitor as though writing to the client, or proposes ADR in a token line with no mechanism and no costs point.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsCorrespondence register between solicitors: precise, unemotional, no bluster, no rhetorical questions, and the open status of the letter stated at the top.Adopts the client's tone, uses aggressive or sarcastic language, or marks the letter without prejudice.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly applies section 35(1)(b) and 35(4) acceptance and section 11(4) so that rejection is not available, and treats clause 9 as a deemed acceptance provision, while recognising that a clause which deems goods accepted after 14 days restricts the buyer's remedy and may itself have to satisfy the requirement of reasonableness if the point is taken.Concedes the right to reject, or analyses clause 9 only as an exclusion clause under the Unfair Contract Terms Act and misses section 35 acceptance altogether.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAlso addresses satisfactory quality under section 14(2) and 14(2A) on the storage evidence, the clause 10 limitation and its exposure under sections 3, 6(1A) and 11 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, and the costs consequences of refusing ADR under the Practice Direction.Deals with acceptance but ignores the counterclaim and clause 10, or asserts that clause 10 is watertight without acknowledging the reasonableness test.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawExcludes every improper threat from the letter and explains to the partner, item by item, why each is improper, keeping any genuine criminal complaint separate from recovery of the debt.Includes any of the winding up, police, Trading Standards, freezing injunction or insolvency publicity threats, or drops them silently without telling the partner why they cannot be sent.

Examiner notes

Two things separate a pass from a fail. First, the acceptance analysis. Candidates see a quality dispute and reach for the Unfair Contract Terms Act, but the decisive point is that Castlebrook installed 250 units and cut 40 more, which is acceptance under section 35(1)(b), so by section 11(4) rejection is gone and only damages remain. Clause 9 is best characterised as a deemed acceptance provision rather than as a straightforward exclusion clause, and a candidate who leads with clause 9 and never reaches section 35 has missed the strongest point on the file. Credit should be given, not withheld, where a candidate also notes that a term deeming goods accepted after 14 days restricts the buyer's remedy and may therefore itself have to satisfy the requirement of reasonableness, which is a point the other side is likely to take. Second, the letter must be free of the client's threats. The trap is that Bella Hollingbourne's list reads like ordinary commercial robustness, and a candidate under time pressure tends either to soften the threats into more polite versions, which does not cure them, or to delete them without explanation, which leaves the partner and the client believing they were merely stylistic. The letter must also stay open. A candidate who marks it without prejudice both loses the ADR costs point under the Practice Direction and misunderstands what the label is for.

Property Practice

Written station 13: Freehold purchase with a restrictive covenant and no legal access

Case and matter analysis  |  Property Practice  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO PARTNER

To: Ruth Adeyemi, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 14 September 2026

Matter: Ferrand, purchase of Unit 4 and yard, Tanners Lane, Marlbrook, HP418923

Subject: Title and search problems, options and recommendation

1. Summary

There are three substantive problems and one professional conduct problem.

1.1 The title has no legal right of way over the only vehicle access. That access strip is not a public highway and a neighbour has asserted ownership of it in writing within the last twelve months.

1.2 A 1968 restrictive covenant prohibits retail sale to the public. That covenant, if enforceable, defeats the showroom, and the client's existing plan to sell finished pieces from the unit would also be a breach.

1.3 A second 1968 covenant prohibits any new building without consent. That defeats the showroom independently of the retail covenant. Local plan policy E3 defeats it a third time as a matter of planning.

1.4 The client has asked us to keep the lender out of it. We cannot do that.

I recommend that we do not exchange on the present terms.

2. Access

2.1 The property register expressly notes that no right of way over the hatched strip is included in the title. The strip is not maintainable at public expense and the search confirms it is not a highway. The property is therefore landlocked as a matter of registered title. Access on foot and by vehicle is a legal necessity for a joinery business receiving timber deliveries.

2.2 The seller's reply to enquiry 4 describes long user without objection since 1968. Long uninterrupted use as of right, without force, secrecy or permission, can give rise to a prescriptive easement, and twenty years of qualifying user would ordinarily be enough. The difficulty is proof. The seller has never occupied the property, the user is her late brother's, and we have no statutory declaration or statement of truth from anyone with direct knowledge. The seller has also not said who owns the strip, and reply 9 says she owns no adjoining land, so she cannot grant a right herself.

2.3 The right cannot be created by section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 or by an implied grant on this sale, because the seller owns nothing over which a right could be implied.

2.4 Enquiry 12 is the critical answer. Mr Whitlock of 3 Tanners Lane wrote in May 2026 claiming to own the strip and saying he intends to gate it. That is a written assertion of rights within the last twelve months. It has two effects. First, it is exactly the kind of interruption or challenge that damages a prescriptive claim and it puts the buyer on notice that access is disputed. Second, it takes the lack of access indemnity policy off the table: Sarsen's indication expressly excludes cover where a person claiming ownership has asserted rights in writing in the last twelve months. So the usual cheap fix is not available.

2.5 Options on access, in order of preference:

(a) Require the seller to obtain an express deed of grant of a right of way with and without vehicles, at all times and for all purposes, from whoever owns the strip, and to procure its registration against the servient title. This is the only outcome that gives a clean title and satisfies the lender. It requires the seller to negotiate with Mr Whitlock and will take time and probably money.

(b) Require the seller to obtain statutory declarations from persons with direct knowledge of user since 1968 and to apply to register a prescriptive easement. Slow, uncertain, and now contested.

(c) Buy with the defect uninsured and unresolved. In my view that is not acceptable. If Mr Whitlock gates the strip the client owns a workshop he cannot get a lorry to.

(d) Withdraw.

3. The retail covenant, covenant (2)

3.1 Covenant (2) prohibits use of the land or any building on it for the sale of goods by retail to members of the public. It is a restrictive covenant which was noted on the register in 1968 and is therefore protected against the buyer. The burden of a restrictive covenant runs in equity where the covenant is negative, was taken for the benefit of identified retained land, was intended to run, and is protected on the register. All of those are satisfied on the face of the entry, which names the Harrowfield Estate as the benefited land.

3.2 The practical question is who can enforce it now. Harrowfield Estates Limited may no longer exist and the estate may have been broken up among many owners. That uncertainty is why indemnity insurance is the standard answer, and Sarsen will insure a retail use of the existing building for 640 pounds. That cover would protect the client, and the lender, against a claim arising from selling finished pieces from the unit as the seller's brother did.

3.3 Two warnings the client must be given. First, the policy is conditional on nobody approaching a potential beneficiary. If we, the client or an agent write to any Harrowfield Estate owner to ask for a release, the insurance is lost and the price of a release goes up. So the choice between insurance and consent has to be made before anyone makes contact, and it cannot be made twice. Second, an application to the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) under section 84 of the Law of Property Act 1925 to discharge or modify the covenant is available in principle, on grounds including obsolescence and that the covenant impedes reasonable user, but it is slow, costs far more than the premium and cannot be done before exchange.

4. The building covenant, covenant (1), and the showroom

4.1 Covenant (1) prohibits erecting any building or structure other than those shown on the 1968 plan without prior written consent, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. The showroom is a new building on the yard. It is therefore prohibited unless consent is obtained from a successor to Harrowfield Estates, and we do not know who that is.

4.2 Sarsen will not insure this. Their indication is explicit: no cover for a proposed development where no planning permission has been obtained. That is not a negotiating position, it is how these policies work. So the showroom cannot be underwritten now.

4.3 Even leaving the covenant aside, the showroom is very unlikely to be permitted. The CON29 reply records that the property is in the Marlbrook Employment Area, that policy E3 permits light industrial Use Class E(g), and that retail Use Class E(a) is not permitted other than where ancillary to an existing lawful use on the same site. A customer showroom for a joinery business could conceivably be argued as ancillary, but a standalone retail showroom on the yard is contrary to policy on the face of the search. There is also no planning history since 1974, so there is no fallback lawful retail use to rely on.

4.4 The realistic advice is therefore that the showroom is not deliverable on this site in the foreseeable future, for three independent reasons: the covenant, the absence of insurance, and planning policy. The client should be told that plainly now, not after completion.

5. Advice to the client

5.1 The workshop use is fine. Unit 4 in the Employment Area is a permitted light industrial use and there is no covenant against it. That is the part of the client's plan that works.

5.2 Selling finished pieces to callers is a breach of covenant (2) but is insurable at 640 pounds. He should take the policy, and he must not contact anyone about the covenant.

5.3 The showroom should be treated as not achievable. If the showroom is the reason he is paying this price, he is paying for something he cannot have.

5.4 Access is the deal breaker. He should not exchange, and no responsible lender will lend, unless either an express right of way is granted and registered, or the Whitlock claim is withdrawn in writing and insurance becomes available. I would put that to the seller as a condition of proceeding.

5.5 On price, the client is right that there is room to renegotiate, and the covenant and access problems are real and documented. But he must understand that his own timetable is the weak point in his position. He has given notice on his existing workshop and it ends on 31 December 2026. He should not disclose that pressure to the other side. If a substitute is needed, a short term extension or storage arrangement is cheaper than buying a landlocked property.

6. Professional conduct

6.1 We act for the buyer and for Cranborne Building Society. The client has asked us to leave the building society out of it and sort the covenant and the access out afterwards. We cannot do that.

6.2 Both defects are plainly material to the lender: a property with no legal access and a covenant restricting use affects the value and the saleability of the lender's security. Under the lender's standard instructions and our duty to the lender as a client, we must report them. Failing to report while continuing to act would be misleading the lender by omission and would breach the duty not to mislead anyone we act for or a third party, and the duties of honesty and integrity.

6.3 There is also a conflict of interest question. The lender's interest is that the defects are reported and the retainer is delayed or the offer revised. The client's stated interest is that they are concealed so that the offer survives. If the client will not authorise disclosure to the lender, we have a conflict between two clients and we must stop acting for one or both, and we cannot disclose the client's confidential information to the lender without consent. That is why the client needs to be told now, in writing, that disclosure to Cranborne is not optional and that the alternative is that we cease to act.

6.4 I suggest we write to the client today confirming the position, and that we do not report to Cranborne until he has had the chance to consider it, but that we do not exchange in the meantime.

7. Next steps before exchange

(a) Written confirmation from the client authorising the report to Cranborne, and the report going out.

(b) Requisition to the seller: identify the owner of the access strip, produce the Whitlock correspondence, and either procure a deed of grant or procure a written withdrawal of the claim.

(c) Statutory declarations of user as a fallback, from persons with direct knowledge.

(d) Bind cover for the covenant (2) retail indemnity, with strict instructions to the client and to the agent that no approach is to be made to any Harrowfield beneficiary.

(e) Revised valuation and any renegotiation of price once the access position is known.

(f) Confirm the client's funding for the balance and the source of the July 2026 sale proceeds for our file, and check the Cranborne offer expiry date against the revised timetable.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client asks the firm to keep the lender out of the title problems and to sort them out after completion. The firm acts for both the buyer and Cranborne Building Society. The lack of legal access and the restrictive covenants are plainly material to the lender's security and must be reported under the lender's instructions and the duty owed to the lender as a client. A competent candidate identifies that concealing them would mislead the lender and breach the duties of honesty and integrity, that a conflict of interest arises between the two clients if the buyer refuses to authorise disclosure, and that the firm must advise the client in writing that disclosure is not optional and must cease to act for one or both clients if he refuses. A second, quieter point is the indemnity insurance condition: the candidate must warn that no approach may be made to any potential covenant beneficiary, and must not make one.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsPicks out the four facts that decide the case: the express no right of way note on the property register, the CON29 confirmation that the strip is not a highway, the Whitlock written claim in reply 12 read against the insurer's twelve month exclusion, and policy E3 read against the proposed showroom. Also spots that the seller owns no adjoining land, so she cannot grant a right herself.Summarises the documents without connecting the Whitlock letter to the insurance exclusion, or misses that the seller cannot grant the right of way because she has no interest in the strip.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsGives the client a straight answer on his actual business plan: the workshop works, occasional sales are insurable for a small premium, the showroom is not deliverable, and he must not exchange until access is resolved. Addresses the December workshop deadline and warns him not to reveal that pressure.Lists legal options without recommending one, or advises the client to proceed and deal with the access later because of his timetable.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured report to the partner with headed sections, one issue per section, a short summary at the front and a clear next steps list. Professional, unemotional, no padding.A narrative with no headings, or a letter addressed to the client rather than a report to the partner.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly states that the noted restrictive covenants bind the buyer, that the burden of a negative covenant runs in equity where it benefits identified retained land and is protected on the register, that there is no legal easement of access and that a prescriptive claim needs evidence of twenty years of user as of right, and that section 84 relief lies to the Upper Tribunal but is slow.Says the covenants are unenforceable because the original covenantee has disappeared, or asserts a prescriptive easement exists as a fact rather than as an evidential claim now under challenge.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with all three defects and with planning, gives the insurance answer and its limits for each, addresses the section 84 route, the express grant route and the statutory declaration route, and links each to what the lender will accept.Deals with the covenant and ignores the access, or ignores the planning policy so advises that the showroom is achievable if the covenant is released.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies without prompting that the firm acts for the lender too, that both defects are material and must be reported, that a conflict arises if the client refuses, and that the firm must advise in writing and cease acting if instructions to conceal are maintained. Also flags the no approach condition on the indemnity policy.Treats the client's request as a matter of preference and simply agrees to report later, or ignores the dual retainer entirely.

Examiner notes

The pass turns on three things: recognising that the lack of legal access is fatal on these facts because the Whitlock letter destroys the insurance route, that the showroom fails independently on covenant, insurance and planning policy, and that the lender must be told. The trap is treating indemnity insurance as a universal answer. Weak candidates recommend insuring everything without reading the Sarsen indication, which expressly excludes both the disputed access and the uninsured proposed development. A second trap is spending the hour reciting the register and the search rather than advising. A third is dealing with the client's request about the lender as a client care point rather than as a conflict and duty to the lender point.

Written station 14: Opposed section 25 notice on a restaurant lease and the negotiation with the landlord

Case and matter analysis  |  Property Practice  |  60 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

REPORT TO PARTNER

To: Marcus Ellery, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 12 February 2027

Matter: Raval, Harbourlight Bistro, 6 Corn Quay, Bristol

Subject: Security of tenure, the section 25 notice, the landlord's grounds and negotiation strategy

1. Summary

1.1 The client has security of tenure. The 2017 attempt to contract out of the Act was void, because a simple declaration was used when a statutory declaration was required.

1.2 The section 25 notice is invalid because it was given less than six months before the termination date it specifies.

1.3 Ground (f) is currently unsupported by the evidence the agent has himself disclosed, and ground (b) is weak.

1.4 The agent's offer of 25,000 pounds is about half the statutory compensation the client would receive if the landlord actually won on ground (f), and it is made on the false premise that she has no right to renew. It should be rejected.

1.5 The client has asked us to tell the agent that a court claim has already been issued. We cannot do that.

2. Does the tenancy have security of tenure

2.1 This is a tenancy of premises occupied by the tenant for the purposes of a business she carries on, so it is within Part II of the Act unless it was validly excluded.

2.2 The exclusion procedure in 2017 failed. The prescribed warning notice was served on 20 June 2017 and the lease was entered into on 25 June 2017, five days later. Because the notice was served less than fourteen days before the tenant entered into the tenancy, the tenant had to make a statutory declaration before an independent person authorised to administer oaths. She made a simple declaration instead, signed by herself alone with no jurat and no independent person. The requirement was not met, so the agreement to exclude sections 24 to 28 is void. Clause 1.4 of the lease has no effect.

2.3 The consequence is that the tenancy does not end on 24 June 2027 by effluxion of time. It continues under section 24 until brought to an end in accordance with the Act. The agent's assertion in the letter of 3 February that the client has no right to renew at all is wrong, and it is the foundation of his 25,000 pound offer.

2.4 We should keep the original 2017 documents safe. They are the client's best asset on this matter.

3. Is the section 25 notice valid

3.1 A section 25 notice has no effect unless it is given not more than twelve nor less than six months before the date of termination specified in it. This notice was served on 10 January 2027 and specifies 24 June 2027. That is five months and fourteen days. The notice is therefore invalid and of no effect.

3.2 It satisfies section 25(4), because the specified date is not earlier than the contractual expiry date, and it appears to be in the prescribed form and to state the grounds relied on. The defect is timing alone, but that is enough.

3.3 The practical effect is limited but useful. The landlord can serve a fresh, valid notice at any time. If a fresh notice were served at the end of February 2027 the earliest termination date it could specify would be about the end of August 2027, and the landlord would need to run the whole opposition process from there. So the defect buys the client roughly two months and, more importantly, tells us that the other side is not being careful.

3.4 We should not point the defect out yet. If we do, a valid notice will be served the same week. There is a judgment call here: the longer the client stays silent, the longer the tenancy runs on the contractual terms at 46,000 pounds, but she also cannot rely on an invalid notice to protect her if she later needs to bring matters to a head. My view is that we say nothing about the timing defect while we negotiate, and that we take the initiative on the process only if negotiation fails.

3.5 The alternative route is a tenant's request for a new tenancy under section 26. That is available where the tenancy was granted for a term of years certain exceeding one year, which this is. It would let the client set the timetable rather than wait. It is a double edged tool, because it commits her to a start date for a new tenancy and invites the landlord to state its grounds of opposition formally. I would keep it in reserve.

4. The landlord's grounds

4.1 Ground (f), demolition or reconstruction. The landlord must show a firm and settled intention, at the date of the hearing, to demolish or reconstruct the premises or a substantial part of them, and that it could not reasonably do so without obtaining possession. Intention has a subjective element, that the landlord genuinely means to do the work, and an objective element, that it has a reasonable prospect of being able to do it.

4.2 On the agent's own letter the objective element is not there yet. There is a pre-application enquiry only, no planning application, funding merely being discussed with the bank, and no board resolution. A company's intention normally requires a board resolution. The client's evidence supports the same conclusion: four years of talk, no site activity, and the neighbouring unit relet on a five year term last autumn, which is not what a landlord assembling a site for immediate reconstruction does.

4.3 The landlord may of course put all of this in place before any hearing, which is why this is a negotiating point rather than an answer. But today the ground is not made out and the agent has disclosed why.

4.4 Section 31A gives the client a second line of defence even if intention is established. If the client agrees to terms in the new tenancy giving the landlord access and facilities to carry out the works, and the works could be done without substantially interfering with her business, the court cannot hold that possession is needed. On a strip out and reconstruction of a whole building that argument is hard, and I would not expect it to succeed here. The section 31A(b) limb, a tenancy of an economically separable part, is also unpromising for a single restaurant unit over ground and basement. We should raise it but not rely on it.

4.5 Ground (b), persistent delay in paying rent. This is a discretionary ground and the court asks whether the tenant ought not to be granted a new tenancy in view of the delay. Six late payments over three years, averaging five weeks, is persistent. But the delays were concentrated in the pandemic period, there have been no arrears and no late payments since March 2024, and there are no arrears now. The court would also consider whether the landlord's position can be protected in the new lease, for example by a rent deposit or a guarantor. Standing alone, ground (b) on these facts is unlikely to defeat a renewal, and the landlord has not forfeited or complained at the time.

4.6 Grounds (b) and (f) are also different in one respect that matters to the client's money. Compensation under section 37 is payable only where the court is precluded from ordering a new tenancy by reason only of ground (e), (f) or (g). If the landlord were to succeed on ground (b) as well, no compensation would be payable at all. That is a real risk in the client's decision making and she must be told about it.

5. What the client would receive

5.1 Compensation on the figures supplied. The rateable value is 48,000 pounds and the multiplier is 1, because the client has occupied since 25 June 2017 and so will not have been in occupation for the whole of the fourteen years preceding termination. Compensation would therefore be 48,000 pounds, payable on quitting, if the landlord succeeded on ground (f) alone.

5.1A One qualification which changes the negotiating arithmetic. Compensation under section 37 is available on a no application basis only where the landlord's notice specifies solely ground (e), (f) or (g). This notice specifies ground (b) as well, so the client cannot simply quit on 24 June 2027 and claim 48,000 pounds. She would have to apply to the court and the landlord would have to be precluded by reason only of ground (f). The 48,000 pounds is therefore a contested outcome rather than a guaranteed floor, and it must be discounted for the ground (b) risk when we price the surrender. It is also a reason to watch what a fresh notice says: a landlord is confined at the hearing to the grounds specified in the notice it has served, so if the landlord serves again and drops ground (b) the no application compensation route reopens, and if it adds ground (g) we face a different case.

5.2 The agent's offer is 25,000 pounds. That is little more than half the statutory figure, it requires her to leave on 24 June 2027, and it is offered on the basis that she has no renewal right, which is wrong.

5.3 If she renews. Rent on a new tenancy is the open market rent for the holding under section 34, disregarding her own occupation and the goodwill of her business. The comparable at 58,000 pounds a year suggests the market has moved well above the passing rent of 46,000 pounds. She has told us she can pay up to about 54,000 pounds. So a renewal is worth having but it is not free, and the gap between 46,000 and the new rent is the real cost of staying.

5.4 Interim rent. If the tenancy continues under the Act while matters are resolved, either party may apply under section 24A for an interim rent. On a rising market the landlord will want one, and it can be backdated to the earliest date that could have been specified in the notice or request. The client should budget for the rent rising before any new lease starts.

6. Deadlines and immediate steps

6.1 On the notice as served, the client's application to court for a new tenancy could not be made after 24 June 2027, unless the parties agree in writing before that date to extend the period. Because the notice is invalid, no such deadline is in fact running, but we must not manage the file on that assumption. If we are wrong about the timing defect, missing that date destroys the client's right to renew altogether.

6.2 I recommend we diarise 24 June 2027 as a hard deadline, work to a date well before it, and seek a written extension agreement from the landlord's solicitors as a matter of routine as soon as negotiations begin. Any extension must be in writing and agreed before the current date expires, and each further extension must be agreed before the previous one runs out.

6.3 The agent's offer is stated to be open for fourteen days, so to 17 February 2027. We should reply within that period, without accepting.

7. Negotiation strategy

7.1 Objective. The client's first choice is to stay. Her fallback is to leave for a sum that properly reflects what she is giving up. Both outcomes are available, so we negotiate from a genuine choice, which is the strongest position there is.

7.2 Our leverage. The exclusion is void, so she has renewal rights. The notice is invalid, although we do not say so yet. Ground (f) is not currently made out on the agent's own account. The landlord has no planning permission, no funding and no board resolution, and a contested renewal would take many months and cost the landlord more than the difference between the parties.

7.3 Their leverage. Time is on the landlord's side in one respect, because it can cure the defects, obtain permission and resolve on the scheme. Ground (b) exists and, if run successfully alongside ground (f), would remove the compensation entitlement. Interim rent will rise.

7.4 Opening position. Reply before 17 February. Reject 25,000 pounds. Say plainly that the tenancy is not contracted out, without at this stage setting out the detailed reasons, and that our client is entitled to a new tenancy. Propose a new fifteen year lease with a break, or a ten year lease, at a rent to be agreed. Invite the landlord, if it genuinely intends to redevelop, to evidence the scheme.

7.5 The two settlement shapes worth pursuing.

(a) Stay. A new lease at up to 54,000 pounds a year, with a landlord's redevelopment break exercisable on not less than twelve months' notice after year five, and an agreement that if the break is exercised the landlord pays a sum equal to statutory compensation. That gives the landlord the flexibility it says it wants and gives the client the certainty she needs to invest.

(b) Go. A surrender on a date the client chooses within a stated window, for a payment of not less than 48,000 pounds, subject to the qualification at 5.1A that the 48,000 pounds is a contested outcome rather than a walk away entitlement and must be discounted for the ground (b) risk, plus a contribution to relocation and fitting out costs, plus release from dilapidations and from any claim for arrears or interest. My opening figure would be 95,000 pounds inclusive, on the basis that she is giving up a profitable business location and a right to renew. I would expect to settle in the region of 60,000 to 70,000 pounds plus a dilapidations release and a rent free period to the departure date.

7.6 Tactics. Keep both options live for as long as possible. Do not disclose that she would consider leaving until the landlord has moved off 25,000 pounds. Do not disclose the 54,000 pound ceiling. Do not disclose the notice defect. Mark the correspondence without prejudice where it contains offers, and keep the without prejudice negotiation separate from the open correspondence on procedure and any extension agreement. Get any extension of the section 29A period recorded in open correspondence, not in a without prejudice letter.

8. Professional conduct

8.1 The client has asked us to tell the agent that a claim for a new tenancy has already been issued, when it has not. We cannot do that and neither can she with our knowledge. A solicitor must not mislead or attempt to mislead another party, whether by act or omission, and must act with honesty and integrity. That a claim may be issued later does not make a statement that it has been issued true today. It would also be a false statement made to obtain a negotiating advantage, so it goes to the heart of the duty.

8.2 I recommend that we tell the client this at once, in writing, and explain the practical point as well as the principle. If the agent asked for the claim number, or checked, the client's credibility on everything else, including her account of the 2017 signing, would be destroyed at the moment it matters most. Her real position is much stronger than the bluff she wants to run.

8.3 If the client insists that we make that statement, we must decline to act on that instruction, and if she maintains it we would have to consider ceasing to act on the matter.

8.4 Two smaller points. The 3 February letter is expressed to be without prejudice as to the offer, so we must handle it accordingly. And we should confirm that no one else occupies or shares the premises, given clause 3.9, because occupation by the tenant for the purposes of her business is the foundation of her protection.

9. Next steps

(a) Confirm to the client in writing that we cannot say a claim has been issued, and why.

(b) Reply to the agent by 17 February rejecting 25,000 pounds and asserting the renewal right, without revealing the notice defect.

(c) Secure a written extension of the section 29A period as soon as negotiations begin, and diarise 24 June 2027 as a hard stop.

(d) Obtain a formal valuation of the open market rent for the holding and a relocation and fitting out cost estimate, so the two settlement shapes can be priced.

(e) Preserve the 2017 documents and take a full statement from the client about the signing.

(f) Advise on interim rent exposure and on the compensation risk if ground (b) is also run.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client instructs the solicitor to tell the landlord's agent that a court claim for a new tenancy has already been issued when it has not, on the basis that it will be issued eventually so the statement is not really untrue. That is a false statement made to gain a negotiating advantage. A competent candidate refuses, explains to the client that a solicitor must not mislead another party by act or omission and must act with honesty and integrity, confirms the refusal in writing, points out that the bluff would destroy her credibility on the far stronger true points in her favour, and makes clear that if the instruction is maintained the firm must decline to act on it and consider ceasing to act. A secondary point of judgment, not of misconduct, is the decision to say nothing about the invalidity of the section 25 notice: staying silent about a defect in the other side's own document is legitimate, while asserting a fact that is untrue is not, and the strongest answers draw that line explicitly.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsExtracts the decisive facts from the documents rather than the narrative: the 20 June notice against the 25 June lease date, the simple declaration with no jurat and no independent person, the 10 January service date against the 24 June termination date, and the agent's own admissions of no planning application, no funding and no board resolution. Also picks up the continuous occupation since 2017, the rent history and the 58,000 pound comparable.Accepts the agent's assertion that the tenancy is contracted out, or reads the notice for its grounds without checking the dates on its face.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsGives the client a real choice between staying and going, prices both, tells her what she loses if ground (b) succeeds alongside ground (f), and warns her about interim rent. Advice is aimed at a restaurant owner with eleven staff and a build up of goodwill, not at an abstract tenant.Advises on the law without telling the client whether to accept the offer, or recommends acceptance of 25,000 pounds without comparing it to the 48,000 pound statutory figure.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured report with the conclusions at the front, the negotiation strategy set out as positions and figures the partner can act on, and a clean separation between what may be said openly and what must not be said.Runs the analysis and the negotiation together so that no clear opening or settlement position emerges, or writes to the client instead of reporting to the partner.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly applies the contracting out requirements, section 25(2), the two elements of intention under ground (f), section 31A, the discretionary nature of ground (b), section 34 rent, section 24A interim rent, and section 37 compensation including the reason it is lost if the landlord also succeeds on ground (b). Compensation correctly calculated at 48,000 pounds using the supplied multiplier.Says the notice is valid, applies the fourteen year multiplier of 2 to a tenant in occupation since 2017, or treats ground (b) as mandatory.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers security of tenure, notice validity, both grounds, section 31A, compensation, rent and interim rent, the section 29A deadline and extension mechanics, the section 26 request as a reserve option, and the negotiation, without leaving any of the partner's six questions unanswered.Answers on the grounds of opposition only and omits the deadline, the compensation figure or the negotiation strategy the partner expressly asked for.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies unprompted that the client's proposed statement about issued proceedings is a lie the firm cannot tell or permit, resolves it with a written explanation to the client and a refusal to act on the instruction, and distinguishes that from the legitimate decision not to volunteer the notice defect.Agrees to make the statement, treats it as a tactical question, or refuses without explaining the distinction between silence and misrepresentation.

Examiner notes

Two findings decide this station and both sit in the documents rather than in the client's account: the 2017 exclusion is void because a simple declaration was used where the notice was served only five days before the lease, and the section 25 notice is invalid because it gives five months and fourteen days rather than the minimum six months. Candidates who miss the contracting out point advise a client who has no rights at all and will accept the 25,000 pounds. On the negotiation, a pass needs concrete numbers and a reason for them, anchored on the 48,000 pound compensation figure supplied and the 58,000 pound comparable, not a general statement that the offer is too low. The commonest traps are asserting that the client will certainly defeat ground (f) rather than that it is not made out on today's evidence, forgetting that success on ground (b) as well as ground (f) would extinguish the compensation entitlement, and forgetting the section 29A deadline and the need for any extension to be agreed in writing before it expires. Candidates are given the rateable value and multiplier and are expected to apply them, not to recall them.

Written station 15: Additional provisions in a transfer of part: easements, reservations and covenants

Legal drafting  |  Property Practice  |  45 minutes

Model answer

TRANSFER OF PART OF REGISTERED TITLE, TITLE NUMBER NYK611204

PANEL 11, ADDITIONAL PROVISIONS

1. DEFINITIONS

1.1 "the Property" means the land transferred by this transfer, being Plot 2 shown edged red on the Plan.

1.2 "the Retained Land" means the land registered under title number NYK611204 remaining vested in the Transferor immediately after this transfer, and any part of it.

1.3 "the Plan" means the plan annexed to this transfer.

1.4 "the Track" means the roadway shown coloured brown on the Plan leading from the public highway at Nether Stowey Road to and past the Property and on to the farmyard.

1.5 "Conduits" means all pipes, drains, sewers, wires, cables, channels and other conducting media and any ancillary apparatus, whether now existing or laid or installed at any time after the date of this transfer.

1.6 "the Septic Tank" means the septic tank and associated soakaway, pipework and apparatus situated in the top field forming part of the Retained Land and shown coloured green on the Plan.

1.7 "the Shared Facilities" means the Track, the Septic Tank and the Conduits serving both the Property and the Retained Land.

1.8 "Fair Proportion" means a fair and reasonable proportion of the cost, according to the extent of the use made by the Property, of maintaining, repairing, cleansing, emptying, renewing and replacing the relevant Shared Facility, such proportion to be determined by the Transferor acting reasonably and certified in writing, and in default of agreement by an independent chartered surveyor appointed on the application of either party by the President for the time being of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, who shall act as an expert and whose decision shall be final and binding save in the case of manifest error, and whose fees shall be borne by the parties equally.

2. RIGHTS GRANTED

2.1 The Transferor transfers the Property with full title guarantee and grants to the Transferee, for the benefit of the Property and each and every part of it, the rights set out in Schedule 1.

3. RIGHTS EXCEPTED AND RESERVED

3.1 There are excepted and reserved out of the Property, for the benefit of the Retained Land and each and every part of it, the rights set out in Schedule 2.

4. COVENANTS BY THE TRANSFEREE

4.1 The Transferee covenants with the Transferor, for the benefit of the Retained Land and each and every part of it and with the intention of binding the Property and each and every part of it into whosoever hands it may come, to observe and perform the covenants set out in Schedule 3.

5. INDEMNITY COVENANT

5.1 The Transferee covenants with the Transferor to observe and perform the restrictive covenants contained in the Conveyance dated 3 September 1998 and referred to in entry number 1 of the charges register of title number NYK611204, so far as they relate to the Property, still subsist and are capable of being enforced, and to indemnify the Transferor against all actions, claims, demands, costs and liability arising from any breach of them after the date of this transfer.

6. DECLARATIONS

6.1 The Property does not have and shall not acquire any right of light or air or any other easement which would restrict or interfere with the free use of the Retained Land for building, rebuilding, alteration or any other purpose, and the Transferee shall not be entitled to object to any development of the Retained Land on the ground of interference with light, air, outlook, privacy or amenity.

6.2 Section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 does not apply to this transfer. The only rights granted to the Transferee are those expressly granted by clause 2 and Schedule 1, and no further rights pass by implication, whether under the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows or otherwise.

6.3 Nothing in this transfer creates any easement or right in favour of the Property over the Retained Land other than as expressly granted.

7. DEED OF COVENANT AND RESTRICTION

7.1 The Transferee covenants with the Transferor not to transfer or grant a lease of the whole of the Property without first procuring that the transferee or lessee enters into a deed of covenant with the Transferor in favour of the Retained Land in the same terms as clause 4, Schedule 3 and this clause 7, including this covenant.

7.2 The Transferee applies to the Chief Land Registrar to enter the following restriction against the title to the Property:

"No disposition of the registered estate, other than a charge, by the proprietor of the registered estate is to be registered without a certificate signed by a conveyancer that the provisions of clause 7.1 of a transfer dated [ ] made between (1) Halbrook Farms Limited and (2) Wren and Copse Developments Limited have been complied with."

8. NOTICES AND MISCELLANEOUS

8.1 Any notice or approval required under this transfer shall be in writing and shall be validly given if delivered to, or sent by first class post to, the party's registered office or last known address.

8.2 The Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 does not apply to this transfer, and no person other than a party to it and their respective successors in title to the Property and the Retained Land may enforce any of its terms.

SCHEDULE 1

RIGHTS GRANTED TO THE TRANSFEREE

1. A right of way at all times and for all purposes, with or without vehicles, over the Track, to and from the public highway at Nether Stowey Road, but not so as to obstruct the Track and not including any right to park on it or to stop on it other than for so long as is reasonably necessary for loading and unloading.

2. The right to the free and uninterrupted passage and running of water, soil, gas, electricity, telecommunications and other services to and from the Property through the Conduits now serving the Property and laid in, on, over or under the Retained Land.

3. The right to drain foul water and effluent from the Property into and through the Septic Tank, together with the right to use it in common with the Transferor and all others entitled.

4. The right, on not less than seven days' written notice except in an emergency, to enter such parts of the Retained Land as are reasonably necessary to inspect, clean, repair, maintain, renew, replace and connect into the Conduits and the Septic Tank, the person exercising the right causing as little damage and inconvenience as reasonably practicable and making good all damage caused to the reasonable satisfaction of the Transferor as soon as reasonably practicable.

5. The right to enter the Retained Land on reasonable prior written notice, except in an emergency, so far as is reasonably necessary to construct, erect, inspect, repair, maintain, renew and paint the boundary fence referred to in paragraph 2 of Schedule 3 and any building on the Property that cannot conveniently be dealt with from the Property, subject to the same conditions as to damage and making good.

6. The right to connect into the Conduits and the Septic Tank at such points as the Transferor may reasonably approve, that approval not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed.

SCHEDULE 2

RIGHTS EXCEPTED AND RESERVED TO THE TRANSFEROR

1. The right of way at all times and for all purposes, with or without vehicles and with or without agricultural machinery and livestock, over any part of the Track that forms part of the Property, and the right for the Transferor and all others authorised by it to continue to use the Track without interruption by the Transferee.

2. The free and uninterrupted passage and running of water, soil, gas, electricity, telecommunications and other services through any Conduits now or at any time after the date of this transfer laid in, on, over or under the Property and serving the Retained Land.

3. The right, on not less than seven days' written notice except in an emergency, to enter the Property to inspect, clean, repair, maintain, renew, replace and lay Conduits serving the Retained Land, causing as little damage and inconvenience as reasonably practicable and making good all damage caused as soon as reasonably practicable.

4. The right of support and shelter for the Retained Land and any building now or later on it from the Property and any building now or later on it.

5. The full and free right to develop, build on, rebuild, alter and use the Retained Land in any manner, and to obtain and implement any planning permission for it, notwithstanding that this may interfere with the light, air, outlook, privacy or amenity enjoyed by the Property or any building on it.

SCHEDULE 3

COVENANTS BY THE TRANSFEREE

1. Not to use the Property otherwise than as a single private dwelling with a garden, and in particular not to carry on any trade, business or profession on it, not to station or keep any caravan, mobile home or other temporary structure on it, and not to erect or permit more than one dwelling on it.

2. Within three months of the date of this transfer to erect, and thereafter to maintain in good and stock proof condition, a stock proof fence not less than 1.2 metres high along the boundary between the Property and the Retained Land marked with a T mark inwards on the Plan.

3. Not to erect any building or structure on the Property, and not to make any external alteration or extension to any building on the Property, until plans, elevations and specifications of it have been submitted to and approved in writing by the Transferor, such approval not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed, and thereafter to build only in accordance with the approved plans.

4. To pay to the Transferor on demand the Fair Proportion of the cost of maintaining, repairing, cleansing, emptying, renewing and replacing the Track, the Septic Tank and the Conduits serving both the Property and the Retained Land, within 21 days of receipt of a written demand accompanied by a certificate of the amount and copies of the relevant invoices.

5. To use the Track and the Septic Tank reasonably and not to do anything that damages them or interferes with their use by the Transferor or any other person entitled to use them, and not to discharge into the Septic Tank anything other than ordinary domestic foul drainage from the single dwelling permitted by paragraph 1.

6. To indemnify the Transferor against all liability arising from any breach of the covenants in this Schedule.

NOTE TO PARTNER

1. The reply to enquiry 6 that went out on 29 September is wrong. The septic tank is on the retained land, as the client confirmed on 7 October. The client has asked that the reply be left as it stands, that the drainage right be left out of the transfer, and that we say nothing about the water pipe, so that the buyer has to buy a right to drain from him in a few years.

2. I have not drafted the transfer that way, and I do not think we can. Leaving an incorrect reply uncorrected once we know it is wrong, and then drafting a transfer designed to take advantage of that error, would mislead the buyer's solicitors. We cannot mislead another party or their adviser by act or by omission, and we cannot take unfair advantage of them. The instruction also asks us to withhold information about the water pipe that we now know matters to a reply already given.

3. Please would you speak to the client. He needs to be told that the reply must be corrected in writing to Trant and Fell before exchange, and that the drainage and services rights must appear in the transfer, which is where the heads of terms at paragraph 5 already put them. If he will not agree, we should not send this draft out and we shall have to consider whether we can continue to act.

4. Two smaller points for the same conversation. The client says he may sell the paddock behind Plot 2 for housing in a few years, so the reservations in Schedule 2 and the declaration at clause 6.1 are deliberately wide and he should understand that the buyer's solicitors will push back on them. And the covenants in Schedule 3, paragraphs 2 to 5, are positive, so they do not by themselves bind a future owner of Plot 2. Clause 7 and the restriction are what carry them forward, and the client should know that they are not negotiable if he wants the fencing and the contributions to survive a resale.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client's email of 7 October reveals that a reply to enquiry 6 already given to the buyer's solicitors is false: the septic tank is on the retained land, not off it. The client instructs the firm to leave the reply uncorrected, to omit the drainage and services rights from the transfer, and to say nothing about the water pipe, so that the buyer must pay for a right to drain in the future. A competent candidate refuses to draft the transfer on that basis, drafts the drainage and services easements in, and tells the partner that the incorrect reply must be corrected in writing before exchange. The point is that a solicitor must not mislead another party or their representative by act or omission and must not take unfair advantage of them, and that a false reply which we know to be false cannot simply be left to stand. If the client refuses to correct it, the firm must not send out the draft and must consider ceasing to act. The candidate must resolve this inside the document by including the rights, not merely by mentioning it.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsDefined terms are set up once and used consistently, each right and covenant is a single self contained obligation in plain language, qualifications such as notice periods, making good and reasonableness are expressed precisely, and no precedent placeholder, square bracket or inapplicable wording survives.Copies the precedent with square brackets or blanks left in, uses undefined expressions such as the track or the tank, or writes long compound clauses in which the obligation cannot be identified.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsBody clauses for definitions, grant, reservation, covenants, indemnity, declarations and the deed of covenant machinery, with the detailed rights and covenants moved into numbered schedules and cross referred correctly. Logical order, consistent numbering, easy for the buyer's solicitor to mark up.Runs everything together as an undifferentiated list, or scatters rights, reservations and covenants so that it is unclear which party owes what to whom.
