Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawGrants and reservations are correctly directed, expressed for the benefit of the Property or the Retained Land and each part of it, the restrictive covenants are drafted so as to be capable of binding successors, the indemnity covenant matches the 1998 entry, and the declarations exclude rights of light and air and disapply section 62 and implied grant.Reserves rights in favour of the buyer or grants rights over the property to the buyer, omits the annexation wording so the covenants benefit no identified land, or purports to make the positive covenants run with the land as drafted.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers every right the plot actually needs, including the right of way, services, foul drainage to the septic tank, connection and rights of entry to repair, every reservation the client needs including services, support and the right to develop, all four heads of covenant in the heads of terms, the contribution machinery with a determination mechanism, and the restriction that keeps the positive covenants alive.Omits the drainage or services rights, omits the reservation of services through Plot 2, omits any mechanism for determining the fair proportion, or imposes positive covenants with no deed of covenant clause and no restriction.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIncludes the drainage and services rights notwithstanding the client's instruction, and tells the partner that the reply to enquiry 6 is false, must be corrected in writing before exchange, and that the firm cannot send the draft out or continue to act if the client refuses.Follows the instruction and leaves the drainage right out, or includes it silently without alerting the partner to the false reply that has already gone to the buyer's solicitors.

Examiner notes

The station separates candidates on two axes. First, completeness of the grant: a transfer of part is failed by omitting the drainage easement, the services easement, the rights of entry to repair, the reservation of services through the plot, or the exclusion of section 62 and Wheeldon v Burrows, any of which leaves a client exposed. Second, the positive covenant problem: the fencing covenant and the contribution to the track and septic tank costs are positive obligations, and a candidate who imposes them without a covenant not to dispose without a deed of covenant and a supporting restriction has drafted covenants that die on the first resale. The main trap is the ethics instruction. A candidate who follows the client's instruction and omits the drainage right has drafted a document that both fails the client's own heads of terms at paragraph 5 and takes advantage of a false reply. A candidate who includes the right but never tells the partner about the incorrect reply has done half the job. Structure matters here: clauses in the body, rights and covenants in schedules, defined terms used consistently, and no square brackets or unadapted precedent wording left in.

Written station 16: Repairing and alienation covenants in a new commercial lease

Legal drafting  |  Property Practice  |  45 minutes

Model answer

ADDITIONAL DEFINITION (for insertion into clause 1 of the lease)

"Schedule of Condition" means the schedule of condition comprising a written report and photographs prepared by Bettridge Frayne, chartered building surveyors, dated 20 January 2027, a signed copy of which is annexed to this lease.

"Group Company" means, in relation to the Tenant, a company which is a subsidiary of the Tenant, a holding company of the Tenant or a subsidiary of such a holding company, within the meaning of section 1159 of the Companies Act 2006, for so long as that relationship subsists.

4.5 REPAIR, DECORATION AND YIELDING UP

4.5.1 The Tenant must keep the Premises in good and substantial repair and condition and, where necessary for that purpose, must renew or replace any part of the Premises.

4.5.2 The Tenant is not obliged by clause 4.5.1 or by any other provision of this lease to put or to keep the Premises, or any part of them, in any better state of repair, decoration or condition than that evidenced by the Schedule of Condition. Where there is any inconsistency between the Schedule of Condition and clause 4.5.1, the Schedule of Condition prevails.

4.5.3 The Tenant is not liable to repair or reinstate damage caused by an Insured Risk, except where the insurance money is irrecoverable in whole or in part because of an act or default of the Tenant or of anyone at the Premises with the Tenant's authority.

4.5.4 The Tenant must in the last year of the Term (however it ends) redecorate the inside of the Premises in a good and workmanlike manner with materials of good quality and in colours no less suitable than those existing at the date of this lease. The Tenant has no obligation to decorate the outside of the Premises.

4.5.5 The Tenant must keep the Premises clean and tidy and must not allow refuse to accumulate at the Premises.

4.5.6 At the end of the Term (however it ends) the Tenant must yield up the Premises to the Landlord with vacant possession, repaired and decorated in accordance with the Tenant's covenants in this lease, subject in every case to clause 4.5.2, and must remove all its fixtures, fittings, signs, goods and equipment and make good all damage caused by their removal.

4.5.7 Nothing in clause 4.5.6 obliges the Tenant to remove any alteration or addition which the Landlord approved in writing, unless the Landlord's approval was given subject to a condition requiring its removal.

4.12 ALIENATION

Prohibited dealings

4.12.1 The Tenant must not assign, underlet, charge, part with possession of, or share the occupation of, part only of the Premises.

4.12.2 The Tenant must not charge or mortgage the whole of the Premises.

4.12.3 The Tenant must not hold the Premises or any part of them on trust for another person, and must not part with possession of or share occupation of the Premises except as expressly permitted by this clause 4.12.

Assignment of the whole

4.12.4 The Tenant may assign the whole of the Premises with the prior written consent of the Landlord, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed.

4.12.5 For the purposes of section 19(1A) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1927, the Landlord and the Tenant agree that the Landlord may withhold its consent to an assignment of the whole of the Premises if any of the following circumstances exists at the date of the Tenant's application for consent or at the date of the proposed assignment:

(a) any sum due under this lease is outstanding, whether or not formally demanded;

(b) there is a subsisting breach of any tenant covenant in this lease which the Landlord has notified to the Tenant in writing;

(c) the proposed assignee is a person who is entitled to claim diplomatic, state or sovereign immunity;

(d) the proposed assignee is a Group Company of the Tenant and, in the Landlord's reasonable opinion, is of lesser financial standing than the Tenant.

4.12.6 For the purposes of section 19(1A) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1927, the Landlord and the Tenant agree that the Landlord may grant consent to an assignment of the whole of the Premises subject to all or any of the following conditions:

(a) that the Tenant enters into an authorised guarantee agreement with the Landlord, in a form which conforms with section 16 of the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 and is otherwise reasonable, guaranteeing the performance by the assignee of the tenant covenants of this lease for so long as the assignee remains bound by them;

(b) that the assignee covenants directly with the Landlord to observe and perform the tenant covenants of this lease from the date of the assignment until it is released by the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995;

(c) that, where the Landlord reasonably requires it having regard to the financial standing of the assignee, a guarantor reasonably acceptable to the Landlord enters into a guarantee of the assignee's obligations in a form reasonably required by the Landlord, or the assignee pays a rent deposit of not more than an amount equal to six months' Rent plus VAT on the Landlord's standard terms;

(d) that any sum then due under this lease is paid on or before completion of the assignment.

4.12.7 Nothing in clauses 4.12.5 and 4.12.6 prevents the Landlord from withholding consent on any other ground on which it is reasonable to do so, or from granting consent subject to any other condition which it is reasonable to impose, and nothing in this clause 4.12 limits the Landlord's duties under section 1 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988.

4.12.8 No condition may be imposed which would require the Tenant to guarantee the performance of the tenant covenants by any person other than its immediate assignee.

Underletting of the whole

4.12.9 The Tenant may underlet the whole of the Premises with the prior written consent of the Landlord, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed, and only where all the following requirements are met:

(a) the underlease is granted without taking any fine or premium and at a rent which is not less than the open market rent of the Premises at the date of grant, payable in advance on the same days as the Rent;

(b) the underlease reserves no rent review, or reserves reviews on the same dates and on substantially the same basis as this lease;

(c) before the underlease is granted the parties to it have completed the notice and declaration procedure under section 38A(3) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 and the underlease is expressed to exclude sections 24 to 28 of that Act;

(d) the underlease contains covenants by the undertenant in substantially the same terms as clauses 4.5 and 4.12 of this lease, and prohibits any further underletting;

(e) before the underlease is granted the undertenant covenants directly with the Landlord to observe and perform the tenant covenants of the underlease and the tenant covenants of this lease, other than the covenant to pay the Rent, for the duration of the underlease.

4.12.10 The Tenant must enforce the covenants in any underlease and must not, without the Landlord's prior written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed), vary the terms of any underlease, accept a surrender of it, or waive any breach of it.

Sharing with a Group Company

4.12.11 The Tenant may share occupation of the whole or any part of the Premises with a Group Company, provided that:

(a) no relationship of landlord and tenant is created between the Tenant and that Group Company and the sharing does not confer on it any right to exclusive possession or any right to remain after it ceases to be a Group Company;

(b) the Tenant gives the Landlord written notice of the name and registered number of the Group Company within ten working days of the sharing beginning, and written notice within ten working days of it ending;

(c) the sharing ends immediately on the company ceasing to be a Group Company or on the end of the Term, whichever is earlier.

Registration

4.12.12 Within one month after any assignment, underletting or other devolution of this lease or of any underlease, the Tenant must give the Landlord's solicitors written notice of it, supply a certified copy of the relevant document and pay a registration fee of 75 pounds plus VAT.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client's email asks the firm to draft the repairing covenant in unqualified full repairing form even though the heads of terms agreed a limit by reference to the schedule of condition, on the express footing that the tenant has no solicitor, will not spot the difference, and is not to have it pointed out. Acting on that instruction would take unfair advantage of an unrepresented party and would be complicity in the client's attempt to mislead the tenant. A candidate must draft the repairing covenant in accordance with the agreed heads of terms, with the Schedule of Condition operating as a genuine cap and expressed to prevail over the general repairing obligation, and must not disguise the position by drafting so as to leave the point obscure. The candidate cannot simply refuse and do nothing either: the client is entitled to be told, outside this document, that the firm cannot draft what has been asked for and why, and to be told that it is open to the client to reopen the point openly with the tenant.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsEvery obligation is expressed as a single, testable requirement. Conditions on consent are listed as lettered sub paragraphs rather than run together. Terms such as Schedule of Condition and Group Company are defined and then used exactly.Consent conditions written as one long sentence, use of woolly wording such as the Landlord may impose reasonable conditions with nothing specified, or the phrase reasonable state of repair which sets no measurable standard.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsClause 4.5 runs repair, then the schedule of condition limit, then insured risks, then decoration, then yielding up. Clause 4.12 separates absolute prohibitions, assignment of the whole, underletting of the whole, group sharing and registration under sub headings.A single undivided alienation clause in which the absolute and qualified prohibitions are mixed, so the reader cannot tell which dealings are barred outright and which need consent.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawThe repairing covenant is expressly limited by the Schedule of Condition with an overriding provision resolving inconsistency, damage by insured risks is carved out, and internal decoration only is imposed. The alienation clause uses section 19(1A) circumstances and conditions, an authorised guarantee agreement limited to the immediate assignee in line with section 16(4), contracted out underleases and direct covenants.A bare full repairing covenant with the schedule of condition merely mentioned, which does not limit the obligation. Or requiring the outgoing tenant to guarantee a subsequent assignee, which section 16(4) prevents, or an absolute bar on assignment of the whole contrary to the heads of terms.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawDeals with all five dealings named by the partner, adds registration of dealings, preserves the landlord's rights under section 1 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988, and covers yielding up, removal of fixtures and reinstatement of alterations.Silence on charging, on sharing with a group company or on part disposals, or an alienation clause that permits underletting without requiring the underlease to be contracted out or the undertenant to covenant directly.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDrafts the repairing covenant limited by the Schedule of Condition, as the heads of terms provide, and does not adopt the precedent's unqualified full repairing wording. Recognises that the client's instruction is to take unfair advantage of an unrepresented party and to mislead it, and that it cannot be followed.Following the client's instruction and drafting an unqualified full repairing covenant, or drafting the limited covenant but burying it so it reads as though the schedule is merely evidential. Either amounts to complicity in misleading the other party.

Examiner notes

The technical divide is the section 19(1A) mechanism. Strong candidates set out named circumstances in which consent may be withheld and named conditions on which it may be granted, and they keep the authorised guarantee agreement within section 16(4) by guaranteeing the immediate assignee only. Weak candidates write consent not to be unreasonably withheld and stop, which gives the client nothing beyond what section 19(1) already implies. The trap is the client's email. It is written in reasonable, commercial language and it appears to be an ordinary instruction about risk allocation. It is not. It asks the candidate to draft a document that departs from the agreed terms in order to catch out a party with no solicitor. Candidates who follow it lose the ethics criterion outright and usually lose legal correctness as well, because the drafted clause no longer reflects the bargain. Candidates who merely mention the schedule of condition in passing, without a clause stating that the tenant need not put the premises in any better condition and that the schedule prevails, have not actually limited anything.

Written station 17: Enforcing estate covenants against a successor in title

Legal research  |  Property Practice  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO PARTNER

To: Ngozi Farrant

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 14 October 2026

Matter: Caldwell, 18 Alder Rise, Kettersham. Meadowbank Estate covenants

1. Summary of advice

1.1 The covenant against carrying on a trade or business is a restrictive covenant. Its burden runs in equity and it is protected by an entry in the charges register of the title to number 12. Its benefit is annexed to Mrs Caldwell's plot. She can enforce it against Mr Vance and the grooming salon is a plain breach.

1.2 The covenant to pay one eighth of the road and drainage costs is positive. Its burden does not run with the freehold, so Mrs Caldwell has no direct claim against Mr Vance on the covenant itself. She does, however, have a good argument under the benefit and burden principle, because the same transfer that imposes the payment obligation grants Mr Vance the right of way and the right of drainage he uses every day. That is the route I would take.

1.3 There is a conduct problem in Mrs Caldwell's instructions which we cannot carry out. It is at paragraph 5 below.

2. The covenant against trade or business

2.1 The burden of a restrictive covenant runs in equity where the four conditions of the rule in Tulk v Moxhay (1848) 2 Ph 774, as that rule has since been settled, are met. Tulk itself decided that equity will restrain a purchaser who takes with notice; the requirement that the covenantee retain land capable of benefiting comes from London County Council v Allen [1914] 3 KB 642, and in registered land the protection requirement is now supplied by the Land Registration Act 2002. All four are met here.

(a) The covenant is negative in substance. Clause 4(a) requires the owner to refrain from using the property other than as a single private dwellinghouse and to refrain from carrying on a trade or business. No expenditure is needed to comply.

(b) It was taken to benefit land retained by the covenantee and it touches and concerns that land. In September 1998 Meadowbank Developments Limited still owned the remaining plots, including Plot 7, which it did not sell until June 1999. The covenant is expressed to be for the benefit of each other plot on the estate. This distinguishes London County Council v Allen [1914] 3 KB 642, where the covenantee held no land capable of benefiting.

(c) The parties intended the burden to run. Clause 4 says so in terms, and section 79(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925 would in any event deem the covenant to be made on behalf of the covenantor's successors in title in the absence of a contrary intention.

(d) The burden is protected. Number 12 is registered land. Entry 1 of the charges register, made on 30 September 1998, records the restrictive covenants in the 1998 transfer. Under section 29(1) and (2)(a)(i) of the Land Registration Act 2002 an interest which is the subject of a notice in the register retains its priority against a purchaser for valuable consideration. Mr Vance bought in March 2021 and took subject to it.

2.2 Mrs Caldwell must also show that the benefit has passed to her. It has, on two independent grounds. First, express annexation: clause 4 states that the covenant is given for the benefit of each and every other plot on the Meadowbank Estate and every part of it, and the estate is edged blue on the transfer plan. That satisfies the requirement in Crest Nicholson Residential (South) Ltd v McAllister [2004] EWCA Civ 410 that the benefited land be identified in, or easily ascertainable from, the instrument. Secondly, statutory annexation under section 78(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925 as construed in Federated Homes Ltd v Mill Lodge Properties Ltd [1980] 1 WLR 594. There is nothing in the transfer amounting to the contrary intention which defeated annexation in Roake v Chadha [1984] 1 WLR 40.

2.3 Breach. Running a dog grooming salon from the converted garage, with commercial vehicles and members of the public attending during the working day, is the carrying on of a trade or business and is a use other than as a single private dwellinghouse. Both limbs of clause 4(a) are broken.

2.4 Remedy. The primary remedy is a prohibitory injunction. It is equitable and therefore discretionary, and the court may award damages in substitution under section 50 of the Senior Courts Act 1981. Mrs Caldwell's position on discretion is good: she objected in writing in August 2022, within months of the salon opening, and again in January 2023, so there is no acquiescence and no material delay.

2.5 Risk to flag. Mr Vance can apply to the Upper Tribunal under section 84(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925 to discharge or modify the covenant. On these facts an application is unlikely to succeed. The estate remains wholly residential so the covenant is not obsolete under ground (a), and under grounds (aa) and (1A) the covenant plainly secures a practical benefit of substantial value to the neighbours in keeping commercial traffic off a private estate road. But an application would be slow and expensive, and Mrs Caldwell should be told that now rather than later.

3. The road and drainage contribution

3.1 Clause 4(c) is a positive covenant. It requires the owner of number 12 to put his hand in his pocket. The burden of a positive covenant does not run with freehold land: Austerberry v Oldham Corporation (1885) 29 Ch D 750, affirmed by the House of Lords in Rhone v Stephens [1994] 2 AC 310. Section 79 of the Law of Property Act 1925 does not change that. Lord Templeman held it to be a word saving provision which is concerned with who is deemed to covenant, not with making the burden run. So there is no claim against Mr Vance on clause 4(c) itself.

3.2 Suing the original covenantor is not a realistic answer. Mr Pryde remains liable in contract on his own covenant and the benefit of it will have passed to Mrs Caldwell at law under section 78 and Smith and Snipes Hall Farm Ltd v River Douglas Catchment Board [1949] 2 KB 500. But he sold in 2009 and any indemnity chain runs through the Hendrys. Pursuing a man who has had nothing to do with the estate for 17 years to recover 1,200 pounds is not proportionate and I would not advise it.

3.3 The better route is the benefit and burden principle. In Halsall v Brizell [1957] Ch 169 estate purchasers who used the estate roads and sewers were required to pay the corresponding contribution. Rhone v Stephens limited the principle, and Davies v Jones [2009] EWCA Civ 1164 restated the conditions, per Sir Andrew Morritt C at [27]: the benefit and the burden must be conferred in or by the same transaction, the enjoyment of the benefit must be conditional on or reciprocal to the burden, and the successor must have or have had the opportunity of rejecting or disclaiming the benefit, not merely the right to receive it.

3.4 Those conditions are satisfied here, and on the road and drainage head Thamesmead Town Ltd v Allotey (1998) 30 HLR 1052 is authority for the client rather than against her: the defendant there was held liable to contribute to the estate roads and sewers he had the right to use and did use, and escaped only on the landscaped and communal areas, over which his transfer gave him no rights at all. The obligation to contribute in clause 4(c) and the rights of way and drainage in clause 5 are in the same transfer, and each is directed at the same physical thing: the road coloured brown and the drain and pumping chamber coloured green. The payment is reciprocal to the rights, not a general estate charge. The facts are close to Wilkinson v Kerdene Ltd [2013] EWCA Civ 44, where chalet owners with express rights over estate roads and drainage were held liable to pay a fair proportion of the cost of maintaining them. Mr Vance uses the road as his only access and discharges into the shared chamber. He can renounce the rights, and if he did he would have no claim to use either, so the element of election is present.

3.5 The recoverable sum is a fair proportion of the cost actually and properly incurred, which on the figures is one eighth of the 9,600 pound resurfacing bill of May 2026, being 1,200 pounds, plus any drainage costs since 2023 on the same basis. We should ask Mrs Caldwell for the invoices before any letter goes out.

4. Sources I have not relied on

4.1 The Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 governs the transmission of covenants in leases. Both plots are freehold, so it has no application.

4.2 The Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 does not assist. By section 10(2) and (3) it does not apply to a contract entered into before 11 May 2000, and the transfer of Plot 4 is dated 22 September 1998.

4.3 Street v Mountford concerns the distinction between a lease and a licence and is irrelevant.

5. Conduct point for the meeting

5.1 We cannot send the letter Mrs Caldwell has asked for. She wants us to threaten to report Mr Vance to the police for tax fraud, and to tell his customers that he has a criminal conviction which she accepts he does not have, in order to make him give way in a private dispute about covenants. Making an allegation we know to be untrue would breach paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits misleading others, and Principle 5, which requires us to act with integrity. Threatening a criminal complaint and adverse publicity in order to extract payment in a civil matter is an abuse of our position under paragraph 1.2 and risks Mrs Caldwell herself committing a criminal offence.

5.2 The way through is to tell her plainly that we will not put those threats in a letter, and that we do not need to. Her case on the salon is strong and she has a real argument on the money. A firm letter before action setting out the covenant, the breach, the remedy sought and a short deadline, with a proper reference to the pre action protocol, will do more than a threat and will not expose her to a counterclaim. If she insists on the threats we cannot act on those instructions and would have to consider ceasing to act.

6. Next steps I suggest

6.1 Obtain the resurfacing and drainage invoices and the estate accounts since 2023.

6.2 Obtain copies of Mrs Caldwell's 2022 and 2023 letters and any reply.

6.3 Confirm from the filed transfer of Plot 7 that the covenants and the plan are in identical form.

6.4 Send a letter before action covering both the breach of clause 4(a) and the contribution on the benefit and burden basis, and canvass whether the other six owners will join in, which would strengthen the position and spread the cost.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client's email instructs the firm to threaten to report the neighbour to the police for tax fraud and to tell his customers he has a criminal conviction, which she accepts he does not have, in order to make him comply in a private covenant dispute. Making a statement known to be untrue breaches paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and Principle 5 (integrity), and using a threat of criminal proceedings and adverse publicity to gain a collateral advantage in a civil matter is an abuse of position under paragraph 1.2, in line with the SRA's warning notice on abusive and improper conduct in disputes. The candidate must refuse those instructions, tell the client plainly and in writing that the letter will not be sent in that form, warn her that the threat could expose her to criminal liability, and offer the legitimate alternative of a letter before action. If she insists, the firm must consider ceasing to act.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses Sources A to F, the 1998 transfer and the charges register entry, and pins each proposition to the right source. Expressly discards Sources G, H and I, and gives the reason in each case, in particular that the 1999 Act cannot apply to a 1998 transfer because of the commencement provision. Does not pad the note with material that does not bear on the two questions asked.Cites the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 or the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 as though it helped, or lists every source in the bundle without distinguishing the relevant from the irrelevant. Ignores the charges register entry, which is the document that makes the covenant bind Mr Vance.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers both of the partner's questions in the first paragraph, then supports them. Gives usable advice for a 9am meeting: the salon can be stopped, the money is recoverable by a different route, the section 84 application is the risk to warn about, and here is what to collect before writing to Mr Vance.Produces an accurate legal essay on covenants which never tells the partner what to say to the client, or which leaves the money question at 'the burden of a positive covenant does not run' without exploring any route to the same result.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA short headed note with numbered paragraphs, a summary at the top and next steps at the bottom. Authorities cited in full but without lengthy quotation. No research trail, no database narrative, no recitation of what the candidate searched for.Writes a research trail despite being told not to, or writes an undifferentiated block of prose in which the partner cannot find the answer to either question.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the Tulk v Moxhay conditions accurately and applies each to these facts, including that the developer still owned Plot 7 in September 1998. Correctly identifies clause 4(c) as positive and applies Rhone v Stephens, including that section 79 does not transmit the burden. Correctly identifies section 29 LRA 2002 as the reason the covenant binds a 2021 purchaser.Says section 79 of the Law of Property Act 1925 makes the burden run, which is exactly what Rhone v Stephens decided it does not do. Or treats the covenant as binding simply because Mr Vance 'had notice', without reference to the register.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with the burden and the benefit separately, gives both express and statutory annexation, addresses Roake v Chadha and Crest Nicholson, covers the remedy and its discretionary nature, flags the section 84 risk, and develops the benefit and burden argument through Halsall, Rhone, Thamesmead, Davies v Jones and Wilkinson v Kerdene, identifying the element of election as the point on which it turns.Establishes that the burden runs but never asks whether the benefit has passed to this claimant, so the answer is only half done. Or asserts Halsall v Brizell without the restrictions imposed by Rhone v Stephens, which is the very point a partner would test.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies unprompted that the instruction to threaten a police report and to publish a false allegation of a criminal conviction cannot be carried out, names the Principles and Code paragraphs engaged, warns that the client risks criminal liability herself, and offers the lawful alternative of a proper letter before action, with the consequence if she insists.Passes over the last two paragraphs of the client's email entirely, or notices the threat but simply says 'this would be unprofessional' without identifying the duty, the risk to the client or what to do instead.

Examiner notes

The station is built so that the two questions have opposite answers, and the pass turns on the candidate keeping them apart. The restrictive covenant is straightforward once the Tulk v Moxhay conditions and the charges register entry are married up. The contribution is the discriminator. A weak candidate stops at 'positive covenants do not run' and delivers nothing the partner can use. A marginal candidate mentions Halsall v Brizell but treats it as a free standing rule. A strong candidate applies the Rhone v Stephens and Davies v Jones conditions and shows why the express rights of way and drainage in clause 5 of the same transfer supply the link and the element of election, then quantifies the claim.

The commonest single error is asserting that section 79 of the Law of Property Act 1925 makes the burden of a positive covenant run. Source D states the opposite in terms, so this error also shows the candidate did not read the bundle.

The decoys are chosen to punish pattern matching. A candidate who sees 'covenants' and 'successors in title' and reaches for the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 has not noticed the land is freehold. A candidate who reaches for the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 has not read the commencement note printed at the foot of the same source.

Ethics is not signposted anywhere in the partner's email. It sits in the last two paragraphs of the client's own message and is easy to skim past when reading for the covenant facts.

Written station 18: Writing to a buyer client when exchange cannot proceed

Legal writing  |  Property Practice  |  30 minutes

Model answer

HALSTEAD VANE LLP

Solicitors

By email and by first class post

Ms Farrah Adeyinka

12b Ferrisgate Court

Leeds

Our ref: PAB/ADE/1044

18 November 2026

Dear Farrah

Your purchase of 14 Corriemore Gardens, Leeds

Thank you for your email this morning and for your calls. I am sorry you have found it hard to reach somebody. You have not done anything wrong in ringing us, and I would rather you rang than sat at home worrying.

I want to be straight with you about three things.

1. We will not be able to exchange contracts on Friday

We are not in a position to exchange contracts on 20 November. I know that is not what you wanted to hear and I am sorry.

I am not able to explain the reason to you. I know how unsatisfactory that sounds. There are situations in which the law does not allow a solicitor to give a client the reason for a delay, and this is one of them. You will remember that the letter you signed on 8 October said that this could happen. I cannot go further than that, and please do not think me rude if I say the same thing again when you ring.

I also cannot tell you when we will be able to move forward, because I do not know. As soon as I am able to tell you anything at all, I will telephone you the same day. You will not have to chase me.

2. What I need you to do now

Please do not agree a date for exchange or completion with the estate agent, with the seller or with anybody else. If they press you, please say that your solicitors are not yet able to confirm a date and ask them to speak to me. Do not let anyone push you into promising a date, because at the moment you cannot keep it.

Please do not send us any further money for the time being. The money you have already sent us is held in our client account and it is untouched.

Please do not make any further arrangement that depends on completing on 11 December. If you have already given notice on your room, speak to your landlord this week and ask whether it can be withdrawn or extended. If it cannot, please tell me, because you may need to make short term arrangements and it is better to know now.

3. About the mortgage

In your email of 16 November you asked us to tell Brightmoor Building Society that the 160,000 pounds is savings. I cannot do that. We act for the building society as well as for you, and neither you nor I can give them an account of your money which is not accurate. That is not me being difficult with you. Telling a lender something untrue in order to obtain a mortgage is a criminal offence, and I would be putting you at risk as well as myself if I did it. So please do not ask me again, and please do not say anything of that kind to the building society yourself.

4. If you are unhappy

You are entitled to complain and I will not take it personally. Our complaints procedure is in the letter you signed on 8 October. In the first instance please contact our Client Care Partner, Miss Delia Okonjo-Sturt, at this office. If you are still unhappy afterwards you may take the matter to the Legal Ombudsman. You are also free to instruct another firm if you wish; if you decide to do that, please speak to me first, because there are things I will need to deal with before any papers or money can be passed on.

I am sorry to be sending you a letter with so little in it. You can ring me on the direct line below at any time and I will take your call.

Yours sincerely

Trainee Solicitor

for Halstead Vane LLP

Direct line 0113 496 0212

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The firm has made an authorised disclosure to the National Crime Agency and is in the notice period. Telling the client why the transaction cannot proceed, or that a report has been made, would be tipping off contrary to section 333A of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, and exchanging or applying the funds without a defence would risk offences under sections 327 and 328. That collides with the ordinary duty to keep a client informed and to explain matters in a way the client can understand. The correct resolution is that the criminal prohibition prevails: the solicitor writes to the client, says clearly that the firm cannot exchange and cannot say why, gives no timescale, invents no substitute explanation, does not return the funds and does not report the source of funds to the lender pending the reporting officer's decision. The client's separate instruction to describe the money to Brightmoor Building Society as savings must be refused outright, because the firm also acts for the lender and must not mislead it, and the client must be warned not to say it herself.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsCovers everything the client actually needs: no exchange on Friday, no reason can be given, no date can be given, do not commit to a date with the agent, send no more money, the money already sent is safe in client account, do not act on the notice given on her room, and the refusal to describe the funds as savings to the lender. Includes the complaints route because she has raised it.Writes a letter which says only 'we cannot exchange on Friday' and leaves out the practical instructions, so the client goes on to agree a completion date with the estate agent the same afternoon. Or omits the savings point, which is the one thing in the file that could expose the client to a criminal charge.
Use a logical structure.SkillsShort numbered sections, worst news first, then what she must do, then the mortgage point, then complaints. Each paragraph does one job. The reader knows after the first two lines where she stands.Buries the fact that exchange will not happen in the middle of a long paragraph of apology, or leads with the complaints procedure, which reads as defensive.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsRecognises that this is a frightened first time buyer with a van booked and notice given, and deals with those human facts directly. Warm without being false. Says plainly that the silence is not a judgment on her, without hinting at what lies behind it. Offers a direct line and a promise to call the same day.Cold and defensive, or the opposite, over reassuring in a way that implies the problem is trivial and will be sorted by Monday. Promising a timescale nobody can keep is a failure of client focus even though it feels kind.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsPlain English throughout. No statutory references, no mention of the Proceeds of Crime Act, no reference to any agency, no jargon and no acronyms. Sentences short. The register is that of a solicitor writing to a lay client under pressure.Quotes or names the statute, or writes 'we are subject to obligations under Part 7' or similar, which both baffles the client and points straight at the thing that must not be disclosed.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawThe letter is consistent with the firm being unable to exchange or apply the funds without a defence, does not offer to return the money, gives no reason for the delay, and does not deny that anything has happened or substitute an invented explanation.Offers to return the 160,000 pounds to the client so that she can 'send it from a different account', which would be a transfer of suspected criminal property without a defence and would also destroy the audit trail. Or tells her the delay is caused by the seller, the lender or the searches, which is a lie to the client.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawHandles the whole picture: exchange, the funds, further payments, the lender, the practical arrangements and the complaint. Deals with the instruction to describe the money as savings, and explains why that cannot be done without revealing why the file has stalled. Leaves the client with instructions she can follow today.Deals only with the delay and never touches the lender, so the client is left free to tell Brightmoor herself that the money is savings. Or refuses the savings instruction while explaining the refusal in terms that reveal the suspicion.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies from document 3 that telling the client why the firm cannot proceed would be an offence, and writes accordingly, giving no reason at all while still treating her honestly. Does not invent a false reason, which would breach the duty not to mislead the client. Recognises that the duty to keep a client informed gives way here, and reflects that in a sentence acknowledging the limit rather than pretending there is none. Says nothing to the lender in the meantime and leaves that to the reporting officer.Tells the client that a report has been made, or that the firm has a concern about her funds, or names an agency. Alternatively, invents a false explanation such as a problem with the seller's title, which avoids one offence by committing a breach of the duty not to mislead the client and will unravel the moment the seller's solicitors are asked about it.

Examiner notes

This is the station where the kindest instinct is the failing one. The client is sympathetic, she has given notice on her room and she is asking a direct question. Candidates want to answer it. The whole assessment is whether the candidate can hold the line and still write something a frightened person can use.

Three distinct failures appear. The first is explicit tipping off, naming the report or the agency. The second is soft tipping off, which is subtler and just as fatal: 'we have concerns about where your money has come from', 'we are required to make certain reports in some circumstances and I cannot say whether we have', or quoting the statute. The third is inventing a cover story, usually a problem with the seller's title or the searches. That avoids the offence but breaches the duty not to mislead the client, and it collapses as soon as she rings the estate agent.

The permitted middle path is a bare statement that the firm cannot proceed and cannot give the reason, coupled with the acknowledgment already in the signed client care letter that there are situations in which the law prevents the firm from explaining. A candidate who uses that document has read the materials.

Two further points separate a clear pass from a marginal one. Nothing in the letter may offer to return the money, and the letter must deal with the instruction to tell the lender the funds are savings. Candidates who deal with the savings point often do it well, but many never notice it because it sits in the middle of the file note rather than in the client's email.

Nothing in the partner's email says 'consider the ethical issues'. It says only that nothing should go in the letter that the partner would not want read out, which is the sort of instruction a real supervising partner gives.

Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)

Written station 19: Challenge to a home made will: execution, capacity and a witness beneficiary

Case and matter analysis  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO ROSALIND FERRIER, PARTNER

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 6 April 2027

Matter: Estate of Marjorie Hollingsworth, deceased. Instructions of Alison Pryce

Subject: Validity of the will dated 11 September 2026

1. Summary

The 2026 will is, on the material we have, very likely to be invalid because it was not executed in accordance with section 9 of the Wills Act 1837. That is our strongest point by a distance and it is a point about what happened, not about the deceased's mind, so it does not depend on medical opinion.

If we are right about execution, the 2026 will has no effect at all, its revocation clause has no effect, and the 2019 will stands. Alison then takes half the estate, worth around £201,100, rather than the £5,000 the 2026 will gives her.

There is a second, independent point. Kayleigh Hollingsworth attested the will and is Nigel's wife. Even if the will were validly executed, section 15 of the Wills Act 1837 makes the gift to Nigel void. Nigel would take nothing under the will.

There is a third line, want of capacity and want of knowledge and approval, which is arguable but weaker and slower. We do not need it if the execution point holds.

2. The facts that matter

Mrs Hollingsworth died on 3 February 2027, a widow, leaving two children and no surviving spouse. The gross estate is about £406,500 (house £340,000, building society £62,400, current account £4,100, plus modest chattels and an engagement ring), less the funeral account of £4,300, so roughly £402,200 net.

The 2026 will was typed by Nigel, the sole substantial beneficiary, from an online form. Alison was not told it was being made. Nigel's wife signed as a witness. The neighbour Trevor Nash signed at his own kitchen table with Mrs Hollingsworth not present and did not see her that day. Mrs Hollingsworth had been diagnosed with vascular dementia in March 2026 and her recorded MMSE score fell from 21 to 18 between March and July 2026, with fluctuating presentation. Nigel was under financial pressure and had asked his mother for money before.

3. Ground one: execution, section 9 Wills Act 1837

Section 9 requires the testator's signature to be made or acknowledged in the presence of two witnesses present at the same time, and requires each witness then to attest and sign, or acknowledge a signature already made, in the presence of the testator.

Mr Nash's account fails both limbs. He was not present with Kayleigh Hollingsworth when Mrs Hollingsworth signed or acknowledged her signature, and he signed in his own house with Mrs Hollingsworth absent. On that account the will was not validly executed and is void.

Two qualifications. First, there is a presumption of due execution where a will contains a proper attestation clause. This will does not have one. It has the words "Signed in our presence" and nothing more, which does not state that the witnesses were present together or that they signed in the testator's presence, so the presumption is weak and the burden on Nigel to prove due execution is a real one. Second, Mr Nash's recollection is of a single evening some seven months ago and he says he thinks there was already ink on the document. His evidence needs to be taken properly and tested, but he is an independent neighbour with nothing to gain and he says plainly that he never saw Mrs Hollingsworth that day.

I rate this ground as strong.

4. Ground two: section 15, the witness beneficiary

Kayleigh Hollingsworth attested the will. She is Nigel's wife. Section 15 makes a beneficial gift void so far as concerns an attesting witness or the spouse of an attesting witness. The gift of residue in clause 4 to Nigel is therefore void even if the will was properly executed.

This is not a challenge to the will, it is a consequence of it. It matters because it is the answer if the court finds the will was validly executed after all. If clause 4 fails, there is no further gift of residue in the will, so the residue passes on a partial intestacy. With no surviving spouse, it goes to the issue on the statutory trusts, that is to Alison and Nigel in equal shares. Alison's £5,000 legacy under clause 3 stands, and she also takes half the residue.

I rate this ground as very strong, because it turns on the face of the document.

5. Ground three: capacity, and knowledge and approval

Testamentary capacity requires the testator to understand the nature of the act and its effects, the extent of the property being disposed of, and the claims to which she ought to give effect, and to be free of any disorder of mind that perverts her sense of right in disposing of her property. The diagnosis of dementia is not itself proof of incapacity. Capacity is decision specific and assessed at the time of execution, and the GP record for October 2026 records that on a good day Mrs Hollingsworth converses normally and gives an accurate account of her circumstances.

What helps us is that the will was rational on its face but a marked departure from the 2019 will, that no capacity assessment was ever carried out, and that no solicitor or medical practitioner was involved. The so called golden rule, that a will for an elderly or seriously ill testator should be witnessed or approved by a medical practitioner who satisfies himself as to capacity and records his examination, was not followed. Failure to follow it does not invalidate a will, but it removes the evidence that would otherwise answer the challenge.

Knowledge and approval is the better of the two. The will was prepared by the person who takes almost the whole estate, the testator was elderly and cognitively impaired, and the other child was kept in the dark. Those are circumstances which excite the suspicion of the court, and the burden is then on Nigel as propounder to prove positively that his mother knew and approved the contents. He has to show she understood what she was signing. There is no attendance note, no letter of instruction and no independent explanation of the document.

Undue influence in probate is a different matter. There is no presumption. Alison would have to prove actual coercion, that Mrs Hollingsworth's will was overborne, and mere persuasion or the opportunity to influence is not enough. On what we have, Nigel's debts and his mother's vulnerability raise suspicion but do not prove coercion. I would not plead undue influence on the present material. Pleading it without a proper evidential basis carries an adverse costs risk.

6. What the estate is worth to Alison on each outcome

Taking a net estate of about £402,200 after the funeral account, and ignoring the modest chattels:

(a) 2026 will invalid for want of due execution. The revocation clause fails with the rest of the will, so the 2019 will is the last valid will. Alison and Nigel take equally, subject to the 28 day survivorship clause, which is satisfied. Alison receives about £201,100.

(b) 2026 will validly executed but clause 4 void under section 15. Alison takes her £5,000 legacy plus half of the residue of about £397,200, so about £203,600. Nigel takes about £198,600 and nothing under clause 4.

(c) 2026 will validly executed, section 15 somehow disapplied, and the capacity and knowledge and approval challenges fail. Alison receives £5,000.

Outcomes (a) and (b) are close in money terms. That matters for strategy: Alison's real exposure is only outcome (c), and outcome (c) requires Nigel to overcome both the execution evidence and section 15.

On inheritance tax, the net estate of about £402,200 is above the nil rate band, so the position needs to be worked through rather than assumed. On outcomes (a) and (b) the house is closely inherited by the deceased's children, so the residence nil rate band should be available in addition to the nil rate band, and it is also worth establishing whether any of the late Mr Hollingsworth's nil rate band was used on his death in 2011, since an unused proportion is transferable. On that footing no tax is likely to arise, but the account cannot be settled until the personal representative is identified and the destination of the residue is known, and the rates and thresholds current at that date will have to be applied.

7. Next steps

(a) Obtain a formal witness statement from Trevor Nash while his recollection is fresh, taken carefully and without leading him, and ask him to confirm whether Kayleigh Hollingsworth was present at any point.

(b) Ask Kayleigh Hollingsworth, through Nigel's solicitors once instructed, for her account of the execution.

(c) Enter a caveat at the Probate Registry to prevent a grant issuing to Nigel while the validity of the will is in dispute. A caveat lasts six months and can be extended. If Nigel warns off the caveat, Alison must enter an appearance setting out her interest.

(d) Send a Larke v Nugus request to whoever, if anyone, was involved in preparing the 2026 will. Since Nigel prepared it himself there is no draftsman to ask, so the request is of limited use here, but the point should be recorded.

(e) Obtain the full GP and memory clinic records, and the carers' daily notes for the period around 11 September 2026, by consent of the personal representatives or by court order.

(f) Obtain an itemised valuation of the house and the engagement ring.

(g) Consider early mediation. Both children want the same house sold and neither gains from spending the estate on costs. A negotiated outcome recorded in a settlement agreement is realistic, and Alison has said she does not want a permanent breach.

8. Our own position on this file

Two matters need your attention before you write to Alison.

First, Alison has asked us to send her the whole of her mother's 2019 file, including any note of what her mother said about Nigel's debts, so that she can use it against him. We cannot do that. Our duty of confidentiality to Mrs Hollingsworth survived her death. The file relates to our former client and the right to waive that confidentiality now rests with her personal representatives, and no personal representative has yet been appointed. The fact that Alison is a beneficiary and an executor named in the 2019 will does not entitle her to the file while there is no grant and while the identity of the personal representative is itself in dispute. We should also consider whether acting for Alison against her late mother's estate creates a conflict with our duties to our former client, and record our conclusion on the file. I would write to Alison explaining, in terms, that we hold the file for the estate and not for her, that we will provide a full and even handed account of the circumstances in which the 2019 will was prepared to all parties on request, and that we will not release confidential material selectively to one side of a dispute.

Second, Alison has told us she removed her mother's engagement ring from the house after the funeral and has asked us not to mention it. That ring is an asset of the estate. It is not hers unless and until it is distributed to her. Handling estate assets in this way risks being treated as intermeddling, which can fix her with the obligations of an executor de son tort. More immediately, we cannot act on an instruction to conceal an estate asset from the other beneficiary, the personal representative or, in due course, HMRC. That would put us in breach of our duty not to mislead others and of our obligation to act with honesty and integrity. I would advise her to return the ring or to hold it and disclose it, tell her plainly that we will not conceal it, and confirm that if she insists on concealment we would have to stop acting. It should also be listed in any schedule of estate assets.

Neither point should be difficult with Alison. She raised both openly, which suggests she has not appreciated the difficulty rather than that she is being deliberately obstructive.

9. Recommendation

Lead on execution, plead section 15 as an alternative, plead want of knowledge and approval, and do not plead undue influence on the present material. Enter a caveat this week. Take Mr Nash's statement. Then invite Nigel to mediate before either side incurs serious costs.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two unflagged issues sit in the attendance note. First, Alison asks for the deceased's 2019 file, including a note of what her mother said about Nigel's debts, to use against her brother. Confidentiality survives death and is owed to the deceased and now to her personal representatives, of whom there are none, so the file cannot be handed to a beneficiary, still less selectively to one side of a probate dispute. The firm should also consider whether acting for Alison against her late mother's estate conflicts with duties owed to a former client. The competent answer is to refuse, explain why, and offer a full and even handed account of the circumstances of the 2019 will to all parties. Second, Alison has removed her mother's engagement ring and asked the firm to say nothing about it. It is an estate asset, taking it risks intermeddling, and the firm cannot act on an instruction to conceal an asset from the personal representative, the other beneficiary or HMRC. The competent answer is to advise her to disclose or return it, tell her the firm will not conceal it, list it in the estate schedule, and make clear the firm would stop acting rather than participate.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsPicks up every fact that drives the analysis: that Nash signed at his own house with the testator absent, that Kayleigh is Nigel's wife and attested, that Nigel typed the will and is the sole substantial beneficiary, that the will has no proper attestation clause, the MMSE trajectory and the fluctuating presentation, Nigel's financial pressure, the absence of any capacity assessment, and the two facts Alison volunteered about the file and the ring. Uses the estate figures to quantify each outcome.Reports the dementia diagnosis as if it settled the matter and never notices either that Nash signed out of the testator's presence or that the second witness is the beneficiary's wife.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsTells the partner in money what Alison gains or loses on each outcome, ranks the grounds by strength rather than listing them, warns about costs and the adverse costs risk of pleading undue influence without evidence, recommends a caveat now, and reflects Alison's stated wish to avoid a permanent family breach by recommending mediation.Sets out the law on each ground without ever saying which one to run, what the estate is worth to Alison, or what should happen this week.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA report addressed to the partner, headed and numbered, with a short summary at the front that answers the question before the reasoning. Plain professional English, no padding.Writes a letter to the client, or produces undifferentiated prose in which the recommendation is buried on the last page.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies section 9 accurately to Nash's account and identifies the failure of both the simultaneous presence requirement and the requirement to attest in the testator's presence. Applies section 15 correctly to the spouse of an attesting witness and works through the consequence that the residuary gift fails and residue passes on partial intestacy to the two children. States the capacity test and the burden on the propounder where suspicious circumstances arise, and correctly says there is no presumption of undue influence in probate.Says section 15 invalidates the whole will, or says that failure to follow the golden rule makes the will void, or asserts a presumption of undue influence because a child prepared the will.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all four attacks and, critically, works out the distribution on each outcome, including the point that an invalidly executed later will effects no revocation, so the 2019 will was never revoked and remains the last valid will. Deals with the survivorship clause, the partial intestacy rule and the evidence needed to prove each ground.Stops at the conclusion that the will is invalid and never says what then governs the estate, or forgets that the revocation clause fails with the rest of the will and assumes an intestacy.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies without prompting that the deceased's file is confidential and cannot be released to a beneficiary while no personal representative exists, considers the former client conflict, and separately identifies that concealing the engagement ring is an instruction the firm cannot follow. Resolves both: explain, refuse, offer an even handed account to all parties, advise that the ring is an estate asset, and warn that the firm would cease to act rather than conceal it.Hands the 2019 file to Alison because she is a beneficiary and a named executor, or notices the ring but treats it as a family matter of no professional concern.

Examiner notes

The pass is decided on whether the candidate reads Trevor Nash's statement properly and sees that section 9 has failed twice over, and whether the candidate notices that the second witness shares Nigel's surname and address and is his wife, which triggers section 15. Both are on the face of the papers. The trap is the dementia diagnosis, which is deliberately prominent and pulls weaker candidates into a long capacity argument that is the weakest ground on these facts and that they then cannot resolve because the medical evidence cuts both ways. The second trap is failing to work through the consequences: an invalid later will revokes nothing, so the 2019 will governs, and a void residuary gift under section 15 produces a partial intestacy rather than a lapse into Nigel's hands. A candidate who reaches the right grounds but never tells the partner what Alison actually receives will struggle on client focused advice.

Written station 20: Drafting will clauses: specific gift, contingent legacy, survivorship and a residuary life interest trust

Legal drafting  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  45 minutes

Model answer

4. GIFT OF PIPPIN COTTAGE

4.1 I GIVE my freehold property known as Pippin Cottage, Lark Lane, Hessett, Suffolk IP30 9RD, or such other property as I may own at my death in substitution for it, together with all furniture, furnishings and other chattels contained in it at my death, to my nephew OWEN BELL of 3 Whitmore Row, Stowmarket, Suffolk absolutely.

4.2 I DIRECT that the gift in clause 4.1 takes effect free of any mortgage, charge or other money obligation secured on the property at my death, and free of the costs of transferring the property and its contents to the beneficiary, and I DIRECT that my Trustees shall discharge that mortgage, charge or other money obligation, and those costs, out of my residuary estate. This direction is given expressly for the purposes of section 35 of the Administration of Estates Act 1925.

4.3 If the said Owen Bell does not survive me by the period specified in clause 6, the gift made by clause 4.1 shall lapse and the property and its contents shall fall into and form part of my residuary estate. No child or remoter issue of the said Owen Bell shall take by substitution.

5. CONTINGENT PECUNIARY LEGACY

5.1 I GIVE the sum of TWENTY FIVE THOUSAND POUNDS (£25,000) to my Trustees to hold on trust for ISLA KERR of 22 Lark Rise, Woolpit, Suffolk if she attains the age of 25 years. I DIRECT that my Trustees shall set this legacy aside as a separate fund as soon as practicable after my death, and that the legacy shall carry the intermediate income of that fund from the date of my death.

5.2 Until the said Isla Kerr attains the age of 25 years, or dies before attaining that age, my Trustees may apply the whole or any part of the income of the legacy for her maintenance, education or benefit as my Trustees in their absolute discretion think fit, and may accumulate any income not so applied and add it to the capital of the legacy. Section 31 of the Trustee Act 1925 shall apply with the modification that the said Isla Kerr shall not become entitled to the income of the legacy on attaining the age of 18 years, and shall not become so entitled unless and until she attains the age of 25 years.

5.3 My Trustees may at any time pay or apply the whole or any part of the capital of the legacy for the advancement or benefit of the said Isla Kerr, including for the purposes of her education or of acquiring an interest in a dwelling for her occupation, and section 32 of the Trustee Act 1925 shall apply accordingly and shall extend to the whole of the legacy.

5.4 The receipt of a parent or guardian of the said Isla Kerr, while she is under the age of 18 years, shall be a complete discharge to my Trustees for any payment made under clauses 5.2 or 5.3.

5.5 If the said Isla Kerr dies before attaining the age of 25 years, the legacy and any accumulations of income shall fall into and form part of my residuary estate.

6. SURVIVORSHIP

6.1 A beneficiary who does not survive me by 30 clear days shall be treated for all the purposes of this my will as having died before me, and the gift to that beneficiary shall take effect accordingly.

6.2 Clause 6.1 does not apply to the gift of my residuary estate to the Suffolk Reed Rivers Trust made by clause 7, and does not apply so as to defeat that gift.

7. RESIDUARY ESTATE

7.1 I GIVE all the residue of my estate, after payment of my debts, funeral and testamentary expenses, any inheritance tax payable by reason of my death on property passing under this my will, and the legacies and directions given by this my will, to my Trustees to hold on the trusts declared by this clause (my "Residuary Fund").

7.2 My Trustees shall pay the income of my Residuary Fund to my brother VAUGHAN MARCHETTI during his life.

7.3 My Trustees may at any time during the lifetime of the said Vaughan Marchetti pay or apply capital out of my Residuary Fund to him or for his benefit as my Trustees in their absolute discretion think fit, provided that the total of all capital so paid or applied shall not exceed one half of the value of my Residuary Fund calculated as at the date of the first such payment or application.

7.4 Subject to clauses 7.2 and 7.3, and on the death of the said Vaughan Marchetti, my Trustees shall hold my Residuary Fund for THE SUFFOLK REED RIVERS TRUST, registered charity number 1082644, of Flatford Mill Lane, Manningtree, Essex CO11 2RX, absolutely, for its general charitable purposes.

7.5 If the said Vaughan Marchetti does not survive me by the period specified in clause 6, my Trustees shall hold my Residuary Fund for the said Suffolk Reed Rivers Trust absolutely, for its general charitable purposes, and the trusts declared by clauses 7.2 and 7.3 shall not take effect.

7.6 If at the date the said charity becomes entitled it has ceased to exist, or has changed its name, or has amalgamated with or transferred its assets to another body, my Trustees shall pay my Residuary Fund to the body which then carries on its work or its successor, and if there is no such body my Trustees shall pay my Residuary Fund to such charitable body or bodies having objects as nearly as possible resembling those of the said charity as my Trustees in their absolute discretion select.

7.7 The written receipt of a person appearing to my Trustees to be a proper officer of the charity or body receiving my Residuary Fund shall be a complete discharge to my Trustees, who shall not be concerned to see to the application of the money.

8. ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS

8.1 Sale and retention. My Trustees may sell, retain or otherwise deal with any part of my estate as if they were absolute owners of it, and shall be under no liability for any loss arising from the retention of any asset in its existing form.

8.2 Investment. My Trustees may invest any money requiring investment in any manner in which they could invest if they were absolute owners, including the acquisition of freehold or leasehold land in any part of the world for investment, for occupation by a beneficiary, or for any other purpose.

8.3 Charging. Any of my Trustees who is a solicitor or other person engaged in a profession or business may charge and be paid all usual professional and other charges for work done by that Trustee or that Trustee's firm in connection with my estate or the trusts of this my will, including work which a trustee not being in a profession or business could have done personally. This provision applies notwithstanding that the Trustee is a sole trustee and without the need for the written agreement of any other Trustee.

8.4 Insurance. My Trustees may insure any asset comprised in my estate against any risk and to any value they think fit, and may pay the premiums out of income or capital as they think fit.

8.5 Appropriation. My Trustees may appropriate any asset of my estate in or towards satisfaction of any legacy, share or interest under this my will at such value as they think fit, without the consent of any beneficiary and without obtaining any valuation, and section 41 of the Administration of Estates Act 1925 shall apply with that modification.

8.6 Trustees abroad. My Trustees may at any time appoint a person or body resident outside the United Kingdom to be a trustee of the whole or any part of my estate, and may on doing so declare that the trusts of that part shall be governed by and take effect under the law of another jurisdiction, and my Trustees shall not be liable for any consequence of a proper exercise of this power.

8.7 Indemnity. My Trustees shall not be liable for any loss to my estate or to any trust fund arising from anything done or omitted in good faith, other than loss arising from that Trustee's own fraud or dishonesty.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

At the end of the attendance note the client says she wants to leave £15,000 to the partner personally, and the partner passes it to the trainee to 'deal with in your drafting as you think right'. A client proposing a gift of significant value to the solicitor advising on the will creates an own interest conflict, and the firm cannot draft the clause on these instructions. The competent candidate simply does not include it, and understands the resolution: advise the client that she must take independent legal advice about the gift from a solicitor with no interest in it, do not draft the clause unless and until that advice has been taken, cease to act on the will if she refuses to take it, and record all of that on the file. Nothing about the rest of the will is affected. A secondary point sits in the estrangement from her son, which raises the prospect of a claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 and is why the letter of wishes matters, but that is a matter for the file note rather than for these clauses.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsClauses read as operative will clauses: single subject per clause, defined terms used consistently, beneficiaries fully identified by full name and address on first mention, amounts in words and figures, no ambiguity about what falls into residue. British spelling. No em-dashes.Copies the precedent's loose wording, refers to beneficiaries by first name only, or writes narrative explanation instead of operative language.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsNumbered 4 to 8 in the order the partner set, with sub-clauses used to separate the gift, the direction about the mortgage and costs, and the lapse provision. The residue clause moves logically from the fund, to the life interest, to the power over capital, to the remainder, to the substitution, to the receipt clause.Runs the whole of clause 4 or clause 7 together as one long sentence, or renumbers the clauses so they no longer fit the will the partner is building.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawReverses the precedent's mortgage wording so the charge is thrown onto residue with the express contrary intention section 35 requires. Removes the substitution of Owen's children, which is contrary to instructions, and provides expressly that the gift lapses into residue if he does not survive, noting that section 33 of the Wills Act 1837 has no application to a gift to a nephew because it saves only a gift to a child or remoter descendant of the testator. Modifies section 31 so that Isla does not take income at 18 when the contingency is 25. Extends section 32 expressly. Gives the life interest with a capped capital power and a proper remainder to the charity, with a substitution if the life tenant predeceases. Uses a 30 day survivorship period and does not let it defeat the charitable gift.Leaves the gift 'subject to any mortgage', which is the opposite of the instruction and is what section 35 provides by default, or relies on a general direction to pay debts out of residue, which section 35 says is not enough.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers everything asked for and the things the precedent's own drafting notes flag: contents of the cottage, costs of transfer, destination on lapse, income and capital powers for a minor, receipt by a parent or guardian, gift over if Isla dies before 25, a longstop if the life tenant predeceases, a charity name change or amalgamation clause, a charity receipt clause, and each of the administrative powers requested including the professional charging clause and the power to appropriate without consent.Drafts a life interest with no provision for what happens if the life tenant dies first, or a charitable gift with no receipt clause and no provision for the charity ceasing to exist, leaving a partial intestacy or a stalled administration.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDoes not draft the £15,000 gift to the partner. Recognises that a client wishing to make a gift of significant value to the solicitor advising on the will creates an own interest conflict, that the firm must advise the client to take independent legal advice from another firm about that gift, and that the firm must decline to act on it if she will not. Omits the clause from the draft and, if any note is unavoidable, records only that the gift is not included and why.Drafts the £15,000 legacy to the partner because the client asked for it, or drafts it 'subject to the client taking advice', which puts the clause into the instrument before the advice the client is entitled to has been given.

Examiner notes

Three technical points decide this station and each is planted in the precedent, which is deliberately wrong. First, the precedent gives the property 'subject to any mortgage', the exact opposite of the instruction, and section 35 makes the charged property primarily liable unless the will expressly says otherwise, so the candidate must both delete the wrong words and add an express direction. A general debts clause will not do. Second, the precedent's contingent legacy leaves section 31 unmodified, so a 14 year old with a gift contingent on reaching 25 would become entitled to the income at 18; the candidate must exclude that. Third, the precedent's residue clause has no provision for the life tenant predeceasing the testator, which on these facts is a real risk since the brother is 74 and in poor health. Weaker candidates transcribe the precedent with the names filled in. The ethics point is the £15,000 gift to the drafting partner, and the correct answer is to leave it out entirely, not to draft it neatly.

Written station 21: Redrafting the legacy, survivorship and residue clauses of a will

Legal drafting  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  45 minutes

Model answer

REPLACEMENT CLAUSES 4 TO 7

Will of Rosalind Anne Pethick, draft dated 2 April 2027

4. LEGACIES

4.1 I GIVE the sum of thirty thousand pounds (30,000 pounds) free of inheritance tax to my sister HAZEL MARGARET INGRAM of 4 Saltmarsh Cottages, Whitchurch, Shropshire absolutely, provided that she survives me by 28 days. If she does not survive me by 28 days this legacy shall lapse and shall fall into and form part of my residuary estate.

4.2 I GIVE the sum of twenty thousand pounds (20,000 pounds) free of inheritance tax to my Trustees to hold on trust for my granddaughter IMMY ROSE PETHICK of 18 Ashenden Row, Shrewsbury if she attains the age of 25 years. If she does not attain that age this legacy shall lapse and shall fall into and form part of my residuary estate.

4.3 WHILE the interest of my granddaughter under clause 4.2 remains contingent my Trustees may:

(a) apply the whole or any part of the income of that legacy for her maintenance, education or benefit as my Trustees in their absolute discretion think fit, and shall accumulate any income not so applied by adding it to the capital of that legacy; and

(b) pay or apply the whole or any part of the capital of that legacy for her advancement or benefit as my Trustees in their absolute discretion think fit.

4.4 The powers in clause 4.3 are in addition to, and not in substitution for, the statutory powers of maintenance and advancement, which shall apply free of any restriction as to amount.

5. GIFT OF MY WATERCOLOUR COLLECTION

5.1 I GIVE my collection of watercolour paintings by artists of the Fenwick Valley and the surrounding area, together with their frames, to THE FENWICK VALLEY MUSEUM TRUST of the Old Corn Exchange, Fenwick Bridge, Shropshire SY5 2LN (registered charity number 1102884) absolutely for its general charitable purposes.

5.2 I DECLARE that the receipt of a person who appears to my Trustees to be a proper officer of that body shall be a full discharge to my Trustees.
