5.3 If that body has ceased to exist at my death, or declines to accept the whole or any part of this gift, then this gift, or so much of it as is declined, shall fall into and form part of my residuary estate.

5.4 I DIRECT that the cost of packing, insuring and delivering any painting accepted under this clause shall be paid out of my residuary estate as a testamentary expense.

6. RESIDUARY ESTATE

6.1 I GIVE all the residue of my estate, after payment of my debts, funeral and testamentary expenses and the legacies given by this will or by any codicil to it, to such of my children VERITY GRACE PETHICK and CALLUM DOUGLAS PETHICK as shall survive me and satisfy the condition in clause 7, and if both, in equal shares absolutely.

6.2 PROVIDED THAT if either of my said children fails to take a share under clause 6.1 but leaves a child or children living at my death who satisfy the condition in clause 7, that child or those children shall take by substitution, and if more than one in equal shares, the share of my residuary estate which their parent would otherwise have taken.

6.3 The share of any such grandchild who is under the age of 18 at my death shall be held by my Trustees on trust for that grandchild contingently on attaining the age of 18 years, and clause 4.3 shall apply to that share as it applies to the legacy given by clause 4.2.

6.4 If either of my said children fails to take a share under clause 6.1 and no substituted gift takes effect under clause 6.2 in respect of that share, that share shall accrue to the other of them, or if that other has also failed to take a share, to the persons who would take that other share under clause 6.2.

7. SURVIVORSHIP

7.1 NO person other than a charity shall take any benefit under this my will unless that person survives me by 28 days.

7.2 Any gift to a person who fails to satisfy the condition in clause 7.1 shall take effect as if that person had died before me.

DRAFTER'S NOTE FOR THE FILE, NOT PART OF THE WILL

Before this draft is sent out, Mrs Pethick should be seen alone so that instructions are confirmed directly by her and free of her daughter's presence, and a contemporaneous note made.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The instructions have come to the firm through Verity Pethick, who is one of the two residuary beneficiaries. She arranged the appointment, gave the background before it, remained in the room, answered for her mother twice and asserted on the residue that her mother had "already decided". The client has never been seen alone. The risk is not incapacity, since the client is 71, in good health, manages her own money and drove herself to the meeting. The risk is that the will may not represent instructions the client has given freely and with knowledge and approval, and that the will could later be challenged on that ground. Under the SRA Principles the solicitor acts for Mrs Pethick alone, and must act in her best interests and with independence, so the competent candidate flags that the draft should not go out until Mrs Pethick has been seen alone, has confirmed the terms herself, and the file records that she did so. The professional charging clause in the precedent bank is a second, smaller trap: the client has expressly said she does not want one, and inserting Precedent F would put a benefit for the firm into the will against instructions.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsClauses read as operative will clauses. Amounts appear in words and figures, beneficiaries are identified by full name and address, defined terms already used in the will ("my Trustees") are picked up rather than reinvented, and each clause does one thing. No stray advice, commentary or square brackets left in the operative text.Writing a memorandum explaining what the clauses would say instead of drafting them, or leaving unfilled precedent square brackets, blank ages or an undefined "the Trustees" in the drafted text.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsNumbered 4 to 7 so the clauses drop into the existing draft. Legacies before residue, residue before the general survivorship condition, and the contingent legacy's administrative powers placed immediately after the legacy they govern. Cross references between clauses are accurate.Renumbering from 1, burying the survivorship condition inside the residue gift so it does not reach the legacies, or scattering the maintenance and advancement powers away from the legacy they attach to.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawThe contingent legacy is given to the trustees to hold on trust, not to a 9 year old outright, and the contingency is 25 rather than 18. The residue gift creates an express substitution for grandchildren rather than relying on section 33 of the Wills Act 1837. The survivorship period is a condition, expressed so a failing gift takes effect as if the beneficiary had predeceased, and the charity is excluded from it so charity exemption is not prejudiced. Failed gifts are directed into residue.Giving the 20,000 pounds to the granddaughter absolutely, which vests at 18 and defeats the instruction, or applying the 28 day survivorship condition to the charitable gift, which would make the gift capable of failing for a reason the client never intended.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawEvery eventuality raised on the file is covered: Hazel predeceasing, Immy dying before 25, the museum declining all or part of the collection, a child predeceasing with issue, a child predeceasing without issue, and a substituted grandchild who is a minor. The trustees are given maintenance and advancement powers over the contingent legacy and over a minor grandchild's substituted share, and a charity receipt clause is included.Leaving a gap that produces a partial intestacy, most often by drafting the museum gift with no gift over if the Trust declines, or by providing for a child dying with issue but not for a child dying without issue.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises that instructions have been taken through Verity, a residuary beneficiary, who arranged the meeting, spoke for the client and answered for her on the residue, and that the client has never been seen alone. Records that the draft must not be sent until Mrs Pethick confirms her instructions directly and in private, with a contemporaneous note. Does not, however, let this displace the task: the clauses are still drafted.Treating the daughter's involvement as ordinary family help and drafting without comment, or the opposite error of writing a long conduct essay and producing no usable clauses. A candidate who alleges that the client lacks capacity, when nothing on the file suggests it, has misread the issue: the concern here is knowledge and approval and freedom from influence, not capacity.

Examiner notes

The pass line is whether the four clauses actually work as a set. The single most common failure is clause 5. Candidates copy Precedent C but drop the closing sentence, so if the museum declines the collection there is no gift over and the paintings pass on a partial intestacy, which is precisely what the file note of 13 April warns against. The second common failure is clause 4.2: the instruction is age 25, and a candidate who gives the legacy to a 9 year old "absolutely" has produced a gift that vests at 18 and has ignored the instruction entirely. Strong candidates also notice that the survivorship condition must exclude the charity, and that a substituted grandchild might be a minor, so the residue clause needs a holding trust of its own. On conduct, a single accurate sentence recording that the client must be seen alone before the draft is sent is worth more than a page of general commentary, and a candidate who writes only commentary and no clauses cannot pass a drafting station.

Written station 22: A legacy to the husband of a person who attested the will

Legal research  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO PARTNER

To: Idris Vaughan

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 3 February 2027

Matter: Boyce deceased, effect of section 15 Wills Act 1837 on the pecuniary legacy and the residue

1. CONCLUSION

1.1 The 75,000 pounds legacy to Nigel Talbot is valid and can be paid once the grant issues. It is saved by section 1 of the Wills Act 1968.

1.2 The residuary gift to Ronan Ngwenya is valid and is unaffected. Section 15 of the Wills Act 1837 does not catch a witness who marries a beneficiary after the will has been attested.

1.3 The will itself is validly executed under section 9 of the Wills Act 1837. Nothing in the attestation puts the will in doubt.

1.4 There is a separate point on which the firm's own position needs to be addressed, at paragraph 5 below, before Mr Talbot is answered.

2. THE LEGACY TO MR TALBOT

2.1 Section 15 of the Wills Act 1837 makes void any beneficial gift to a person who attests the will, or to the wife or husband of a person who attests it. Freya Talbot attested. She was, at 12 March 2026, the wife of Nigel Talbot, who takes 75,000 pounds. On the bare wording of section 15 his legacy would be void.

2.2 That was the law until 1968. In the Estate of Bravda, deceased [1968] 1 WLR 479 the Court of Appeal held that where two independent witnesses had already validly attested, the additional signatures of two beneficiaries could not be treated as surplusage, and their gifts were void. The result was regarded as unsatisfactory and Parliament reversed it.

2.3 Section 1(1) of the Wills Act 1968 provides that for the purposes of section 15 the attestation of a will by a person to whom, or to whose spouse, a disposition is given is to be disregarded if the will is duly executed without that attestation, and without that of any other such person. By section 1(2) the section applies to the will of any person dying after 30 May 1968. Mr Boyce died on 8 January 2027, so it applies.

2.4 The will therefore has to be tested by asking whether it was duly executed under section 9 leaving Mrs Talbot's signature out of account. Section 9 requires the testator's signature to be made or acknowledged in the presence of two or more witnesses present at the same time, each of whom attests and signs. Disregarding Mrs Talbot, two witnesses remain: Deborah Craven and Peter Halloran. Both signed in the deceased's presence and in the presence of each other, immediately after he signed. The will was accordingly duly executed without Mrs Talbot's attestation.

2.5 Section 1(1) also requires that the will be duly executed without the attestation of any other person falling within section 15. Neither of the two remaining witnesses falls within section 15:

(a) Mr Halloran took a legacy of 10,000 pounds under the will as originally made, but that gift was revoked by the codicil of 2 May 2026 and he takes nothing. There is now no beneficial disposition to him or to his spouse, so he is not within section 15. The codicil itself was witnessed by two members of staff who take nothing, so it raises no separate issue.

(b) Deborah Craven was unmarried when she attested. She is dealt with at paragraph 3 below.

2.6 Mrs Talbot's attestation is therefore disregarded, section 15 does not bite, and Mr Talbot's legacy of 75,000 pounds stands.

2.7 One caution. The saving in section 1(1) depends on there being two other qualifying witnesses. It works here only because neither Mr Halloran nor Miss Craven is a person within section 15. If either of them had been, the will could not have been duly executed without the attestation of "any other such person", both attestations would have had to be counted, and Mr Talbot's legacy would have failed. The point is finer than it looks and should be recorded on the file.

3. THE RESIDUARY GIFT TO MR NGWENYA

3.1 Deborah Craven attested on 12 March 2026 when she was unmarried. She married the residuary beneficiary, Ronan Ngwenya, on 5 September 2026, during the deceased's lifetime.

3.2 Section 15 avoids a gift to a person who attests or to "the wife or husband of such person". The relationship must exist at the time of attestation. That is precisely the point decided in Thorpe v Bestwick (1881) 6 QBD 311, where the witness was single when she attested and afterwards married the legatee in the testator's lifetime. The legacy was held valid. Lopes J held that the disability created by the section is not one that can be acquired by a subsequent event.

3.3 The residuary gift to Mr Ngwenya is therefore unaffected, and Miss Craven remains a witness whose attestation counts for the purposes of paragraph 2.5 above.

4. IF THE POSITION HAD BEEN OTHERWISE

4.1 For completeness, section 15 would not have invalidated the will. It avoids only the gift, and expressly preserves the witness as a competent witness to prove execution. A failed pecuniary legacy would have fallen into residue; a failed residuary gift would have passed on intestacy.

4.2 The extract from Fennimore, Practical Will Drafting, 6th edition, 1962 states the position as absolute and says that nothing can be done after the event. That was correct when it was written but it predates the Wills Act 1968 and should not be relied on.

5. THE FIRM'S POSITION, AND WHAT TO TELL THE EXECUTOR

5.1 This firm drafted the will and our then trainee attended to supervise execution. Allowing a beneficiary's wife to sign as one of three witnesses was an error. It has caused no loss because of section 1 of the Wills Act 1968, but the outcome turned on the fact that two other unaffected witnesses happened to sign.

5.2 Mr Talbot has already asked whether, if there were a problem, "the solicitors would have to make it good". A will draftsman can owe a duty of care to a disappointed beneficiary: Ross v Caunters [1980] Ch 297, the reasoning of which was confirmed on a different basis in White v Jones [1995] 2 AC 207. Mr Talbot is not our client and we cannot advise him. He should be told plainly that his legacy is valid and will be paid on the grant, and that we cannot advise him on any question about the firm's own conduct.

5.3 Because the firm has an interest of its own in the answer to the question the executor has asked, the position should be disclosed to her rather than left on the file, and the matter reported internally under the firm's own procedures so that insurers can be notified if that is required. Our advice to the executor is unaffected by the firm's interest, and on this analysis she suffers no prejudice, but she should be told that the point arises from our own file so that she can decide for herself whether she wants independent advice.

5.4 Advice to the executor, in short terms: the relative who told her that "a witness cannot inherit" is describing a rule that exists but that does not apply here. She may pay the 75,000 pounds legacy when the grant issues, and she may distribute the residue to Mr Ngwenya in the ordinary way.

6. SOURCES NOT RELIED ON

6.1 The bundle contains material that does not bear on the question. Banks v Goodfellow (1870) LR 5 QB 549 and Gill v Woodall [2010] EWCA Civ 1430 go to testamentary capacity and to knowledge and approval. Neither is in issue: the deceased read the will, questioned the residue and nothing suggests any want of capacity or approval. Section 18 of the Wills Act 1837 concerns revocation by the testator's own marriage, not a witness's marriage, and the deceased did not marry. Section 3 of the Succession (Scotland) Act 2016 is an Act of the Scottish Parliament applying in Scotland and has no application to an estate in England and Wales.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The firm drafted this will and its own trainee supervised an execution at which the wife of a 75,000 pounds legatee signed as a witness. That was a mistake, and if the will had been attested by only two witnesses, or if one of the other two had also been within section 15, the legacy would have been void and the firm would have been exposed to a claim by Mr Talbot on the Ross v Caunters and White v Jones line of authority. The legacy is in fact saved by the Wills Act 1968, but the firm has an interest of its own in the question the executor has asked, which engages the own interest conflict provisions of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and the duty to act in the client's best interests. The competent candidate discloses the error to the executor rather than burying it, reports it internally so that insurers can be notified if the firm's arrangements require it, tells Mr Talbot only that his legacy is valid and will be paid, and declines to advise him about the firm's own conduct because he is not the firm's client and the firm cannot advise on a potential claim against itself.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsRelies on section 15 of the Wills Act 1837, section 1 of the Wills Act 1968 and Thorpe v Bestwick, uses Bravda to explain why the 1968 Act exists, and uses Ross v Caunters only for the conduct point. Cites accurately by name, year and reference. Positively discards the capacity, knowledge and approval, section 18 and Scottish material, and identifies the 1962 textbook as superseded.Building the answer on Banks v Goodfellow or Gill v Woodall because the will is being questioned, or quoting the 1962 textbook's statement that nothing can be done after the event, which states the law as it stood before the Wills Act 1968.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the two questions the executor actually asked, in the order she asked them, and tells the partner what to say to her: the legacy may be paid on the grant, the residue is unaffected, and the relative's rule of thumb is real but does not apply here. Deals with what to say to Mr Talbot, who is not the client.Producing an accurate essay on section 15 that never states whether the executor may pay, or advising Mr Talbot directly when he is not the firm's client.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA note to a partner: conclusion first, numbered paragraphs, no research trail, no narration of databases searched. Statutory language is quoted only where the exact words matter, in particular the words "and without that of any other such person".Setting out the search process, or reciting long passages of the sources without applying them to the three named witnesses.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly concludes that section 1 of the Wills Act 1968 saves the Talbot legacy because the will was duly executed under section 9 by the two remaining witnesses, and that Thorpe v Bestwick saves the residuary gift because Miss Craven was unmarried when she attested. Applies the 1968 Act to a death in 2027 and notes it applies to wills executed before as well as after 1968.Concluding that the Talbot legacy is void by reading section 15 alone and stopping there, or concluding that the residuary gift fails because the witness later married the residuary beneficiary.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawWorks through all three witnesses, not just Mrs Talbot. Sees that the saving in section 1(1) requires that no other witness falls within section 15, and that this is only satisfied because the codicil revoked Mr Halloran's legacy and because Miss Craven was unmarried at the time. States what would have happened if the gift had failed, that the will itself remains valid and that the legacy would have fallen into residue.Dealing only with Mrs Talbot and never testing whether the other two witnesses are themselves within section 15, which is the step the whole answer turns on. Missing the effect of the codicil on Mr Halloran's position is the usual route to that failure.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises that the firm drafted the will and supervised an execution at which a beneficiary's wife signed, that the firm therefore has an own interest in the answer, and that Mr Talbot's question about whether the solicitors would "make it good" is a claim question the firm cannot advise on. Proposes disclosure to the executor, an internal report and notification of insurers if required, and a plain non advisory response to Mr Talbot.Treating the good news as the end of the matter, so the firm's own error is never disclosed because it caused no loss, or the opposite error of advising Mr Talbot on the strength of a negligence claim against the candidate's own firm.

Examiner notes

The station separates candidates at one step. Nearly everyone finds section 15 and sees the problem. The pass depends on then finding section 1 of the Wills Act 1968 in the bundle and, critically, applying its second limb: the attestation is disregarded only if the will is duly executed without it "and without that of any other such person". That forces the candidate to examine all three witnesses. The codicil revoking Mr Halloran's legacy and the fact that Miss Craven was unmarried on 12 March 2026 are the two facts that make the saving work, and a candidate who never mentions them has reached the right answer for the wrong reason. The most common failure is the opposite: a confident note concluding that the legacy is void, based on section 15 and the 1962 textbook, which states the pre 1968 law. The Bravda editorial note is the signpost. Two decoys catch weaker candidates: Banks v Goodfellow and Gill v Woodall look attractive because the will is being questioned, but capacity and knowledge and approval are not in issue anywhere on these facts. The Scottish Act and section 18 should be discarded in a line each.

Written station 23: Two legacies said to be held on undisclosed trusts

Legal research  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO PARTNER

To: Aurelio Nkanga

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 9 September 2027

Matter: Colefax deceased, clause 4 and clause 5 legacies

1. CONCLUSION

1.1 Clause 4. There is a valid fully secret trust. Mr Mawdsley takes the 150,000 pounds as trustee for Miss Nkemdi and cannot keep it.

1.2 Clause 5. The half secret trust in favour of Elias Vardy fails, because the terms were not communicated to Mrs Osei until 11 November 2024, some eight weeks after the will was executed. Mrs Osei does not take beneficially. She holds the 100,000 pounds on a resulting trust for the estate, so it falls into residue and passes to the Harlestone Riverside Trust under clause 6.

1.3 The two legacies are governed by different rules on timing, and that difference is the whole of the case. It is what produces two opposite answers on facts that look similar.

1.4 What Mr Mawdsley has told our assistant solicitor cannot be dealt with as he has asked. See paragraph 5.

2. CLAUSE 4, THE GIFT TO MR MAWDSLEY

2.1 Clause 4 gives 150,000 pounds to Mr Mawdsley "absolutely". Nothing on the face of the will suggests a trust, so this is the fully secret category.

2.2 The elements are those set out by Brightman J in Ottaway v Norman [1972] Ch 698: the testator's intention to subject the primary donee to an obligation in favour of a secondary donee, communication of that intention to the primary donee, and acceptance of the obligation, expressly or by acquiescence.

2.3 All three are established on Mr Mawdsley's own account:

(a) Intention. Mrs Colefax told him the money was to go to Miss Nkemdi and gave her reason for not naming her in the will. The obligation was directed at a named person and a defined sum.

(b) Communication. Made in terms on 2 September 2024 at the Fox and Garland. Both the identity of the beneficiary and the extent of the obligation, the whole of the legacy, were communicated.

(c) Acceptance. "Of course, whatever you want" is an express acceptance. Even had he said nothing, acquiescence would suffice on Ottaway.

2.4 Timing is not a problem here. Ottaway confirms that for a fully secret trust it is immaterial whether the communication and acceptance precede or follow the execution of the will, provided they occur in the testator's lifetime. This communication in fact came sixteen days before the will was signed, so the point does not arise.

2.5 The absence of writing is not a problem either. The trust is of a sum of money, not of land, so section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925 has no application. Ottaway itself was proved on oral evidence.

2.6 The evidential position needs stating plainly, because it is the source of Mr Mawdsley's confidence. The only direct evidence of the trust is his own account. The court applies the ordinary civil standard but looks for clear evidence before fastening a trust on somebody who takes absolutely on the face of the will. Here the account is an admission against his own interest, made to a solicitor and recorded in a file note. It is strong evidence, and it does not cease to be evidence because he has since changed his mind about what he wants to do.

2.7 Mr Mawdsley therefore takes the 150,000 pounds as trustee and must pay it to Miss Nkemdi.

3. CLAUSE 5, THE GIFT TO MRS OSEI

3.1 Clause 5 declares a trust on the face of the will: the money is given to Mrs Osei "to be held by her upon trusts which I have already communicated to her". This is the half secret category, and a stricter rule on timing applies.

3.2 In Blackwell v Blackwell [1929] AC 318 the House of Lords held such trusts enforceable, but on the footing that where the will itself shows the legatee takes as trustee the communication must be made before or at the time of the execution of the will. A testator may not declare a trust in his will and reserve to himself a power to fill in its terms afterwards by an unattested instrument.

3.3 That is exactly what happened here. Mrs Osei's attendance note of 18 September 2024 records that Mrs Colefax was to let her have the details "shortly". Nothing had been communicated at or before execution. The name of Elias Vardy and the terms of the trust reached her only in the letter of 11 November 2024, eight weeks later. The trust fails.

3.4 In re Keen, Evershed v Griffiths [1937] Ch 236 gives the same answer from the other direction and disposes of two arguments that might be made for Mr Vardy:

(a) It confirms as an independent ground that a testator cannot reserve the power to make future unattested dispositions. The 11 November letter is precisely such a disposition.

(b) It shows that the clause 5 wording cannot be used to cure the defect. In Keen the will contemplated a future notification while the actual communication had been earlier, and the trust failed because parol evidence may not contradict the express terms of the will. Here the position is reversed: clause 5 says the trusts had "already" been communicated when in fact they had not. The evidence again contradicts the will. The past tense in clause 5 would have been an advantage to Mr Vardy if the communication had genuinely preceded execution. It is of no help where it did not.

3.5 The same conclusion follows from In the Goods of Smart [1902] P 238 if the letter is treated as a document to be incorporated by reference. A document can only be incorporated if it was in existence at the date of the will. The 11 November letter was not.

3.6 In re Boyes, Boyes v Carritt (1884) 26 Ch D 531 settles where the money goes. A legatee who has accepted an obligation cannot take beneficially, but where the terms were not properly communicated he holds on a resulting trust for the estate. Mrs Osei has in any event confirmed she makes no personal claim. The 100,000 pounds therefore falls into residue and passes to the Harlestone Riverside Trust under clause 6.

3.7 There is one distinction from Boyes worth recording. In Boyes nothing at all was communicated in the testator's lifetime. Here the terms were communicated, but too late to satisfy the rule for a half secret trust. The result is the same.

4. WHAT THE EXECUTORS SHOULD DO

4.1 Clause 5. Pay Mrs Osei nothing. Add the 100,000 pounds to residue and account for it to the Harlestone Riverside Trust, with a short written explanation, since the charity is entitled to know why the residue is larger than the will suggests. Mr Vardy should be told in writing that the intended gift has failed, and why, so that he can take his own advice. He is 19 and should not simply hear nothing.

4.2 Clause 4. Pay the 150,000 pounds to Mr Mawdsley, because that is what the will directs and the executors' duty under the will is to pay the legacy. The executors do not administer the secret trust, and they should not withhold the legacy on the strength of an account they have from a third party. What the executors must not do is distribute the estate as though they know nothing about it. See paragraph 5.

4.3 If Mr Mawdsley maintains his position, Miss Nkemdi's remedy is a claim against him personally as trustee. She does not presently know of any of this. The executors should consider whether it is proper for them to leave her in ignorance of a trust of which they have been informed, and if the position is not resolved they may apply to the court for directions rather than decide it for themselves.

5. THE CONDUCT POINT ON MR MAWDSLEY

5.1 Mr Mawdsley is not our client. He came to this firm, told our assistant solicitor that he had accepted an obligation to pass on the whole legacy, then said that he intended to keep it because nothing is in writing and nobody could contradict him, and asked us not to tell the executors.

5.2 We cannot agree to that. We act for the executors. They are entitled to know material information we hold about the estate they are administering, and we cannot conduct the administration on a basis we know to be incomplete. Nor can we allow the firm's silence to be used to make a plan of that kind work.

5.3 Mr Mawdsley should be told, in writing, that we act for the executors and not for him, that we cannot advise him, that we are not able to keep what he told us from our clients, and that he should take his own independent advice before doing anything further. He should be given the opportunity to correct or add to what he said before anything is passed on.

5.4 The conversation and the file note should then be reported to the executors, and the matter recorded on the file.

6. SOURCES NOT RELIED ON

6.1 Section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925 requires writing only for a declaration of trust respecting land. Both legacies are of money. Section 53(2) also preserves resulting, implied and constructive trusts.

6.2 King v The Chiltern Dog Rescue [2015] EWCA Civ 581 concerns a donatio mortis causa. There was no lifetime delivery and no gift made in contemplation of impending death. Neither legacy is a deathbed gift.

6.3 Fuller v Strum [2001] EWCA Civ 1879 concerns knowledge and approval. The will is not challenged. Mrs Colefax read it through, there is a full attendance note and nothing excites suspicion about the execution itself.

6.4 Ainslie, The Law of Trusts in Scotland states that Scots law has no doctrine corresponding to the English secret trust. That is a description of another jurisdiction and has no bearing on an estate in England and Wales.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Mr Mawdsley volunteered to the firm's assistant solicitor that he had accepted an obligation to pass the entire 150,000 pounds to Miss Nkemdi, then said that as there was nothing in writing and nobody who could contradict him he intended to keep it, and asked that the executors not be told. He is not the firm's client and no retainer or client confidentiality arises from his visit. The firm acts for the executors, who are entitled to material information about the estate they are administering, and the firm cannot allow its silence to be the thing that makes his plan work or conduct the administration on a basis it knows to be incomplete. The competent candidate refuses the request, writes to Mr Mawdsley making clear that the firm acts for the executors, cannot advise him and cannot keep what he said from its clients, invites him to correct or add to his account and tells him to take independent advice, then reports the conversation and the file note to the executors. The candidate also considers Miss Nkemdi, who has no idea any of this exists, and advises the executors that if the position is not resolved the proper course is an application to the court for directions rather than the executors deciding a contested trust question themselves.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses Ottaway v Norman for clause 4, Blackwell v Blackwell and In re Keen for clause 5, In re Boyes for the destination of the failed legacy, and In the Goods of Smart as a supporting route. Cites accurately. Discards the Law of Property Act, donatio mortis causa, knowledge and approval and Scottish material, each in a line, and says why.Treating section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925 as fatal to the clause 4 trust because nothing was in writing. The subsection applies to land, and both legacies are of money.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsTells the executors what to pay and to whom, in figures, for both legacies. Recognises that the executors administer the will and not the secret trust, so they pay Mr Mawdsley his legacy while still passing on what they know. Deals with telling Mr Vardy and telling the charity.Advising the executors to refuse to pay the clause 4 legacy to Mr Mawdsley and to pay Miss Nkemdi directly, which is not the executors' function and is not what the will directs, or leaving Mr Vardy to find out for himself.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsConclusion first, then one section per legacy so the contrast is visible, no research trail. The timing rule is stated once, precisely, and then applied twice.Setting out the whole law of secret trusts before reaching the facts, so the two legacies are never separately analysed and the answer runs out of time on clause 5.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawGets both answers and the reason for the difference: for a fully secret trust communication and acceptance may come at any time in the testator's lifetime, whereas for a half secret trust the communication must be at or before execution. Concludes correctly that the clause 5 money passes on a resulting trust into residue and so to the charity, not to Mrs Osei and not to Mr Vardy.Applying one rule to both legacies. A candidate who applies the strict half secret timing rule to clause 4 wrongly fails a valid trust; a candidate who applies the relaxed fully secret rule to clause 5 wrongly upholds a failed one. Either error loses the station.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with all three elements of the fully secret trust separately rather than asserting the conclusion, addresses the evidential weakness of an oral trust and why an admission recorded in a file note meets it, uses In re Keen's contradiction point on the past tense in clause 5, and works out where the 100,000 pounds actually goes rather than stopping at "the trust fails". Notes that no writing is required for a trust of money.Concluding that the clause 5 trust fails and stopping there, so the note never says whether Mrs Osei keeps the money, it passes on intestacy, or it augments residue. Failing to see that the residuary gift is to a charity, so the failure has a real beneficiary, is part of the same omission.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSees that Mr Mawdsley has told the firm he accepted the obligation and now intends to keep the money, and has asked the firm to keep that from its own clients. Concludes that the firm cannot agree, that he must be told the firm acts for the executors and cannot advise him and cannot withhold what he said, that he should take independent advice, and that the executors must then be told. Considers whether Miss Nkemdi can properly be left in ignorance and raises an application to the court for directions if the position is not resolved.Agreeing to keep the conversation confidential because Mr Mawdsley asked, which confuses a duty owed to a client with a request from a third party and would leave the firm assisting a plan it knows about. The opposite error is to treat the firm as owing Mr Mawdsley advice, or to write to Miss Nkemdi directly without instructions from the executors.

Examiner notes

This station is built on one distinction and rewards candidates who state it before applying it. For a fully secret trust, where the will shows an absolute gift, communication and acceptance may happen at any point in the testator's lifetime, before or after execution. For a half secret trust, where the will itself shows the legatee takes as trustee, communication must be at or before execution. Clause 4 satisfies the first, clause 5 fails the second by eight weeks, and the two legacies therefore go in opposite directions on facts that look parallel. Candidates who identify only one category and apply its rule to both get one answer right by accident and the other wrong. The second discriminator is what happens to the failed 100,000 pounds. Many notes conclude that the clause 5 trust fails and stop, leaving the executors no better off. In re Boyes supplies the answer: the trustee cannot take beneficially where she accepted an obligation, so the money is held on a resulting trust for the estate and augments residue, which here means the charity receives it. The In re Keen contradiction point is the mark of a strong answer: clause 5 asserts that the trusts had "already" been communicated when they had not, and parol evidence cannot contradict the will. Weaker candidates seize on section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925 and fail the clause 4 trust for want of writing, forgetting that the subsection is about land. The donatio mortis causa, knowledge and approval and Scottish sources should each be dismissed in one line.

Written station 24: Without prejudice letter to a claimant's solicitors proposing settlement of a claim against an estate

Legal writing  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  30 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

Haleworth Croft LLP

Solicitors

2 Crown Chambers

Northwich

Harrow and Vance

17 Bellamy Street

Northwich

3 March 2027

WITHOUT PREJUDICE SAVE AS TO COSTS

Dear Sirs

Estate of Margaret Ellwood deceased

Your client: Mr Dennis Ashcroft

Our clients: the executors, Rosalind Ellwood and Toby Ellwood

We have your letter of 24 February 2027 and have taken instructions.

Our clients accept that your client is entitled to bring a claim. They do not accept the claim as you have put it, and in particular they do not accept the sum sought. They would nonetheless prefer to resolve this without proceedings, and this letter contains an offer.

1. What is agreed

Our clients accept that your client lived with the deceased at 9 Thurlby Lane from March 2017 until her death on 14 October 2026, that they lived in the same household as a couple, and that he cared for her in her final year. They do not dispute his standing to apply under section 1(1)(ba). They speak of him without hostility and one of them asked us to record that he was good to their mother.

2. Why the claim as put is not accepted

2.1 The standard. Your client is not a surviving spouse. Under section 1(2)(b) the provision that falls to be considered is what would be reasonable for his maintenance, not what would be a fair share of the estate. A claim for one half outright is a claim on the spouse standard and there is no basis for it.

2.2 His resources. He owns 4 Coldstream Court outright and it is unencumbered. We are instructed that the tenant vacated in December 2026 and that the flat has been empty since. Your letter presents him as having nowhere to live while describing an asset that is a one bedroom flat standing empty. If that is wrong we will consider anything you send us, but as matters stand his housing need is capable of being met from his own property.

2.3 His income. He has the state pension, an occupational pension of £3,900 and rental income which will resume when the flat is relet, together with savings of £11,000. Those are modest resources and our clients do not say he has no need. They say the need is a maintenance need of limited size, not a claim to half of an estate.

2.4 The deceased's decision. The will was made on 19 May 2021, four years into the relationship. The deceased knew of the relationship and knew of the flat. Her reasons are relevant under section 3(1)(g), and testamentary freedom remains the starting point.

2.5 The beneficiaries. Our clients accept they are both in work. Section 3 requires their resources and needs to be weighed, not disregarded, and the fact that a beneficiary is employed does not turn the estate into a fund available to a claimant.

3. The estate

So that you can advise your client properly, we enclose the estate schedule. It shows a net estate of £726,650 before any award, comprising 9 Thurlby Lane at £395,000, a second property at 11 Sallowfield Road at £215,000 which is let, bank balances of £72,500, quoted investments of £41,500, a car and contents. No inheritance tax is payable. Your letter refers only to 9 Thurlby Lane and we do not want your client's advice to proceed on an incomplete picture.

4. Our clients' offer

Without prejudice save as to costs, and in full and final settlement of all claims your client has or may have against the estate, the deceased or our clients in any capacity, our clients offer:

(a) a lump sum of £72,000, payable within 28 days of a signed settlement agreement or within 14 days of completion of the sale of 9 Thurlby Lane, whichever is the later;

(b) a licence for your client to occupy 11 Sallowfield Road on the expiry of the current tenancy, rent free save for utilities and council tax, for six months, to allow him to arrange the reletting or occupation of his own flat. If he would prefer not to wait for that tenancy to end, our clients will instead pay a further £4,800 towards rented accommodation, in place of the licence;

(c) each party to bear its own costs;

(d) the settlement to be recorded in a written agreement containing a full and final release, with no admission of liability.

The offer is open for acceptance for 21 days from the date of this letter, after which it is withdrawn without further notice. It is made without prejudice save as to costs and our clients reserve the right to draw it to the attention of the court on the question of costs.

5. The time limit

The grant issued on 6 January 2027, so the six month period under section 4 expires on 6 July 2027. Our clients do not want your client driven to issue merely to protect his position, and issuing would add cost on both sides for no benefit.

We therefore propose a standstill agreement in the usual form, suspending the running of time under section 4 until 30 September 2027, our clients undertaking not to take any point on the expiry of the period during that time and not to distribute the estate in the meantime beyond ordinary administration expenses. If you send us a draft we will turn it round within three working days.

6. Mediation

If the offer is not accepted, our clients propose mediation before any proceedings are issued, at a date within eight weeks, costs of the mediator to be shared. They will not decline an invitation to mediate.

We look forward to hearing from you within 21 days.

Yours faithfully

Haleworth Croft LLP

Enc: Estate schedule as at 14 October 2026

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Paragraph 6 of the attendance note records one executor instructing the firm to tell the other side that the estate is all tied up in the house and that there is nothing else in it. Paragraph 7 records that the estate in fact includes a second property worth £215,000, savings of £68,200 and investments of £41,500, and that the claimant's solicitors appear not to know of the second property. The instruction is an instruction to make a statement the firm knows to be false. A competent candidate refuses it without being asked to consider ethics, states the true composition of the estate in the letter, encloses or offers the schedule, and explains that the claim can still be resisted honestly on the maintenance standard and the claimant's own empty flat. Saying nothing about the estate while knowing the other side is working from an incomplete picture is equally objectionable as misleading by omission. The point engages the SRA Principles on honesty and integrity and paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits misleading others whether by act or omission. There is a secondary point that the executors are also the sole beneficiaries, so the firm must be alert to the difference between their duties as personal representatives and their personal interest in defeating the claim.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the nine year cohabitation, the date and terms of the 2021 will, the empty flat at 4 Coldstream Court, the pension and rental figures, the true net estate of £726,650 including the second property, the grant date of 6 January 2027 and the resulting section 4 expiry.Argues the merits in the abstract without deploying the empty flat, the date of the will or the size and composition of the estate, so the letter contains an offer with no reasons behind the figure.
Use a logical structure.SkillsMarks the letter without prejudice save as to costs at the head, concedes what is not in issue, then sets out the grounds of resistance, then the estate, then the offer as numbered terms with a deadline, then the standstill and mediation.Buries the offer in a paragraph of narrative, gives no deadline, or omits the without prejudice marking so that a settlement offer becomes an open document.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsWrites to a professional opponent who must be able to advise his own client on it: concedes standing rather than fighting a hopeless point, gives the other side the material it needs to value the claim, keeps the door open with a standstill and mediation, and pitches the offer at a figure the executors have authorised while leaving room to move.Writes an aggressive letter that concedes nothing and offers nothing usable, or opens at the executors' full authority of £90,000 so there is nowhere left to go.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsSolicitor to solicitor: firm, courteous, no rhetoric, no personal remarks about the claimant, terms stated so precisely that they could be transcribed into an agreement without further negotiation about what they mean.Adopts the tone of the letter of claim and trades insults about the relationship, or writes in a soft client facing register that leaves the offer terms vague on timing, costs and the scope of the release.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly identifies the claimant as a cohabitant under section 1(1)(ba), correctly applies the maintenance standard in section 1(2)(b) rather than the spouse standard, deploys the section 3 factors including section 3(2A), and correctly states the section 4 six month period as running from the grant on 6 January 2027.Applies the surviving spouse standard, or asserts that the claim is bound to fail because the deceased was entitled to leave her estate as she wished, or dates the six month period from the death rather than from the grant.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers standing, the standard, the applicant's resources, the beneficiaries' position, the deceased's reasons, the size and nature of the net estate, the forms of order available under section 2 so that the offer of a licence is properly grounded, the section 4 deadline and a standstill, and the risk of distribution pending the claim.Argues the merits and makes an offer but never addresses the limitation position at all, leaving the other side no option but to issue, or ignores that a court can order a licence or transfer of property and so offers only cash.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses to write that the estate is tied up in the house with nothing else in it, because the schedule shows a second property worth £215,000 and £114,000 of bank and investment assets. Puts the true position to the other side, provides the schedule, and resolves the point without abandoning the client: the estate can be described accurately and the claim still resisted on the maintenance standard.Adopts Toby's instruction and describes the estate as consisting of the house, or dodges it by saying nothing at all about the estate while knowing the other side is proceeding on an incomplete picture, which is misleading by omission.

Examiner notes

This is a negotiation on paper and it is marked as one. A pass requires an actual offer: a number, a payment mechanism, a costs position, a scope of release and a deadline. Candidates who write a strong merits letter and end with an invitation to make proposals have not done the task. The two substantive discriminators are the maintenance standard, which disposes of the claim for half the estate in one sentence, and the empty flat at 4 Coldstream Court, which is the fact that changes the value of the claim and which sits in paragraph 4 of the attendance note rather than in the letter of claim. The limitation point is the quiet third one: the grant issued on 6 January 2027, and a letter that does not offer a standstill forces the other side to issue proceedings, which is precisely what the executors are paying to avoid. The trap is Toby's instruction in paragraph 6, which is phrased as commercial common sense and is an instruction to lie. A candidate who repeats it fails the ethics criterion outright, and a candidate who quietly omits any description of the estate has only half seen the point.

Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures

Written station 25: Proposed purchase of a trading unit from a director's own company

Case and matter analysis  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO HELENA BRAITHWAITE-OKONJO

Client: Larkspur Fabrication Limited

Matter: Proposed acquisition of Unit 7 Foxholme Trading Estate

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 14 January 2027

1. Summary of advice

The purchase is a substantial property transaction under section 190 Companies Act 2006 and cannot lawfully proceed on the current board resolution alone. It requires approval by ordinary resolution of the members, either before completion or as a condition of the contract. Iain Rothbury has not made an adequate declaration of interest, and the independent valuation of £395,000 suggests the company is being asked to pay £85,000 more than the property is worth. We should advise the board, not Mr Rothbury alone, that the transaction must be paused, the valuation disclosed to all three directors, and the price renegotiated or independently re-tested before any approval is sought. We also have a conflict and confidentiality problem which must be resolved before we go any further.

2. Relevant facts

The company proposes to buy a freehold unit for £480,000 from Rothbury Holdings Limited. Mr Rothbury is a director of our client and the sole shareholder and sole director of the seller. The company's net assets are £3,140,000. An independent valuation dated 21 November 2026, commissioned by the seller and covering the whole freehold including the yard, gives a market value of £395,000. Mr Rothbury told the board only that he had 'a small interest' in the seller, did not mention the valuation, and has asked us not to send it to the other directors. He holds 550 of the 1,000 issued shares.

3. Substantial property transaction, section 190

Rothbury Holdings is a company controlled by Mr Rothbury and is therefore a person connected with him. The company is acquiring a non-cash asset from a connected person. The asset is substantial: at £480,000 it exceeds £100,000, so the second limb of section 191(2) is satisfied and the 10% test does not need to be considered.

Members' approval by ordinary resolution is therefore required. It can be given before the arrangement is entered into, or the arrangement can be made conditional on approval being obtained, which is the safer route because it allows the company to sign but not be bound. Approval can be given by written resolution or at a general meeting. Section 190 does not disenfranchise the interested member, so Mr Rothbury may vote his 550 shares and can pass an ordinary resolution on his own. That is a significant practical point: compliance with section 190 will not on its own protect the minority or cure the price problem.

The consequences of proceeding without approval are set out in section 195. The arrangement would be voidable at the company's instance, and Mr Rothbury, Rothbury Holdings and any director who authorised the arrangement would be liable to account for any gain and to indemnify the company for its loss. Ms Devereux-Ng, who voted in favour, is exposed to that liability. Mr Tasker abstained, which helps him but is not a complete answer if he took no further step.

4. The board resolution of 8 January 2027

The articles are the unamended model articles. Model article 14 provides that where a proposed decision of the directors concerns an actual or proposed transaction or arrangement with the company in which a director is interested, that director is not to be counted as participating in the decision making process for quorum or voting purposes. None of the exceptions applies: the members have passed no ordinary resolution disapplying the article, the interest is not one which could be said to be unlikely to give rise to a conflict, and it does not arise from any permitted cause.

Mr Rothbury was interested in the purchase. He owns and controls the seller. He nonetheless chaired the meeting and voted in favour, and the minute records his vote as one of the two in favour. The resolution is accordingly defective, and the company should not act on it.

The defect is curable. Excluding Mr Rothbury there are still two directors, which is the quorum under model article 11. The board should meet again, Mr Rothbury should make a full declaration under section 177 and then take no part in the quorum or the vote, and Ms Devereux-Ng and Mr Tasker should take the decision on a properly informed basis with the valuation in front of them. The minute should record the exclusion and record that the remaining two directors constituted a quorum.

5. Directors' duties

Declaration of interest, section 177. Mr Rothbury had to declare the nature and extent of his interest before the company entered into the transaction. Saying he had 'a small interest' was neither accurate nor complete: he owns and controls the seller. He must now make a full declaration, and section 177(3) requires a further declaration where an earlier one was inaccurate.

Conflict of interest, section 175. The duty to avoid conflicts does not apply to a conflict arising from a transaction with the company, because that is dealt with by section 177, but the underlying conflict remains real and is what model article 14 addresses by excluding him from the quorum and the vote.

Duty to promote the success of the company, section 172, and duty of reasonable care, skill and diligence, section 174. Steering the company towards paying £480,000 for an asset his own surveyor valued at £395,000, while withholding that valuation from his co-directors, is capable of being a breach of both. Ms Devereux-Ng's decision to vote through a purchase of this size with no valuation, after asking for one and being brushed off, is also open to criticism under section 174.

Ratification. A breach can be ratified by ordinary resolution under section 239, but on ratification Mr Rothbury's votes and those of anyone connected with him are disregarded. He therefore cannot ratify his own breach. Ratification would depend on Ms Devereux-Ng and Mr Tasker, who together hold the remaining 450 shares.

6. Options for the company

(a) Do not proceed. The company has no obligation to buy and the lease does not expire until 30 September 2027, so there is time.

(b) Proceed at a renegotiated price supported by a fresh independent valuation instructed by Larkspur, not by the seller, with the contract conditional on members' approval under section 190 and with Mr Rothbury absenting himself from the board decision.

(c) Proceed at £480,000 with section 190 approval passed on Mr Rothbury's votes. This is technically achievable but leaves the company having overpaid, leaves the directors exposed under sections 172 and 174, and creates an obvious platform for a minority shareholder complaint later. I do not recommend it.

I recommend option (b).

7. Professional conduct

Our client is the company, and our instructions come from the board as a whole. Mr Rothbury has asked us to withhold the valuation from his co-directors. We cannot do that. Withholding information material to the company's decision would put us in breach of our duty to act in the best interests of our client and would risk us misleading the other directors. The valuation itself came to us from Mr Rothbury in his capacity as a director of our client and in connection with this matter, so there is no obstacle to putting it before the whole board.

I have also considered our conflict position. We act for Larkspur alone. Rothbury Holdings is on the other side of this transaction and its interests conflict with our client's on price and on the terms of sale, so we cannot act for it and it should be told in writing to instruct its own solicitors. If the firm has acted for Rothbury Holdings or for Mr Rothbury personally on any earlier matter, that should be checked on the system before we go further, because a duty of confidentiality to a former client would need to be considered alongside our duty to keep the board informed.

If Mr Rothbury insists that the valuation is not shown to the board, we should tell him plainly that we cannot continue on that basis and we should consider ceasing to act, giving the company reasonable notice.

8. Next steps

1. Write to all three directors enclosing the valuation and this analysis.

2. Instruct an independent valuation for Larkspur.

3. Confirm to Rothbury Holdings that it must take separate advice.

4. Prepare a conditional contract and the section 190 ordinary resolution once the price is settled.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The majority shareholder director instructs the firm to withhold from his fellow directors an independent valuation showing the company is about to overpay by £85,000, and asserts that he controls the company so can approve whatever is needed. The client is the company and instructions come from the board, so the firm cannot suppress information material to the board's decision without acting against its client's interests and misleading the other directors. A competent candidate says the valuation must go to the whole board, is clear that the firm acts for Larkspur alone and cannot also act for Rothbury Holdings on the opposite side of the same transaction so the seller must instruct its own solicitors, and states that if the director persists the firm should cease to act on reasonable notice.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsPicks out every fact that drives the analysis: the seller is controlled by a director, the £480,000 price against £395,000 market value, net assets of £3,140,000, the vague 'small interest' disclosure, the abstention and the vote in favour, the 550 share holding, and the request to withhold the valuation. Facts are used, not merely listed.Recites the board minute at length but never draws out that Rothbury Holdings is a connected person, or misses that the valuation covers the yard and so defeats the director's stated objection to it.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsGives the board real options with a clear recommendation, explains that section 190 approval can be obtained on the majority's votes alone but does not solve the overpayment, and sets out practical next steps with an order and a reason.Stops at 'an ordinary resolution is required' and offers no advice on price, on the exposure of the other two directors, or on what the board should actually do next.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA properly headed report to the partner, in short numbered sections, within the word limit, with a summary of advice at the front.Writes a letter to the client instead of a report to the partner, or produces undivided prose that buries the recommendation.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies section 190 and section 191 accurately, identifies Rothbury Holdings as a connected person, applies the £100,000 limb rather than fumbling the 10% test, states the section 195 consequences correctly, and identifies that the articles are the unamended model articles and that model article 14 excluded Mr Rothbury from the quorum and the vote on the purchase, so that the board resolution of 8 January 2027 is defective and must be re-taken by the other two directors.Treats the transaction as requiring a special resolution, or asserts that the interested member cannot vote on the section 190 resolution, confusing section 190 approval with section 239 ratification, or takes the board resolution at face value, so that the report never tells the partner the board decision itself has to be taken again without the interested director.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers section 177 and the inadequacy of the declaration, sections 172 and 174 in relation to the price and the withheld valuation, section 195 liability of the approving director as well as the interested director, and the section 239 restriction on ratification votes.Deals only with section 190 and ignores the directors' general duties entirely, or ignores the exposure of Ms Devereux-Ng who voted in favour.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies that the client is the company and not the majority shareholder, refuses to withhold the valuation from the board, recognises that the firm acts for Larkspur alone, that Rothbury Holdings is on the other side of the transaction and must be told to instruct its own solicitors, and that any earlier retainer for Mr Rothbury or his company should be checked for a former client confidentiality issue, and states what the firm will do if the director insists, including ceasing to act.Accepts the instruction not to send the valuation to the other directors, or treats the request as a confidentiality question owed to Mr Rothbury personally.

Examiner notes

A pass turns on getting section 190 right and then going further. The trap is to stop at 'members' approval by ordinary resolution' and treat the station as a one point question. The third discriminator, and the one most candidates miss, is model article 14. The minute states in terms that the chair voted, and the chair is the seller. On the unamended model articles he could not be counted for quorum or voting purposes, so the resolution is defective and the answer to the partner's first question includes re-taking it. The other two discriminators are, first, appreciating that the interested member's votes count for section 190 approval but not for section 239 ratification, so procedural compliance is easy but ratification of the underlying breach is not; and second, refusing the instruction to withhold the valuation. Candidates who treat the majority shareholder as the client rather than the company will fail the ethics criterion however good the company law is.

Written station 26: Excluded minority shareholder and a proposed buy out

Case and matter analysis  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

REPORT TO RAVINDER CHAUDHRY-BLOOM

Client: Delphine Marchetti-Hall

Matter: Coppergate Interiors Limited, exclusion and proposed buy out

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 11 May 2027

1. Summary

Delphine has a strong unfair prejudice petition. The company is a quasi partnership, she has been excluded from management and starved of any return while the other two have more than doubled their own pay. The likely remedy is an order that they buy her shares at a price valued pro rata and without a minority discount, which the accountants put at about £340,000. The offer of £110,000 is a discounted minority figure and is not a reasonable offer. The settlement terms are worse than the price: clause 5.3 would gag her from speaking to a regulator, a tax authority or law enforcement, and we cannot advise her to sign it. I recommend we counter at £340,000 with a costs contribution, hold firm on no minority discount and on the removal of clause 5.3, and use her costs exposure as a reason to settle early rather than as a reason to accept a low figure.

2. The claims

Unfair prejudice, section 994 Companies Act 2006. Delphine must show that the company's affairs have been conducted in a manner unfairly prejudicial to her interests as a member. The strength of the claim rests on the company being a quasi partnership: three former colleagues, each contributing capital, each working full time, each a director from incorporation, sharing profit by dividend, and no shareholders' agreement. Where a company is formed on that basis the courts recognise a legitimate expectation of participation in management, and exclusion from management is the paradigm case of unfair prejudice.

Her removal as a director is open to challenge on its own terms, and we should not accept Hesketh Vane's assertion that it was validly passed. The attendance note records that the general meeting of 12 March 2027 was held on short notice. Under section 307 of the Companies Act 2006 a general meeting of a private company may be called by shorter notice than 14 days only if that is agreed by a majority in number of the members having a right to attend and vote who together hold at least 90 per cent in nominal value of the shares carrying that right. Mr Okoye-Brandt and Ms Sedgemoor hold 75 per cent between them, and Delphine, who holds the other 25 per cent, did not agree: she attended and spoke against. On the face of it the meeting was not validly called. Separately, section 168(2) requires special notice of a resolution to remove a director, which by section 312 must be given to the company at least 28 days before the meeting and passed on to the members with the notice of the meeting or, if that is not practicable, by advertisement or other permitted means at least 14 clear days beforehand. Neither requirement sits with a meeting on short notice, and section 169 gave her the right to have written representations circulated. We should ask Hesketh Vane, before we respond on price, to confirm the date on which notice of the meeting was given, the date on which special notice of the resolution was received by the company, whether all the members consented to short notice, and to provide a copy of the notice and the minutes.

If the removal was invalid Delphine remains a director, with the right to be paid, to attend board meetings and to see the company's books. That does not change the shape of her section 994 claim, because even a procedurally impeccable removal would be unfair on a quasi partnership, but it is an independent point and a real lever in the negotiation, and it is inconsistent with the other side's opening assertion that she has no complaint arising from her removal.

The exclusion is aggravated by two further matters:

(a) No dividend since March 2026, so she now receives nothing at all from her investment.

(b) The doubling of the other two directors' salaries from £70,000 to £145,000 each. The accountants regard the increase as above a commercial rate and calculate that it removed about £150,000 from distributable profits in one year. Paying away profits as remuneration to the majority, so that nothing is left to distribute to the excluded minority, is itself prejudicial conduct.

The rebate concerns she raised in 2026 give context and explain the timing, but we should not pitch the case on an allegation of impropriety we cannot yet evidence.

3. Remedies

The usual remedy on a successful petition is an order under section 996 that the majority buy the petitioner's shares. On a quasi partnership where the petitioner has been unfairly excluded, the court's normal approach is to value the shares pro rata to the value of the whole company, with no minority discount, because the petitioner is not a willing seller of a minority stake but someone being forced out. On the accountants' figures that is approximately £340,000.

The court will also decide the valuation date and can direct adjustments for conduct, including adding back excessive remuneration. Both points favour Delphine here.

Just and equitable winding up is available in principle but is a remedy of last resort, and it would destroy value. It is a threat to be used sparingly, not a route we want.

A derivative claim is not the right vehicle. Her complaint is about the conduct of the company's affairs towards her as a member, not primarily about a wrong done to the company.

4. What is wrong with the offer

(a) Price. £110,000 sits at the bottom of the discounted range in the accountants' note. It applies a discount of roughly 68% to the pro rata figure. On the likely court approach no discount applies at all, so the offer is short by about £230,000.

(b) A reasonable offer can defeat a petition. If the majority made a proper offer, pro rata, with an independent valuer, equality of access to information and a contribution to costs, that could remove the unfairness and leave her without a remedy. This offer does none of those things, so it does not protect them.

(c) Clause 5.3. It purports to prevent her from communicating with any regulatory body, tax authority, law enforcement agency or court, without limit of time, with immediate repayment of the whole price if she breaches it. That goes far beyond a legitimate confidentiality clause. We should not advise her to sign it and we should not be party to putting it forward. It must come out, and clauses 5.1, 5.2 and 5.4 must be narrowed accordingly.

(d) Clause 6.1 waives unknown and future claims. It should be limited to claims arising out of her shareholding and directorship up to the date of the agreement.

(e) The 14 day deadline is pressure, not a real constraint.

5. Negotiation strategy

Her objectives, in order: a fair price, a clean exit, speed, and limited costs exposure. She has told us she cannot fund a long fight, so our aim is a negotiated exit within a few months, not a trial.

Opening position. Respond promptly on a without prejudice save as to costs basis. Counter at £340,000 as the pro rata figure, plus a contribution to costs, payment in full on completion, and deletion of clause 5.3. Set out the quasi partnership analysis, the exclusion, the withheld dividends and the remuneration add back, and enclose the accountants' note in outline so they understand the case is evidenced.

What we can concede. The precise figure within the range the accountants' own numbers support. Their enterprise value range is £1.30 million to £1.45 million, and the £1.36 million equity figure at the midpoint implies net debt of about £15,000, so the equity range is about £1.285 million to £1.435 million and a 25 per cent pro rata share is about £321,000 to £359,000. We open at the midpoint of £340,000 and have room to move down towards £321,000, but not below it, because below £321,000 we are conceding more than the only valuation evidence on the file supports. Payment in two or three instalments over a short period with security or a personal guarantee, if that unlocks the deal. A properly drawn mutual confidentiality clause and a non disparagement clause that runs both ways. A reasonable non solicitation of customers for a limited period. Dropping the costs contribution if the price is right.

What we cannot concede. Any minority discount, which is the whole battleground. Any restriction on reporting to a regulator, tax authority or law enforcement. Any clawback of the entire consideration for a breach of confidentiality.

Process. Propose a joint instruction of an independent valuer with access to the books, or a short mediation. Either gives a fast route to a number and controls costs. Make clear that if no agreement is reached we will present a petition, and that the offer they have made will not protect them on costs.

6. Professional conduct

Two points.

First, we should not advise Delphine to accept clause 5.3, and if the other side press it we should say plainly why it is objectionable. A non disclosure clause must not prevent a person from reporting to a regulator or to law enforcement.

Second, the folder of company emails and management accounts Delphine downloaded on 3 January 2027. Those documents belong to the company, not to her, whatever email account they sat in. We should tell her not to send them to us, not to review them and not to use them, and we should take her instructions on quarantining and returning them. If we take them in and use them, we risk a serious problem for her and for us later. We can obtain the same financial information properly through disclosure or through a jointly instructed valuer.

7. Next steps

1. Advise Delphine in writing on the offer, on costs, and on the documents she must not send us.

2. Reply to Hesketh Vane rejecting the offer and countering at £340,000 with clause 5.3 deleted.

3. Propose a jointly instructed valuer or a mediation within eight weeks.

4. Prepare a draft petition in the background so the timetable is credible.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two unflagged points. The draft settlement contains a non disclosure clause that in terms prevents the client from communicating with any regulatory body, tax authority, law enforcement agency or court, without time limit and with repayment of the whole consideration on breach. A solicitor must not advise a client to accept, or seek to impose, a confidentiality term that prevents a report to a regulator or to law enforcement, and the clause must be struck out rather than traded away for a higher price. Separately, the client has downloaded company emails and management accounts to a personal drive and offers to send them to the firm. Those documents belong to the company. The competent candidate declines them, tells the client not to use or circulate them, and obtains the financial information properly through a jointly instructed valuer or disclosure.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsDraws out the quasi partnership indicators, the sequence of exclusion, the cessation of dividends, the salary increase and its effect on distributable profits, the pro rata and discounted valuation figures, the terms of clause 5.3, and the downloaded documents.Narrates the falling out without identifying the facts that make the company a quasi partnership, or overlooks the salary increase, which is the second head of prejudice.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsAnswers the client's real question, which is whether to take the money, with a clear recommendation, a specific counter figure, a costs aware strategy that respects her inability to fund a long fight, and a concession list that separates what is tradable from what is not.Sets out the law on section 994 and stops, giving no counter figure and no view on whether the offer should be accepted.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA report to the partner with a front end summary and a distinct negotiation section, precise about figures and about what is and is not conceded.Writes to the client rather than the partner, or produces a discursive essay with the negotiation advice scattered through it.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies section 994 correctly, recognises that even a valid removal does not preclude a finding of unfair prejudice on a quasi partnership, and identifies the buy out order as the normal remedy valued pro rata without a minority discount. Tests rather than assumes the validity of the removal, and identifies that a general meeting of a private company can be held on short notice only with the agreement of a majority in number holding at least 90 per cent in nominal value, which the two continuing shareholders could not give on a 75 per cent holding, and that special notice under sections 168(2) and 312 is not compatible with short notice.Concludes there is no claim because the removal resolution was validly passed, or accepts the other side's assertion that the removal was validly passed and so never notices that the meeting was held on short notice which 75 per cent of the members could not authorise, or accepts the minority discount as the correct measure and treats £110,000 as broadly right.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAdds the excessive remuneration and dividend starvation heads, addresses the valuation date and conduct adjustments, explains that a properly made offer could defeat the petition and why this one does not, and correctly discards winding up and a derivative claim with reasons.Deals only with exclusion from management, ignores the remuneration point, or advances a derivative claim as the primary route.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses to advise the client to accept a clause preventing disclosure to a regulator, tax authority or law enforcement, insists it is deleted, and deals firmly with the company documents the client downloaded by telling her not to send or use them.Treats clause 5.3 as an ordinary confidentiality term to be traded for price, or accepts the downloaded folder as useful evidence.

Examiner notes

This station separates candidates on two things. First, the minority discount.
