A candidate who accepts that a 25% holding is worth a discounted figure has failed the client by about £230,000, and the accountant's note deliberately supplies both figures to see which one the candidate reaches for. Second, the negotiation section must be a strategy and not a summary: an opening number, a target range, an explicit list of what may be conceded and what may not, and a process proposal that controls cost, because the client has said she cannot fund a long fight. A third discriminator is buried in one phrase of the attendance note: the meeting of 12 March 2027 was held on short notice. Seventy five per cent cannot authorise short notice in a private company, and special notice of a removal resolution cannot be squared with it either, so the removal is very probably invalid. Candidates who take the other side's word for it lose a free point. The trap is clause 5.3. Many candidates read it as ordinary boilerplate and offer to negotiate it down, when the correct answer is that a clause barring a report to a regulator or law enforcement cannot be advised on or imposed at all.

Written station 27: Liquidator's allegations against a former director

Case and matter analysis  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO MARGUERITE OLLERENSHAW

Client: Gareth Llewellyn-Fisk

Matter: Sablefield Interiors Limited (in liquidation), liquidator's allegations

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 4 June 2027

1. Summary

All three allegations are serious and, on the present material, all three are likely to succeed to a substantial degree. The vehicle sale is a transaction at an undervalue with a connected person and the statutory defence looks unavailable. Both September payments are preferences, and both carry a presumption of the necessary desire as against Gareth which we will struggle to rebut, the payment to Brantwood because his personal guarantee was discharged by it so that he is himself a person preferred. The wrongful trading claim is strong from about October 2026 and arguable from July 2026. Gareth also faces a real prospect of disqualification. I recommend an early approach to the liquidator with a view to a negotiated settlement rather than a defended trial. Separately, Gareth has asked us to prepare a board minute recording a meeting that was never minuted and to say he did not see the March accounts until November. We cannot do either and he must be told so plainly.

2. Allegation 1, the vehicle sale

Test. A transaction at an undervalue is a gift or a transaction for a consideration significantly less in value than the consideration provided by the company, entered into within two years ending with the onset of insolvency, at a time when the company was unable to pay its debts or where it became unable to do so in consequence.

Application. The sale was on 14 May 2026, well within two years of the 12 February 2027 onset. The company received £15,000 for a fleet independently valued at £46,000 and £48,000. On any view that is significantly less. Imogen Llewellyn-Fisk is Gareth's spouse and so an associate of a director and a connected person, which means insolvency at the time is presumed and the burden is on us to show the contrary. Given that the March 2026 management accounts show net liabilities of £512,000, cash of £31,000, a fully drawn overdraft, HMRC arrears of £206,000 and £389,000 of trade creditors over 90 days overdue, we cannot rebut that presumption.

Defence. Section 238(5) requires all three of good faith, the purpose of carrying on the business, and reasonable grounds for believing the transaction would benefit the company. The second limb is arguable: moving to subcontracted couriers saved about £4,000 a month and the proceeds went into the company's account to pay wages. The third limb is the problem. Selling to the director's wife with no valuation, at about a third of value, does not support reasonable grounds for believing the transaction benefited the company. The fact that she sold four vehicles within three months and did not use them undermines the account further.

Evidence needed. Contemporaneous documents on the courier decision and the saving, any condition reports or MOT records for the vehicles, the sale invoices, and what the four vehicles fetched on resale. If they resold near the liquidator's valuations the position worsens.

Likely outcome. An order restoring the position, in practice payment of the difference, in the region of £31,000 to £33,000.

3. Allegation 2, the two payments on 9 September 2026

Test. A preference is a payment or other step which puts a creditor, surety or guarantor into a better position on insolvent liquidation than they would otherwise be in, made at a relevant time, where the company was influenced by a desire to produce that effect. The relevant time is six months before onset, or two years where the recipient is connected. The company must have been insolvent at the time or become so in consequence.

(a) The £60,000 to Gareth. He is a director and therefore a connected person, so the two year period applies and 9 September 2026 is comfortably inside it. He is a creditor of the company for his loan, and repayment plainly put him in a better position than the dividend he would receive in the liquidation, which on the figures will be small. Because he is connected, the desire to prefer is presumed. To rebut it he would have to show the payment was made for some proper commercial reason unconnected with improving his own position. His own explanation is that he needed the money for his mortgage. That does not rebut the presumption, it confirms it. This allegation will succeed.

(b) The £84,000 to Brantwood. This payment prefers two people on two different footings and must be analysed twice.

Against Brantwood. Brantwood is a creditor and was paid in full while no other unsecured creditor received anything. Brantwood is not connected, so the six month period applies and 9 September 2026 is within six months of the 12 February 2027 onset. There is no presumption of desire against Brantwood, so the liquidator must prove it, and genuine commercial pressure is a real answer: Brantwood was threatening to sue and the company needed continuing supply.

Against Gareth. This is the point the liquidator will press and it is much harder for us. Section 239(4)(a) applies not only to a creditor but to a surety or guarantor for the company's debts. Gareth guaranteed Brantwood's debt on 3 March 2024, and paying Brantwood £84,000 discharged his personal exposure pro tanto, so it put him into a better position on an insolvent liquidation than he would otherwise have been in. He is therefore a person preferred in his own right. Because he is a director he is connected with the company under section 249(a), so the relevant time is the two year period in section 240(1)(a), not six months, and the desire to produce that effect is presumed against him under section 239(6). To rebut it he would have to show the company was influenced only by pressure from Brantwood and not at all by the release of his guarantee. He accepted in our meeting that he knew the guarantee was there, no other creditor was paid, and he took £60,000 for himself on the same day. I do not think the presumption can be rebutted, and an order can be made against him under section 241 as the person benefited.

Evidence needed. The Brantwood correspondence and any letter before claim, evidence of supply continuing after payment and of what alternative suppliers were available, the guarantee itself, and the bank statements for the period.

Likely outcome. £60,000 recoverable with little prospect of resistance, and £84,000 likely to be recovered from Gareth personally on the guarantee analysis, whatever the position as against Brantwood itself.

4. Allegation 3, wrongful trading

Test. The company has gone into insolvent liquidation. The question is whether, at some point before winding up, Gareth knew or ought to have concluded that there was no reasonable prospect of the company avoiding insolvent liquidation, judged by the standard of a reasonably diligent person with the general knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of someone carrying out his functions, and with the knowledge and experience he actually has.

Application. Two candidate dates.

The liquidator will argue for 20 April 2026, when the board received accounts showing balance sheet insolvency, a forecast inability to pay debts from July 2026, and an accountant's memorandum recommending immediate advice from a licensed insolvency practitioner and declining to treat the company as a going concern. Gareth read them. He is the sole executive director, so the objective standard is that of a competent managing director, and his actual knowledge was high.

Our answer to that date is that the accountant identified two routes out, new funding of £600,000 or the Hollisbrook contract, and that a director may properly continue for a period while a genuine rescue is pursued. That is a real argument for April to about September 2026.

It collapses from October 2026. Gareth accepted in terms that after October there was no realistic chance. The Hollisbrook contract was never signed and no funding arrived. Between October 2026 and January 2027 the company took £212,000 of customer deposits, of which £198,000 was never fulfilled or refunded. Taking deposits from customers who will never be supplied, at a time when the director accepts there was no realistic chance, is close to the worst version of this claim.

Defence. Section 214(3) requires every step with a view to minimising loss to creditors that he ought to have taken. He took none. He did not take insolvency advice until January 2027, did not stop taking deposits, did not ring fence them and did not call a creditors' meeting. The defence is not available on these facts.

Likely outcome. A contribution measured by the increase in net deficiency from the relevant date. If the date is October 2026 the deposits figure of £198,000 is the obvious anchor, and the liquidator will argue for more.

5. Other exposure

Misfeasance under section 212 gives the liquidator a summary route for breach of the duties to promote the success of the company and to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence, and covers the same ground.

Disqualification is a real risk and is separate from any money claim. The conduct here, a connected party sale at an undervalue with no valuation, self repayment, payment of a guaranteed creditor and continued deposit taking with no insolvency advice, is the pattern that produces disqualification, for a period between 2 and 15 years. Gareth should understand that settling the liquidator's claims does not resolve the disqualification risk, although cooperation and early settlement help.

6. Recommendation

We should make an early, without prejudice approach to the liquidator, concede the £60,000 repayment and the undervalue element, recognise that the £84,000 is very likely recoverable from him on the guarantee analysis, and negotiate on quantum and on the wrongful trading date. Defending everything would be expensive and, on this evidence, would fail on at least two heads while worsening his position on conduct. We should advise Gareth in writing on the realistic range of his total exposure and on the disqualification risk, and take his instructions on his ability to fund a settlement.

7. Professional conduct

Gareth has asked us to prepare a board minute dated May 2026 recording a decision that was never minuted, and has asked whether it would help to say he did not see the March management accounts until November 2026. We cannot prepare a document that gives the false impression of being a contemporaneous record, and we cannot advance a case we know to be untrue. He told us he received the accounts on 20 April 2026 and read them. Putting forward November would be misleading the liquidator and, in due course, the court.

We should tell him this directly, explain that a document created now and presented as a May 2026 minute would seriously aggravate his position if discovered, and record the advice on the file. If he insists on either course, we must cease to act.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client asks the firm to prepare a board minute dated May 2026 recording a decision that was never minuted, on the basis that the meeting happened and writing it up now is a formality, and asks whether it would help to say he first saw the March management accounts in November 2026 when he has already told the firm he received and read them on 20 April 2026. Creating a document that presents itself as a contemporaneous record, and advancing an account the solicitor knows to be false, would mislead the liquidator and the court. A competent candidate refuses both, explains that a manufactured minute would seriously worsen the client's position if discovered, records the advice on file, and states that if the client insists the firm must cease to act.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsFixes the key dates against the 12 February 2027 onset, identifies the wife and the director as connected persons, uses the accountant's memorandum and the October 2026 admission as the two candidate wrongful trading dates, and picks up the personal guarantee and the unfulfilled deposits.Recites the liquidator's letter without testing each date against the statutory period, or misses that Brantwood is not connected so a different period and no presumption apply.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsReaches a view on likely outcome and quantum for each head, recommends early negotiated settlement with reasons, and tells the client about disqualification as a separate risk that money does not cure.Sets out the tests without any assessment of prospects, or advises defending everything with no regard to cost or to the client's conduct exposure.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsOne section per allegation, each with test, application, defence, evidence and likely outcome, and a summary at the front giving the overall picture.Runs the three allegations together so that the preference analysis and the wrongful trading analysis contaminate each other.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies the correct relevant time to each claim, applies the connected person presumptions to the right parties, recognises that the guaranteed payment to Brantwood preferred both an unconnected creditor and a connected surety so that the two year period and the presumption of desire apply as against the client himself, states the section 238(5) defence as cumulative, and states the wrongful trading test and the every step defence accurately. A weak answer applies the six month preference period to the director's £60,000, treats the Brantwood payment as raising no presumption at all merely because Brantwood is unconnected, or reverses the burden by requiring the liquidator to prove desire where the person preferred is connected.Applies the six month preference period to the director's £60,000, or reverses the burden by requiring the liquidator to prove desire where the recipient is connected.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all three claims, distinguishes the position of the connected and unconnected recipients, identifies the guarantee as the route to a preference order against the client personally, considers both candidate wrongful trading dates, and adds misfeasance and disqualification.Omits the significance of the personal guarantee, or ignores disqualification, which is the consequence the client cares about most once it is explained.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses to prepare a minute presented as a contemporaneous May 2026 record, refuses to advance the November account which the client has already contradicted, explains the consequences to the client, records the advice, and states that the firm must cease to act if he insists.Treats the minute as a harmless tidying up exercise because the meeting is said to have happened, or offers to draft it with a note that it was prepared later.

Examiner notes

The pass point is disciplined application of three different tests with three different relevant times and two different presumptions. The commonest technical error is treating both September payments identically: the director is connected, so on his own £60,000 the two year period and the presumption of desire apply. The Brantwood payment is the real discriminator, because it prefers two people on two different tests. Against Brantwood, which is unconnected, the six month period applies and the liquidator must prove desire, so commercial pressure is a real answer. Against the client, whose personal guarantee was discharged by the payment, section 239(4) makes him a person preferred in his own right, and because he is connected the two year period applies and desire is presumed against him. A strong candidate separates the two. The second discriminator is the wrongful trading date. Weak candidates pick 20 April 2026 and stop; strong candidates argue that a genuine rescue attempt could justify continuing for a period and then concede that the position is indefensible from October 2026, which is when unfulfilled customer deposits start accruing. The ethics trap is deceptively soft, because the client frames the minute as mere paperwork for a meeting that really happened.

Written station 28: Retirement clause for a partnership agreement

Legal drafting  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  45 minutes

Model answer

18. RETIREMENT

Notice of retirement

18.1 A Partner may retire from the Firm by giving to each of the other Partners not less than six months' written notice expiring on any date, or such shorter notice as all of the other Partners may agree in writing.

18.2 A Partner shall be deemed to have retired from the Firm with immediate effect on the date on which any of the following occurs:

18.2.1 he is removed from the register of veterinary surgeons, or his registration is suspended;

18.2.2 a bankruptcy order is made against him;

18.2.3 he has been unable by reason of ill health or incapacity to perform his duties under this Agreement for an aggregate of more than nine months in any period of twelve months.

18.3 Where a Partner is deemed to have retired under clause 18.2, the Retirement Date is the date on which the relevant event in clause 18.2 occurs, and this clause 18 applies to that Partner as the Outgoing Partner and to the other Partners as the Continuing Partners in the same way as on a retirement under clause 18.1.

Continuation of the Firm

18.4 The retirement of a Partner shall not dissolve the Firm. The Continuing Partners shall carry on the practice of the Firm in partnership together, and this Agreement shall continue to apply to them.

18.5 With effect from the Retirement Date the Outgoing Partner's share in the capital, assets, profits and losses of the Firm shall accrue to the Continuing Partners in the proportions in which they share profits between themselves immediately after the Retirement Date.

Accounts and payment out

18.6 The Firm shall instruct the Firm's accountants to prepare accounts of the Firm made up to the Retirement Date. The Firm shall use reasonable endeavours to procure that those accounts are signed off within three months after the Retirement Date. Those accounts shall be binding on the Outgoing Partner and the Continuing Partners save in the case of manifest error.

18.7 Subject to clause 18.9, the Firm shall pay to the Outgoing Partner:

18.7.1 the balance standing to the credit of his capital account as shown by the accounts prepared under clause 18.6;

18.7.2 the balance standing to the credit of his current account as shown by those accounts; and

18.7.3 his share of the profits of the Firm to the Retirement Date as shown by those accounts.

18.8 The sums payable under clause 18.7 shall be paid by twelve equal monthly instalments, the first instalment falling due one month after the date on which the accounts prepared under clause 18.6 are signed off. Interest shall accrue on the outstanding balance from the Retirement Date at the rate of 4% per annum and shall be paid with each instalment. The Firm may at any time pay all or any part of the outstanding balance early without penalty.

18.9 The Firm may set off against any sum payable under clause 18.7 any sum then due from the Outgoing Partner to the Firm.

18.10 The Outgoing Partner shall not be entitled to any payment in respect of the goodwill of the Firm, which has never been and shall not be valued in the accounts of the Firm.

Indemnity and continuing liability

18.11 The Continuing Partners shall jointly and severally indemnify the Outgoing Partner and keep him indemnified against all debts, liabilities and obligations of the Firm, whether incurred before or after the Retirement Date, and against all claims, demands, costs and expenses arising out of them, except to the extent that any such liability arises from the Outgoing Partner's own fraud, wilful default or breach of this Agreement.

18.12 As soon as reasonably practicable after the Retirement Date the Continuing Partners shall:

18.12.1 give written notice of the Outgoing Partner's retirement to every client, supplier, bank and other person who has had dealings with the Firm before the Retirement Date;

18.12.2 cause notice of the Outgoing Partner's retirement to be advertised in the London Gazette;

18.12.3 remove the Outgoing Partner's name from the Firm's notepaper, website, signage, practice literature and from its registrations with the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, NHS bodies and insurers; and

18.12.4 procure the removal of the Outgoing Partner from every bank mandate, direct debit authority and other authority under which he can bind the Firm.

18.13 The Outgoing Partner shall not after the Retirement Date hold himself out, or knowingly permit himself to be held out, as a partner in or as being connected with the Firm, and shall not use the name of the Firm.

18.14 The Outgoing Partner and the Continuing Partners shall each execute all such documents and do all such things as the other may reasonably require in order to give effect to this clause 18.

Confidentiality

18.15 The Outgoing Partner shall not at any time after the Retirement Date use or disclose to any person any confidential information of the Firm, including information relating to its clients, their animals, its employees, its suppliers, its fees or its business methods, except:

18.15.1 to the extent that the information is or becomes public other than through his breach of this clause;

18.15.2 to the extent required by law or by any court or regulatory authority of competent jurisdiction; or

18.15.3 for the purpose of making a report or disclosure to the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, to any other regulator, or to any law enforcement agency.

Restrictions

18.16 The Outgoing Partner shall not, for a period of twelve months from the Retirement Date:

18.16.1 carry on or be engaged, concerned or interested in any veterinary practice within three miles in a straight line of either of the Firm's surgeries at Ashgrove Lane, Craven Arms and at Pellingford Road, Church Stretton;

18.16.2 solicit or endeavour to entice away from the Firm, or deal with or accept instructions from, any person who was a client of the Firm at the Retirement Date and with whom the Outgoing Partner had material dealings in the twelve months ending on the Retirement Date;

18.16.3 solicit or endeavour to entice away from the Firm, or employ or engage, any person who was at the Retirement Date a Partner in or an employee of the Firm and with whom the Outgoing Partner worked in the twelve months ending on the Retirement Date.

18.17 Nothing in clause 18.16.1 prevents the Outgoing Partner from holding for investment purposes not more than 3% of any class of securities listed or dealt in on a recognised investment exchange.

18.18 Each of the restrictions in clause 18.16 is a separate and independent restriction. If any restriction is held to be void or unenforceable but would be valid and enforceable if part of its wording were deleted or the period or area were reduced, that restriction shall apply with such modification as is necessary to make it valid and enforceable.

18.19 The Outgoing Partner acknowledges that the restrictions in clause 18.16 are no greater than is reasonably necessary to protect the legitimate business interests of the Firm.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two points are buried in the attendance note. A continuing partner asks for a five year, twenty five mile restraint to be inserted anyway, expressly to frighten the outgoing partner into signing, even after being told it is very unlikely to be enforceable. Drafting a restriction the firm knows to be excessive, for the purpose of intimidating the other side, is not something a solicitor should do, and the competent candidate drafts the reasonable covenant the partners actually agreed. The confidentiality clause should also be drafted so it cannot bar a report to the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, to another regulator or to law enforcement. Both of those points are resolved inside the drafting and are what the ethics criterion marks. Separately, the outgoing partner has telephoned asking the firm to check the clause is fair to him too. The firm acts for the partnership, and his interests conflict with those of the continuing partners on payment terms, indemnity and covenants, so the firm cannot advise him and he must be told to take independent advice. That conversation is for the partner and does not belong in the clause, and the candidate is not expected to address it in the document.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsUses the agreement's defined terms consistently, drafts in short numbered sub clauses with one obligation each, states who owes what to whom, and avoids ambiguity about dates, rates and periods.Reproduces the vagueness of the old clause, for example 'the Firm shall pay him what is due', or uses undefined expressions such as 'the retiring vet' alongside the defined 'Outgoing Partner'.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsGroups the clause into a sensible sequence, notice and deemed retirement, continuation, accounts and payment, indemnity and protection from continuing liability, confidentiality, restrictions, with headings and consistent numbering.Drafts an undifferentiated block of sub clauses in the order of the attendance note, so payment terms sit between the covenants and the deemed retirement events.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawProvides accurately for the agreed commercial terms, uses the 4% rate and the twelve instalments as instructed, and drafts restrictions limited to three miles and twelve months with a severance provision, so that the restraint stands a real prospect of being enforceable.Inserts the five year, twenty five mile covenant the partner asked for, which would very probably be an unreasonable restraint of trade and unenforceable, or invents an interest rate instead of using the one given.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers every instructed term and, importantly, deals with continuing liability properly: notice to existing clients and counterparties, London Gazette advertisement, removal from the mandate, no holding out, and an indemnity extending to debts incurred after the retirement date.Omits the London Gazette advertisement and the notice to existing customers, so the outgoing partner remains exposed to being treated as an apparent member of the firm, or gives an indemnity limited to pre retirement debts only.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDeclines to draft the deliberately excessive covenant put forward to frighten the outgoing partner, drafts the reasonable restriction the partners agreed, and drafts confidentiality so that it cannot prevent a report to the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, another regulator or law enforcement.Drafts the five year covenant on instructions, or drafts an unqualified perpetual confidentiality obligation that would on its face bar the outgoing partner from reporting a clinical or regulatory concern.

Examiner notes

The document is the whole of the answer, so the ethics criterion has to be satisfied through the drafting itself and not through a commentary. Two things separate a pass from a fail. First, protection from continuing liability: an outgoing partner remains at risk of being treated as an apparent member by anyone who dealt with the firm and has not been told he has gone, so a competent clause requires actual notice to existing clients and counterparties and a London Gazette advertisement, and backs it with an indemnity that covers debts incurred after the retirement date, not just before it. Candidates who give only a pre retirement indemnity have missed the point of the clause. Second, the covenant. The attendance note tempts the candidate to draft the five year, twenty five mile restraint that a partner still wants; drafting it is both bad law and a conduct failure, and the answer is the twelve month, three mile version with severance. A strong candidate also carves regulatory and law enforcement reporting out of the confidentiality obligation without being asked.

Written station 29: Pre emption on transfer clause in a shareholders' agreement

Legal drafting  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  45 minutes

Model answer

9. TRANSFER OF SHARES: PRE EMPTION

9.1 Restriction on transfer

No Shareholder shall Transfer any Share, or any interest in any Share, except in accordance with this clause 9. Any purported Transfer in breach of this clause 9 shall be of no effect, and the Shareholders shall procure that the Board declines to register it and that the Company does not enter the transferee in the register of members.

9.2 Permitted transfers

Clauses 9.3 to 9.11 do not apply to a Transfer of Shares by a Shareholder:

(a) to that Shareholder's spouse, civil partner or adult child;

(b) to the trustees of a trust under which no person other than that Shareholder and the persons described in clause 9.2(a) has any beneficial interest; or

(c) where the Shareholder is a body corporate, to a wholly owned subsidiary of that Shareholder,

provided in each case that the transferee first executes and delivers to the Company a Deed of Adherence, and provided that if the transferee under clause 9.2(c) ceases to be a wholly owned subsidiary of the transferor it shall immediately Transfer the Shares back to the transferor.

9.3 Transfer Notice

9.3.1 A Shareholder who wishes to Transfer any Shares (the Seller) shall give written notice to the Company (a Transfer Notice) specifying the number of Shares it wishes to Transfer (the Sale Shares) and the price per Share at which it is willing to sell them (the Proposed Price).

9.3.2 A Transfer Notice, once given, may not be withdrawn except under clause 9.6.3.

9.3.3 A Transfer Notice constitutes the Company the agent of the Seller for the sale of the Sale Shares in accordance with this clause 9.

9.4 Deemed Transfer Notice

9.4.1 A Shareholder shall be deemed to have given a Transfer Notice in respect of all of the Shares then held by it, without specifying a Proposed Price, immediately on the occurrence of any of the following:

(a) the Shareholder dies;

(b) a bankruptcy order is made against the Shareholder, or the Shareholder enters into any composition or arrangement with its creditors generally;

(c) where the Shareholder is a body corporate, a liquidator, administrator or administrative receiver is appointed over it or any of its assets; or

(d) the Shareholder ceases for any reason to be a director of the Company, or (where the Shareholder is or has been an employee of the Company) ceases for any reason to be an employee of the Company, and for the avoidance of doubt it is sufficient that the Shareholder ceases to hold either office or employment and it is not necessary that the Shareholder ceases to hold both.

9.4.2 On a deemed Transfer Notice no Proposed Price is specified, clause 9.6.1 does not apply, and the price of the Sale Shares shall be the Fair Value determined under clause 9.6.2.

9.4.3 This clause 9.4 applies to every Shareholder without exception and irrespective of the number of Shares held.

9.5 Offer to Continuing Shareholders

9.5.1 Within 5 Business Days of receipt or deemed receipt of a Transfer Notice the Company shall offer the Sale Shares in writing to each Shareholder other than the Seller (each a Continuing Shareholder), stating the number of Sale Shares, the price and the date by which the offer must be accepted.

9.5.2 The Sale Shares shall be offered to the Continuing Shareholders in the proportions which the number of Shares held by each of them bears to the total number of Shares held by all of them, in each case excluding the Sale Shares.

9.5.3 Each Continuing Shareholder may accept its entitlement in whole or in part by written notice to the Company within 20 Business Days of the date of the offer, and may in that notice state that it wishes to be offered further Sale Shares not taken up by others.

9.5.4 If any Sale Shares are not accepted, the Company shall within 5 Business Days offer them to those Continuing Shareholders who accepted their full entitlement and indicated that they wished to take more, in the proportions set out in clause 9.5.2, and that Continuing Shareholder shall have 10 Business Days to accept. The process in this clause 9.5.4 shall be repeated until either all the Sale Shares have been accepted or no Continuing Shareholder wishes to take any more.

9.5.5 An acceptance given under this clause 9.5 is irrevocable, but is conditional on the price being determined where clause 9.6 applies and on the Seller not withdrawing under clause 9.6.3.

9.6 Price

9.6.1 If Continuing Shareholders accept all the Sale Shares at the Proposed Price, the price shall be the Proposed Price.

9.6.2 If the Proposed Price is not accepted, or if clause 9.4 applies, the price shall be the fair value of the Sale Shares (the Fair Value) determined by an independent chartered accountant (the Valuer) agreed between the Seller and the Continuing Shareholders or, failing agreement within 10 Business Days of the date on which either of them first proposes a Valuer, appointed on the application of any of them by the President for the time being of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales. The Valuer shall act as an expert and not as an arbitrator and, in the absence of fraud or manifest error, the Valuer's determination shall be final and binding on the parties. The Valuer shall determine the Fair Value as that proportion of the value of the entire issued share capital of the Company which the Sale Shares bear to that entire issued share capital, without any discount or premium by reason of the Sale Shares constituting a minority or a majority holding. The Company shall give the Valuer access to such information as the Valuer reasonably requires.

9.6.3 Within 10 Business Days of being notified of the Fair Value the Seller may withdraw the Transfer Notice by written notice to the Company, in which case the Sale Shares shall not be sold and the Seller may not give a further Transfer Notice for 6 months. This clause 9.6.3 does not apply to a deemed Transfer Notice under clause 9.4.

9.6.4 The Valuer's costs shall be borne as to one half by the Seller and as to the other half by those Continuing Shareholders who accept Sale Shares, in proportion to the Sale Shares accepted, save that (a) where a Proposed Price was specified and the Fair Value is within 5 per cent of the Proposed Price, those Continuing Shareholders shall bear all of the Valuer's costs, and (b) on a deemed Transfer Notice under clause 9.4, where no Proposed Price is specified, the Valuer's costs shall be borne as to one half by the Seller and as to the other half by those Continuing Shareholders who accept Sale Shares, in proportion to the Sale Shares accepted.

9.7 Completion of sales to Continuing Shareholders

Completion of the sale of accepted Sale Shares shall take place at the registered office of the Company at 11.00 on the tenth Business Day after the later of the last acceptance and the determination of the Fair Value, when the Seller shall deliver a duly executed stock transfer form and the relevant share certificate, or an indemnity for a lost certificate, against payment of the price in cleared funds.

9.8 Enforcement of sale

If the Seller fails to complete, the Company shall be entitled to receive the price on the Seller's behalf and any director of the Company (other than the Seller or, where the Seller is a body corporate, any director appointed by it) is irrevocably authorised as the Seller's attorney to execute the stock transfer form on the Seller's behalf, and the Board shall register the transfer. The Company shall hold the price on trust for the Seller without interest pending delivery of the share certificate.

9.9 Sale to a third party

9.9.1 Any Sale Shares not accepted under clause 9.5 may be Transferred by the Seller to any person within 60 days of the expiry of the last acceptance period, provided that:

(a) the price is not less than the Proposed Price or, where clause 9.6.2 applied, the Fair Value;

(b) the terms are no more favourable to the buyer than those on which the Sale Shares were offered to the Continuing Shareholders;

(c) the Transfer is of all and not some only of the unaccepted Sale Shares, and is a bona fide sale for cash consideration; and

(d) the buyer has first executed and delivered to the Company a Deed of Adherence.

9.9.2 The Board shall not register any Transfer under clause 9.9.1 unless the Seller has satisfied the Board that each of the conditions in clause 9.9.1 has been met.

9.10 Company's obligations

The Shareholders shall exercise their voting rights, as shareholders and, so far as the law permits, as directors, to give effect to this clause 9 and to procure that the Company does so.

9.11 Time

Time is of the essence in relation to each period specified in this clause 9.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The firm is asked to act for all three shareholders and the company on the same agreement. Dr Fasso then asks for clause 9.4 to be drafted so that the deemed transfer notice bites only on a holder of fewer than 50 shares, which on its face looks general but in fact exempts her alone, and she says the others do not need to know and will not read it closely. There are two points and a competent candidate deals with both inside the document. First, this is a conflict of interest between clients on the same matter: the shareholders have differing interests in the very clause being drafted, and there is no substantially common interest and no competing for the same objective, so the firm cannot act for all of them on this clause. Second, and more immediately, drafting the disguised carve out would mean producing a document intended to mislead the other two clients, which is a breach of the duties of honesty and integrity and of the prohibition on misleading others, and it would also be a breach of the duty to act in the best interests of each of those clients. The candidate resolves it by drafting the clause as the heads of terms provide, applying to every shareholder, and by stating expressly that it applies irrespective of the size of the holding, so that the point cannot be lost. The conversation about the conflict is for the partner and does not belong in the clause.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsUses the defined terms exactly as they appear in clause 1 and does not redefine them. Introduces new defined terms such as Transfer Notice, Sale Shares, Continuing Shareholder, Proposed Price and Fair Value cleanly at first use. Uses "shall" for obligations and "may" for options consistently. Every period is expressed in Business Days from a stated trigger event, so no obligation is left floating.Keeps the previous adviser's vague wording such as "a fair price", "act reasonably and in good faith" or "anybody at any price", which cannot be enforced because it gives the court nothing to measure. Or redefines terms already defined in clause 1, creating an internal conflict.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsFollows the actual sequence of events: prohibition, permitted transfers, transfer notice, deemed transfer notice, offer round and second round, price and valuation, completion, default, third party sale, then supporting provisions. Sub clauses are numbered so that later clauses can cross refer to them, and the cross references are correct.Drafts the price mechanism before the offer mechanism, or buries the deemed transfer notice inside the general transfer notice clause, so the reader cannot follow what happens when. Or writes long unnumbered paragraphs that cannot be cross referred to at all.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawRecognises that the model articles contain no pre emption on transfer and that a shareholders' agreement binds only the parties, so the clause must both prohibit a non complying transfer and oblige the shareholders to procure that the Board refuses to register it. Makes acceptances irrevocable but conditional. Provides a workable expert determination with a fallback appointor and expressly excludes a minority discount. Gives the Seller a right to withdraw after valuation but disapplies that right on a deemed transfer notice, since otherwise a departing employee could always defeat the compulsory transfer.Drafts a clause that says a shareholder "shall not" transfer without offering the shares first, but provides no consequence, so the transfer still passes title and the Board can still register it. Or gives the Seller an unqualified right to withdraw, including on a deemed transfer notice, which destroys the compulsory transfer the heads of terms require.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers every point in the heads of terms, including the proportionate offer excluding the sale shares, the repeating second round among those who took their full entitlement, the appointment mechanism for the valuer and who bears the valuer's costs including the 5 per cent qualification, the 60 day third party window with the price floor and no better terms condition, the Deed of Adherence, the closed list of permitted transfers with the subsidiary claw back, and the deemed transfer triggers of death, bankruptcy and ceasing to be an employee or director. Adds the machinery a working clause needs, such as completion, a power of attorney on default and time of the essence.Omits the second round of offers, so shares not taken up go straight to an outsider, or omits the Deed of Adherence, so a buyer takes the shares free of the agreement. Or leaves out any default machinery, so the only remedy against a Seller who refuses to complete is a fresh action for specific performance.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDrafts clause 9.4 so that it applies to every shareholder without distinction, and says so expressly. Does not insert Dr Fasso's fifty share carve out in any form, whether openly or by the disguised threshold she suggested. The document that is produced is the one all three clients agreed in the heads of terms.Drafts the deemed transfer notice so that it applies only to a shareholder holding fewer than 50 Shares. That single line hands the largest shareholder a secret advantage over the two clients the firm is also acting for, it does not reflect the heads of terms all three signed, and it is drafted to be missed. It fails this criterion on its own.

Examiner notes

The pass or fail turns on two things: whether the clause is enforceable at all, and whether the candidate resisted the carve out. On enforceability, remember the model articles contain no pre emption on transfer, which the partner points out. A shareholders' agreement is only a contract between the parties, so a clause that merely says a shareholder shall not transfer without offering first leaves the transfer perfectly valid once made. The clause has to prohibit the transfer, make a non complying transfer of no effect and oblige the shareholders to procure that the board declines to register it. Candidates who write elegant machinery but leave that out have drafted something that fails the moment a shareholder ignores it. On ethics, the trap is the way the request is buried at the end of an attendance note among perfectly ordinary instructions, and the fact that Dr Fasso frames it as a drafting preference rather than as deceit. A surprising number of candidates simply give the client what she asked for because she holds half the shares and appears to be the person instructing. She is not the only client. The other classic error is forgetting the second round of offers, which is expressly in the heads of terms and is the point of a proportionate pre emption clause in a three shareholder company.

Written station 30: Retirement and profit share clauses in a partnership agreement

Legal drafting  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  45 minutes

Model answer

8. PROFITS, LOSSES AND DRAWINGS

8.1 Partnership Shares

The net profits of the Business remaining after the payments required by clauses 8.2 and 8.3, and the losses of the Business, shall belong to and be borne by the Partners in the following shares (each a "Partnership Share"):

Mr Fenwick Adeyemi-Rowe 45 per cent

Ms Corinne Vasiliev 35 per cent

Mr Otto Lindqvist 20 per cent

8.2 Partners' salaries

8.2.1 Before any division of profits under clause 8.1, each Partner shall be paid out of the profits of the Business the following annual salary:

Mr Fenwick Adeyemi-Rowe 62,000 pounds

Ms Corinne Vasiliev 58,000 pounds

Mr Otto Lindqvist 46,000 pounds

8.2.2 The salaries in clause 8.2.1 are a first charge on the profits of the Business and are payable in equal monthly instalments in arrear whether or not the profits of the Business are sufficient to pay them.

8.2.3 If in any accounting period the profits are insufficient to pay the salaries and the interest under clause 8.3 in full, the deficiency shall be treated as a loss of the Business and borne by the Partners in their Partnership Shares.

8.2.4 The salary of a Partner shall be apportioned on a daily basis for any period of less than a full accounting period.

8.3 Interest on capital

Before any division of profits under clause 8.1, and after payment of the salaries under clause 8.2, each Partner shall be paid interest on the amount of that Partner's capital for the time being at the rate of 4 per cent a year, accruing daily and payable at each Accounting Date. This clause 8.3 applies in place of clause 4.3.

8.4 Drawings

8.4.1 Each Partner may draw monthly on the last Working Day of each month, on account of that Partner's salary and Partnership Share, such sum as the Partners shall determine in advance for the accounting period in question. If the Partners do not determine a rate for an accounting period, the rate for the previous accounting period shall continue to apply.

8.4.2 If on the signing of the Accounts for an accounting period it appears that a Partner has drawn more than the total of that Partner's salary, interest on capital and Partnership Share of profit for that period, that Partner shall repay the excess to the Partnership within 30 days of the date on which the Accounts are signed.

8.4.3 A sum repayable under clause 8.4.2 and not repaid when due shall carry interest at 4 per cent a year from the due date until payment.

8.5 Current accounts

A current account shall be maintained in the Accounts for each Partner, to which shall be credited that Partner's salary, interest on capital and Partnership Share of profit, and to which shall be debited that Partner's drawings, share of losses and any other sum owing by that Partner to the Partnership.

8.6 Variation

No variation of clause 8.1, 8.2 or 8.3 shall have effect unless it is in writing and signed by all the Partners.

9. RETIREMENT OF A PARTNER

9.1 Voluntary retirement

Any Partner may retire from the Partnership by giving to each of the other Partners not less than 6 months' written notice expiring on an Accounting Date. This clause 9.1 applies to each Partner on the same terms.

9.2 Compulsory retirement

A Partner shall be treated as having retired, and shall cease to be a Partner:

(a) on the Accounting Date falling at the end of the accounting period in which that Partner attains the age of 68;

(b) immediately on that Partner being removed from the register of veterinary surgeons maintained by the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, or being suspended from that register;

(c) immediately on a bankruptcy order being made against that Partner, or on that Partner entering into any composition or arrangement with his or her creditors generally; or

(d) on the date on which the other Partners give written notice to that Partner, where that Partner has by reason of ill health been unable to perform his or her duties under this agreement for an aggregate of 9 months in any period of 12 months.

Clause 9.2(a) applies to each Partner without exception, and may be disapplied in a particular case only by the agreement in writing of all the Partners.

9.3 Continuation of the Partnership

9.3.1 The Partnership shall not be dissolved by the retirement of a Partner under this clause 9, and the continuing Partners shall carry on the Business.

9.3.2 On and from the date on which a Partner ceases to be a Partner (the "Retirement Date"), the Partnership Share and the share of capital and goodwill of the outgoing Partner (the "Outgoing Partner") shall accrue to the continuing Partners in the proportions which their Partnership Shares bear to each other immediately before the Retirement Date.

9.3.3 Section 42 of the Partnership Act 1890 shall not apply as between the Outgoing Partner and the continuing Partners, and the Outgoing Partner shall be entitled only to the payments provided for by clause 9.4.

9.3.4 Where the Retirement Date is not an Accounting Date, the Partnership shall instruct the Partnership's accountants to prepare a set of accounts of the Partnership made up to the Retirement Date on the same bases and using the same policies as the Accounts, and in this clause 9 references to the Accounts at the Retirement Date are references to those accounts. Those accounts shall be prepared as soon as reasonably practicable and in any event within 3 months of the Retirement Date, and shall be binding on the Outgoing Partner and the continuing Partners save in the case of manifest error.

9.4 Payments to the Outgoing Partner

9.4.1 The Partnership shall pay the Outgoing Partner:

(a) the amount of that Partner's capital as shown in the Accounts at the Retirement Date;

(b) the credit balance (if any) on that Partner's current account at the Retirement Date, together with that Partner's salary, interest on capital and Partnership Share of profit down to the Retirement Date; and

(c) that Partner's share of the goodwill of the Business, calculated in accordance with clause 9.5.

9.4.2 The Partnership may set off against any sum payable under clause 9.4.1 any sum owing by the Outgoing Partner to the Partnership, including any excess drawings under clause 8.4.2.

9.4.3 The sums payable under clauses 9.4.1(a) and 9.4.1(b) shall be paid within 3 months of the Retirement Date or, if later, within 21 days of the date on which the accounts referred to in clause 9.3.4 are signed.

9.4.4 The sum payable under clause 9.4.1(c) shall be paid by four equal instalments, the first 3 months after the Retirement Date and the remainder at intervals of 6 months thereafter, and interest at 4 per cent a year shall accrue on the outstanding balance from the Retirement Date and be paid with each instalment.

9.4.5 If any instalment is more than 21 days late the whole of the balance then outstanding, with accrued interest, shall become immediately payable on written demand by the Outgoing Partner, and shall be a debt due from the continuing Partners jointly and severally.

9.5 Valuation of goodwill

The share of the Outgoing Partner in the goodwill of the Business shall be that Partner's Partnership Share immediately before the Retirement Date of a sum equal to one and one half times the average annual net profit of the Business for the three completed accounting periods ending on or before the Retirement Date, calculated before partners' salaries under clause 8.2 and interest on capital under clause 8.3, save that where the Retirement Date is not an Accounting Date the profit for the period from the last Accounting Date to the Retirement Date shall be annualised on a daily basis and substituted for the earliest of those three accounting periods. The calculation shall be made by the Partnership's accountants, who shall act as experts and not as arbitrators, and whose certificate shall in the absence of fraud or manifest error be final and binding. Their fees shall be borne by the Partnership.

9.6 Indemnity and release

9.6.1 The continuing Partners shall indemnify the Outgoing Partner against all debts, liabilities and obligations of the Partnership incurred before, on or after the Retirement Date, other than any liability arising from that Partner's own fraud or wilful default.

9.6.2 The continuing Partners shall use all reasonable endeavours to procure the release of the Outgoing Partner from the guarantee given to Wrekinshire Mutual Bank plc, and from any other guarantee or security given by that Partner in respect of the Partnership, as soon as reasonably practicable and in any event within 3 months of the Retirement Date.

9.7 Notice to the world

9.7.1 The continuing Partners shall as soon as practicable after the Retirement Date, and in any event within 14 days, cause notice of the change in the constitution of the Partnership to be published in the London Gazette, notify in writing every client, supplier and bank of the Partnership which has had dealings with the Partnership, and remove the name of the Outgoing Partner from the Business premises, stationery and website.

9.7.2 The Outgoing Partner shall not after the Retirement Date hold himself or herself out, or knowingly permit himself or herself to be held out, as a partner in the Partnership, and shall sign any document reasonably required to give effect to this clause 9.

9.8 Continuing obligations

Clauses 9.4 to 9.7 continue to bind the parties after the Retirement Date.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The firm acts for the partnership, which means for all three partners. Mr Adeyemi-Rowe emails privately, marked "keep this between us", asking for two changes: a shorter notice period for himself than for the others, and a compulsory retirement age that can be overridden by a majority, which he explains will in practice mean him alone, on the footing that the other two will assume it means everyone. This is a conflict of interest between clients on the same matter and it is also an instruction to produce a document intended to mislead the other two clients into signing something different from what they agreed on 15 June. A solicitor cannot act for one client against the interests of another client on the same matter, cannot keep from one client information material to that client's matter, and cannot draft a document designed to deceive. The candidate resolves it in the document: clause 9.1 gives the same 6 month period to every partner, clause 9.2(a) applies to every partner and is disapplied only by the written agreement of all of them, and neither private change appears. Explaining that to Mr Adeyemi-Rowe, and telling him that the firm cannot keep it from the others, is for the partner and not for the clause.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsUses the defined terms from clause 1 correctly, in particular Accounting Date, Accounts, Working Day and Partnership Share, and gives Partnership Share the definition that clause 1 says is to be found in clause 8. Introduces Retirement Date and Outgoing Partner as defined terms and then uses them consistently. Figures are written once, clearly, with the percentages and the sterling amounts unambiguous.Uses "business day" when the agreement defines "Working Day", or writes profit shares in a narrative sentence so that the arithmetic has to be worked out by the reader. Or leaves Partnership Share undefined, so clause 1, clause 12 and clause 11 all cross refer to something that does not exist.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsClause 8 runs in the order in which money moves: shares, salaries as a first charge, interest on capital, drawings, current accounts, then variation. Clause 9 runs in the order events happen: voluntary retirement, compulsory retirement, continuation, payments, valuation, indemnity and release, notice to the world. Sub clauses are numbered so that clause 9.4 can refer back to clause 8.4.2 and does so accurately.Mixes the retirement payments in with the definition of retirement, or deals with goodwill valuation before establishing that goodwill is payable at all. Or produces two undifferentiated blocks of prose that cannot be cross referred to.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawDisplaces the Partnership Act 1890 defaults that would otherwise apply, since the partners' agreement overrides them under section 19 and section 24 only applies subject to agreement. In particular displaces equal shares under section 24(1), the rule in section 24(6) that a partner is not entitled to remuneration, and section 42 as regards the outgoing partner's post retirement entitlement. Provides expressly that the partnership continues so that a retirement notice does not operate as a section 32(c) dissolution notice. Deals with the section 36 point by requiring the London Gazette notice and actual notice to existing clients, since the Gazette alone protects only against those who had no previous dealings.Drafts a retirement clause that says a partner may retire on notice but does not say that the partnership continues. Against sections 26 and 32(c) that leaves a real risk that the notice dissolves the whole firm, which is the exact outcome the partners said they must avoid. Or relies on the London Gazette notice alone, leaving each outgoing partner exposed under section 36(1) to existing clients.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers every point in the partners' note, including that salaries are payable whether or not profits cover them and that any shortfall is a loss borne in the profit sharing proportions, that interest on capital is 4 per cent, the monthly drawings and the 30 day repayment of excess drawings, the four compulsory retirement triggers, accrual of the outgoing share to the continuing partners in their own proportions, the payment timetable, the goodwill formula, the indemnity, the release from the Wrekinshire Mutual Bank guarantee and the holding out point. Answers Otto's question at paragraph 13 of the note by making the instalments accelerate on default and the debt a joint and several debt of the continuing partners.Omits the accrual provision, so nobody knows who takes the outgoing partner's share. Or omits the set off for excess drawings, or fails to make the salaries a first charge payable irrespective of profits, which was the specific point the partners raised. Or ignores Otto's question entirely, leaving the outgoing partner with instalments and no remedy on default.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDrafts clause 9.1 with a single 6 month notice period applying to all three partners, as agreed at the meeting, and says so. Drafts compulsory retirement at 68 so that it applies to every partner and can be disapplied only by the agreement of all the partners, not by a majority. Does not include either of Mr Adeyemi-Rowe's private changes.Gives Mr Adeyemi-Rowe a 6 month notice period and the other two 12 months, or drafts the age 68 proviso as a majority decision. Either implements one client's secret instruction against the interests of the other two clients of the same firm, in a document all three will sign believing it records what they agreed.

Examiner notes

The technical heart of this station is that a general partnership is not a company. Under sections 26 and 32(c) of the Partnership Act 1890 a notice by one partner to leave a partnership of undefined duration can dissolve the whole firm, and the partners have said in terms that the practice must keep going. A retirement clause that permits retirement on notice but never says that the partnership continues between the others, and never says who takes the outgoing share, is the classic fail here. So is forgetting section 42, which would otherwise let a retired partner claim a share of post retirement profits or 5 per cent interest on the value of his share, and section 36, where a Gazette notice alone leaves the outgoing partner exposed to clients who dealt with the firm before. The ethics trap is well disguised. Mr Adeyemi-Rowe's email is polite, plausible and sounds like ordinary senior partner housekeeping, and his second request is dressed up as a general power. Candidates who lift the profit and retirement figures straight from the meeting note but take the notice periods from his email have implemented a secret instruction against two other clients of the firm and cannot pass the ethics criterion. Watch also for the candidate who never defines Partnership Share, when clause 1 of the existing agreement says the definition is to be found in clause 8.

Written station 31: Whether a corporate finance advisory firm needs FCA authorisation for a company sale mandate

Legal research  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

RESEARCH NOTE

To: Hester Vanbrugh-Iyer, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 4 November 2026

Client: Calderstone Advisory LLP

Subject: Whether the proposed Thrapston Ceramics mandate can be taken on without FCA authorisation

1. SUMMARY OF ADVICE

1.1 Steps 3 and 4 of the proposed mandate are regulated activities. Advising the shareholders on which offer to accept, and on whether to take cash or shares in the buyer, is advising on investments under article 53 of the Regulated Activities Order. Introducing the shareholders to a buyer and negotiating heads of terms is arranging deals in investments under article 25.

1.2 However, in every scenario Calderstone is contemplating, the transaction is a sale of the entire issued share capital of Thrapston Ceramics Limited. Provided the conditions in the sale of a body corporate exclusion are met, both the arranging and the advising fall outside the general prohibition. On the facts as I have them the exclusion is available for the 100 per cent sale. The 90 per cent scenario also satisfies it, on either limb, provided the counterparty condition is met.

1.3 Calderstone should not rely on the professional firms exemption in section 327 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. The incidental condition in section 327(4) is very unlikely to be satisfied by a dedicated corporate finance team charging a transaction based success fee, and the section 327(3) condition would be breached by any unaccounted for benefit. The sale of a body corporate exclusion is a better and safer answer.

1.4 The information memorandum is a financial promotion. It may be sent to the 18 authorised firms and, on the facts, to the 14 trading companies. It must not be sent to the 8 individuals in its present form. The sale of a body corporate exemption in article 62 of the Financial Promotion Order is likely to be available and, if it is, cures the whole distribution list, but Calderstone should not rely on it for the individuals without first confirming that the conditions are met in the particular case.

1.5 There is a conflict and disclosure problem on our own side which must be dealt with before Friday. It is at paragraph 6 below.

2. IS THIS A REGULATED ACTIVITY?

2.1 By section 19 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) no person may carry on a regulated activity in the United Kingdom unless authorised or exempt. Breach is an offence under section 23 and, by section 26, renders the agreement unenforceable against the other party and gives that party a right to recover what it has paid. Calderstone's fee agreement with the shareholders would therefore be unenforceable if it were in breach, which is a commercial as well as a criminal risk.

2.2 By section 22 an activity is regulated if it is of a specified kind, carried on by way of business, and relates to a specified investment. Shares in a body corporate are a specified investment: article 76 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 (RAO). Calderstone would be acting by way of business, for a fee and a success fee.

2.3 Advising. Article 53 RAO specifies advising a person, in his capacity as an investor, on the merits of buying or selling a particular investment which is a security. Step 3 is precisely that: advice to the four shareholders on which offer to accept for their own shares, and on the merits of taking shares in the buyer instead of cash. PERG 2.7.15 confirms that advice on whether to accept a particular offer, and on cash versus shares, is advice on the merits in relation to a particular investment. It is not generic advice and it is not the mere provision of information.

2.4 Arranging. Article 25(1) RAO specifies making arrangements for another person to buy or sell a particular investment. Article 25(2) covers arrangements with a view to a person participating in them buying or selling. Article 26 excludes arrangements which do not or would not bring about the transaction. Step 4, negotiating price and heads of terms with the preferred buyer and introducing the shareholders to that buyer, is intended to bring about the sale, so article 26 does not help: see PERG 2.7.7A and 2.7.7B.

2.5 Steps 1 and 2, preparing and circulating the memorandum, would also be capable of amounting to arranging under article 25(2), and are in any event caught by the financial promotion restriction dealt with at paragraph 5 below.

3. THE SALE OF A BODY CORPORATE EXCLUSION

3.1 This is the answer that actually solves the problem. Article 70 RAO (activities carried on in connection with the sale of a body corporate) excludes from article 25 (by article 70(5)) and from article 53 (by article 70(6)) arrangements made and advice given in connection with a transaction to acquire or dispose of shares in a body corporate other than an open ended investment company, in materially the same terms as article 62 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005 (FPO), where either:

(a) the object of the transaction may reasonably be regarded as the acquisition of day to day control of the affairs of the company; or

(b) the shares consist of or include 50 per cent or more of the voting shares and the acquisition is between parties each of whom is a body corporate, a partnership, a single individual or a group of connected individuals.

3.2 The rationale, as PERG 8.14 explains, is that a transfer of control of a business is in substance a commercial transaction rather than an investment transaction.

3.3 On the primary scenario the entire issued share capital of 400 ordinary shares is being sold. The object of the transaction is plainly the acquisition of day to day control, so limb (a) is satisfied and article 70(5) and (6) take Calderstone's arranging and its advice on the sale outside the general prohibition. One element needs to be separated out. Advice on whether to take shares in the buyer rather than cash has two parts. Advice on the structure and consequences of a paper element, and on what the shareholders should press for in the negotiation, is given in connection with the disposal of Thrapston and is within article 70(6). Advice on the intrinsic investment merits of holding a minority stake in the buyer is advice on the acquisition of a different investment, and the acquisition of that stake is not itself a transaction of the kind described in article 70(1), so the exclusion should not be relied on for it. Calderstone should confine itself to the first and tell the shareholders to take advice from an authorised person on the second.

3.4 On the 90 per cent scenario the answer is the same. A sale of 90 per cent of the voting shares still has as its object the acquisition of day to day control, so limb (a) is again satisfied. Limb (b) would also be satisfied on the 50 per cent threshold, provided the sellers are a group of connected individuals within the meaning of the article, which requires each of them to be a director or manager of the company, a close relative of such a person, or a trustee for such a person. I do not have that information about the four shareholders and it should be checked. The retention of 10 per cent for two years does not disturb limb (a), because the test is directed at the object of the transaction rather than at whether 100 per cent changes hands.

3.5 The practical advice is that the exclusion must be established transaction by transaction. If, on a future mandate, Calderstone were to advise on the sale of a minority stake, the exclusion would not be available and the analysis at paragraph 4 would become critical.

4. THE PROFESSIONAL FIRMS EXEMPTION

4.1 Ms Achterberg may expect to be told that Calderstone is covered because it is an ICAEW firm. It should not rely on that here.

4.2 Section 327 FSMA disapplies the general prohibition for a member of a profession, but only if every one of the conditions in subsections (2) to (7) is met. Three matter here.

4.3 Section 327(3): Calderstone must not receive from a person other than its client any pecuniary reward or other advantage for which it does not account to its client. Calderstone's fee is payable by the shareholders, who are its clients, so on the facts given this condition appears to be satisfied. It would not be if Calderstone were also to take anything from the buyer.

4.4 Section 327(4): the manner of the provision of the service must be incidental to the provision of professional services. This is the condition Calderstone fails. PROF 2.1.13G restates the condition, explaining that professional services are services which do not themselves constitute the carrying on of a regulated activity, and PROF 2.1.14G states that the FCA considers that regulated activities cannot be a major part of the practice of the firm, and that the relevant factors include the scale of the regulated activity in proportion to the professional services provided, whether and to what extent the activity is held out as a service in its own right, and the impact of the activity on the fees charged. A firm with a dedicated corporate finance team, holding the service out and charging a transaction based success fee, will find it difficult to show that the activity is incidental. Calderstone has a growing corporate finance team, is taking the mandate as a standalone engagement, and is charging 1.5 per cent of consideration. The advice is that section 327(4) is not satisfied.

4.5 Section 327(5) and (6). By section 327(5) the firm must not carry on, or hold itself out as carrying on, any regulated activity beyond those which the rules of its designated professional body, made under section 332(3), allow, or one in relation to which it is an exempt person. Calderstone is holding itself out as offering a corporate finance service in its own right, which is the very thing subsection (5) is directed at, and the ICAEW's own rules would have to be checked to see what they permit. By section 327(6) the activity must not be of a description, or relate to an investment of a description, specified by the Treasury in the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Professions) (Non-Exempt Activities) Order 2001. Separately, the requirement that a regulated activity arise out of, or be complementary to, the provision of a particular professional service to a particular client is imposed by section 332(4) and by the designated professional body's own scope rules made under section 332(3); it appears as rule 2.1(b) of the SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules in Source G, and the ICAEW's rules contain an equivalent. A corporate finance mandate taken on its own merits does not arise out of Calderstone's audit or tax work.

4.6 The exemption is in any event policed by rules made by the designated professional body under section 332(3), and the FCA may direct under section 328 that section 327(1) does not apply to a specified extent. So this is not a route Calderstone can safely take without reference to the ICAEW's own rules.

4.7 Conclusion: advise Calderstone to rely on the sale of a body corporate exclusion, and not on section 327.

5. THE INFORMATION MEMORANDUM

5.1 By section 21(1) FSMA a person must not, in the course of business, communicate an invitation or inducement to engage in investment activity unless authorised or unless the content is approved by an authorised person. Contravention is an offence under section 25. Calderstone is not authorised.

5.2 A memorandum describing the business and inviting recipients to offer for the entire share capital is both an invitation and an inducement: PERG 8.4.4. Entering into an agreement to buy shares is engaging in investment activity within section 21(8). So the restriction is engaged, and the question is whether an exemption in the FPO applies.

5.3 The 18 private equity houses and corporate finance arms of banks. Article 19 FPO exempts a communication made only to recipients whom the communicator believes on reasonable grounds to be investment professionals, which includes an authorised person. These recipients are authorised. The memorandum may be sent to them.

5.4 The 14 trading companies. Article 49 FPO exempts a communication made only to a body corporate with called up share capital or net assets of not less than the prescribed amount, given to us as 5,000,000 pounds. Each has turnover exceeding 50,000,000 pounds. Turnover is not the same as share capital or net assets, so Calderstone must satisfy itself on reasonable grounds as to net assets before relying on article 49. Article 19 may also apply to any of them whose ordinary activities involve acquiring companies, but that should not be assumed.

5.5 The 8 individuals. Article 48 FPO exempts a communication to a high net worth individual, but only where the individual has signed a statement in the prescribed terms within the preceding twelve months confirming annual income of not less than 100,000 pounds or net assets of not less than 250,000 pounds, and only where the prescribed warning accompanies the communication. Calderstone has no statement from any of them. The fact that the partners believe them to be wealthy and know they have bought businesses before is not enough. As matters stand the memorandum must not be sent to these eight.

5.6 Article 62 FPO. The sale of a body corporate exemption applies to any communication in connection with a transaction to acquire or dispose of shares in a body corporate where the conditions at paragraph 3.1 above are met. On the primary scenario the object is the acquisition of day to day control, so article 62 is likely to be available and would exempt the communication to every recipient including the eight individuals. But the exemption depends on the character of the transaction, and at the point when the memorandum goes out no buyer has been identified and it is not certain that any resulting acquisition will meet the conditions. My advice is that Calderstone should rely on articles 19 and 49 for the two categories where it plainly can, and should not send the memorandum to the eight individuals unless it either obtains the prescribed certificate and gives the prescribed warning under article 48, or has the content approved by an authorised person under section 21(2)(b).

5.7 Article 12 FPO, which disapplies the restriction for a communication received outside the United Kingdom, is not in point: all the recipients are in the United Kingdom.

6. OUR OWN POSITION

6.1 The file note records that this firm is to receive 10 per cent of Calderstone's success fee on mandates introduced by us, that two of the four Thrapston Ceramics shareholders are our clients on other matters, and that this firm made the introduction in September. Nobody has told the shareholders.

6.2 Under paragraph 5.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors we may only make or receive a referral if the arrangement is in the client's best interests and the clients are informed of any financial interest we have in referring them, and of any relevant fee sharing arrangement. That disclosure has not been made and it must be, in writing, to the two shareholders who are our clients.

6.3 More seriously, we now have a financial interest in Calderstone taking this mandate on and completing it at the highest possible price, because our fee rises with theirs. We are advising Calderstone on whether the mandate is lawful at all. That is an own interest conflict, or at least a significant risk of one, within paragraph 6.1 of the Code, and it engages Principle 5 (integrity) and Principle 7 (acting in the best interests of each client). Advising that a course is lawful while standing to gain financially if it proceeds is exactly the position paragraph 6.1 is directed at.

6.4 My advice is that before Friday the firm should (a) disclose the fee arrangement in writing to the two shareholder clients and to Calderstone, (b) consider whether the arrangement should be given up in relation to this matter, and (c) not give the perimeter advice unless satisfied there is no own interest conflict. Nothing in this note should go to Ms Achterberg until that has been resolved.

7. SOURCES RELIED ON

Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, sections 19, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 327, 328 and 332.

Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001, articles 25, 26, 53, 70 and 76.

Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order 2005, articles 19, 48, 49 and 62.

FCA Handbook, PROF 2.1.13G and 2.1.14G, and FCA Perimeter Guidance Manual, PERG 2.7.7A, 2.7.7B, 2.7.15, 8.4.4 and 8.14.
