SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paragraphs 5.1 and 6.1, and SRA Principles 5 and 7.

I have not relied on the extracts from the Companies Act 2006, the Insolvency Act 1986 or the Consumer Rights Act 2015, none of which bears on the perimeter question. The SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules govern this firm rather than Calderstone, which is regulated by the ICAEW, and I have referred to them only by way of comparison.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The partner's own note records that the firm receives 10 per cent of Calderstone's success fee on introduced mandates, that the firm made the introduction, that two of the four selling shareholders are also clients of the firm, and that nobody has told them. Two obligations follow. The first is disclosure: under paragraph 5.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors a referral arrangement is permissible only if it is in the client's best interests and the client is told in writing of the financial interest and of any relevant fee sharing arrangement, and that has not happened. The second, and the more serious, is an own interest conflict under paragraph 6.1. The firm is being asked whether Calderstone may lawfully take on a mandate, and the firm's own fee goes up if the mandate proceeds and the price is high. Advising on the lawfulness of a transaction from which the adviser stands to profit is a significant risk of an own interest conflict, and it engages Principle 5 on integrity and Principle 7 on acting in the best interests of each client. A competent candidate raises it in the note, does not bury it, and gives the partner practical steps: disclose the arrangement in writing to the shareholder clients and to Calderstone, consider whether the fee share should be waived on this matter, and hold the advice until the position is resolved.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses Sources A, B, C and F, which together answer the question, and uses Source G only for the firm's own conduct position. Identifies Sources D, E and H as irrelevant and says so briefly rather than padding the note with them. Within the relevant sources, picks the provisions that matter: sections 19, 21, 22, 26 and 327 FSMA, articles 25, 26, 53, 70 and 76 RAO, articles 19, 48, 49 and 62 FPO, and the FCA guidance on the incidental condition at PROF 2.1.13G and 2.1.14G.Works through every source in the bundle in turn, including the Companies Act, the Insolvency Act and the Consumer Rights Act, which wastes most of the hour and signals that the candidate cannot tell what the question is about. Or misses the guidance on the incidental condition, which is the source that actually decides the section 327 point.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the three questions the partner asked, in that order, and answers them. Says in terms that Calderstone can take the mandate but should rely on the sale of a body corporate exclusion rather than on section 327, and that the memorandum must not go to the eight individuals as things stand. Answers Ms Achterberg's own question about the 90 per cent scenario. Identifies the further information needed, in particular whether the shareholders are a group of connected individuals and the net asset position of the 14 companies.Sets out the law accurately and then stops, leaving the partner to decide whether the mandate can be taken. Or hedges everything, so the note contains no answer the partner can give the client on Friday. Or ignores the 90 per cent scenario, which the client expressly raised.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA note to a partner: headed, numbered, with a summary of advice at the front so the partner can read the first page and know the answer. Citations given precisely and in full at first use, then shortened. No research trail, no narrative of what the candidate looked at first.Writes a letter to the client instead of a note to the partner, or writes a chronological account of the research process. Or cites loosely, for example "the FSMA rules on promotions", which in the one station where citation is expected is not good enough.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly characterises step 3 as article 53 advising and step 4 as article 25 arranging, and correctly rejects the article 26 exclusion because these arrangements are intended to bring the transaction about. Correctly concludes that the section 327 incidental condition fails on these facts and gives the reason. Correctly applies article 48 to conclude that a belief that the individuals are wealthy is no substitute for a signed statement in the prescribed terms.Concludes that Calderstone is fine because it is an ICAEW firm and section 327 therefore applies, without ever testing the incidental condition. Or treats the 14 companies' turnover as satisfying article 49, when article 49 turns on called up share capital or net assets and the note gives turnover. Or concludes that no regulated activity is involved at all because Calderstone is only advising its own clients on selling their own company.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all three questions and the consequences: the criminal offence under section 23, and, commercially more important to this client, the unenforceability of Calderstone's own fee agreement under section 26. Deals with each of the three categories of recipient separately rather than treating the distribution list as one. Deals with the 90 per cent variant. Notes that the sale of a body corporate exclusion has to be established transaction by transaction, so this answer does not solve the problem for a future minority stake mandate.Answers the regulated activity question and the section 327 question and then runs out of time before the financial promotion question, which is a third of what the partner asked for. Or treats the whole distribution list as a single question and gives one answer for all 40 recipients.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots the undisclosed 10 per cent success fee share, identifies both the disclosure obligation under paragraph 5.1 of the Code owed to the two shareholder clients and the own interest conflict under paragraph 6.1 arising from advising on the lawfulness of a transaction from which the firm profits, and gives the partner concrete steps: disclose in writing, consider giving up the fee share on this matter, and do not release the advice until it is resolved.Treats the note added by the partner as background colour and never mentions it, or mentions the referral fee but says only that it should be disclosed, missing that the firm's fee rises with the value of the very transaction it is being asked to bless. Or, worse, advises that the arrangement is fine because referral fees are lawful.

Examiner notes

The bundle is deliberately overfull. Sources D (Companies Act), E (Insolvency Act) and H (Consumer Rights Act) are decoys and answer nothing, and Source G is only half relevant, since the SRA Scope Rules govern this firm and not an ICAEW firm, although the Code extracts in it are directly in point on the ethics. Candidates who cannot discard the decoys spend forty minutes on them. The legal trap is section 327. Most candidates know there is a professional firms exemption and reach for it, because Calderstone is a professional firm and the client expects that answer. It fails, and the source that shows it fails is the FCA guidance on the incidental condition at PROF 2.1.13G and 2.1.14G: a dedicated corporate finance team, held out as a service, charging 1.5 per cent of consideration, is not carrying on an incidental activity. The answer the client actually needs is the sale of a body corporate exclusion in article 70 of the Regulated Activities Order, which is at the end of Source B and appears again as article 62 in Source C. A candidate who finds it, applies both routes into it and answers the 90 per cent variant is into A territory. The other reliable discriminator is the eight individuals. Article 48 requires a signed statement in the prescribed terms within the last twelve months plus the prescribed warning, and the figures are given, so no recall is needed. Candidates who say the eight can be approached because the partners reasonably believe them to be wealthy have missed the point of the certification regime. Finally, watch the fee note: it is written in the partner's own voice, which makes candidates read it as authorised rather than as the problem.

Written station 32: Ratifying a director's breach of duty and identifying whose votes count

Legal research  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO CALLUM REES

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 3 February 2027

Client: Ardenshaw Fabrications Limited

Subject: Proposed ratification of Mrs Fairhurst's conduct, availability and voting

1. Summary

1.1 Mrs Fairhurst has breached section 175 of the Companies Act 2006 on the Calderhay contract, and sections 177 or 182 and section 190 on the press brake. Her explanation that the Company could not have serviced the contract is no defence.

1.2 Two separate resolutions are needed, not one. A section 239 ratification resolution deals with her personal liability. A section 196 affirmation resolution deals with the voidability of the press brake sale. The voting rules are different on each, which is the point Mrs Fairhurst has missed.

1.3 On the section 239 resolution her 38 per cent and her husband's 10 per cent cannot be counted in favour. The remaining votes are Mr Prescott 22 per cent, Ms Kyriakou 18 per cent and Hollinbrook 12 per cent. On the stated positions the resolution fails unless Hollinbrook votes in favour, and even then it carries only 34 to 18.

1.4 More fundamentally, the Company appears to be insolvent on a balance sheet basis and is showing signs of cashflow distress. On BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA the members cannot ratify at all once creditors' interests are engaged. My advice is that a ratification resolution should not be put at present.

1.5 Separately, I cannot prepare the board minute Mrs Fairhurst has asked for. See section 7.

2. Matter one, the Calderhay contract

2.1 Section 175(1) requires a director to avoid a situation in which she has a direct or indirect interest that conflicts or possibly may conflict with the interests of the company. Section 175(2) applies the duty in particular to the exploitation of any property, information or opportunity, and says in terms that it is immaterial whether the company could take advantage of it.

2.2 Mrs Fairhurst learned of the Calderhay opportunity because she was managing director of the Company. She routed it to a company she wholly owns. Her answer, that the Company lacked plant capacity, is squarely answered by section 175(2) and by Regal (Hastings) Ltd v Gulliver, where the directors were liable to account even though the company could not itself have taken the opportunity and had suffered no loss. Bhullar v Bhullar confirms that the question is not whether the company could have taken the opportunity but whether the director learned of it by reason of her position and whether there was a real possibility of conflict.

2.3 There has been no board authorisation. Section 175(4)(b) and (5)(a) would have permitted the directors of a private company to authorise the situation, the Company's constitution containing nothing invalidating that, but section 175(6) requires the quorum to be met without counting the interested director and the matter to be agreed without her votes. Nothing of the kind happened. The point in section 175(5) about a public company needing an enabling constitutional provision does not arise, because the Company is private.

2.4 She is also in breach of section 172(1) in failing to report the approach, and the conduct engages section 176 to the extent she has received a benefit by reason of her office.

2.5 Remedies. By section 178 the consequences are the same as for breach of the corresponding equitable principle. The Company can seek an account of the profits made by Fairhurst Metalwork Limited, equitable compensation, and, on the Cook v Deeks analysis, a declaration that the benefit of the framework agreement is held on constructive trust for the Company. It could also seek rescission of any related transaction and, in principle, injunctive relief.

3. Matter two, the press brake

3.1 Section 190(1)(a) prohibits a company entering into an arrangement under which a director acquires a substantial non cash asset from the company unless approved by resolution of the members or made conditional on such approval.

3.2 Is the asset substantial? Section 191(2) provides that an asset is substantial if its value exceeds 10 per cent of the company's asset value and is more than 5,000 pounds, or exceeds 100,000 pounds. The Company's net asset value by the most recent statutory accounts was 610,000 pounds, so the 10 per cent figure is 61,000 pounds. On the price paid, 46,000 pounds, the first limb is not met. On the independent valuations of 92,000 to 105,000 pounds it is comfortably met, since the value exceeds 61,000 pounds and exceeds 5,000 pounds. Section 191 speaks of the value of the asset and not the price paid, and I advise the partner to proceed on the basis that the asset was substantial. On the upper valuation the second limb, exceeding 100,000 pounds, would also be met.

3.3 No members' resolution was obtained. The Company therefore entered into the arrangement in contravention of section 190.

3.4 Consequences. Under section 195(2) the transaction is voidable at the instance of the Company. None of the bars in section 195(2) applies: the press brake still exists and is in Mrs Fairhurst's possession, so restitution is possible, the Company has not been indemnified, and no third party has acquired rights. Separately and additionally, section 195(3) makes Mrs Fairhurst liable to account for her gain and to indemnify the Company for its loss whether or not the transaction is avoided. Section 195(4)(d) also exposes any other director who authorised the sale, which needs investigating.

3.5 She is also in breach of section 177 if she failed to declare her interest before the sale, or section 182 if the declaration was to be made afterwards. She has made no declaration at all. Note that section 175 does not apply to this matter, because section 175(3) takes transactions with the company outside that duty.

4. Which resolutions are needed

4.1 Two, doing different work.

4.2 A section 239 resolution to ratify her conduct amounting to breach of duty. This is what releases her personal liability, on both matters. It must be a resolution of the members: section 239(2).

4.3 A section 196 resolution affirming the press brake transaction, so that it may no longer be avoided under section 195. Section 196 requires affirmation within a reasonable period. The sale was on 14 November 2026 and we are now in February 2027, so this should be done promptly if it is to be done at all. Affirmation under section 196 stops avoidance. It does not by itself release the section 195(3) liability to account, which is why the section 239 resolution is still needed.

5. Whose votes may be counted, and the arithmetic

5.1 On the section 239 resolution. Section 239(4) provides that where the resolution is proposed at a meeting it is passed only if the necessary majority is obtained disregarding votes in favour by the director, if a member, and by any member connected with her. Section 239(5)(b) applies the Part 10 meaning of connected. Section 252(2)(a) and section 253(2)(a) make a director's spouse a connected person. Mr Daniel Fairhurst is her husband, so he is connected. Hollinbrook Ventures LLP is an outside investor with no board seat and nothing in the file connects it to her.

5.2 So Mrs Fairhurst's 380,000 votes and Mr Fairhurst's 100,000 votes, 48 per cent between them, cannot be counted in favour. Three points of detail. First, the disregard is only of votes in favour: if either of them voted against, that vote would count, and section 239(5)(c) confirms that the identification of the persons caught does not depend on how the votes are cast. Second, they are not excluded from the meeting. They may attend, count in the quorum and speak. Third, if the resolution were proposed as a written resolution instead, section 239(3) makes neither of them an eligible member at all.

5.3 The arithmetic on the stated positions. The votes capable of counting in favour are Mr Prescott 220,000, Ms Kyriakou 180,000 and Hollinbrook 120,000. Ratification is by ordinary resolution, so a simple majority of the votes cast, after the disregard, is required. Mr Prescott supports, Ms Kyriakou opposes, Hollinbrook is unknown. If Hollinbrook votes in favour the resolution carries 340,000 to 180,000. If Hollinbrook votes against or does not vote, it fails, 220,000 to 180,000 being a majority only if Hollinbrook abstains, which on those numbers it would be. To be precise: if Hollinbrook abstains, Mr Prescott's 220,000 in favour beats Ms Kyriakou's 180,000 against and the resolution carries; if Hollinbrook votes against, the resolution is lost 220,000 to 300,000. Everything therefore turns on Hollinbrook, which is why Mrs Fairhurst's arithmetic is wrong. Her own 48 per cent is worth nothing on this resolution.

5.4 On the section 196 resolution. Section 196 contains no equivalent of section 239(3) or (4), and no other provision disenfranchises the interested member. Mrs Fairhurst and Mr Fairhurst may therefore vote their 48 per cent on the affirmation resolution. With Mr Prescott's 22 per cent, that carries. The result is the paradoxical but correct position that she can save the transaction from being unwound but cannot release herself from the liability to account.

5.5 Section 239(6)(a) preserves the validity of a decision taken by unanimous consent of the members. Unanimity is not achievable here given Ms Kyriakou's stated position, so that route is closed.

6. What would defeat a ratification even if the numbers were there

6.1 Creditors' interests. This is the decisive point. Section 172(3) makes the duty subject to any rule of law requiring directors to consider the interests of creditors. In BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA the Supreme Court held that the duty is modified where the company is insolvent or bordering on insolvency, or where an insolvent liquidation or administration is probable, and that shareholder ratification cannot authorise a breach of the modified duty, because in that situation the shareholders are not the only persons for whose benefit the duty is owed.

6.2 The Company's management accounts show net liabilities of 84,000 pounds, the bank facility is fully drawn and repayable on demand, trade creditors are being paid at 71 days against 30 day terms and two suppliers have stopped supply. That is at the least a company bordering on insolvency. On that footing a section 239 resolution would be liable to be treated as ineffective, and the directors who procured it would be exposed in their own right. I advise that no ratification resolution be put until the Company's solvency has been properly assessed.

6.3 Acts incapable of ratification. Section 239(7) preserves the rules as to acts that cannot be ratified. Cook v Deeks holds that a majority cannot by their own votes make a present to themselves of property belonging in equity to the company. Because section 239(4) already strips out Mrs Fairhurst's and her husband's votes, this category is narrower than it once was, and I do not think it independently defeats a resolution carried by disinterested members. It matters more as an answer to the suggestion that the 48 per cent settles the question.

6.4 Derivative claim. If ratification fails, Ms Kyriakou or Hollinbrook could seek permission to bring a derivative claim under section 260(3). Section 263(2)(c) requires permission to be refused if the act has been ratified, which is a further reason to be sure any ratification is effective before relying on it, and section 263(4) requires the court to have particular regard to the views of members with no personal interest, which here means Ms Kyriakou and Hollinbrook.

7. Mrs Fairhurst's two requests

7.1 The backdated minute. I cannot prepare a board minute dated 5 September 2026 recording an authorisation that was never given. It would be a false record of a company meeting, created to make the position appear tidy, and its purpose would be to mislead the members who are about to vote and anyone later reviewing the file. Preparing it would breach Principles 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the SRA Principles, and paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits misleading clients, the court or others either by our own acts or omissions or by being complicit in the acts or omissions of others. It would also risk criminal liability for Mrs Fairhurst and for us. The request must be refused in writing, and if she persists we should consider our position on the retainer and whether a report is required.

7.2 Who our client is. Our client is the Company, not Mrs Fairhurst. Her request that my advice go to her alone and not to Ms Kyriakou cannot be met. Advice given to the Company belongs to the Company and must be available to the board as a whole. Acting on her instruction would put us in a conflict between our client's interests and hers under paragraph 6.2 of the Code, and would breach paragraph 7.1's requirement that we act in the best interests of each client. I recommend we write to the whole board confirming who we act for and circulating this note to all three directors.

8. Sources not relied on

8.1 North-West Transportation Co Ltd v Beatty is superseded on the point for which it would be cited. Section 239 was enacted long after it and now disregards the interested director's votes in favour. It cannot be used to support Mrs Fairhurst's arithmetic.

8.2 The Partnership Act 1890 material and Bentley v Craven concern a partnership. Ardenshaw is a company with a share capital and the statutory machinery in sections 190 to 196 and 239 applies instead. The absence of any disenfranchising rule in partnership law is not transferable.

8.3 The UK Listing Rules related party provisions apply only to companies with equity shares admitted to listing. Ardenshaw is a private company and they impose nothing on it.

8.4 Ashgrove Holdings Pty Ltd v Leeming is a decision of an Australian court on the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth), which has no application here and contains a civil penalty regime with no English equivalent.

9. Recommended next steps

9.1 Do not convene the general meeting yet. Obtain a solvency assessment and, if needed, insolvency advice for the board.

9.2 Obtain the Company's statutory accounts to 31 March 2026 and a formal valuation of the press brake as at 14 November 2026, to fix the section 191 position.

9.3 Investigate who else authorised the press brake sale, for the purposes of section 195(4)(d).

9.4 Write to the whole board confirming that we act for the Company, refusing the request for the minute, and circulating this advice.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two unflagged points sit in paragraph 7 of the file note. First, Mrs Fairhurst asks for a board minute recording an authorisation that was never given, dated 5 September 2026, before the diversion of the contract. That is the creation of a false company record whose purpose is to mislead the members about to vote. It must be refused outright: SRA Principles 1, 2, 4 and 5, and paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which forbids misleading clients or others by the solicitor's own acts or by being complicit in the acts of others. The refusal should be recorded in writing and the firm should consider whether to continue acting. Second, she asks that the advice go to her alone and not to Ms Kyriakou. The client is the Company. Advice given to the Company belongs to the Company and must reach the whole board. Following her instruction would breach paragraphs 6.2 and 7.1 of the Code. The competent candidate spots both and resolves them by writing to the board as a whole.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses Sources A, B, C and D and cites the provisions that decide the question: sections 175, 177, 182, 190, 191, 195, 196, 239, 252 and 253 of the Companies Act 2006, together with Regal (Hastings), Bhullar, Cook v Deeks and Sequana. Discards Sources E, F, G and H expressly, identifying North-West Transportation as superseded by section 239 rather than as good law.Relies on North-West Transportation v Beatty for the proposition that the interested member may vote, which is exactly the answer Mrs Fairhurst wants and is wrong. Or ignores the practitioner extract at Source D and so never separates the section 239 resolution from the section 196 resolution.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers all four of the partner's questions, gives the actual arithmetic on the actual shareholdings and states the outcome on each of Hollinbrook's possible positions, and gives a clear recommendation not to put the resolution yet because of the solvency position.Sets out the law on ratification without ever working the numbers, so the partner still cannot tell Mrs Fairhurst whether her 48 per cent counts. Or gives the arithmetic but no recommendation.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsNumbered note with a summary at the front, the two matters separated, and the two resolutions separated with their voting rules set out one at a time. Figures stated precisely and consistently.Runs the two matters and the two resolutions together so it is impossible to see which voting rule applies to which resolution, or writes a research trail rather than advice.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly applies section 239(4) to disregard votes in favour by Mrs Fairhurst and, via sections 252 and 253, by her husband as a connected person, correctly notes that only votes in favour are disregarded and that those members may still attend and count in the quorum, and correctly applies section 191(2) using the value of the press brake and the 610,000 pound net asset figure rather than the price paid.Treats Mr Fairhurst as an unconnected shareholder because he is not a director or employee, and so leaves his 10 per cent in the count. Or applies the section 191 10 per cent test to the 46,000 pound price rather than to the asset's value and wrongly concludes that section 190 was not engaged. Or says Mrs Fairhurst may not attend or be counted in the quorum.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers both matters and both resolutions, explains that section 196 affirmation stops avoidance but does not release the section 195(3) liability to account, spots that section 196 contains no equivalent disenfranchisement so Mrs Fairhurst may vote on that resolution, deals with section 175(2) and Regal (Hastings) as the answer to the no loss argument, and identifies the Sequana creditors' interests point as capable of defeating a ratification outright. Also notes the derivative claim consequence under sections 260 and 263.Stops at section 239 and never addresses the press brake as a separate section 190 problem needing its own resolution. Or misses the insolvency material in the file note entirely, so the fourth question the partner asked goes unanswered. Or accepts the capacity argument as a defence to section 175.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses the request for a board minute dated 5 September 2026 in unequivocal terms, identifies it as the creation of a false record intended to mislead the members and any later reader, cites Principles 1, 2, 4 and 5 and paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors including complicity in the acts of others, and advises that the refusal be put in writing. Separately identifies that the client is the Company and not Mrs Fairhurst, so her instruction to withhold the advice from Ms Kyriakou cannot be followed, citing paragraphs 6.2 and 7.1.Deals with the minute as a practical difficulty, saying it would be better not to, rather than refusing outright. Or addresses the minute but misses the who is the client point and the instruction to keep advice from a fellow director, which is the second half of the ethics issue.

Examiner notes

This station separates candidates in three places. The first is the connected person analysis. Mr Fairhurst holds 10 per cent, is not a director and is not an employee, and weak candidates therefore treat his votes as available. Sections 252(2)(a) and 253(2)(a) make a spouse a connected person, so nearly half the register drops out and Mrs Fairhurst's confident arithmetic collapses. The second is the recognition that two resolutions are required and that they have different voting rules: section 239 disenfranchises her on ratification, while section 196 contains no equivalent provision so she may vote to affirm the press brake sale. Candidates who put everything into one resolution cannot pass the comprehensiveness criterion. The third is the solvency material, which is presented as ordinary trading background in paragraph 5 of the file note. Net liabilities, a fully drawn on demand facility, creditors at 71 days and two suppliers on stop engage the modified duty in Sequana, and the members cannot ratify a breach of a duty that is no longer owed for their benefit alone. The traps are the decoys. North-West Transportation v Beatty is seductive because it states in terms the proposition the client wants, and a candidate who cites it without noticing the editorial note and paragraph 12.03 of Source D has got the law backwards. The Partnership Act material, the Listing Rules and the Australian decision are all off point and cost time. On section 191, the marking distinguishes between candidates who apply the 10 per cent test to the value of the asset, which is what the section says, and those who apply it to the 46,000 pound price and wrongly conclude that section 190 was never engaged.

Written station 33: A director's personal liability for wrongful trading and what amounts to taking every step

Legal research  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO PARTNER

To: Adaeze Okonjo

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 8 March 2027

Matter: Rosalind Kirkbride - Calderbrook Interiors Limited (in creditors' voluntary liquidation)

Subject: Wrongful trading, the relevant date, and the section 214(3) defence

1. Summary of advice

1.1 The liquidator's claim is under section 214 of the Insolvency Act 1986. On the material we have, the statutory conditions in section 214(2) are likely to be made out against Mrs Kirkbride, and the relevant date is more likely to be 2 July 2026 than the 30 April 2026 date the liquidator has pleaded.

1.2 Her defence, that she took sensible steps, is not the statutory defence. Section 214(3) requires her to show she took every step with a view to minimising the potential loss to creditors. On these facts she cannot show that, principally because she continued to take customer deposits for work the company could not perform and stopped paying HMRC while the position deteriorated, and because she did not take insolvency advice until 22 December 2026 despite being told to do so in July.

1.3 Her realistic exposure is a contribution measured by the increase in the net deficiency from the relevant date, subject to causation. If the relevant date is 2 July 2026 the arithmetic reduces the claim from £432,000 to about £384,000, and there are further causation arguments on part of that figure. She should be advised to negotiate rather than to defend on the basis she has put forward.

1.4 There is a serious professional conduct problem in her email of 6 March 2027 which we must address before we reply to the liquidator at all. It is at section 6 below.

2. The claim, and which provision applies

2.1 The company went into creditors' voluntary liquidation on 15 January 2027 and did not at any stage enter administration (Document 3). The applicable provision is therefore section 214 of the Insolvency Act 1986 (Source A), on the application of the liquidator. Section 246ZB (Source B) is the administration equivalent and has no application here.

2.2 This is not a fraudulent trading case. Section 213 (Source C) requires actual dishonesty in the carrying on of the business. Nothing in the liquidator's letter alleges dishonesty and it would be wrong to advise Mrs Kirkbride on that footing. It is right to warn her, however, that on a section 214 declaration the court may of its own motion make a disqualification order under section 10 of the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986 (Source D), for up to 15 years. No section 6 proceedings have been intimated.

2.3 The separate duty to consider creditors' interests confirmed in BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA [2022] UKSC 25, given effect through section 172(3) of the Companies Act 2006 (Source I), is engaged on these facts but is a different claim, brought for breach of duty. It is not what the liquidator has pleaded. It matters only in that it gives the liquidator an alternative route, and it should be flagged to the client as a risk if she takes an aggressive stance.

3. Are the section 214(2) conditions met

3.1 Section 214(2)(a): the company has gone into insolvent liquidation, since its assets (£61,000) are plainly insufficient to pay its debts (£803,000) and the expenses of the winding up: section 214(6).

3.2 Section 214(2)(c): Mrs Kirkbride was a director throughout. That is not in issue.

3.3 Section 214(2)(b) is the real question: at some time before the commencement of the winding up did she know, or ought she to have concluded, that there was no reasonable prospect that the company would avoid going into insolvent liquidation. The standard is the mixed objective and subjective standard in section 214(4): the general knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of a person carrying out her functions as managing director, and also her own actual knowledge and experience, which after twelve years running the business is considerable. Under Re Produce Marketing Consortium Ltd (No 2) [1989] BCLC 520 (Source E) she is fixed not only with what she knew but with what a reasonably diligent director would have ascertained.

3.4 The liquidator relies on 30 April 2026. I doubt that date. As Snowden J put it in Re Ralls Builders Ltd (No 2) [2016] EWHC 1812 (Ch) (Source G), insolvency is a necessary but not a sufficient condition, and a balance sheet insolvent company may still have a real prospect of rescue. At the end of April 2026 the company had suffered a large one off bad debt, had a board resolution to cut costs and seek refinancing, and did in fact make real cuts in May. A director could rationally have taken the view then that the company might trade out. Brooks v Armstrong [2015] EWHC 2289 (Ch) (Source F) confirms that directors are not to be judged with hindsight, and that the applicant must plead and prove the date it relies on.

3.5 The better date is 2 July 2026, when Vellacott Grieve told her in writing that the company was balance sheet insolvent, would not be able to meet its liabilities as they fell due beyond the autumn, and needed insolvency advice now. From that point the only thing said to stand between the company and insolvent liquidation was the Brackenhill refinancing. That refinancing was never reduced to writing, never the subject of any commitment, and as at 19 December 2026 was conditional on committed new equity the company plainly could not produce. On Ralls Builders that is not a reasonable prospect but a hope. If the partner prefers a later date, 1 September 2026, when the company stopped paying HMRC altogether, is the fallback.

3.6 I would advise that the conditions in section 214(2) are made out, with the relevant date at 2 July 2026.

4. The section 214(3) defence, and what "every step" requires

4.1 The burden is on Mrs Kirkbride. Section 214(3) provides that the court shall not make a declaration if satisfied that, after the condition in section 214(2)(b) was first satisfied, the director took every step with a view to minimising the potential loss to the company's creditors as, assuming her to have known there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvent liquidation, she ought to have taken.

4.2 Three points follow, and they are the answer to her case as she has put it.

(a) The steps must have been taken after the relevant date. Her redundancies (15 May 2026), the change in quoting policy and the approach to asset based lenders all pre date 2 July 2026 and do not count towards the defence at all, whatever else may be said for them.

(b) The test is every step, not some steps. Brooks v Armstrong (Source F) is explicit: the subsection is not satisfied by showing that some steps, even sensible steps, were taken, and the measure is what a reasonably diligent director in her position ought to have taken.

(c) The steps must be directed at minimising loss to creditors, not at saving the company for its members. Again Brooks v Armstrong: steps taken to trade out of difficulty for the company's own sake are not the same thing, though they may coincide. Everything Mrs Kirkbride did after July 2026 was directed at keeping the business alive in the hope of the Brackenhill facility.

4.3 Against that, the steps she ought to have taken and did not are obvious and are the ones the liquidator will point to. She did not take the insolvency advice she was expressly told to take on 2 July 2026 until 22 December 2026. She held no board or management review of the solvency position and recorded nothing after 28 April 2026. She did not stop incurring new liabilities: she stopped paying PAYE, national insurance and VAT from September 2026, so that £191,000 of Crown debt accrued after the relevant date, and she took £96,000 of customer deposits between September and December 2026 for work the company never started. Snowden J's observation in Ralls Builders on precisely that combination, that it amounts to the involuntary financing of continued trading by creditors who have no say, is directly against her.

4.4 My conclusion is that the section 214(3) defence is not available. She should be told this plainly, because she is currently proceeding on the basis that it is a complete answer.

5. Quantum, and where the argument actually is

5.1 The jurisdiction is compensatory, not penal: Re Produce Marketing Consortium (No 2) (Source E) and Re Continental Assurance Co of London plc (No 4) [2007] 2 BCLC 287 (Source H). The court must be satisfied that the continuation of trading caused loss to creditors as a body; if the creditors as a whole are no worse off than they would have been on a liquidation at the relevant date, no contribution should be ordered however unwise the trading was (Ralls Builders, Continental Assurance).

5.2 The usual starting point is the increase in net deficiency between the relevant date and liquidation, but on the appeal in Brooks v Armstrong that approach must not be applied mechanically and is subject to causation (Source F).

5.3 The liquidator has taken 31 March 2026 (£310,000) to 15 January 2027 (£742,000) and claims the difference, £432,000. If the relevant date is 2 July 2026 the correct comparator is the 30 June 2026 figure of £358,000, giving an increase of £384,000. That is a real saving and is the first argument to run.

5.4 Within that figure, the £191,000 of post relevant date Crown debt and the £96,000 of customer deposits are the hardest elements to resist, because both are new liabilities to creditors who received nothing in return. The £77,000 increase in trade creditors and the £68,000 of trading losses are more arguable: we would need to show what part of the trade creditor increase was matched by work in progress or goods actually received and realised in the liquidation.

5.5 The court retains a discretion as to the contribution, if any. Her own unpaid £40,000 loan does not reduce the contribution as a matter of law, though it is a point of mitigation on the exercise of discretion. It is not a defence and she should not be encouraged to think it is.

6. Matters arising from Mrs Kirkbride's email of 6 March 2027

6.1 There are three, and we cannot reply to Pellowe Strand until they are resolved.

6.2 The board minute. She has asked us to send to the liquidator's solicitors, as a board minute of the company, a document she typed last week, signed and dated 14 September 2026. Whatever she genuinely discussed, that document is not a contemporaneous record and holding it out as one would be a false statement to a third party. We cannot send it. We must tell her that we will not, and explain why. If she wants to put her recollection forward she may do so in a witness statement or in correspondence, dated and described honestly as her present recollection. She should also be warned that producing a fabricated minute in the proceedings risks a contempt finding and would transform a compensatory claim into a case about her honesty, with the disqualification and section 213 consequences that follow.

6.3 The £45,000. She has asked us to conceal from the liquidator payments of £45,000 taken from the company in October and November 2026 and described in the books as a management charge. We cannot do that. We cannot mislead the liquidator's solicitors, whether by a positive statement or by omitting something which makes what we do say misleading, and if asked what payments were made to her we cannot answer in a way that leaves out those payments. As a practical matter the payments are in the bank statements and the liquidator will find them. They are also very likely recoverable in their own right, and they will be treated as post relevant date extractions if we do not deal with them first.

6.4 Her brother. She has asked us to present Neil Kirkbride as having had nothing to do with the company after 30 June 2026. On our own chronology he continued to attend weekly management meetings and to sign off pricing until 14 November 2026. "Director" in section 214 includes a shadow director (section 214(7)). We cannot advance a positive case about his role which we know to be untrue. As it happens it is not in her interests either, since if he is liable he is a co contributor.

6.5 How to handle it. I suggest we see her, explain that our duty not to mislead the court or a third party overrides her instructions on these points, and confirm the position in writing. If she maintains the instruction to send the minute or to conceal the £45,000 we would have to stop acting, and we should tell her that now rather than later. We must not tip off the liquidator as to the reason for any withdrawal, and our duty of confidentiality survives the retainer. There is nothing so far which requires a report under the money laundering regime, but if she persists in an attempt to conceal the extraction of company money from the liquidator we will need to take advice from the firm's MLRO before doing anything further.

7. Recommended advice to the client

7.1 The claim is soundly based in principle and the defence she is relying on will fail.

7.2 The date is worth fighting: pleaded at 30 April 2026, likely to be 2 July 2026, which takes about £48,000 off the claim before any causation argument.

7.3 Causation is worth fighting on the trade creditor and trading loss elements, roughly £145,000 of the £384,000.

7.4 The Crown debt and the customer deposits, roughly £287,000, are very difficult, and the deposits carry a reputational risk of their own.

7.5 She should be advised to make a realistic proposal within the 21 day period, supported by evidence of means, and to do so before the £45,000 emerges from the bank statements rather than after.

7.6 We should not reply to Pellowe Strand until the matters at section 6 are resolved.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Document 4 contains three unflagged conduct problems. First, the client has fabricated a board minute after the event, signed and dated it 14 September 2026, and asks the firm to send it to the liquidator's solicitors as one of the company's board minutes. Second, she asks the firm to conceal £45,000 she extracted from the company in October and November 2026 as a purported management charge, and to say nothing about it even if asked directly what payments were made to her. Third, she asks the firm to present her brother as having had no involvement after his resignation, when the firm's own chronology shows he attended management meetings and priced contracts until 14 November 2026 and may therefore be a shadow director. A competent candidate refuses all three, explaining that a solicitor must not mislead the court, the liquidator or the liquidator's solicitors, whether by a false statement or by an omission which makes what is said misleading, and must not be complicit in another person doing so; advises the honest route of a dated witness statement of present recollection and voluntary disclosure of the payments; warns of contempt, disqualification and a possible fraudulent trading allegation if a fabricated document is deployed; and makes clear that if the instructions are maintained the firm must cease to act, without telling the other side why, with confidentiality surviving the retainer, and with the MLRO consulted before anything further is done if she persists in trying to conceal the extraction of company money.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses section 214 as the governing provision and says why, expressly discounting section 246ZB because the company never entered administration and section 213 because no dishonesty is alleged. Uses Produce Marketing for imputed knowledge, Brooks v Armstrong for the date and for the meaning of every step, Ralls Builders for reasonable prospect and the refinancing point, Continental Assurance for causation and quantum. Notes section 10 CDDA and the Sequana creditor duty as adjacent risks without confusing them with the claim pleaded. Ignores the Partnership Act extract entirely. Uses the figures in Document 3 rather than only those in the liquidator's letter.Works through every source in the bundle in turn, giving the Partnership Act, section 213 and section 246ZB the same weight as section 214, or treats Sequana as if it were the claim being made. Equally poor is a note which cites only section 214 and no case law at all, when this is the one station where authorities are expected.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the two questions the partner actually asked, tells the partner plainly that the client's own understanding of the defence is wrong, quantifies the exposure with a figure and identifies which parts of the claim are worth fighting and which are not. Gives the partner something to say to the client within the 21 day deadline.Produces an accurate essay on wrongful trading which never reaches a view on whether this client is liable, never gives a number, and leaves the partner with nothing to tell Mrs Kirkbride.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured note with headings, short paragraphs, a conclusion at the front, accurate citation and no research trail. Language a partner can lift into a client letter.A narrative of the research process, long undigested quotations from the sources, or a note which buries the conclusion on the last page.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies the section 214(4) mixed objective and subjective standard to a managing director of twelve years' experience, identifies a defensible relevant date and justifies departing from the liquidator's date, and states the section 214(3) defence accurately, in particular that the steps must post date the relevant date, must be every step, and must be directed at minimising creditor loss rather than saving the company.States the defence as taking reasonable steps or acting in good faith, or credits the client with the May 2026 redundancies and the approach to lenders when those pre date any tenable relevant date. Also fails: treating balance sheet insolvency at 31 March 2026 as by itself proving no reasonable prospect.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers liability, the defence, causation and quantum, recalculates the increase in net deficiency from the chosen relevant date, separates the elements which are hard to resist from those which are arguable, notes the court's discretion, notes shadow directorship of the brother under section 214(7), and notes the disqualification risk under section 10 CDDA.Stops at liability and never addresses quantum, or simply adopts the liquidator's £432,000 without noticing that the comparator must move with the relevant date. Missing the brother's possible shadow directorship altogether.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies all three limbs of the email: the fabricated board minute, the instruction to conceal the £45,000, and the instruction to misrepresent the brother's role. Refuses each, explains that a solicitor must not mislead a third party or the court and must not allow a client's instructions to do so, advises the honest alternative (a witness statement of present recollection, disclosure of the payments), warns of the consequences, and states that the firm must stop acting if the instructions are maintained, without tipping off. Notes that confidentiality survives and that the MLRO should be consulted if she persists in concealing the extraction.Deals only with the backdated minute and treats the £45,000 as merely a bad commercial fact, or agrees to stay silent about the payments on the footing that there is no duty to volunteer information. Worst is a note which simply advises withdrawal without first explaining the position to the client, or which proposes to tell the liquidator why we are withdrawing.

Examiner notes

The station separates candidates on two things. The first is the meaning of "every step" in section 214(3). Weak candidates repeat the client's own case, that she took sensible steps and so has a defence. A pass requires three points: the steps must come after the date on which the condition in section 214(2)(b) was first satisfied, so the May 2026 redundancies are irrelevant; the statutory word is every, not some, and the burden is on the director; and the steps must be aimed at minimising loss to creditors rather than at rescuing the company for its members. The second is the relevant date. The liquidator has pleaded 30 April 2026 and the papers are deliberately arranged so that a candidate who accepts that date without argument loses the client about £48,000 and misses the point that a bad debt plus a bank refusal, followed by real cost cutting, may still leave a rational prospect of trading out. The stronger answer moves the date to the accountant's written warning of 2 July 2026, after which the only hope was an unwritten, uncommitted refinancing. The trap is the bundle. Four of the ten sources are there to be discarded: the Partnership Act extract is irrelevant to a company, section 213 requires dishonesty which nobody alleges, section 246ZB applies only where a company has entered administration and Document 3 says in terms that this company never did, and the Sequana material describes a different claim. Candidates who work dutifully through all ten run out of time before reaching quantum. On quantum, the compensatory nature of the jurisdiction and the causation limit on the net deficiency measure are what turn a competent answer into a strong one. Finally, no credit is available for a note which resolves the section 214 analysis beautifully and then agrees to send the fabricated minute, or which quietly says nothing about the £45,000.

Written station 34: Email to a first time director about a purchase from his own company

Legal writing  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  30 minutes

Model answer

From: Trainee Solicitor, Halberd and Rowe LLP

To: Tobias Renn

Date: 11 May 2026

Subject: Unit 7 Calder Road, what has to happen before Larchgate can buy it

Dear Tobias,

Thank you for your email. I can help, but the purchase cannot simply be signed off by you, and there are two points I need to be straight with you about before anything else.

Who we act for

We act for Larchgate Interiors Limited, the company, and not for you personally and not for Renn Holdings Limited. That matters here because on this deal the company is the buyer and you, through Renn Holdings, are effectively the seller. Your interests and the company's interests are not the same, so we cannot look after your side as well. Please take your own solicitor's advice on Renn Holdings' position. Everything below is written to you in your role as a director of Larchgate.

The purchase needs shareholder approval

Renn Holdings is treated in law as connected with you, because you hold all of its shares and that is well above the 20 per cent level that makes a company connected with a director.

Because of that, this is what the Companies Act calls a substantial property transaction. An asset is substantial if it is worth more than 100,000 pounds, or if it is worth more than 5,000 pounds and more than 10 per cent of the company's net assets. Unit 7 is going in at 240,000 pounds. That is above 100,000 pounds, and it is also above 10 per cent of Larchgate's net assets, which on the last accounts is 141,200 pounds. It clears both tests.

So the company cannot enter into this purchase unless the shareholders approve it by ordinary resolution, or unless the contract is made conditional on that approval. In practice that means Nadia and Alan have to be asked, in a general meeting or by written resolution, and told what they are approving. An ordinary resolution needs more than half of the votes, and you hold 30 per cent, so you cannot carry it on your own.

What you personally have to do

First, you must declare the nature and extent of your interest in the purchase to the other directors, and you must do it before the company commits itself. The cleanest way is at a board meeting, minuted.

Second, under the company's articles you are not to be counted in the quorum or the vote on the board decision to buy, because you are interested in it. Nadia and Alan should take that decision.

Third, as a director you owe the company a duty to act in the way you consider, in good faith, would be most likely to promote its success. You cannot exercise that duty properly on this purchase while you are on the other side of it, which is another reason to leave the decision to the other two.

The survey

I cannot leave the surveyor's figure of 185,000 pounds out of what the shareholders are told, and I am afraid you should not either. The shareholders are being asked to approve the company paying 240,000 pounds for the unit. The valuation the company itself obtained is directly relevant to that decision. Withholding it would mean the approval was given on incomplete information, and would expose you personally to the argument that you did not act in the company's best interests. If you feel the valuation is too low, the answer is to say so and explain why, or to obtain a second valuation, not to keep the first one back.

What happens if the steps are missed

If the company buys the unit without shareholder approval, the purchase is voidable by the company, which means the company can unwind it. Separately, and whether or not it is unwound, you and Renn Holdings would have to account to Larchgate for any gain made out of the deal and would have to compensate the company for any loss it suffers. That is a personal exposure for you, so this is worth doing properly.

Next steps

I suggest we convene a board meeting this week at which you declare your interest and then step out of the vote, and that we prepare a written resolution to the shareholders with a short explanatory note attaching the valuation. Please do not exchange contracts or confirm the deal to the agent until that is done.

Please call me if any of this is unwelcome or unclear. It is normal for a first year as a director to throw up something like this, and it is straightforward to fix if we take the steps in the right order.

Kind regards,

Trainee Solicitor

Halberd and Rowe LLP

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two issues sit unflagged in the facts. First, Tobias writes as though the firm acts for him and asks it to look after Renn Holdings too. The retainer is with the company. Acting for both sides of a substantial property transaction where the company is buying from its own director's company is an own interest and client conflict, and the candidate must say plainly that the firm acts for Larchgate alone and that Tobias should instruct his own solicitor. Second, Tobias asks the candidate to keep the 185,000 pound valuation from Nadia and to present the agreed price as the price. Complying would mean the members approve a transaction on information the candidate knows to be incomplete, and would put the candidate's duty to the company client, and the duty not to mislead, in breach. A competent candidate refuses politely, explains that the shareholders being asked to approve must be told, and offers the constructive alternative of a second valuation.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the price of 240,000 pounds, the net asset figure of 1,412,000 pounds and the resulting 10 per cent figure of 141,200 pounds, the 100,000 pound limb, Tobias's 100 per cent holding in Renn Holdings, his 30 per cent holding in Larchgate against Nadia's 45 per cent, the unamended Model Articles, and the 185,000 pound valuation. Every fact used is one that changes the advice.Advises in the abstract that shareholder approval is needed without working the price against either threshold, or ignores that 30 per cent cannot carry an ordinary resolution, or never mentions the valuation at all.
Use a logical structure.SkillsDeals with the retainer point first because it governs everything else, then the company's step, then the director's personal steps, then the valuation, then consequences, then next steps. Short headed sections that a non lawyer can navigate.One unbroken block of text, or the sequencing reversed so the consequences of breach appear before the reader knows what the requirement is, or the retainer point buried at the end as an afterthought.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsAnswers the question Tobias actually asked, which is whether he can just sign, and tells him plainly that he cannot and what to do instead. Recognises that he is a first time director, gives him the practical route through (board meeting, declaration, step out of the vote, written resolution) and tells him what not to do before then. Addresses his personal exposure because that is what will motivate him.A technical exposition of sections 190 and 191 with no instruction to Tobias about what he should actually do on Monday morning, or advice pitched to the company in the abstract that never engages with his stated intention to exchange.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsPlain English throughout for a lay reader with no legal training. Concepts such as connected person, ordinary resolution and voidable are used but explained in a few words each. Firm without being cold, given the candidate has to refuse two of his requests. Fits comfortably in the reading time of a busy director.Latin, unexplained jargon, or statutory quotation dropped in raw. Alternatively a letter so softened that Tobias could read it and still believe he may sign, or so blunt that it reads as an accusation of dishonesty.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly identifies Renn Holdings as a person connected with Tobias on the 20 per cent test, correctly treats the unit as a substantial non cash asset under both limbs, correctly requires an ordinary resolution of the members or a contract conditional on it, and correctly states the section 177 declaration must be made before the company enters the arrangement.Treats the transaction as caught only because Tobias is a director, missing that the counterparty is a connected company; or says a special resolution is needed; or says the declaration can be made after exchange; or states the contract is void rather than voidable.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all four strands: members' approval, the section 177 declaration, the article 14 bar on counting in quorum and vote, and the consequences under section 195 of accounting for gain and indemnifying loss. Also brings in the duty to promote the success of the company as the reason the price and the valuation cannot be brushed aside.Stops at shareholder approval and never reaches the declaration of interest, the voting restriction in the articles or the personal liability to account, leaving Tobias unaware of his own exposure.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies that the client is the company, not Tobias and not Renn Holdings, declines to act for him on the other side of the same transaction, and tells him to take independent advice. Refuses to conceal the valuation from Nadia and Alan and explains why, without lecturing. Recognises the own interest conflict in Tobias directing the company's advisers on a deal he is selling into.Agrees to look after Tobias's side as well, or simply stays silent on the request to keep the survey from Nadia, or promises to withhold it. Any of these is a fail on this criterion no matter how good the company law is.

Examiner notes

The pass is decided by whether the candidate answers the question asked, which is whether Tobias can sign the contract himself, and by whether the two ethical requests in his email are dealt with rather than ignored. Strong candidates do the arithmetic on both limbs of the substantial asset test and show why 30 per cent cannot carry the resolution. The trap is the tone. Candidates who realise the requests must be refused often write to Tobias as though he were the opponent, which loses marks on recipient focus; candidates who keep the warmth often quietly drop the refusal, which loses marks on ethics. The station rewards doing both at once. A second trap is spending the whole 30 minutes on section 190 and never reaching section 177, article 14 or the personal liability to account, which caps the comprehensiveness criterion.

Written station 35: Letter to a lender responding to pre-drawdown confirmations sought

Legal writing  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  30 minutes

Model answer

Trescothick Vane LLP

Sian Morcombe

Relationship Director

Brecon Vale Bank plc

Commercial Lending, Newport

3 February 2027

Dear Ms Morcombe

Thurlow Precision Engineering Limited, facility of 450,000 pounds

Your letter of 30 January 2027

We act for Thurlow Precision Engineering Limited. We do not act for Brecon Vale Bank plc and nothing in this letter is intended as advice to the bank, which we understand is separately advised on the facility and the security. We respond to your numbered requests in turn.

1. Incorporation and standing

We confirm that Thurlow Precision Engineering Limited is a private company limited by shares, incorporated in England and Wales on 4 June 2011 with company number 07641228. A search of the register at Companies House carried out by this firm on 2 February 2027 showed the company on the register, with no outstanding filings shown and no strike off action recorded. That confirmation is given by reference to the search on that date and to the information appearing on the public register.

2. Power to borrow and to grant security

We confirm that the company's articles of association are the Model Articles for private companies limited by shares with one amendment, article 4A, adopted by special resolution on 9 September 2018. Article 4A empowers the directors to exercise all the powers of the company to borrow money and to mortgage or charge the whole or any part of its undertaking, property and assets, present and future, and to issue debentures, without limit as to amount. There is no borrowing limit in the articles.

3. Board authority

We confirm that a meeting of the board was held on 14 January 2027 at which both directors were present, so that the meeting was quorate throughout. The board resolved that the company enter into the facility agreement and the debenture in the form produced to the meeting, and authorised any one director to execute them on behalf of the company. We have seen the signed minute of that meeting.

4. The sum of 180,000 pounds

We are not able to give the confirmation sought in your paragraph 4. That request asks us to confirm both the origin of a payment made into the company's bank account and our own satisfaction as to the source of those funds. Neither is a matter on which this firm is in a position to give a confirmation to a third party. We did not receive or handle the payment, and any confirmation as to where money credited to the company's account came from is a matter for the company and for the bank into which the money was paid, rather than for the company's solicitors. If the bank requires that information it should obtain it directly from the company.

5. Solvency

We are not able to give the confirmation sought in your paragraph 5 either. Whether the directors have disclosed to you all matters relevant to the company's solvency is a matter within the directors' knowledge and not within ours, and a solicitor is not in a position to certify a company's solvency or a director's disclosure to its lender. Confirmations of that kind are conventionally sought from the directors themselves, and if the bank wishes to have them we suggest they are requested from the board directly and in writing.

We are sorry that we cannot assist on your paragraphs 4 and 5. Nothing in this letter should be taken as any confirmation, express or implied, on the matters raised in them, and the bank should not rely on this letter in relation to them.

The confirmations in paragraphs 1 to 3 above are given to the bank for the purposes of the facility only and are given as at the date of this letter.

Yours sincerely

Aled Trescothick

Partner

Trescothick Vane LLP

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The 180,000 pounds arrived from an offshore entity, for no consideration, with no shares issued, no loan agreement and no documentation, from a person the client can name only as Ray, and the client has told the candidate not to go digging. That is a suspicion of money laundering and it triggers a required disclosure to the firm's nominated officer as soon as is practicable. At the same time the candidate must not disclose that a report has been or may be made, which rules out saying anything to the bank or to the client that would reveal it. Cutting across both is the duty not to mislead others: the bank has asked for a confirmation the firm cannot honestly give, and the client wants the drawdown. A competent candidate does three things: reports internally to the nominated officer and raises it with the partner rather than in the letter, declines paragraphs 4 and 5 on grounds that are genuinely true and structural (the firm did not handle the payment and cannot certify solvency or the directors' disclosure), and gives nothing that would let the bank infer a suspicion. The creditor position, the broken time to pay arrangement, the statutory demand expiring on 11 February 2027 and the net liabilities are the reason the solvency confirmation cannot be given and are also matters for separate advice to the directors on their duties as the company approaches insolvency, but none of that goes in this letter.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsGives the bank the specific facts it can act on: incorporation date, company number, the date of the Companies House search, article 4A and its adoption by special resolution, the date and quorum of the board meeting, and the authority for a single director to execute. Draws the confirmations from the documents on the file rather than from assertion.Confirms points 1 to 3 in bare terms with no dates, no company number and no reference to article 4A, so the bank cannot see what the confirmation rests on. Or, at the other extreme, imports facts from the file note about the creditors, HMRC, the statutory demand or Verdanto, none of which belong in this letter.
Use a logical structure.SkillsOpens by identifying who the firm acts for and that it does not act for the bank, then answers the bank's five points in the bank's own numbering, then closes with a clear statement of the scope of the confirmations given. The reader can match the reply to the request line by line.Answers only the three easy points and leaves 4 and 5 unaddressed, or addresses them so obliquely that the bank cannot tell whether a confirmation has been given. Silence on a requested confirmation is the worst structural failure here.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsWritten to a lender's relationship director whose credit sanction depends on the reply. Gives cleanly what can properly be given, declines the rest in terms that are commercially normal and not alarming, and tells the bank where it should go instead: to the company on source of funds and to the directors on solvency. Serves the client's interest in an orderly drawdown without serving it dishonestly.Treating the bank as an opponent and refusing curtly with no route forward; or the opposite, trying to please the client by giving comfort on paragraphs 4 and 5 in hedged language that a lender would read as a confirmation.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsFormal third party correspondence, no advice to the recipient, careful scoping of every confirmation, and an express statement that nothing in the letter is a confirmation on paragraphs 4 and 5. The refusals are unambiguous. Nothing in the wording invites the reader to ask why.Wording that reveals the real reason for the refusal, for example that the firm has concerns about the payment or about the company's ability to pay its debts. Also fails: vague phrases such as we are not currently in a position to confirm, which read as a signal rather than a scope limit.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly confirms corporate capacity and board authority by reference to article 4A, the quorum and the resolution, and correctly identifies that the company's power to borrow without limit comes from the amended article rather than being assumed. Correctly treats source of funds and solvency as matters outside a solicitor's proper certification.Confirming solvency, or confirming that the directors have made full disclosure to the bank, neither of which the firm can know. Also, confirming the board authority without checking that the meeting was quorate or that a single director was authorised to execute.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with all five requests, scopes the three confirmations given as at the date of the letter and for the purposes of the facility only, states that the firm does not act for the bank, and states expressly that the bank should not rely on the letter in relation to paragraphs 4 and 5, closing off any argument of implied assumption of responsibility to the lender.Giving the three confirmations without any scoping or reliance wording, so the firm has given an open ended certification to a non client. Or leaving the reader to infer from silence that paragraphs 4 and 5 are answered.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises that the 180,000 pounds gives rise to a suspicion which must be reported internally to the firm's nominated officer, and that the report and any suspicion must not be disclosed to the bank or to the client. Resolves the tension by declining paragraphs 4 and 5 on neutral, structural grounds that are true and complete in themselves, so the firm neither misleads the bank nor tips anyone off. Keeps the reporting point out of the letter and raises it with the partner instead, as the partner's email invites.Three distinct fails: writing anything in the letter that discloses or hints at a suspicion or an internal report; giving the paragraph 4 or paragraph 5 confirmation to keep the client happy, which misleads the bank; or refusing in terms so pointed that the bank would understand the firm suspects the client, which is tipping off by another route.

Examiner notes

This station tests restraint. The candidate is holding information that would answer the bank's questions and must not use it. A pass requires the three confirmable points to be given properly and paragraphs 4 and 5 to be declined in wording that is true, complete and uninformative. The commonest fail is over-disclosure: candidates who have correctly spotted the money laundering point often want credit for it and put it in the letter, which is the tipping off offence in the clearest possible form. The second commonest is the opposite, giving a soft confirmation on source of funds because the client is under pressure to draw down, which misleads the lender. A third and subtler fail is a refusal so pointed that its meaning is obvious, for example saying the firm has been unable to satisfy itself as to the origin of the funds. The partner's email deliberately says to raise anything the partner needs to know in person and not in the letter, which is the only prompt the candidate gets; there is no instruction to consider ethics and none will be given.

Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)

Written station 1: Contested bail and allocation on an either way fraud by false representation

Case and matter analysis  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO CALLUM ASHGROVE, PARTNER

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 3 February 2027

Re: Nadia Fenwick, fraud by false representation. Marlbury Magistrates' Court, 4 February 2027

1. The offence and where the fight is

The charge is fraud by false representation under sections 1 and 2 of the Fraud Act 2006. The Crown must prove that she made a representation, that it was false in the sense that it was untrue or misleading and she knew it was or might be, that she made it dishonestly, and that she intended to make a gain for herself. The offence is complete when the representation is made, so the fact that the money was paid adds to the picture but is not an element.

Two elements are effectively conceded. She accepts she raised and approved the invoices, and she accepts they were paid to her own account, so the making of a representation and an intended gain are not in issue. The fight is on falsity and on dishonesty, and in reality it is one fight: was the work done and was the arrangement authorised.

Her case is that the design work was genuinely carried out and that the finance director, Mr Renwick, verbally authorised the separate invoicing. If a jury or bench accepts that, the representation was not false and she was not dishonest. If Mr Renwick is believed, the representations were false and the dishonesty finding follows almost automatically on those facts, because there is no innocent reading of invoicing your employer for work you did not do.

Strength of the Crown's case:

(a) 19 invoices, 47,850 pounds, all under her own 5,000 pound approval limit, which supports a deliberate structuring.

(b) No corresponding work in the project system.

(c) Two invoices reference a campaign the company says was cancelled.

(d) Renwick Hollis's account is squarely against her.

Points for the defence:

(e) She used a sole trader account in her own name, not a concealed vehicle. That is a poor way to run a fraud and is a genuine point on dishonesty.

(f) She gave a full account in interview rather than staying silent, and her account has been consistent since.

(g) The design work may exist on her personal laptop, which has not been seized. That is our most important line of enquiry and we should preserve and image the laptop now, and disclose it to the Crown at the right moment.

(h) The case ultimately turns on one word against another on the verbal authorisation. Mr Renwick has an obvious institutional interest in denying it.

The case is arguable but not strong for us on paper. A great deal will depend on the laptop and on any messages between her and Mr Renwick in February 2026.

2. Bail

Section 4 of the Bail Act 1976 gives her a right to bail. The Crown must satisfy the court that there are substantial grounds for believing one of the paragraph 2 exceptions applies. On the papers the Crown will run failure to surrender and interference with witnesses.

Failure to surrender. The Crown's material is that she mentioned a job offer in Malaga, that she was arrested at Marlbury Airport on a warrant, and that she has a 2019 conviction for failing to surrender. Our answers:

(a) The flight was a return flight to visit her sister, landing back at Bristol on 6 February. Counsel must have the booking confirmation from the sister in court. Without it this point fails.

(b) She was arrested on a warrant she did not know existed. Attending an airport is not evidence of flight if the return leg is documented.

(c) She turned the Malaga job down in December.

(d) The 2019 failure to surrender is nearly eight years old, is on a driving matter, was dealt with by a fine, and she says she was in hospital. It is a relevant antecedent under paragraph 9(c) but it is old and low level.

(e) Community ties under paragraph 9(b) are real: she has held the tenancy at 12 Sallowfield Road since 2021, her mother lives in Marlbury and she sees her most days, and she has been offered part time work locally.

Interference with witnesses. The only named witness of substance is Mr Renwick. She is suspended and has no reason or route to approach him, and a condition dealing with it removes the risk.

Nature and seriousness under paragraph 9(a). We must be realistic with the court.
