On the guideline extract we have, an amount between 20,000 and 100,000 pounds with abuse of trust and sustained offending sits in a range with a starting point of about 2 to 3 years before mitigation and plea. So a custodial sentence is a real prospect on conviction, which strengthens the Crown on flight risk. The answer is a conditions package strong enough to meet it.

Package to offer:

(i) Residence at 12 Sallowfield Road, Marlbury, with a condition to live and sleep there each night.

(ii) Surrender of her passport and any travel documents to Marlbury Police Station, and a condition not to apply for any travel document.

(iii) A condition not to enter any airport, seaport or international rail terminal.

(iv) Reporting to Marlbury Police Station three times a week, reducible later.

(v) A condition not to contact directly or indirectly Mark Renwick or any current employee of Renwick Hollis Group Limited, and not to enter the company's premises.

(vi) Security of 3,000 pounds offered by her sister, or the sister as surety if the court prefers, subject to the sister being able to satisfy the court as to means and to the source of the funds. Her sister lives in Malaga, so a surety who cannot readily attend is worth less than a security lodged with the court, and I would offer it as security.

Taken together that meets both exceptions. Counsel should expect bail to be dealt with at the end of the hearing, after plea before venue and allocation, because that is the statutory sequence and because the court will not remand until it knows where the case is going. Counsel should therefore make the bail application on the paragraph 2 exceptions and on the conditions package, and should resist any suggestion that the court's decision to decline jurisdiction is itself a reason to remand in custody: allocation goes to the adequacy of the magistrates' sentencing powers, not to the risk of absconding.

3. Allocation and venue

This is an either way offence. The court must first put the charge and invite an indication of plea under section 17A of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980. She will indicate not guilty, so the court then takes the allocation decision under sections 19 to 21 and the allocation guideline. The court asks whether its sentencing powers are adequate. The general limit for a single either way offence in the magistrates' court is 12 months. The guideline range here starts at about 2 to 3 years' custody. On any realistic view the magistrates will decline jurisdiction and send the case to the Crown Court. Counsel should be prepared for that and should not waste credibility resisting it.

If, contrary to expectation, the magistrates accept jurisdiction, she would then have the right to elect. My recommendation would still be Crown Court trial. The case turns on the credibility of a verbal arrangement between an employee and a finance director, and on documents recovered from a personal laptop. A jury is the better tribunal for that, and Crown Court disclosure and case management will serve us better. The counterweight, which she must be told, is greater sentencing powers, longer delay and higher cost exposure.

She should also be told, before any plea is taken, that a guilty plea at the first hearing attracts the maximum reduction, and that the reduction falls away as the case goes on. She is not pleading guilty, but she is entitled to know the arithmetic before she commits.

4. A matter that must be dealt with before counsel is instructed

Our client has instructed us to tell the court that she lives at her mother's address at 8 Gorse Lane, when she does not live there, and to say nothing about 12 Sallowfield Road. Her sister confirms she has never lived at Gorse Lane. We cannot do that. Putting a residence she does not occupy before the court as the basis for a residence condition would be misleading the court, and a solicitor must not mislead the court or be complicit in another person doing so. The obligation is not diluted by the fact that the instruction came from the client, and it is not cured by counsel saying it rather than us.

I have not repeated the instruction to counsel and I have recorded it on the file. The right course is:

(a) Explain to her, before the hearing, why we cannot advance a false address, and that a residence condition tied to an address she does not live at would be breached on the first night and would destroy her credibility on bail for the rest of the case.

(b) Explain that the true position is better for her anyway: a tenancy she has held since 2021 is a stronger community tie than staying at her mother's house.

(c) If she maintains the instruction, we cannot act on it. We may continue to act on the true facts, but we cannot advance the false address, and if she insists we must cease to act. If we do cease to act we say nothing to the court about why, because the reason is privileged, and we tell the court only that we are professionally embarrassed.

Nothing she has told us in confidence is disclosed to the court either way.

Trainee Solicitor

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client instructs the firm to tell the court she lives at her mother's address at 8 Gorse Lane because it sounds more settled, and to say nothing about her own flat, where she will in fact be living. Her sister's email confirms she has never lived at Gorse Lane. Advancing that address as the basis for a residence condition would mislead the court, which a solicitor must never do and must not allow another person to do on the solicitor's behalf, including counsel. A competent candidate refuses the instruction, does not repeat it to counsel, explains to the client that the truth is better for her because a tenancy held since 2021 is a stronger community tie, and states that if she insists the firm must cease to act, telling the court only that it is professionally embarrassed, because the reason is privileged and confidential.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsExtracts the facts that decide the bail application and the allocation decision: the return flight and the sister's evidence, the arrest on a warrant she did not know about, the age and nature of the 2019 failure to surrender, the tenancy since 2021 and the local family, the 5,000 pound approval limit, the invoices in her own name, the unseized laptop, and the guideline range.Summarises the fraud allegation at length and reaches bail with no factual material to answer the Crown's two objections, or overlooks that the airport arrest was on a warrant she says she did not know about.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsAdvises the partner on what to do tomorrow: a specific conditions package answering each exception, the recommendation to deal with bail first, the realistic expectation that jurisdiction will be declined, and the credit for plea arithmetic the client must be told before any plea.Sets out the law on bail and allocation without recommending any condition, or offers a generic list of conditions that does not answer failure to surrender or interference with witnesses.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured report to the partner in short numbered sections, honest about the weaknesses, in British English and within a workable length.Writes an advocacy speech or a client letter rather than a report, or buries the misleading address problem in a closing line.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies section 2 of the Fraud Act 2006 element by element, identifies that the making of the representation and intended gain are conceded so the fight is falsity and dishonesty, applies the section 4 right to bail with the paragraph 2 exceptions and paragraph 9 considerations, and applies the 12 month general limit against the guideline range.Treats payment of the money as an element of the offence, or reverses the burden by arguing the defendant must persuade the court to grant bail rather than the Crown must make out an exception.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers the whole of the task: offence analysis, both bail exceptions with the answer to each, a full conditions package including security and its practical weakness where the surety lives abroad, allocation with reasons, election if jurisdiction were accepted, and the practical next step of preserving and imaging the laptop.Deals with bail but not allocation, or asserts the magistrates will keep the case without measuring the guideline range against the 12 month limit.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies unprompted that the client has asked the firm to put a false residential address before the court, refuses to advance it, explains why the true address is in fact the stronger point, and sets out the consequences if she insists, including ceasing to act while preserving privilege.Treats the address instruction as a tactical choice, passes it to counsel to decide, or proposes to disclose the client's confidential instruction to the court as the way of resolving it.

Examiner notes

The pass line is a bail application built out of the actual facts rather than a recitation of Schedule 1. Candidates must answer both exceptions the Crown will run and offer conditions that are matched to them, including passport surrender and a no airport condition against flight risk and a non contact condition against interference. The commonest failure is to treat bail as an argument about seriousness rather than about risk and how conditions manage it. The second trap is allocation. Weak candidates argue for summary trial because the client wants the case over quickly, without measuring a 2 to 3 year guideline starting point against the 12 month general limit in the magistrates' court, which makes a declination of jurisdiction close to inevitable. The third trap is the security offered by a sister who lives in Malaga: candidates should notice that a surety who cannot attend is worth less than a security lodged with the court. The ethics point is deliberately dressed as a small practical tidying up of the client's address and is missed by candidates who read the attendance note quickly.

Written station 2: Drafting a defence statement on a theft alleging a belief in a legal right

Legal drafting  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  45 minutes

Model answer

IN THE CROWN COURT AT ASHCOMBE

CASE NUMBER: T20260419

REGINA

-v-

MARCUS TEBBUTT

DEFENCE STATEMENT

Served under sections 5 and 6A of the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996

1. THE NATURE OF THE DEFENCE

1.1 The defendant denies count 1. He accepts that on 3 August 2026 he attended the site at Pikelow Lane, Ashcombe, and that he removed 44 insulation boards and a drum of armoured cable in his own van. He accepts that this was an appropriation of property belonging to Halloway Construction Limited.

1.2 The defendant denies that the appropriation was dishonest. He relies on section 2(1)(a) of the Theft Act 1968. He appropriated the property in the belief that he had in law the right to deprive Halloway Construction Limited of it, because he believed the company owed him 3,140 pounds in unpaid overtime and untaken holiday pay and that he was entitled to take goods of about that value in place of the money owed.

1.3 In the further alternative the defendant relies on section 2(1)(b) of the Theft Act 1968. He had been told by the site manager, Chris Naismith, that surplus material on the Pikelow Lane site was written off and treated as waste, and he had seen other site workers remove such material without objection. He believed the company would have consented to the removal had it known of the appropriation and the circumstances of it.

1.4 The defendant relies on his belief as it was genuinely held. It is not necessary for the defence that the belief was reasonable.

1.5 The defendant does not dispute that the value of the property removed was in the region of 3,200 pounds.

2. MATTERS OF FACT ON WHICH ISSUE IS TAKEN WITH THE PROSECUTION, AND WHY

2.1 The defendant takes issue with the evidence of Fiona Delacourt that no outstanding sums were owed to him. He disputes it because he worked approximately 190 hours of overtime which was never paid and accrued 14 days of holiday which he never took, and because he requested payment on three occasions, twice by text message to Ms Delacourt and once in person, and was told only that the final payment of 812 pounds represented the whole of his entitlement.

2.2 The defendant takes issue with the evidence of Fiona Delacourt that the material removed was not surplus and was allocated to plots 14 to 19. He disputes it because he had been told by the site manager, Chris Naismith, that overs on that job were written off and treated as waste, and because he had seen other site workers remove such material without objection.

2.3 The defendant takes issue with the assertion that he acted covertly or without the knowledge of the company. He disputes it because he attended the site at about 14:40 on a working day, drove in through the manned main gate in a van bearing his own name, told the gateman Ivan Roscoe what he was taking, permitted his registration number to be recorded in the gate log, and loaded the material in the open in full view of the site camera.

2.4 The defendant does not take issue with the fact of the removal, the identity of the material removed, or the fact that he had been dismissed on 28 July 2026.

3. PARTICULARS OF THE MATTERS OF FACT RELIED ON FOR THE PURPOSES OF THE DEFENCE

3.1 The defendant was employed by Halloway Construction Limited as site foreman at Pikelow Lane from March 2024 until his dismissal on 28 July 2026.

3.2 By the date of his dismissal the defendant had worked approximately 190 hours of unpaid overtime and had accrued 14 days of untaken holiday. He calculated the sum owed to him at 3,140 pounds by reference to his wage slips.

3.3 The defendant requested payment of that sum on three occasions, twice by text message to Fiona Delacourt and once in person. He received a final payment of 812 pounds on 31 July 2026 and no further sum.

3.4 During his employment the defendant was told by the site manager, Chris Naismith, on more than one occasion that surplus material on the Pikelow Lane site was written off and treated as waste. The defendant observed other site workers removing surplus material without objection from the company.

3.5 On 3 August 2026 the defendant attended the site at about 14:40 in his own van, which bears his name. He entered through the manned main gate. He informed the gateman, Ivan Roscoe, that he was taking the insulation boards and the cable. His registration number was recorded in the gate log. He loaded the material in the open, in daylight, within the field of view of the site camera.

3.6 The defendant selected a quantity of material which he believed to be of approximately the value of the sum owed to him, and no more.

3.7 The defendant retains all of the material at his home address at 41 Wrenfield Close, Ashcombe. He informed the police of that fact in his interview under caution on 11 August 2026, and the material remains available for inspection or collection.

3.8 The defendant made no attempt to sell, use or otherwise dispose of the material.

4. POINTS OF LAW AND AUTHORITIES

4.1 Section 2(1) of the Theft Act 1968 provides that an appropriation is not to be regarded as dishonest where the defendant holds the belief there described. Where section 2(1) applies, dishonesty is not made out and the general test of dishonesty does not arise. The belief need not be reasonable, provided it is genuinely held.

4.2 The burden of proving each element of the offence, including dishonesty, rests upon the prosecution throughout, to the criminal standard.

4.3 No point is taken at this stage as to the admissibility of any evidence or as to abuse of process. The defendant reserves the right to take any such point in the light of further disclosure.

5. ALIBI

5.1 No alibi is relied on.

6. REQUEST FOR DISCLOSURE

6.1 The gate log for the Pikelow Lane site for 3 August 2026, and for the preceding six months, on the basis that it records the defendant's attendance and registration number and may record other attendances by former or current workers removing material, which is capable of assisting the defence on paragraphs 2.2 and 2.3 above.

6.2 The full site camera footage for 3 August 2026, and not only the extract relied on, on the basis that it shows the manner of the loading and is capable of assisting the defence on paragraph 2.3.

6.3 Any statement, note or record of any account given by Ivan Roscoe, including any first account taken by an officer, on the basis that it is capable of confirming that the defendant told him what he was taking.

6.4 Any statement, note or record of any account given by or sought from Chris Naismith, on the basis that it is capable of confirming what the defendant was told about surplus material.

6.5 The company's records of materials written off as waste on the Pikelow Lane site, and any internal policy or instruction as to the removal of surplus material, on the basis that they are capable of supporting paragraph 3.4.

6.6 The company's payroll, timesheet and holiday records for the defendant for the whole of his employment, on the basis that they are capable of supporting paragraphs 3.2 and 3.3.

6.7 The text messages sent by the defendant to Fiona Delacourt requesting payment, and any reply, if in the possession of the prosecution.

Signed: ......................................

Owen Brackley, Solicitor for the Defendant, Marlow Quayle Solicitors

Dated: ...................... October 2026

COVERING NOTE FOR THE PARTNER

1. The statement is drafted on the section 2(1)(a) belief in a legal right, with section 2(1)(b) in the alternative. Both come straight out of his proof, and the surrounding facts, the daylight attendance, the gate log, the named van, telling the gateman and keeping everything in the garage, all support a genuinely held belief. Section 6(1) may still be argued by the Crown on the basis that he treated the goods as his own to dispose of regardless of the company's rights, but if the section 2(1) belief is accepted the count fails on dishonesty in any event.

2. I have not included the alibi the client asked for, and I have stated positively that no alibi is relied on. He has told you in his proof that he drove to the site on 3 August, that he told the gateman what he was taking and that the material is in his garage. An assertion that he was in Cardiff all that day and was never there would therefore be a statement we know to be untrue. We cannot draft or serve a document putting that before the court, and we could not call Mr Verity to say it. I have not named Mr Verity anywhere in the statement.

3. He also needs to be told, before he signs anything off, that the two accounts cannot both be run. They are mutually inconsistent, and under section 11 of the 1996 Act a court or jury may draw proper inferences where inconsistent defences are given in a defence statement or where a defence is run at trial that was not mentioned in it. Putting both in would destroy the section 2(1) defence, which is the good one.

4. Please could you see him with me to explain this and to confirm his instructions on the statement as drafted. If he insists on the Cardiff account being included or advanced, we cannot act and will have to come off the record, telling the court no more than that we are professionally embarrassed.

5. One query for you: he says he sent two text messages to Ms Delacourt asking for the money. Do we have his handset or a download? If we do not, we should get it before 26 October, because those messages are the best independent support for paragraph 3.3.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client's own proof of evidence admits that he drove to the site on 3 August 2026, told the gateman what he was taking and still has the material in his garage. He then instructs the firm to plead in the alternative that he was in Cardiff all day and was never there, saying a friend will give evidence to that effect. Drafting and serving a defence statement containing that assertion would put before the court a fact the firm knows to be untrue, and calling the friend would be calling evidence known to be false. A competent candidate does not plead the alibi, states expressly that no alibi is relied on, does not name the proposed witness, explains to the partner why, warns that the two accounts are mutually inconsistent so that inferences could be drawn under section 11 of the 1996 Act and the good defence would be destroyed, and records that if the client insists the firm must cease to act, telling the court only that it is professionally embarrassed.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsFormal, precise drafting throughout. Numbered paragraphs, one proposition each, no narrative padding, British English, and language a court would accept in a served document rather than a summary of the client's proof in his own words.Reproduces the proof of evidence as continuous prose, writes in the first person as the client, or uses loose language such as saying the client felt the company had been unfair rather than stating the belief relied on.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsFollows the precedent's six headings in order and puts the right material under each: the defence and the defences relied on in section 1, disputed facts with reasons in section 2, positive facts in section 3, law in section 4, the alibi position in section 5, and a properly reasoned disclosure request in section 6.Collapses sections 2 and 3 so that no reason is given for any matter in issue, omits the alibi heading altogether, or leaves the precedent's square bracket prompts in the served draft.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawPleads the defence correctly: the appropriation is admitted, dishonesty is denied by reference to section 2(1)(a), with section 2(1)(b) in the alternative, and it is stated that the belief need not be reasonable and that the burden remains on the prosecution.Denies the appropriation, which the client's own account admits, argues the general test of dishonesty without ever reaching section 2(1), or asserts that the client had a legal right to the goods rather than that he believed he had.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawComplies with the whole of section 6A: nature of the defence, each matter in issue with the reason for it, positive particulars, the point of law, and an express statement that no alibi is relied on, together with a disclosure request that gives a reason for each item sought.Omits the reasons required by section 6A(1)(c), leaves the alibi section blank rather than stating that no alibi is relied on, or asks for disclosure with no basis stated for any item.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses to plead the Cardiff account, states positively that no alibi is relied on, does not name the proposed witness anywhere, and explains to the partner why the account cannot be advanced and what must happen if the client insists.Pleads the alibi in section 5 with the witness's details, or hedges by pleading both accounts in the alternative, which puts a statement known to be untrue before the court and would attract inferences for inconsistent defences.

Examiner notes

This station is deliberately a good defence spoiled by a bad instruction. The pass line is a defence statement that admits the appropriation and denies dishonesty under section 2(1)(a), because a candidate who denies the taking has not read the proof. The section 6A discipline is the second half of the pass line: every matter in issue needs the reason for it, not just the assertion, and section 6A(2) means the alibi heading must be answered one way or the other rather than left blank. The trap is the client's request for a fallback account. Weak candidates plead it in the alternative, on the reasoning that alternative defences are permissible. Alternative defences are permissible, but not an alternative the solicitor knows to be false, and here the client's own instructions place him at the site. Candidates who plead both also fail to see the practical damage: inconsistent defences invite proper inferences under section 11 and would sink the section 2(1) belief, which is the defence that could actually win. Marks are also lost by candidates who leave the precedent's bracketed prompts in a document the partner is asked to sign and serve.

Written station 3: Skeleton written bail application in a contested fraud remand

Legal drafting  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  45 minutes

Model answer

IN THE MAGISTRATES' COURT AT ASHGROVE

REGINA -v- LORCAN WHITBEY

SKELETON ARGUMENT IN SUPPORT OF AN APPLICATION FOR BAIL

Hearing: 5 March 2027 at 10:00

A. INTRODUCTION

1. The defendant is aged 29 and is charged with one offence of fraud by false representation, contrary to sections 1 and 2 of the Fraud Act 2006. The total sum alleged is £11,240 across eleven invoices. He indicates a not guilty plea.

2. He was charged on 3 March 2027, refused police bail, and remanded into custody at HMP Netherfold on 4 March 2027 when the case was adjourned for this contested hearing. This is the defendant's first application for bail before this court and it is made on the merits.

3. The defendant is entitled to bail under section 4(1) of the Bail Act 1976 unless the court is satisfied that one of the exceptions in Schedule 1 applies. The burden of establishing substantial grounds under paragraph 2 rests on the prosecution.

4. The court is asked to note two matters of fact which the defence puts before it at the outset rather than leaving to be discovered.

4.1 The address recorded by the police, 4 Sedgewood Row, is no longer available to the defendant and the defence does not ask the court to release him to it. A different and verified address is proposed at paragraph 21 below.

4.2 The defendant was granted police bail on 8 February 2027 in respect of an allegation of theft of a bicycle, listed at Marlow Grange Magistrates' Court on 30 March 2027. That matter has not been discontinued so far as the defence is presently aware. The alleged offence in the present case is said to have been committed between 1 September 2026 and 20 January 2027, that is before the grant of police bail on 8 February 2027, so paragraph 2A of Schedule 1 Part I is not engaged. The defence draws the matter to the court's attention because it is relevant to the paragraph 9 assessment and because the court should have a complete picture.

B. THE PROSECUTION OBJECTIONS

5. The prosecution objects under paragraph 2 of Part I of Schedule 1 to the Bail Act 1976, contending that there are substantial grounds for believing that the defendant would, if released:

5.1 fail to surrender to custody (paragraph 2(a));

5.2 commit an offence while on bail (paragraph 2(b));

5.3 interfere with witnesses or otherwise obstruct the course of justice (paragraph 2(c)).

6. The defence answers each in turn. The correct question in each case is not whether a risk can be imagined but whether there are substantial grounds for the belief, and whether any such risk can be met by conditions under section 3(6).

C. RESPONSE TO EACH OBJECTION

Objection 1: failure to surrender

7. The single failure to surrender is now nearly four years old. It arose in June 2023 when the defendant had moved address and did not receive the notice of hearing. He attended court of his own motion the following morning. The court record confirms the voluntary surrender. That is the conduct of a man who returns to court, not one who absconds.

8. Since that date the defendant has completed a suspended sentence order of 12 weeks suspended for 12 months without any breach, and has attended every appointment required of him. His record as respects the fulfilment of his obligations under previous grants of bail, which is the express paragraph 9(c) consideration, is otherwise unblemished.

9. The defendant answered questions in interview and advanced a positive account. He was suspended on 22 January 2027 and dismissed on 9 February 2027 but did not leave the area and was arrested at an address in Ashgrove. He has lived in Ashgrove all his life.

10. The proposed address at paragraph 21.1 is verified and the occupier has been spoken to. A surety is offered. A man who absconds forfeits his uncle's savings, which is a real and personal restraint.

11. As to the probable method of dealing with the defendant under paragraph 9(a), this is an allegation of £11,240 obtained by an employee over some months. It is a serious allegation. It is not, however, one which makes an immediate custodial sentence inevitable on a first fraud conviction with a guilty character reference, and the defendant indicates a not guilty plea with an identified evidential answer. The incentive to abscond is correspondingly limited.

Objection 2: commission of further offences on bail

12. The defendant has three convictions for dishonesty, the most recent in 2023. There is nothing between 2023 and the present allegation. The pattern relied on is a historic one.

13. The alleged offending is workplace specific. It depended entirely on the defendant's position as an assistant contracts administrator at Brancaster Facilities Limited with authority to approve invoices up to £2,000. He was suspended on 22 January 2027 and dismissed on 9 February 2027. The opportunity relied on by the prosecution no longer exists and cannot be recreated.

14. The defendant has an offer of casual warehouse shifts from Rothbury Logistics at their Ashgrove depot, evidenced by text message, beginning the week after next. Lawful work reduces rather than increases the risk relied on.

15. As to paragraph 9(d), the strength of the evidence is not all one way. The defendant accepts the account is his but says the arrangement was authorised orally by his then line manager, Mr Hadrian Voke, and that an email chain on his former work account refers to it. That material has not yet been obtained. Remand in custody makes it markedly harder for the defendant to assist in recovering it.

Objection 3: interference with witnesses

16. The defendant accepts sending two text messages to Ms Ines Carraway on 12 February 2027. That was before charge, at the point of his dismissal, and the messages are on their face expressions of distress. The second message is capable of being read as a request that she give a particular account and the defence does not seek to minimise it.

17. There has been no contact of any kind since 12 February 2027, a period of three weeks, including a period after the defendant knew he was under investigation. There has been no attendance at her home or workplace, no third party approach and no repetition.

18. This is the objection most obviously capable of being met by condition rather than by remand. A condition of no contact, direct or indirect, with the named witness, coupled with an exclusion zone around her place of work, addresses the risk directly and is enforceable, breach being an arrestable matter under section 7 of the Bail Act 1976.

Overall

19. Taking the paragraph 9 considerations together, the defendant has settled community ties in Ashgrove, a verified address, an available surety, an offer of employment, a single and explained failure to surrender nearly four years ago, a completed suspended sentence order, and a positive case to advance. The prosecution cannot establish substantial grounds on any of the three limbs once the conditions below are in place.

20. If the court is against the defendant on any limb, the defence invites the court to consider whether the risk identified can be managed by a condition before concluding that only custody will do.

D. PROPOSED CONDITIONS

21. The defendant offers the following conditions, each of which is directed to a purpose in section 3(6) of the Bail Act 1976.

21.1 Residence at 27 Halloway Terrace, Ashgrove, and nowhere else, with a requirement to be present at that address between 22:00 and 06:00 daily. The occupier, Mr Sefton Whitbey, has confirmed the room is available immediately and that he is content for the address to be given to the court. Purpose: section 3(6)(a), to secure surrender.

21.2 A surety in the sum of £1,000 to be entered into by Mr Sefton Whitbey, who is the defendant's uncle, is retired, is at the address for most of the day, has savings of approximately £4,000 and has no convictions. He will attend court to be taken through his obligations. Purpose: section 3(6)(a). The court is invited to find him suitable under section 8.

21.3 A condition not to contact, directly or indirectly, Ms Ines Carraway, or any other person named by the prosecution as a witness in these proceedings. Purpose: section 3(6)(c).

21.4 A condition not to enter the premises of Brancaster Facilities Limited at Marchwood Business Park, Ashgrove. Purpose: section 3(6)(b) and (c).

21.5 A condition to report to Ashgrove police station on Mondays and Thursdays between 09:00 and 19:00. Purpose: section 3(6)(a).

21.6 A condition to surrender his passport to Ashgrove police station within 24 hours of release and not to apply for any international travel document. Purpose: section 3(6)(a).

21.7 A condition not to hold or operate any bank account other than his existing personal account, details of which will be provided to the officer in the case, and not to undertake any work involving the approval or submission of invoices. Purpose: section 3(6)(b).

22. The defendant is content for the court to add a condition requiring him to attend any interview with his solicitor under section 3(6)(e) and to make himself available for the preparation of any report under section 3(6)(d).

E. CONCLUSION

23. The court is invited to grant conditional bail on the terms set out at paragraph 21, alternatively on such terms as the court considers necessary.

Served by: Coombe Vessey LLP, solicitors for the defendant

Dated: 4 March 2027

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two related points sit in the conference note. First, the client instructs the firm to give his mother's address to the court when the solicitor has spoken to the mother and knows the address is not available. The firm cannot put an address before the court which it knows the client cannot occupy, so it proposes only the uncle's address, which has been verified with the occupier, and it does not ask the court to release the client to the police recorded address at 4 Sedgewood Row, which is no longer available to him. Second, the client asks the firm to keep quiet about the outstanding theft allegation listed on 30 March 2027 and to allow the court to proceed on the basis that it is finished, which he confirms he has no basis for saying. The firm cannot state or imply that the matter is concluded, and cannot advance the application on a basis it knows to be wrong. It is not, however, free simply to volunteer the matter against the client's instructions, because the client's affairs are confidential under paragraph 6.3 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs and no exception applies. The two duties are reconciled by taking the client's instructions before filing. The skeleton as drafted relies on there having been nothing since 2023, so that argument cannot be run while the pending charge is suppressed. The competent candidate therefore either states the true position with the client's agreement, or drops any argument that depends on the absence of recent matters, and records that if the client insists that the application be advanced on the footing that the theft matter is finished, the firm cannot act and must cease to act, telling the court only that it is professionally embarrassed and giving no reasons, because the reasons are privileged. The candidate also analyses the pending matter correctly rather than fearing it. Paragraph 2A of Schedule 1 Part I is not a discretionary exception of the paragraph 2 kind: it provides that bail may not be granted where the defendant was on bail in criminal proceedings on the date of the offence, unless the court is satisfied that there is no significant risk of his committing an offence while on bail. It is therefore a prohibition with a statutory escape, and where it bites it displaces the section 4 right to bail unless the court is affirmatively satisfied. It is not engaged on these dates, because the charge period ends on 20 January 2027 and the police bail was granted on 8 February 2027. Confidentiality applies to the client's own words in conference throughout, so the skeleton records objective facts and never the conversation.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsShort numbered paragraphs written for an advocate to speak from. Each condition is stated in terms a court could pronounce and a police officer could enforce, with the address, the times, the police station and the named witness all specified. Measured tone that concedes the weak points rather than overselling.Emotive advocacy in place of argument, or conditions written so loosely that they could not be entered on a bail record, for example "the defendant will stay away from witnesses" or "he will live at a suitable address".
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsThe precedent's five sections are used. The three objections are listed once, then answered one by one in the same order, and the conditions section pairs each proposed condition with the section 3(6) purpose and therefore with the objection it neutralises. The reader can see at a glance that nothing has been left unanswered.A single undifferentiated narrative of the client's good points, so that the court has to work out for itself which passage answers which objection, or a conditions list bolted on at the end with no link back to any objection.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawThe right to bail under section 4 is correctly stated, with the paragraph 2 exceptions correctly framed as requiring substantial grounds and with the burden on the prosecution. Each proposed condition is tied to a purpose actually listed in section 3(6). Paragraph 2A is correctly analysed and correctly held not to apply, because the alleged offence predates the grant of police bail on 8 February 2027.Treating the defendant as bearing the burden of showing he should be released, inventing conditions with no section 3(6) purpose such as a general good behaviour requirement, or misapplying paragraph 2A by asserting that the defendant was on bail at the time of the offence when the charge period ends on 20 January 2027.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawAll three objections are answered on their own terms, the paragraph 9 factors are worked through rather than recited, the surety is addressed by reference to section 8 with his means, character and proximity, and the outstanding Marlow Grange matter is dealt with openly. The skeleton also takes the alternative position that any residual risk is met by conditions.Answering only the objections that are easy, typically the failure to surrender, and passing over the witness contact, which is the objection the bench will be most concerned about. Also offering a surety without any of the section 8 material the court needs to assess suitability.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawThe candidate refuses to put the mother's address before the court and uses the verified uncle's address instead, and does not ask the court to release the client to the police recorded address which is no longer available. On the outstanding Marlow Grange matter the candidate recognises that there is no duty to volunteer material adverse to the client, but that the skeleton cannot both suppress the pending charge and rely on there having been nothing since 2023. Either resolution earns full credit: stating the position openly where the client's instructions to do so have been obtained, or drafting the skeleton so that no argument depends on the absence of recent matters and recording that the client's instructions must be taken before filing.Proposing residence at 12 Larkspur Road because the client asked for it, when the occupier has refused. Equally a fail is a skeleton which suppresses the outstanding theft matter while still arguing that there has been nothing since 2023, which is misleading the court by advancing an argument the drafter knows to be false, or which asks the court to release the client to 4 Sedgewood Row when that address is no longer available to him. Some candidates go too far the other way and volunteer the client's own words from the conference, which breaches confidentiality without any need.

Examiner notes

A pass turns on answering all three objections and offering a condition package that is actually anchored in section 3(6). The single biggest discriminator is what the candidate does with the address. A weak candidate writes "residence at 12 Larkspur Road" because that is what the client said, missing that the solicitor has already telephoned the mother and been told no. A middling candidate spots the problem and simply omits any address, which leaves the bail application without its most important condition and will fail on comprehensiveness. A strong candidate uses the verified uncle's address, supports it with the section 8 surety material, and turns the whole thing into a strength. The second discriminator is the outstanding Marlow Grange matter. Many candidates will either suppress it or assert that paragraph 2A applies. Neither is right. Paragraph 2A is not a discretionary exception; it says the defendant may not be granted bail if he was on bail in criminal proceedings on the date of the offence, unless the court is satisfied there is no significant risk of his offending on bail. That is why it matters that on these dates it is not engaged at all: the charge period ends on 20 January 2027 and the police bail was granted on 8 February 2027, so the defendant was not on bail in criminal proceedings on the date of the alleged offence. A candidate who has read the dates says so, and a candidate who asserts that it applies has put his own client under a materially harder test than the law requires. The related conduct point is that the skeleton positively relies on there having been nothing since 2023, so the pending matter cannot be left out while that argument is run; a candidate who instead drops the argument, or who records that the client's instructions on disclosing the matter must be taken before the skeleton is filed, is doing the same job by a different route and should not be marked down for it.

Written station 4: Bad character propensity notice in a handling stolen goods trial

Legal research  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

RESEARCH NOTE

To: Rosalind Ackworth, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 21 September 2026

Matter: R v Gethin Amory, Crown Court at Farrowmede, T2026/0912, trial 3 November 2026

Subject: Prosecution bad character notice under section 101(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003

1. SUMMARY OF ADVICE

1.1 The 2023 handling conviction is very likely to be admitted. It is an offence of the same description, it is recent, and its facts closely mirror the present allegation: cash at well below value, identifying marks removed, storage in a rented unit. That is the modus operandi point Hanson identifies as making a conviction genuinely probative.

1.2 The 2010 shop theft is weak. It is 16 years old, the defendant was 19, and it has no feature in common with the present allegation. On Hanson it is the paradigm old conviction with no special feature shared with the offence charged, and there is nothing in a 2010 shop theft that could be said to show a propensity continuing into a 2026 receiving allegation.

1.3 The 2014 handling conviction is disputed on the facts. The client says it belongs to his brother, who gave the client's name and date of birth. That has to be investigated at once, because if it is right the prosecution is asking the jury to hear a conviction that is not his.

1.4 The 2024 excess alcohol conviction should not be admitted at all. It is neither the same description nor the same category, it says nothing about propensity to handle stolen goods and nothing about propensity to be untruthful.

1.5 The propensity to untruthfulness limb at paragraph 4 of the notice is misconceived on Hanson and should be resisted.

1.6 The notice is out of time. There is a real procedural point, though it is unlikely on its own to keep the 2023 conviction out.

1.7 There is a conflict of interest issue on the file which needs a decision from you before anything else happens, and I deal with it at section 6.

2. QUESTION 1: WHAT CAN PROPERLY COME IN THROUGH GATEWAY (d)?

The framework

2.1 Evidence of the defendant's bad character is admissible only through one of the gateways in section 101(1) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The common law rules are abolished by section 99(1). The prosecution relies on gateway (d), evidence relevant to an important matter in issue between the defendant and the prosecution.

2.2 By section 103(1)(a) the matters in issue include whether the defendant has a propensity to commit offences of the kind charged, except where such a propensity makes it no more likely that he is guilty. Propensity may be established under section 103(2) by convictions for an offence of the same description or the same category, but section 103(3) disapplies that route where the court is satisfied, by reason of the length of time since the conviction or for any other reason, that it would be unjust.

2.3 Handling stolen goods and theft both fall within the Theft Category prescribed by the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (Categories of Offences) Order 2004, and two handling offences are of the same description because the statement of offence would be in the same terms.

2.4 R v Hanson [2005] EWCA Crim 824 sets the three questions: does the history establish a propensity to commit offences of the kind charged; does that propensity make it more likely he committed this offence; and is it unjust to rely on the convictions, and in any event would the proceedings be unfair. Hanson also holds that being of the same description or category is neither exhaustive nor necessarily sufficient, that the fewer the convictions the weaker the evidence of propensity, and that old convictions with no special feature shared with the offence charged are likely seriously to affect the fairness of the proceedings adversely, unless despite their age they can properly be said to show a continuing propensity.

2.5 The issue in this trial is narrow. Possession is admitted. The only question is knowledge or belief that the goods were stolen. That narrowness cuts both ways. It means a genuine propensity to handle is highly relevant, and it means a conviction that says nothing about that state of mind has no work to do.

Conviction (c), handling, 19 January 2023

2.6 This is the prosecution's real case and we should expect it to be admitted. It is an offence of the same description within section 103(4)(a). It is three years old. Most importantly the facts share several significant features with the present count: goods bought for cash at well below value, identifying marks deliberately removed (serial numbers ground off there, plates removed here), and storage in a rented lock up. On Hanson those shared features are what turns a same description conviction into evidence of propensity, and they bear directly on the only issue in the case, which is whether he knew or believed. Question 1 and question 2 of Hanson are both answered against us.

2.7 Our arguments against it are limited. We can say that a single qualifying conviction is a thin basis for propensity, and Hanson accepts that a single conviction will often not show propensity. But Hanson qualifies that immediately: it may do so where the modus operandi has significant features shared with the offence charged, which is this case. I would advise you not to expect to keep it out and to prepare instead for how it is presented and how the jury is directed about it.

Conviction (a), theft (shop), 12 March 2010

2.8 This is within the Theft Category, so section 103(2)(b) is technically satisfied. It should nonetheless be excluded.

2.9 It is 16 years old at trial. The defendant was 19 at the time and the penalty was a £120 fine. It has no feature in common with a receiving allegation: shop theft involves taking, not receiving, and tells the jury nothing about whether this man knew mowers were stolen when he bought them. Hanson says in terms that old convictions with no special feature shared with the offence charged are likely seriously to affect the fairness of the proceedings adversely, unless despite their age they can properly be said to show a continuing propensity, and a single fine for shop theft when the defendant was 19 shows nothing continuing. Section 103(3) allows the court to disapply the same category route where by reason of the length of time it would be unjust, and section 101(4) requires the court on an exclusion application to have particular regard to the length of time. This is the strongest of our exclusion arguments after the excess alcohol conviction.

Conviction (b), handling, 4 November 2014

2.10 On its face this is the same description as the present count and is 12 years old. If it is properly the defendant's, it would strengthen the propensity case, though the facts (three car stereos for £30 in a public house) are of a different order to the present allegation and the age of it supports a section 103(3) and section 101(4) argument.

2.11 The real point is different. The client's instruction is that the conviction is not his, and that his brother gave the client's name and date of birth on arrest in 2014. If that is right, the prosecution is proposing to put before the jury a conviction that belongs to somebody else. We should:

(a) obtain the full antecedents printout and the memorandum of conviction for 4 November 2014, which will show the address, date of birth and any custody photograph or fingerprint reference;

(b) require the prosecution to prove the conviction and its attribution to this defendant, which it must do if the fact is disputed;

(c) set out in the exclusion application under rule 21.4(5)(c) precisely which facts in the notice we dispute, which is exactly what that rule requires.

2.12 I would not advise taking a position on this in correspondence until we have the memorandum of conviction. If the attribution is correct, the client's account that his brother used his name is itself an assertion the jury could hold against him.

Conviction (d), driving with excess alcohol, 7 June 2024

2.13 This should be resisted outright and I would expect the prosecution to abandon it. It is not an offence of the same description as handling and is not in the Theft Category, so section 103(2) does not assist the prosecution at all. That is not fatal in itself, because Hanson confirms section 103(2) is not exhaustive, but the prosecution would then have to show some other route by which drink driving makes it more likely that this defendant knew these mowers were stolen. There is none. On Hanson question 2, the propensity does not make it more likely he is guilty, and section 103(1)(a) itself excludes a propensity which makes it no more likely that he is guilty.

Propensity to be untruthful

2.14 Paragraph 4 of the notice asserts propensity to be untruthful under section 103(1)(b). Hanson holds that propensity to untruthfulness is not to be equated with propensity to dishonesty, and that previous convictions are only likely to show it where the defendant pleaded not guilty and gave an account the jury must have disbelieved, or where the offence itself involved making false statements or representations. None of these four convictions is of that character on the material we have, and we do not know how any of them was disposed of. This limb should be resisted and the prosecution put to proof on how the convictions were entered.

3. QUESTION 2: THE APPLICATION TO EXCLUDE

3.1 We should make an application under section 101(3) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The court must not admit evidence under gateway (d) if, on an application by the defendant, it appears that admission would have such an adverse effect on the fairness of the proceedings that the court ought not to admit it. Section 101(3) is a duty, not a discretion, once the adverse effect is established. By section 101(4) the court must have regard in particular to the length of time between the previous matters and the offence charged, which is our best point on conviction (a) and a good point on conviction (b).

3.2 We should also invite the court to hold, under section 103(3), that it would be unjust to apply the same description or same category route to convictions (a) and (b) by reason of the length of time since them.

3.3 Section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 remains available as a general power to exclude prosecution evidence and can be relied on in the alternative, but on gateway (d) the specific and stronger provision is section 101(3) and that is what the application should be founded on.

3.4 Prospects, conviction by conviction:

(a) 2010 shop theft: good prospects of exclusion. Sixteen years old, no shared feature, minor penalty, defendant aged 19.

(b) 2014 handling: prospects depend entirely on attribution. If it is not his, it cannot be admitted at all. If it is his, we have a respectable but not strong age and dissimilarity argument.

(c) 2023 handling: poor prospects of exclusion. Plan for it to go in.

(d) 2024 excess alcohol: very good prospects. It has no bearing on the issue.

3.5 If the 2023 conviction is admitted, two things follow. First, we should ask the judge to admit it in an agreed form limited to the fact of the conviction and the basic circumstances, rather than allowing the prosecution to lead detail which invites the jury to try the earlier case again. Second, we should ask for a direction that propensity is not by itself proof of guilt and that the jury must not convict wholly or mainly on the previous conviction.

4. QUESTION 3: THE PROCEDURAL POINT ON THE NOTICE

4.1 Under rule 21.4(3)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Rules 2025 a prosecutor in the Crown Court must serve notice of intention to introduce a defendant's bad character not more than 10 business days after the not guilty plea. The plea was entered on 24 August 2026 and the notice was served on 18 September 2026, which is more than 10 business days later. The notice is therefore out of time.

4.2 We should say so in the application and require the prosecution to apply for an extension. Rule 21.6 allows the court to extend a time limit even after it has expired, and Hanson records that the Court of Appeal will be slow to interfere with a judge's ruling on the consequences of non compliance with the notice requirements. I would not advise you to expect the notice to be struck out on this ground alone.

4.3 The point still has value. It supports our objection generally, it is a reason for the court to look critically at a notice which also includes an obviously bad conviction and a misconceived untruthfulness limb, and it gives us a proper basis to ask for the notice to be narrowed rather than extended.

4.4 Our own objection must be served on the court officer and every other party not more than 10 business days after service of the notice under rule 21.4(5)(b), that is by 2 October 2026 counting business days from 18 September 2026. The application must state which facts in the notice we dispute and which we admit, which is where the dispute over conviction (b) is formally raised. Please diarise this.

5. SOURCES I HAVE DISCARDED

5.1 Makin v Attorney-General for New South Wales [1894] AC 57 and DPP v P [1991] 2 AC 447 state the common law similar fact rules. Those rules were abolished by section 99(1) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 and admissibility is now governed exclusively by the statutory gateways. Neither case should be cited on this application.

5.2 Sections 114 and 116 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 govern hearsay. No hearsay issue arises. The convictions will be proved by memorandum of conviction, not as hearsay statements.

5.3 The note on section 101 of the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 and the Moorov doctrine is Scots law. Scotland is a separate jurisdiction with no gateway scheme and a corroboration requirement, and the material has no application in the Crown Court at Farrowmede. The coincidence that the relevant Scottish section is also numbered 101 is a trap and nothing more.

5.4 Clause 2 of the Criminal Evidence (Previous Convictions) Bill 2026 would require prosecution leave for convictions more than ten years old. It is not in force, no commencement regulations have been made, and it cannot be relied on. Had it been in force it would have helped us on convictions (a) and (b), which is worth knowing but is not a submission we can make.

5.5 Section 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 I have not discarded but have relegated to the alternative, for the reason at paragraph 3.3.

6. CONDUCT POINT REQUIRING YOUR DECISION BEFORE WE PROCEED

6.1 The file note records that Mr Vaughan Amory, the client's brother, telephoned on 19 September 2026 asking this firm to act for him on a handling charge arising out of the same Wrentham Park compound, saying that the brothers "should both be saying the same thing".

6.2 We cannot act for him. There is a conflict of interest within paragraph 6.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors. Our client's instruction is that his brother gave the client's name at a police station in 2014 and that a conviction on the client's record belongs to the brother. Advancing that instruction is directly adverse to the brother. The brother's own suggestion that both should say the same thing is itself a reason to keep the representation separate, and neither of the exceptions in paragraph 6.2 can apply where the clients are effectively in dispute about the very facts we would have to advance. I would decline the retainer and record the reason.

6.3 We must also be careful about what we say to him when we decline. Everything our client has told us about the 2014 conviction is confidential under paragraph 6.3 of the Code and cannot be given as the reason. A short letter declining to act, without reasons, is sufficient. He should be advised to instruct his own solicitors promptly.

6.4 Finally, the client should be advised not to discuss the evidence in this case with his brother. Both are facing allegations arising out of the same compound and any co ordination of accounts would expose him to a serious further allegation.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The partner's file note records that the client's brother has telephoned asking this firm to act for him on a handling charge arising out of the same compound, and has said the two brothers "should both be saying the same thing". Acting for both would be a conflict of interest under paragraph 6.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors. The client's own instructions are directly adverse to the brother, since he says the brother gave the client's name at a police station in 2014 and that a conviction on his record is really the brother's. Neither the substantially common interest exception nor the competing for the same objective exception is available on these facts, so no consent can cure it, and the brother's own suggestion that the accounts be aligned makes the risk plain. The competent candidate advises declining the retainer, declines without giving reasons so that the client's confidential instructions under paragraph 6.3 are not disclosed, records the decision, tells the brother to instruct his own solicitors promptly, and advises the client not to discuss the evidence with his brother at all.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsSections 99, 101(1)(d), 101(3), 101(4), 103(1) to (4), the Categories of Offences Order, Hanson and Criminal Procedure Rules 2025 Part 21 are all used and correctly cited. Each of the four decoys is named and rejected with a reason: Makin and DPP v P (abolished by section 99), sections 114 and 116 (hearsay, no hearsay issue), the Scottish note (separate jurisdiction, no gateway scheme), and the 2026 Bill (not in force). Section 78 is correctly kept as an alternative rather than treated as the primary route.Arguing admissibility by reference to DPP v P or striking similarity, which is the abolished common law test, or citing the Scottish material because its section number happens also to be 101. Citing the Bill is worse still, because it has no legal effect.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsThe note gives a conviction by conviction prospects assessment rather than a general discussion, tells the partner frankly that the 2023 conviction will probably go in, and turns to what to do about that: agreed limited form, a direction to the jury, and evidence about the disputed 2014 conviction. Concrete next steps are given with the rule 21.4(5)(b) deadline calculated.Setting out the law on gateway (d) without ever saying which convictions will actually be admitted, or giving an optimistic assessment on the 2023 conviction that the partner cannot rely on when advising the client about plea.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsNumbered, headed, with a summary at the top that a partner can act on in two minutes. Each conviction is dealt with under its own heading. Citations are accurate and given once. British spelling, no em-dashes, no research trail.Treating the four convictions as a single block so that the reader cannot see that they stand or fall separately, or reciting long statutory extracts without applying them.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawThe Hanson three questions are applied to each conviction separately. Same description and same category are correctly distinguished, with the two handling convictions being the same description and the shop theft only in the same category. Excess alcohol is correctly identified as neither, engaging the section 103(1)(a) exception because the propensity makes it no more likely he is guilty. The untruthfulness limb is correctly rejected on Hanson's distinction between untruthfulness and dishonesty.Treating every previous conviction as automatically admissible because the defendant has a dishonesty record, or conflating dishonesty with untruthfulness and conceding the section 103(1)(b) limb. Another frequent error is arguing the admissibility of the 2023 conviction only on age, missing that its shared modus operandi is precisely what makes it probative.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawThe section 101(3) exclusion application, the section 101(4) time factor, the section 103(3) injustice route and section 78 as an alternative are all covered. The Part 21 timetable is worked out in both directions: the prosecution notice is late under rule 21.4(3)(b), and our own objection is due within 10 business days under rule 21.4(5)(b). The dispute over the attribution of the 2014 conviction is handled as an evidential issue requiring the memorandum of conviction, not merely asserted.Missing the late service of the notice entirely, or spotting it and overclaiming that the notice must therefore be excluded, when rule 21.6 lets the court extend even after expiry. Also failing to diarise the defendant's own 10 business day deadline, which is the deadline that can actually cost the client his objection.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawThe candidate identifies the brother's request that the firm act for him as a conflict of interest under paragraph 6.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, notes that the client's instructions are directly adverse to the brother and that the brother has proposed the two of them say the same thing, and advises declining the retainer. The candidate also protects the client's confidentiality when declining, and advises the client not to discuss the evidence with his brother.Reading the file note as background about the 2014 conviction and never noticing that the firm has been asked to act for a second, conflicting client. A partial answer identifies the conflict but then tells the brother what the client has said about the 2014 conviction, or anything else from which the client's instructions could be worked out, which breaches confidentiality under paragraph 6.3 of the Code. Saying no more than that the firm cannot act because of a conflict of interest is correct and is not a breach.

Examiner notes

The discriminator is whether the candidate treats the four convictions separately or as a block. A weak answer says the client has a bad record and the convictions will probably come in. A pass takes each conviction through the Hanson three questions and reaches a different answer for each. The 2023 handling conviction is meant to go in, and candidates who fight it to the exclusion of everything else have misread where the value lies: the winnable arguments are the 2010 shop theft on age and dissimilarity, the excess alcohol conviction on relevance, and the untruthfulness limb on the Hanson distinction between untruthfulness and dishonesty, which many candidates concede without noticing. The bundle carries four decoys, each failing for a different reason, and the Scottish source is deliberately baited with a section number of 101. Candidates should also notice both halves of the Part 21 timetable; spotting that the prosecution notice is late is worth a mark, but forgetting that the defence objection has its own 10 business day deadline is the error that would cost the real client his application. Finally, the conflict of interest is disguised as a note about the disputed 2014 conviction, and candidates who read that note only for its evidential content will miss the professional conduct criterion entirely.

Written station 5: Special reasons for not disqualifying following a drink driving conviction

Legal research  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

RESEARCH NOTE

To: Peter Vaisey, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 8 February 2027

Matter: R v Doughty, Pentrebrook Magistrates' Court, 2 March 2027

Subject: Special reasons for not disqualifying on a guilty plea to driving with excess alcohol

1. Summary of advice

1.1 Driving with excess alcohol carries obligatory disqualification for at least twelve months under section 34(1) of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988. The only route to avoiding it is a finding of special reasons.

1.2 The laced drink argument is now unavailable to us. On the client's corrected instructions of 5 February she knew during the evening that her drink had been laced. That destroys the second limb of the test in Pugsley v Hunter. We cannot run the argument, and we cannot call Mr Ilsley to say she did not know.

1.3 The emergency argument is available in principle under DPP v Bristow but on these facts it is weak. She drove nine miles on a main road when the obvious alternative was to telephone for help.

1.4 The loss of her job is not capable of being a special reason. It is personal to her, not to the offence.

1.5 There is a professional conduct problem arising from what the client now proposes. It is dealt with at paragraph 6, and it must be resolved before anything else is done on the file.

2. The statutory starting point

2.1 Section 5(1)(a) of the Road Traffic Act 1988 is an offence involving obligatory disqualification. Section 34(1) of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 requires the court to disqualify for at least twelve months unless it finds special reasons to disqualify for a shorter period or not at all. Section 44(1) provides the equivalent discretion for endorsement.

2.2 Section 35 of the same Act, which allows a court to mitigate the normal consequences of a totting up disqualification where there are grounds including exceptional hardship, does not apply. This is not a penalty points case. The client has a clean licence, so there is no question of twelve or more points. The exceptional hardship material and the Trust policy are not admissible on the section 34 question, because section 35 has no application to an obligatory disqualification.

3. What amounts to a special reason

3.1 R v Wickins (1958) 42 Cr App R 236 sets the four conditions. The matter must be a mitigating or extenuating circumstance, must not amount in law to a defence, must be directly connected with the commission of the offence, and must be one the court ought properly to take into account. Wickins also holds that a circumstance peculiar to the offender rather than to the offence cannot be a special reason, and that hardship and loss of employment are expressly excluded.

3.2 It follows that the client's likely dismissal under clause 7.2 of the Trust policy cannot be a special reason, however serious it is for her. It is relevant only as personal mitigation on the level of fine and on the length of any disqualification within the range the court chooses.

4. The laced drink argument

4.1 Pugsley v Hunter [1973] 1 WLR 578 requires the defendant to prove three things on the balance of probabilities: that the drink was laced, that she did not know or suspect it, and that but for the added alcohol she would have been under the limit. Even then the court retains a discretion and must consider whether she ought nevertheless to have realised she was unfit to drive.

4.2 On the instructions of 4 February all three limbs were arguable, although the third would have required a report from a forensic scientist. Pugsley v Hunter is clear that in the ordinary case scientific evidence is needed and that the court should not be invited to speculate.

4.3 On the corrected instructions of 5 February the second limb fails on the client's own account. She tasted the alcohol, worked out that spirits had been added and continued to drink. She knew. The argument cannot be advanced.

5. The emergency argument

5.1 DPP v Bristow [1998] RTR 100 asks how the facts would have appeared to a sober, reasonable and responsible friend of the defendant present at the time but not a driver, and whether that person would have advised her to drive. The court will look at what she believed, whether that belief was reasonable, what alternatives there were, the distance, the manner of the driving and the level of alcohol.

5.2 In her favour: the belief that her elderly mother had fallen and could not get up was genuine and reasonable; she drove normally; there is no suggestion of bad driving; and she is of previous good character.

5.3 Against her: she could have telephoned for an ambulance or asked a neighbour, which Bristow says will usually defeat the argument; she drove nine miles on a main road with other traffic; and her reading of 61 was nearly double the limit, which is well into the second band of the Magistrates' Court Sentencing Guidelines. Chatters v Burke [1986] 1 WLR 1321 confirms that the possibility of contact with other road users is the most important factor where distance is relied on, and driving on a main road for nine miles gives that possibility in full.

5.4 My assessment is that the emergency argument is properly arguable but is more likely than not to fail. It should be advanced only if the client understands that risk and gives instructions to run it. Section 15(2)(a) of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 means the reading of 61 must be taken as the proportion at the time of driving, and the only escape, under section 15(3), is proof of drinking after she stopped driving, which is not this case, so there is no scope for arguing that she was lower when she set off.

6. Professional conduct

6.1 The client has told us that she knew her drink had been laced but wants Mr Ilsley to tell the court that she did not, because that is what the court needs to hear. We cannot allow that.

6.2 Paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors provides that we must not mislead or attempt to mislead the court, either by our own acts or omissions or by allowing or being complicit in the acts or omissions of others, including the client. Calling Mr Ilsley to give an account we know to be untrue, or advancing a laced drink special reason on instructions we know to be false, would breach that paragraph and the SRA Principles on integrity, on upholding the constitutional principle of the rule of law and the proper administration of justice, and on maintaining public trust.

6.3 The correct course is to explain to the client, before the hearing, that she remains fully entitled to plead not guilty and put the prosecution to proof, and that we can advance any argument that is consistent with her true instructions, but that we cannot put forward a version we know to be false. If she insists on the laced drink argument we must cease to act. We should not tell the court why we are withdrawing, because her instructions remain confidential under paragraph 6.3 of the Code, and we should say only that we are professionally embarrassed.

6.4 Nothing should be said to Mr Ilsley that could be taken as inviting or shaping a false account.

7. Advice to give the client

7.1 Tell her that a disqualification of at least twelve months is the starting point and that the guideline range for a reading of 61 is seventeen to twenty two months.

7.2 Tell her that the laced drink point is gone on her own account, and explain why we cannot run it.

7.3 Tell her that the emergency point can be argued but is likely to fail, and that if she wants to run it she will have to give evidence and be cross examined about why she did not telephone for help.

7.4 Tell her that the loss of her job cannot avoid disqualification but is proper mitigation on length and on the fine, and that it is worth putting the Trust policy before the court for that limited purpose.

7.5 Advise her that a full early guilty plea attracts the maximum reduction for a plea, and that she should consider the drink drive rehabilitation course, which the court may offer and which can reduce the disqualification period.

8. Sources not relied on

8.1 Section 35 of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 and the exceptional hardship test apply only to totting up disqualifications and have no application here. The Trust policy is relevant to mitigation, not to special reasons. Section 15(2)(a) of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 is relevant only to close off an argument about the reading and does not assist us affirmatively.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client's corrected instructions of 5 February are that she did realise her drink had been laced, but she wants her colleague to tell the court she did not because that is what the court needs to hear. A competent candidate identifies without prompting that advancing the laced drink special reason, or calling that evidence, would mislead the court contrary to paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and the SRA Principles on integrity and the proper administration of justice. The resolution is to explain the position to the client, to advance only what is consistent with her true instructions, to remind her she may still put the prosecution to proof, and to cease acting if she insists, without disclosing her confidential instructions to the court.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsRelies on section 34(1) and section 44(1) of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988, R v Wickins, Pugsley v Hunter, DPP v Bristow and Chatters v Burke, cites them properly, and says expressly that section 35 exceptional hardship and the Trust policy do not go to special reasons.Argues exceptional hardship under section 35 on a clean licence, which is the planted decoy, or relies on the Trust policy as the special reason.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the partner's actual questions: what she must prove, to what standard, what evidence is needed, and a candid prospects assessment, followed by practical points on plea credit and the rehabilitation course.Sets out the law on special reasons without ever saying whether this client is likely to keep her licence, or gives false reassurance that a genuine emergency will succeed.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsNumbered note, advice summarised at the front, authorities cited in the body rather than listed, no research trail.Recites each source in turn in the order it appeared in the bundle, with no synthesis and no conclusion.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly applies the three limb Pugsley v Hunter test and identifies that the second limb fails on the corrected instructions, and correctly applies the Wickins rule that hardship and loss of employment are personal to the offender and cannot be special reasons.Runs the laced drink argument anyway on the original instructions, or treats the burden as resting on the prosecution rather than on the defendant on the balance of probabilities.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with all three candidate special reasons, laced drink, emergency and hardship, applies the Bristow sober friend test to the nine mile drive and the availability of a telephone call, and notes the residual judicial discretion and the effect of section 15(2).Deals only with the laced drink point and never considers the emergency, or considers the emergency without applying the sober and responsible friend test or the alternatives to driving.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots that the client wants a witness to say something she has admitted is untrue, refuses to advance it, cites the duty not to mislead the court, advises the client of her right to put the prosecution to proof, and advises withdrawal without disclosing the reason if she insists.Ignores the second attendance note entry, or advises simply calling Mr Ilsley because he is willing to say it, or proposes to tell the court that the client has lied, breaching confidentiality.

Examiner notes
