The pass turns on noticing that the second attendance note entry has destroyed the laced drink argument, and on saying so rather than working up the argument the client wants. The main trap is the exceptional hardship decoy: the client has a clean licence and a job at risk, which invites candidates into section 35, when section 35 only bites on a totting up disqualification and this is an obligatory disqualification under section 34. The second trap is treating loss of employment as capable of being a special reason, which Wickins expressly rules out.

Written station 6: Email to the Crown Prosecution Service proposing acceptable pleas

Legal writing  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  30 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

From: Callum Fenwick, Fenwick Sabir Solicitors

To: Priya Ramanathan, Crown Prosecution Service, Wetherfield Complex Casework Unit

Date: 3 August 2026

Subject: R v Ryan Peter Alsop, Wetherfield Crown Court, trial listed 12 October 2026, offer of plea

Dear Ms Ramanathan

I act for Ryan Alsop in the above matter. I write with my client's express written authority to offer a plea and to invite the Crown to accept it.

The offer

Mr Alsop offers to plead guilty to count 2, unlawful wounding contrary to section 20 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861, in full satisfaction of the indictment, on the written basis set out below. The offer is made on the basis that count 1 would lie on the file on the usual terms.

The basis of plea

Mr Alsop accepts, and has always accepted, that he caused the wound to Mr Croyde's cheek and that he was reckless as to whether some harm would result. His basis is as follows.

1. He was holding a pint glass which he had picked up from the bar shortly before the argument began. He did not pick it up in order to use it as a weapon.

2. Mr Croyde pushed him twice before he swung his arm.

3. He swung his arm once, in temper. He did not aim at the face and did not have the glass in mind.

4. He accepts causing the wound and accepts recklessness as to some harm.

5. He did not intend to cause really serious harm.

6. He did nothing further after the blow and remained at the scene.

That basis is signed by Mr Alsop and I attach it. If the Crown accepts the plea but not the basis, I would ask you to say so now so that a hearing under the Newton procedure can be listed rather than the trial.

Why I invite you to accept

The issue between us is intent, and only intent. I put the following points to you.

First, the glass. Your own CCTV shows Mr Alsop holding the glass at the bar for around forty seconds before any argument started. That is inconsistent with the glass being picked up as a weapon and is consistent with his account that it was simply in his hand.

Secondly, the medical evidence. Dr Oyelaran describes a single laceration of even depth, with no fracture, no eye injury and no involvement of the facial nerve, and expressly says that the absence of multiple lacerations and the even depth are more consistent with a single sweeping contact than with a thrusting or grinding action. That evidence supports a single reckless swing rather than a deliberate glassing.

Thirdly, the conduct after the blow. Mr Alsop did not pursue Mr Croyde, did not strike again and did not leave the scene.

Fourthly, the sequence. On his account, which the CCTV does not contradict, he was pushed twice before he swung.

I do not suggest that count 1 is unarguable. I say that the intent to cause really serious harm is the weakest part of it, and that a jury is likely to find the section 20 count proved and to be far less certain about section 18.

Why this is in the public interest

A plea to section 20 on this basis reflects the seriousness of what Mr Alsop actually did. He accepts causing a permanent facial scar to Mr Croyde. The Crown Court retains ample sentencing powers on a section 20 count, and Mr Alsop's basis does not seek to minimise the injury or to blame Mr Croyde for it. Acceptance would also spare Mr Croyde from having to give evidence about a distressing incident and would resolve the case in October or sooner.

Mr Alsop is 23 and has one previous conviction, a public order matter in 2023 dealt with by a fine.

The complainant's views

I recognise that under the Attorney General's Guidelines you will wish to take Mr Croyde's views into account before deciding, and that the decision is yours alone. I would be grateful if you could confirm whether he has been consulted, and I appreciate that this may take a little time.

Timescale

The offer is open and does not expire. I would be grateful for a decision, if possible, by 24 August 2026, so that if it is accepted the matter can be listed for a plea hearing and Mr Croyde can be told promptly, and if it is not, both sides can prepare for trial on 12 October.

I am happy to speak on the telephone if that would help.

Yours sincerely

Callum Fenwick

Partner

Fenwick Sabir Solicitors

Enclosure: signed basis of plea dated 31 July 2026

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two traps sit in the clerk's email. First, the pupil's note records the client as accepting he would be convicted of section 18 in any event. That is not what he said. The detailed conference note of 31 July records that he has always denied any intent to cause really serious harm, and his signed authority of the same date says the same, so the pupil's note is second hand and wrong. Repeating it to the prosecutor would mislead her about the client's instructions and would breach paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and the duty to act with integrity under the SRA Principles. Secondly, the client's mother has asked the firm to tell the CPS that the client has a diagnosed condition affecting impulse control. There is no diagnosis on the file, no assessment and no instruction from the client. Instructions come from the client and not from a relative, and asserting an unevidenced diagnosis would be a misleading assertion of fact. A competent candidate leaves both out, and states positively in the email that the offer is made on the client's express written authority.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the CCTV showing the glass held for around forty seconds, the specific findings in Dr Oyelaran's report, the two pushes, the single blow, remaining at the scene, the single 2023 public order conviction, and the trial date.Recites the whole case history the CPS already has, or asserts the client did not intend serious harm without pointing to any evidence supporting it.
Use a logical structure.SkillsThe offer first, then the numbered basis of plea, then the reasons to accept, then the public interest, then the complainant and a timescale, under headings, with the basis attached.Runs the offer, the argument and the basis together so the reviewing lawyer cannot see what precisely is being offered or on what terms.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsWritten for a prosecutor: engages with the Attorney General's Guidelines tests of public interest, adequate sentencing powers and the complainant's views, acknowledges the decision is the prosecutor's, and asks for a Newton hearing if the basis is disputed.Writes as though to a client or a partner, argues the case as if to a jury, or is aggressive and tells the prosecutor the section 18 count is hopeless.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsProfessional correspondence register, short paragraphs, no overstatement, courteous, and short enough to be read in one sitting as the partner asked.Overstates the strength of the defence case, uses emotive language about the complainant, or produces a long recitation of the evidence the recipient already holds.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly identifies that the only live difference between section 18 and section 20 on these facts is the specific intent to cause grievous bodily harm, that recklessness as to some harm suffices for section 20, and correctly deploys the Newton procedure where a basis is disputed.Confuses the mental elements, for example arguing that the client lacked intent so cannot be guilty of section 20 either, or offering a plea to section 20 while disputing that he caused the wound.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAddresses each of the Attorney General's Guidelines requirements: seriousness properly reflected, adequate sentencing powers, the basis capable of belief on the evidence, and the complainant's views, and deals with what happens if the basis is not agreed.Makes the offer without engaging with the guidelines at all, or omits any mention of the complainant or of what happens if the Crown accepts the plea but disputes the basis.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawConfirms the offer is made with express written authority, does not repeat the untrue assertion that the client expects to be convicted of section 18, and says nothing about an alleged impulse control diagnosis for which there is no evidence, no assessment and no instruction from the client.Tells the CPS the client accepts he would be convicted of section 18, which is untrue, or asserts the unverified diagnosis reported by the client's mother, which would mislead the prosecutor and act on a third party's instructions rather than the client's.

Examiner notes

The pass turns on writing a genuine plea negotiation rather than an argument. The candidate must state precisely what is offered and on what basis, in full satisfaction of the indictment, and must engage with the tests the prosecutor is actually required to apply under the Attorney General's Guidelines. Weak answers advocate the innocence of the client, which is not the point, since the client is offering to plead guilty to a serious offence. The trap is the clerk's email, which reads like housekeeping and contains both ethics points: candidates who mine it for extra ammunition put an untrue concession and an unverified diagnosis into correspondence with the prosecution.

Dispute Resolution

Written station 7: Warehouse fall claim with a disputed system of work and an apportionment argument

Case and matter analysis  |  Dispute Resolution  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO ROWAN ADEYEMI

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 3 February 2027

Client: Ms Priya Sandhu

Proposed defendant: Norvell Distribution Limited (Norvell)

1. SUMMARY

1.1 Liability in negligence is good. The system of work was unsafe and the ladder was defective. I put the prospects of establishing breach at about 80 per cent.

1.2 The claim is significantly reduced by two separate points which candidates often confuse. First, causation: the joint orthopaedic evidence is that the accident accelerated a pre existing back condition by four years only. Second, contributory negligence: Ms Sandhu did not fetch an available platform and was not wearing safety footwear. My estimate of contributory negligence is 20 to 25 per cent.

1.3 My full value of the claim before any deduction is about GBP 80,000. After a 25 per cent reduction the likely recovery is about GBP 60,100.

1.4 Limitation expires on 11 March 2027. That is five weeks away and it drives everything below.

2. RELEVANT FACTS

2.1 Accident on 11 March 2024 at 06.22 at Norvell's Bicester site. Ms Sandhu fell about 1.6 metres from step ladder SL-114 while picking from the third shelf of bay F12 onto a concrete floor.

2.2 Norvell's own accident report records that ladder SL-114 was inspected the following day, that one anti slip foot was missing, and that the ladder was scrapped. That is an admission by the defendant that the equipment was defective and it is the strongest document in the case.

2.3 Ms Sandhu reported the missing foot verbally to the shift supervisor, Callum Reece, the week before the accident. She did not record it in the defects book and says nobody used it.

2.4 Four of the eight mobile picking platforms were out of service. Ms Sandhu says Mr Reece told the 6am briefing to use the ladders because the vans were waiting. Two possible witnesses, Bev Osgood and a picker called Tomas.

2.5 Ms Sandhu did not fetch one of the four working platforms, which were in the far aisle and would have taken about ten minutes to bring, because her monitored pick rate was behind.

2.6 She was wearing her own trainers. Her issued safety boots had split and she had asked twice for replacements.

2.7 Injuries: displaced fracture of the right distal radius treated by internal fixation, and lower back symptoms. 25 weeks off work, returning on 2 September 2024 on 22 hours instead of 37.5.

2.8 Documented pre existing L4/L5 disc protrusion in 2019 with physiotherapy in 2019 and 2020, settled by 2021.

3. LIABILITY IN NEGLIGENCE

3.1 Norvell owed Ms Sandhu the ordinary employer's duty to take reasonable care for her safety, which includes providing safe plant and equipment, a safe place of work and, above all, a safe system of work, and supervising that system so that it is actually followed. The duty is non delegable.

3.2 Breach is established on at least three bases.

3.2.1 Equipment. The ladder was missing an anti slip foot. Norvell's own report says so and says the ladder was scrapped. A ladder in that condition on a concrete floor was not reasonably safe.

3.2.2 Inspection and reporting. The defect had been reported verbally to the supervisor a week earlier and nothing was done. Norvell will say it was not recorded in the defects book. That is an answer only if the defects book was in fact used and enforced. If pickers habitually reported verbally and Norvell tolerated it, the reporting system existed on paper only, and a system which is not enforced is not a safe system.

3.2.3 System of work. Half the mobile platforms were out of service and pickers were, on Ms Sandhu's account, told to use ladders to keep the vans moving, against a monitored pick rate which penalised the safer and slower option. An employer must take account of the fact that employees under production pressure will take short cuts, and must design the system so that the safe method is the practicable one.

3.3 The weakness is Norvell's assertion in the accident report that the immediate cause was overreaching and that the correct equipment was available. Both are contested. We need the maintenance records for the platforms to prove that four were out of service.

3.4 Causation of the accident itself is straightforward. A ladder with a missing foot on concrete rocked and she fell. But for the defective ladder and the pressure to use it she would not have fallen.

4. CAUSATION AND THE EXTENT OF THE INJURY

4.1 This is a different question from whether Norvell caused the fall. It is how much of Ms Sandhu's present condition the fall is responsible for. A defendant is liable only for the damage its breach actually caused.

4.2 Wrist. Mr Marchetti attributes the fracture wholly to the accident, with a permanent 20 per cent loss of extension and a 10 per cent risk of osteoarthritis. This head is unaffected by the pre existing condition.

4.3 Back. Mr Marchetti's opinion is that the degenerative change at L4/L5 is constitutional and that the accident accelerated symptoms which would have arrived anyway by about March 2028. The consequence is that Norvell is liable for four years of back symptoms and no more. It is not liable for the back related restriction on lifting and standing after March 2028, because that would have happened in any event.

4.4 The practical effect on the future loss of earnings claim is severe and Ms Sandhu must be told about it early. Mr Marchetti says the wrist injury alone would not have prevented a return to full time stock picking. The claim for continuing reduced earnings therefore runs only to March 2028 and not for life. Any advice that ignores this will overstate the claim by a large multiple.

4.5 The acceleration period also determines which Judicial College bracket applies to the back. Four years is less than five, so category (c)(ii) at GBP 9,000 to GBP 15,000 applies and not category (c)(i).

4.6 Mr Marchetti is instructed jointly. We should put written questions to him on whether the four year acceleration would have been shorter without the physically demanding nature of the job, and on whether the wrist restriction alone reduces her earning capacity at all.

5. CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE

5.1 Norvell will plead contributory negligence and will succeed to some extent. Damages are reduced to the extent the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility for the damage.

5.2 The platform. Four platforms were working and she chose not to fetch one. That is a real criticism. It is tempered by the fact that the choice was produced by the employer's own pick rate monitoring and by the supervisor's instruction, and courts consistently make allowance for the fact that employees act in the heat of a production line and are not to be judged too finely.

5.3 The footwear. She wore trainers rather than the issued boots. This is a weaker point for Norvell than it looks. Her boots had split and she had asked twice for replacements, which is itself a failure by the employer. More importantly, causation must be shown for contributory negligence too. Norvell must show the footwear contributed to the fall or the injury. A fall caused by a rocking ladder is unlikely to have been prevented by safety boots, and the injuries were to the wrist and back and not the foot. I would resist this limb almost entirely.

5.4 Not using the defects book is a point about the reporting system rather than about the accident, given that she reported the defect verbally to the supervisor.

5.5 My assessment is a reduction of 20 to 25 per cent. I would advise Ms Sandhu to expect 25 per cent and treat anything lower as a good outcome.

6. QUANTUM

6.1 General damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity.

Wrist, category (c), less severe with permanent stiffness and pain: I would put this at GBP 21,000, toward the middle to upper part of the bracket given the surgery, the permanent loss of extension and the osteoarthritis risk.

Back, category (c)(ii), acceleration over a period shorter than five years: GBP 13,000.

Allowing for overlap between the two injuries rather than adding them mechanically, I assess general damages at GBP 31,000.

6.2 Past loss of earnings. 25 weeks at GBP 486 net, less statutory sick pay of GBP 116.75 per week. Net loss GBP 369.25 per week for 25 weeks, which is GBP 9,231.25.

6.3 Past partial loss of earnings from return to work on 2 September 2024 to today, 3 February 2027, which is approximately 126 weeks at GBP 201 per week net (GBP 486 less GBP 285), which is GBP 25,326.

6.4 Future partial loss of earnings from today to March 2028, approximately 57 weeks at GBP 201, which is GBP 11,457. This stops in March 2028 for the reason in paragraph 4.4. Subject to Mr Marchetti's answer on whether the wrist alone restricts her, there may in addition be a Smith v Manchester award for handicap on the open labour market, which I would put at no more than about GBP 4,000 on the present evidence. I have not included that figure in the total below.

6.5 Gratuitous care. 3 hours per day for 10 weeks is 210 hours, and 1 hour per day for 8 weeks is 56 hours, a total of 266 hours at GBP 12.50, which is GBP 3,325. A discount of about 25 per cent is conventionally applied to gratuitous care to reflect the absence of tax and other commercial elements, giving about GBP 2,494.

6.6 Other special damages: travel GBP 340, medication GBP 128, spectacles GBP 165, total GBP 633.

6.7 Total full value: GBP 31,000 plus GBP 9,231.25 plus GBP 25,326 plus GBP 11,457 plus GBP 2,494 plus GBP 633, which is GBP 80,141.25, say GBP 80,000. Interest is claimable on general damages and on past losses.

6.8 After a 25 per cent contributory reduction the likely net recovery is about GBP 60,100, and about GBP 64,100 if a 20 per cent reduction is achieved. Recovery of state benefits under the Compensation Recovery Unit scheme will need to be checked because statutory sick pay was paid.

7. LIMITATION AND TIMETABLE

7.1 The accident was on 11 March 2024. The primary limitation period for personal injury is three years from the date of the cause of action accruing or the date of knowledge, so it expires on 11 March 2027. That is five weeks from today. Everything else is subordinate to this.

7.2 The pre action protocol for personal injury cannot realistically be completed in five weeks. The correct course is to issue a protective claim form now and then serve it late in the four month period for service while the protocol is completed, agreeing a stay if necessary. Do not allow the protocol to run past the limitation date.

7.3 Steps this week:

(a) Issue a protective claim form in the County Court. The claim value places it above the fast track and it is likely to be allocated to the multi track or the intermediate track depending on value and complexity, so plead accordingly.

(b) Send the letter of claim to Norvell and to its insurer.

(c) Request the maintenance records for the eight picking platforms, the defects book for the six months before the accident, the toolbox talk records, the risk assessment for picking at height, the CCTV if any survives and the pick rate data for the shift.

(d) Obtain the full 2019 to 2021 medical records for the lumbar spine so we are not surprised on disclosure.

(e) Take a witness statement from Bev Osgood, subject to paragraph 8 below, and trace Tomas through Norvell's shift records.

(f) Put written questions to Mr Marchetti on the acceleration period and on the wrist alone.

(g) Confirm funding and check for any before the event legal expenses insurance on her home policy.

8. PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT

8.1 Ms Sandhu said that Bev Osgood 'will say whatever I need her to say about the briefing' and asked whether her statement could be taken first so that Ms Sandhu could go through it with her afterwards and get it lined up. That must be dealt with before anybody speaks to Ms Osgood.

8.2 We cannot take a statement on that basis. Coaching a witness, or allowing a party to rehearse or align a witness's account, would put before the court evidence that is not the witness's own recollection. It would breach the SRA Principles requiring honesty, integrity and the upholding of public trust, and the provisions of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors on not misleading the court and not being complicit in another person doing so. It also risks the whole claim, because a witness whose evidence is shown to have been shaped destroys the credibility of the client along with it.

8.3 The resolution is to tell Ms Sandhu clearly that she must not discuss her evidence with Ms Osgood or any other witness, that any statement we take must be Ms Osgood's own account in her own words, and that if Ms Osgood does not support the account about the 6am briefing then we run the case on the documents and on the missing anti slip foot, which is the stronger evidence anyway. We should take Ms Osgood's statement ourselves, alone, and record on the file that this advice was given and when.

8.4 If Ms Sandhu later insists on approaching witnesses to align their accounts we would have to consider whether we can continue to act.

8.5 There is nothing to report to the SRA at this stage. No false evidence has been produced.

9. ADVICE TO THE CLIENT

9.1 She has a good claim on liability and Norvell's own accident report helps her.

9.2 She should expect a deduction of about a quarter for her own share of the responsibility.

9.3 The back element of the claim is limited to the four year acceleration, so her earnings claim ends in 2028 and not at retirement. She needs to hear this now rather than at a settlement meeting.

9.4 Realistic net recovery is in the region of GBP 59,000 to GBP 63,000 before any benefit recoupment.

9.5 She must not discuss her evidence with any other witness.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

At paragraph 10 of the file note the client says Bev Osgood 'will say whatever I need her to say' and asks for Ms Osgood's statement to be taken first so the client can go through it with her afterwards and get it lined up. Nothing flags this. Taking a statement on that footing, or allowing the client to rehearse a witness, is witness coaching. It would place evidence before the court which is not the witness's own recollection, contrary to the SRA Principles on honesty, integrity and public trust and to the provisions of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors on not misleading the court and not being complicit in another person doing so. The competent candidate instructs the client not to discuss her evidence with any witness, takes Ms Osgood's statement alone and in her own words, explains that the documentary evidence of the missing anti slip foot is stronger than the disputed briefing anyway, records the advice on the file, and recognises that persistence by the client would raise the question of ceasing to act.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsUses the accident report's own note that a foot was missing and the ladder was scrapped as the central document, identifies the four out of service platforms, the monitored pick rate, the verbal report to the supervisor, the split boots, the 11 March 2024 accident date and the documented 2019 lumbar history. Separates what is proved from what depends on contested oral evidence.Summarises the client's account and treats it as established. Fails to notice that the defendant's own document admits the defect, or fails to spot the 11 March 2027 limitation date at all.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsAdvises the client in terms she can act on: good liability, expect roughly a quarter off, the earnings claim ends in March 2028 and not at retirement, a realistic net figure, and the instruction not to speak to witnesses. Tells her the bad news about the acceleration period now rather than later.Gives a purely academic liability analysis with no figure and no advice on what she should expect. Presents the acceleration finding as a technicality instead of the thing that cuts her future loss claim short.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA numbered report to the partner with a summary at the front, separate sections for breach, causation, contributory negligence, quantum and timetable, and arithmetic set out so it can be checked.Runs breach, causation and contributory negligence together in one narrative so it is impossible to see which reduction applies to what. Quantum given as a single unexplained figure.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly states the employer's non delegable duty and applies it to equipment, inspection and system of work. Correctly treats the acceleration opinion as a limitation on the extent of recoverable damage, not as a defence to liability. Correctly applies contributory negligence as a reduction to the extent just and equitable, and recognises that the footwear point requires the defendant to show it contributed to the fall or the injury. Correctly identifies the three year personal injury limitation period expiring 11 March 2027 and picks the Judicial College bracket that matches an acceleration of under five years.Treats the pre existing back condition as defeating the claim, or ignores it and values the back as a fresh injury. Uses the over five year bracket for a four year acceleration. Treats contributory negligence as an all or nothing defence. Misses limitation, or notices it and still recommends completing the protocol before issuing.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers every head: general damages for both injuries with an allowance for overlap, past full loss, past and future partial loss ending at the acceleration date, gratuitous care with the conventional discount, other special damages, interest and benefit recoupment. Deals with both limbs of contributory negligence separately and gives a percentage. Sets out disclosure to be requested and questions for the expert.Omits the gratuitous care claim or the discount on it. Runs the future loss of earnings to retirement despite the expert evidence. Gives no percentage for contributory negligence, or gives one with no reasoning. Says nothing about what documents to obtain from the employer.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots without prompting that the client is proposing to align Ms Osgood's evidence with her own, identifies witness coaching as a breach of the SRA Principles and the prohibition on misleading the court, and resolves it by instructing the client not to discuss her evidence, taking any statement in the witness's own words and alone, recording the advice, and noting that the documentary case is stronger in any event.Misses the remark at paragraph 10 of the file note. Or treats it as merely unhelpful and proposes to take Ms Osgood's statement first as the client suggested, which is exactly the wrong response.

Examiner notes

Two separate reductions are in play and the commonest failure is to merge them. The acceleration opinion goes to causation and limits what damage the accident is responsible for at all. Contributory negligence is a percentage cut applied afterwards to what remains. A candidate who applies a contributory percentage to a back claim running to retirement has made a large error even if the percentage is right. The second trap is limitation. The accident date of 11 March 2024 and the report date of 3 February 2027 are given for a reason, and a candidate who recommends working through the pre action protocol before issuing has advised the client into a time barred claim. A third trap is treating the footwear as a strong contributory point without asking whether trainers had anything to do with a rocking ladder or a wrist fracture. The strongest answers notice that the defendant's own accident report proves the defect and build the case on the documents rather than on the disputed 6am briefing.

Written station 8: Defence to a negligence claim for repeated flooding from drainage works

Legal drafting  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 minutes

Model answer

IN THE COUNTY COURT AT NORWICH Claim No. K20YJ441

BETWEEN:

CORVELL COFFEE LIMITED

Claimant

and

MARLBROOK GROUNDWORKS LIMITED

Defendant

DEFENCE

Introduction

1. Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Particulars of Claim are admitted.

2. Paragraph 3 is admitted, save that the Defendant will say that it carried out the Works as contractor for the site owner, Wetherfold Estates Limited, and in accordance with a drainage design prepared by Hearne and Pike Consulting Engineers, drawing reference HP-2019-14 revision C, who were engaged directly by Wetherfold Estates Limited. The Defendant was not engaged to design the drainage system and did not do so. The Defendant had no contract with the Claimant.

Limitation

3. The claim in respect of the flood of 14 August 2020 is statute barred and the Defendant relies on section 2 of the Limitation Act 1980.

PARTICULARS

(a) The claim is founded on tort. The cause of action in respect of that flood accrued when the damage was suffered, namely on 14 August 2020.

(b) The six year period expired on 14 August 2026.

(c) The claim form was issued on 20 October 2026, more than six years after the cause of action accrued.

(d) Accordingly the Claimant is not entitled to bring the claim in respect of the flood of 14 August 2020, that is to say the sums of GBP 26,400 and GBP 18,000 pleaded at paragraph 7(a) of the Particulars of Claim, and that part of the claim is denied on that ground alone.

(e) Section 14A of the Limitation Act 1980 does not assist the Claimant. The damage was patent on the day it occurred and the Claimant then had the knowledge required for bringing an action. If the Claimant contends otherwise, it is required to plead the date on which it says it first had that knowledge.

4. Paragraphs 5 to 10 below are pleaded without prejudice to paragraph 3 above.

Duty

5. As to paragraph 4, it is admitted that in carrying out the Works the Defendant owed a duty to take reasonable care not to cause physical damage to property at Unit 4, Wetherfold Yard. It is denied that the Defendant owed any duty in respect of the design of the drainage system, which was the responsibility of Hearne and Pike Consulting Engineers.

Breach

6. Paragraph 5 is denied. The Defendant's answer to each of the particulars of negligence is as follows.

(a) As to particular (a), the gradient of the outfall pipe was specified by Hearne and Pike Consulting Engineers on drawing HP-2019-14 revision C as 1 in 80. The Defendant did not select the gradient. Further, the drainage survey obtained by the Claimant on 2 October 2025 records the outfall pipe as 'free running, no defect noted'. It is denied that the gradient of the outfall pipe caused or contributed to any of the flooding alleged. As to the gradient actually achieved on site, the Defendant will say that the level of the connection at the site boundary constrained the fall which could be laid and that the Defendant's site records show that the fall achieved on 19 June 2019 was less than that shown on the drawing. The Defendant will rely on those records at trial. It is denied that laying the pipe to the fall permitted by the existing connection level was a failure to take reasonable care, and in any event it is denied that it caused the damage alleged for the reasons at (b) and at paragraphs 7 and 8 below.

(b) As to particular (b), it is admitted that no silt trap was installed. No silt trap was shown on drawing HP-2019-14 revision C. The Defendant was not engaged to design the system and it is denied that it was negligent in building what the engineer had specified.

(c) Particular (c) is denied. The completed system was tested on 4 July 2019 by Hearne and Pike Consulting Engineers in the presence of the Defendant and passed. The Defendant will rely on the signed test certificate of that date.

(d) Particular (d) is denied. The system as constructed had been designed by a consulting engineer, had been tested and had passed. The Defendant had no contract or other relationship with the Claimant, had never been in communication with the Claimant, and there was no matter of which it was aware which called for a warning to be given.

Causation and the floods of 3 November 2022 and 9 September 2025

7. Paragraph 6 is admitted only to the extent that the Defendant admits that water entered Unit 4 on 14 August 2020, on 3 November 2022 and on 9 September 2025. It is denied that any of those events was caused by any act or omission of the Defendant.

8. The Defendant's positive case is as follows.

(a) The flood of 14 August 2020 was caused by exceptional rainfall of 51mm in two hours, being the heaviest rainfall recorded in Norwich for many years, and not by the condition of the drainage system. The Defendant will rely on the Meteorological Office records for that date.

(b) In or about April 2022, and after the Works were complete, Wetherfold Estates Limited constructed a timber bin store in the yard directly over the yard gully which takes surface water into the outfall. The Defendant was not consulted about that structure, had no involvement in it and had left the site almost three years earlier. The Defendant will rely on photographs taken on a site visit in June 2022 showing the gully wholly covered by the bin store.

(c) The floods of 3 November 2022 and 9 September 2025 were caused by the obstruction of the yard gully by that bin store, which prevented surface water reaching the outfall at all. The Defendant will rely on the Claimant's own drainage survey of 2 October 2025, which records the gully as 'obstructed by structure above' and records the outfall pipe as 'free running, no defect noted'.

(d) The construction of the bin store was the act of a third party for which the Defendant is not responsible and which broke any chain of causation between the Works and the floods of 3 November 2022 and 9 September 2025.

Loss and damage

9. Paragraph 7 is denied. Further and in any event, as to each head of loss:

(a) The sums claimed at paragraph 7(a) are not recoverable for the reason given at paragraph 3 above and are in any event denied. If, which is denied, the Defendant is liable in respect of that flood, the Claimant is required to prove the damage to flooring, fixtures and stock and the alleged five week closure. No inventory, invoice or accounting evidence has been produced.

(b) The sums claimed at paragraph 7(b) and 7(c) are denied for the reasons at paragraph 8 above. Further, the Claimant is required to prove each item of physical damage and each period of closure. The Defendant does not admit the business interruption figures of GBP 7,200 and GBP 14,400, no accounts, management information or loss adjuster's report having been produced, and the Defendant reserves the right to plead further once the Claimant's financial documents have been disclosed.

(c) The cost of the drainage survey claimed at paragraph 7(d) is not admitted. It is in any event a survey which supports the Defendant's case as to the cause of the flooding.

Interest

10. As to paragraph 8, no interest is due because no sum is due. If, which is denied, the Defendant is held liable, the rate and period of any interest awarded under section 69 of the County Courts Act 1984 are matters for the court.

11. Save as expressly admitted, each and every allegation in the Particulars of Claim is denied.

STATEMENT OF TRUTH

The Defendant believes that the facts stated in this defence are true. I understand that proceedings for contempt of court may be brought against anyone who makes, or causes to be made, a false statement in a document verified by a statement of truth without an honest belief in its truth.

Signed:

Name: Warren Dacre

Position: Contracts Director, Marlbrook Groundworks Limited

Date: 6 February 2027

Tinsdale Roche LLP, Solicitors for the Defendant

[Note for the partner, not part of the draft: I have not pleaded that the Works were built in accordance with drawing HP-2019-14 revision C so far as the gradient of the outfall is concerned, because the site diary entry of 19 June 2019 shows that they were not. Paragraph 6(a) is drafted so that it is accurate and still runs our real defence, which is that the fall was constrained by the existing connection level and that the outfall was in any event free running. I have told Mr Dacre that the site diary is a disclosable document, that it must be preserved and copied to the file now, and that we cannot draft around it. Please confirm you are content before the defence is verified.]

The conduct issue hidden in this station

At paragraphs 8 and 9 of the file note the client produces a 2019 site diary recording that the outfall was laid nearer 1 in 200 than the 1 in 80 shown on the drawing, then asks that it be left out, that the defence plead compliance with the drawing, and that the firm hold the diary rather than copy it onto the file. Nothing flags this. Pleading compliance with the drawing would put before the court, verified by a statement of truth, a positive case the drafter knows to be untrue, contrary to the SRA Principles on honesty, integrity and public trust and to the provisions of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors on not misleading the court and not being complicit in another person doing so. The suggestion that the diary be kept off the file also invites a breach of the duty to preserve documents which are or are likely to be disclosable. The competent candidate advises the client that the diary must be preserved and placed on the file and will have to be disclosed, declines to plead compliance with the drawing, and drafts the gradient paragraph so that it is accurate while still running the genuine defences that the fall was constrained by the existing connection level and that the outfall was free running and did not cause the flooding. The candidate reports the position to the supervising partner before the defence is verified, as the precedent's own drafting note requires.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsAnswers the particulars of claim paragraph by paragraph in the same order and in short numbered paragraphs. Admits, does not admit or denies with precision and uses each of those three responses where it is the correct one. No argument, no evidence recited at length, no rhetoric.Writes a narrative account of the client's version instead of responding to the pleading. Uses 'not admitted' for facts plainly within the Defendant's own knowledge, such as whether it installed a silt trap. Uses bare denials with no reasons.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsFollows the precedent: responses in pleading order, limitation under its own heading, the positive case under its own heading, quantum dealt with head by head, the sweep up denial, and a statement of truth. Makes clear that the substantive defence is pleaded without prejudice to the limitation point.Buries the limitation point inside a paragraph about breach, or omits the sweep up denial or the statement of truth. Deals with all three floods in one undivided paragraph so it is impossible to see which defence answers which event.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawPleads limitation expressly under section 2 of the Limitation Act 1980, correctly identifies that the cause of action in negligence for property damage accrues when the damage occurs, applies it to 14 August 2020 against issue on 20 October 2026, and confines the bar to that flood only. Correctly separates the duty owed as contractor from the design responsibility of the engineer. Pleads the bin store as a third party act breaking the chain of causation.Pleads limitation against the whole claim, which is wrong because the 2022 and 2025 floods are in time. Or misses limitation altogether, which loses about GBP 44,400 of the claim for no reason. Says the cause of action accrued in 2019 when the Works were done. Denies any duty at all rather than denying a duty in respect of design.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawAnswers all four particulars of negligence separately, answers all three flooding events separately with a distinct positive case for each, uses the Claimant's own survey against it, deals with each head of loss including the survey cost and the interest claim, and reserves the position on quantum pending disclosure.Leaves one or more of the four particulars of negligence unanswered, which is taken as an admission. Answers the 2020 flood and treats the other two as following automatically. Pleads 'loss and damage is denied' and nothing more, contrary to the precedent's own drafting note.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDoes not plead that the outfall was laid in accordance with the drawing, because the site diary shows otherwise. Drafts paragraph 6(a) so that it is truthful and still advances the real defence on causation. Tells the partner about the diary, advises the client it is disclosable and must be preserved, and refuses to hold it off the file.Pleads compliance with the drawing as the client asked, verified by a statement of truth, which is misleading the court. Or agrees to keep the diary off the file, or says nothing about it at all and simply avoids the subject in the draft.

Examiner notes

Two things separate a pass from a fail. The first is answering every one of the four particulars of negligence and every one of the three floods separately, because an allegation not dealt with is taken to be admitted. The second is the limitation point, which is worth about GBP 44,400 and is available only against the 2020 flood. Candidates make one of two opposite errors: they miss limitation entirely, or they plead it against the whole claim and so give up a good point on the two floods that are in time. The date of accrual is the date of the damage and not the date of the Works, and the section 14A extract is there as the answer the Claimant may run, not as something the Defendant should plead for it. The ethics trap sits in the gradient. A candidate who pleads that the Works were built in accordance with the drawing has written a false case into a document verified by a statement of truth, and the fact that the client asked for it is no answer. The strongest candidates notice that the truthful version of that paragraph is not actually weaker, because the real defence is that the outfall was free running and the gully was blocked by somebody else's bin store.

Written station 9: Defence to a construction defect claim against a contractor

Legal drafting  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 minutes

Model answer

IN THE COUNTY COURT AT CHELMSFORD

Claim No.

BETWEEN:

KESTREL PARK DEVELOPMENTS LIMITED

Claimant

and

(1) BRAMLEY AND HOYT CONSTRUCTION LIMITED

(2) DANIEL HOYT

Defendants

DEFENCE OF THE FIRST DEFENDANT

1. Paragraph 1 of the Particulars of Claim is admitted.

The contract

2. Paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 are admitted. The First Defendant will refer to the Contract dated 6 February 2026 at trial for its full terms, meaning and effect. The First Defendant will rely in particular on clauses 2.4, 4.6, 12.1, 12.3 and 17.1.

3. Further, and as pleaded at paragraph 4 of the Particulars of Claim, it was an express term of the Contract at clause 2.4 that the Claimant's architect was responsible for the design of the Works and that the First Defendant was not responsible for the adequacy of any design prepared by or on behalf of the Claimant. The design of the Works, including the render system, the blockwork substrate and the movement joint layout, was prepared by Halstow Architects Limited and is contained in the Contract Documents listed in Schedule 2, in particular drawing HAL-406 rev C.

The alleged oral warranty

4. Paragraph 5 is denied. At the site meeting on 12 March 2026 the Second Defendant said that the manufacturer of the render system offers a 25 year guarantee on that system, which is correct. The Second Defendant did not warrant that the render would not crack and gave no warranty of his own or on behalf of the First Defendant.

5. Further or alternatively, if, which is denied, any statement was made at the site meeting on 12 March 2026 which amounted to a warranty, no such warranty was given by or on behalf of the First Defendant. The Second Defendant had no authority, actual or ostensible, to give warranties on behalf of the First Defendant outside the terms of the written Contract.

6. Further or alternatively, if, which is denied, any statement made on 12 March 2026 amounted to a warranty, that statement post-dated the Contract by some five weeks and did not vary it. The Contract was not varied at any time, whether in writing or at all, and no consideration moved from the Claimant for any such variation. Clause 17.1 of the Contract, by which the Contract constitutes the entire agreement between the Claimant and the First Defendant, confirms that the parties' bargain is contained in the written Contract alone.

7. Paragraph 6 is denied. The Claimant did not rely on any warranty, for the reasons pleaded at paragraphs 4 to 6 above. If and to the extent that the Claimant approved the render system, it did so on the advice of its own architect, who had specified that system in the Contract Documents before the site meeting took place.

Practical completion and the alleged defects

8. Paragraph 7 is admitted.

9. As to paragraph 8, it is admitted that cracking has appeared in the render to the north and east elevations of Units 1, 2 and 4 and that the cracks follow the line of the blockwork joints. The width and extent of the cracking are not admitted and the Claimant is required to prove them.

10. Paragraph 9 is denied. The cracking was not caused by any breach of clause 4.2 of the Contract by the First Defendant, and there was no warranty of the kind alleged.

11. As to the Particulars of Breach under paragraph 9:

(a) Sub paragraph (a) is denied. The render was applied in two coats to a total thickness of approximately 13mm on each of Units 1, 2 and 4. The First Defendant will rely on its daily site diary and on the delivery notes for the second coat material.

(b) Sub paragraph (b) is admitted, in that no movement joints were formed in the render. It is denied that the absence of movement joints was a breach of contract by the First Defendant. No render movement joints were shown on drawing HAL-406 rev C or elsewhere in the Contract Documents. The design of the movement joint layout was the responsibility of the Claimant's architect under clause 2.4, and by clause 4.6 the First Defendant was not obliged to depart from the Contract Documents.

(c) Sub paragraph (c) is denied. The render was applied in September 2026, not December 2026. The First Defendant's daily site diary records air temperatures of between 7 and 11 degrees Celsius throughout the rendering works.

12. The First Defendant's positive case is that the cracking was caused by the absence of movement joints in the render, which is a defect in the design prepared by the Claimant's architect and for which the First Defendant is not responsible under clause 2.4 of the Contract. The cracking follows the line of the blockwork joints, which is consistent with movement in the substrate that unjointed render cannot accommodate.

Loss and damage

13. Paragraph 10 is denied. If, which is denied, the First Defendant is liable to the Claimant, the sums claimed are excessive and are not admitted.

14. As to the Particulars of Loss and Damage:

(a) Sub paragraph (a) is not admitted. The Claimant is required to prove that the whole of the render to Units 1, 2 and 4 requires stripping and reapplying and that £214,000 is a reasonable cost of doing so. If the cracking is the result of the absence of movement joints, the remedial works would in any event involve the formation of movement joints which the Contract never required the First Defendant to provide, and the cost of which is not recoverable from the First Defendant.

(b) Sub paragraph (b) is denied. The First Defendant is unable to admit or deny that Unit 4 has been unable to be let, or the rent at which it would have been let, and requires the Claimant to prove both. Further, by clause 12.3 of the Contract the First Defendant is not liable for loss of rent howsoever arising, and the claim at sub paragraph (b) is accordingly excluded.

15. Further and in any event, by clause 12.1 of the Contract the First Defendant's liability under or in connection with the Contract, whether in contract, tort, breach of statutory duty or otherwise, does not in aggregate exceed the Contract Sum of £1,840,000.

16. If, which is denied, the Claimant contends that clauses 12.1 and 12.3 do not satisfy the requirement of reasonableness under sections 3 and 11 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, the First Defendant will contend that both clauses were fair and reasonable terms to be included having regard to the circumstances which were, or ought reasonably to have been, known to or in the contemplation of the parties when the Contract was made. The Claimant is an experienced property developer which contracted at arm's length for a sum of £1,840,000, the cap is set at the full Contract Sum rather than at any lesser figure, and the Claimant was free to price an alternative form of contract.

Interest

17. Paragraph 11 is noted. It is denied that the Claimant is entitled to any sum, and accordingly denied that it is entitled to interest.

18. Save as expressly admitted above, each and every allegation in the Particulars of Claim is denied.

Dated 30 April 2027

Kilbride Farrant LLP, solicitors for the First Defendant

STATEMENT OF TRUTH

The First Defendant believes that the facts stated in this defence are true. I understand that proceedings for contempt of court may be brought against anyone who makes, or causes to be made, a false statement in a document verified by a statement of truth without an honest belief in its truth.

Signed:

Name: Margaret Ubsdell

Position held: Company Secretary, duly authorised by the First Defendant

Date:

NOTE TO THE PARTNER

The draft is a defence for the First Defendant alone. We should not act for Mr Hoyt as well. The company's instructions are that if any warranty was given on 12 March 2026 then Mr Hoyt gave it personally and without authority, and that case is pleaded at paragraph 5. That is the company's best answer to the claim against it and it is directly adverse to Mr Hoyt, whose only answer is that no warranty was given at all. There is a conflict of interest between two existing or prospective clients on the same matter, and neither of the exceptions applies: the two do not have a substantially common interest and they are not competing for the same objective. Mr Hoyt should be told at once that we cannot act for him and that he needs his own solicitor without delay, because his own defence is due on the same date. We also need his separate instructions before the First Defendant's case on authority is served, and we should confirm to the company in writing that anything Mr Hoyt has told us in his capacity as a director is confidential to the company's retainer.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The company secretary's letter contains a request that reads like ordinary cost control: Mr Hoyt is a director, it is all one dispute, so please act for him too and send one bill. It cannot be done. The company's strongest answer to the warranty allegation is that if anything was said, Mr Hoyt said it on his own account and had no authority to bind the company. That case is fatal to Mr Hoyt personally, because it leaves him exposed on the claim against him while giving the company an escape. There is a conflict of interest between two clients on the same matter under paragraph 6.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, and neither exception is available: the two do not have a substantially common interest, and they are not competing for the same objective in the sense the rule means. The competent candidate drafts for the First Defendant only, heads the document accordingly, and tells the partner that Mr Hoyt must be told now that the firm cannot act for him and that he needs separate representation urgently, since his own defence falls due on 6 May 2027. A candidate who goes further will note that information Mr Hoyt gave in his capacity as a director belongs to the company's retainer and that his own position must not be prejudiced by delay in telling him.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsUses the settled vocabulary of a defence accurately and consistently: admitted, denied, not admitted, unable to admit or deny and required to prove, and the conditional formula if, which is denied. Reasons for each denial are given in one or two sentences. No argument, no evidence recited at length and no rhetoric.Using not admitted and denied interchangeably, or denying facts the client accepts, such as the existence of the contract, the date of practical completion or the presence of cracking. Writing the client's letter of instruction out in narrative form instead of converting it into pleaded responses.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsCorrect heading naming both defendants but pleading for the First Defendant only. Responds paragraph by paragraph to the particulars of claim in the same order, sub paragraph by sub paragraph where the claimant has particularised. Positive case is pleaded where a denial requires it. Ends with a general traverse, a date, and a statement of truth.Grouping several unrelated paragraphs of the claim into a single response so that some allegations are never dealt with. Under CPR 16.5(5) an allegation not dealt with is taken to be admitted, so a missing response is a substantive loss, not a formatting slip. Omitting the general traverse or the statement of truth.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawPleads the design responsibility answer correctly by reference to clauses 2.4 and 4.6, so that the absence of movement joints is admitted as a fact but denied as a breach. Denies the factual particulars the site records contradict and gives the client's version, as CPR 16.5(2)(b) requires. Pleads want of authority and the entire agreement clause against the alleged oral warranty. Pleads clauses 12.1 and 12.3 and anticipates the reasonableness challenge under sections 3 and 11 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, recognising that the burden of proving reasonableness is on the party relying on the clause.Denying the absence of movement joints, which the client accepts, instead of admitting the fact and denying that it is a breach. Ignoring the exclusion clauses altogether and simply denying the rent claim on causation. Asserting the exclusion clauses as if they were unanswerable, without recognising that this is the contractor's own standard form and so section 3 of the 1977 Act is engaged.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawEvery paragraph and every sub paragraph of the particulars of claim is answered. Deals separately with the three alleged particulars of breach, because the client's answer to each is different. Pleads the warranty answers in the alternative, so that the denial that anything was said, the want of authority and the entire agreement clause each stand on their own. Deals with quantum, causation of the rent loss, the exclusion of loss of rent and the overall cap. Identifies the documents relied on.Answering the warranty allegation only by denying that anything was said, so that the defence collapses if the judge prefers the claimant's witness. Failing to plead the client's positive case on causation, which leaves the defence as a bare denial and invites an application to strike out or for further information.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots that the firm cannot act for both the company and Mr Hoyt. The company's pleaded case is that any warranty was given by Mr Hoyt personally and without authority, which is directly adverse to him. This is a conflict of interest between two clients on the same matter and neither the substantially common interest nor the competing for the same objective exception applies. Drafts for the First Defendant only, says so in the heading, and tells the partner that Mr Hoyt must be advised immediately to instruct his own solicitor because his defence is due on the same date. A strong answer also notes the confidentiality position between the company and its director.Accepting the company secretary's suggestion and drafting a joint defence for both defendants to save costs, which is the invited answer. A joint defence cannot coherently plead that the Second Defendant acted without authority, and drafting it would put the firm in breach of the conflict rules and leave Mr Hoyt without a defence he can properly advance. Failing to warn about Mr Hoyt's own deadline is also a serious omission.

Examiner notes

The centre of gravity of this station is the difference between denying a fact and denying that a fact is a breach. The client admits there are no movement joints in the render. A weak candidate denies it because it appears in the particulars of breach. The right answer admits the fact, denies the breach, and explains why: the movement joint layout was the architect's design, clause 2.4 puts design on the employer and clause 4.6 relieves the contractor of any duty to depart from the contract documents. The second discriminator is the exclusion clauses. Candidates who spot clauses 12.1 and 12.3 usually stop there. The file note says the contract is the contractor's own standard form, which engages section 3 of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, and section 11(5) puts the burden of proving reasonableness on the contractor. A defence that pleads the clauses without anticipating that challenge is incomplete. The trap is the request to act for Mr Hoyt too. It is buried in the last paragraph of a long instruction letter and is framed as a favour to the client. Acting for both is impossible on this pleaded case and a candidate who drafts a joint defence will fail the ethics criterion.

Written station 10: Costs consequences of beating a claimant's own settlement offer at trial

Legal research  |  Dispute Resolution  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO GEORGINA ATTLEE

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 21 June 2027

Matter: Tarnwood Joinery Limited v Silverbrook Interiors Limited, Claim No. K90YM213

Subject: Part 36 costs consequences, costs hearing 9 July 2027

1. Summary

1.1 The letter of 2 October 2026 was a valid Part 36 offer. The defendant's expiry argument fails on C v D [2011] EWCA Civ 646 and on CPR 36.9(2).

1.2 Our client beat its own offer, so CPR 36.17(1)(b) is engaged and the court must make the orders in CPR 36.17(4) unless it considers it unjust to do so.

1.3 We should ask on 9 July for enhanced interest on the judgment sum, indemnity costs from 24 October 2026, interest on those costs, and an additional amount of £13,750.

1.4 The only real answer open to the defendant is that it would be unjust to make those orders under CPR 36.17(5). On Smith v Trafford Housing Trust that is a formidable obstacle for it and I do not think it succeeds here.

1.5 The email chain received on 18 June contains privileged advice which appears to have been sent to us in error. I deal with that at section 6 and it needs to be addressed before anything else is done.

2. Was the letter a valid Part 36 offer

2.1 CPR 36.5(1) requires a Part 36 offer to be in writing, to make clear that it is made pursuant to Part 36, to specify a relevant period of not less than 21 days within which the defendant will be liable for the claimant's costs under rule 36.13 or 36.23 if the offer is accepted, to state whether it relates to the whole of the claim or to part of it, and to state whether it takes account of any counterclaim.

2.2 Our letter does all five things. It is in writing. It says in terms that it is made pursuant to Part 36 and is intended to have the consequences of that Part. It specifies a relevant period of 21 days and refers to rule 36.13. It offers to settle the whole of the claim including interest. It states that it does not take account of any counterclaim.

2.3 The defendant's point is the sentence saying the offer is open for acceptance for 21 days only and will then automatically expire. Its argument is that an offer which lapses of its own accord cannot be a Part 36 offer.

2.4 That argument fails on C v D [2011] EWCA Civ 646. The Court of Appeal considered materially the same wording. Rix LJ held that the letter must be construed as a whole and in its context, and that where a letter states in terms that it is made under Part 36 and is intended to have Part 36 consequences the court leans strongly against a construction which would deprive it of them. The reference to 21 days identifies the relevant period during which the offeree may accept and obtain its costs under the rule; it is not a self executing time limit. Rimer LJ agreed that a genuinely time limited offer would not be a Part 36 offer, but held that on its proper construction that offer was not time limited. The same construction applies to our letter, which is if anything clearer than the letter in C v D because it uses the defined term relevant period and cross refers to rule 36.13.

2.5 There is a second and independent answer. CPR 36.9(2) provides that an offeror withdraws a Part 36 offer or changes its terms by serving written notice on the offeree. We never served any such notice. CPR 36.9(4)(b) does allow an offer to be automatically withdrawn in accordance with its terms after expiry of the relevant period, but that only operates where the offer is properly construed as containing such a term, and on C v D this one is not. In any event, no notice of withdrawal was served and CPR 36.17(7)(a), which disapplies paragraph (4) for a withdrawn offer, is not engaged.

3. The consequences we can ask for

3.1 CPR 36.17(1)(b) applies where judgment against the defendant is at least as advantageous to the claimant as the proposals in the claimant's own Part 36 offer. By CPR 36.17(2), in a money claim at least as advantageous means better in money terms by any amount however small. Judgment was for £137,500 against an offer of £120,000, so the test is comfortably met.

3.2 Where paragraph (1)(b) applies, the court must, unless it considers it unjust to do so, order the four things in CPR 36.17(4). We should ask for each of them.

3.3 Interest under CPR 36.17(4)(a). Interest on the whole or part of the sum awarded, excluding interest, at a rate not exceeding 10 per cent above base rate for some or all of the period starting with the date the relevant period expired. The relevant period expired on 23 October 2026. Base rate is 4 per cent, so the ceiling is 14 per cent. We should ask for the enhanced rate on £137,500 from 24 October 2026 to 14 June 2027. Note the ceiling is a maximum and not an entitlement, and the court will fix a rate it regards as appropriate.

3.4 Indemnity costs under CPR 36.17(4)(b). Costs on the indemnity basis from 24 October 2026. This matters for two reasons beyond the basis of assessment: on the indemnity basis any doubt about reasonableness is resolved in our client's favour, and proportionality does not apply. Our budgeted standard basis costs for that period are about £96,000, so the recovery should exceed that figure.

3.5 Interest on costs under CPR 36.17(4)(c), again at a rate not exceeding 10 per cent above base rate, so a ceiling of 14 per cent.

3.6 The additional amount under CPR 36.17(4)(d). The case has been decided and there has been no previous order under that sub-paragraph, so the additional amount is available. The prescribed percentage for an award up to £500,000 is 10 per cent of the sum awarded. The sum awarded is £137,500. Ten per cent of that is £13,750. That is well within the £75,000 cap. I have calculated the additional amount on the judgment sum of £137,500 and not on the interest of £9,400, because sub-paragraph (4)(d)(i) applies the percentage to the sum awarded to the claimant by the court and the rule deals with interest separately in paragraph (4)(a).

4. What the defendant can say

4.1 The expiry argument fails for the reasons at section 2.

4.2 CPR 36.17(7) does not help it. The offer was not withdrawn and no notice was served. Its terms were never changed. It was made on 2 October 2026, more than eight months before trial, so it was not made less than 21 days before trial.

4.3 That leaves only the injustice argument under CPR 36.17(4) and (5). The court must take into account all the circumstances including the terms of the offer, the stage at which it was made, the information available to the parties at the time, the parties' conduct as to giving information to allow the offer to be evaluated, and whether the offer was a genuine attempt to settle.

4.4 On Smith v Trafford Housing Trust [2012] EWHC 3320 (Ch), the burden on the party resisting the ordinary consequences is a formidable obstacle. Something more than the ordinary disadvantage of being the paying party is needed. The question is not whether the defendant acted reasonably in refusing the offer but whether it would be unjust to apply the consequences the rule prescribes.

4.5 The likely line of attack is that the offer of £120,000 against a claim of £180,000 was not a genuine attempt to settle. That should fail. The discount was £60,000, a third of the sum claimed, which is a real and meaningful concession rather than a derisory one. Huck v Robson and Jockey Club Racecourses confirm that even a 5 per cent discount can be a genuine attempt to settle, and that the offeree's own view that the claim was worth nothing does not make the rule unjust; a discount of a third is comfortably on the right side of that line.

4.6 The defendant might also say it lacked information to evaluate the offer in October 2026 under CPR 36.17(5)(c) and (d). We should check what disclosure and what expert material it had by then, so that we can meet this at the hearing. If it had the material it needed, the point goes nowhere.

4.7 Carver v BAA plc [2008] EWCA Civ 412 is in the bundle and the defendant may be tempted by it, because it allowed the court to look beyond the money at the wider picture. It should not be relied on. Its effect was reversed and CPR 36.17(2) now provides expressly that more advantageous means better in money terms by any amount however small. A margin of £17,500 is decisive.

5. Sources I have not relied on

5.1 CPR 44.13 and 44.14 apply to personal injury and fatal accident claims. This is a commercial contract claim and qualified one way costs shifting has no application.

5.2 CPR 36.22 to 36.24 apply only to claims to which Section VI, VII or VIII of Part 45 applies, that is claims within the extended fixed recoverable costs regime. This is a £180,000 commercial contract claim which is not within any fixed recoverable costs regime, so CPR 36.17 applies unmodified and rule 36.24 is not engaged.

5.3 Chartbrook Ltd v Persimmon Homes Ltd [2009] UKHL 38 concerns the construction of contracts and the inadmissibility of pre contractual negotiations. The construction of a Part 36 offer is governed by C v D and the scheme of Part 36 itself.

6. The email received on 18 June 2027

6.1 The chain forwarded to us at 17:52 on 18 June includes, below the covering message, an internal message from the defendant's solicitor to his client headed privileged and confidential, advice to client. It records counsel's view that the expiry argument is very weak, gives a figure for the defendant's realistic exposure, and advises the client not to disclose any of it to us.

6.2 That material is plainly privileged and it is plainly not intended for us. It has been forwarded by mistake.

6.3 I stopped reading as soon as it was apparent what the document was. We must notify Marlin Deane immediately and in writing that we have received it, confirm that we have not read beyond the point at which its nature became apparent, and ask for their instructions on destroying or returning it. We must not use it, refer to it at the hearing, or deploy the knowledge that counsel thinks their argument is weak or that their exposure is put at £110,000 to £120,000. If the client asks us to use it we must refuse and explain why. If Marlin Deane does not accept that the privilege stands, that is a matter for an application to the court, not something we resolve by using the document in the meantime.

6.4 We should also consider whether the firm can continue to act if we have absorbed enough of it to be embarrassed. My view is that we can, because nothing in it changes the analysis at sections 2 to 4, which stands on the rule and the authorities alone, but the partner should form her own view.

7. Recommended steps before 9 July

7.1 Serve a short skeleton relying on C v D and CPR 36.9(2) on validity, and on CPR 36.17(1)(b), (2) and (4) on consequences.

7.2 Prepare a schedule showing the enhanced interest calculation on £137,500 from 24 October 2026 to 14 June 2027 at the rate contended for, the costs claimed on the indemnity basis from 24 October 2026, and the additional amount of £13,750.

7.3 Pull together what the defendant had by 2 October 2026 on disclosure and experts, to meet any argument under CPR 36.17(5)(c) and (d).

7.4 Write to Marlin Deane about the misdirected email today, before any further correspondence about the hearing.

Sources relied on: CPR 36.5, CPR 36.9, CPR 36.17; C v D [2011] EWCA Civ 646; Smith v Trafford Housing Trust [2012] EWHC 3320 (Ch); Carver v BAA plc [2008] EWCA Civ 412, considered and not relied on.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The last document in the bundle is a covering email from the defendant's solicitor with the solicitor's own internal advice to his client left below it in the chain. It is headed privileged and confidential, advice to client. It records counsel's opinion that the defendant's expiry argument is very weak and that C v D is against it, puts the defendant's realistic exposure at £110,000 to £120,000, and tells the client to say none of it to the other side. It has obviously been forwarded by mistake. The material is privileged and the privilege belongs to the defendant, not to us. The solicitor must stop reading as soon as the nature of the document is apparent, notify the other side promptly and in writing, and seek their instructions on returning or destroying it. The document cannot be used, referred to at the costs hearing, or exploited in settlement discussions, and the knowledge of the opponent's stated exposure figure cannot be traded on. Using it would breach the SRA Principles on integrity and on public trust and paragraph 1.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits abusing a position by taking unfair advantage of others. If the client instructs the firm to use it, the firm must refuse and explain why. The candidate should also consider whether the firm can continue to act, and a good answer reasons that it can, since the analysis stands on the rule and the reported authorities without needing the document at all.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses CPR 36.5 to test validity, CPR 36.9 on withdrawal, CPR 36.17 for the consequences, C v D for the construction of the expiry wording and Smith v Trafford Housing Trust for the injustice discretion. Cites each properly. Identifies Carver as superseded rather than ignoring it or applying it. Discards CPR 44.13 and 44.14, CPR 36.24 and Chartbrook with a line of reasoning each. Takes the operative dates and figures from the chronology and uses them.Relying on Carver v BAA as good law, which produces the wrong answer on whether a £17,500 margin is enough. Applying CPR 36.24 or the fixed costs regime to a £180,000 commercial claim, or discussing qualified one way costs shifting, which belongs to personal injury litigation only.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers each of the partner's four questions in order and gives the money figure she asked for. Sets out what to ask the court for on 9 July as a list of orders. Adds the practical preparation that follows: a schedule of the interest calculation, and checking what information the defendant held in October 2026 so that the injustice argument can be met.Producing a general account of Part 36 without ever saying whether the October letter was valid, or omitting the additional amount calculation altogether when the partner asked for it in terms. Failing to identify what orders are actually to be sought at the hearing.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsShort numbered paragraphs under headings, a summary at the front carrying the answer and the £13,750 figure, precise rule references down to the sub paragraph, and no research trail. Distinguishes clearly between what the court must do and what it may do.Quoting CPR 36.17 at length rather than applying it. Describing the enhanced interest and the additional amount as entitlements without noting that the rate is a ceiling and that the whole of paragraph (4) is subject to the court's view on injustice.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawConcludes the offer was valid, for the right two reasons. Applies CPR 36.17(1)(b) and (2) correctly to a judgment of £137,500 against an offer of £120,000. Runs the consequences from 24 October 2026, the day after expiry of the relevant period, not from the date of the offer. Calculates the additional amount as 10 per cent of £137,500, that is £13,750, on the sum awarded rather than on the sum offered or on the costs, and notes the £75,000 cap. Uses base rate of 4 per cent to give a ceiling of 14 per cent.Calculating the additional amount as 10 per cent of the offer, or of the difference between the offer and the judgment, or of the costs. Running indemnity costs from the date of the offer rather than from the expiry of the relevant period. Treating the enhanced interest rate of 10 per cent above base as an automatic award rather than a maximum.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with all four limbs of CPR 36.17(4), not just costs. Tests the offer against every requirement of CPR 36.5(1) rather than only the disputed sentence. Gives the independent CPR 36.9(2) answer as well as the C v D answer. Works through CPR 36.17(7) and explains why none of its three limbs applies. Anticipates the injustice argument under CPR 36.17(5), identifies the genuine attempt to settle point as the one the defendant will run, and answers it on Smith.Stopping at indemnity costs and never mentioning enhanced interest, interest on costs or the additional amount, which is what the partner asked for. Concluding the offer is valid and then failing to consider whether the defendant has any answer at all, so the note gives the partner nothing to prepare against.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises that the forwarded chain contains the opponent's privileged advice sent in error, stops reading, and says so. Advises that the other side be notified in writing immediately, that instructions be sought on returning or destroying the material, and that neither the document nor the knowledge gained from it may be used at the hearing or in negotiation. Says that if the client asks for it to be used the firm must refuse. Considers whether the firm remains able to act.Using the material. A candidate who writes that the defendant's own counsel thinks the argument is weak, or who advises the partner to press for settlement at just under £110,000 because that is the opponent's stated exposure, fails this criterion outright. Reading the whole thing and saying nothing about it is equally serious.

Examiner notes

Two things separate a pass from a fail. The first is arithmetic and rule mechanics. The additional amount is 10 per cent of the sum awarded, so £13,750 on a judgment of £137,500. Candidates get this wrong in three ways: applying the percentage to the offer, to the difference between offer and judgment, or to the costs. They also frequently run indemnity costs from the date of the offer rather than from 24 October 2026, the day after the relevant period expired, and they present the enhanced interest ceiling of 10 per cent above base as an automatic award when the rule says not exceeding.
