The second is the misdirected email. It arrives at the end of a long bundle, it is genuinely useful, and the partner's email invites the candidate to read it. A candidate who quotes it back, or who advises settling just under the opponent's stated exposure figure, has failed the ethics criterion no matter how good the Part 36 analysis is. Note also the two decoys most likely to catch a candidate who is reading fast: Carver v BAA looks directly on point and is no longer good law, and CPR 36.24 looks like part of the general Part 36 machinery, and CPR 36.17(1) is expressly subject to it, but it applies only to claims within the extended fixed recoverable costs regime in Sections VI to VIII of Part 45.

Written station 11: Advising a client on a Part 36 offer and a counter offer

Legal writing  |  Dispute Resolution  |  30 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

Marchant Vellacott LLP

Solicitors

Broad Street, Ludlow

Ms Priya Ambrose

The Sarn Bakehouse

Ludlow

11 February 2027

Dear Priya

Your claim against Coldridge Catering Equipment Limited: their offer of £30,000

Thank you for your email of last night. I understand why the figure feels low. Below I set out what this offer actually is, what happens on each route open to you, and what I recommend. Please read the section on costs carefully, because the costs rules are what make this decision difficult.

1. What the offer is

The defendant has made what is called a Part 36 offer. That is a formal offer under the court rules. It is not an ordinary letter. It carries automatic consequences on costs, which is why it has to be taken seriously even though you think the figure is too low.

The offer is £30,000 to settle the whole claim, including interest. You have 21 days from yesterday to accept, so the deadline is 3 March 2027. The judge who hears the trial will not be told about the offer until after deciding the case, so it cannot prejudice your claim.

2. What happens if you accept within the 21 days

You receive £30,000. The defendant also pays your legal costs up to the date you accept, assessed on the standard basis. In practice that usually means recovering most, but not all, of what you have spent, so you should expect a shortfall of perhaps 20 to 30 per cent that comes out of your own pocket. Your costs so far are about £24,000 plus VAT.

3. What happens if you accept late

If you let the 21 days pass and then accept, the court will normally order that the defendant pays your costs only up to 3 March, and that you pay the defendant's costs from 3 March to the date you accept. That is a real risk if we drift.

4. What happens if you reject it and go to trial

There are two outcomes to plan for.

If you beat £30,000 at trial, even by a pound, the offer falls away and the usual rule applies: the defendant pays your damages and a large part of your costs.

If you do not beat £30,000, you will still have won your case but you will pay a heavy price. The court must normally order you to pay the defendant's costs from 3 March onwards, plus interest on those costs, as well as bearing your own. Our costs from now to the end of the trial are estimated at £38,000 plus VAT, and the defendant's are likely to be similar. A judgment of, say, £28,000 could leave you worse off than accepting today.

5. What the claim is realistically worth

Counsel puts your prospects of recovering something at about 60 per cent and a realistic award, if you win, at around £52,000. The oven itself is a strong claim. The £21,000 loss of profit on the hotel contract is the weak part, because the hotel gave three reasons for ending the contract and only one was about deliveries, and because the defendant did not know about that contract when it sold you the oven. Counsel would not value that head above about £11,000, and it may fail altogether.

Putting that together, £30,000 is below what the claim is worth but it is not a nuisance offer, and there is a genuine risk that a judge awards you less than £30,000 if the loss of profit claim fails.

6. My recommendation

Do not accept £30,000. Instead, make your own Part 36 offer promptly, so that the pressure runs both ways.

You asked me to offer £55,000. I would advise offering £42,000. An offer has to be a genuine attempt to settle to attract the full protection of the rules, and £55,000 is above what counsel thinks the claim is worth, so it risks being treated as a tactic rather than an offer. £42,000 is defensible, recovers the oven and something for the lost profit, and is a figure I think we have a real chance of beating at trial.

If you make that offer and the defendant refuses it, and you then equal or beat £42,000 at trial, the court must normally order the defendant to pay you: interest on your damages at up to 10 per cent above base rate; your costs on the indemnity basis from the end of their 21 day period, which is a more generous basis of assessment; interest on those costs; and an extra 10 per cent of the amount awarded, capped at £75,000. On a £45,000 award that additional amount alone would be £4,500. That is a powerful lever and it is the main reason to make a formal offer rather than a casual one.

7. Two things I cannot say on your behalf

You have asked me to tell the other side that Marcus will give evidence that the oven was faulty from the first week, and that you have a buyer for the bakehouse at £310,000 who will pull out unless the case settles by March.

I am not able to write either of those things. Marcus has told you he cannot remember that first week and does not want to give evidence, and there is no buyer. A solicitor is not permitted to make a statement to another party that he knows to be untrue, and I would be doing exactly that. This is not a technicality about my professional rules. If it later emerged, and in litigation these things usually do emerge, it would damage your credibility with the judge on everything else, and your credibility is worth more to this claim than any short term pressure.

There is a related practical point. If Marcus cannot support the first week, we need to know that now and plan around it. The defendant's own engineer's reports record a 34 degree variance across the middle deck, and that documentary evidence is stronger than any recollection of dates.

8. What I need from you

Please telephone me by 4pm on Friday 13 February with your instructions on the £42,000 offer. I would like it served next week, so that its 21 day period expires well before the trial window in May.

If you would prefer to talk any of this through before deciding, I am free on Thursday morning.

Yours sincerely

Trainee Solicitor

for Marchant Vellacott LLP

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client instructs the solicitor to tell the other side two things she knows to be false: that her head baker will give evidence about the first week when he has said he cannot remember and will not attend, and that a purchaser has offered £310,000 for the business and will withdraw unless the claim settles by March, when there is no purchaser. Passing either on would breach paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits misleading others, and Principle 5 on integrity. Conveying a false statement of a third party's evidence would also risk misleading the court in due course. A competent candidate does not simply leave the statements out. The candidate declines them expressly in the letter, gives a short and non judgmental explanation, and converts the problem into practical advice, namely that the defendant's own engineer's reports are stronger evidence than a witness who cannot remember, and that the firm needs to know now that Marcus will not attend. Recommending £42,000 rather than the client's £55,000 also engages rule 36.17(5)(e), because an offer that is not a genuine attempt to settle may lose its costs protection.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the figures that matter: the £30,000 offer, the 3 March deadline, costs of £24,000 to date and £38,000 to trial, counsel's 60 per cent and £52,000, and the weakness in the £21,000 loss of profit head, and links each to the decision.Recites the rule text without applying any of the client's own numbers, so she cannot see what she gains or loses.
Use a logical structure.SkillsMoves in a clear order: what the offer is, accept in time, accept late, reject and lose, valuation, recommendation, the instructions that cannot be followed, and a deadline for a reply.Mixes advice, costs and rule mechanics together so the client cannot find the recommendation.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsWritten for a baker with no litigation experience, explains the costs risk in cash terms, gives a firm recommendation rather than a menu, and offers a call.Hedges completely, tells her the decision is entirely a matter for her and gives no view, or lectures her about her tone.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsPlain English, short sentences, no untranslated rule numbers or Latin, courteous about her anger without being either patronising or evasive.Quotes CPR 36.13(5) and 36.17(3) at a lay client, or writes as though to a fellow solicitor.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly states that acceptance in time gives standard basis costs to the date of acceptance, that late acceptance shifts costs from expiry, and that failing to beat the offer gives the defendant its costs from expiry plus interest even though the client has won.Says she keeps her costs if she wins at trial regardless of the offer, or overlooks that failing to beat the offer reverses costs from the expiry of the relevant period.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAlso explains the claimant's own offer under rule 36.17(4), including enhanced interest, indemnity costs, interest on costs and the additional 10 per cent capped at £75,000, and warns that an offer must be a genuine attempt to settle.Deals only with the defendant's offer and says nothing useful about what a claimant's own Part 36 offer would achieve, or promises the full 36.17(4) consequences as automatic with no mention of the genuine attempt requirement.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses in the letter itself to convey the false evidence and the invented buyer, explains why in terms the client can accept, and turns it into practical advice about the documentary evidence and about Marcus.Drafts the counter offer including the statements about Marcus and the buyer, or stays silent about them and simply omits them without telling the client why.

Examiner notes

This is a negotiation station in the form of a letter. A pass requires the candidate to explain the three costs outcomes correctly and to give a recommendation. A grade A candidate goes further and turns the letter into a negotiating plan: reject, make a calibrated claimant's offer, and use rule 36.17(4) as leverage. The commonest failure is to treat the station as a Part 36 essay and forget that the reader is a baker. The second commonest is to handle the ethics point by silently dropping the two false statements from the counter offer. That is not enough. The client asked for them, believes they are fair game, and will simply ask again or say them herself unless she is told plainly that they cannot be said and why. A candidate who accepts the £55,000 instruction without comment has also missed that an offer pitched above the claim's realistic value can forfeit the very costs protection the client is trying to buy.

Written station 12: Which of four communications can be put before the court

Legal writing  |  Dispute Resolution  |  30 minutes

Model answer

INTERNAL NOTE

To: Gideon Ashcombe

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 10 March 2027

Matter: Merridale Foods Limited v Pentlow Logistics Limited, ref AR/MFL/3307

Subject: Admissibility of the four communications received 3 to 9 March, and the client's instructions

Summary

Three of the four cannot be used at all. What we can use is the maintenance and job card material sent on 5 March, which is disclosable in any event and gets us to the same evidence as the admission in the 3 March letter. The paralegal's email of 9 March 18:04 is an obvious mistake and needs a call to Ilbury Nash today. The client's instructions cannot be carried out and he should be told so before 24 March.

1. Communication A, letter of 3 March marked without prejudice

Not admissible. It opens by saying it is written with a view to exploring settlement, it makes an offer, and the admissions about the failed service and the incomplete temperature log are made in that context. That is a genuine attempt to settle an existing dispute, so the rule applies. The fact that the admissions are damaging to Pentlow is the reason the privilege exists, not a reason to disapply it. None of the exceptions is engaged: no settlement was concluded, there is no impropriety in the letter, delay is not in issue, and the letter is marked simply without prejudice rather than without prejudice save as to costs, so it cannot even be shown to the court on costs. The privilege is also joint, so our client cannot waive it unilaterally.

2. Communication B, email of 5 March marked without prejudice

The label is wrong and does not bite. This email makes no offer and contains no settlement discussion. It is a response to our protocol request of 20 February. Providing documents under a pre-action protocol is not a negotiation aimed at settlement. Separately, and more importantly, the maintenance history and job cards are pre-existing documents which are not privileged in themselves and do not become privileged by being sent under a without prejudice heading. They are disclosable and we can use them.

This is the useful point. If the job cards show that the refrigeration unit failed its service on 19 January 2026 and was not re presented, we prove that fact from Pentlow's own records without touching the 3 March letter. Please can Priya go through both PDFs today and report on what they actually show.

3. Communication C, email of 9 March 14:22, unmarked

Also inadmissible, notwithstanding the absence of a heading. It is in the same chain, it refers back to the 3 March letter and to a settlement telephone call, and it increases the offer. In substance it is a settlement communication, and substance governs. It is not open correspondence and it cannot go in the trial bundle. It is not a Part 36 offer and it is not marked save as to costs, so it is of no use to us on costs either.

4. Communication D, email of 9 March 18:04 with counsel's advice

This was addressed to Mr Pentlow of the defendant company and reached us by an error in their distribution list. It is plainly privileged and plainly sent by mistake, and it is obvious on its face. We must not read any further. I have not opened the attachment and I have secured the paralegal's copy, but the covering email itself discloses counsel's assessment.

Proposed action, which needs your approval today:

(a) telephone the supervising solicitor at Ilbury Nash and tell them what has happened;

(b) confirm in writing that we have not opened the attachment, that we have deleted it and the covering email from our systems, and that we have not passed the contents to our client;

(c) record on the file who saw it and what was read;

(d) do not use it, do not refer to it in negotiation or at the mediation, and do not put it in any bundle;

(e) do not tell Ivor Merridale what it says. That is uncomfortable, because he already knows roughly what it says from his own reading of the paralegal's email, but we cannot confirm, discuss or act on the contents.

If it later appears that we have taken in enough of the advice that we cannot put it out of mind, Ilbury Nash may apply to restrain this firm from continuing to act. Dealing with it openly today is the best protection against that. Please let me know if you would prefer to make the call yourself.

5. The client's instructions

None of Ivor Merridale's four requests can be met, and he needs to hear that from you rather than discover it on 24 March.

Handing the 3 March letter to the judge would put privileged material before the court and would rightly attract criticism and a costs order. Putting the 9 March offer in the trial bundle is the same problem in a different form. Forwarding counsel's advice to him or to the brokers, and quoting it at a mediation, would be using material we know was sent by mistake and would be taking unfair advantage of the other side. Sending the 3 March letter to Chilled Freight Monthly is the worst of the four: it publishes a privileged settlement communication, exposes our client to an injunction and to a claim, and would be a serious breach by this firm.

I suggest the message to him is short and positive. He does not need the 3 March letter, because Pentlow's own service records prove the same facts and can be used in open court.

6. Next steps on the file

(a) Priya to analyse the service history and job cards and produce a one page schedule of the January 2026 service failure and any subsequent entries.

(b) Serve a request under Part 18 in open correspondence asking Pentlow to say whether the refrigeration unit failed its scheduled service on 19 January 2026, whether it was re presented, and whether the temperature log was completed at two hourly intervals on 14 August 2026. If they answer, we have the admissions openly. If they refuse, we can seek an order at the case management conference on 24 March.

(c) Consider a notice to admit facts once the job cards are analysed.

(d) Costs protection. Their offers are of no use to either side on costs as matters stand. We should make our own offer under Part 36, or at least mark our next offer without prejudice save as to costs, so that we are protected. On a claim of £190,000 with costs already at £31,000, that should be done before the case management conference.

(e) Diarise the 14 day expiry of the £55,000 offer, which falls on 23 March, and take the client's instructions on it separately.

Please let me know on (4) and (5) before you leave tonight.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Communication D is counsel's advice to the opposing party, sent to this firm by an obvious error in the sender's distribution list and read by the firm's paralegal before the mistake was appreciated. The receiving solicitor must not read further than is needed to appreciate the position, must notify the sending firm at once, must return or destroy the material, must not use it and must not pass the contents to the client, even though the client has expressly asked for it and wants to quote the figures at a mediation. Using it would be taking unfair advantage contrary to paragraph 1.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and would offend Principles 2 and 5, and the firm may be restrained from continuing to act if it has absorbed the contents. There is a second, quieter issue in the client's instruction to send the without prejudice letter to a trade magazine, which would publish a privileged settlement communication and expose both client and firm. A competent candidate resolves both by acting openly and immediately, and by telling the client what cannot be done rather than simply not doing it.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the distinguishing features of each communication: the settlement purpose and offer in A, the protocol request of 20 February answered by B, the chain and the telephone call behind C, and the addressee and distribution list error behind D, together with the 24 March hearing and the 23 March expiry.Discusses the without prejudice rule in the abstract without pinning the analysis to what each of the four documents actually says.
Use a logical structure.SkillsTakes the four communications in turn under headings, then the client's instructions, then next steps, with a short summary at the top that the partner can act on immediately.Answers only the admissibility question and ignores the client's instructions or the next steps the partner asked for.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsWritten for a partner leaving for a hearing: gives a view rather than options, names who does what, flags the two decisions needed tonight, and proposes how the client should be told.Writes a letter to the client by mistake, or lists possibilities without recommending anything, leaving the partner to decide everything.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsInternal register. Concise, direct, no letter formalities, no client facing softening, no citations padded out for effect.Adopts a formal correspondence style with Dear Sirs and Yours faithfully, or writes at such length that the partner cannot use it before leaving.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly holds A and C inadmissible on substance rather than on their labels, correctly holds that the label on B does not apply and that the pre-existing records are disclosable and usable, and correctly notes the privilege is joint and cannot be waived by the client alone.Decides admissibility by the presence or absence of the heading, so treats C as open because it is unmarked, or treats the maintenance records as privileged because the covering email was mislabelled.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAlso covers the recognised exceptions and why none applies, the difference between without prejudice and without prejudice save as to costs, the consequence that neither party's offers are currently usable on costs, and the Part 18 and notice to admit route to getting the same facts openly.Identifies the rule but never explains the without prejudice save as to costs point, so misses that neither offer currently gives anyone costs protection and that our own offer needs to be made before the case management conference.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawTreats the mistakenly sent counsel's advice as an obvious error: stops reading, notifies Ilbury Nash at once, deletes or returns it, records who saw it, refuses to pass the contents to the client, and recognises the risk of being restrained from acting.Reads or forwards the attachment, tells the client what counsel advised, or plans to deploy the figures at the mediation.

Examiner notes

The discriminator is whether the candidate decides admissibility by substance or by heading. Weak candidates work through the four documents by looking at the top of each one, which produces exactly the wrong answers on B and C: they treat the maintenance records as protected because the email was mislabelled, and they treat the unmarked offer as open because nobody typed the words. A strong candidate reverses both, then sees the practical consequence, which is that the maintenance records give us the same facts as the privileged admission and can be used in open court. The second discriminator is the costs point. Both of Pentlow's offers are marked without prejudice only, or not marked at all, so neither party has any costs protection at present, and the answer is to make a Part 36 offer before the case management conference. Candidates who stop at inadmissible and go no further usually pass on law and fail on client focus. The trap is Communication D, which sits at the end of a long bundle and reads like a gift. Any candidate who forwards it, quotes it or tells the client what it says has failed the ethics criterion however good the rest of the note is.

Property Practice

Written station 13: Joint purchase of a mixed use property in Wales with unusual funding

Case and matter analysis  |  Property Practice  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO PARTNER

To: Gwilym Prosser, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 5 February 2027

Matter: Wierzbicki and Nkemelu, purchase of 44 Sanctuary Row, Newport, CYM204118

Subject: Co-ownership, land transaction tax, and matters requiring your decision

1. Summary and recommendation

1.1 The file cannot proceed in its present state. In my view there are reasonable grounds to suspect that this transaction involves the proceeds of crime, and separately the clients have asked us to take part in a scheme to understate the price so as to reduce land transaction tax. That is tax fraud and we cannot do it.

1.2 My recommendation is that I report internally to the firm's nominated officer today, that no further step is taken on the matter and no funds are accepted until the nominated officer has decided whether to make a suspicious activity report and whether a defence against money laundering is needed, and that nothing is said to either client about that report.

1.3 The co-ownership and tax points below still need to be worked through, because if the matter is cleared to proceed they have to be dealt with properly, and because the answers we give the clients on them must be correct.

2. Money laundering and source of funds

2.1 The following features of this file are red flags, and they are cumulative rather than individually decisive.

(a) Speed and pressure. Instructions taken nine days ago, completion demanded by 28 February, a stated risk of losing the property and a rival buyer. Artificial urgency is a classic feature.

(b) A cash purchase of 360,000 pounds with no lender. There is no third party doing any diligence on the funds except us.

(c) A third party payment of 155,000 pounds from Kalvary Trading Group, a company in Dubai, said to be owned by the client's cousin, coming direct to our client account, not through the client's own account, with a numeric reference and no documentation. The stated reason, settlement of an old debt owed personally by the cousin, does not explain why a company is paying it. On the firm's procedures at 5.1 that payment cannot be accepted without evidence of the third party's identity, the reason for the payment and the third party's own source of funds.

(d) 145,000 pounds said to be eleven years of savings from a cash business, with the client saying he cannot produce statements and that they would not show much anyway. That is an unevidenced source of funds and the client has pre-empted the request.

(e) A request to return any surplus from client account to the cousin's account in Dubai. That is using the client account as a banking facility, which 5.4 prohibits, and it is a request to move money out to an account other than the one it came from.

(f) A client we have never met, Ms Nkemelu, with no identification at all, said to be abroad, whose instructions are being relayed by the other client, together with a request that we do not email her about the money.

(g) Two requests to keep matters out of writing, on the funding and on Ms Nkemelu's contribution.

2.2 Taken together these give reasonable grounds to suspect that the funds, or some of them, are criminal property. Under the firm's procedures at 6.1 I must make an internal report to the nominated officer at once and take no further step until told to do so. If the nominated officer decides that we would otherwise be concerned in an arrangement facilitating the acquisition or control of criminal property, the transaction must not proceed until a defence against money laundering has been obtained from the National Crime Agency, and the statutory notice periods will make the 28 February date impossible.

2.3 Tipping off. Under 6.3 and the underlying law we must say nothing to either client, or to the agent or the seller's solicitors, about the internal report or about any suspicious activity report. That is why I have not contacted the clients. If the matter is delayed, any explanation given to the clients must be truthful but must not reveal the report. In practice we say that we are not in a position to proceed and, if we cease to act, we do not give reasons.

2.4 Client due diligence is in any event incomplete and must be completed before the firm carries out the transaction. Ms Nkemelu has provided nothing. A photocopy passport and a utility bill for Mr Wierzbicki taken by a paralegal is thin. Ms Nkemelu has not been met, so she must be verified electronically or by certified copies from a suitable certifier. The third party payer must also be identified. This transaction is unusually large for these clients, involves a third party payer in another jurisdiction and has features with no apparent economic purpose, so enhanced due diligence and enhanced ongoing monitoring are required under 4.6. We cannot take instructions for Ms Nkemelu from Mr Wierzbicki. She is a client in her own right and we must take instructions from her, satisfy ourselves that she is giving them freely and advise her separately.

3. The proposed price apportionment and land transaction tax

3.1 Land transaction tax applies because the property is in Wales. Stamp duty land tax does not. LTT is administered by the Welsh Revenue Authority. The shop with a self contained flat above is mixed use, so the non-residential rates apply to the whole price.

3.2 On the true price of 360,000 pounds the tax on the file figures is: nothing on the first 225,000 pounds; 1 per cent on the slice from 225,000 to 250,000 pounds, which is 250 pounds; and 5 per cent on the slice from 250,000 to 360,000 pounds, which is 5,500 pounds. Total 5,750 pounds.

3.3 On the proposed contract figure of 285,000 pounds the tax would be: nothing on the first 225,000 pounds; 250 pounds on the slice to 250,000 pounds; and 5 per cent on 35,000 pounds, which is 1,750 pounds. Total 2,000 pounds. The scheme therefore seeks to avoid 3,750 pounds of tax.

3.4 The scheme does not work and it is not lawful. An apportionment to chattels only takes an amount out of chargeable consideration if it genuinely reflects the value of chattels. Most of what is listed is not chattels at all. Shutters and flooring fixed to the building are fixtures and form part of the land. Goodwill on a transfer of land of this kind is in substance part of the price. Barber's chairs may be chattels, but they belong to the barber as tenant of the shop, not to the seller, so the seller cannot sell them and no part of the price can be apportioned to them. A receipt for 75,000 pounds against that list would be a false document.

3.5 Filing a return stating a price of 285,000 pounds when the price is 360,000 pounds is a false return to the WRA. That is tax fraud, not tax planning, and the agent's assurance that everybody does it is worthless. We cannot draft the contract that way, we cannot file the return and we cannot allow the clients to do it while we act. If the clients insist we must cease to act.

3.6 The clients must also be told, if the matter proceeds, that the return must be filed and the tax paid within 30 days beginning with the day after completion, and that interest and penalties follow late filing and late payment.

4. Co-ownership

4.1 The clients want both names on the title and the survivor to take the whole. That is a beneficial joint tenancy. It is almost certainly the wrong answer here and it was chosen without advice.

4.2 They are business partners, not a couple, and they are contributing very unequally, 300,000 pounds and 60,000 pounds. Under a joint tenancy the right of survivorship operates on death, so if Ms Nkemelu died first Mr Wierzbicki would take the whole property and her 60,000 pounds would pass out of her estate to him, and if Mr Wierzbicki died first Ms Nkemelu would take a property she contributed one sixth of, and his estate and his family would get nothing. Neither outcome reflects what they have actually put in, and neither can be changed by a will, because survivorship takes effect regardless of a will.

4.3 The right answer on these facts is a tenancy in common in unequal shares, recorded as a declaration of trust, with the shares reflecting their contributions or such other split as they agree. The declaration should be made in the transfer, by completing the relevant panel of the TR1 to state that they hold on trust for themselves as tenants in common in the stated shares, or by a separate deed of trust referred to in the transfer. A declaration in the transfer signed by both is conclusive as between them, which is exactly why it must be correct and must be what they both actually want. A restriction will be entered on the register so that capital money is not paid to a single trustee.

4.4 The declaration of trust should also deal with the matters that cause the disputes: who pays the outgoings and the cost of works, how income from the barber's lease is split, what happens if one of them wants out, and a mechanism for one to buy the other. They should each be advised to make a will.

4.5 If they insist on a joint tenancy after advice, that can be done, but the advice must be recorded and they must be told about severance in writing.

4.6 There is a conflict of interest point. Their interests on the co-ownership terms are not the same, and Ms Nkemelu's position under the joint tenancy proposal is materially worse than under a tenancy in common in shares. We are being asked to accept that proposal on her behalf from the other buyer, without ever speaking to her. We cannot advise both of them on the split unless we have taken instructions from each of them separately and are satisfied there is no conflict. If a conflict emerges, one of them must take independent advice.

5. Ms Nkemelu

5.1 She is our client. We have never spoken to her, we have no identification for her, all her instructions come through Mr Wierzbicki, and he has asked us twice not to put things about the money in writing to her or about her contribution. That last request, that her contribution should not be recorded, is inconsistent with the declaration of trust she needs.

5.2 Whether or not the money laundering issue is resolved, we cannot act for her on this basis. We must speak to her directly, verify her identity, take her own instructions and satisfy ourselves that she is acting freely.

6. Next steps, in order

(a) Today: internal report to the nominated officer setting out the matters in section 2. No further step on the file, no funds accepted, nothing said to the clients about the report.

(b) Await the nominated officer's decision on a suspicious activity report and on a defence against money laundering, and follow it.

(c) Do not accept the 155,000 pounds from Kalvary Trading Group into client account. If it arrives before we have decided, take instructions from the nominated officer; do not pay it away and do not return it to a different account.

(d) Whatever else happens, write to both clients confirming that we cannot record a price of 285,000 pounds or apportion 75,000 pounds to those items, explaining why, and that if they wish to proceed on that basis we shall cease to act. Timing of this letter to be settled with the nominated officer so as not to prejudice any investigation.

(e) Contact Ms Nkemelu directly. Complete client due diligence and enhanced due diligence for both clients.

(f) If and when the matter is cleared to proceed: advise both clients on joint tenancy against tenancy in common, take separate instructions on the shares, prepare the declaration of trust, and revise the completion timetable, which cannot be 28 February.

(g) Diarise the 30 day LTT filing and payment deadline against the eventual completion date.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two issues sit unflagged in the papers. First, the funding carries multiple money laundering red flags: artificial urgency, a large cash purchase with no lender, an unevidenced source of funds from a cash business, a 155,000 pound third party payment from an overseas company direct to client account, a request to send surplus funds out to a different account, incomplete client due diligence and a client who has never been met. A competent candidate treats these cumulatively, reports internally to the firm's nominated officer at once, takes no further step, does not accept or pay away the funds, and says nothing to the clients that would amount to tipping off. Second, the proposed apportionment of 75,000 pounds of the price to fixtures, goodwill and the tenant's own chattels is a scheme to file a false land transaction tax return. The candidate must refuse to draft or file on that basis, advise the clients plainly, and cease to act if they insist. There is also a conflict and capacity to instruct issue: instructions for Ms Nkemelu are being relayed by the other buyer and she has provided no identification.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsAssembles the red flags from three separate documents and treats them cumulatively: urgency, unmet client, no identification for the second buyer, cash business with no statements, the Dubai company payment direct to client account, the surplus refund request and the two requests to keep things out of writing. Identifies the unequal 300,000 to 60,000 contributions and that the clients are business partners.Reports each document in turn without drawing the funding facts together, or misses that the barber's chairs belong to the tenant and not to the seller.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsTells the partner plainly what must happen and in what order, distinguishes what can be said to the clients from what cannot, and gives correct co-ownership advice aimed at what these two clients actually need, including outgoings, income from the lease, exit and wills.Advises writing immediately to the clients explaining the money laundering concern, or simply records the clients' instruction that the survivor should take the whole property.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA clear report with headed sections, the recommendation at the front, arithmetic set out plainly and a numbered next steps list. No hedging about whether the tax scheme is acceptable.Long, unstructured, or so cautious about the tax scheme that the partner cannot tell whether the candidate is refusing it.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrect on land transaction tax applying in Wales instead of stamp duty land tax, on mixed use attracting the non-residential rates, on the arithmetic using the rates supplied, on fixtures against chattels, and on the difference between a beneficial joint tenancy with survivorship and a tenancy in common in shares recorded by a declaration of trust.Applies stamp duty land tax to a Welsh property, calculates the tax on a slab rather than a banded basis, or says a will can override survivorship under a joint tenancy.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers the money laundering duties, the due diligence gaps, the tax scheme, the co-ownership structure and the declaration of trust, the register restriction, the 30 day filing and payment deadline, and the conflict and instructions problem affecting Ms Nkemelu.Deals only with the money laundering and never answers the two questions the partner actually asked, or deals only with co-ownership and tax and ignores the funding.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies both the money laundering duty to report internally and take no further step, and the refusal to be party to a false tax return, and resolves each with a concrete step. Recognises the tipping off restriction and the problem of taking one client's instructions from another.Names the red flags but recommends proceeding with more paperwork, discloses the suspicion to the clients, or fails to refuse the apportionment scheme.

Examiner notes

This station fails candidates who treat the money laundering material as a client care problem. The pass requires an internal report to the nominated officer, a halt on the transaction, and express recognition of the tipping off restriction, which candidates routinely forget when they then draft a letter telling the client exactly why the file has stalled. On tax, the trap is to accept the chattels apportionment as legitimate planning; the strongest candidates notice that the shutters and flooring are fixtures, that goodwill on a land transfer is in substance price, and that the barber's chairs belong to the tenant and cannot be sold by the seller at all. On co-ownership, the trap is to record the clients' stated wish for survivorship without advising against it given the unequal contributions and the fact that they are business partners. Candidates are given the LTT rates in the materials and are expected to apply them; they are not expected to recall them. A candidate who says stamp duty land tax applies to a Newport property has made a substantive error.

Written station 14: Special conditions for a sale of part of a registered freehold

Legal drafting  |  Property Practice  |  45 minutes

Model answer

SPECIAL CONDITIONS

1. Definitions and interpretation

1.1 In these special conditions:

"the Plan" means the plan drawn by Verrall Surveying and dated 2 September 2026 annexed to this contract;

"the Property" means the land at the rear of 12 Fernbank Rise, Ludlow, Shropshire SY8 2QT shown edged red on the Plan, being part of the land registered at HM Land Registry under title number SL418902;

"the Retained Land" means the remainder of the land registered under title number SL418902, being 12 Fernbank Rise, Ludlow and its garden, shown edged blue on the Plan;

"the Driveway" means the driveway at the side of 12 Fernbank Rise shown coloured brown on the Plan;

"the Drain" means the foul drain and all associated pipes, manholes and inspection chambers now laid under the Property and serving the Retained Land;

"the 1968 Conveyance" means the Conveyance dated 4 March 1968 made between (1) The Fernbank Estate Company Limited and (2) Harold Gilmore Peake referred to at entry 1 of the charges register of title number SL418902;

"the Transfer" means the transfer of the Property to the Buyer in the form annexed to this contract.

1.2 The Standard Conditions of Sale (Fifth Edition, 2018 Revision) are incorporated in this contract. Where there is any conflict or inconsistency between a standard condition and a special condition, the special condition prevails. Standard condition 1.1.1(e) applies to the expression "working day" in these special conditions.

2. Sale of part and title guarantee

2.1 The Seller will sell and the Buyer will buy the Property with full title guarantee.

2.2 The Property is sold as part only of the land in title number SL418902. The Buyer is to apply to HM Land Registry for the registration of the Transfer and for the opening of a new title.

2.3 The Buyer accepts the Property boundaries as shown on the Plan and may not raise any requisition or objection about them.

3. Title and incumbrances

3.1 The Property is sold subject to, and with the benefit of, the matters contained or referred to in the property register and the charges register of title number SL418902 so far as they relate to the Property and are still subsisting and capable of taking effect, and in particular subject to the restrictive covenants contained in the 1968 Conveyance.

3.2 The Seller has supplied the Buyer with official copies of the register and title plan of title number SL418902 dated 9 September 2026. The Buyer buys with full knowledge of them and of the replies given by the Seller's conveyancer to the Buyer's pre contract enquiries, and may raise no requisition or objection on the title save as to matters arising after the date of this contract.

3.3 Neither the 1968 Conveyance nor a certified copy or examined abstract of it is available. The Buyer may raise no requisition or objection about the contents of the 1968 Conveyance or about the Seller's inability to produce it. Standard condition 3.1.4 continues to apply.

3.4 Nothing in this contract limits the Seller's duty to disclose incumbrances of which the Seller knows or ought to know and which the Buyer could not discover on inspection.

4. Rights granted to the Buyer

4.1 The Transfer will grant to the Buyer, for the benefit of the Property and each and every part of it and its owners and occupiers from time to time and those authorised by them:

4.1.1 a right of way at all times and for all purposes on foot and with or without vehicles over and along the Driveway, for the purpose of access to and egress from the Property only, but not any right to park or to leave any vehicle standing on the Driveway;

4.1.2 the right to connect into and thereafter to use the Drain for the passage of foul water from the Property, and the right to lay a connecting pipe from the Property to the Drain along the route shown by a green dotted line on the Plan;

4.1.3 the right to enter on so much of the Retained Land as is reasonably necessary to inspect, maintain, repair, cleanse and renew the connecting pipe referred to in special condition 4.1.2, on not less than ten working days' prior written notice except in an emergency, causing as little damage and disturbance as possible and making good all damage caused to the reasonable satisfaction of the Seller.

4.2 The Transfer will contain a covenant by the Buyer to pay to the owner of the Retained Land on demand a fair proportion, according to use, of the cost of maintaining, repairing and resurfacing the Driveway. The right granted by special condition 4.1.1 is granted on condition that the Buyer complies with that covenant.

5. Rights reserved to the Seller

5.1 The Transfer will reserve to the Seller, for the benefit of the Retained Land and each and every part of it and its owners and occupiers from time to time:

5.1.1 the right to the free and uninterrupted passage of foul water through the Drain;

5.1.2 the right to enter on the Property with or without workmen, materials and equipment so far as reasonably necessary to inspect, maintain, repair, cleanse and renew the Drain, on not less than ten working days' prior written notice except in an emergency, causing as little damage and disturbance as possible and making good all damage caused to the reasonable satisfaction of the Buyer;

5.1.3 the right to the free passage of gas, water, electricity, soil and telecommunications through any other conduit now in, on or under the Property and serving the Retained Land, with rights of entry on the terms set out in special condition 5.1.2;

5.1.4 the right to build on and to develop the Retained Land in accordance with any planning permission from time to time granted, notwithstanding any interference with the access of light or air to the Property.

6. No implied rights

6.1 Except for the rights expressly granted by special condition 4, the Buyer takes no right or easement over the Retained Land or over any other land of the Seller.

6.2 Section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 does not apply to the Transfer and no right is to pass to the Buyer under the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows.

6.3 The Transfer will contain an agreement and declaration that the Buyer is not entitled to any right of light or air which would restrict or interfere with the free use of the Retained Land for building or any other purpose.

7. Buyer's covenants

7.1 The Transfer will contain covenants by the Buyer with the Seller, for the benefit of the Retained Land and each and every part of it and with the intention of binding the Property and each and every part of it into whosoever hands the same may come, in the following terms:

7.1.1 within three months of the date of the Transfer to erect along the boundary between the Property and the Retained Land shown by a broken black line on the Plan a close boarded fence not less than 1.8 metres in height and thereafter to maintain that fence in good repair and condition;

7.1.2 not to use the Property otherwise than as a single private dwellinghouse with its garden, and not to carry on any trade or business on the Property;

7.1.3 not to erect on the Property any building other than one detached dwellinghouse together with a garage and one domestic outbuilding.

7.2 The Transfer will contain a covenant by the Buyer with the Seller to observe and perform the restrictive covenants contained in the 1968 Conveyance so far as they relate to the Property and are still subsisting and capable of taking effect, and to indemnify the Seller against all actions, claims, demands and liability arising from any future breach of them.

8. Deposit

8.1 On the date of this contract the Buyer is to pay a deposit of 31,000 pounds, being 10 per cent of the purchase price, to the Seller's conveyancer as stakeholder.

8.2 The deposit is to be paid by electronic means from an account held in the name of the Buyer's conveyancer at a clearing bank to the account of the Seller's conveyancer at a clearing bank, in accordance with standard condition 2.2.4.

8.3 No part of the deposit may be paid in cash. No part of the deposit may be paid after the date of this contract.

9. Vacant possession, completion and contract rate

9.1 The Property is sold with vacant possession on completion.

9.2 The completion date is 30 October 2026 and standard condition 6.1.1 is varied accordingly. Time is not of the essence unless a notice to complete has been served.

9.3 Completion is to take place by 2.00 pm on the completion date. Standard condition 6.1.2 applies to money received after that time.

9.4 The contract rate is the Law Society's interest rate from time to time in force.

10. General

10.1 The Buyer enters into this contract in reliance only on the written replies given by the Seller's conveyancer to the Buyer's written pre contract enquiries, and not in reliance on any other statement made by or on behalf of the Seller. Nothing in this special condition limits or excludes liability for fraud or for fraudulent or reckless misrepresentation.

10.2 The Buyer buys with knowledge of planning permission reference 26/03318/FUL granted by Shropshire Council on 6 August 2026 and the Seller gives no warranty that any development of the Property may lawfully be carried out.

10.3 A person who is not a party to this contract has no right under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 to enforce any of its terms.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The attendance note records that 25,000 pounds of the deposit is to be brought to the office in cash by the buyer's father, that the client wants a special condition permitting it, and that the buyer's own solicitor has not been told. Three things follow. First, the firm's policy forbids accepting cash in any amount and forbids agreeing any term that contemplates it, so the candidate must not draft the condition requested and must instead draft a deposit condition that complies with standard condition 2.2.4 and expressly excludes cash. Second, a large cash sum from a third party in a cash based trade, offered without explanation and deliberately concealed from the buyer's own conveyancer, is a money laundering warning sign that requires an internal report to the Money Laundering Reporting Officer and source of funds enquiries before exchange, with no tipping off. Third, the client's instruction to say nothing that would slow the deal down cannot be followed to the point of misleading the buyer's conveyancer, which would breach the duty not to mislead others. The candidate resolves it by drafting the compliant condition and reporting the cash offer internally.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsConditions are short, numbered and unambiguous. Rights and covenants are defined once and then used consistently. Defined terms are capitalised and each is actually used. No loose wording such as reasonable access or suitable fence.Long undivided paragraphs, terms used before they are defined, or vague drafting such as a right of way over the driveway with no statement of who has it, for what and for whose benefit.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsDefinitions first, then title, then rights granted, then rights reserved, then covenants, then deposit and completion. Grants and reservations are kept apart and each is stated to be for the benefit of identified land.Grants and reservations mixed together in one clause, deposit and completion buried inside the rights clauses, or the schedule left in the order of the partner's numbered list rather than in a logical drafting order.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawExcludes section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 and the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows, grants the easements to the buyer and reserves the drainage rights to the seller with proper entry and making good provisions, annexes the positive fencing covenant and the user covenant to the retained land, adds an indemnity covenant for the 1968 covenants, and varies standard condition 6.1.1 to fix 30 October 2026.Failing to exclude implied grant on a sale of part, so the buyer takes rights over the retained land the sellers never agreed to. Reserving nothing for the drain, or purporting to reserve rights without any entry or making good machinery.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers every item in the partner's list, deals with the missing 1968 conveyance, states vacant possession, the completion time, the contract rate and the deposit, and preserves the seller's duty of disclosure rather than trying to exclude it wholesale.Omitting the indemnity covenant, omitting vacant possession, or drafting a blanket clause that the buyer takes the property subject to all incumbrances whether or not disclosed, which is an attempt to contract out of the duty of disclosure.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDrafts a deposit condition that requires payment by electronic means from the buyer's conveyancer's client account in accordance with standard condition 2.2.4, expressly prohibits cash and expressly prohibits payment after exchange. Does not draft the condition the client asked for.Drafting the condition the client asked for, permitting 25,000 pounds in cash and part payment a week after exchange. This is a firm policy breach and a money laundering red flag and it fails this criterion outright.

Examiner notes

This station passes or fails on two things. The first is the sale of part discipline: a candidate who does not exclude section 62 and the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows, and who does not reserve the drainage rights, has given away rights over the retained land and cannot reach a pass on legal correctness. The second is the deposit. The trap is that the partner's email lists nine tasks and item 9 simply says deal with the deposit, so a candidate working quickly drafts an ordinary 10 per cent condition, or worse drafts exactly what the client asked for because the client asked for it. Both miss the point. The instruction to read the attendance note is the only signpost, and the attendance note is where the cash offer sits. Weak candidates also write a covering note explaining the ethics. There is no client focused advice criterion in drafting, so the answer is the special conditions and nothing else, and the ethics point has to be resolved inside the drafting itself.

Written station 15: Licence to assign a commercial lease

Legal drafting  |  Property Practice  |  45 minutes

Model answer

DATED 2027

(1) CHERITON WHARF PROPERTIES LIMITED

(2) HOLLOW LANE FABRICATION LIMITED

(3) TARN METALWORKS LIMITED

LICENCE TO ASSIGN

Unit 12, Cheriton Wharf, Feeder Road, Bristol BS2 0TQ

THIS DEED is made on [ ] 2027

BETWEEN

(1) CHERITON WHARF PROPERTIES LIMITED (company number 05512099) whose registered office is at [address] (the "Landlord");

(2) HOLLOW LANE FABRICATION LIMITED (company number 08331764) whose registered office is at [address] (the "Tenant"); and

(3) TARN METALWORKS LIMITED (company number [ ]) whose registered office is at [address] (the "Assignee").

BACKGROUND

A. This deed is supplemental to a lease dated 4 June 2021 made between (1) the Landlord and (2) the Tenant of Unit 12, Cheriton Wharf, Feeder Road, Bristol BS2 0TQ for a term of 15 years from and including 4 June 2021 (the "Lease"). The Premises are registered at HM Land Registry under title number BL674455 and the Landlord's reversion is registered under title number BL661204.

B. The Landlord is entitled to the immediate reversion to the Lease and the Tenant is the tenant under the Lease.

C. The Tenant has applied to the Landlord for consent to assign the whole of the Premises to the Assignee. The Landlord has agreed to grant consent on the terms of this deed.

OPERATIVE PROVISIONS

1. INTERPRETATION

1.1 In this deed, unless the context otherwise requires:

"AGA" means the authorised guarantee agreement in clause 5;

"Assignment" means the assignment of the whole of the Premises by the Tenant to the Assignee in accordance with this deed;

"Premises" means the premises demised by the Lease;

"Rent Deposit Deed" means the rent deposit deed of the same date as this deed made between the Landlord and the Assignee;

"Tenant Covenants" means the tenant covenants of the Lease within the meaning of the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995.

1.2 Words and expressions defined in the Lease have the same meanings in this deed unless otherwise stated.

1.3 A reference to a statute includes any amendment, extension or re enactment of it for the time being in force.

1.4 Where a party comprises more than one person, their obligations are joint and several.

1.5 Clause headings do not affect the interpretation of this deed.

2. LICENCE TO ASSIGN

2.1 Subject to clause 2.2 and to the conditions in clause 3, the Landlord consents to the Assignment.

2.2 The consent in clause 2.1:

2.2.1 is given for one assignment only, being an assignment of the whole of the Premises by the Tenant to the Assignee, and for no other dealing;

2.2.2 takes effect only when every condition in clause 3 has been satisfied;

2.2.3 lapses and is of no effect if the Assignment has not been completed within three months after the date of this deed;

2.2.4 does not authorise any further assignment, underletting, charging, parting with possession or sharing of occupation of the whole or any part of the Premises;

2.2.5 does not release the Tenant from, or waive, any breach of the Tenant Covenants existing at the date of this deed or at the date of the Assignment.

2.3 Except as expressly provided in this deed, the Lease continues in full force and effect.

3. CONDITIONS

3.1 The Landlord's consent is conditional on all of the following being satisfied on or before completion of the Assignment:

3.1.1 the Assignee entering into the covenants in clause 4;

3.1.2 the Tenant entering into the AGA in clause 5;

3.1.3 the Assignee paying to the Landlord's solicitors, to be held on the terms of the Rent Deposit Deed, the sum of 45,000 pounds together with VAT on that sum, being an amount equal to six months' Rent, and the Assignee entering into the Rent Deposit Deed;

3.1.4 all sums due under the Lease at the date of the Assignment being paid;

3.1.5 the Tenant paying the Landlord's costs under clause 6.

3.2 The Landlord's solicitors are not obliged to accept the sum referred to in clause 3.1.3 from any person other than the Assignee, and may decline to accept or to retain it, without the Landlord being in breach of this deed, where the Landlord's solicitors have not completed to their satisfaction the identity checks and source of funds checks required of them by law and by their own procedures in respect of the payer and the origin of the money. Where the sum is not accepted, the condition in clause 3.1.3 is not satisfied.

4. ASSIGNEE'S COVENANTS

4.1 The Assignee covenants with the Landlord that, from the date of the Assignment, it will pay the rents reserved by the Lease and observe and perform the Tenant Covenants, and that it will continue to do so until it is released from them by the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995.

4.2 The Assignee covenants with the Landlord to enter into the Rent Deposit Deed on or before completion of the Assignment.

4.3 The Assignee covenants with the Landlord that, within one month after the Assignment, it will:

4.3.1 give written notice of the Assignment to the Landlord's solicitors, together with a certified copy of the transfer, and pay the registration fee of 100 pounds plus VAT required by clause 3.14.9 of the Lease; and

4.3.2 apply to HM Land Registry to register the Assignment and this deed against title number BL674455, and supply the Landlord with official copies of the register showing the Assignee as registered proprietor as soon as they are available.

5. TENANT'S COVENANTS AND AUTHORISED GUARANTEE AGREEMENT

5.1 The Tenant covenants with the Landlord to complete the Assignment in accordance with this deed.

5.2 This clause 5 is an authorised guarantee agreement within section 16 of the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995.

5.3 The Tenant guarantees to the Landlord that the Assignee will pay the rents reserved by the Lease and observe and perform the Tenant Covenants, and that if the Assignee fails to do so the Tenant will pay or make good the default to the Landlord on demand.

5.4 The Tenant's liability under this clause 5 is that of principal debtor and is not affected by:

5.4.1 any time, indulgence, waiver or concession given by the Landlord to the Assignee;

5.4.2 any variation of the Lease, save that the Tenant is not liable in respect of any increase in liability arising from a variation to which it has not consented;

5.4.3 the Landlord's refusal to accept a tender of rent;

5.4.4 the insolvency of the Assignee or the disclaimer of the Lease.

5.5 If the Lease is disclaimed and the Landlord gives the Tenant written notice within six months after the disclaimer, the Tenant must take a new lease of the Premises for the residue of the term that would have remained, at the same rents and on the same terms as the Lease, the new lease to take effect from the date of the disclaimer, and must execute it and pay the Landlord's costs.

5.6 The Tenant's liability under this clause 5 ends on the date the Assignee is released from the Tenant Covenants by the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995. Nothing in this deed requires the Tenant to guarantee the performance of the Tenant Covenants by any person other than the Assignee, and any provision of this deed which purports to do so is of no effect to that extent.

6. COSTS

6.1 The Tenant must pay the Landlord's reasonable legal and other proper costs and disbursements of and incidental to the Tenant's application for consent and this deed, in the sum of 1,450 pounds plus VAT. That sum is payable on the earlier of completion of the Assignment and the date 14 days after written demand, and is payable whether or not the Assignment is completed and whether or not the Tenant's application is withdrawn.

7. GENERAL

7.1 Nothing in this deed releases the Tenant or any guarantor of the Tenant from any liability under the Lease arising before the Assignment.

7.2 Any guarantee given to the Landlord in respect of the Tenant's obligations under the Lease continues in respect of the Tenant's obligations under this deed, including the AGA, so far as the law allows.

7.3 A person who is not a party to this deed has no right under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 to enforce any of its terms.

7.4 This deed and any dispute arising out of it are governed by the law of England and Wales, and the parties submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of England and Wales.

EXECUTED as a deed by the parties on the date at the beginning of this deed.

EXECUTED as a deed by CHERITON WHARF PROPERTIES LIMITED acting by a director in the presence of a witness

Director .............................

Witness signature .............................

Witness name and address .............................

EXECUTED as a deed by HOLLOW LANE FABRICATION LIMITED acting by a director in the presence of a witness

Director .............................

Witness signature .............................

Witness name and address .............................

EXECUTED as a deed by TARN METALWORKS LIMITED acting by a director in the presence of a witness

Director .............................

Witness signature .............................

Witness name and address .............................

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The rent deposit of 45,000 pounds is to reach the firm from Vestrik Holdings SA, an offshore company with no documented connection to the assignee, whose involvement the assignee refuses to explain, with pressure to move the money on quickly. The assignee is a company incorporated two months ago with no accounts. The firm holds no due diligence on the assignee or on the payer, and the client has said he does not care where the money comes from and that questions will kill the deal. Those are classic money laundering warning signs: an unexplained third party payer, an offshore corporate structure, an urgency to pass funds on, and a refusal to provide information. The candidate must not draft the deposit condition so that the firm is bound to accept the money. The condition should require payment by the assignee and should be drafted so that it is not satisfied unless the money is actually accepted, which allows the firm to complete identity and source of funds checks first. Outside the document the candidate must report the position to the firm's Money Laundering Reporting Officer, must not proceed with the transaction while suspicion is unresolved, and must not tell the client, the assignee or their solicitor that a report has been made. The client's commercial instruction cannot override that.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsDefined terms are set up once and used throughout. The grant of consent is expressed in one short clause with its limits in a separate sub clause list. The guarantee provisions read as obligations, not as narrative.Recitals used to create obligations, definitions listed but never used, or a consent clause whose limits are buried in a long sentence so that the scope of the consent is unclear.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsRuns parties, background, interpretation, licence, conditions, assignee's covenants, tenant's covenants and AGA, costs, general, attestation. Conditions precedent are separated from continuing covenants.Mixing the conditions on which consent is given with the covenants that survive the assignment, or omitting the attestation clauses so the document cannot take effect as a deed.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawConsent is limited to one assignment, is conditional, and lapses after three months. The AGA guarantees the immediate assignee only and ends on the assignee's release, in line with section 16(4). The assignee covenants directly until released by the 1995 Act. Executed as a deed as clause 3.14.4 requires.An AGA that guarantees successive assignees, or that continues after the assignee's release, which section 16(4) prevents. Or open ended consent that would authorise any future dealing and waive the alienation covenant.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers the rent deposit and the rent deposit deed, notice and registration of the assignment, the registration fee, the landlord's costs whether or not the assignment completes, preservation of existing breaches and of any existing guarantee, and third party rights.Omitting registration at HM Land Registry, omitting the costs provision, or failing to preserve pre assignment liability, so the tenant and its guarantor escape accrued breaches.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises that money for the deposit is being pushed through the firm from an unconnected offshore company with no explanation and no documents, and drafts so that the condition is only satisfied if the money is accepted after identity and source of funds checks. Does not draft any provision obliging the firm to receive or pass on the money.Drafting a clause simply requiring payment of 45,000 pounds from Vestrik Holdings SA, or naming the third party payer as the source, which commits the firm to receiving unverified offshore funds under pressure to move them on quickly.

Examiner notes

The technically decisive point is section 16(4). Many candidates draft the authorised guarantee agreement in wide terms so that the outgoing tenant guarantees the assignee and anyone after it. That is void to that extent and it fails legal correctness. A pass needs the guarantee tied to the immediate assignee and expressed to end on that assignee's statutory release, plus the disclaimer and new lease provision that gives the guarantee real value. The trap is the file note. It looks like background about a rent deposit, and the partner's email mentions it in one line at the end. Candidates who skim it draft a flat condition requiring 45,000 pounds to be paid by Vestrik Holdings SA, which is exactly what the assignee's solicitor asked to be confirmed, and in doing so commit the firm to receiving offshore money it knows nothing about. The ethics criterion is decided by whether the drafting leaves the firm free to refuse the money, and by whether the candidate recognises that this is a matter for the Money Laundering Reporting Officer rather than for the client to decide.

Written station 16: Enforcing a roadway maintenance covenant against a successor in title

Legal research  |  Property Practice  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO DOMINIC ELSTREE

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 5 May 2027

Matter: HB/2027/1902, Fanshawe, Plot 3 Harrowgate Barns

Subject: Recovery of 2,920 pounds from the owner of Plot 5 towards roadway resurfacing

1. Summary

1.1 Mr Bewley is right that he is not bound by the positive covenant in the 1998 transfer simply because he now owns Plot 5. The burden of a positive covenant does not run with freehold land.

1.2 He is nonetheless very likely to be liable, on a different basis. The 1998 transfer that imposed the payment obligation is the same transfer that granted the right of way he uses every day. Under the principle of conditional benefit and burden he cannot take the benefit of the right of way without accepting the correlative burden of contributing to the upkeep of the roadway. On these facts each of the conditions for that principle is satisfied.

1.3 I would advise Mrs Fanshawe that the claim to one fifth of the cost, 2,920 pounds, is strong, but that it belongs to whoever actually paid Torvale Surfacing, so she can recover in her own name only what she herself paid out on Mr Bewley's behalf and the four paying owners should claim together. I would advise her that a letter before claim setting out the benefit and burden argument is the right first step, and that a claim in the county court is proportionate if he does not pay. I would also advise her that she cannot compel him to keep the benefit, so if he ever genuinely gave up the right of way the argument would stop working for the future.

1.4 There is a conflict of interest that has to be dealt with before you telephone her. It is at paragraph 6 below.

2. The burden of the positive covenant does not run

2.1 Clause 5.1 of the 1998 transfer is a positive covenant. It requires the owner of Plot 5 to spend money.

2.2 The burden of a positive freehold covenant does not pass to a successor in title, at law or in equity: Rhone v Stephens [1994] 2 AC 310. Lord Templeman held that equity cannot compel an owner to comply with a positive covenant entered into by his predecessor without flatly contradicting the common law rule that a person cannot be made liable on a contract to which he was not a party.

2.3 Section 79 of the Law of Property Act 1925 does not help. It was held in Rhone v Stephens to be a word saving provision concerned with the identity of the covenantor, and it does not make the burden of a positive covenant enforceable against a successor.

2.4 The entry in the charges register of title SL220419 does not change this. Under section 32(3) of the Land Registration Act 2002 the fact that an interest is the subject of a notice does not mean the interest is valid; the entry protects priority only. A noted covenant that is unenforceable in substance remains unenforceable.

2.5 So a claim brought simply on the covenant against Mr Bewley as owner of Plot 5 would fail.

3. Conditional benefit and burden

3.1 The route to recovery is the principle in Halsall v Brizell [1957] Ch 169. Upjohn J held that a person cannot take a benefit under a deed without subscribing to the obligations under it, and that successors who used the estate roads and sewers were bound to contribute to the cost of their upkeep. That is very close to our facts.

3.2 Rhone v Stephens confirmed the principle but limited it. The burden must be relevant to the exercise of the right. On the facts of Rhone the obligation to repair a roof was an independent provision, unconnected to the right of support, so the principle did not apply.

3.3 The conditions were restated by Sir Andrew Morritt C, the Chancellor of the High Court, in Davies v Jones [2009] EWCA Civ 1164 at [27]. Taking them in the order convenient here:

(a) the receipt or enjoyment of the benefit must be relevant to the imposition of the burden, in the sense that the former must be conditional on or reciprocal to the latter;

(b) the benefit and the burden must be conferred in or by the same transaction;

(c) the person on whom the burden is imposed must have, or have had, the opportunity of rejecting or disclaiming the benefit, not merely the right to receive it.

3.4 Applying those conditions:

(a) Relevance. The covenant in clause 5.1 is to pay one fifth of the cost of maintaining, repairing and resurfacing the very roadway over which clause 4 grants the right of way. The burden could not be more closely connected to the benefit. This is not the independent obligation that failed in Rhone v Stephens. Note also that clause 5.2, the fencing covenant, and clause 5.3, the user covenant, are not connected to the right of way in the same way, so this argument reaches the roadway contribution only.

(b) Same transaction. Both the grant and the covenant are in the transfer of 22 September 1998.

(c) Opportunity to renounce. Mr Bewley enjoys the right of way as an easement appurtenant to Plot 5. He can release or abandon it. He has not done so and he uses the roadway several times a day, including for deliveries of building materials. The fact that he has no wish in practice to give it up, there being no other vehicular access to Plot 5, is not fatal: in Wilkinson v Kerdene Ltd [2013] EWCA Civ 44 chalet owners with express rights over estate roads were held liable to contribute although none of them had ceased to use the roads or wished to do so. What matters is that the right is one he is free to release, which it is.

3.5 On that basis Mr Bewley is liable to pay one fifth of the reasonable cost of the resurfacing so long as he continues to take the benefit of the right of way.

4. Who can sue, and for how much

4.1 Mrs Fanshawe has the benefit of the covenant in her own right. Clause 5 of the 1998 transfer states that the covenant is given to the transferor and, as separate covenants, to the owner or owners for the time being of Plots 1 to 4. She is the owner of Plot 3 and can therefore sue in her own name. Section 78 of the Law of Property Act 1925 would in any event annex the benefit to her land, but we do not need to rely on it because the covenant is expressly made with the owners for the time being.

4.2 The transferor, Harrowgate Farms Limited, was dissolved in 2004, so nothing can be done through it.

4.3 The sum claimed is one fifth of 14,600 pounds, which is 2,920 pounds. Clause 5.1 makes the sum payable on demand to the person or persons incurring the cost, so the four owners who paid the contractor are the proper claimants. If Mrs Fanshawe paid only her own fifth, she is entitled to claim only what she has actually paid out on his behalf, and the four owners should really claim together. I would check who actually paid Torvale Surfacing before any letter goes out.

4.4 The cost must be reasonable. Three quotations were obtained and the lowest was accepted, the road was potholed, and Mr Bewley was sent the quotations and did not object. That is good evidence of reasonableness.

5. Other routes, and why they are weaker

5.1 Chain of indemnity. The original covenantor, Mr Trent, remains liable in contract for the whole of the covenant, and the 2023 transfer to Mr Bewley contained an indemnity covenant in Mr Trent's favour. In principle the claimants could sue Mr Trent, who would then claim on the indemnity. In practice Mr Trent is in New Zealand and we have no address, so this route is not worth pursuing. It is also not directly available to Mrs Fanshawe against Mr Bewley, because she is not a party to the 2023 indemnity.

5.2 Restrictive covenant doctrine. The rule in Tulk v Moxhay is not in point. It applies only to covenants restrictive of the use of land. Clause 5.1 is positive and requires payment, so equity will not enforce it against a successor. Clause 5.3, the covenant not to use Plot 5 otherwise than as a single private dwellinghouse, would run under that doctrine, but it is not what we are trying to enforce.

5.3 Land charges. Registration under the Land Charges Act 1972 is irrelevant here. All five titles are registered with title absolute, so the Land Charges Act regime does not apply, and in any event it concerns restrictive covenants only.

5.4 Leasehold covenants. The Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 has no application. These are freehold plots, not a tenancy.

5.5 Welsh law. The Renting Homes (Wales) Act 2016 has no application. Harrowgate Barns is in Shropshire, so the law of England applies, and in any event that Act deals with residential occupation contracts, not freehold covenants.

5.6 Land Registry guidance. The extract from Practice Guide 19 in the bundle is from an edition withdrawn on 16 March 2026 and should not be relied on. It also says nothing about enforceability, only about how entries are made and removed.

6. Conflict of interest

6.1 The matter search run on 4 May 2027 shows that our Shrewsbury office is currently acting for Mr Garrick Alan Bewley on the remortgage of Plot 5, matter HB/2026/4417, with activity as recent as 28 April 2027. He is therefore a current client of the firm.

6.2 Advising Mrs Fanshawe on a claim against Mr Bewley, and writing a letter before claim to him, would put us in conflict between two current clients.
