There is no substantially common interest, and this is not a situation of competing for the same objective, so neither exception applies and informed consent cannot cure it.

6.3 There is also a confidentiality risk. We hold confidential information about Mr Bewley from the remortgage file, including information about his lender and his financial position, which is material to the enforcement decision. We cannot use it for Mrs Fanshawe and we cannot disclose it to her.

6.4 Before you telephone Mrs Fanshawe I suggest you speak to Danielle Okri and to our compliance officer for legal practice. Realistically the firm cannot act for Mrs Fanshawe on a claim against Mr Bewley. She should be told promptly, told the reason so far as we can without breaching Mr Bewley's confidentiality, and referred to another firm without delay so she loses no time. We should not charge her for work done on the claim itself after today, and the 900 pounds estimate should be revisited.

7. What to tell the client, assuming the conflict is resolved

7.1 The short answer to her question is yes, he can be made to pay, but not on the ground she expects. He is not caught by the covenant as such. He is caught because he uses the road that the same deed gave him the right to use.

7.2 Practical next steps for whoever acts:

(a) confirm who actually paid the contractor and get the invoice, the three quotations and proof of payment;

(b) send a letter before claim to Mr Bewley setting out the Halsall v Brizell argument, enclosing the 1998 transfer, and giving him a reasonable period to pay;

(c) if he does not pay, issue in the county court. A claim of 2,920 pounds falls in the small claims track, so recoverable costs will be very limited even if she wins. She should be told this plainly before she spends money on the claim, because the costs of a fully argued benefit and burden point could easily exceed the sum in issue.

7.3 For the future, the covenant will keep causing this argument at every resurfacing, and each new owner will run it again. Her options are:

(a) a deed of covenant from each owner, and a requirement that each future buyer enters into a direct deed of covenant with the other owners before any sale, which would need everyone's agreement now;

(b) a formal maintenance arrangement between the five owners recording how costs are apportioned, quotations obtained and payment demanded;

(c) leaving matters as they are and relying on benefit and burden each time, which works but repeats the argument.

Option (a) is the cleanest and she should raise it with the other owners while four of the five are cooperating.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The matter opening printout shows that the firm's Shrewsbury office is acting for Mr Bewley, the intended defendant, on a live remortgage of the very plot in dispute, with activity eight days ago. Advising Mrs Fanshawe on a claim against him would put the firm in conflict between two current clients. Neither the substantially common interest exception nor the competing for the same objective exception applies, so consent cannot cure it. There is also a distinct confidentiality problem, because the firm holds confidential information about Mr Bewley's finances and his lender which is material to Mrs Fanshawe's decision whether to sue, and which cannot be used for her or disclosed to her. The competent response is to raise it with the fee earner on the other file and with the firm's compliance officer, to accept that the firm cannot act against Mr Bewley, to tell Mrs Fanshawe promptly and refer her elsewhere without delay so that she is not prejudiced, and to revisit the costs estimate. The printout is presented as a routine file opening document and the partner's email does not mention it.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsCRITERION: Identify and use relevant sources and information. GRADE_A: Uses Rhone v Stephens, Halsall v Brizell, Davies v Jones, section 79 of the Law of Property Act 1925 and section 32 of the Land Registration Act 2002, and states in terms why Tulk v Moxhay, the Land Charges Act 1972, the 1995 Act, the Welsh Act and the superseded practice guide extract are not in point. Cites cases and sections accurately. COMMON_FAIL: Building the answer on Tulk v Moxhay or on the Land Charges Act, or relying on the superseded practice guide extract, or citing nothing and asserting the law. Simply ignoring the decoys without explaining that they were considered and rejected also loses marks, because the partner needs to know they were dealt with.Building the answer on Tulk v Moxhay or on the Land Charges Act, or relying on the withdrawn practice guide, or citing nothing and asserting the law. Simply ignoring the decoys without explaining that they were considered and rejected also loses marks, because the partner needs to know they were dealt with.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the question the client actually asked, gives the amount, the proper claimant, the next steps and a frank warning that a small claim of 2,920 pounds recovers almost no costs. Adds the practical fix for future resurfacing.A correct academic analysis of the running of covenants with no advice on whether to sue, who sues, or whether it is worth it.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA short note with numbered paragraphs, a summary at the top, and one point per paragraph. Plain professional English suitable for a partner about to telephone a client.A discursive essay, or a research trail describing which sources were searched and in what order, which the partner expressly did not want.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly separates the covenant analysis from the conditional benefit and burden analysis, and applies each of the three Davies v Jones conditions to these facts rather than reciting them. Correctly identifies that section 32(3) means the register entry proves nothing about enforceability.Concluding that the covenant binds Mr Bewley because it is noted in the charges register, or because section 79 makes it run. Both are wrong and both are the answers the bundle invites.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with the standing of the client to sue, the correct claimant, the chain of indemnity and why it fails in practice, reasonableness of the cost, the limit of the argument to the roadway covenant only, and the risk that abandonment of the easement would end liability for the future.Stopping at the conclusion that he is liable, without addressing who may sue, how much, or the fact that the fencing and user covenants are not caught by the same argument.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots that the firm's other office acts for Mr Bewley on a live matter, identifies it as a conflict between two current clients with no applicable exception, identifies the separate confidentiality problem, and proposes a concrete resolution including prompt referral elsewhere and revisiting the costs estimate.Missing the conflict entirely, or noting it and then advising the partner to press on with a letter before claim, or suggesting the client's consent can cure a conflict of this kind.

Examiner notes

The bundle is designed to push candidates towards the wrong answer twice. First, the covenant is noted in the charges register and the withdrawn practice guide explains how such notes are made, which tempts candidates into concluding that a noted covenant must therefore bind. Section 32(3) of the Land Registration Act 2002 disposes of that. Second, Tulk v Moxhay is the case most candidates remember, and it is about the wrong class of covenant. The Land Charges Act extract is about unregistered land and about restrictive covenants, so it is wrong twice over. The Welsh Act and the 1995 Act are there to see whether candidates check jurisdiction and tenure before reading a provision. A pass requires Rhone v Stephens for the negative proposition and Halsall v Brizell with the Davies v Jones conditions for the positive one, applied to these facts. A grade A answer also tells the partner, in one line each, why the four unused sources were rejected. The commonest fail is a candidate who reaches the right legal conclusion, writes it up well, and never opens the client care printout, so the conflict is missed and the note recommends writing a letter before claim to another of the firm's own clients.

Written station 17: Prescriptive right of way and an unregistered easement on a purchase

Legal research  |  Property Practice  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO PARTNER

To: Callum Beavan

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 3 February 2027

Matter: Oyelaran, purchase of The Old Granary, Pentre Lane, Ashcombe

1. Summary

1.1 The claim to a prescriptive right of way over the stone track is not safe. Two documents on the file damage it: the 2011 wayleave letter and receipt, and the sign at the foot of the track. Either could defeat it, and together they mean I would not report the title as good on the strength of the statutory declaration.

1.2 The farm's right over the rear yard is the opposite. If it has arisen at all, it is a legal easement and it will bind Mr Oyelaran as an overriding interest.

1.3 There is a conduct problem. The statutory declaration at document 10 states things which the 2011 letter at document 11 contradicts, and the reply to enquiry 19 is inconsistent with what our own client saw on site. We cannot put that declaration forward to an insurer or to the lender as it stands. This is at paragraph 5.

2. The track. Has a right of way been acquired by prescription?

2.1 A prescriptive easement requires user as of right, that is nec vi, nec clam, nec precario, by and against freehold owners, for the relevant period. The test is objective and asks how the user would have appeared to a reasonable owner of the servient land: R v Oxfordshire County Council, ex parte Sunningwell Parish Council [2000] 1 AC 335. Prescription rests on the servient owner's acquiescence in open user: Dalton v Angus and Co (1881) 6 App Cas 740.

2.2 Three routes are available. Common law prescription fails at once, because use plainly began in 1997 and not before 1189. That leaves lost modern grant, which requires twenty years' user as of right at any time, and section 2 of the Prescription Act 1832, which requires twenty years' user without interruption. By section 4 of the 1832 Act that period must be the twenty years next before the action in which the right is questioned, which is a real limitation on the statutory route here.

2.3 The 2011 wayleave. Document 11 is a letter from the farm's agent offering to permit the use to continue on payment of an annual wayleave of 75 pounds, together with a receipted invoice for that sum paid on 2 April 2011. Where user is accompanied by payment to the servient owner the natural inference is that the user was enjoyed by leave and is therefore precario: Gardner v Hodgson's Kingston Brewery Co Ltd [1903] AC 229. Mere toleration would not have that effect, because toleration is not permission: Mills v Silver [1991] Ch 271. But this was not toleration. Permission was offered in writing, a price was set and the price was paid.

2.4 The sellers say the payment was a one off contribution to resurfacing. That is arguable, because only one invoice was ever raised and nothing was paid after 2012, so it can be said that any permission was spent and that user reverted to being as of right thereafter. It is not a bad argument but it is not one I would want to be running at a client's expense after he has bought the house.

2.5 Whichever view is taken of the 2011 payment, the arithmetic is against us. If the payment broke the period, user as of right ran from September 1997 to March 2011, which is thirteen and a half years, well short of the twenty needed for lost modern grant. Time would then start again no earlier than the expiry of the wayleave year on 25 March 2012.

2.6 The sign. Our client saw a weathered board at the foot of the track reading 'PRIVATE DRIVE. NETHERFOLD FARM. ACCESS BY PERMISSION ONLY.' A clear and visible sign asserting that the land is private is enough to make continued user contentious, and the servient owner need do nothing more: Winterburn v Bennett [2016] EWCA Civ 482. From the date the board went up the user is vi and no longer as of right. We do not know when it was erected. That matters to the earlier period, because a board already in place would have made the user contentious from the day it went up; it cannot rescue the later period, which even on the most favourable view has run only since March 2012 and so stands at under fifteen years today. This must be established before exchange.

2.7 Conclusion on the track. There may be a prescriptive right but it is contestable on two independent grounds. The title is not one I would certify to the lender as carrying a legal right of way.

2.8 Sources I have discounted. Section 62 of the Law of Property Act 1925 and the rule in Wheeldon v Burrows (1879) 12 Ch D 31 both operate only on a conveyance by a person who owned both parcels, and their further requirements differ: Wheeldon presupposes prior unity of ownership and occupation, whereas section 62 requires prior diversity of occupation unless the use was continuous and apparent. Neither can apply here, because The Old Granary and the stone track have never been in common ownership. Schedule 6 to the Land Registration Act 2002 concerns registration of an adverse possessor of an estate in land. We are not claiming the track, only a right over it, so it does not apply. The Party Wall etc. Act 1996 is not in point at all.

3. The farm's right over the rear yard

3.1 The reply to enquiry 7 admits use by tractor and trailer twice a year to reach the top field, unobjected to and undocumented. On the same principles as above that use looks to be as of right, and if it has run for twenty years an easement will have arisen by lost modern grant. An easement acquired by prescription takes effect as a legal easement, because it is presumed to have been granted for an interest equivalent to a fee simple absolute in possession.

3.2 Priority is governed by section 29 of the Land Registration Act 2002. Mr Oyelaran's purchase is a registrable disposition for valuable consideration, so on registration it postpones any interest whose priority is not protected. Nothing appears on the register. So the question is whether the easement falls within paragraph 3 of Schedule 3.

3.3 It does. Paragraph 3 excepts a legal easement from overriding status only where it is both outside the buyer's actual knowledge and not obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, and even then the exception does not apply if the person entitled proves exercise within the year ending with the disposition. Here all three limbs point the same way. Mr Oyelaran has actual knowledge, because the reply to enquiry 7 tells him and he saw the ruts and the gate himself. The right is obvious on inspection, for the same reason. And on the sellers' own account the farm used the yard in June and September 2026, which is within the year ending with completion.

3.4 Conclusion. The farm's right will bind Mr Oyelaran. He cannot obstruct the yard, and this affects where the pottery deliveries and any parking can go. He should be told before exchange.

4. What I recommend

4.1 Raise a requisition asking the sellers to obtain an express deed of grant of a right of way over the track from Mr Netherfold, at the sellers' cost, before exchange. That is the only outcome which gives Mr Oyelaran and Carrowdale a good title, and it is the sellers' problem to solve, not ours.

4.2 If the sellers will not or cannot do that, the alternative is a lack of access indemnity policy. Two warnings. Approaching Mr Netherfold for a grant will normally prejudice or exclude cover, so we must choose one route and not both, and take the insurer's position before anybody writes to the farm. And the policy must be applied for on a full presentation, which means telling the insurer about the 2011 wayleave letter and receipt and about the sign. A policy obtained on an incomplete presentation can be avoided, which would leave our client with nothing at the only moment he needs it.

4.3 Establish when the board at the foot of the track was erected. A dated photograph, the selling agent's old particulars or historic street imagery may settle it.

4.4 Report both matters to Carrowdale Building Society. An absent legal right of vehicular access and any proposal to rely on a policy instead of good title are material and require the lender's consent.

4.5 Advise Mr Oyelaran in writing of the farm's right over the yard and of its effect on the pottery.

4.6 Do not exchange on 26 February unless 4.1 or 4.2 is resolved and the lender has consented.

5. Conduct

5.1 The statutory declaration at document 10 says at paragraph 3 that use was at no time with permission and that no payment was ever made, and at paragraph 4 that no sign was ever erected. The 2011 letter and receipt in the sellers' own bundle contradict the first. Our client's own site visit contradicts the second, as does the reply to enquiry 19.

5.2 We now know that. If we submit the declaration to an insurer, or rely on it in a certificate of title to Carrowdale, without disclosing the 2011 letter and the sign, we mislead them by omission. Paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors prohibits misleading others, whether by our own acts or omissions or by being complicit in the acts or omissions of others, including our client, and Principle 5 requires us to act with integrity. The duty is not softened by the fact that the declaration was made by the seller rather than by us.

5.3 Mr Oyelaran's comment that he will sign whatever is needed to get the purchase through must be handled carefully rather than taken up. We should advise him in writing that any insurance proposal or lender certificate must be complete and accurate, that a policy taken out on anything less is worthless, and that if he instructs us to proceed on an incomplete presentation or to withhold the position from Carrowdale we cannot act on those instructions and would have to cease to act for him and for the lender.

5.4 We should also ask the sellers' solicitors to take their client's instructions on the inconsistency between document 10 and document 11 and on the reply to enquiry 19. We do not accuse anybody. We put the documents side by side and ask for the position to be corrected.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The seller's statutory declaration swears that use of the track was never permissive, that no payment was ever made and that no sign was ever erected. Document 11 in the seller's own bundle is a written offer of permission with a receipted wayleave payment, and the client has seen a sign on site, which also makes the reply to enquiry 19 wrong. Once the solicitor knows this, relying on the declaration to obtain a lack of access indemnity policy, or reporting the title to Carrowdale without disclosing it, would mislead the insurer and the lender by omission, contrary to paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and Principle 5. The client's remark that he will sign whatever is needed is the invitation to do it. The candidate must advise that any proposal or certificate must be a full presentation, must report the position to the lender, must ask the sellers' solicitors to correct the declaration and reply, and must tell the client that if he instructs otherwise the firm will have to cease to act for him and for the lender.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsWorks from Sources A to E and, crucially, reads documents 3 and 4 against each other and against the attendance note. Uses Gardner and Winterburn for the two attacks on the prescriptive claim and Schedule 3 paragraph 3 for the yard. Rejects Source F on the ground stated in the source itself, that common ownership is required, and rejects Sources G and H with a one line reason each.Analyses the prescription question from the statutory declaration alone and never opens document 11, so the whole answer is built on a factual premise the file contradicts. Or treats Schedule 6 adverse possession as the answer to a question about a right of way.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsGives the partner a decision, not a discussion: do not exchange on 26 February unless an express grant is obtained or a properly disclosed policy is in place with the lender's consent. Deals with the practical consequences the client cares about, including access for the pottery and the effect of the farm's right on the rear yard.Concludes that the position is 'arguable' or 'a matter for the court' and stops, leaving the partner with nothing to tell a buyer who is due to exchange in three weeks.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured note, two questions answered separately and in the order the partner asked them, with a summary at the top and numbered recommendations. Full citations, no long quotations, no research trail.Runs the two access questions together so it is unclear which land is dominant and which is servient, which is fatal to the reader's understanding of the second question.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the nec vi nec clam nec precario test correctly and objectively, distinguishes toleration from permission on Mills v Silver, applies Gardner to the wayleave payment and Winterburn to the sign. On the yard, gets the direction of Schedule 3 paragraph 3 right, recognising that it is an exception which the buyer must bring himself within, and that exercise within the previous year defeats the exception.Reads Schedule 3 paragraph 3 backwards and concludes that the farm's right does not bind because it is not on the register. Or asserts that the 1832 Act gives an absolute right after twenty years, ignoring the words 'next before some suit or action' in section 4 and the forty year rule.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all three routes to prescription and explains why common law fails on these dates. Works out the consequences of the 2011 payment for the length of the qualifying period, gives the seller's contrary argument that the payment was a one off, and says why it is still not safe. Deals with the effect of the prescriptive easement being legal rather than equitable, which is what makes Schedule 3 available at all.Identifies lost modern grant but never counts the years, so the effect of the 2011 payment on the qualifying period is never worked out. Or ignores the sign entirely because it appears only in the attendance note and not in the sources.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots the contradiction between the statutory declaration and the 2011 letter and reply 19 without being prompted, identifies the duty not to mislead the insurer and the lender by omission, deals with the client's offer to sign anything, and states the consequence if the client insists. Also proposes the proportionate step of asking the sellers' solicitors to correct the position rather than making an accusation.Notes the inconsistency as a factual weakness in the prescription claim but never treats it as a conduct problem, so recommends an indemnity policy without addressing disclosure to the insurer, which is the step that would make the policy worthless.

Examiner notes

The whole station turns on whether the candidate reads document 11. It is placed after the statutory declaration and is labelled as included 'for completeness' with a soothing note from the seller's solicitor, which is exactly how such a document arrives in practice. A candidate who accepts the declaration at face value produces a confident and entirely wrong answer, and also misses the ethics criterion, so the same omission costs marks twice.

The second discriminator is direction of travel on Schedule 3 paragraph 3. Weak candidates read it as a list of conditions the easement must satisfy to override and conclude that an unregistered right cannot bind. It is drafted as an exception, and it is defeated by exercise within the preceding year. The facts give actual knowledge, visible ruts and a gate, and use in June and September 2026, so all three limbs point the same way and there is no excuse for getting it wrong.

Good candidates count the years. Use from 1997 broken by permission in 2011 gives fourteen, not twenty. Candidates who never do the arithmetic tend to conclude the right is established because the use has gone on 'for nearly thirty years'.

Source F is the trap for the well drilled candidate, who sees an access problem and reaches for section 62 and Wheeldon v Burrows. The source itself states the requirement of prior common ownership, and there has never been any here. Schedule 6 punishes the candidate who confuses prescription with adverse possession. The Party Wall etc. Act 1996 is a pure decoy.

The indemnity policy point is where competent and strong candidates separate. Recommending a policy is sound. Recommending a policy without dealing with disclosure of the 2011 letter and the sign, and without warning that an approach to the neighbour will prejudice cover, is advice that would fail the client at the moment he relied on it.

Written station 18: Writing to the seller's solicitor after adverse search results

Legal writing  |  Property Practice  |  30 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

HALSTEAD VANE LLP

Solicitors

SUBJECT TO CONTRACT

By email

Marchmont Vale LLP

For the attention of Mr H Salchow-Dean

Your ref: HSD/HALLOWAY/2211

Our ref: NF/KADRI/0913

9 March 2027

Dear Sirs

Miss G Halloway-Frett to Mr and Mrs K Kadri

7 Thorn Lea, Hebbleworth, Lancashire

We have now received and reported to our clients on the local authority search dated 3 March 2027 and the drainage and water search dated 2 March 2027. Three matters arise. We set them out below with our proposals, and we should be grateful for your client's instructions by 4pm on Friday 19 March 2027.

1. Thorn Lea is not adopted

The reply to CON29 question 2.1 confirms that the roads and footpaths abutting the property are not maintainable at public expense. The Council holds no agreement under section 38 of the Highways Act 1980 and no road bond. Your client's reply to enquiry 4.1 confirms that there is no formal maintenance arrangement and that the six owners contribute informally.

The consequence for our clients is twofold. They will be liable to contribute to the cost of maintaining Thorn Lea for as long as they own the property, with no agreed mechanism and no cap. Separately, their lender requires either access to an adopted highway or evidence of adequate maintenance arrangements for the private access before completion.

Please let us have:

(a) copies of any deed, rentcharge, licence or maintenance agreement relating to Thorn Lea, including any right of way granted to the property and any covenant to contribute;

(b) confirmation of who owns the surface of the lane;

(c) the invoices for the resurfacing referred to in reply 4.1 and for any works in the last six years;

(d) confirmation of whether any of the six owners has ever refused to contribute.

If there is no documented right of way and no documented maintenance obligation, we will need to consider an appropriate indemnity policy at your client's expense, and we will need to report the position to Pennine Crest Bank.

2. The 2019 rear extension has no building regulation completion certificate

Planning permission HB/2019/0884 was granted on 14 May 2019. The Council holds no completion certificate, no final certificate from an approved inspector and no initial notice. Your client's reply to enquiry 7.2 confirms that she does not have one.

Our clients are buying a two storey extension which has never been certified as complying with the Building Regulations. That is a matter for their lender and for any future buyer, and it is a matter for them personally, because nobody has confirmed that the structure is sound.

We invite your client to choose one of the following, and we should be grateful if she would tell us which before anybody contacts the Council, because an approach to the Council will prevent an indemnity policy from being available:

(a) apply for a regularisation certificate at her own cost and provide it before exchange; or

(b) provide, at her own cost, a building regulations indemnity policy in a form approved by us, extending to our clients, their successors in title and their lender, together with a copy of the proposal so that we can confirm the presentation is complete.

Option (b) is quicker but it does not tell our clients that the extension is sound. That is why the price is raised below.

3. A public sewer runs beneath the extension

The Northmoor Water plc public sewer map shows a 150mm public foul sewer running under the rear elevation on a line passing beneath the 2019 extension. Northmoor Water plc has no record of a build over agreement or of any consent. Your client's reply to enquiry 7.5 that she is not aware of any works over or near a public sewer will need to be revisited in the light of the search.

The undertaker retains the right to enter to repair or replace the sewer, and our clients could be exposed to the cost of removing or altering part of the extension. Again there are two routes and they cannot both be taken:

(a) your client applies to Northmoor Water plc for a retrospective build over agreement at her own cost; or

(b) your client provides, at her own cost, a build over indemnity policy on the same terms as at 2(b) above.

Please note that if your client applies to the water undertaker or to the Council on either matter, no policy will be available on that matter afterwards. We ask that no approach is made until the route is agreed between us.

4. The price

Our clients remain willing to proceed and they like the house. They are not willing to proceed at 425,000 pounds on the present information. Taken together, the three matters mean that they are buying a property with no adopted access and no agreed maintenance regime, an uncertified two storey extension, and a public sewer running under that extension. Each of those will have to be disclosed by our clients when they in turn come to sell.

Our clients instruct us to invite your client to reduce the price to 410,000 pounds. In the alternative, they would be content to proceed at 425,000 pounds if your client provides, before exchange and at her own cost, a regularisation certificate for the extension, a build over agreement from Northmoor Water plc, and the documentation at paragraph 1 above.

We should say plainly that our clients are troubled by all three matters and that they are not prepared to exchange until they are resolved one way or the other. Their mortgage offer expires on 30 June 2027, and we would prefer to reach agreement in the next fortnight rather than lose it.

We look forward to hearing from you by 4pm on Friday 19 March 2027.

Yours faithfully

Halstead Vane LLP

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client has instructed the firm to tell the seller's solicitors that the buyers will withdraw on Friday unless the price is reduced by 15,000 pounds, while telling the firm in the same breath that they will buy the house anyway. Passing that on would be a statement of fact the solicitor knows to be untrue, in breach of paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits misleading others by the solicitor's own acts or omissions or by being complicit in the acts or omissions of the client, and in breach of Principle 5. The candidate must not include the threat. The instruction is not a licence to write a weak letter either: the solicitor may properly say that the buyers are unwilling to exchange until the matters are resolved, may press the reduction hard, and may rely on the genuine deadline created by the mortgage offer. The candidate should also record that the client must be told why the threat was not used.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsAll three search results are stated accurately with their sources and dates, matched against the seller's own replies to enquiries 4.1, 7.2 and 7.5, and the consequence of each is spelled out. The lender's requirement at clause 5.4.3 and the expiry of the mortgage offer are used, because both give the letter its urgency. The documents requested at paragraph 1 are specific.Recites the search results without saying what they mean for the buyers, so the seller's solicitor has nothing to take instructions on. Or misses the sewer altogether, because it is in the second search rather than the local authority search.
Use a logical structure.SkillsOne numbered section per issue, each following the same pattern of finding, consequence, proposal, followed by a separate section on price and a clear deadline. Marked SUBJECT TO CONTRACT. Headed with the parties, the property and both references.Runs the three issues into continuous prose so that the proposals are hard to extract, or omits SUBJECT TO CONTRACT on a letter that discusses the price of an unexchanged sale.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsServes the clients' actual objective, which is to buy this house at a lower price and not to lose it. Offers the seller a genuine choice on each issue and an alternative to the reduction, which gives her a way to say yes. Firm about the buyers' position without threatening anything the buyers will not do.Writes a hostile letter that demands 15,000 pounds and threatens withdrawal, which is both untrue and contrary to the clients' real objective of keeping the house and the school place.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsSolicitor to solicitor register. Precise about what is asked for and by when. No hectoring, no sarcasm, no unnecessary explanation of law the recipient knows. The one place law is spelled out is the warning that an approach to the Council or the undertaker destroys the policy option, which the recipient needs before her client picks up the telephone.Writes to the other side's solicitor in the register of a letter to a lay client, explaining what a search is, or alternatively adopts a combative tone that invites the seller to dig in.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawGets the legal effect of each finding right: an unadopted road means no public maintenance liability and a private contribution obligation, an absent completion certificate leaves the risk of local authority action and a defect on any future sale, and building over a public sewer without consent exposes the owner to the undertaker's rights of entry and to the cost of alteration. Uses the given stamp duty figures correctly as background and does not attempt to calculate any tax.Says the extension is unlawful or must be demolished because there is no completion certificate, which confuses building regulations with planning, and the search confirms planning permission was granted and no enforcement notice is registered.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAddresses all three matters plus the lender, offers both the remedial route and the insurance route on each, states that they are alternatives and not cumulative, and specifies the terms a policy must have, namely cover for the buyers, their successors and the lender, and a full presentation.Proposes both a regularisation application and an indemnity policy on the same matter, which the practice note in the materials says destroys the policy. Or forgets the lender entirely.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDeclines to state that the buyers will withdraw on Friday, because the attendance note records that they will not. Instead puts the clients' position truthfully and still forcefully: they are troubled, they will not exchange until the matters are resolved, and there is a real deadline in the mortgage offer. A note or covering line to the partner flagging that the client's instruction cannot be followed and must be taken up with her is a mark of a strong answer.Writes 'our clients instruct us that they will withdraw on Friday unless the price is reduced by 15,000 pounds', which is a statement of fact the solicitor knows to be untrue and breaches paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and Principle 5. Softening it to 'our clients may withdraw' without any basis is the same error in a quieter voice.

Examiner notes

This is a negotiation station dressed as a search results letter. The buyers want the house, so the candidate is negotiating from a weaker position than the client thinks, and the letter has to be firm without lying.

The ethics point is placed where a hurried candidate will read past it. Mrs Kadri's instruction sits at the end of a long attendance note about school places and mortgage offers, and it is phrased as the sort of thing clients really do say. Candidates who simply obey it write an otherwise competent letter and fail the conduct criterion. Candidates who notice it sometimes overcorrect and produce a letter with no pressure in it at all, which fails the client focus criterion instead. The pass lies in finding the truthful pressure that is genuinely available: three unresolved defects, an unwillingness to exchange until they are dealt with, and a mortgage offer with a real expiry date.

On substance, the discriminator is the alternatives point in the practice note. A candidate who asks the seller both to apply for regularisation and to provide an indemnity policy has proposed something that cannot work, and worse, may prompt the seller to telephone the Council and destroy the cheaper option. Warning the other side not to approach the Council or the water undertaker until the route is agreed is the single most practically valuable sentence in the letter.

The stamp duty figures are supplied deliberately and no candidate should be calculating anything. Marks are not available for tax arithmetic here, and a candidate who invents a rate has misread the materials.

Marking SUBJECT TO CONTRACT is a small point that reliably separates candidates who have done residential conveyancing from those who have only read about it.

Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)

Written station 19: Cohabitant's claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 and settlement strategy

Case and matter analysis  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  60 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

REPORT TO DUNCAN WHITLOW, PARTNER

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 2 September 2027

Matter: Estate of Raymond Frayling, deceased. Claim by Paulette Naismith

Subject: Merits, time, and settlement strategy

1. Summary

Miss Naismith is plainly an eligible applicant. She has a real claim which is likely to succeed on liability, and the only serious question is quantum. Her opening figure of £185,000 is high. My assessment is that a court would be likely to award between £90,000 and £150,000, or the equivalent secured by a life interest in a modest property, and that a negotiated settlement in the region of £110,000 to £130,000 would be a good outcome for Dean.

The urgent point is time. The grant issued on 12 May 2027. The six month period under section 4 expires on 12 November 2027, which is ten weeks away. We must deal with that this month.

Dean has given us two instructions we cannot carry out, and there is a further problem with his position as executor. Those are dealt with at section 7 and they need your attention before you reply to him.

2. Eligibility

Section 1(1)(ba) with section 1(1A) admits a person who, throughout the whole of the two years ending immediately before the death, was living in the same household as the deceased and as his wife. Miss Naismith moved in in June 2022 and was there when he died in January 2027, so about four years and seven months, comfortably more than the two year minimum, and the period ran right up to the death. Dean accepts they lived as a couple and were treated as such. That the deceased never called her his wife does not matter. The test looks at the reality of the household, not the label.

She is therefore eligible under section 1(1)(ba). She is also very likely eligible under section 1(1)(e), because he housed her, met every outgoing and paid her around £600 a month, which is a substantial contribution in money or money's worth towards her reasonable needs and is not commercial. Eligibility is not worth fighting.

3. The standard, and the section 3 factors

Because she is not a spouse or civil partner, section 1(2)(b) applies. The question is what provision it would be reasonable in all the circumstances for her to receive for her maintenance. That is a lower standard than the spouse standard. Maintenance is not limited to subsistence but it does not extend to everything she might reasonably want, and it is directed at her income and housing needs rather than at giving her a share of the estate. She is not entitled to a share simply because they lived together.

The court applies a two stage approach. First, was reasonable financial provision made? Second, if not, what provision should be made? Both are judged objectively at the date of the hearing, not at the date of death.

Applying section 3 and section 3(2A):

(a) Her resources and needs. Age 58. Earnings of £11,500 gross from 20 hours a week. Savings of £3,100. No occupational pension and several years before the state pension. Rent of £725 a month, which on those earnings she cannot sustain. This is a strong housing need and a real income shortfall. It is the heart of her claim.

(c) The beneficiaries' resources and needs. Dean is 44, employed as a quantity surveyor with household income of around £96,000, a home of his own, and he has already received £60,000 from the pension death benefit. He has no need of this estate. Craig is 41, earns about £34,000, rents, and is divorced, so his position is weaker than Dean's, and that helps us to a degree. Neither brother is in need in the way Miss Naismith is.

(d) The deceased's obligations. He took her out of a secure tenancy, housed her for four and a half years and supported her financially. That is a real obligation and the court will treat it as one, whatever the will says.

(e) Size of the estate. Net £446,600 on the schedule, with the house under offer at £388,000, so a little below the probate value. The estate is comfortably large enough to meet a maintenance award without hardship to the beneficiaries. That cuts against us.

(g) Conduct and other matters. The pension death benefit of £120,000 is not part of the net estate, because the scheme trustees paid it at their discretion. It does not form part of what the court can order against. It is highly relevant under section 3(1)(c), because it means the two beneficiaries have already received £60,000 each outside the estate. Dean should not expect the court to ignore it. Nor will the court be impressed by the fact that she was asked to leave the house in April 2027, three months after the death.

Section 3(2A) adds her age, the length of cohabitation and her contribution to the welfare of the family. Four and a half years is a moderate period. It is not a long cohabitation and that is our best point on quantum.

4. Likely award

Her primary case, that the estate should buy her a house outright, is unlikely to be granted in that form. Where the applicant is a cohabitant claiming on the maintenance standard, the court often meets a housing need by settling a property on her for life, or by giving a right to occupy, with reversion to the estate beneficiaries, rather than by transferring capital outright. That reflects the fact that maintenance is about her needs during her life, not about enriching her estate.

Taking a realistic view, I would expect an award of the order of:

- a capitalised sum in the range £90,000 to £150,000; or

- a life interest in a small property purchased out of the estate for around £150,000, with the capital reverting to Dean and Craig on her death, plus a modest cash sum of £15,000 to £25,000 for moving and furnishing.

A life interest structure is worth more to Dean in the long run than a straight payment of the same headline figure, because the capital comes back. It is also easier to defend as maintenance. I would open on that basis.

If she issued and won at the top of the range, the estate would also be at risk on her costs, which on a claim of this kind are easily £40,000 to £60,000 a side to trial. The costs risk is a bigger driver of settlement than the difference between our figure and hers.

5. Time, and what must happen now

The six month period from the grant of 12 May 2027 expires on 12 November 2027. After that she needs the court's permission to apply out of time, which is discretionary and not to be relied on either way. Ten weeks is not long.

Two consequences.

First, we should not simply let the clock run in the hope she misses it. That would be a strategy of delay rather than a defence, and if she issues in time it will have achieved nothing except costs. In practice, if settlement talks are progressing, the sensible course is either that she issues a protective claim which is then stayed, or that the parties enter a written standstill agreement extending time. If a standstill is used it must be in writing, must be signed by all parties who could be affected, and must have a clearly defined end date and a mechanism for termination. The courts have criticised loose standstill agreements in this field, so I would prefer a protective claim form with a stay, or a firm dated standstill drafted by us.

Second, section 20 protects a personal representative who distributes after the end of the six month period against a later, out of time claim. It does not protect a personal representative who distributes before that period expires, and it does not protect against a claim brought in time. Dean has already transferred £30,000 to Craig. He must make no further distribution before 12 November 2027, and he should retain enough to meet a realistic award and costs. If he distributes and the claim succeeds, he is personally liable to make good the shortfall, and there is a real question whether he could recover the £30,000 from Craig. He needs to be told this in writing.

6. Negotiation strategy

Objective. Settle before 12 November 2027, for a capital equivalent within the range £110,000 to £130,000, structured so that as much as possible returns to the estate on her death, with each side bearing its own costs.

Steps I recommend:

(a) Reply to the letter of claim within the 28 days, on a without prejudice basis, neither admitting nor denying the claim but proposing mediation and asking for full disclosure of her means: bank statements, savings, pension position, tenancy agreement, payslips. Her figures are all self reported at present.

(b) Agree a standstill or a stayed protective claim so that time is not the driver.

(c) Mediate. Claims under the 1975 Act are well suited to mediation, the parties know each other, and the court expects parties to engage in alternative dispute resolution. A refusal to engage carries a costs risk. Mediation also allows an outcome the court could not order, for example an agreed contribution towards her removal costs or an agreed period of continued occupation.

(d) Offers. Make a Part 36 offer once we have her financial disclosure. A Part 36 offer that she fails to beat at trial shifts costs from the end of the relevant period and is the most effective pressure available. Keep the without prejudice save as to costs correspondence tidy.

(e) Range for Dean. Open at £70,000 payable on completion of the sale of 4 Bardsley Grove. Target £110,000 to £120,000. Reserve position £150,000 or a settled property of that value with reversion. Below £70,000 there is nothing in it for her and she will issue.

(f) Craig must be brought in. He is a beneficiary and his half share is exposed to any award. He cannot be bound by a settlement he is not party to, and we cannot advise him, for the reason given at section 7.

7. Implementing a settlement

If the claim is settled before proceedings are issued, the settlement should be recorded in a written compromise agreement signed by Miss Naismith, Dean as executor, Dean personally and Craig, releasing all claims under the 1975 Act and against the estate.

The redirection of estate assets to Miss Naismith is most efficiently given effect by a deed of variation. If the deed is made within two years of the death, is in writing, is signed by the beneficiaries giving up their entitlement, contains the statement that section 142(1) of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 is to apply, and is not made for consideration in money or money's worth, the redirection is read back to the date of death for inheritance tax, with an equivalent statement under section 62(6) of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 for capital gains tax. Two years from 14 January 2027 gives until 14 January 2029, so there is time. Note that an order of the court under section 2 of the 1975 Act is itself read back to the death for inheritance tax purposes without any deed, so if a consent order is made in issued proceedings that route is available instead.

On the figures given to us, the estate has the nil rate band of £325,000 and the residence nil rate band of £175,000 available, the residence passing to the deceased's two sons who are lineal descendants, so on a net estate of £446,600 no inheritance tax arises. A variation in favour of Miss Naismith, who is not a spouse and not a charity, does not create a liability on these figures. That should be checked against the account before any deed is signed, and the point that a variation can increase the tax and then requires the personal representatives to join in and to notify HMRC within six months should be kept in mind.

8. Matters you need to know before replying to Dean

Three points, and none of them can be left.

First, Dean has instructed us to write to Miss Naismith's solicitors saying the estate is worth almost nothing once debts, funeral and costs are paid. That is untrue. The net estate is £446,600 against date of death liabilities of £9,000. Estate administration costs of £2,600 have been incurred since the death; they reduce what is available for distribution but are not deductible in computing the estate for inheritance tax. We cannot make a statement we know to be false to the other side. Doing so would breach our duty not to mislead others and our obligation to act with honesty and integrity, and it would also be seen for what it is the moment the estate accounts are disclosed. We should tell Dean plainly that we will not send that letter, and that if he insists we would have to cease acting.

Second, he wants to distribute the estate this month so there is nothing left to claim against. Quite apart from the fact that it would not work, because the court can order provision out of the net estate and can look at what the personal representative has done, it would expose him personally. Section 20 gives him no protection for a distribution made inside the six month period. He has already paid £30,000 to Craig and should be advised to have it repaid or at least to hold the balance of the estate intact. Advising him of the personal liability is the answer here, and the advice should go in writing.

Third, and separately, Dean is both the executor and a beneficiary. His duty as executor is to hold the estate for those entitled and to remain neutral on the claim while preserving the assets, and it conflicts directly with his personal interest in defeating it. We should confirm in writing whether we are retained by him as executor, personally, or both, and record the position. Craig is the other beneficiary, has taken no advice, and Dean has said Craig will do whatever he is told. We should not accept instructions from Dean on Craig's behalf and we should write to Craig recommending that he takes his own advice before any settlement is agreed, because his half share is at risk and his interests may not be identical to Dean's.

9. Recommendation

Confirm the retainer and the conflict position in writing. Tell Dean today that the estate must not be distributed further before 12 November 2027 and that we will not send the letter he has asked for. Reply to Hallamby Vine within 28 days without prejudice, propose mediation, request financial disclosure and agree a written standstill or a stayed protective claim. Aim to settle in the range £110,000 to £130,000, preferably as a life interest in a purchased property with reversion to the estate, implemented by a deed of variation or a consent order.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client, who is both sole executor and a beneficiary, instructs the firm to tell the claimant's solicitors that the estate is worth almost nothing, which is false on the estate schedule, and to distribute the estate at once so there is nothing left to claim against. The firm cannot make a statement to a third party which it knows to be untrue, and cannot assist a distribution designed to defeat a claim, which would also expose the client to personal liability because section 20 protects him only against out of time claims after the six month period has run. Separately, his duty as personal representative to preserve the estate and remain even handed conflicts with his personal interest as beneficiary, and his brother Craig, whose half share is at risk, has taken no advice and is said to do whatever he is told. The competent candidate refuses the letter, advises in writing against any further distribution and about the £30,000 already paid to Craig, defines whether the firm acts for the client as executor, personally or both, declines to take instructions on Craig's behalf, writes to Craig recommending independent advice, and makes clear the firm would cease to act rather than mislead the other side.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsExtracts the facts that decide eligibility and quantum: the exact cohabitation period against the two year minimum, her age, earnings, savings and rent, the beneficiaries' respective means, the £120,000 pension benefit paid outside the estate, the grant date of 12 May 2027, and the £30,000 already paid to Craig. Notes that her financial figures are self reported and unverified.Repeats the letter of claim's figures without checking them against the estate schedule, or misses the grant date and therefore the whole time issue.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsGives the partner a usable settlement range with an opening figure, a target and a walk away point, explains why a life interest is worth more to the client than a lump sum of the same headline value, prices the costs risk, and sets a clear timetable against the 12 November deadline.Analyses the section 3 factors thoroughly and then stops, offering no figure, no range and no strategy, so the partner cannot act on the report.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured report to the partner with numbered sections, a front loaded summary and a closing recommendation. Figures set out clearly. Nothing addressed to the client or the other side.Drafts the without prejudice letter to the other side instead of the report the partner asked for, or produces a shapeless narrative.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly applies section 1(1)(ba) with section 1(1A) and the alternative under section 1(1)(e) with section 1(3). Correctly identifies the maintenance standard under section 1(2)(b) and does not apply the surviving spouse standard. Applies section 3 and section 3(2A) individually to these facts. Gets section 4 and section 20 right, including that section 20 does not protect a distribution made inside the six month period.Applies the spouse standard because they lived as a couple, treats her as entitled to a share of the estate rather than to maintenance, or says section 20 protects the executor if he waits six months from the date of death rather than from the grant.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers eligibility, standard, the two stage test, every relevant section 3 factor, quantum with a reasoned range, the forms of order available under section 2 including a settlement of property, the time limit and the standstill or protective claim options, the personal representative's exposure, and the mechanism for implementing settlement, recognising that reading back is achieved by a consent order under section 2 read back under section 146 of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 and that a section 142 deed of variation is excluded because the redirection would be made for consideration in money's worth.Deals with the claim on its merits and omits the time limit, the executor's personal liability or how a settlement would actually be documented.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies without prompting that the firm cannot write a letter it knows to be false about the value of the estate, that assisting a distribution designed to defeat the claim is not something the firm can do and would expose the client personally, and that the client's dual role as executor and beneficiary creates a conflict which requires the retainer to be defined and Craig to be told to take independent advice. Resolves each: refuse, advise in writing, define the retainer, and warn that the firm would cease acting if pressed.Sends the misleading letter because it is what the client wants, or notices the conflict but offers no resolution beyond naming it.

Examiner notes

This is the negotiation station. A candidate who produces a competent merits analysis and stops there cannot pass on client focused advice, because the partner asked in terms for options, a strategy, a range and a mechanism. The strongest answers convert the section 3 analysis into a number, explain why a life interest with reversion serves the client better than an outright lump sum of the same size, and drive everything against the 12 November deadline. The commonest legal error is applying the surviving spouse standard because the couple lived as husband and wife; section 1(2)(b) applies and the standard is maintenance. The second commonest is treating the £120,000 pension death benefit as part of the net estate; it is not, because the trustees paid it at their discretion, but it is squarely relevant to the beneficiaries' resources under section 3(1)(c). The third is misreading section 20 as a shield for an early distribution. Ethically, a candidate who drafts the letter the client asked for has failed the conduct criterion whatever else the report contains.

Written station 20: Drafting a deed of variation redirecting a share of residue to grandchildren and a charity

Legal drafting  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  45 minutes

Model answer

DEED OF VARIATION

relating to the estate of GORDON ASHWELL deceased

THIS DEED OF VARIATION is made the [ ] day of [ ] 2027

BETWEEN

(1) NINA ASHWELL of 78 Calverley Lane, Leeds LS13 1NN (the "Original Beneficiary");

(2) ROSA ASHWELL of 5 Beckett Gardens, Leeds LS13 4TP and THEO ASHWELL of 5 Beckett Gardens, Leeds LS13 4TP (together the "New Individual Beneficiaries");

(3) WHARFEDALE RIVERBANK RESTORATION, a charity registered in England and Wales under number 1149330, of 8 Kirkgate, Otley, West Yorkshire LS21 3HA (the "Charity"); and

(4) CALLUM ASHWELL of 4 Sedbergh Way, Harrogate, North Yorkshire HG2 8DF (the "Executor").

RECITALS

(A) GORDON ASHWELL of 12 Fernbeck Road, Harrogate, North Yorkshire HG2 8LP (the "Deceased") died on 8 March 2027 having made a will dated 22 April 2019 (the "Will"). The Deceased died domiciled in England and Wales.

(B) By clause 2 of the Will the Deceased appointed the Executor to be the sole executor and trustee of the Will. Probate of the Will was granted to the Executor out of the Principal Registry of the Family Division on 9 July 2027.

(C) By clause 6 of the Will the Deceased gave the residue of his estate to such of his children, the Executor and the Original Beneficiary, as survived him, and if both in equal shares absolutely. Both survived the Deceased. The Original Beneficiary accordingly became entitled to one half of the residuary estate of the Deceased (the "Original Entitlement").

(D) The estate of the Deceased has not yet been distributed and the Original Beneficiary has not received the Original Entitlement or any part of it.

(E) The Original Beneficiary wishes to vary the dispositions made by the Will in the manner set out in this Deed, and the Executor has agreed to join in this Deed for the purpose of giving effect to it.

(F) This Deed is made within the period of two years after the death of the Deceased.

OPERATIVE PROVISIONS

1. VARIATION

1.1 The Original Beneficiary hereby varies the dispositions made by the Will so that the Will takes effect, and shall be read and construed, as if the Deceased had by the Will given:

1.1.1 the sum of SIXTY THOUSAND POUNDS (£60,000) to Rosa Ashwell absolutely;

1.1.2 the sum of SIXTY THOUSAND POUNDS (£60,000) to Theo Ashwell absolutely; and

1.1.3 the sum of FORTY FIVE THOUSAND POUNDS (£45,000) to the Charity absolutely for its general charitable purposes,

in each case out of, and to the extent only of, the Original Entitlement.

1.2 Subject to clause 1.1, the Original Entitlement and the remaining dispositions of the Will shall continue to have effect unaltered, and the Original Beneficiary remains entitled to the balance of the Original Entitlement.

1.3 The sums given by clause 1.1 shall be paid out of the Original Entitlement and shall not be paid out of, or reduce, the share of the residuary estate to which the Executor is beneficially entitled under the Will.

1.4 The written receipt of a person appearing to the Executor to be a proper officer of the Charity authorised to give it shall be a complete discharge to the Executor in respect of the sum given by clause 1.1.3, and the Executor shall not be concerned to see to its application.

2. NO CONSIDERATION

2.1 The variation effected by this Deed is not made for any consideration in money or money's worth, other than consideration consisting of the making, in respect of another of the dispositions of the property comprised in the estate of the Deceased, of a variation or disclaimer to which section 142(1) of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 applies.

2.2 No party to this Deed has paid, promised or agreed to pay any sum or to give any other benefit to the Original Beneficiary in return for the variation effected by this Deed.

3. INHERITANCE TAX

3.1 The Original Beneficiary and the Executor, being all of the relevant persons, declare that they intend that section 142(1) of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 shall apply to the variation effected by this Deed.

4. CAPITAL GAINS TAX

4.1 The Original Beneficiary declares that she intends that section 62(6) of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 shall apply to the variation effected by this Deed.

5. INDEPENDENT ADVICE

5.1 The Original Beneficiary confirms that she has been advised to take, and has had the opportunity to take, independent legal advice on the effect of this Deed, and that she enters into this Deed freely and with a full understanding of its effect.

6. FURTHER ASSURANCE

6.1 Each party shall at the request and cost of the Executor do all such acts and execute all such documents as may reasonably be required to give effect to this Deed.

7. COUNTERPARTS

7.1 This Deed may be executed in any number of counterparts, each of which when executed and delivered is an original, and all the counterparts together constitute one and the same deed.

8. GOVERNING LAW

8.1 This Deed and any dispute arising out of it are governed by the law of England and Wales.

IN WITNESS of which this Deed has been executed and delivered on the date first written above.

EXECUTED as a DEED by NINA ASHWELL )

in the presence of: ) ..............................

Witness signature ..............................

Witness name ..............................

Witness address ..............................

Witness occupation ..............................

EXECUTED as a DEED by ROSA ASHWELL )

in the presence of: ) ..............................

Witness signature ..............................

Witness name ..............................

Witness address ..............................

Witness occupation ..............................

EXECUTED as a DEED by THEO ASHWELL )

in the presence of: ) ..............................

acting by a duly authorised officer ) ..............................

as executor of the estate of Gordon Ashwell deceased )

in the presence of: ) ..............................

Witness signature ..............................

Witness name ..............................

Witness address ..............................

Witness occupation ..............................

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two things sit in the attendance note. Callum, who is the firm's client, says Nina is hopeless with paperwork and should be got to sign without being confused by the tax point, and he asks whether the deed can record a £5,000 payment he promised her for agreeing to the variation, then says he would rather it was not written anywhere. The firm acts for Callum, not for Nina, and Nina's interests in giving up £165,000 are not the same as his. The firm must not take unfair advantage of her, must not procure her signature to a document she does not understand, and must not advise her. The deed should recite that she has been advised to take independent legal advice, and she should be written to separately recommending it. On the £5,000, a payment for making the variation is consideration in money or money's worth, which takes the deed outside section 142(1) and section 62(6) entirely, so the deed cannot both recite it and achieve its purpose. Nor can the firm draft a clause stating that no consideration passes while knowing of a promised payment, because that would be a false statement made to HMRC. The competent candidate declines to draft either version, tells the client the payment must either be abandoned or the reading back given up, and takes instructions afresh.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsParties fully and correctly identified with addresses and the charity by its registered number. Defined terms introduced once and used consistently. Sums in words and figures. The redirection is expressed unambiguously as coming out of the Original Beneficiary's share alone. No em-dashes, British spelling.Leaves the precedent's square bracket placeholders unfilled, or describes the redirection so loosely that it is unclear whether the gifts come out of Nina's share or off the top of residue.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsConventional deed structure: title, date, parties, recitals establishing death, date of will, grant, entitlement and the two year period, then operative clauses, then execution blocks with attestation for each individual and a corporate execution block for the charity.Runs the recitals and the operative provisions together, or omits the execution and attestation blocks so the document could not be executed as a deed.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawDeletes recital (E) of the precedent, which recites consideration and would defeat section 142 and section 62(6) altogether. Includes an express statement that section 142(1) is intended to apply, made by the Original Beneficiary, and a statement that section 62(6) is intended to apply. Correctly identifies who must make each statement and joins the executor. States that the deed is made within two years and that no consideration passes.Reproduces the consideration recital, or omits the section 142(1) statement, either of which stops the variation being read back and destroys the whole purpose of the deed.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawDeals with everything the transaction needs: the three separate redirected gifts in the right amounts, the express point that they come out of Nina's share only and not Callum's, the balance remaining hers, a charity receipt clause, an independent advice recital, further assurance, counterparts, governing law, and proper execution by every party including the charity.Redirects the money without saying which share it comes out of, forgets the capital gains tax statement even though the estate contains an investment portfolio and a house sold at a gain after death, or leaves the charity out of the parties so it never becomes bound.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses to record the £5,000 payment Callum says he promised Nina, because it would be consideration and would destroy the reading back, and equally refuses to conceal it, since a deed which states that no consideration passes when the firm has been told otherwise would be a false statement to HMRC. Recognises that the firm acts for Callum and not for Nina, does not purport to advise her, and builds in a recital that she has been advised to take independent legal advice. Does not act on the instruction to get her to sign without understanding the tax effect.Drafts the no consideration clause knowing about the promised £5,000 and says nothing, or treats Nina as a client of the firm and advises her within the deed.

Examiner notes

The precedent contains a planted fatal defect: recital (E) recites that the original beneficiary has received a sum in consideration for the variation. Consideration in money or money's worth takes the variation outside section 142(1) and section 62(6), so a candidate who reproduces that recital has drafted a deed that achieves nothing, however well the rest is written. The second planted point is the missing capital gains tax statement, which the precedent's own drafting note hints at: without a statement under section 62(6) of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 the redirection is treated as a disposal by the original beneficiary of her interest in the unadministered estate. It does not touch the executor's own sale of the house in October 2027, on which any gain is assessed on the personal representatives. The third is deciding who must be a party: the original beneficiary must make the statements, the charity and the two children should be parties so they are bound and can give a receipt, and the executor need only join where the variation increases the tax, though joining him is ordinary practice and here he is also the paying party. The commonest structural failure is redirecting the gifts without saying that they come out of Nina's half share, which would silently take money out of Callum's share too. The ethics point is the promised £5,000: it cannot be recited without destroying the deed and cannot be concealed without making a false statement, so the answer is to draft neither and go back for instructions.

Written station 21: A specific gift of a house sold by an attorney before death

Legal research  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO PARTNER

To: Salome Bhatt

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 22 June 2027

Matter: Farrow deceased, gift of Wrenfield Lodge and the Corley Building Society proceeds account

1. CONCLUSION

1.1 The specific gift of Wrenfield Lodge in clause 3 has adeemed. Mr Farrow takes nothing under that clause.

1.2 He is not entitled to the 481,940 pounds in the Corley account. The preservation provision in Schedule 2, paragraph 8 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 does not apply, because the house was sold by an attorney under a lasting power of attorney and not under an order of the Court of Protection or by a deputy.

1.3 The proceeds fall into residue and pass to Mrs Farrow-Brace. Mr Farrow keeps the 25,000 pounds pecuniary legacy in clause 4.

1.4 The codicil of 11 March 2025 does not save the gift. Republication does not put back into the estate property that had already been sold six months earlier.

1.5 There are two matters on which the partner needs to make a decision before we write to anyone, at paragraphs 5 and 6 below.

2. ADEMPTION

2.1 A specific gift takes effect only if the property answering its description forms part of the estate at death. By section 24 of the Wills Act 1837 the will speaks from death as to the property comprised in it, unless a contrary intention appears. Clause 3 gives "my freehold property known as Wrenfield Lodge", identified by postal address and by title number CH480221. That is a specific gift of one identified asset, and there was no such asset in the estate on 19 November 2026.

2.2 The test is whether the thing given can still be found in the estate, allowing for a change of name or form only. In In re Slater, Slater v Slater [1907] 1 Ch 665 Cozens Hardy LJ put it as asking where the thing given is, and said that tracing is only permissible where what is found has changed in name and form only but is substantially the same thing. Shares exchanged for stock in a successor undertaking were held to be a different thing, and the gift adeemed.

2.3 In re Slater also decides the point Mr Farrow's argument turns on. The court held that the motive for the change, and whether the change was made by the testator or without the testator's knowledge, is immaterial. It follows that Mrs Farrow's loss of capacity and her ignorance of the sale do not preserve the gift.

2.4 Mr Farrow will rely on In re Dorman, deceased [1994] 1 WLR 282, where an attorney closed the deposit account which was the subject of the gift and opened a new one at the same branch, and the legacy was held not to have adeemed. Dorman does not help him. The change there was administrative and the asset was in substance the same asset, a deposit account with the same bank. Here a freehold house has been converted into cash. That is a change of substance, not of name or form. The point is the same one the Court of Appeal drew in Slater.

2.5 The fact that the proceeds were paid into a separate account named "M E Farrow, Wrenfield proceeds", and were never spent, does not alter the analysis. Ademption is decided on the words of the will and on what is in the estate at death, not on the label an attorney puts on a bank account. The will gives a house. There is no house.

3. THE MENTAL CAPACITY ACT 2005

3.1 Schedule 2, paragraph 8 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 exists to prevent exactly this outcome. Where P's property has been disposed of, and a person would have taken an interest in it under P's will but for the disposal, and property representing it belongs to P's estate at death, that person takes the same interest in the property representing it.

3.2 Each of paragraph 8(1)(b) and (c) is satisfied here. Mr Farrow would have taken Wrenfield Lodge but for the sale, and the Corley account plainly represents the house.

3.3 Paragraph 8(1)(a) is not satisfied. It requires the disposal to have been made by virtue of an order made or directions given by the court under section 16, or by a deputy appointed by the court. The sale on 14 September 2024 was made by Mrs Farrow-Brace as attorney under a lasting power of attorney registered in April 2019. No application was ever made to the Court of Protection. A disposal by an attorney is outside the paragraph, as the annotated edition confirms.

3.4 Section 101 of the Mental Health Act 1983 is in similar terms, but it was repealed by Schedule 7 to the 2005 Act with effect from 1 October 2007 and cannot be relied on.

3.5 The practical consequence is that the ademption could have been avoided at the time, either by applying for an order of the court authorising the sale, which would have brought paragraph 8 into play, or by applying for a statutory will under section 18(1)(i) of the 2005 Act. Neither was done. That cannot now be cured: a statutory will can only be made during P's lifetime.

4. THE CODICIL

4.1 The codicil of 11 March 2025 confirms the will, and confirmation republishes it, so that the will is read as if made on 11 March 2025. Republication does not assist Mr Farrow. The house had already been sold on 14 September 2024, six months before the codicil. Republication changes the date from which the will speaks, not the contents of the estate. If anything it puts the gift on worse ground, because at the date the will is treated as made the property described in clause 3 was already gone.

4.2 The codicil is relevant in one other way. It shows that Mrs Farrow had testamentary capacity in March 2025, certified by an independent doctor, and that she made a fresh testamentary instrument after the sale without altering clause 3. If she was capable of making a codicil then, she was capable of being advised then that clause 3 had been overtaken by the sale. That is a matter for paragraph 6 below.

5. WHAT TO ADVISE THE EXECUTOR

5.1 As a matter of law the estate should be distributed as follows: 25,000 pounds to Mr Farrow under clause 4, the chattels and the whole of the residue including the 481,940 pounds to Mrs Farrow-Brace under clause 5.

5.2 Mr Farrow should be told the outcome and the reason for it in writing, with the two statutory references, so that he can take his own advice. He should not be told simply that "the house was sold for care fees and the gift has gone".

5.3 Mrs Farrow-Brace should be advised that Mr Farrow has two possible routes and that both should be raised with her now rather than after distribution:

(a) A claim against her personally as attorney, on the footing that a reasonable attorney faced with selling property that was the subject of a specific gift in the donor's will, with the donor lacking capacity, should have applied to the Court of Protection. We cannot advise on the strength of that claim, for the reason at paragraph 6.

(b) A claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975. On the facts this looks weak.
