Ilott v The Blue Cross [2017] UKSC 17 confirms that for an adult child the standard is maintenance, that being a child of the deceased and receiving little or nothing is not itself a claim, and that the applicant's own resources are central. Mr Farrow is 61, working, owns his home outright, describes himself as comfortably off and was never maintained by his mother. He also receives 25,000 pounds. The claim should be mentioned to the executor because of the six month time limit running from the grant, and because distributing the residue before that period expires carries a risk for her personally, but it is not a claim we would expect to succeed.

5.4 The commercial answer may be a deed of variation by Mrs Farrow-Brace redirecting part of the residue to her brother. That is her decision alone and she should not be pressed. It should be put to her as an option, with the point that a variation made within two years of death can be given effect for inheritance tax and capital gains tax purposes if the correct statements are included.

6. THE FIRM'S POSITION AND THE EXECUTOR'S INSTRUCTION

6.1 This firm acted on the sale of Wrenfield Lodge in September 2024, on the attorney's instructions. Whether the ademption point was raised with her at the time is not apparent from the file and needs to be established before we advise her on any claim against her as attorney, because if it was not raised the firm has an interest of its own in the answer and cannot advise on it.

6.2 Mrs Farrow-Brace has asked that her brother not be shown the sale file or the account statements and be told only that the house was sold for care fees. We can decline to volunteer documents which belong to the estate and to which he has no automatic right, and there is nothing improper in a considered decision about what an executor discloses to a residuary or specific beneficiary. What we cannot do is give him an account which is designed to leave him with a false impression of how the money was handled or of why his gift has failed. The instruction as given should not be followed in that form.

7. SOURCES NOT RELIED ON

7.1 Section 20 of the Administration of Justice Act 1982 allows rectification only for a clerical error or a failure to understand instructions. The will said exactly what Mrs Farrow intended in 2016. There is nothing to rectify, and in any event the six month limit would apply.

7.2 Section 33 of the Wills Act 1837 concerns a beneficiary who predeceases the testator leaving issue. Mr Farrow is alive.

7.3 Kilmarnock, Succession in Scotland describes the Scots doctrine of ademption and the surrogatum, and legal rights, jus relictae and legitim. This is the law of Scotland and has no application to an estate in England and Wales. The Scots qualification for alienation by a guardian or continuing attorney is precisely the qualification English law does not make outside Schedule 2, paragraph 8, and it must not be borrowed.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two issues sit in the facts and neither is flagged. First, the executor, who is also the attorney who sold the house and the residuary beneficiary who gains 481,940 pounds from the ademption, has instructed the firm to tell her brother only that the house was sold for care fees and the gift has gone, and not to go into how the money was handled. An executor has a measure of discretion about what documents she volunteers, but a solicitor must not give a beneficiary an account calculated to create a false impression, and the instruction in that form must not be followed. Second, this firm acted on the sale in September 2024 on the attorney's instructions. If the ademption risk was not raised with her at the time, the firm has an interest of its own in the question whether the attorney should have applied to the Court of Protection before selling, and it cannot advise her on that question while its own conduct is in issue. The competent candidate says both things plainly, proposes that the 2024 file be checked before any advice is given on a claim against the attorney, and advises that Mr Farrow be given the true reason his gift has failed in writing so that he can take his own advice.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsBuilds the answer on section 24 of the Wills Act 1837, Schedule 2 paragraph 8 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, In re Slater and In re Dorman, and uses the republication text for the codicil. Uses Ilott only to dismiss the 1975 Act claim. Identifies section 101 of the Mental Health Act 1983 as repealed and the Scottish text as another jurisdiction, and disposes of section 20 of the 1982 Act and section 33 of the Wills Act 1837 briefly.Applying section 101 of the Mental Health Act 1983 as if it were in force, or importing the Scots surrogatum rule from the Kilmarnock extract, which produces the opposite answer and reads plausibly because the paragraph is about attorneys.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsSays who takes what, in figures, and what to do next. Addresses the son's actual argument that the account is the house in another form and explains why it fails. Flags the six month period from the grant, the risk of distributing early, and the deed of variation as an option for the executor to consider and not a recommendation.A correct analysis of ademption which never states the distribution, or advising the executor to make a variation as though it were a legal requirement.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsConclusion first, numbered, no research trail. The Slater and Dorman distinction is drawn in two or three sentences rather than by summarising both reports at length.Long quotation from every source in the bundle, or narrating which sources were looked at and in what order.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawConcludes the gift adeems, that paragraph 8 fails on limb (1)(a) alone because the disposal was by an attorney under a lasting power rather than by the court or a deputy, and that the codicil does not revive the gift. Correctly identifies that Slater makes the testator's ignorance and lack of capacity irrelevant.Concluding that paragraph 8 applies because the Corley account obviously represents the house, which satisfies limb (1)(c) but never tests limb (1)(a). This is the single most common wrong answer and it looks well reasoned.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all four strands: ademption, the statutory preservation provision, the effect of the codicil and republication, and what the son may do next. Notes that the ademption was avoidable at the time by a Court of Protection application or a statutory will, and that a statutory will is no longer possible. Deals with the pecuniary legacy in clause 4, which survives.Answering only the ademption question and never dealing with the codicil, or overlooking that the 25,000 pounds legacy is unaffected, so the note tells the executor the son takes nothing at all.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies both points. First, the executor's instruction that her brother be told only that the house was sold for care fees, which the firm cannot follow if the effect is to leave him with a false impression. Second, that the firm itself acted on the sale, so it has a possible interest of its own in whether the attorney should have applied to the Court of Protection, and cannot advise the executor on a claim in which the firm may be implicated. Proposes checking the 2024 sale file before advising further.Treating the executor's instruction as an ordinary decision about disclosure and saying nothing about it, or missing entirely that the firm acted on the sale and advising confidently on the strength of a claim against the attorney.

Examiner notes

The trap is Schedule 2, paragraph 8 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005. The provision reads as though it is made for these facts, and two of its three limbs are satisfied: the son would have taken the house but for the sale, and the ring fenced Corley account plainly represents it. Candidates who see that stop, conclude that the son takes the 481,940 pounds and lose the station. The whole question is limb (1)(a): the disposal must be by an order or direction of the court under section 16, or by a court appointed deputy. It was neither. It was made by an attorney under a registered lasting power, and no Court of Protection application was ever made. Candidates who lift the repealed section 101 of the Mental Health Act 1983, or who borrow the Scots surrogatum rule from the Kilmarnock extract, arrive at the same wrong answer by two other routes. The second discriminator is In re Slater, which disposes of the emotional pull of the facts by holding that the motive for the change, and whether the testator knew of it, is immaterial. Strong candidates also see that In re Dorman is being offered to them as the son's best argument and distinguish it properly, on substance against form, rather than ignoring it. Answering the codicil point takes three sentences and is worth having: republication moves the date the will speaks from, and does not put a sold house back into the estate.

Written station 22: Validity of an undocumented direction to executors and of an oral arrangement over a cottage

Legal research  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  60 minutes

Model answer

RESEARCH NOTE

To: Marianne Ostler, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 22 January 2027

Matter: Estate of Harold Fenwick deceased

Subject: Clause 4 and clause 5, and the executors' position

1. Summary of advice

1.1 Clause 4 fails. The arrangement over the £150,000 does not bind the executors and Mr Sowden has no enforceable claim to it. The fund falls into residue and passes to Neil Fenwick under clause 6. There are two independent reasons, either of which is fatal.

1.2 Clause 5 stands. Douglas Fenwick holds Stint Cottage on a fully secret trust for Ada Fenwick, contingent on her attaining 30. He takes nothing beneficially.

1.3 Separately, Neil's request that the lunch conversation should not be mentioned cannot be acted on, and it raises a conflict that has to be dealt with before Monday. That is at paragraph 5.

2. Clause 4, the £150,000

2.1 Clause 4 gives the money to the trustees 'to hold upon such trusts as I may hereafter make known to them'. The existence of a trust appears on the face of the will but its objects do not. This is a half secret trust.

2.2 The doctrine is established by Blackwell v Blackwell [1929] AC 318. Equity enforces the arrangement because it acts on the conscience of the person who accepted the obligation, and because the testator relied on that acceptance in making his will in that form. Viscount Sumner identified the three requirements as intention, communication and acceptance. The trust operates outside the will and so does not offend section 9 of the Wills Act 1837.

2.3 The first difficulty is timing. Where the will itself discloses the trust, communication must be made before or at the time the will is executed. Communication afterwards will not do, because the testator would then be altering the destination of his estate by an act done after execution and without the section 9 formalities. That is the footing on which Blackwell proceeded and it was confirmed in Re Keen, Evershed v Griffiths [1937] Ch 236. Lord Wright MR held that the trusts 'must be described in the will as established prior to, or at least contemporaneously with, its execution'. Here the will was executed on 1 March 2024 and the only communication was on 18 June 2024, more than three months later. On that ground alone the trust fails.

2.4 The second difficulty is the wording of clause 4 itself. The words 'as I may hereafter make known to them' point to a future notification. In Re Keen the equivalent words reserved to the testator a power to make future unwitnessed dispositions of his estate, which cannot stand with section 9. The same reasoning was applied in Re Bateman's Will Trusts [1970] 1 WLR 1463, where 'as shall be stated by me in a sealed letter' was held void for exactly that reason and the fund fell into residue. Clause 4 is on all fours with Re Bateman.

2.5 It follows that even a communication made on 1 March 2024 would not have saved this clause, because the words used would have contradicted it. In Re Keen a sealed envelope handed over before execution was treated as a good communication at the date of handing over, but the clause still failed because its wording was inconsistent with what had actually happened. Clause 4 has both defects.

2.6 The consequence is a resulting trust. The executors hold the £150,000 for the estate, and it passes under the residuary gift in clause 6 to Neil Fenwick.

3. Clause 5, Stint Cottage

3.1 Clause 5 is an absolute gift to Douglas on the face of the will. Nothing in the will suggests a trust. This is a fully secret trust and a different rule applies.

3.2 The requirements are set out by Brightman J in Ottaway v Norman [1972] Ch 698: an intention by the testator to subject the primary donee to an obligation in favour of the secondary donee, communication of that intention to the primary donee, and acceptance of the obligation, expressly or by acquiescence. All three are present. The deceased told Douglas in February 2024 what he intended, identified Ada and the age of 30, gave his reason, and Douglas agreed.

3.3 Timing is not a problem here. Because the will is absolute on its face, communication and acceptance may take place at any point in the testator's lifetime, before or after execution. It is enough that the donee's conscience was affected before death. The communication here was in fact before execution, so the point does not arise.

3.4 Evidence. The standard is the ordinary civil standard of the balance of probabilities, Re Snowden [1979] Ch 528, subject to Brightman J's warning in Ottaway that the court looks for clear evidence before fastening a trust on property given absolutely by a duly executed will. We have the contemporaneous diary entry of 11 February 2024, we have Douglas's own account against his own interest, and we have Neil's acceptance that his father said something of the sort. That is a strong evidential position.

3.5 The counterfactual confirms the analysis. In Wallgrave v Tebbs (1855) 2 K & J 313 the donees took beneficially precisely because nothing had been communicated and nothing accepted. Had Douglas never been asked, or never agreed, the cottage would have been his outright.

3.6 Douglas therefore holds Stint Cottage on trust for Ada contingent on her reaching 30. He should be told not to deal with the property as his own, and the trust should be documented now by a declaration of trust so that the position is clear on the register and to any future purchaser or lender.

4. Sources I have not relied on

4.1 Section 15 of the Wills Act 1837 (Source A) does not apply. The will was witnessed by two members of Havelock and Pyne who take no benefit and are not married to anyone who does.

4.2 The Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 (Source G) and Ilott v The Blue Cross [2017] UKSC 17 (Source H) are not in point. Mr Sowden is a former business partner. He is not a spouse, former spouse, cohabitant, child or child of the family, and on the file he was not being maintained by the deceased immediately before the death, so he is not within section 1(1). Ada is a granddaughter and is not being deprived of anything.

4.3 Sen v Headley [1991] Ch 425 (Source I) is not in point. There was no gift in contemplation of impending death and no parting with dominion or with the indicia of title.

4.4 Re Rose [1952] Ch 499 (Source J) is not in point. Nothing here turns on an incomplete transfer of shares or on the perfection of a lifetime gift.

5. The executors' position and what I suggest you say on Monday

5.1 Neil has asked that the lunch conversation should not be mentioned to the Probate Registry or to the family, and has linked that request to his position as residuary beneficiary and payer of our bill. We cannot act on it. We must not mislead anyone, whether by act or omission, and the fact that clause 4 fails as a matter of law does not entitle anyone to suppress the conversation. The failure of the trust is a conclusion the executors are entitled to reach with advice; it is not a reason to conceal the facts that produced it. That engages the SRA Principles on upholding the rule of law and the proper administration of justice, acting with honesty and with integrity, and acting in a way that maintains public trust, together with paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors.

5.2 There is also an own interest conflict. Neil is an executor, and as executor he owes duties to the estate and must administer it properly. He is also the residuary beneficiary and takes the £150,000 personally if clause 4 fails. He is not free to take the point in his own interest and then bury the evidence for it. Douglas has not been consulted and may take a different view.

5.3 We act for both executors jointly. If Neil maintains his position after being advised, we have a conflict of interest between two clients on a matter in which they have differing interests, and we would have to stop acting for one or both and tell them to take separate advice. I suggest you put this to both of them together on Monday and record the advice in writing.

5.4 Client focused options. The executors should be told plainly that the deceased's wish for Mr Sowden was genuine but does not bind them, and that this is a legal answer they are entitled to rely on. If Neil wishes to give effect to his father's wish, the practical route is a deed of variation of the residuary gift within two years of the death, executed by Neil as the beneficiary whose entitlement is being redirected. He should take his own advice on the tax consequences of that. Mr Sowden should be told the position, courteously and in writing, so that he is not left with an expectation. Douglas should be advised on the declaration of trust over Stint Cottage and on his duties to Ada until she is 30.

5.5 Next steps: (i) a joint meeting with both executors; (ii) a letter to each recording the advice on clause 4, clause 5 and the conflict; (iii) a declaration of trust for Stint Cottage; (iv) a letter to Mr Sowden once the executors have decided; (v) if the conflict is not resolved, a written notice that we cannot continue to act for both.

Trainee Solicitor

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Paragraph 7 of the file note records Neil Fenwick, who is both an executor and the residuary beneficiary, asking that the June 2024 lunch conversation be left out of anything sent to the Probate Registry or to the family, and linking that request to the fact that he pays the firm's bill. It reads as housekeeping. It is an instruction to conceal a material fact by a client with a direct personal interest in the outcome. A competent candidate identifies it without prompting, advises that the firm cannot mislead anyone by act or omission and that the legal failure of clause 4 gives no licence to suppress the facts, identifies the conflict inside Neil's own position between his duty as executor and his personal benefit as residuary beneficiary, identifies that the firm acts for both executors and that their interests on this question now differ so that there is a conflict of interest between two current clients, and resolves it by advising both executors together, recording the advice in writing, and ceasing to act for one or both if Neil maintains his position. The point engages the SRA Principles on honesty, integrity and public trust, paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors and the conflict of interest provisions in paragraph 6.2 of that Code. There is no own interest conflict here in the sense the Code uses that term, because the firm has no interest of its own in whether clause 4 succeeds or fails, and a candidate who says so should not be marked up for it.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses Blackwell v Blackwell, Re Keen, Re Bateman's Will Trusts, Ottaway v Norman and Wallgrave v Tebbs, cites each accurately with its citation, ties section 9 of the Wills Act 1837 to the reasoning, and states positively that section 15, the 1975 Act, Ilott, Sen v Headley and Re Rose do not apply and why.Works through the 1975 Act because Mr Sowden looks hard done by, or discusses donatio mortis causa, and cites no case for the half secret and fully secret trust rules beyond a bare mention of secret trusts.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsTells the partner what to say to each executor separately, explains that Douglas holds the cottage for Ada and must not treat it as his own, identifies the deed of variation as the practical route if Neil wants to honour his father's wish, and lists concrete next steps including a declaration of trust and a letter to Mr Sowden.Produces a correct academic answer on secret trusts and stops there, giving the partner nothing to say on Monday and no next steps.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA numbered note that opens with the two conclusions in two sentences, separates clause 4 from clause 5, quotes only the words that matter, and stays within the length a partner will read before a meeting.A narrative research trail describing what was searched and in what order, or a long recitation of each case's facts before any conclusion is reached.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly holds that clause 4 fails, gives both the late communication ground and the Re Keen and Re Bateman future disposition ground, states that the fund falls into residue on a resulting trust and passes to Neil, and correctly holds that clause 5 is a valid fully secret trust for Ada contingent on 30.Applies the fully secret trust timing rule to clause 4 and concludes that the June 2024 conversation is good enough because it happened in the testator's lifetime, so Mr Sowden takes the £150,000.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with intention, communication and acceptance for both clauses, addresses the wording of clause 4 as a separate and independent defect, addresses the standard and sufficiency of the evidence for the cottage, applying the ordinary civil standard with Ottaway's requirement of clear evidence, and explains what would have happened absent communication by reference to Wallgrave v Tebbs.Decides clause 4 on timing alone and never notices that the words 'as I may hereafter make known' would have defeated the clause even with a timely communication, or ignores the evidential question on the cottage altogether.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots Neil's request unprompted, states that the firm cannot suppress the conversation and that the legal failure of clause 4 is no justification for concealment, identifies the conflict inside Neil's own position between his duty as executor and his personal benefit as residuary beneficiary, identifies the resulting conflict of interest between the firm's two joint clients, and sets out a resolution including advising both together, recording it in writing and ceasing to act if the position is maintained.Treats paragraph 7 of the file note as background, or notices it but resolves it by simply saying 'we should be careful', without naming the conflict between the two executors or saying what the firm will do if Neil persists.

Examiner notes

The pass turns on treating the two clauses under two different rules. Candidates who learned one line about secret trusts apply a single timing rule to both and get one of them wrong. The commonest error is to save clause 4 by reasoning that communication in the testator's lifetime is enough, which is the fully secret rule and does not apply where the will discloses the trust. The second trap is stopping at timing on clause 4 and missing that the wording itself is fatal under Re Keen and Re Bateman, which matters because it is the point that survives even if the candidate is wrong about the date. The third trap is the 1975 Act, which is in the bundle because Mr Sowden is elderly and poor and looks like a claimant, and is not. The fourth is paragraph 7 of the file note, which is the ethics issue and is written to look like a routine instruction from a paying client.

Written station 23: Letter to a recently widowed client explaining the first steps in administering her husband's estate

Legal writing  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  30 minutes

Model answer

Pryor Vance LLP

Solicitors

8 Castlegate

Deverton

Mrs Eileen Thorne

14 Fenner Rise

Deverton

26 January 2027

Dear Mrs Thorne

Your husband's estate

Thank you for your letter. I am very sorry about Raymond's death, and I am sorry that you have been worrying about all of this on top of everything else. I hope this letter settles most of it. Nothing in it needs to be dealt with today.

You raised three things and I will take them in your order. There is then one point about the will that I need to explain to you properly, and one decision I would like you to make when you feel ready.

The house

You will not have to move and the house does not have to be sold.

You and Raymond owned 14 Fenner Rise together as what the law calls beneficial joint tenants. That means that on his death his share passed to you automatically. It did not pass under the will and it does not have to wait for anything. The house is now yours alone. We will write to the Land Registry to have the register put into your sole name, which is a short piece of paperwork and costs very little.

Whatever you were told at church, it does not apply here.

Inheritance tax

There will be no inheritance tax to pay on Raymond's estate.

Anything a husband or wife leaves to the other is free of inheritance tax, with no limit on the amount. Raymond left everything to you, so the whole estate is covered by that exemption. That is true of the house, the accounts, the car and the contents.

There is a second piece of good news for the future. Because Raymond did not need to use his own tax free allowances, the unused part of them can be claimed on your own death and added to yours. In practical terms your children should have roughly double the tax free amount to work with when the time comes. I mention it now only so that you know it is there. It is worth reviewing your own will at some point, but there is no hurry and it is a separate piece of work.

What has to happen next

Some of Raymond's money was in accounts in his sole name: the current account of about £11,400, the cash ISA of £62,000 and the savings account of £37,000. Deverton Building Society has written to say it will not release the sole accounts until it sees a grant of probate.

A grant of probate is a document from the Probate Registry confirming who is entitled to deal with the estate. It is not a court case. Nobody has to attend anywhere and nobody is arguing about anything. It is an application on paper.

The steps are:

1. We write to each bank, the building society and the pension provider to confirm the balances at the date of death.

2. We prepare the probate application and the inheritance tax information. Because everything passes to you, this is the shorter form.

3. The Probate Registry issues the grant. That usually takes about eight to sixteen weeks from the date of the application at present.

4. We send the grant to the building society and the bank, close the sole accounts and transfer the money to you.

5. We settle the funeral account of £4,180 and the utility and council tax arrears of about £900 out of the estate.

6. We transfer the house at the Land Registry and deal with the car.

The joint current account of £6,200 is already yours by survivorship and the building society should release it without waiting for the grant. If it will not, tell me and I will write to it this week.

The funeral account can usually be paid direct from the deceased's account before the grant is issued if the building society is asked properly, so please do not pay it yourself unless you want to.

What this will cost

It will not run into thousands upon thousands, and you will not be asked for money up front.

Our charges are based on the time spent, at £245 per hour plus VAT. On an estate of this size and shape we would expect the total to be between £2,400 and £3,600 plus VAT. On top of that there is the probate application fee of £300, plus £1.50 for each extra copy of the grant. I will tell you straight away if anything happens that is likely to take the cost above that range.

Our charges are paid out of the estate, not out of your own pocket, and they are paid at the end rather than as we go along. I will send you a full written estimate with the next letter.

The will names me as executor, and what that means for you

There is something in the will you should know about, because it affects your choices and I would rather you heard it from me.

When Raymond made his will in 2019 he appointed Alison Pryor, a partner in this firm, as his sole executor. The will also contains what is called a charging clause, which allows this firm to charge for the work of administering the estate and to be paid out of the estate.

That means the firm has an interest in the arrangement, and you are entitled to know that and to think about it. So please understand the following.

You are not obliged to instruct this firm. Miss Pryor is named as executor, but she is not obliged to act either. She can formally step down before doing anything further, which is called renouncing. If she does, then because you inherit the whole estate under the will you would be entitled to apply for the grant yourself. You could then either do the work yourself, or instruct us, or instruct any other firm you choose. If Miss Pryor does act as executor, the firm will charge under the charging clause as I have described.

I am telling you this because it is your decision and not ours. If you would like some time to think about it, or would like to speak to another solicitor first, that is entirely reasonable and we will not take it amiss.

Your son Peter

Peter is right that some people deal with an estate themselves, and it is perfectly lawful. He is not wrong and he is plainly trying to look after you.

The honest position is this. If Miss Pryor renounces and you take the grant yourself, Peter could help you complete the forms and you would save our charges. What you would take on is responsibility. The person who takes out the grant is personally answerable for getting the tax position, the debts and the distribution right, and for the consequences if they are wrong. In an estate like this, where everything passes to you and there is no tax to pay, those risks are modest. Peter would also need to know that he cannot take the grant himself, because he is not the executor and, as things stand, is not entitled to apply while you are alive and entitled.

So it is a real choice, not a false one. You could reasonably decide either way, and I am happy to talk it through with you and with Peter together if that would help.

What I need from you

There is no rush, but when you feel able:

1. Let me know whether you would like this firm to act, or would prefer to consider the alternatives I have set out.

2. Post or bring in the building society letter, the pension letters, the car registration document and Raymond's last bank statements.

3. Do not pay any bills in Raymond's name out of your own money before speaking to me.

If anything in this letter is unclear, or if you would rather go through it on the telephone, please ring me and I will call you back at a time that suits you. If it is easier, bring Peter or your daughter with you to the next meeting.

With sympathy and best wishes

Yours sincerely

Trainee Solicitor

For Pryor Vance LLP

The conduct issue hidden in this station

A partner of the candidate's own firm is the sole executor named in the will and the will contains a charging clause, so the firm stands to earn fees from an appointment it drafted. The client, newly bereaved and anxious about cost, is being told by her son that she does not need a solicitor at all. There is an own interest issue and a plain risk of the client being carried along without a real choice. A competent candidate raises it unprompted: discloses the appointment and the charging clause, explains that the client is not obliged to instruct the firm, explains that the partner may renounce and that the client, as the residuary beneficiary taking the whole estate, could then apply for the grant herself or instruct any other firm, gives clear and complete costs information including the hourly rate, the likely range and the disbursements, treats the son's suggestion fairly rather than dismissing it, and invites the client to take independent advice if she wishes. This engages the SRA Principles on acting with integrity, in the best interests of the client and in a way that maintains public trust, together with the Code obligations not to take unfair advantage and to give the client the best possible information about the likely overall cost.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the actual figures and names from the file: the £360,000 house held as beneficial joint tenants, the sole accounts of £11,400, £62,000 and £37,000, the joint account of £6,200, the funeral account of £4,180, the arrears of about £900, the hourly rate, the estimated range and the £300 probate fee, and the building society's refusal to release without a grant.Writes a generic 'what happens when someone dies' letter with no figures, so the client cannot tell whether her own house is safe or what her own bill will be.
Use a logical structure.SkillsAnswers her three questions in the order she asked them, under headings she would recognise, then adds the executor point and a short list of what she needs to do, so the letter can be read once and acted on.Opens with a long account of the law of survivorship and inheritance tax and leaves the answers to her actual questions scattered through the letter or never reached.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsOpens with a genuine and brief expression of sympathy, answers the house question first and unequivocally because it is what frightens her, tells her nothing needs doing today, is fair to Peter rather than dismissive of him, offers a telephone call and offers to see her with a family member.Correct in law but cold in tone, or the reverse: so much sympathy that the client still does not know whether she has to leave her home.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsPlain English throughout. Explains 'beneficial joint tenants', 'grant of probate', 'renouncing' and 'charging clause' in the sentence in which each first appears. Short sentences. No Latin, no section numbers, no abbreviations she would not know.Uses 'survivorship', 'spouse exemption', 'transferable NRB', 'IHT400' or 'personal representative' without explanation, or writes to a 71 year old lay client in the register of a note to counsel.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates correctly that the house passes by survivorship outside the will and need not be sold, that the spouse exemption means no inheritance tax is payable, that the unused nil rate band and residence nil rate band are transferable on her own death, that a grant is nonetheless needed because of the sole accounts, and that the joint account passes to her without a grant.Says the house forms part of the estate and passes under the will, or calculates tax against the nil rate band and residence nil rate band and produces a liability, having missed that the spouse exemption disposes of the whole estate.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers the grant, the reduced reporting position because the estate is exempt, the debts and funeral account as estate liabilities, the Land Registry transfer, the transferable allowances for the future, the option of Miss Pryor renouncing so that the client may apply as residuary beneficiary, and the fact that Peter cannot apply himself while his mother is alive and entitled.Deals with tax and the grant but never explains what actually happens to the sole accounts, the funeral bill or the house title, so the client is told the law but not the administration.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawVolunteers that a partner of the firm is the named executor and that the will contains a charging clause, explains that the firm therefore has an interest, states plainly that the client is free to instruct another firm, sets out the alternative of renunciation followed by an application by the client as residuary beneficiary, gives the best possible information on cost including the rate, the range and the disbursements, and invites her to take independent advice without discouragement.Simply announces that Miss Pryor is the executor and that the firm will charge under the charging clause, presenting it as settled, or treats Peter's suggestion as an obstacle to be talked down rather than a legitimate option the client is entitled to weigh.

Examiner notes

Two things separate a pass from a fail. The first is whether the candidate answers the question the client actually asked. She is frightened of losing her home, so the survivorship answer must come early and must be unqualified; a letter that reaches it in the fourth paragraph after a discussion of the nil rate band has failed her. The second is the executor point. It is not flagged anywhere in the partner's email, and the partner is the beneficiary of the appointment, so a candidate who writes to please the partner will omit it. The trap on the law is the tax calculation: the materials deliberately supply the nil rate band and the residence nil rate band, and a candidate who reaches for them instead of the spouse exemption will produce a tax bill on an estate that has none, which is exactly the outcome the client has been told to fear. The third trap is Peter, who invites a defensive answer; the fair answer is that he is right that it can be done without a solicitor, wrong that he could take the grant himself, and that the decision is his mother's.

Written station 24: Internal note to a partner on the attestation of a will after an interim distribution

Legal writing  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  30 minutes

Model answer

INTERNAL NOTE

To: Priya Ramanathan, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 17 May 2027, 4.15pm

Matter: Estate of Colin Weatherby deceased, ref WEA/1

Subject: Attestation of the will, effect on the March distributions, recommended action

1. Bottom line

1.1 The will is valid and the grant stands. Nothing here touches the validity of the will or of the appointment of Nadia as executor.

1.2 The £80,000 legacy to Bridget Hallam is void. Her husband Martin Hallam attested and they were married at the date of attestation. That £80,000 was paid out on 3 March 2027 without authority and falls to be recovered. It belongs to residue, and therefore to Nadia.

1.3 The £40,000 legacy to Lewis Okafor is good and was correctly paid. Priscilla Okafor attested, but she did not marry Lewis until 8 April 2023, eleven months after the will was signed. Section 15 bites only where the marriage existed at the date of attestation. Engagement and cohabitation are not enough.

1.4 The Wills Act 1968 does not save the Hallam legacy. It disregards the attestation of an interested witness only where the will is duly executed without it. There were only two witnesses here, so removing Martin Hallam leaves one and the will would not be duly executed. Priscilla Okafor is not an interested witness for these purposes, so she does not make up the number.

1.5 Mrs Hallam has asked us not to tell Nadia. We cannot agree to that and I deal with it at section 4.

2. Consequences of the March distribution

2.1 Nadia paid £80,000 to a person with no entitlement. That is a distribution in breach of duty, however innocently made and whatever advice she was given. As executor she is prima facie personally liable to account to the estate, and the person prejudiced is Nadia herself as residuary beneficiary. That limits the practical exposure considerably, but it does not remove the obligation to get the money back into the estate.

2.2 Recovery routes. The estate can claim the £80,000 from Mrs Hallam as a payment made under a mistake, and a recipient of estate money to which she was never entitled is liable to repay. Mrs Hallam says she has spent £26,000 on a car and course fees, so a change of position argument may be raised on part of it. On the facts, the money was spent between March and May, and paying off an existing debt is not usually treated as an irreversible change of position, so I would not concede it. The realistic outcome is repayment of the balance now and terms for the remainder.

2.3 Section 61 Trustee Act 1925. If Nadia is exposed, she acted honestly and on the firm's advice, which is the paradigm case for relief. I mention it for completeness rather than because I expect it to be needed, since she is the only person prejudiced.

2.4 Our own position. The advice to distribute in March was given by this firm on a home made will that we did not draft, and the attestation was on the face of the document. That is a matter for you and I have not put anything to the client about it. It should go to the COLP and to the insurers before anything is said to Nadia about how the payment came to be made. The firm's own position must not be allowed to shape the advice she is given.

3. The residue

3.1 Residue currently held: £356,400. If the £80,000 is recovered in full, residue becomes £436,400, all of it Nadia's.

3.2 No distribution of residue should be made until the Hallam position is resolved, and I would not release anything further today.

3.3 Estate accounts prepared on the current figures are wrong and should not be sent out.

4. Mrs Hallam's request

4.1 She has asked us twice not to raise the point with Nadia, on the footing that if nobody says anything it will go through.

4.2 We cannot do that. We act for Nadia. This is material information about her own estate and her own money and she is entitled to be told. Withholding it to protect a third party who is not our client would put us in breach of our duty to our own client and would mean the firm knowingly allowing the estate to be misapplied.

4.3 Nor can the request be treated as confidential in a way that binds us. Mrs Hallam is not a client. She was told at the outset of the call that we act for the executor. The information about the attestation comes from the will itself in any event, not from her.

4.4 She is unrepresented and has an interest directly opposed to our client's. We must not advise her, must not appear to advise her, and must not take advantage of the fact that she does not have her own solicitor. She should be told in writing, in neutral terms, that we act for the executor only, that we cannot advise her, and that she should take her own advice promptly. We should not press her for repayment in the same conversation in which we tell her that.

4.5 I have not returned her call and I suggest nobody does until you have spoken to Nadia.

5. Recommended next steps, in order

5.1 Today. You telephone Nadia this evening and tell her the position on both legacies, that the £80,000 falls into her residue, and that we are not distributing residue until it is resolved. Confirm in writing tomorrow.

5.2 Today. Report internally to the COLP and notify insurers of a circumstance. Do not correspond with Mrs Hallam before that is done.

5.3 Tomorrow. Short letter to Mrs Hallam: we act for the executor, we cannot advise her, she should take independent advice, and we will write again once instructed. Do not make a demand in that letter.

5.4 Within seven days. Once Nadia has decided, a letter of claim to Mrs Hallam or her solicitors seeking repayment of £80,000, with a proposal for instalments on the £26,000 element if that is what Nadia wants. Nadia may prefer a compromise, and as the only person affected she is entitled to take that view provided she is properly advised.

5.5 Within seven days. Written confirmation to Mr Okafor that his legacy is unaffected, so that he is not left in doubt if he hears about this from the Hallams.

5.6 Ongoing. Revised estate accounts once the position is settled. Residue not to be distributed before then.

6. What I need from you

6.1 Confirmation that you will make the call to Nadia rather than me.

6.2 A decision on whether the file is to be reallocated given the advice given in March.

Trainee Solicitor

The conduct issue hidden in this station

There are two issues and both are unflagged. The first is Mrs Hallam's request, recorded in the attendance note, that the firm should not raise the attestation point with Nadia because 'if nobody says anything it will just go through'. The firm acts for the executor. Agreeing would mean withholding material information from its own client to the client's financial detriment and knowingly allowing estate money to remain misapplied. No confidentiality protects the request, because Mrs Hallam is not a client, was told at the outset that the firm acts for the executor, and the underlying fact appears on the face of the will. A competent candidate refuses, tells the partner the client must be told today, and separately recognises that Mrs Hallam is an unrepresented person whose interests are directly opposed to the client's, so she must be told in writing that the firm cannot advise her and that she should take her own advice promptly, and must not be pressed for repayment in the same conversation. The second issue is the firm's own position: the interim distribution in March was made on this firm's advice on a will whose attestation was on its face. That is an own interest conflict under paragraph 6.1, which admits of no exception. It must be reported to the compliance officer and notified to insurers, Nadia must be told promptly and in writing that the March distribution was made on this firm's advice and what that may mean for her, she must be advised to take independent advice on any claim against the firm, and the firm's own exposure must not be allowed to shape the advice she is given. Both engage the SRA Principles on integrity, on acting in the best interests of each client and on public trust, together with the Code duties to keep the client informed of material information, not to abuse the firm's position, and not to take unfair advantage of an unrepresented person.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the two marriage dates against the will date of 4 May 2022, the fact that there were only two witnesses, the March payments of £80,000 and £40,000, the residue of £356,400, the £26,000 Mrs Hallam says she has spent, and the fact that Nadia is the sole residuary beneficiary.Notes that a witness's spouse took a legacy without recording either marriage date, so the note cannot distinguish the two legacies and the partner cannot use it.
Use a logical structure.SkillsLeads with the conclusions in a short bottom line section, then consequences, then the telephone call, then a numbered and prioritised action list with owners and timing, so the partner can act from it without reading twice.Works up to the conclusion through a discussion of section 15, so the partner reaches the answer on the second page, or gives recommendations as loose prose with no order of priority.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsWritten for a partner who is about to telephone the client: tells her what to say, what not to say, who should say it, what must happen before Mrs Hallam is contacted, and asks two specific questions back. Recognises that the practical exposure is limited because the only person prejudiced is the residuary beneficiary herself.Produces an accurate analysis with no recommendation, or drafts a letter to the client instead of the internal note that was asked for.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsInternal register: short numbered paragraphs, technical terms used without explanation because the reader is a solicitor, no condolences, no client facing softening, no recitation of statutory wording beyond what the point requires.Writes in the register of a client letter, explaining what a legacy is and expressing sympathy, or quotes section 15 at length instead of applying it.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly holds the Hallam legacy void under section 15 because the marriage predated attestation, correctly holds the Okafor legacy valid because the marriage postdated it, correctly states that the will and the grant remain valid, and correctly states that the void legacy falls into residue.Voids both legacies because both witnesses were connected to a legatee, or concludes that the will itself is invalid and the estate passes on intestacy.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAddresses the Wills Act 1968 and explains why it does not save the legacy with only two witnesses, addresses the executor's personal liability for a distribution made without authority, addresses recovery from the recipient and the change of position argument on the £26,000, addresses section 61 relief, and addresses the hold on residue and the estate accounts.Reaches the right answer on section 15 and stops, saying nothing about how the £80,000 is to be recovered, nothing about the executor's exposure, and nothing about halting the distribution of residue.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses Mrs Hallam's request outright, explains that the duty is owed to the executor and that the information is material to her own entitlement, explains that no confidentiality attaches because Mrs Hallam is not a client and the point comes from the will itself, identifies that Mrs Hallam is unrepresented with an opposed interest and must be told to take her own advice rather than advised or pressed, and separately identifies that the firm's own advice to distribute in March creates an own interest conflict, requiring a report to the COLP and to insurers, prompt written disclosure to Nadia of what happened, and a recommendation that she take independent advice on any claim against the firm.Agrees to say nothing to the client for the time being, or simply notes the request without deciding what to do about it, or spots the duty to the client but misses the firm's own position and starts making demands on an unrepresented third party in the same breath as telling her she needs a solicitor.

Examiner notes

The discriminator is the pair of marriage dates. Section 15 catches the spouse of an attesting witness only where the marriage existed at the date of attestation, and the file gives 12 September 2009 for the Hallams and 8 April 2023 for the Okafors against a will dated 4 May 2022. A candidate who voids both legacies, or saves both, has not read the chronology. The second discriminator is the Wills Act 1968, which looks like a rescue and is not one here, because with only two witnesses the will is not duly executed once the interested witness is disregarded. The third is that the note must be a note: the partner asked for an internal document and said she is telephoning the client that evening, so a candidate who produces a warm letter to Nadia has failed the task regardless of the legal analysis. The trap is the attendance note. It reads as a distressed beneficiary asking for sympathy and is in fact a request that the firm conceal material information from its own client, and it sits alongside a second, quieter problem in the fact that the March payment was made on the firm's own advice.

Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures

Written station 25: Funding and ownership concerns on a share purchase

Case and matter analysis  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO DUNCAN FERREIRA-NEALE

Client: Meridian Kite Holdings Limited

Matter: Proposed acquisition of Brackenhall Logistics Limited

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 3 March 2027

1. Summary

This matter carries a cluster of serious money laundering warning signs. In my view we have reasonable grounds to suspect that the funds coming into this transaction are criminal property, and there is a real risk that the transaction is being used to move money rather than to buy a haulage business. I recommend that you make an internal report to the MLRO today, that no further step is taken on the transaction and no funds are moved, that the £180,000 already received is not applied and not returned, and that we say nothing to the client about our concerns.

2. The features that give cause for concern

(a) Overpayment with no interest in value. The price is £4.2 million for a company with net assets of £780,000 and turnover of £2.1 million. The client did not negotiate, does not want a valuation and says the price is simply what the seller asked. Paying substantially over the odds is a classic method of moving value.

(b) Refusal of due diligence. A genuine buyer of a £4.2 million business wants to know what it is buying. Refusing due diligence while insisting on a fixed and short timetable suggests the purpose of the transaction is not the acquisition itself.

(c) Opaque ownership. The client company was incorporated eight weeks ago, is owned by a company in a high risk jurisdiction, and the director says he does not know who ultimately owns it. Its persons with significant control register is unconfirmed. We are therefore unable to identify the beneficial owner, which is a mandatory element of customer due diligence.

(d) Identity gaps. There has been no face to face contact, the passport was supplied only as an image by email, and the utility bill is in a different name.

(e) Third party funding. £600,000 is to come from Ovrell Trade Services, a company with no connection to the buyer group, coupled with an instruction not to ask it any questions. Unexplained third party funding with a request not to enquire is a strong warning sign.

(f) Unexplained receipt. £180,000 has arrived from an individual, Anatol Preisz, who does not appear anywhere on the matter, from an overseas bank.

(g) A payment deliberately kept out of the documents. The client wants £250,000 paid directly to the seller personally and not recorded in the share purchase agreement. That is an instruction to disguise part of the consideration. It also puts the written record of the transaction at odds with the truth.

(h) Use of client account as a banking facility. The client asked us to hold funds for several weeks before completion and to return them, if the deal fails, to a different account from the one they came from. Returning funds to a different account is a recognised laundering technique and we must not do it.

(i) The request to be told first. The client has asked to be told before we act on any concern. That is an invitation to tip off, and it also shows an awareness that concerns might arise.

Taken individually a few of these might be explicable. Taken together they are not.

3. The firm's obligations

Customer due diligence. We cannot complete customer due diligence because we cannot identify the beneficial owner behind Kestrelmoor Partners. Enhanced due diligence is required in any event: a high risk third country is involved, the transaction is unusually large relative to the target, and it has no apparent economic purpose. Enhanced measures include establishing the source of funds and the source of wealth, which we have not done. Where due diligence cannot be completed, we must not carry out the transaction, must not establish or continue the business relationship, and must consider making a disclosure.

Internal report. Under the firm's procedures, and under the failure to disclose offence which applies to us as a regulated sector business, anyone who knows or suspects, or has reasonable grounds to suspect, money laundering must report to the MLRO as soon as practicable. The threshold is suspicion, not proof, and it is plainly met. The report is to the MLRO, in the firm's prescribed form, today. The MLRO decides whether a suspicious activity report goes to the National Crime Agency.

Authorised disclosure and consent. If we proceeded, we would risk committing a principal offence by becoming concerned in an arrangement which facilitates the acquisition, retention or control of criminal property. To obtain a defence we need an authorised disclosure and appropriate consent before acting. The notice period is 7 working days beginning with the first working day after disclosure, and if consent is refused there is a moratorium of 31 calendar days from refusal. On any view the 20 March completion date cannot be met, and we should not treat that date as achievable.

The £180,000 already held. It must not be applied to the matter, must not be paid onward and must not be returned to any account, including the account it came from, without the MLRO's decision and, if required, consent. Returning it could itself be a prohibited act.

4. What we can and cannot say to the client

We must not tell the client that a report has been made or is being considered, or say anything likely to prejudice an investigation. That rules out telling him that compliance has concerns, that funds are held pending a decision, or that the delay is caused by anti money laundering issues. His express request to be told first cannot be met and should not be answered on its own terms.

We can say neutral things that are true and do not disclose the position: that we are not in a position to proceed to completion on 20 March, and that we are unable to act on the instruction to pay part of the consideration off the record.

We must refuse the instruction to pay £250,000 outside the agreement. Documenting a transaction so that it does not record the true consideration would mislead others who rely on the documents, and we cannot be party to it.

5. Can we continue to act

Not on the present basis. We cannot complete due diligence, so we cannot carry out the transaction. If the MLRO decides that we should cease to act, that decision must be implemented carefully. We can tell the client that we are unable to continue and give reasonable notice, but we must not give a reason that amounts to tipping off. A short, neutral withdrawal is the right approach.

6. Next steps

1. Internal report to the MLRO today, with a copy of this analysis.

2. Freeze all activity on the matter, and instruct accounts to hold the £180,000 and take no action on it.

3. No communication with the client on the substance until the MLRO has decided.

4. Record on the file the reasoning, the time and the date of each step.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Three unflagged issues sit in the papers. The client asks to be told first if anyone has concerns, which is an invitation to tip off and must be refused without explanation. The client instructs the firm to pay £250,000 of the price directly to the seller and keep it out of the share purchase agreement, which would produce a document that does not record the true transaction and would mislead anyone relying on it, so it must be refused. The client asks the firm to hold funds with no underlying transaction and to return them to a different account, which the firm must refuse. A competent candidate refuses all three, reports internally to the MLRO on suspicion rather than proof, and takes no step that reveals the report.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsExtracts the full pattern of warning signs, including the price against net assets, the refusal of due diligence, the unidentifiable beneficial owner, the third party payer, the unexplained £180,000 from a stranger, the off the record £250,000, the banking facility request and the request to be told first.Picks out two or three warning signs, typically the overseas element and the speed, and misses the £250,000 undocumented payment or the request to return funds to a different account.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsTells the partner exactly what to do and in what order, deals expressly with the money already received, states that the 20 March date cannot be met, and separates what may be said to the client from what may not.Says the firm should 'report and consider its position' without addressing the £180,000, the completion date or the wording that can safely be used with the client.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA structured report with the warning signs grouped and the obligations set out in sequence, written soberly and without overstatement.A breathless narrative that asserts the client is a criminal, or an unstructured list of red flags with no legal consequence attached to any of them.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the suspicion threshold correctly, identifies the failure to disclose obligation in the regulated sector, explains the need for an authorised disclosure and consent before acting, uses the 7 working day and 31 day periods as given in the materials, and applies the tipping off prohibition accurately.Requires proof or certainty before reporting, reports to the National Crime Agency directly rather than through the MLRO, or invents a consent period instead of using the one supplied.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers customer due diligence and beneficial ownership, the triggers for enhanced due diligence and source of funds and wealth, the consequence of being unable to complete due diligence, the reporting duty, consent, the handling of the funds already held, and the banking facility prohibition.Deals only with reporting and ignores due diligence entirely, or ignores the £180,000 sitting in client account, which is the live problem.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses the instruction to keep £250,000 out of the agreement because it would make the documents misleading, refuses to return funds to a different account, declines the client's request to be told first, and explains how to cease acting without tipping off.Agrees to tell the client why there is a delay, or proposes to return the £180,000 to the sender as a way of getting rid of the problem.

Examiner notes

This station is passed by candidates who report on suspicion and then think about the money already in the account. The commonest fail is to write a good list of red flags, conclude 'we should report', and then advise telling the client that completion is delayed for compliance reasons, which is tipping off and destroys the ethics criterion. The second trap is the £180,000: returning it to the sender feels tidy and cautious but may itself be a prohibited act, and a strong candidate says it must be held pending the MLRO's decision. A third discriminator is spotting that the off the record £250,000 is a separate integrity problem, not merely another warning sign.

Written station 26: Scope of the firm's role on a share sale and reinvestment of the proceeds

Case and matter analysis  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

REPORT TO GIDEON HALLORAN-WEISS

Client: Rosalind Aikman-Pryce

Matter: Sale of Thornbeck Analytics Limited and related instructions

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 22 September 2027

1. Summary

We can act on the sale of Thornbeck and on the sale of the Fennimore stake, because the sale of a body corporate exclusion covers the first and, on analysis, the second falls outside it and has to be handled under section 327 instead. We can advise Rosalind on the legal and commercial merits of taking shares instead of cash, but we cannot advise her on whether Calderbrook shares are a good investment. We cannot advise her on the Ardenshaw fund or arrange her subscription to it: that is a prohibited activity and no exemption is available. We must not accept the 2% introduction fee on the terms proposed. I recommend we write to Rosalind setting out clearly what we will and will not do and telling her to take advice from an authorised person on items 2, in part, 3 and 4.

2. The framework

Under section 19 FSMA 2000 no person may carry on a regulated activity in the United Kingdom unless authorised or exempt. This firm is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.

An activity is regulated if it is a specified activity carried on by way of business in relation to a specified investment. Shares are specified investments, and so are units in a collective investment scheme. The specified activities in play are dealing as agent, making arrangements for another person to buy or sell a particular investment, and advising on the merits of buying or selling a particular investment.

There are two ways out. Either an exclusion in the Regulated Activities Order applies, so the activity is not regulated at all, or the activity is regulated but falls within the section 327 exemption for members of a profession. The exclusion route is much the better one where it is available, because it takes the activity outside the regime altogether.

3. Item 1, the sale of Thornbeck

Negotiating and completing the sale of Rosalind's shares involves arranging and, arguably, dealing as agent, in relation to shares. On the face of it these are regulated activities.

The article 70 exclusion applies. Rosalind is selling 100% of the voting shares in Thornbeck, so the 50% threshold is comfortably met and the object of the transaction is the acquisition of day to day control. The parties are a single individual and a body corporate, which satisfies the second condition. Thornbeck is not an open ended investment company.

So articles 14, 25 and 53 do not apply, and we can negotiate the agreement, advise on its terms and take the matter to completion without touching the general prohibition. That covers the whole of item 1.

4. Item 2, cash or Calderbrook shares

This needs to be split.

We can advise on the legal and structural questions: what warranties and indemnities she gives either way, what happens to her risk profile if part of the price is deferred in shares, whether the Calderbrook shares are subject to restrictions on transfer or a lock in, what rights the shares carry, and the negotiating consequences of pressing for all cash. Advice of that kind is legal and commercial advice about the transaction, not advice on the merits of an investment.

What we cannot do is answer the question she has actually asked, which is whether Calderbrook shares are a good thing to hold. That is advice on the merits of acquiring a particular investment and is a specified activity.

Does article 70 rescue it? The share for share element forms part of the same transaction for the acquisition of 100% of Thornbeck, so there is a respectable argument that advising on it is done in connection with that transaction and falls within the exclusion. But the exclusion is directed at the acquisition or disposal of control of the target, and advising her on the investment quality of a 0.4% holding in a listed plc is not naturally part of that. I would not rely on it. The safe course is to advise on the deal terms and tell her to take advice from an authorised person on whether to hold Calderbrook stock.

5. Item 5, the Fennimore stake

Rosalind is selling 8% of Fennimore Print Limited to her nephew. Article 70 does not apply: 8% is well short of 50% and there is no acquisition of day to day control.

So arranging that sale is a regulated activity. We would have to rely on section 327. The conditions are satisfiable here: we are a firm regulated by the SRA and the Law Society is a designated professional body; the work is incidental to the professional service of documenting a share transfer for a client we are already acting for; arranging a sale of unlisted shares between individuals is not on the prohibited list, because it is not a recommendation to buy a particular investment and does not involve a packaged product or a collective investment scheme; and we receive no third party reward. We should record the analysis on file and refer it to the Compliance Officer for Legal Practice under paragraph 6 of the compliance manual before proceeding.

One caution. We can arrange and document the transfer. We must not advise the nephew, or Rosalind, that £45,000 is a good price for the shares as an investment. If she needs a view on value she needs a valuer, not us.

6. Item 3, the Ardenshaw fund

This is the clearest point in the file, and the answer is no.

Units in a collective investment scheme are a specified investment. Advising Rosalind on whether the Ardenshaw Balanced Growth Fund is right for her is advising on the merits of a particular investment. Arranging her subscription is making arrangements for her to subscribe. Both are regulated activities and no exclusion in the Regulated Activities Order applies. Article 70 is irrelevant because this is not a transaction in the shares of a body corporate whose control is changing.

Section 327 does not save it either. Recommending that a client buys units in a collective investment scheme, and arranging for a client to do so, are within the prohibited activities in the Non-Exempt Activities Order, and a fund of this kind is a packaged product. An activity on the prohibited list cannot be carried on in reliance on section 327 at all.

There is a second problem even if the first did not exist. Section 327 requires the activity to be incidental to the provision of professional services. Selecting an investment fund for a client's spare cash is a free standing financial service, not something incidental to acting on a share sale.

We must therefore tell Rosalind that we cannot advise on the fund and cannot arrange the subscription, and that she needs an FCA authorised financial adviser.

7. Item 4, the introduction fee

We should not accept it as proposed. Three reasons.

First, it is a fee for introducing her to an investment we are not permitted to recommend or arrange, so it is payment for something we cannot lawfully do.

Second, even where a professional firm can act under section 327, the exemption requires the firm not to receive any pecuniary reward from a person other than the client for which it does not account to the client. A 2% introduction fee of £40,000, retained by us, would break that condition.

Third, and independently of FSMA, we must not put ourselves in a position where our own financial interest could affect the advice we give. A £40,000 fee turning on Rosalind subscribing to a particular fund is exactly that. Any referral must be in her best interests, she must be told about any financial arrangement, and any benefit must be accounted for to her with her informed written consent.

The accountant has also asked us not to raise the fee with her again because she has 'already agreed it'. We should decline that request. Her agreement was given in an email at the end of a list, without any explanation of the amount, the effect on the advice or the alternatives. That is not informed consent. If we go any further with this we must put the position to her in writing ourselves.

8. Consequences of getting it wrong

Breaching the general prohibition is a criminal offence under section 23, punishable by imprisonment or a fine. Any agreement made in the course of carrying on a regulated activity in breach of the general prohibition is unenforceable against the other party, who may recover money paid and compensation. So Rosalind's own subscription could be unwound and we could be liable to her. There would also be regulatory consequences for the firm and for the individuals involved.

9. Next steps

1. Reply to Rosalind confirming we will do items 1 and 5, will advise on the deal terms of item 2, and will not do item 3, the investment merits part of item 2, or item 4.

2. Recommend she instructs an FCA authorised adviser and offer to send her the papers she needs.

3. Write to Mr Skelmond declining the introduction fee.

4. Refer the item 5 section 327 analysis to the COLP and record it on the file.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The accountant proposes that the firm takes a 2% introduction fee of £40,000 from the fund manager and asks that the fee is not raised with the client again because she has 'already agreed it' in a single line of an email. The fee gives the firm a direct financial interest in the client subscribing to a particular investment, which is an own interest conflict, and the client's throwaway agreement is not informed consent. It also breaks the section 327 condition against retaining a third party reward without accounting to the client. A competent candidate declines the fee, refuses the request to stay silent, and puts the position to the client in writing directly rather than through the accountant.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify relevant facts.SkillsSeparates the five requests and pulls out the facts that decide each: 100% of Thornbeck against 8% of Fennimore, the plc shares as part consideration, the fund being a collective investment scheme, the 2% fee of £40,000, and the accountant's request not to raise the fee again.Treats the instructions as one undifferentiated question about financial services, so the article 70 analysis is applied to everything or to nothing.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsGives the partner a plain list of what the firm will and will not do, tells the client where to go instead, and preserves as much useful legal advice as the rules allow rather than refusing the whole instruction.Concludes 'this is a regulated activity so we cannot help' across the board, including on matters the firm can plainly do, or gives no practical answer on the share versus cash question.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsDeals with the requests in order under headings, with a clear yes or no on each, and a summary at the front.A general essay on FSMA that never reaches a decision on any of the five items.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies the general prohibition, identifies the specified investments and activities correctly, applies article 70 accurately to the 100% sale and correctly rules it out for the 8% sale, and applies section 327 and the prohibited activities list correctly to the fund.Uses article 70 to justify the fund subscription, or concludes that section 327 permits recommending a collective investment scheme because the firm is a solicitors' firm.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all five items, splits item 2 into the part the firm can advise on and the part it cannot, addresses the incidental condition as a separate obstacle from the prohibited activities list, and states the section 23 and sections 26 and 27 consequences.Answers only on the fund, misses that the Fennimore sale falls outside article 70, or omits the consequences of breach entirely.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRefuses the introduction fee, identifies the own interest conflict it creates, rejects the accountant's request not to raise it with the client again, and explains that a line in the client's email is not informed consent.Accepts the fee on the basis that the client said she does not mind, or treats the fee as purely a FSMA condition and misses the conflict and informed consent dimension.

Examiner notes

The station rewards candidates who work item by item rather than reaching for a single answer. Two traps recur. The first is treating article 70 as a general licence: it plainly covers the 100% sale of Thornbeck, and candidates who then apply it to the 8% Fennimore stake or to the fund subscription lose the correctness criterion. The second is section 327. Many candidates recite the five conditions and conclude the firm can advise on the fund because it is a solicitors' firm and the work relates to a matter it is handling. The answer is that recommending or arranging units in a collective investment scheme sits on the prohibited list, so section 327 never gets off the ground, and separately the activity is not incidental to any professional service. A strong candidate also refuses the introduction fee for conflict reasons and not only because it breaks a FSMA condition.

Written station 27: Board minute approving a supply agreement and a related party transaction

Legal drafting  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  45 minutes

Model answer

MINUTES OF A MEETING OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF MERIDIAN FOUNDRY LIMITED (the Company)

Held at Unit 9 Thornaby Vale Industrial Estate on 5 October 2026 at 14.00

PRESENT

Ms Ovie Lambert (chair)

Mr Rasheed Anwar

Ms Beatrix Okere

Mr Callum Threlfall

IN ATTENDANCE

Ms Ovie Lambert, company secretary

Ms Nadia Speight of Speight and Coyne, solicitors, by invitation

1. CHAIR, NOTICE AND QUORUM

1.1 Ms Lambert took the chair.

1.2 The chair reported that notice of the meeting, with the papers, had been given to each director on 28 September 2026 in accordance with article 9, and that a quorum of directors was present in accordance with article 11.

1.3 The chair declared the meeting duly convened and open.

2. DECLARATION OF INTEREST

2.1 Mr Anwar declared that he is the freehold owner of Unit 14 Thornaby Vale Industrial Estate, the property the subject of item 4 below, that he would receive the whole of the purchase price of 265,000 pounds personally, and that he had given written notice of the nature and extent of that interest to each of the other directors on 21 September 2026. The declaration was made before the Company entered into any transaction or arrangement in respect of the property.

2.2 The board noted the declaration and that, under article 14 as amended by the special resolution passed on 3 April 2024, Mr Anwar was not to be counted for quorum or voting purposes on item 4.
