2.3 No director declared any interest in the matter the subject of item 3 below.

3. SUPPLY AGREEMENT WITH CALDERBECK ALLOYS LIMITED

3.1 There was produced to the meeting the final form supply agreement between the Company and Calderbeck Alloys Limited for a term of five years from 1 November 2026, providing for a minimum annual spend of 480,000 pounds, an annual price review on each 1 November by reference to a published index, and termination by either party on six months' written notice for convenience at any time after the third anniversary of commencement.

3.2 The board considered the terms of the agreement, and in particular the level of the minimum annual spend and the terms on which the Company could exit, and was satisfied that entering into the agreement would be most likely to promote the success of the Company for the benefit of its members as a whole.

3.3 IT WAS RESOLVED THAT:

(a) the supply agreement produced to the meeting be and is approved; and

(b) any two directors be and are authorised to execute the supply agreement on behalf of the Company in the form produced, with such non material amendments as the directors executing it think fit, and to do all such other acts as may be necessary to give effect to it.

4. PROPOSED PURCHASE OF UNIT 14 THORNABY VALE INDUSTRIAL ESTATE FROM MR ANWAR

4.1 Mr Anwar, having made the declaration recorded at paragraph 2.1, withdrew from the meeting before the discussion and did not vote. The remaining three directors constituted a quorum.

4.2 There was produced to the meeting a written valuation of Unit 14 dated 22 September 2026 prepared by Hurst and Ballantyne, chartered surveyors, giving a value in the range 262,000 pounds to 270,000 pounds.

4.3 The board considered the valuation, the proposed price of 265,000 pounds, and the fact that the Company already occupies Unit 14 under a short lease at a rent of 24,000 pounds a year, and was satisfied that the purchase at that price was in the interests of the Company and would be most likely to promote its success for the benefit of its members as a whole.

4.4 The board noted that Mr Anwar is a director of the Company, that Unit 14 is a non cash asset, and that its value exceeds 100,000 pounds, so that it is a substantial non cash asset within section 191 of the Companies Act 2006. The board further noted that under section 190 of that Act the Company may not enter into the arrangement unless it has been approved by a resolution of the members or is conditional on such approval being obtained.

4.5 IT WAS RESOLVED THAT:

(a) the Company enter into a contract to purchase the freehold of Unit 14 Thornaby Vale Industrial Estate from Mr Rasheed Anwar at a price of 265,000 pounds, such contract to be expressly conditional upon the approval of the members of the Company by ordinary resolution in accordance with section 190 of the Companies Act 2006; and

(b) subject to and conditional upon that approval being obtained, any director other than Mr Anwar be and is authorised to agree the remaining terms of the contract and transfer and to execute them on behalf of the Company.

4.6 Mr Anwar returned to the meeting and was informed of the resolution.

5. MEMBERS' APPROVAL

5.1 The board considered the means by which the approval of the members should be sought.

5.2 IT WAS RESOLVED THAT:

(a) the approval of the members be sought by way of a written resolution under Chapter 2 of Part 13 of the Companies Act 2006;

(b) the company secretary be and is authorised to circulate to every eligible member the proposed written resolution, together with a memorandum setting out the terms of the proposed arrangement, and to do so before or at the same time as the resolution is circulated; and

(c) the company secretary be and is authorised to take all steps necessary to procure the passing of the written resolution.

6. ANY OTHER BUSINESS

6.1 There was no other business.

7. CLOSE

7.1 There being no further business the chair declared the meeting closed at 15.20.

.............................................

Ms Ovie Lambert

Chair

Dated: 6 October 2026

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The company secretary reports that Mr Anwar wants the minute dated 21 September 2026 and the approval recorded as given on that date, so that it matches emails he has already sent to the seller's agent. A minute is the company's statutory record under section 248 of the Companies Act 2006 and it must record what actually happened. Backdating it would create a false document capable of misleading the other shareholders, the company's auditors and any buyer of the company, and it would be a breach of the duty to act with honesty and with integrity and of the prohibition on misleading others. A competent candidate simply does not do it: the minute records a meeting held on 5 October 2026, is dated when it is signed, and records the written declaration of 21 September 2026 as a declaration and nothing more. The candidate does not need to lecture the client inside the minute, and should not; the resolution of the issue shows in the document being accurate.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsWrites in the settled register of a board minute, in the past tense, using "IT WAS RESOLVED THAT" for each operative decision and reporting language for the narrative. Each resolution is a single sentence that can be read out of context and still make sense. No commentary, no advice to the client and no editorialising about Mr Anwar's request.Writes the minute as a narrative of who said what, so that no resolution is separately identifiable, or slips into advisory language such as "the board should note that it must obtain members' approval", which turns the minute into a memorandum.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsUses a conventional minute structure with heading, present, in attendance, chair and quorum, declarations of interest, then a separately numbered and headed item for each item of business in the order taken, then any other business and close, with signature and date blocks. Numbering is consistent and every resolution is separately identified.Runs the supply agreement, the property purchase and the members' approval together under one heading, or omits the present, quorum and notice section altogether, so that the minute does not evidence that the meeting was validly held.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawRecords Mr Anwar's declaration of the nature and extent of his interest and that it was made before the Company entered into the arrangement, applies article 14 as amended so that he is excluded from both quorum and vote on item 4, and records that the remaining three directors still formed a quorum under article 11. Makes the purchase resolution expressly conditional on members' approval under section 190, rather than an unconditional approval. Dates the minute correctly and records the meeting as held on 5 October 2026.Records the purchase as unconditionally approved by the board, so that the minute evidences the Company entering into an arrangement in breach of section 190. Or counts Mr Anwar in the quorum or in the vote on item 4, when article 14 in the amended form set out in the materials excludes him from both, and the unamended model article would also have excluded him because none of the exceptions in article 14(3) applies. Or fails to record the exclusion and the fact that the remaining three directors still constituted a quorum under article 11. Or backdates the minute or the resolution to 21 September 2026.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers every item actually transacted, including the authority for any two directors to execute the supply agreement, the authority to execute the property documents given to a director other than Mr Anwar, and the resolution to seek the members' approval by written resolution. Records the board's decision that a memorandum setting out the terms of the proposed arrangement be circulated with the written resolution, which section 190 does not require but which is what the board resolved and is proper practice if the members are to reach an informed decision. Identifies the asset as substantial by reference to the 100,000 pound limb of section 191 and records the board's reasoning on the valuation.Omits the signing authorities, so the minute records a decision but confers no power to execute anything, or omits item 3 on members' approval, or fails to record the valuation and the board's consideration of it, leaving no evidence that the directors turned their minds to the price.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDoes not backdate. Dates the minute the day it is made and records the meeting on its true date of 5 October 2026, and records the declaration as having been given on 21 September 2026 only because that is what actually happened. The candidate's document is an accurate record, and the candidate does not incorporate Mr Anwar's request in any form, whether by dating the minute earlier or by describing the board as having approved the purchase on 21 September.Dates the minute or the resolution 21 September 2026, or writes a form of words that leaves the reader to infer approval was given then. That is the creation of a misleading document and is a breach of the duty to act with honesty and integrity, and it fails this criterion outright however good the rest of the drafting is.

Examiner notes

Two things separate a pass from a fail. The first is whether the purchase resolution is made conditional on members' approval. Section 190 is set out in the materials, the value plainly exceeds 100,000 pounds and the whole point of item 3 was that the members had to approve it, so a board minute that unconditionally approves the purchase is legally wrong on the face of it. The second is the date. The trap is that the backdating request arrives in a note appended to the partner's rough notes, after the substance, and the partner says she will deal with the rest, which many candidates read as permission to leave it alone. It is not. The candidate deals with it by producing an accurate minute. A weaker candidate writes a good looking minute and then dates it 21 September because the client asked, and fails the ethics criterion. The other common error is failing to record the effect of article 14 at all, or recording Mr Anwar as having been counted in the quorum or as having voted. Note that the unamended model article 14 would exclude him too, because none of the exceptions in article 14(3) applies to a director selling his own property to the company; what the amendment of 3 April 2024 does is strip those exceptions out, so that the only route by which an interested director could be counted is an ordinary resolution of the members disapplying the article, and none has been passed. The minute should record the exclusion and record that the remaining three directors still formed a quorum under article 11.

Written station 28: Confidentiality provision in a settlement agreement with a departing finance director

Legal drafting  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  45 minutes

Model answer

12. CONFIDENTIALITY

12.1 Definition

In this clause 12, "Confidential Information" means (a) the amount of the Settlement Sum and the other financial terms of this agreement; (b) the content of the negotiations leading to this agreement; and (c) information which is not in the public domain relating to the Company's clients and counterparties, its client lists, its pricing and risk models and its counterparty credit lines. Confidential Information does not include the fact that the Employee's employment has ended, the wording in Schedule 2 or the wording in Schedule 3.

12.2 The Employee's obligation

Subject to clause 12.3, the Employee shall not disclose Confidential Information to any person, and shall not use it for any purpose other than a purpose permitted by this agreement.

12.3 Permitted disclosures

Nothing in this agreement, and nothing in this clause 12, prevents the Employee from, or shall be treated as discouraging her from, making any of the following disclosures, and she is under no obligation to notify the Company or to obtain its consent before or after doing so:

(a) reporting any misconduct, any wrongdoing, or any breach of a legal or regulatory obligation, whether by the Company, by any of its officers or employees, or by any other person, to the Financial Conduct Authority, the National Crime Agency, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the police, any other regulator or law enforcement agency, or any body having supervisory or investigatory functions in relation to the Company;

(b) co operating with any criminal investigation or prosecution, or with any investigation, review or enquiry by any body referred to in clause 12.3(a), including responding to any question put to her by any of them, and giving evidence to a court or tribunal;

(c) making a protected disclosure within the meaning of section 43A of the Employment Rights Act 1996;

(d) making any disclosure required or permitted by law, by any court or tribunal of competent jurisdiction, or by any binding rule of any regulatory body;

(e) making any disclosure under Part 7 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, or to a nominated officer of the Company;

(f) making any disclosure to the auditors of the Company, to the chair or any member of its audit committee, to any of its non executive directors, or to any person conducting an investigation, review or enquiry on behalf of the Company or of its audit committee, including responding to any question put to her by any of them;

(g) discussing this agreement, her employment or the circumstances of its ending with her spouse, civil partner or immediate family, with a medical practitioner, therapist or counsellor treating her, with her insurers, with His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, or with her legal, financial or other professional advisers, in each case (other than a disclosure to a public body or a legal adviser) on the basis that the person to whom the disclosure is made keeps it confidential;

(h) confirming to a prospective employer, or to a body regulating the Employee, the fact and dates of her employment, her job title and the reason for the ending of her employment as set out in Schedule 2, and making any disclosure required by any body regulating the Employee; and

(i) enforcing this agreement, or defending any claim brought against her.

12.4 The report of 3 March 2027

Nothing in this agreement requires the Employee to withdraw the internal memorandum she sent to the chair of the audit committee on 3 March 2027, to state that the matters set out in it were mistaken, to take or refrain from taking any step in relation to it, or to refrain from co operating with the audit committee's review of it.

12.5 The Company's obligation

The Company shall not, and shall procure that its officers and its Human Resources and senior management personnel shall not, disclose Confidential Information to any person, save (a) to those of its officers, employees and professional advisers who need to know it, (b) to its auditors, insurers and regulators, (c) as required by law or by any regulatory body, and (d) as required to enforce this agreement.

12.6 Non disparagement

Neither the Employee nor the Company (acting by its officers and its Human Resources and senior management personnel) shall make any statement about the other which is intended to disparage the other, save that nothing in this clause 12.6 prevents either party from making any disclosure permitted by clause 12.3 or from giving a truthful account of any matter to any person to whom a disclosure is permitted by clause 12.3.

12.7 Remedies

12.7.1 If the Employee breaches clause 12.2, the Company's remedies are damages and, if the court thinks fit, injunctive relief. The Employee is not required to repay the Settlement Sum or any part of it, and no sum is payable by way of liquidated damages or indemnity costs, by reason of any breach of this clause 12.

12.7.2 Clause 12.7.1 does not apply to, and no remedy of any kind is available in respect of, any disclosure permitted by clause 12.3 or any matter within clause 12.4.

12.8 Severance

If any provision of this clause 12 is or becomes invalid or unenforceable, it shall be deemed modified to the minimum extent necessary to make it valid and enforceable, or if modification is not possible it shall be deemed deleted, and the deemed modification or deletion shall not affect the validity or enforceability of the rest of this clause 12 or of this agreement.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

This is the SRA warning notice on non disclosure agreements, unflagged. The chief executive has drafted a clause that would prevent his former finance director from speaking to the Financial Conduct Authority, the National Crime Agency, HMRC, the police, the company's auditors, her own family, her doctor and her own advisers, would require her to withdraw a report that the company may have failed to make a required money laundering disclosure and to say it was mistaken, and would claw back the entire settlement sum if she spoke to anyone. He has also said he will withdraw the agreed reference if she will not sign, which is oppressive leverage. A solicitor must not use a non disclosure agreement to prevent a person reporting misconduct or a regulatory breach to a regulator or law enforcement agency, to prevent co operation with a criminal investigation, to prevent a protected disclosure, or to prevent disclosure to family, a medical professional, an insurer or a professional adviser, and must not include clauses known to be unenforceable or use oppressive tactics. Section 43J of the Employment Rights Act 1996 makes the protected disclosure element void in any event, and a term purporting to prevent a disclosure under Part 7 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 would put the client's former employee at risk of committing an offence. The candidate resolves it inside the document, by drafting a confidentiality clause that protects the settlement figure and the company's genuine trade secrets while expressly preserving every carve out, by deleting the withdrawal of the report and by replacing the clawback with an ordinary damages and injunction remedy that cannot apply to a permitted disclosure. The instruction to make it "as wide as it will possibly go" is not one that can be followed.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsWrites the carve outs in plain, unqualified language a departing employee can read and rely on, for example "Nothing in this agreement prevents the Employee from", with no requirement to notify the Company first and no consent requirement attached. Defines Confidential Information tightly rather than prohibiting disclosure of "any matter whatsoever".Writes carve outs which are then hedged, for example "provided that the Employee shall first notify the Company" or "save where the Company consents". A carve out subject to the employer's consent is not a carve out, and it is the exact chilling effect the warning notice is aimed at.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsPuts the restriction first, then the definition of what is actually confidential, then the permitted disclosures as a single clearly signposted clause that expressly overrides everything else, then the mutual obligation, non disparagement, remedies and severance. The carve outs are prominent, not buried at the end of a long sub clause.Buries the permitted disclosures in a proviso at the end of clause 12.1, or scatters them across several sub clauses, so a reader cannot tell what she is free to do. Or keeps the original numbering and simply crosses out clause 12.2, leaving a clause with no carve outs at all.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawUnderstands that clause 12.1 of the draft, in so far as it purports to preclude a protected disclosure, is void under section 43J of the Employment Rights Act 1996, and that a clause purporting to stop a report to the National Crime Agency under Part 7 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 is contrary to law and would expose Ms Feilding to criminal liability. Removes the clawback of the whole Settlement Sum on any breach, which bites on the disclosures the clause must preserve, is oppressive in that it is calculated to deter her from making them, and is in any event at risk of being unenforceable as a penalty under Cavendish Square Holding BV v Talal El Makdessi, being a detriment out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the Company in enforcing confidentiality. Removes the acknowledgment that damages would not be an adequate remedy and the reference to an injunction without notice, which do not bind the court.Keeps a prohibition on approaching the FCA or the NCA in any form, or keeps clause 12.3 requiring the withdrawal of the report and a statement that it was mistaken. Either of those makes the whole clause improper, and the second is an attempt to influence the substance of a report about a suspected failure to report money laundering.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawProtects what the Company is legitimately entitled to protect: the settlement figure, the negotiations and its genuine confidential information such as client lists, pricing model and credit lines. Includes the full set of carve outs: regulators and law enforcement, co operating with an investigation, protected disclosures, disclosures required by law, disclosures under Part 7 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, family, medical practitioner, insurers, HMRC and professional advisers, and confirming basic employment facts to a prospective employer. Makes the confidentiality mutual, deals with the announcement and the reference, and adds severance.Produces a clause consisting only of carve outs, protecting nothing, so the client gets no confidentiality at all and the settlement figure can be published. Or forgets that the obligation should be mutual, so the Company remains free to discuss the terms while Ms Feilding cannot.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawProduces a clause that on its face preserves every carve out the SRA warning notice requires, and does not include anything the drafter knows is unenforceable. Does not include the withdrawal of the report, does not include any clause deterring contact with a regulator, and does not use the reference in Schedule 2 as leverage. The clause is drafted so that Ms Feilding, reading it, would understand that she remains free to speak to the FCA and the NCA.Softens the original rather than removing it, for example by requiring Ms Feilding to give the Company notice before contacting a regulator, or by keeping the whole sum clawback so that the practical effect is still to deter her. Drafting a clause the drafter knows to be unenforceable, in the hope it will frighten her into silence, is itself a breach and fails this criterion.

Examiner notes

This station is failed in two opposite directions. The larger group of candidates does what the client asked, tidying the grammar of Mr Whyle-Baptiste's draft and perhaps softening clause 12.2 to require the company's prior consent before Ms Feilding contacts a regulator. That is still an improper non disclosure agreement and it fails both application of law criteria and the ethics criterion. The smaller group overcorrects and writes a page of carve outs with no operative restriction at all, which is legally ineffective and gives the paying client nothing. A pass needs both halves: a real, enforceable protection of the settlement figure, the negotiations and the company's genuine confidential information, and a prominent, unqualified permitted disclosures clause. The single most reliable marker of a strong answer is that no carve out is made conditional on notifying or obtaining the consent of the company. Two details separate an A from a B: expressly disapplying the remedies clause to permitted disclosures, and expressly stating that nothing in the agreement requires Ms Feilding to withdraw the report of 3 March 2027 or to say it was mistaken. Note also that clause 12.3 of the draft is not merely unenforceable, it is an attempt to suppress a report about a suspected failure to make a money laundering disclosure, and a candidate who leaves any trace of it in the redraft cannot pass the ethics criterion.

Written station 29: Warranty limitations and a tax indemnity in a share purchase agreement

Legal drafting  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  45 minutes

Model answer

7. LIMITATIONS ON THE SELLERS' LIABILITY

7.1 Application

7.1.1 This clause 7 applies to any Claim. Clauses 7.1.2, 7.6 and 7.7 apply also to a claim under clause 8. The other provisions of this clause 7 apply to a claim under clause 8 only where clause 8.3 expressly so provides.

7.1.2 Nothing in this clause 7 or in this agreement limits or excludes the liability of a Seller for fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation or wilful concealment by that Seller.

7.2 Thresholds

7.2.1 The Sellers shall have no liability for a Claim unless the amount of that Claim exceeds 7,500 pounds.

7.2.2 The Sellers shall have no liability for a Claim unless the aggregate amount of all Claims which each exceed 7,500 pounds equals or exceeds 75,000 pounds, in which case the Sellers shall be liable for the whole of that aggregate amount and not merely the excess over 75,000 pounds.

7.2.3 Clauses 7.2.1 and 7.2.2 do not apply to a claim under clause 8, to a claim under the Title and Capacity Warranties, or to a claim to which clause 7.1.2 applies.

7.3 Cap

7.3.1 The aggregate liability of the Sellers under this agreement, including under clause 8, shall not exceed 3,400,000 pounds.

7.3.2 Clause 7.3.1 does not apply to a claim under the Title and Capacity Warranties or to a claim to which clause 7.1.2 applies, and the liability of the Sellers in respect of any such claim is unlimited.

7.4 Time limits

7.4.1 The Sellers shall have no liability for a Claim unless the Buyer has given the Sellers written notice of it, stating in reasonable detail the nature of the Claim and, so far as reasonably practicable, the Buyer's estimate of the amount claimed:

(a) in the case of a Claim under the Warranties relating to Tax, or a claim under clause 8, on or before the seventh anniversary of Completion;

(b) in the case of any other Claim, other than under the Title and Capacity Warranties, on or before the second anniversary of Completion.

7.4.2 There is no time limit for a claim under the Title and Capacity Warranties or for a claim to which clause 7.1.2 applies.

7.4.3 A Claim notified under clause 7.4.1 shall be treated as withdrawn, and the Sellers shall have no liability for it, unless proceedings in respect of it have been issued and validly served on the Sellers within 9 months of the date of the notice. Where the Claim is based on a contingent liability, the 9 month period runs from the date on which that liability becomes an actual liability which is due and payable.

7.5 Disclosure

7.5.1 The Sellers shall have no liability for a Claim to the extent that the matter giving rise to it is fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter, with sufficient detail to enable the Buyer to make a reasonably informed assessment of the matter and of its likely effect on the Company.

7.5.2 No other disclosure, and no knowledge or means of knowledge of the Buyer, limits the liability of the Sellers. In particular, the Sellers shall not be entitled to rely on the Buyer having made or being able to have made any enquiry, on the Buyer's actual, constructive or imputed knowledge, or on any document being in a data room or otherwise made available to the Buyer.

7.5.3 Clause 7.5.1 does not apply to a claim under clause 8.

7.6 Liability of the Sellers

The liability of the Sellers under this agreement is joint and several.

7.7 No double recovery and insurance

7.7.1 The Buyer is not entitled to recover more than once in respect of the same loss.

7.7.2 The Sellers shall have no liability for a Claim to the extent that the Buyer or the Company has actually recovered from an insurer, in respect of the same loss, a sum in cleared funds net of the costs of recovery.

7.8 Third party claims

7.8.1 If the Buyer becomes aware of a claim by a third party which may give rise to a Claim, the Buyer shall give the Sellers written notice of it within 20 Working Days, shall keep the Sellers informed of its progress, and shall consult the Sellers before making any admission of liability or entering into any settlement.

7.8.2 The Buyer shall have conduct of any such third party claim and shall have the final decision on how it is dealt with, provided that the Buyer acts in good faith. The Sellers shall reimburse the Buyer's reasonable costs of dealing with any third party claim to the extent that it gives rise to a Claim for which the Sellers are liable.

7.9 Acts after Completion

The Sellers shall have no liability for a Claim to the extent that it arises from an act of the Buyer or the Company after Completion which is outside the ordinary course of the Company's business as carried on at Completion and which the Buyer knew, or ought reasonably to have known, would give rise to the Claim. This clause 7.9 does not apply where the act was required by law, by a Tax Authority, or by this agreement.

8. INDEMNITY: CUSTOMS DUTY AND IMPORT VAT ON IMPORTED HULL SECTIONS

8.1 Indemnity

The Sellers shall indemnify the Buyer, and shall keep the Buyer indemnified, on demand and pound for pound, against:

(a) any customs duty, import VAT, or other Tax which the Company is or becomes liable to pay to any Tax Authority in respect of the importation of prefabricated hull sections from Norway during the period from 1 March 2023 to Completion, including any liability arising from the classification of those goods under an incorrect commodity code or from the understatement of the customs value of those goods;

(b) all interest, penalties, fines and surcharges arising in connection with any liability within clause 8.1(a);

(c) any Tax, interest, penalty or surcharge arising from the making or the failure to make any disclosure to a Tax Authority in respect of any matter within clause 8.1(a) at any time before Completion; and

(d) all reasonable costs and expenses properly incurred by the Buyer or the Company in connection with any matter within clauses 8.1(a) to 8.1(c), including the reasonable fees of accountants, customs advisers and lawyers, and the reasonable costs of dealing with the enquiry opened by His Majesty's Revenue and Customs by letter dated 14 January 2027.

8.2 After tax basis

If any payment under this clause 8 is subject to Tax in the hands of the recipient, or would be but for the use of a relief, the amount payable shall be increased so that the recipient retains, after that Tax, a sum equal to the amount it would have retained had the payment not been subject to Tax.

8.3 Relationship with clause 7

8.3.1 Clauses 7.2 and 7.5 do not apply to a claim under this clause 8. In particular, the Sellers are not entitled to rely on any disclosure in the Disclosure Letter, or on the Buyer's knowledge of any matter, in answer to a claim under this clause 8.

8.3.2 Clause 7.3 applies to a claim under this clause 8, so that a claim under this clause 8 counts towards and is subject to the cap in clause 7.3.1. Clauses 7.1.2, 7.6 and 7.7 also apply to a claim under this clause 8, so that no limitation applies to fraud, the liability of the Sellers under this clause 8 is joint and several, and the Buyer may not recover more than once in respect of the same loss or recover to the extent that it or the Company has actually recovered the same loss from an insurer.

8.3.3 A claim under this clause 8 must be notified in accordance with clause 7.4.1(a).

8.4 Payment

The Sellers shall pay any sum due under this clause 8 within 10 Working Days of written demand by the Buyer or, if later, 5 Working Days before the date on which the Tax in question is due and payable to the Tax Authority without incurring interest or a penalty. Any sum not paid when due shall carry interest at 4 per cent a year above the base rate of the Bank of England from the due date until payment, both before and after judgment.

8.5 Conduct of the enquiry

8.5.1 The Buyer shall notify the Sellers in writing of any assessment, demand, enquiry or other communication from a Tax Authority which may give rise to a claim under this clause 8, within 20 Working Days of receipt.

8.5.2 The Buyer shall have conduct of any such matter. The Buyer shall keep the Sellers informed, shall provide the Sellers with copies of material correspondence, and shall consult the Sellers and consider in good faith any written representations they make within 10 Working Days of being consulted, before submitting any substantive response to the Tax Authority or entering into any settlement.

8.5.3 Nothing in this clause 8.5 requires the Buyer or the Company to withhold, delay or alter any disclosure to a Tax Authority which the Buyer or the Company is required by law to make, or to take any step which the Buyer reasonably considers may be misleading to a Tax Authority.

8.6 Survival

This clause 8 continues in force after Completion.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The buyer's managing director asks for the indemnity to be drafted so that the seller's solicitors will not notice how wide it is: a neutral heading, no reference to the commodity code or the Norwegian imports, and wording that reads as boilerplate. He also volunteers that he learned privately from the target's finance director that the sellers already know the classification is wrong. A solicitor may drive a hard bargain for a client and may certainly draft a wide indemnity that a buyer is commercially entitled to ask for, but must not deceive or mislead others, including another party's solicitor, whether by act or omission. Drafting a clause with a deliberately misleading heading and deliberately obscured scope, for the purpose of stopping the other side's advisers from understanding what they are signing, crosses that line. The candidate resolves it by drafting the indemnity plainly and openly, with an accurate heading, an express identification of the subject matter, and an express statement that disclosure does not defeat it. The client loses nothing he is entitled to: the clause is just as protective when it is honest. Whether to tell the sellers what the finance director said is not a matter for the clause, and the candidate should not include anything about it in the document.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsUses the agreed clause 1 definitions exactly, in particular Claim, Tax, Tax Authority, Title and Capacity Warranties and Working Day, and does not redefine them. Each limitation is expressed as a single obligation with its exceptions identified by cross reference rather than repeated. The indemnity is drafted as an on demand, pound for pound obligation in words that leave no room for argument about measure of loss.Writes the indemnity in warranty language, for example "the Sellers warrant that no duty is payable", which puts the buyer back into proving loss, causation and mitigation and defeats the purpose of an indemnity. Or invents new definitions that conflict with clause 1.
Structure the document appropriately and logically.SkillsClause 7 runs from application and the fraud carve out, through thresholds, cap, time limits, disclosure, joint and several liability, double recovery and insurance, third party conduct and post completion acts. Clause 8 states the indemnity, then the after tax gross up, then its relationship with clause 7, then payment, conduct and survival. Each exclusion from a limitation is stated once, in the sub clause it belongs to.Scatters the carve outs, so that fraud, the title warranties and the clause 8 indemnity are excepted in some sub clauses and silently caught by others. Or drafts clause 8 without saying anywhere how it interacts with clause 7, leaving it arguable that the thresholds and the disclosure defence apply to it.
Draft a document which is legally correct.Application of lawReverses each of the seller friendly positions to the agreed position and gets the mechanics right: the aggregate threshold is a tipping basket, not an excess basket, so once 75,000 pounds is reached the whole sum is recoverable. Liability is joint and several, not joint. Disclosure is limited to fair disclosure with sufficient detail, and constructive and deemed knowledge are expressly excluded. Provides that no limitation applies to fraud, and gives the buyer an uncapped, unlimited time claim on title and capacity. Drafts clause 8 so that a disclosure of the HMRC letter cannot defeat it, which is the whole reason a specific indemnity is being asked for.Leaves the disclosure clause covering knowledge or reasonable enquiry, which on these facts is fatal, because the HMRC letter of 14 January 2027 will be disclosed and would defeat any warranty claim. Or reproduces the excess basket in clause 7.1 of the seller's draft instead of a tipping basket. Or leaves liability joint, so the buyer must sue both sellers together.
Draft a document which is legally comprehensive.Application of lawCovers every point in the heads of terms, including the individual and aggregate thresholds, the cap and its carve outs, the three tier time limits, the 9 month issue and serve provision with its contingent claim variant, the fair disclosure standard, joint and several liability, no double recovery, the insurance recovery limit and the conduct provisions with the buyer's costs met. Clause 8 covers duty, import VAT, interest, penalties, the cost of the enquiry, the after tax gross up, the payment mechanic tied to the date the tax is due, default interest and conduct.Drafts the indemnity to cover the duty only, leaving the buyer to bear the interest, the penalty of up to 30 per cent and the adviser costs. Or omits the after tax gross up, which the heads of terms expressly require. Or leaves out the payment date, so the sellers may pay after HMRC's due date and the company still bears the interest.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDrafts clause 8 openly. Heads it as a specific indemnity for the customs duty and import VAT on the imported hull sections, identifies the goods, the period and the HMRC enquiry of 14 January 2027 by reference, and states plainly in clause 8.3 that disclosure and the thresholds do not apply to it. The buyer's position is fully protected and nothing is concealed from the other side's advisers. Also declines to draft any conduct provision that would allow a required disclosure to a Tax Authority to be withheld or altered.Follows the client's instruction: heads the clause "General tax matters", avoids naming the commodity code or the Norwegian imports, and buries the anti disclosure wording so that the seller's solicitors are likely to miss it. That is drafting a document intended to mislead another party's advisers, and it fails this criterion however commercially effective the clause is.

Examiner notes

Two technical points decide this station. The first is the tipping basket. The seller's draft gives an excess basket at 500,000 pounds; the heads of terms require a tipping basket at 75,000 pounds, so that once the aggregate is reached the sellers pay the whole amount. Candidates who write "liable only for the excess" have given away the agreed position. The second is disclosure, and it is the reason clause 8 exists at all. The HMRC letter of 14 January 2027 will be disclosed in the Disclosure Letter, so any warranty claim on the customs point is dead. A specific indemnity is only worth having if it is expressly taken outside the disclosure clause and outside the thresholds, and a candidate who drafts a fine indemnity and then leaves clause 7.5 applying to it has produced something worthless. The ethics trap is unusually easy to miss because the client is not asking for anything substantively improper: he is entitled to the indemnity, and the anti disclosure wording is correct. What he is asking for is camouflage. Candidates who follow the instruction usually do so without noticing they have, because heading a clause "General tax matters" feels like a stylistic choice rather than a deception. Look for a clause 8 that names its subject matter in its own heading. That single feature separates the candidates who spotted it from those who did not.

Written station 30: Share sale advice, regulated activity and the professional firms exemption

Legal research  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO RUTH CALDERBANK

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 14 September 2026

Matter: Ubhi and others, proposed sale of Harewood Precision Engineering Limited

Subject: Financial services perimeter, whether we may act on the investment elements

1. Summary of advice

1.1 Advising the shareholders on the merits of accepting loan notes rather than cash is prima facie advising on investments under article 53 of the Regulated Activities Order. Putting the deal together with the buyer's corporate finance advisers is prima facie arranging deals in investments under article 25.

1.2 Both are nevertheless taken outside the regulated activity altogether by the sale of body corporate exclusion in article 70, because the sellers are disposing of 100 per cent of the voting shares and the three of them are a group of connected individuals. On that footing we do not need the professional firms exemption at all and we may do both pieces of work.

1.3 The proposed introduction fee from Kesteven is the real problem. It does not by itself take us outside article 70, but if we ever have to fall back on Part XX of the Act, an unaccounted for fee would destroy the exemption. Independently, we cannot keep it without telling the sellers. I deal with this at section 5.

2. Is either piece of work a regulated activity?

2.1 An activity is a regulated activity if it is of a specified kind, carried on by way of business, and relates to a specified investment: section 22(1) of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. We plainly act by way of business.

2.2 The investments. The ordinary shares in Harewood are shares in a body corporate and are a specified investment under article 76 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 (SI 2001/544). The buyer's unsecured loan notes are instruments creating or acknowledging indebtedness and are a specified investment under article 77.

2.3 Advising on the loan notes. Article 53(1) specifies advice given to a person in his capacity as an investor on the merits of his buying, selling, exchanging, redeeming or holding a particular investment. Mr Ubhi has asked whether the notes are worth having as against cash. That is advice on the merits of acquiring a particular article 77 investment, not an explanation of the legal effect of the loan note instrument. The distinction is drawn at paragraph 9.14 of the practitioner extract at Source D and I agree with it. Explaining what the instrument says would not be article 53 advice. Telling them whether to take it is.

2.4 Dealing with Kesteven to structure and conclude the sale. Article 25(1) specifies making arrangements for another person to buy or sell a particular investment. Negotiating the terms of the share sale on the sellers' behalf and bringing it to signature is making arrangements for them to sell the Harewood shares, a specified investment under article 76. Article 25(2) would in any event catch arrangements with a view to a person participating buying or selling.

2.5 Both activities are therefore specified activities relating to specified investments and would be regulated activities unless an exclusion applies.

3. Does an exclusion apply?

3.1 Article 70, sale of body corporate. This excludes from both article 25 and article 53 any activity carried on for the purposes of or in connection with the acquisition or disposal of shares in a body corporate, provided both limbs of article 70(1) are met.

3.2 Limb (a), the shares. The exclusion applies where the shares consist of or include 50 per cent or more of the voting shares, or the object of the transaction may reasonably be regarded as the acquisition of day to day control. The sellers are disposing of the entire issued ordinary share capital and the buyer will replace the board on completion. Limb (a) is comfortably satisfied on either alternative.

3.3 Limb (b), the parties. The disposal must be between parties each of whom is a body corporate, a partnership, a single individual or a group of connected individuals. The buyer, Fentonbridge Industrial Holdings Limited, is a body corporate. The sellers are three individuals, so they must be a group of connected individuals within article 70(2). All three are directors of Harewood, which brings each of them within article 70(2)(a) in their own right. Mr Ubhi and Mrs Ubhi-Nolan are in any event siblings and so close relatives within article 70(2)(b). Limb (b) is satisfied.

3.4 The wording of article 70 is deliberately wide, covering any transaction and any activity entered into or carried on for the purposes of or in connection with the acquisition or disposal. Advice on whether to take loan notes as part of the consideration for those shares is given in connection with the disposal, and the negotiation with Kesteven plainly is. Both pieces of work fall inside the exclusion.

3.5 Article 67, the necessary part exclusion. I would not rely on this. It requires the activity to be capable of being regarded as a necessary part of our other professional services, and article 67(2) withdraws it entirely where the activity is separately remunerated. If we raise a distinct fee for the loan note advice we lose it. Source D at paragraph 9.11 makes the same point, and it was the ground on which the firm in Hallowfield v Brenchley Partners failed. Article 70 is the better and safer answer and we should not need article 67.

4. If we are wrong about article 70, does Part XX help?

4.1 If for any reason article 70 did not apply, for example if the deal were restructured so that the sellers sold only a minority stake, we would have to rely on the exemption in section 327 of the Act. The firm holds no Part 4A permission, so the general prohibition in section 19 would otherwise bite.

4.2 The section 327 conditions, applied to us, would be:

(a) section 327(2), we are controlled and managed by members of a profession, satisfied;

(b) section 327(3), we must not receive from a person other than the client any pecuniary reward for which we do not account to the client, dealt with at section 5 below, and this is where we are exposed;

(c) section 327(4), the manner of provision of the service must be incidental to our professional services, satisfied if the advice is given as part of the sale retainer rather than as a standalone investment advisory engagement;

(d) section 327(5), only one designated professional body has made rules, the Solicitors Regulation Authority, satisfied;

(e) section 327(6), the activity must not be one specified by the Treasury. Article 4 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Professional Firms) Order 2001 (SI 2001/1227) specifies dealing as principal, accepting deposits, insurance as principal, collective investment schemes and the rest. Advising and arranging on a share sale are not on that list, satisfied;

(f) section 327(7), no FCA order or direction under sections 328 or 329 applies to us, satisfied.

4.3 We would also have to satisfy the SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules. Rule 2.1 prohibits us from carrying on any regulated activity except an exempt regulated activity, and rule 2.2 imposes conditions mirroring section 327, including at rule 2.2(a) that the activity arise out of or be complementary to a particular professional service to a particular client, and at rule 2.2(c) that we account to the client for any third party benefit. Rule 3.1 lists prohibited activities. None of them is engaged. In particular we would not be recommending a packaged product to a retail client under rule 3.1(e), because loan notes issued by a corporate buyer as deal consideration are not a packaged product.

5. The Kesteven introduction fee

5.1 This needs dealing with before you call Mr Ubhi. Kesteven has offered the firm 1 per cent of any sums the sellers place with its wealth management arm, and has suggested there is no need to tell the sellers.

5.2 We cannot accept it on that basis. Section 327(3) of the Act permits a third party benefit only where we account to the client for it, and section 327(8) defines client widely enough to catch the three sellers. Rule 2.2(c) of the Scope Rules says the same. Source D at paragraph 9.20 makes the point that a failure to account destroys the exemption for the whole of the activity, not just the tainted part.

5.3 Independently of the financial services position, paragraph 4.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors requires us to account properly to clients for any financial benefit we receive as a result of their instructions unless they have agreed otherwise. Paragraph 1.4 requires us not to mislead clients, and staying silent about a fee we are being paid out of their transaction would mislead by omission. Principles 2, 4 and 5, upholding public trust, acting with honesty and acting with integrity, all point the same way.

5.4 My recommendation is that we tell the sellers in writing about the offer, the amount and the basis of it, before any introduction is made, and that we either account to them for the fee or decline it. We should also consider whether steering them to the buyer's own adviser creates a conflict of our own interest with theirs under paragraph 6.1 of the Code. I would decline the fee rather than manage it.

6. Consequences of getting this wrong

6.1 Carrying on a regulated activity without authorisation or exemption contravenes section 19 and is a criminal offence under section 23, punishable on indictment by up to two years' imprisonment or a fine or both.

6.2 The commercial consequence is worse for the client than for us. Under section 26(1) an agreement made in the course of carrying on a regulated activity in contravention of the general prohibition is unenforceable against the other party, and under section 26(2) that party may recover what it paid and compensation for its loss. Applied here, the share sale agreement itself could be attacked.

6.3 There would also be a breach of rule 2.1 of the Scope Rules and a reportable regulatory failure.

7. Sources I have not relied on

7.1 Hallowfield v Brenchley Partners is a decision on the Financial Services Act 1986, which was repealed in its entirety by the 2000 Act with effect from 1 December 2001. Its reasoning on separate remuneration is a useful illustration of the article 67 point but it is not authority on the current statutory scheme and I have not treated it as binding.

7.2 The Partnership Act 1890 extract is not in point. Harewood is a private company limited by shares. There is no partnership and no partnership share.

7.3 The Listing Rules and Prospectus Regulation Rules extract is not in point. Harewood is a private company with no securities admitted to a regulated market or the official list. Section 755 of the Companies Act 2006 is also not engaged, because this is a transfer of existing shares between private parties and not an offer to the public.

7.4 The overseas regulator's guidance note has no application. It governs a different jurisdiction under a different statute and expressly says the two regimes are not equivalent.

8. Next steps

8.1 Confirm to Mr Ubhi that we can advise on the loan notes and can deal with Kesteven on the transaction, on the footing that this is a sale of the whole voting share capital by the three directors.

8.2 Keep the retainer letter clear that the loan note advice is given as part of the sale work and is not separately charged as investment advice, so that our position does not depend on article 67.

8.3 Write to all three sellers about the Kesteven fee before any introduction, and record the decision on the file.

8.4 If the deal is restructured so that less than the whole share capital is sold, or so that a seller who is not a director or close relative joins, revisit article 70(1)(b) immediately, because the exclusion could be lost.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Kesteven has offered the firm an introduction fee of 1 per cent of any sums the sellers place with its wealth management arm, and has said there is no need to tell the sellers. The candidate must spot this without prompting. It bites twice. Under section 327(3) of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 and rule 2.2(c) of the SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules a third party benefit is only permissible if the firm accounts to the client for it, so an undisclosed fee would destroy the professional firms exemption if the firm ever needed it. Independently, paragraph 4.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors requires the firm to account properly for any financial benefit received as a result of the client's instructions, paragraph 1.4 prohibits misleading the client including by omission, and paragraph 6.1 raises an own interest conflict in steering the sellers towards the buyer's adviser. The competent resolution is written disclosure to all three sellers before any introduction, and either accounting to them for the fee or, better, declining it.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses Sources A, B, C and D, and cites the specific provisions that decide the question: sections 19, 22, 23, 26 and 327 of the Act, articles 25, 53, 67, 70, 76 and 77 of the Regulated Activities Order, article 4 of the Professional Firms Order and rules 2 and 3 of the SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules. Positively identifies Sources E, F, G and H as irrelevant and says why, rather than ignoring them silently.Cites the Act generally without pinning the answer to article 70, or works through the section 327 conditions without ever asking whether an exclusion means the activity is not regulated in the first place. Treats Hallowfield as good law, or wastes time on the Partnership Act, Listing Rules or the overseas guidance.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the partner's four numbered questions directly and gives her something she can say on the telephone tomorrow: yes we can do both pieces of work, here is the reason, and here is the one thing that must be dealt with first. Flags the restructuring risk to article 70(1)(b) as a live watch point.Produces an abstract essay on the financial services perimeter that never tells the partner whether the firm may take the instruction, or hedges so heavily that no decision can be taken from it.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA short headed note with a summary at the front, numbered paragraphs, and the two limbs of article 70 separated and applied one at a time. No research trail. British spelling throughout.A narrative of the candidate's research process, or a note that runs the exclusion and the exemption together so the reader cannot see which one is doing the work.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly classifies the shares under article 76 and the loan notes under article 77, correctly identifies advising under article 53 and arranging under article 25, and correctly applies both limbs of article 70, showing that the three sellers are a group of connected individuals because they are directors of the target and, as to two of them, close relatives.Concludes that article 70 cannot apply because the sellers are individuals rather than a body corporate, having missed the group of connected individuals limb. Or treats advice on the legal effect of the loan note instrument as article 53 advice, or treats genuine merits advice as mere legal advice, and so gets the classification the wrong way round.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with both activities, not just the advice; explains why article 67 is unsafe because of the separate remuneration rule in article 67(2); works through the section 327 conditions as the fallback; checks article 4 of the Professional Firms Order and rule 3.1 of the Scope Rules and finds neither engaged; and states the consequences under sections 23 and 26, including that the share sale agreement itself could be unenforceable.Answers only on the loan note advice and forgets the arranging activity, or stops at the conclusion that article 70 applies without addressing the consequences question the partner asked, or omits section 26 unenforceability entirely.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots the Kesteven introduction fee unprompted, links it to section 327(3) and rule 2.2(c) as well as to paragraph 4.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors on accounting for financial benefits and paragraph 1.4 on not misleading clients, rejects the suggestion that the sellers need not be told, and recommends written disclosure before any introduction with the fee either accounted for or declined. Considers the own interest conflict in steering clients to the buyer's adviser.Treats the introduction fee as a commercial matter for the partner, or mentions it only as a section 327(3) technicality without recognising the separate conduct duty to account and not to mislead. Worst of all, accepts the suggestion that it is an arrangement between professionals which need not trouble the sellers.

Examiner notes

The pass turns on sequencing. A candidate who goes straight to section 327 and works diligently through its conditions can still fail, because the correct answer is that no exemption is needed: article 70 of the Regulated Activities Order takes the whole of the work outside the regulated activity. Strong candidates ask the exclusion question first and reach Part XX only as a fallback. The trap most candidates fall into is limb (b) of article 70(1). Seeing three individual sellers, they conclude that the parties test is failed because the sellers are not a body corporate, and they never look at the definition of a group of connected individuals in article 70(2), which is satisfied here because all three are directors of the target and two are siblings. The second trap is the decoy bundle. Hallowfield is a Financial Services Act 1986 case superseded by the 2000 Act, the Partnership Act extract is irrelevant to a company, the Listing Rules and section 755 material applies to public offers and listed companies rather than a private share transfer, and the overseas guidance is from a different jurisdiction which says on its face that it is not equivalent. A candidate who spends fifteen minutes on any of those will not finish. The best answers say briefly why each is discarded, which is itself evidence of source selection. Finally, the introduction fee is unflagged and easy to read as background colour in an attendance note. It is the ethics point and a candidate who says nothing about it cannot pass that criterion.

Written station 31: Payments and asset transfers before an administration: preference or transaction at an undervalue

Legal research  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

RESEARCH NOTE

To: Marged Efans, Partner

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 14 June 2027

Matter: Gareth Prydderch. Claims by the joint administrators of Harlech Fabrication Limited (in administration)

Subject: Preference and transaction at an undervalue. Relevant time periods, burden of proof and remedies

1. Summary of advice

1.1 The client's belief that the six month period saves the loan repayment is wrong. He was a director and therefore a person connected with the company, so the applicable period is two years, not six months (Insolvency Act 1986, s 240(1)(a) and s 249(a)). The repayment on 12 August 2026 is well inside that period.

1.2 On the loan repayment the administrators have a strong claim under s 239. The client is a creditor, the payment plainly improved his position, the company was insolvent at the time, and because he is connected the requisite desire is presumed against him under s 239(6). On the facts he has told us he will find it very hard to rebut that presumption. I would advise settlement negotiations rather than a defence on the merits.

1.3 On the van, the transfer is within the two year period for a transaction at an undervalue (s 238, s 240(1)(a)). Because the transfer was to a person connected with the company, the insolvency requirement in s 240(2) is presumed against the client, but the presumption is rebuttable and the management accounts to 31 January 2026 show net assets of £84,900. That is the client's best point on this claim. The undervalue itself, £4,000 against a valuation of £22,000, will be difficult to defend.

1.4 Mrs Prydderch is not protected as a good faith purchaser. She is an associate of a director and so, under s 241(2A), is presumed not to have acted in good faith.

1.5 There is a conduct issue arising out of the client's email of 12 June 2027 which must be dealt with before anything is sent to the other side. I deal with it at section 6.

2. The payment of £180,000 on 12 August 2026: preference

2.1 The statutory test. Section 239(4) applies where the recipient is one of the company's creditors and the company does something which has the effect of putting that person in a better position, in the event of the company going into insolvent liquidation, than he would have been in otherwise.

2.2 The client was a creditor. He lent the company £180,000 in March 2023 under an unsecured loan repayable on demand. Full repayment of an unsecured debt at a time when the estimated dividend to unsecured creditors is 2 pence in the pound is the clearest possible improvement in position. Both limbs of s 239(4) are satisfied.

2.3 Relevant time. Section 240(1)(b) gives six months for an unconnected preference, but s 240(1)(a) gives two years where the preference is given to a person connected with the company otherwise than by reason only of being an employee. By s 249(a) a person is connected with a company if he is a director of it. The client was a director throughout, and was the sole director from 6 September 2024. The two year period therefore applies.

2.4 The date the period runs from. The period ends with the onset of insolvency. Under s 240(3)(c), where the section applies because an administrator was appointed by the holder of a qualifying floating charge, the onset of insolvency is the date the notice of intention to appoint was filed or, if none was filed, the date the appointment took effect. The administrators were appointed out of court by Cwmbran Trade Finance Limited on 4 March 2027 and there was no administration application. Assuming no notice of intention to appoint was filed, the onset of insolvency is 4 March 2027 and the two year period runs back to 4 March 2025. The payment on 12 August 2026 falls comfortably inside it. We should ask the administrators to confirm whether a notice of intention to appoint was filed, because an earlier date would only move the window further back and would not assist the client.

2.5 Insolvency at the time. By s 240(2) the time is not a relevant time unless the company was unable to pay its debts within s 123 at that time, or became so in consequence. Note that the presumption in the closing words of s 240(2) applies only to a transaction at an undervalue, not to a preference, so on this claim the administrators must prove insolvency. They will do so easily. At 31 July 2026 the company had net liabilities of £104,200 and at 31 August 2026 net liabilities of £297,600, so the balance sheet test in s 123(2) is met. £240,000 of trade debt was more than ninety days overdue and three suppliers had placed the company on stop, which satisfies the cash flow test in s 123(1)(e). The payment of £180,000 itself made matters worse.

2.6 Desire. Section 239(5) requires that the company was influenced in deciding to give the preference by a desire to produce the effect in s 239(4)(b). Re MC Bacon Ltd [1990] BCLC 324 establishes that s 239 replaced the old "dominant intention" test. Millett J held that it is enough that the decision was influenced by the requisite desire, and that a man is taken to desire that which he positively wishes to bring about. The older authority in the file, Peat v Gresham Trust Ltd [1934] AC 252, states the dominant intention test under the pre 1986 legislation and no longer represents the law. It should not be relied on.

2.7 Because the client was connected with the company otherwise than as an employee, s 239(6) presumes that the company was influenced by the requisite desire unless the contrary is shown. The burden is on the client. Re MC Bacon shows the way such a presumption is rebutted: a company acting only under genuine commercial pressure, with no real alternative if it is to continue trading, is not influenced by a desire to improve the creditor's position. That reasoning does not help here. The client has told us he asked for the money back because he was worried about the company and wanted his money out before anything happened. That is a positive wish to improve his own position. He knew from the aged creditors report that suppliers were unpaid. There was no board minute, no other director to persuade, and no third party pressure. In practice he was the company for this purpose.

2.8 Conclusion on the loan. The claim under s 239 is very likely to succeed. I would put his prospects of defending it at low.

3. The van transferred on 9 January 2026: transaction at an undervalue

3.1 The statutory test. Under s 238(4)(b) a company enters into a transaction at an undervalue if it enters into a transaction for a consideration the value of which, in money or money's worth, is significantly less than the value of the consideration the company provided.

3.2 The comparison here is £4,000 received against a van valued at £22,000, a shortfall of £18,000. Phillips v Brewin Dolphin Bell Lawrie Ltd [2001] UKHL 2, [2001] 1 WLR 143 confirms that the valuation exercise is objective and that the court looks at what the company in reality received rather than at the face of the paperwork. The client's own view that £4,000 was "about right" is not determinative. Two further facts point strongly against him: the company obtained no valuation at all, and the company went on using the van until the administration without paying anything for it, so it received no collateral benefit either. On the evidence we have, this is a transaction at an undervalue.

3.3 Relevant time. Mrs Prydderch is the wife of a director. By s 435(2) a person is an associate of an individual if that person is the individual's spouse, and by s 249(a) a person connected with a company includes an associate of a director. She is therefore connected with the company and the two year period in s 240(1)(a) applies. Running back from 4 March 2027, the period begins on 4 March 2025. The transfer on 9 January 2026 is inside it. In any event the two year period in s 240(1)(a) applies to every transaction at an undervalue, connected or not, so the point is not decisive.

3.4 Insolvency at the time, and who must prove it. This is the client's strongest argument. Section 240(2) requires that the company was unable to pay its debts within s 123 at the time, or became so in consequence. The closing words of s 240(2) presume that requirement satisfied, unless the contrary is shown, where the transaction at an undervalue is entered into with a person connected with the company. Mrs Prydderch is connected, so the presumption applies and the burden is on the client to rebut it.

3.5 The presumption is rebuttable and the figures may allow us to rebut it. The management accounts show net assets of £91,400 at 31 December 2025 and £84,900 at 31 January 2026, so the balance sheet test in s 123(2) is not met at the transaction date on those figures. On cash flow, the company met its debts as they fell due until about May 2026, so the s 123(1)(e) test also appears not to be met in January 2026. The loss of a £22,000 asset for £4,000 did not by itself make the company unable to pay its debts, so the second limb of s 240(2) is not engaged either. We would need the underlying ledgers, and the administrators may attack the management accounts as unaudited or as carrying assets at inflated book value, particularly the laser cutting bed and any stock and work in progress. Subject to that, this is a real defence.

3.6 The section 238(5) defence. There is a separate defence where the company acted in good faith and for the purpose of carrying on its business and there were reasonable grounds for believing the transaction would benefit the company. I do not think it is available. Selling a working van at less than a fifth of its value to the sole director's wife, and then continuing to use it for free, was not for the purpose of carrying on the business and could not reasonably have been thought to benefit the company.

3.7 Conclusion on the van. The undervalue is likely to be established. The client's prospects turn almost entirely on rebutting the presumption of insolvency as at 9 January 2026.

4. What order the court could make

4.1 Under s 238(3) and s 239(3) the court must make such order as it thinks fit for restoring the position to what it would have been if the transaction had not been entered into or the preference given. Section 241(1) sets out the specific powers, which include vesting property back in the company under s 241(1)(a), vesting property representing the proceeds under s 241(1)(b), and requiring a person to pay a sum in respect of benefits received under s 241(1)(d).

4.2 On the loan, the likely order is repayment of £180,000, together with interest. The money is still identifiable in the client's savings account, which makes an order straightforward and removes any argument that he has changed his position.

4.3 On the van, the court could order the van to be transferred back or, more likely, order payment of the shortfall of £18,000, since the company received £4,000 and restoration of the position does not require the client's wife to be stripped of what she paid for.

4.4 Mrs Prydderch's position. Section 241(2) protects a person who received a benefit from the transaction in good faith and for value, but s 241(2)(a) protects only an interest acquired from a person other than the company. She acquired directly from the company, so that limb does not assist her. Even if it did, s 241(2A)(b) presumes an absence of good faith where the recipient was connected with, or an associate of, the company or the person with whom the company dealt. As the wife of the sole director she falls squarely within that. She should take her own advice. We cannot act for both her and Mr Prydderch if their interests conflict.

5. Sources in the bundle which do not assist

5.1 Peat v Gresham Trust Ltd [1934] AC 252 states the dominant intention test for fraudulent preference under the pre 1986 companies legislation. Section 239 replaced it with the "influenced by a desire" test, as Re MC Bacon Ltd explains. It must not be cited to the administrators.

5.2 Sections 9 and 24 of the Partnership Act 1890 are irrelevant. Harlech Fabrication Limited is a company limited by shares, not a partnership, and the client's exposure is under the Insolvency Act, not through joint liability as a partner.

5.3 Section 656 of the Companies Act 2006 applies only to public companies. Harlech Fabrication Limited is a private company, so no duty to convene a meeting on serious loss of capital arose.

5.4 Section 99 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016 deals with unfair preferences in Scottish sequestration. It has no application to an English company in administration in England and Wales.

6. A matter which must be resolved before we do anything else

6.1 The client's email of 12 June 2027 tells us that he has instructed the company's former bookkeeper to go back into the accounting records and re date the van invoice to 2 January 2025, and asks us to send that document to the administrators and to suppress the original. Re dating the invoice would put the transaction outside the two year period. That is the whole purpose of the change.

6.2 We cannot use the altered invoice and we cannot put it forward as genuine. Doing so would be misleading the administrators and, if proceedings are issued, the court. That would breach SRA Principle 1 (upholding the constitutional principle of the rule of law and the proper administration of justice), Principle 2 (upholding public trust and confidence in the profession), Principle 4 (acting with honesty) and Principle 5 (acting with integrity). It would also breach paragraph 1.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, which prohibits misleading or attempting to mislead clients, the court or others, either by our own acts or omissions or by allowing or being complicit in the acts or omissions of others, and paragraph 2.1, which prohibits misusing or tampering with evidence or attempting to do so.

6.3 I suggest you speak to the client at once and advise him that the original invoice must be restored on the accounting system, that both versions must be preserved, and that we cannot advance any case based on the altered document. He should be told that altering records to defeat an office holder's claim risks far more serious consequences than the claim itself, including an application for a disqualification order and possible criminal exposure. Preserving the altered document also matters because the administrators may in due course ask for the accounting records and any attempt to conceal the change would compound the problem.

6.4 If he refuses and insists that we deploy the altered invoice, we cannot continue to act. Paragraph 3.1 of the Code requires us to act only on instructions from the client, but we may not act on an instruction to mislead. We would have to cease acting and give him reasonable notice. Our duty of confidentiality under paragraph 6.3 would prevent us from telling the administrators why we had withdrawn, and we would give notice without explanation. Whether an exception to confidentiality arises, and whether a report should be made to the SRA under paragraph 7.7 as a serious breach, are matters for you and the firm's COLP, and I have not formed a view on them.

6.5 Separately, the client's second question, whether we can simply tell the administrators the repayment was out of time because it was more than six months before the administration, cannot be answered as he hopes. That statement would be wrong in law for the reasons in section 2.3 and we must not make it.

7. Recommended next steps

7.1 Deal with the invoice point with the client before replying to Bratherton Quayle LLP.

7.2 Ask Bratherton Quayle to confirm whether a notice of intention to appoint was filed, and to provide the Kelsall valuation and the instructions given to the valuer, so we can consider a valuation challenge on the van.

7.3 Obtain the underlying nominal ledger, aged creditor and aged debtor listings and any stock records as at 9 January 2026, with a view to rebutting the s 240(2) presumption of insolvency on the van claim.

7.4 Advise the client that the £180,000 must remain untouched, and open discussions about a global settlement. Given the strength of the s 239 claim, an early commercial resolution which limits his exposure on the van is likely to serve him better than a defended trial.

7.5 Advise Mrs Prydderch in writing to take independent advice, and record on the file that we do not act for her.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

In Document 4 the client tells the solicitor he has had the company's former bookkeeper re date the van sales invoice in the accounting system from January 2026 to 2 January 2025, which would place the transaction outside the two year relevant time, and asks the firm to send the altered invoice to the administrators and suppress the original. He also asks the firm to assert that the loan repayment is out of time on the six month period, which is legally wrong. Nothing in the partner's email flags either point. A competent candidate refuses to use the altered document, identifies breaches of SRA Principles 1, 2, 4 and 5 and of paragraphs 1.4 and 2.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, advises the client that the original entry must be restored and both versions preserved, declines to advance the six month argument, and explains that if the client insists the firm must cease to act, give notice without disclosing the reason because of the duty of confidentiality in paragraph 6.3, and refer the question of a report to the SRA under paragraph 7.7 to the partner and the COLP.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses sections 238, 239, 240, 241, 249, 435 and 123 of the Insolvency Act 1986 together with Re MC Bacon Ltd and Phillips v Brewin Dolphin, and expressly discards the four decoys, explaining in a sentence each why Peat v Gresham Trust is superseded, why the Partnership Act 1890 does not apply to a company, why Companies Act 2006 section 656 applies only to public companies, and why the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016 is another jurisdiction. Draws the dates and figures out of Document 3 rather than guessing them.Cites Peat v Gresham Trust as good law and applies a dominant intention test, or works through the Partnership Act or the public company provision as though it applied, or relies on the six month period without noticing section 240(1)(a).
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers all four of the partner's numbered questions in terms, tells the partner plainly that the client's own six month analysis is wrong, gives a realistic view of prospects on each claim separately, identifies rebutting the section 240(2) presumption on the van as the client's one real defence, and recommends practical next steps including settlement and independent advice for the wife.Writes an abstract essay on preferences and undervalue transactions without ever saying what the client should be told, or gives no view on prospects, or treats the two transactions as a single undifferentiated claim.
