Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsA properly structured note to a partner with headings, short numbered paragraphs, an opening summary that could be read on its own, and accurate citation. No research trail, no narration of database searching.Sets out the search process, quotes long slabs of the statutory extracts without applying them, or produces undifferentiated prose in which the partner cannot find the answer to any of the four questions.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly identifies the client as connected under section 249(a) so that the two year period in section 240(1)(a) applies to the preference; correctly identifies the onset of insolvency under section 240(3)(c) as the date the out of court appointment took effect, 4 March 2027; correctly applies the presumption of desire in section 239(6) against the client and the presumption of insolvency in section 240(2) as applying to the undervalue claim only; correctly identifies Mrs Prydderch as an associate under section 435(2) and applies section 241(2A).Applies the section 240(2) insolvency presumption to the preference claim as well, which the statute confines to a transaction at an undervalue; or treats the onset of insolvency as the date of the administrators' letter or of the winding up; or concludes the loan repayment is out of time.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers both transactions, both limbs of the relevant time test, who bears each burden, the section 238(5) defence and why it fails, the valuation approach in Phillips v Brewin Dolphin, the range of orders under section 241(1), and the position of the third party recipient under section 241(2) and (2A).Deals only with the loan repayment, or omits the section 238(5) defence, or says nothing about what order the court would actually make or about the wife's position, so the partner cannot advise on outcome.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots the re dated invoice in Document 4 unprompted, refuses to deploy it, identifies the relevant SRA Principles and paragraphs 1.4 and 2.1 of the Code, advises restoration of the original and preservation of both versions, and sets out what happens if the client insists, including ceasing to act, giving notice without breaching confidentiality, and escalating the reporting question to the partner and the COLP. Also refuses to advance the knowingly wrong six month argument.Reads the email as helpful evidence and relies on the re dated invoice to argue the transaction is outside the two year period, or notices the problem but resolves it by saying only that the client should be reminded to be honest, without addressing the firm's own duties or what to do if he refuses.

Examiner notes

The station turns on one clean statutory point that candidates routinely get wrong under time pressure: the six month period in section 240(1)(b) applies only where the recipient is not connected with the company, and a director is connected under section 249(a), so the period is two years. Candidates who accept the client's framing fail the application of law criteria outright. The second discriminator is the asymmetry of the presumptions. Section 239(6) presumes desire against a connected recipient on a preference, but the insolvency presumption in the closing words of section 240(2) is confined to transactions at an undervalue. Weak candidates apply both presumptions to both claims and so miss that insolvency on the loan repayment must actually be proved by the administrators, easy though that is here, and miss that on the van the burden of showing solvency sits with the client and is his only real defence. The third discriminator is the decoy handling. Four of the twelve sources are irrelevant, and the most dangerous is Peat v Gresham Trust, which reads as directly on point but states a test abolished by section 239. A candidate who argues dominant intention has applied the wrong law to the strongest claim against the client. The trap is that the facts invite sympathy for a director who lent his own money to his own company, and candidates soften the advice accordingly. The correct advice is blunt: the preference claim is very likely to succeed, the money should not be spent, and settlement is the sensible course.

Written station 32: Enforceability of a restrictive covenant given on a share sale, compared with one in an employment contract

Legal research  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  60 minutes

Model answer

NOTE TO PARTNER

To: Fergus Ardleigh

From: Trainee Solicitor

Date: 2 November 2027

Matter: Kelbrook Holdings Limited - covenants given by Dr Imogen Slaithwaite

Subject: Enforceability of the share purchase agreement covenants and the service agreement covenants

1. Summary of advice

1.1 Kelbrook should sue on clause 11 of the share purchase agreement, not on clause 18 of the service agreement.

1.2 The two are judged by different standards. A covenant given by the vendor of a business or of shares in it, in return for the price, is treated far more generously to the buyer than a covenant given by an employee. That distinction runs from Nordenfelt through Herbert Morris v Saxelby to Dawnay, Day and Quantum Advisory. On these facts clause 11.1, 11.2 and 11.3 are in my view enforceable in full.

1.3 Clause 18 is weaker in every respect: Kelbrook is not a party to it, it protects a narrower interest, it is expressed in terms which Tillman v Egon Zehnder shows are too wide because there is no investment carve out, and it expires on 30 June 2028 in any event. There is also no customer non solicitation clause in it at all.

1.4 Kelbrook has an interim injunction, damages and a contractual right of set off against the £250,000 deferred consideration. It should not exercise the set off unilaterally before quantifying a claim.

1.5 Mr Nuttall's email of 1 November 2027 asks us to do two things we cannot do. That is at section 7 and needs to be resolved before anything is sent.

2. The legal framework

2.1 A contractual restriction on a person's freedom to trade is void as a restraint of trade unless the covenantee shows it protects a legitimate interest and goes no further than is reasonably necessary to protect it, and that it is not contrary to the public interest: Nordenfelt v Maxim Nordenfelt Guns and Ammunition Co Ltd [1894] AC 535 per Lord Macnaghten (Source A); Tillman v Egon Zehnder Ltd [2019] UKSC 32 (Source E).

2.2 Reasonableness is judged as at the date the contract was made, not with hindsight: Office Angels Ltd v Rainer-Thomas [1991] IRLR 214 (Source F) and Quantum Advisory Ltd v Quantum Actuarial LLP [2021] EWCA Civ 227 (Source G). So the correct question is what was reasonable on 3 April 2026, not what Dr Slaithwaite has since done.

3. Why the two documents are not judged alike

3.1 This is the heart of the answer and it is worth being precise about it.

3.2 On a sale of a business or of shares in it, the covenant is part of the consideration. The buyer has paid for the goodwill and the vendor would otherwise be free to destroy the very asset sold. Lord Watson in Nordenfelt put the vendor's covenant on "a different footing" from the master and servant case. Lord Atkinson in Herbert Morris Ltd v Saxelby [1916] 1 AC 688 (Source B) described the two classes as "separated by a broad line of demarcation", with the court leaning in favour of the covenant on a sale of goodwill and against it in the employment case. Millett J said the same in Allied Dunbar (Frank Weisinger) Ltd v Weisinger [1988] IRLR 60 (Source C), and added the two features that matter most here: a substantial sum expressly attributed in part to goodwill, and parties separately advised and of broadly equal bargaining power.

3.3 In the employment case the protectable interest is confined to trade connection and trade secrets or equivalent confidential information. Protection against mere competition is not a legitimate interest, and the employee's own skill and knowledge cannot be restrained at all: Herbert Morris and Office Angels.

3.4 A vendor who is also an employee does not therefore get the benefit of the employment approach across both documents. In Dawnay, Day & Co Ltd v de Braconier d'Alphen [1997] IRLR 442 (Source D) the Court of Appeal held that the court looks at the capacity in which the covenant was given and the consideration for which it was given, tests each document in its own context, and does not read down a commercial covenant merely because a narrower one appears in the service agreement. That last point disposes of the argument Dr Slaithwaite is bound to run, namely that a four year covenant cannot be reasonable when the same parties thought twelve months enough in the service agreement.

4. Clause 11 of the share purchase agreement

4.1 Legitimate interest. Kelbrook bought the goodwill of a business whose customer relationships were personal to Dr Slaithwaite. £1.4 million of the price was attributed to goodwill, of which £630,000 was referable to her shareholding. Recital (C) records that the covenants were a material part of the consideration. That is a plain legitimate interest, and a stronger one than any employer could assert.

4.2 Duration. Four years is long by employment standards and unremarkable by sale of business standards. Nordenfelt upheld twenty five years, Allied Dunbar upheld two years across the whole United Kingdom on a smaller transaction. Here the period was negotiated down from five years by Dr Slaithwaite's own solicitors, which on Dawnay, Day and Quantum Advisory is strong evidence of what the parties regarded as reasonable between themselves. Given that she personally knew every significant customer and that calibration contracts run over several years, four years is defensible.

4.3 Area. "England and Wales" matches the actual footprint of the business, whose customers are all in England and Wales. An area covenant is an appropriate form of protection for a business supplying physical equipment and on site calibration, and the area is no wider than the business it protects. Office Angels is the contrast: the area there was both too wide and useless because the business was conducted by telephone. Neither criticism applies here.

4.4 Subject matter. "Restricted Business" is defined by reference to the business actually carried on at completion. It does not extend to metrology outside the aerospace supply chain. That is a properly limited definition.

4.5 "Or be interested in". Tillman shows those words on their ordinary meaning catch any shareholding, which without a carve out makes the covenant too wide. Clause 11.4 supplies the carve out, permitting up to three per cent of listed securities. Clause 11 is therefore not vulnerable on the Tillman point at all, and if it were, clause 11.5 is an express severance provision and the blue pencil test in Tillman could be applied.

4.6 Breach. On the client's account she is carrying on and is interested in a competing business in Keighley (clause 11.1), she has solicited and accepted the custom of Hathersage Aerostructures, a customer in the twelve months before completion (clause 11.2), and she has solicited and now employs Mr Roebuck and Ms Kaczmarek, both employed at completion in a technical capacity (clause 11.3). Her 80 per cent holding in Deepdale is far outside the clause 11.4 carve out, which is limited to listed securities in any event.

4.7 Conclusion. I consider clause 11 enforceable and clearly breached.

5. Clause 18 of the service agreement

5.1 Kelbrook is not a party. The contracting employer is Ganton Precision Limited. Kelbrook cannot sue on it, though as sole shareholder it can procure Ganton to do so. That alone makes it the second choice.

5.2 It is judged on the employment footing. The interest is limited to trade connection and confidential information, and Dr Slaithwaite's own skill as a metrologist cannot be restrained.

5.3 Clause 18.2 restrains her from being "interested in" any competing business, with no carve out for a small investment shareholding. That is the precise defect in Tillman. It could probably be cured by severing "or interested in", but the burden would be on Ganton to show no major change in the overall effect of the restraints, and there is no severance clause in this agreement to assist.

5.4 The area is the United Kingdom, which is wider than the business, whose customers are all in England and Wales, and the scope catches "any business carried on by the Company", tested at the termination date rather than at the date of the contract. Both are open to attack on Office Angels reasoning.

5.5 There is no customer non solicitation clause in the service agreement, so the Hathersage conduct is not caught by it at all.

5.6 It expires on 30 June 2028. Clause 11 runs to 3 April 2030.

5.7 Conclusion. Clause 18 adds nothing that clause 11 does not do better. I would not plead it. If we do plead it in the alternative it should be through Ganton as claimant and with the severance argument set out.

6. Remedies

6.1 Interim injunction. This is the real remedy. Kelbrook should apply promptly for interim injunctive relief restraining breach of clauses 11.1 to 11.3, supported by evidence from Mr Nuttall and, if he will give it, the Hathersage purchasing manager. Delay is fatal to this sort of application, and Kelbrook has known of Deepdale since at least October 2027. An undertaking in damages will be required and the client must be told what that means. A speedy trial should be sought.

6.2 Damages. Loss of the Hathersage contract, being 11 per cent of turnover, plus recruitment and disruption costs for the two engineers. This will take an accountant to quantify.

6.3 Set off against the deferred consideration. Clause 3.4 expressly permits set off against the £250,000 of any sum due from Dr Slaithwaite under the agreement, including in respect of a breach of clause 11. That is a genuine contractual right, but it bites on sums due, so Kelbrook cannot simply withhold the whole £250,000 in April 2028 on an unquantified claim without risking a claim for the balance and undermining its own position on an injunction application. The right course is to quantify, notify and set off the quantified sum, and to say so in correspondence now.

6.4 Springboard relief and claims against Deepdale for inducing breach of contract are possible but are not covered by the sources provided and I have not advised on them.

6.5 Competition Act 1998. Source H raises the point that a vendor non compete which goes beyond what the transfer reasonably requires may fall outside the ancillary restraints principle. The note suggests two to three years is the usual reference point where goodwill or know how is transferred. This is worth a line in our risk assessment, because Dr Slaithwaite may raise it, but it is not a ground on which I would expect a four year covenant on this transaction to be struck down, and it does not change the advice.

6.6 The Consumer Rights Act 2015 extract has no application. Dr Slaithwaite sold shares in her own company and was employed as a director; she was not a consumer within section 61(4) in either capacity. The unfair prejudice provisions in the Companies Act 2006 are also irrelevant: she is no longer a member of Ganton and no petition arises.

7. Matters arising from Mr Nuttall's email of 1 November 2027

7.1 The letters to the investor and the customers. Mr Nuttall wants strongly worded letters sent to Mr Brigham and to four customers threatening to join them and seek their costs, expressly "whether or not you think the claims against them would actually get anywhere", with the stated aim of collapsing Deepdale without ever reaching court. We cannot write those letters. We must not make an allegation or bring a claim which is not properly arguable, and we must not use our position to take unfair advantage of a third party, particularly one like Mr Brigham who may well have no legal advice. A letter to a third party asserting a legal claim we do not believe in is an abuse. What we can properly do is write to Deepdale and to Dr Slaithwaite, and, if there is a genuine and arguable case of inducing breach of contract against a specific recipient, write to that recipient setting out that case accurately and without threats we are not prepared to carry out.

7.2 The threatened report to HMRC and to the accreditation body. Mr Nuttall wants us to tell Dr Slaithwaite that unless she closes her business and signs an agreement not to speak about why she left, we will report the £9,000 holiday expense to HMRC and to her accreditation body. We cannot do that either. Threatening to make a report to a revenue authority or a regulator in order to obtain an advantage in an unrelated civil dispute is an improper threat and takes unfair advantage of the other party. Nor can we demand a wide agreement not to speak about the circumstances of her departure as the price of dropping that threat: an agreement whose purpose or effect is to stop a person reporting a matter to a regulator or a law enforcement or tax authority is improper, and the SRA has issued a warning notice about the misuse of non disclosure agreements. The expense claim, if it is a genuine breach of duty by a former director, is a separate matter which Ganton can pursue on its merits, and any regulatory or tax reporting obligation must be considered on its own footing and not traded away.

7.3 How to handle it. We should see Mr Nuttall, explain that our duty not to abuse our position and not to make unarguable allegations limits what we can send, and confirm the position in writing. He is likely to accept it once he understands that a letter of that kind would damage the injunction application, which is the remedy he actually wants: a judge asked to grant discretionary equitable relief will be shown the correspondence. If he insists, we cannot act on those instructions and would have to consider ceasing to act on this aspect of the matter.

8. Recommendation

8.1 Sue on clause 11 of the share purchase agreement, with Kelbrook as claimant.

8.2 Apply promptly for an interim injunction and a speedy trial.

8.3 Send a proper letter before claim to Dr Slaithwaite and to Deepdale Metrology Limited, without the threats requested.

8.4 Notify Dr Slaithwaite of the intention to set off against the deferred consideration once the claim is quantified, and do not simply withhold it.

8.5 Do not plead clause 18 unless Ganton is joined, and only in the alternative.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Document 4 contains two unflagged conduct problems. First, the client instructs the firm to send letters to Dr Slaithwaite's investor and to four customers alleging that they are knowingly assisting a breach and threatening to join them to proceedings and seek their costs, expressly "whether or not you think the claims against them would actually get anywhere", with the stated purpose of collapsing the competing business without ever reaching court. A solicitor must not make an allegation or threaten a claim which is not properly arguable, and must not use the firm's position to take unfair advantage of a third party, especially one who is unrepresented. Second, the client instructs the firm to threaten to report a £9,000 expense claim to HMRC and to a professional accreditation body unless Dr Slaithwaite closes her business and signs an agreement not to speak about why she left. That is an improper threat made to gain an advantage in a civil dispute, and the proposed silence agreement is a misuse of a non disclosure agreement of the kind the SRA has warned against, because its effect would be to buy off a report to a tax authority and a regulator. A competent candidate refuses both, explains why in terms of not abusing the firm's position and not advancing unarguable claims, points out that such correspondence would also damage the very injunction application the client wants, offers the proper alternatives of a normal letter before claim and, if there really is a director's breach of duty over the expense, a separate claim by Ganton on its merits, and states that if the client insists the firm cannot act on those instructions.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Identify and use relevant sources and information.SkillsUses Nordenfelt, Herbert Morris, Allied Dunbar, Dawnay Day, Tillman, Office Angels and Quantum Advisory for the purposes they actually serve, and in particular uses the employment authorities as the contrast which proves the point rather than as the test to be applied to the share purchase agreement. Discards the Consumer Rights Act and section 994 outright and deals with the Competition Act extract in a line or two as a risk rather than a ground of invalidity. Uses the detail in Documents 1 to 3, including the £630,000 goodwill attribution, the negotiation history, the clause 11.4 carve out and the absence of one in clause 18.Applies Herbert Morris and Office Angels to clause 11 as though a share sale covenant were an employment covenant, and concludes that four years and England and Wales must be too wide. Also poor: an answer which spends time on the Consumer Rights Act or on unfair prejudice, or which treats the Competition Act note as fatal to clause 11.
Provide advice which is client focused and addresses the client's problem.SkillsAnswers the question the partner asked, which is which claim to bring, and says so at the front. Deals with the practical remedies including the interim injunction, the urgency point and the contractual set off, and tells the partner what to advise Mr Nuttall about withholding the £250,000.A correct account of the restraint of trade doctrine which never chooses between the two clauses, or which analyses enforceability and then ignores remedies altogether. Advising the client simply to keep the £250,000 because the contract mentions set off, without the quantification point.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language.SkillsHeaded note, conclusion first, clause by clause analysis, proper citation, no research trail, no lifting of long quotations from the sources.Reproduces the extracts at length and leaves the partner to do the applying, or writes a single undivided narrative in which the two documents are discussed together and become confused.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the test accurately, identifies the correct legitimate interest for each document (goodwill purchased for clause 11; trade connection and confidential information only for clause 18), applies the sale of business approach to clause 11 and the employment approach to clause 18, and correctly judges reasonableness as at 3 April 2026. Applies Tillman to clause 18 and explains why clause 11.4 answers the same point for clause 11.Assuming that because Dr Slaithwaite was an employee every covenant she gave is an employment covenant, or reading clause 11 down to twelve months because clause 18 says twelve months, which Dawnay Day expressly forbids. Also fails: judging reasonableness by what she has since done rather than as at the date of the agreement.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all three limbs of clause 11 and matches each to the conduct alleged, notes that Kelbrook is not a party to the service agreement, notes the expiry dates of both sets of restrictions, deals with severance, and covers injunction, damages and set off. Notes that the covenants are separate and independent under clause 11.5.Analyses only the non compete and never reaches the customer and employee covenants, or misses that Kelbrook cannot sue on the service agreement at all. Missing that clause 11.2 catches the Hathersage approach while clause 18 contains no customer covenant.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies both limbs of the email. Refuses to send threatening letters to the investor and customers asserting claims the firm does not believe are arguable, and explains that a solicitor must not make unarguable allegations or take unfair advantage of a third party, particularly an unrepresented one. Refuses to threaten a report to HMRC and to the accreditation body in order to extract closure of the business and a silence agreement, identifying that as an improper threat and as a misuse of a non disclosure agreement to suppress a report to a regulator or tax authority. Explains the honest alternatives and what happens if the client insists.Treating the letters to third parties as merely aggressive tactics to be softened, or advising that the HMRC point is "good leverage" provided the allegation is true. Truth is not the issue; the impropriety is using the threat to obtain an advantage in the civil dispute. Also fails: spotting one limb and not the other.

Examiner notes

The whole station turns on one distinction: a covenant given by a vendor of shares, as part of the consideration and to protect goodwill the buyer has paid for, is judged far more generously than a covenant given by an employee. Candidates who miss it strike down a perfectly good four year covenant by applying employment reasoning to it, and then advise the client to sue on the twelve month service agreement covenant, which is the weaker instrument on every measure. The bundle is arranged to encourage exactly that error. Herbert Morris v Saxelby and Office Angels are the natural decoys, in the sense that they are real, well known and directly on the topic of restrictive covenants, but they set the test for the wrong document. A strong candidate uses them as the contrast, noting Lord Atkinson's "broad line of demarcation", and then relies on Nordenfelt, Allied Dunbar, Dawnay Day and Quantum Advisory for the covenant that actually matters. Dawnay Day is the source that answers the defendant's best argument, that a four year covenant cannot be reasonable when the parties agreed twelve months in the service agreement: the court tests each document in its own context and does not read the commercial covenant down. The Consumer Rights Act and section 994 extracts are pure decoys and should be discarded in a sentence or not mentioned. The Competition Act extract is the harder decoy because it is genuinely arguable, and the discriminating answer flags it as a risk without letting it drive the advice. Two further traps sit in the drafting: clause 11.4 gives the share purchase covenant the investment carve out that Tillman shows is needed, while clause 18 has none, and Kelbrook is not a party to the service agreement at all, so it could not sue on clause 18 even if it wanted to. Finally, no strong grade is available to a candidate who advises the client to withhold the whole £250,000 without quantifying the claim, or who softens rather than refuses the letters Mr Nuttall has asked for.

Written station 33: Response to a warranty claim under a share purchase agreement and an offer to settle

Legal writing  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  30 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

EMAIL 1: TO THE BUYER'S SOLICITORS

From: Wenlock Gaidry LLP

To: Hollowell Grange LLP, for the attention of the fee earner having conduct

Date: 21 October 2027

Subject: WITHOUT PREJUDICE SAVE AS TO COSTS - Marrable Industrial Group Limited and Ellis Fenwick - share purchase agreement dated 12 January 2027

Dear Sirs

Marrable Industrial Group Limited and Ellis Fenwick

Share purchase agreement dated 12 January 2027 relating to Thornsett Coatings Limited

We have your letter of 4 October 2027 and have taken our client's instructions. This email is written without prejudice save as to costs. Our client's position on each head of claim is set out below, followed by a proposal which is made to bring this matter to an end without either party incurring further cost.

Liability is denied. Our client reserves all of his rights under the agreement, including under Schedule 5.

1. The notice

Your letter is given within the 18 month period in paragraph 4 of Schedule 5, which expires on 12 July 2028. It does not, however, comply with the rest of that paragraph in relation to heads 2 and 3. Paragraph 4 requires the notice to state in reasonable detail the nature of the claim and the matter giving rise to it. Head 2 identifies no stock lines, no book values and no basis for the assertion that the stock cannot be sold at book value. Head 3 identifies no ground of claim and no date. We reserve our client's position on the validity of the notice in respect of both. If your client wishes to preserve those heads it should serve a compliant notice, and it should do so before 12 July 2028.

2. Beckhampton Rail Components Limited

This head is denied.

Warranty 9.4 is given so far as our client is aware and is limited to a customer which has given notice to terminate or has notified the Company in writing of an intention to terminate. Your client's own case is that notice was given on 2 March 2027, which is after completion. Nothing in your letter identifies any written notification received before completion.

In any event, paragraph 5 of Schedule 5 excludes liability to the extent that the matter was fairly disclosed. Disclosure 14 disclosed that the Beckhampton agreement was terminable on three months' notice by either party, that Beckhampton had put its powder coating requirements out to competitive tender in November 2026, that the Company had tendered, and that the outcome was not known. Your client bought a business in which the loss of this customer on three months' notice was a disclosed and live possibility, and it knew from the due diligence responses that Beckhampton represented about 18 per cent of turnover. It cannot now recover for the risk it was told about and priced.

We do not accept the measure of loss either. Three years of gross margin is not the right measure for a contract terminable on three months' notice, and paragraph 7 of Schedule 5 required your client to take all reasonable steps to mitigate. We have seen nothing about what steps were taken to replace the volume between June 2027 and today.

3. Stock

This head is denied.

Disclosure 21 disclosed that stock lines TC/440 to TC/468 had been held for more than 24 months. To the extent the claim concerns those lines it is excluded by paragraph 5.

Beyond that, the completion stock take was carried out by your client's own accountants and your client signed off the completion accounts in March 2027 without adjustment. The review you rely on was carried out in August 2027, some seven months after completion, and no account appears to have been taken of paragraph 6, which excludes liability to the extent that the matter arises from an act or omission of the Buyer or the Company after completion, including how the stock has since been held and managed.

4. Employment

This head fails in any event.

Warranty 15.2 speaks as at completion. Mr Danczuk was dismissed in February 2027 and issued his claim in April 2027, both after completion. There was no current or threatened claim at completion.

Separately, the claim is put at £12,000. Paragraph 1 of Schedule 5 provides that our client is not liable for a claim unless that claim on its own exceeds £15,000, and that a claim below that figure is disregarded entirely and does not count towards the aggregate in paragraph 2. This head therefore falls away and cannot be aggregated.

5. The aggregate threshold

Once head 3 is removed, the heads which remain must together exceed £75,000 before any liability arises at all. If, as we say, the Beckhampton head fails, the remaining claim is below the threshold and nothing is payable.

6. Proposal

Our client's position is that the claim as formulated is bad. He is nevertheless a pragmatic man who would prefer to close this rather than spend money arguing about it, and he is in a position to pay immediately from cleared funds.

On that basis, and strictly without prejudice, our client offers £60,000 in full and final settlement of all claims of any kind under or in connection with the share purchase agreement, whether or not raised in your letter, payable within 10 business days of a signed settlement agreement, each party bearing its own costs.

The offer is open for acceptance for 21 days. It is made on the express basis that the settlement agreement will release our client from all warranty, indemnity and other claims under the agreement, so that both parties can draw a line.

If your client is not minded to accept, we invite it to respond with a properly particularised claim, including the mitigation information referred to at paragraph 2 above and the stock detail referred to at paragraph 1, so that any further discussion can be a useful one. We would also suggest a without prejudice meeting or a short mediation in preference to proceedings, and our client is willing to contribute to the cost of one.

We look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully

Wenlock Gaidry LLP

EMAIL 2: TO THE CLIENT

From: Wenlock Gaidry LLP

To: Ellis Fenwick

Copy: Loveday Trescothick

Date: 21 October 2027

Subject: Marrable claim - your email of yesterday evening

Dear Ellis

Thank you for your email of 20 October. I have sent our reply to Hollowell Grange today and a copy is attached. Before you read it, I need to explain one thing I have not done.

You asked me to state that you had no knowledge before completion of any customer intending to end its relationship with the company. On what you have told me about Mr Naylor's call on 6 January 2027, that statement would not be true, and I cannot make it. We are not permitted to make a statement to the other side which we know to be untrue, and we cannot let a letter of ours give a false impression, whether by what it says or by what it leaves out. That is not a matter of tactics or of what can be proved. It applies whether or not there is a note of the call and whether or not anyone else was on it.

What I have done instead is put the points that are properly open to you, and there are good ones. Warranty 9.4 is limited to a customer which has given notice or has notified the company in writing, and there was nothing in writing before completion. The tender process and the three month termination right were both disclosed, and disclosure is a complete answer to that extent. The loss claimed is far too high for a contract terminable on three months' notice.

You should understand two further things. First, the call is not something I can conceal if a court or the other side asks a question which cannot be answered honestly without it, for example if you were to give a witness statement or evidence about your knowledge before completion. Second, this is a good reason to settle now rather than litigate, because in proceedings you would be asked about your knowledge directly and on oath.

I have offered £60,000 as you authorised and I have asked for a full and final release of all claims, not just the three raised. I will let you know as soon as we hear.

If you would like to talk any of this through, please call me.

Kind regards

Wenlock Gaidry LLP

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Document 4 is the whole of it and nothing draws attention to it. The client discloses that six days before completion the buyer's target customer told him by telephone that the tender had gone against the company and the work would move in the spring, that he said nothing to the buyer, and he instructs the firm to state in terms to the buyer's solicitors that he had no knowledge before completion of any customer intending to end its relationship, adding that there is no note and no other witness. A solicitor cannot make that statement. The firm must not mislead the other side, either by a positive assertion or by an omission or half truth which creates a false impression, and cannot be complicit in a client doing so. The competent response is to refuse the instruction, to write to the other side using only points which are true and properly arguable, in particular that warranty 9.4 is limited to notice given or a written notification received and that nothing in writing was received before completion, to explain to the client in writing why the assertion cannot be made and that this does not turn on whether the call can be proved, to warn him that his pre completion knowledge would be tested on oath in proceedings, which is itself a reason to settle now, and at the same time to respect confidentiality by not disclosing the call to the buyer's solicitors. If the client insists on the false assertion the firm must stop acting.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the facts that matter to each head: the 2 March 2027 notice date, Disclosure 14 and Disclosure 21, the buyer's own completion stock take and sign off in March 2027, the February 2027 dismissal and April 2027 tribunal claim, the £12,000 figure against the £15,000 de minimis, and the £3.2 million consideration. States the offer figure, the payment timescale, the acceptance period and the requirement for a full and final release.A general denial which does not engage with the dates, or an offer made with no figure, no deadline and no scope, so the recipient cannot act on it. Reciting the whole transaction history instead of the facts which answer the claim.
Use a logical structure.SkillsAnswers the claim head by head in the order used by the other side, deals with the threshold and de minimis points after the individual heads because they depend on the outcome of those heads, and puts the offer last with its terms clearly separated. Headed and numbered.Mixes the offer into the denials so it is unclear what is admitted, what is denied and what is offered, or opens with the offer before any position has been established.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsThe email to the buyer's solicitors is written to persuade a sophisticated opponent to settle: firm on liability, specific about what is missing from their claim, and constructive about how to close. It reflects the client's instruction to settle quickly, to open at about £60,000, to use immediate payment as a lever and to get a full and final release. The client email deals plainly with what the client actually asked for and tells him what happens next.Writing to the other side's solicitors as though writing to a client, with explanations of what a warranty is, or ignoring the client's actual commercial instructions and offering nothing at all. Also fails: disclosing the client's £150,000 authority, or telling the other side about the 6 January call, which confidentiality does not permit.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsCorrect solicitor to solicitor register, correctly marked without prejudice save as to costs, no discourtesy, no unnecessary aggression, no jargon in the client email. Short sentences, headings, and finished within the word count a 30 minute exercise allows.Failing to mark the email without prejudice at all, or marking the client email as if it were the letter to the other side. Hostile or personal language, or an unstructured block of text.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies the awareness qualification and the written notification requirement in warranty 9.4 to the pre completion position, applies the disclosure exclusion in paragraph 5 to Disclosures 14 and 21, applies paragraph 1 correctly so that the £12,000 head is disregarded entirely and cannot be counted towards the £75,000 aggregate, and applies paragraph 6 to the post completion stock position. Notes that warranty 15.2 speaks as at completion.Treating the £12,000 head as reducing the claim rather than dropping out entirely, or aggregating it towards the £75,000 threshold, which paragraph 1 expressly forbids. Arguing that the notice is out of time when it plainly is not, since the 18 month period runs to 12 July 2028.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all three heads, the notice requirements in paragraph 4 in respect of particularity as well as timing, the de minimis and aggregate provisions, mitigation under paragraph 7, the post completion exclusion in paragraph 6, and the measure of loss for a contract terminable on three months' notice. Notes the cap of £1,280,000 or, better, recognises it is not engaged and does not waste words on it.Dealing only with the Beckhampton head because it is the largest, and ignoring the stock and employment heads, or missing the disclosure letter entirely, which is the strongest point the client has.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises that the client has asked the firm to assert to the other side something the firm now knows to be untrue, and refuses. The letter to the buyer's solicitors contains no statement that the client had no pre completion knowledge, and is drafted so that its silence does not create a false impression: it says only that nothing in writing was received before completion, which is true. The client is told plainly, in writing, that the assertion cannot be made and why, that this does not depend on whether the call can be proved, and that his knowledge would be explored on oath if the matter is litigated. Confidentiality is respected, so the call is not revealed to the other side.Writing the sentence the client asked for, or writing something which stops just short of it but is designed to convey the same false impression, for example "our client first learned of any intention to terminate in March 2027". Equally wrong at the other extreme is volunteering the content of the 6 January call to Hollowell Grange, which breaches confidentiality. A candidate who says nothing to the client at all about the instruction cannot pass this criterion.

Examiner notes

This is a negotiation exercise carried out in writing, so a letter which only denies liability and makes no offer cannot pass however good the contractual analysis is. The client has authorised up to £150,000, wants to open at about £60,000 and wants a full and final release covering everything, not just the three heads pleaded. A strong answer opens at £60,000, gives the recipient a reason to take it seriously by pointing to immediate payment from cleared funds, imposes a deadline, and asks for the missing particulars so that any further round is productive. Weak answers either reveal the £150,000 authority or make an unfocused offer with no terms. On the law, the discriminating point is paragraph 1 of Schedule 5: the £12,000 employment head does not merely reduce the claim, it is disregarded entirely and cannot be counted towards the £75,000 aggregate, which changes the arithmetic of the whole claim. The second discriminating point is the disclosure letter, which is the client's best answer on both the Beckhampton and the stock heads and which many candidates never open. A common error is to argue that the notice is out of time; it is not, and saying so wastes the strongest genuine notice point, which is that heads 2 and 3 are not particularised as paragraph 4 requires. The ethics point is the hardest thing on the paper because the client's instruction is superficially reasonable and comes with the reassurance that nothing can be proved. Candidates who write the sentence he asked for fail, and so do candidates who write a cleverly worded substitute intended to convey the same false impression. The correct line is narrow: say only what is true, say nothing that creates a false impression, do not reveal the call to the other side, and tell the client in writing why.

Written station 34: Email to the buyer's solicitors countering the warranty package on a share sale

Legal writing  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  30 minutes  |  involves negotiation

Model answer

From: Trainee Solicitor, Fenwick Marrable LLP

To: Rebecca Kestrel, Kestrel Fairbairn LLP

Date: 17 September 2026

Subject: Project Anvil, warranty package, subject to contract

Dear Rebecca,

Thank you for your email of yesterday. We have taken our clients' instructions and set out their position below, taking your points in your order. This email is subject to contract.

1. Cap

Our clients cannot accept a cap at 100 per cent of the consideration for the commercial warranties. They are selling to fund their retirement and cannot leave the entire price exposed. They will agree an aggregate cap of 50 per cent of the consideration, that is 1,600,000 pounds, for the commercial warranties, with 100 per cent of the consideration reserved as the cap for the tax covenant and for the title and capacity warranties. That gives your client full recovery on the risks that go to what it is actually buying.

2. Time limits

Six years across the whole schedule is not agreed. Our clients will give 18 months from completion for the commercial warranties and seven years for tax. Eighteen months gives your client two audited year ends after completion, which is the period in which a commercial warranty issue realistically surfaces. The longer tax period reflects the fact that tax risk is not within your client's control to discover.

3. De minimis

Our clients require an individual claim threshold of 5,000 pounds and an aggregate threshold of 50,000 pounds. The purpose is not to shelter small breaches. It is to keep both parties out of a claims process over sums that will cost more to argue than they are worth. Your client is buying a working business and some minor variance from a warranty is inevitable in any trading company.

4. Disclosure

General disclosure of the data room must stand. Your client's advisers had 1,140 documents available to them for six weeks and conducted their due diligence on that basis. Our clients are, however, prepared to meet you on the fairness point. They will agree that the data room is disclosed only to the extent that a document is fairly disclosed, meaning disclosed in sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. That protects your client from anything buried, without reopening six weeks of diligence.

5. Knowledge

Our clients will give flat warranties on title to the shares, their capacity, and the accounts. They ask for an awareness qualification on three areas only: customer disputes, employee claims, and product performance in the field. Each of those depends on what a third party may assert rather than on any fact within our clients' knowledge. Mr Ottley has in any event been outside the operational side of the business since 2024. We suggest the qualification is expressed as the actual awareness of the sellers having made reasonable enquiry, which is a standard your client can test.

6. Restrictive covenants

Four years across the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland goes further than is needed and, we would say, further than is enforceable. Our clients will accept two years from completion, limited to England and Wales. Mrs Ashcombe is retiring and Mr Ottley is moving to a non executive role in an unrelated sector, so neither presents the competitive risk the drafting is aimed at. A covenant that is no wider than necessary to protect the goodwill your client is buying is also the covenant most likely to be enforced if it ever has to be.

7. Personal guarantees

Our clients want the Ryedale Bank guarantees released at least as much as your client does, and they will use their best endeavours to obtain the release.

I am afraid we cannot give the undertaking you ask for. An undertaking given by this firm has to be something within our own control. What you have asked us to undertake is that our clients will procure a release and that Ryedale Bank will execute a deed of release by a given date. Neither our clients nor this firm can compel the bank to do anything, its credit committee has not yet considered the matter, and it has given no commitment. We are not able to promise a third party's act.

We suggest the point is dealt with in the agreement rather than by undertaking, and we propose the following, which we think gives your client better protection than an undertaking would:

a. a seller obligation in the share purchase agreement to use best endeavours to obtain the release of the guarantees on or before completion;

b. release of the guarantees as a condition to completion, so your client is not obliged to complete without it, with either party able to walk away if it is not satisfied by a long stop date; and

c. repayment of the overdraft in full out of the completion monies, which is the step the bank has indicated it needs before it will release.

If your client would prefer, we will write to Ryedale Bank jointly this week to press for a decision before exchange.

We should be glad to speak before Friday if it would help your client's board to have the reasoning directly. I am available tomorrow morning.

Kind regards,

Trainee Solicitor

Fenwick Marrable LLP

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The buyer's solicitor demands, as a precondition of exchange, an undertaking from the candidate's firm that the sellers will procure the release of the Ryedale Bank guarantees and that the bank will execute a deed of release by completion. An undertaking is personally binding on the solicitor who gives it and must be performed. Here performance depends entirely on two people outside the firm's control: the clients, and a bank whose credit committee has not considered the matter and which has committed to nothing. Giving it would expose the candidate and the firm to a liability they cannot discharge. The commercial pressure to give it is real, because the buyer says it will not exchange without it. A competent candidate refuses clearly, explains the reason, and replaces the undertaking with contractual protection: a best endeavours covenant, release as a completion condition with a long stop date, and repayment of the overdraft from the completion monies. A second, quieter point is that the candidate must not present the relationship manager's informal remark as a bank commitment in order to make the refusal more palatable.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the figures the sellers have actually authorised: 50 per cent of 3,200,000 pounds giving 1,600,000 pounds, 18 months and seven years, 5,000 pounds and 50,000 pounds, two years and England and Wales. Uses the 1,140 documents and six week data room window as the reason on disclosure, Mr Ottley's departure from operations in 2024 on knowledge, and the bank's non committal position on the guarantees.Gives positions without the numbers, or invents numbers the client never authorised, or concedes beyond the instructed limits. Omitting the data room facts leaves the disclosure position asserted rather than argued.
Use a logical structure.SkillsAnswers the buyer's seven points in the buyer's own order and numbering, so the recipient can put the two emails side by side. Each point states the position, then the reason, then any alternative. The guarantee point, which needs the most, is given the most space.Reorders or merges the points so the recipient has to reconcile them, or answers only six, or buries the refusal of the undertaking inside a paragraph about something else.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsWritten for an experienced opposing solicitor who has to sell the outcome to her own client's board on Friday. Every refusal carries a reason she can repeat, and every no is paired with a workable alternative. Advances the sellers' commercial interests without needless concession, and offers a call before the board meets.A flat list of rejections with no reasoning, which gives the recipient nothing to take to her board; or the opposite, a conciliatory email that concedes the cap or the time limits because the buyer called them requirements.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsSolicitor to solicitor register. Technical terms used without explanation because the recipient is a corporate partner. Courteous and firm, never combative. Marked subject to contract. Refuses the undertaking in terms that are unambiguous but not accusatory.Explaining what a warranty is, which is wrong for this reader; or hostile phrasing that hardens the negotiation; or ambiguity about whether the undertaking is being given, which is the single most dangerous drafting failure in the station.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawTreats the warranty limitations correctly as contractual allocations of risk, distinguishes the tax covenant and title and capacity warranties from commercial warranties in justifying different caps and periods, applies the fair disclosure standard correctly, and applies the restraint of trade principle correctly in explaining that a covenant must go no further than is reasonably necessary to protect the goodwill being bought.Treating warranties and indemnities as interchangeable, asserting the four year covenant is simply void without reference to reasonableness and the interest protected, or suggesting a solicitor's undertaking can be given and then discharged by best endeavours.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with all seven points and, on the guarantee, sets out a complete substitute mechanism: contractual best endeavours obligation, release as a condition to completion with a long stop, and repayment of the overdraft out of completion monies. Notes the effect of the subject to contract marking given the heads of terms are binding only as to exclusivity and confidentiality.Refusing the undertaking and stopping there, leaving the buyer with no route to the protection it needs, which is what turns a negotiation email into a deal breaker. Also, silence on any one of the seven points.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises that the undertaking sought would bind the firm to procure the acts of the sellers and of Ryedale Bank, neither of which is within the firm's control, and that an undertaking must be performed once given. Declines it expressly, explains why, and offers the contractual alternative. Does not overstate the bank's position to keep the deal moving, since the relationship manager's informal comment is not a commitment.Giving the undertaking, or giving it in softened wording such as confirming the guarantees will be released, which is the same promise dressed differently. Also fails: repeating the relationship manager's informal remark as though the bank had agreed, which misleads the other side.

Examiner notes

This is the negotiation station and it is marked as a negotiation, not as a legal opinion. A candidate who states seven positions correctly but gives no reasons will not pass the recipient focus criterion, because the recipient's job is to persuade her own client's board on Friday and she needs material to do it with. Equally, a candidate who softens every position to keep the deal sweet has not advanced the sellers' interests. The deciding point is paragraph 7. Roughly speaking, candidates split three ways: those who give the undertaking, who fail on ethics whatever else they do; those who refuse it and stop, who pass ethics but stall the deal and lose ground on comprehensiveness; and those who refuse it and put a complete contractual mechanism in its place, who are the grade A performances. Watch for the softened undertaking, phrased as a confirmation rather than an undertaking, which candidates often believe is a safe middle course. It is not. It is the same promise.

Written station 35: Internal note to a partner on an investor fundraising for a partnership incorporating

Legal writing  |  Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures  |  30 minutes

Model answer

From: Trainee Solicitor

To: Verity Loxdale

Date: 22 June 2027

Subject: Marchwood Joinery, new instruction, my view before you reply

Verity,

My view is that we can do the corporate work but not the fundraising as they have asked for it, and that we should not open a file at all until the conflict at point 4 is resolved.

1. We cannot do the promotion, the investor advice or the fee

We are not FCA authorised. Advising a person on the merits of subscribing for shares, and arranging a subscription, are regulated activities. Our Part 20 exemption only covers activity that arises out of, or is complementary to, a professional service we are providing to a particular client. The twelve investors are not our clients, and advising them that this is a sound investment is the object of the exercise rather than something incidental to work we are doing for Marchwood, so the exemption does not reach it and the general prohibition applies. Helena's reason for wanting it, that they will believe it more from a solicitor, is the reason we must not do it. There is a shorter answer as well. Recommending to an individual that he or she subscribe for shares is specified as a non-exempt activity by article 6 of the Non-Exempt Activities Order 2001, and an activity specified under section 327(6) can never be an exempt regulated activity however incidental it is. So even if the investors were somehow our clients, we could not do this piece of work.

The information memorandum is a separate problem. An invitation to subscribe for shares is a financial promotion, and we cannot communicate it in the course of business unless an authorised person approves its content or an exemption applies. Twelve friends, former customers and business network contacts, none of them professional investors, are unlikely to fall within the high net worth or sophisticated investor exemptions, and I would not run that assessment on the partners' description of who these people are.

The fee has to be refused too. A percentage of the money raised is payment for the promotion rather than for professional services, it cannot be reconciled with the incidental basis of the exemption, and it gives us our own financial interest in the raise succeeding.

We can incorporate the company, do the business transfer, the articles, the subscription agreement and the shareholders' agreement, acting for the company. For the promotion and the investors they need an authorised firm.

2. The draft memorandum

It says there is no material litigation, when the Halden claim for 47,800 pounds has been issued. It names Colm as a current principal, which he has not been since 31 January 2027. And it says it was prepared with our assistance, which invites investors to rely on us for a document we have not settled. If it goes out in that form we would be complicit in misleading the investors. The last line comes out unless we have approved the whole document, and the litigation and the change of principals must be stated accurately.

3. The retirement was never notified

No Gazette notice, no letter to customers or suppliers, and Colm's name still on the letterhead, the invoices and the website through the spring. Halden is a customer of nine years standing, so it is entitled to treat all apparent members of the old firm as members until it has actual notice, and it had none. I expect Colm to remain liable for the March order on that basis and on holding out. That the order postdates his retirement does not help him, so the answer to his request to come off the claim is no. Helena and Priya should Gazette the change, write to every customer and supplier and change the letterhead, invoices and website today, because the exposure runs on new orders until they do. Incorporating does not move the existing partnership debts.

4. The conflict, which decides whether we take this on

Colm is our client on his personal file and has told us in confidence about the petition of 4 June 2027, listed for 13 August 2027, and asked that Helena and Priya are not told until after the shares are issued. We cannot disclose it without his consent. It is also material to the Marchwood matter, so if we act there we owe a duty to inform our client of it that we could not perform. There is also a live conflict between Colm and the other two over the shareholding he says he was promised, which Helena did not confirm.

I recommend you speak to Colm first, put it to him that he must tell them or consent to our telling them, and that if he refuses we decline the Marchwood instruction, keep his confidence and give no reason beyond a conflict of interest. If he consents, we act for the company only and all three take separate advice.

5. What to say this week

We would be glad to do the corporate work; we cannot promote the shares, advise the investors or be paid out of the raise, and they need an authorised firm for that; the memorandum cannot go out as drafted; they should Gazette the retirement and write to customers today; and there is one point we must resolve before we can open the file, without saying what it is.

Trainee Solicitor

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The firm holds confidential information from Colm Draycott, its own client on a separate personal file, that a bankruptcy petition was presented against him on 4 June 2027 and is listed for 13 August 2027, and he has expressly asked that Helena and Priya are not told until after the shares are issued. That information is material to the Marchwood incorporation and fundraising, on which the firm is being asked to act. Confidentiality prevents disclosure without his consent, and the duty to make a client aware of material information cannot be performed while the firm keeps it, so the two retainers cannot sit together. The correct resolution is to go back to Colm, press him to disclose or to consent, and decline the Marchwood instruction if he will not, giving conflict of interest as the reason and nothing more. Sitting alongside it are three further points: a live conflict between Colm and the other two over his claimed shareholding; the risk of being complicit in a misleading document, since the draft memorandum denies material litigation when the Halden claim has been issued, names Colm as a current principal, and invites reliance on the firm's involvement; and an own interest conflict in being paid a percentage of the money raised.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Include relevant facts.SkillsUses the facts that drive each conclusion: the firm is not FCA authorised but is an exempt professional firm, the twelve individuals are not professional investors, the percentage fee proposal, the absence of a Gazette notice and of any notice to customers, Halden's nine year trading history and the 6 March 2027 order date against the 31 January 2027 retirement, the memorandum's no material litigation statement against the 47,800 pound claim, and the 4 June 2027 petition.Writing generally about financial services and partnership law without anchoring to the letterhead, the Gazette omission, Halden's status as an existing customer or the specific wording of the memorandum. Also, reciting facts with no conclusion attached to them.
Use a logical structure.SkillsOpens with the recommendation, then takes the issues in the order that matters, closing with what the partner should actually say to the client this week. Each section reaches a conclusion. The partner could act on it without reading twice.A survey of issues with the answer withheld until the end or never given at all, which is exactly what the partner said she did not want. Or the conflict point raised first in the final line, after the reader has already been told the firm can act.
Advice and content is client and recipient focused.SkillsWritten for the supervising partner, not for the client. Gives a view, states what the firm can and cannot take on, flags the risk to the firm, and hands her usable words for the client call including the point that the reason for the delay cannot be given. Distinguishes what she should say from what she must not say.Drafting the client letter instead of the internal note, or hedging every conclusion so the partner still has to decide everything herself. Also fails to separate the internal analysis from what may be communicated externally, which on these facts is a confidentiality breach waiting to happen.
Use clear, precise, concise and acceptable language which is appropriate to the recipient.SkillsInternal register: direct, unadorned, no client facing softening, technical terms used without explanation because the reader is the head of corporate. Short sentences, headed sections, a stated view rather than a discussion. Confidential material handled with visible care even inside an internal document.Client letter register, complete with reassurance and pleasantries, which wastes the reader's time; or so telegraphic that the reasoning cannot be followed; or explaining the general prohibition to a corporate partner as though she were a lay reader.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly identifies advising on the merits of subscribing and arranging as regulated activities caught by the general prohibition, correctly applies the prohibition on activities specified under section 327(6), namely that a recommendation to an individual to subscribe for shares is a non-exempt activity under article 6 of the Non-Exempt Activities Order 2001 and so can never be an exempt regulated activity, correctly treats the memorandum as a financial promotion needing approval by an authorised person or an exemption, and correctly concludes on section 36 and section 14 that Colm remains exposed to Halden as an existing customer with no notice of the change.Assuming the Part 20 exemption covers everything a solicitor does, which is the commonest error on this material. Also: concluding Colm is not liable because the order postdates his retirement, or treating the Gazette notice as sufficient for a customer who had dealt with the firm before.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers the four strands: the regulated activities and the fee basis, the financial promotion, the continuing partnership exposure with the practical steps to stop it running, and the position on incorporation not transferring existing partnership debts. Separates what the firm may still do from what it may not, so the partner has a workable scope.Dealing with the financial services point and stopping, so the Halden exposure and the urgent practical steps on the letterhead, Gazette and customer notices are never raised. Or spotting the partnership point and never reaching the memorandum's misleading statements.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies the confidentiality and disclosure clash directly: the bankruptcy petition is confidential to Colm, it is material to the Marchwood matter, and the firm cannot both keep it and discharge its duty to inform. Resolves it by seeking Colm's consent first and declining the Marchwood instruction if he refuses, giving no reason beyond conflict. Also identifies the conflict between Colm and the other two over his shareholding, the risk of being complicit in a misleading memorandum, and the own interest conflict in a percentage of the raise.Recommending disclosure of the petition to Helena and Priya, which breaches confidentiality; or proposing an information barrier so the firm can keep both retainers, which does not cure a duty of disclosure the firm cannot perform; or acting for the company and all three individuals on the incorporation without addressing the conflict at all. Silence on the memorandum's no material litigation statement is also a fail here, because letting it go out would make the firm complicit.

Examiner notes

Two things separate a pass from a fail. The first is whether the candidate writes to the partner or to the client. This is an internal note and the register must change: a view, not a survey, and no client facing reassurance. Candidates who cannot switch register lose two skills criteria at once. The second is the confidentiality clash, which is the hardest ethics point in this batch because both of the obvious answers are wrong. Telling Helena and Priya breaches Colm's confidence. Carrying on and saying nothing leaves the firm unable to perform its duty of disclosure to the Marchwood client. Candidates frequently reach for an information barrier, which does not help, because the problem is a duty the firm cannot discharge rather than information leaking between teams. The grade A answer goes back to Colm for consent and is prepared to decline the instruction. On the law, the recurring error is assuming the exempt professional firm registration lets a solicitor do anything a client asks in the course of a transaction; the Scope Rules extract in the materials is there to be read, and the prohibition on activities specified under section 327(6) answers Helena's request directly, because a recommendation to an individual to subscribe for shares is a non-exempt activity.

Oral stations printed in this book (1-10)

These 10 oral stations are printed in Part 3 of the book with a full role play script, numbered 1 to 10 in the order they appear there.

Oral station 1: Contested bail application in the magistrates' court on a dwelling burglary charge

Advocacy  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

May it please you, madam. I appear for Mr Okafor. My learned friend appears for the prosecution.

This is an application for bail. Mr Okafor is 27, he has been in custody since Sunday evening, and he is presumed innocent of a burglary which, on the papers as they presently stand, rests on a single fingerprint on the outside of a window frame he says he handled last November while doing two days of gardening and gutter clearing at that address.

May I take it in four parts. First, the framework. Second, the two grounds the Crown advance and why neither is made out. Third, the strength of the evidence, which the court is expressly entitled to weigh. Fourth, the conditions I invite you to impose, because I recognise that the court will want reassurance and I do not shrink from that.

The framework, shortly. Mr Okafor has a general right to bail. The burden is not on me to earn it; it is on the Crown to displace it, and to do so by satisfying you that there are substantial grounds for believing one of the statutory exceptions is made out. Substantial grounds, madam, not a risk, not a possibility, not an understandable anxiety. If at the end of this application you are left thinking that something might go wrong, the Crown have not discharged that burden.

The first ground is failure to surrender. The Crown rely on one matter, from June 2021, almost five years ago. It was dealt with by a fine of 80 pounds, which tells you what the court thought of it, and the court record shows he attended later that same day. It was not an absconding. Since then he has been before this court once, in 2023, and he answered his bail. He was made subject to a twelve month community order and the probation record before you says "good engagement, attended all appointments". He also completed a suspended sentence order in 2022 without breach. So his actual record of compliance over the last five years is complete, and the single blemish is old, minor and answered.

Set against that are his ties. He has an eight month old daughter, Ada. His partner, Ms Pryce, works Tuesday to Saturday at a nursery and relies on him for childcare on those days. She has telephoned my office and is willing to attend this afternoon. He has work at Feltridge Logistics; his shift manager telephoned my office this morning, said the work remains open to him and described him as someone who turns up and gets on with it. A man with a baby, a partner who needs him at home and a job that is being held open is not a man with the means or the motive to disappear.

The second ground is the commission of further offences. The Crown call it a pattern. Madam, three convictions between 2019 and 2023, the last of them nearly three years ago, is not a pattern; it is a receding history. He has committed no offence for nearly three years. He has never, on the record before you, committed an offence while on bail. That is the very thing the Crown must show substantial grounds to fear, and the one indicator of it is entirely absent from his antecedents.

I come to the strength of the evidence, which the statute expressly permits you to weigh. The Crown put their case at its highest as a fingerprint at the point of entry. It is not that. It is a fingerprint on the external frame of the window. There is not a mark on the internal surfaces, not on the catch, not on the drawer that was opened. Mr Okafor gave an account in interview, immediately and with a solicitor present, that he did two days of gardening and gutter clearing at that address in November for cash and handled the rear windows. Mrs Prentice's own statement does not contradict him. She says her son arranges odd jobs for her and she cannot rule it out. Her son is abroad and has not been spoken to.

What else is there? A neighbour who could not see the man's face, who accepts the lighting is poor, and who gives a partial registration as "something like WK57". That leads to a car registered to the defendant's cousin, who says several family members borrow it and he cannot say who had it. There is no identification procedure. There is no CCTV. Nothing was recovered on arrest and nothing has been recovered since. The cell site material is six weeks away. This is not a case where a man will look at the evidence and conclude that flight is his only option.

Madam, the Crown say no condition can meet their concerns. I invite you to reject that, because the conditions I offer meet each concern directly.

Residence at Flat 12 Barrow House. That is where he was arrested and where he has been living for seven weeks with Ms Pryce and their daughter. Ms Pryce is the sole tenant, she has confirmed to my office that she is content for him to live there and for a tag to be fitted, and she is here or can be here this afternoon to say so. I make clear that I put forward that address and no other, because that is the address that has been checked.

A curfew, electronically monitored. This offence is said to have been committed at 03:40. A tagged curfew answers the night hours precisely. I ask that it run from 21:00 to 06:00 rather than to 07:00, because his early shifts start at 07:00 and a curfew that costs him his job would work against the very stability the court is trying to secure.

Reporting to Kingsmoor police station twice a week, on days that do not clash with his shifts.

An exclusion zone covering Ashcombe Row, and no contact directly or indirectly with Mrs Prentice or Mr Tapp. Those conditions protect the complainant and the witness and cost the court nothing.

I do not ask for anything beyond that, and I do not offer conditions that would serve no purpose, because conditions are only properly imposed where they are necessary and proportionate to a specific risk.

Madam, on 6 February an elderly woman's home was broken into and I do not minimise that for a moment. But the question today is not who did it. It is whether the Crown have shown substantial grounds for believing that this man, with a baby, a partner, a job held open, a clean bail record for five years and an answer to the only forensic evidence in the case, would abscond or offend if released under an electronically monitored curfew. In my submission they have come nowhere near it.

Unless I can assist you further, that is my application.

The test the application turns on

Section 4 of the Bail Act 1976 gives the defendant a general right to bail, which the court must grant unless one of the exceptions in Schedule 1 applies. For an imprisonable indictable offence the relevant exceptions in Part 1 of Schedule 1 require the court to be satisfied that there are substantial grounds for believing that, if released on bail, the defendant would fail to surrender to custody, would commit an offence while on bail, or would interfere with witnesses or otherwise obstruct the course of justice. The burden of displacing the right to bail is on the prosecution, and the standard is substantial grounds for belief, not a mere risk or possibility. In deciding whether a ground is made out the court takes into account the factors set out in Schedule 1, including the nature and seriousness of the offence and the probable method of dealing with the defendant, his character, antecedents, associations and community ties, his record in relation to previous grants of bail, and the strength of the evidence against him. Where bail is granted, conditions may be imposed under section 3(6) of the Bail Act 1976 only where necessary for one of the statutory purposes, and they must be proportionate to the risk they address.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client has instructed the firm to tell the court that he will live at his mother's address at 6 Herndale Court, that it is agreed, and that his mother should not be contacted beforehand. Nobody has spoken to the mother. To advance that address as available and agreed would be to make an assertion of fact to the court with no proper basis, and would risk misleading the court, which the SRA Principles and the Code of Conduct for Solicitors prohibit; an advocate may only put forward statements and submissions which are properly arguable, and may not mislead the court by act, by omission or by being complicit in a client's deception. The competent candidate spots that the instruction cannot be followed as given, and resolves it openly rather than by silence: advance Flat 12 Barrow House, which the tenant has confirmed by telephone and is willing to attend to confirm, or ask the court to put the case back so that the mother can be telephoned and, if she consents, offer her address properly. The candidate should also advise the client, in conference or during a short adjournment, that a false or unverified address is more likely to lose him bail than gain it, and that if he insists on the false assertion the firm cannot make it. The confidentiality of the client's instruction is preserved: the candidate does not tell the court what the client asked them to do.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsCorrect address throughout for a District Judge in the magistrates' court. Announces appearance and the appearance of the prosecutor.
