Concedes the unattractive parts of the record openly and without defensiveness, never over claims, never argues with the bench, and stops the moment the judge speaks.Calling the District Judge "your worships" or "sir" when she is addressed as madam or judge, talking over her interruptions, or adopting an emotive register about the client's baby rather than a professional one.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsSignposts the structure at the outset and keeps to it: framework and burden, then each Crown ground answered in turn, then the strength of the evidence, then the conditions package, then a short conclusion. The judge can tell at any moment which part of the argument she is in.A chronological retelling of the police case followed by an undifferentiated list of good points, so that community ties, evidence and conditions are mixed together and no Crown ground is ever squarely answered.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsTurns each Crown point around rather than merely denying it: the single failure to surrender becomes evidence of five years of subsequent compliance, and the fingerprint becomes evidence of how thin the case is. Puts the burden on the Crown at every stage and offers conditions from a position of strength, not concession.Pleading rather than arguing. Asserting that the client is a family man and would not abscond, with no engagement with why the Crown's grounds fail, and no reason given for preferring bail beyond sympathy.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsAnswers each question directly and at once, then returns to the thread. Where the judge asks who confirmed the address, gives a straight answer and, if needed, asks courteously for the case to be put back. Adjusts the remaining submission to reflect what has already been dealt with by question and answer.Deflecting a question with "I will come to that" and never coming to it, or abandoning the prepared submission entirely after the first interruption and never recovering the structure.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsDeploys the facts that actually matter: the fingerprint is on the external frame with nothing inside, the occupier cannot exclude the gardening work, the identification is a partial registration on a cousin's car, nothing was recovered, the failure to surrender was answered the same day and fined, the 2023 order was completed with good engagement, the partner is the tenant and is willing to attend, and the shift starts at 07:00.Omitting the strength of the evidence altogether, or missing that the client's shift start time makes a 07:00 curfew end unworkable, or failing to mention that the partner has offered to attend court to confirm the address.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the general right to bail accurately, identifies the two exceptions actually relied on, and applies the correct standard of substantial grounds for belief with the burden on the prosecution. Treats seriousness and likely disposal as a statutory factor going to the grounds, not as a ground in itself.Reversing the burden by inviting the court to be satisfied the client will not abscond, or asserting that bail must be refused because the offence is serious, or applying a "real risk" test instead of substantial grounds.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawWorks through the relevant statutory factors rather than one of them: nature and seriousness and probable disposal, character, antecedents, associations and community ties, record on previous grants of bail, and strength of the evidence. Then applies the separate test for conditions, that each must be necessary for a statutory purpose and proportionate.Arguing only community ties, ignoring the strength of the evidence as a factor the court is entitled to weigh, and offering a recited menu of conditions without explaining why any of them is necessary.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawSpots unprompted that the mother's address cannot be advanced, advances only the address that has been confirmed, and if pressed says candidly that a second address has not been verified and asks for the case to be put back rather than asserting it. Preserves the client's confidentiality while doing so, and would advise the client of the position at the first opportunity.Telling the court that the client will reside at 6 Herndale Court and that it is agreed, or saying nothing about the address at all and hoping the point is not reached, or announcing to the judge that the client tried to get the advocate to lie, which breaches confidentiality.

Examiner notes

The pass or fail line here is the address. A candidate who tells District Judge Halloran that the client will live at his mother's, when the conference note shows plainly that the mother knows nothing about it, has misled the court and will not recover on the ethics criterion whatever else they do. The commonest trap is that the note buries the instruction at paragraph six under a heading about address, so candidates who skim read the materials in preparation walk straight into it. The second discriminator is whether the candidate argues the correct test. Weak candidates argue that their client is a nice man with a baby and never mention the burden, the standard of substantial grounds, or the statutory factors. Strong candidates make the Crown carry the burden throughout, weigh the strength of the evidence as a factor in its own right, and offer a conditions package in which every condition is justified by reference to the ground it answers. A third and subtler discriminator is the curfew timing: a candidate who offers a 07:00 curfew end without noticing that the client's shifts start at 07:00 has not read the conference note properly. Do not reward the candidate who simply reads out the Crown's own proposed conditions and adopts them; that is capitulation, not advocacy.

Oral station 2: Application to exclude a confession in the Crown Court on a charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm

Advocacy  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

May it please Your Honour. I appear for Mr Lisle, my learned friend for the Crown.

This is an application to exclude the interview of 4 October. I put it two ways, in this order. Primarily under section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, on the reliability limb, where the burden is on the Crown to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the confession was not obtained in consequence of what was said and done. In the alternative under section 78, as a matter of Your Honour's discretion.

Can I make one thing clear at the outset. I do not invite Your Honour to decide whether what Mr Lisle said in that room was true. That is not the question on either limb. The question is how it was obtained.

May I take Your Honour to the circumstances existing at the time, because on the section 76 reliability limb they are the whole of the case.

Mr Lisle was 19. His full scale IQ, on the unchallenged report of Dr Marchetti, is 63. His comprehension of abstract questions falls in the lowest two per cent for his age. He scores in the high range for interrogative suggestibility and in the high range for compliance. Dr Marchetti's opinion, and the Crown have served no evidence to contradict it, is that he is likely to agree with a proposition put by a person in authority in order to end an unpleasant situation, particularly where he is tired, distressed or believes agreement will get him out. And he does not understand the second limb of the caution even when it is explained to him three times in simplified language by a psychologist across a table.

Now, Your Honour, what happened to that young man in Ravensworth custody suite.

At 23:41 he asked for a solicitor. It is in the custody record in terms. At 00:05 a referral was made. At 00:52 DC Aldous wrote, "Solicitor not yet attended. Interview to commence, DP consents." There is no entry authorising an urgent interview. There is no recorded authority from any superintendent or inspector to delay legal advice. The interview began at 01:15. The solicitor arrived at 02:31, eight minutes after it ended.

And Your Honour will want the first page of the transcript, because it answers the Crown's only point on legal advice. The Crown say he consented, and they point to DC Aldous's log entry at 00:52. This is what the tape records. The caution is put. Mr Lisle asks, "Is Katie coming?" He is told, "This is about you, Jordan, not Katie." He then says, in terms, "I want the solicitor. They said one was coming." DC Aldous answers, "He is not here yet and we cannot sit about all night. You said you were happy to go on." There is no audible reply, and the interview proceeds. So the recorded consent on which the Crown rely is contradicted by the Crown's own recording. There was no waiver. Code C paragraph 6.6 prohibited this interview from beginning at all, and the only route by which it could have begun after a change of mind, paragraph 6.6(d), requires the detainee's agreement recorded in writing or on the interview record and the authority of an officer of at least inspector rank. Neither exists. What the custody record actually shows is a request for a solicitor at 23:41, a renewed request on tape at the start of the interview, and an interview conducted regardless.

At 23:46 the custody sergeant's own risk assessment recorded that this detained person appeared to have difficulty understanding questions and repeated them back, that he had a support worker named Katie at Elmbank, that he had reading and writing difficulties, and that he appeared anxious and tearful. The box asking whether he appeared to be a vulnerable person requiring an appropriate adult was left blank. It was never completed and it was never reviewed. The appropriate adult scheme has confirmed in writing that they hold no record of any call out that night.

So the two safeguards that exist for precisely this suspect, a solicitor and an appropriate adult, were both absent, one of them after he had asked for it.

May I turn to what was said and done. Page 10 of the transcript, at about 02:05, after he had been in custody for nearly three hours and had denied the assault repeatedly. Detective Constable Prewitt says: "Callum has already been in here. Callum has told us what happened and Callum has put you right in it." Mr Lisle answers, "No", when asked if he understands. He then says, "Has he?" and then, "I don't know."

Your Honour will note that Mr Frayne was released with no further action on 20 October.

Then DC Aldous: "Jordan, look at me. You have been here since eleven o'clock. I have got a lad here with a broken nose. You are nineteen. This does not have to take all night. Get this done and you can be out of here."

And the very next thing this young man says is: "If I say it can I go home?"

That question, Your Honour, is the application. It is the moment where the transcript records, in his own words, the operative reason for what followed. He is not told that saying it will not get him home. He is told, "Let us deal with what happened first." He then says, "All right. I hit him. Can I go now?" And the very next thing after that is, "I want Katie."

Of the twenty six questions that follow, he answers "I don't know" to twenty two.

On the statutory language, the things said and done are the false or at best unverified assertion that a co accused had implicated him, and the plain suggestion that admission would end his detention. The question for Your Honour is whether those things were likely, in the circumstances existing at the time, to render unreliable any confession which might be made in consequence. The circumstances are an IQ of 63, high suggestibility, high compliance, no solicitor after a request, no appropriate adult, and the small hours of the morning. In my submission the answer is obvious, and the Crown cannot begin to discharge the burden of proving beyond reasonable doubt that the confession was not so obtained.

I accept at once, as the Crown say, that breaches of the Codes are not automatically fatal. The question is whether they are significant and substantial and what they caused. These are not paperwork slips. Each breach removed a safeguard that exists to prevent exactly the exchange at page 10. A solicitor would have intervened at "get this done and you can be out of here". An appropriate adult would have been there to help him understand what was being put to him and to say that he did not.

If Your Honour were against me on section 76, I invite Your Honour to exclude under section 78. The unfairness is this. The Crown's case is the confession and nothing else. There has been no identification procedure. The only description is "a lad in grey, skinny, maybe eighteen or nineteen". The CCTV does not show the assault. The person who pointed Mr Lisle out has never been traced and is not a witness. Strip out the interview and there is no case; keep it in, and a jury will convict on the answers of a man with an IQ of 63 given after he asked for a lawyer, was refused one and was told he could go home.

The Crown say all of this goes to weight. On the first limb it does not, because if the burden is not discharged the court shall not admit the confession and there is no room for weight. On the second, cross examination cannot recreate what a solicitor and an appropriate adult would have changed in that room.

Finally, and only as a fallback, I recognise that section 77 provides for a warning to the jury where a case depends substantially on a confession by a person with a mental disability made without an independent person present. I say that is a reason to exclude, not an alternative to excluding. A warning does not answer a confession that should never have been obtained.

Your Honour, I invite you to rule the interview inadmissible. If Your Honour considers that the factual account of what happened in that suite is in issue, the proper course is for the Crown to call the interviewing officers on a voir dire, since it is the Crown who carry the burden.

Unless I can assist further, that is my application.

The test the application turns on

Two routes, argued in the alternative. Under section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, where the defence represent to the court that a confession was or may have been obtained by oppression of the person who made it, or in consequence of anything said or done which was likely, in the circumstances existing at the time, to render unreliable any confession which might be made by him in consequence of it, the court shall not allow the confession in evidence except in so far as the prosecution prove to the court beyond reasonable doubt that it was not so obtained. The burden is therefore on the prosecution and the standard is the criminal standard, the question is how the confession was obtained and not whether it is in fact true, and the reliability limb is assessed against the circumstances existing at the time, which include the characteristics of the particular suspect. Under section 78 the court has a discretion to refuse to allow prosecution evidence if, having regard to all the circumstances including the circumstances in which the evidence was obtained, its admission would have such an adverse effect on the fairness of the proceedings that the court ought not to admit it; breaches of the PACE Codes of Practice are not automatically fatal, and the question is whether the breaches were significant and substantial and what their effect on fairness was. The Codes engaged here are the right to legal advice under section 58 and Code C, and the requirement under Code C that an appropriate adult be present where an officer has any reason to suspect that a detained person is vulnerable. Section 77 provides a further safeguard, a warning to the jury where the case depends wholly or substantially on a confession by a person with a mental disability made without an independent person present, but that is a fallback and not an answer to exclusion.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client has told the firm in conference that he did throw the punch, and has asked the advocate to get the interview excluded and then tell the court he was not there. Two duties collide and both must be respected. First, confidentiality: what the client said in conference is privileged and must not be disclosed to the court, to the prosecution or to anyone else, and nothing in the submission may hint at it. Second, the duty not to mislead the court and to make only assertions which are properly arguable: the advocate may not advance a positive case of alibi or of innocence knowing it to be false, may not call the client to give a false account, and may not suggest to a witness that someone else threw the punch. What remains permissible is substantial and the competent candidate identifies it clearly: the advocate may challenge the admissibility of the confession, because the section 76 question is how it was obtained and not whether it is true, and may put the prosecution to proof at trial on identification and on every element. The correct handling in the station is therefore to make the application entirely on the manner in which the confession was obtained, never to assert that the client is innocent or that the confession is false, and never to reveal the instruction. Beyond the hearing the candidate should advise the client that a positive false case cannot be run, that self defence may be a proper issue on his own account, and that if he insists on advancing an account the firm knows to be untrue the firm must cease to act.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsCorrect address for a Circuit Judge throughout. Measured and unemotional about facts that invite indignation, which makes the indignation land. Concedes the Crown's correct proposition about Code breaches at once and then defeats it, rather than resisting it.Attacking the officers personally, describing the interview as a disgrace or the officers as liars, or using magistrates' court forms of address in the Crown Court.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsStates at the outset that the application is put primarily under the first route and in the alternative under the discretion, then takes the circumstances existing at the time, then the Code breaches, then what was said and done, then the alternative discretionary argument, then the fallback. The judge always knows which limb is being argued.Running the two routes together so that burden, standard and test are blurred, or narrating the custody record chronologically without ever separating admissibility from weight.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsBuilds the argument on the transcript itself, particularly the sequence of the inducement followed immediately by the question about going home, so that the conclusion appears to come from the document rather than from the advocate. Holds the Crown to their burden rather than trying to prove the negative.Reciting the breaches as a list with no causal argument, so that the submission amounts to saying the police got the paperwork wrong, without ever explaining why that means this confession cannot safely be admitted.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsAnswers the question of law when a question of law is asked, rather than retreating into the facts. Deals sensibly with the question about hearing evidence, recognising that it is for the Crown to call the interviewing officers because the burden is theirs on the first limb.Answering "under section 78" and nothing more when asked under what power and where the burden lies, or offering to call the client to give evidence on the voir dire without appreciating what that would expose him to.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsUses the request for a solicitor at 23:41, the renewed request on the interview recording itself ("I want the solicitor. They said one was coming") and the officer's reply, which contradicts the custody log entry that the detained person consented, the absence of any recorded authority to delay, the interview at 01:15 with the solicitor arriving at 02:31, the uncompleted vulnerability box on the risk assessment, the scheme's written confirmation of no call out, the psychologist's IQ, suggestibility and compliance findings, the exact words of the inducement and the reply, the twenty two "I don't know" answers, the fact that the co accused was released with no further action, and the absence of any identification procedure or forensic evidence.Missing that the client asked for a solicitor before the interview, which converts the point from an omission into a refusal, or missing the no further action decision on the co accused, which undermines the assertion made to induce the admission.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the reliability limb accurately, including that the court looks at anything said or done in the circumstances existing at the time and at whether it was likely to render unreliable any confession made in consequence, and that the truth of the confession is irrelevant to that question. States the burden as being on the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt and the discretion under the fairness provision correctly.Putting the burden on the defence, applying a balance of probabilities standard, arguing that the confession should be excluded because it is untrue, or confusing oppression with the reliability limb and arguing oppression on facts that do not support it.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers both statutory routes, identifies the specific Code requirements engaged, the right to legal advice and the requirement for an appropriate adult where there is any reason to suspect vulnerability, applies the significant and substantial approach to breaches, and deals with the jury warning provision as a fallback which is a reason to exclude rather than an answer to exclusion.Arguing one route only, or ignoring the appropriate adult point entirely and relying solely on the denial of legal advice, or failing to answer the Crown's argument that the points go to weight.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawMakes the whole application on how the confession was obtained, never asserts that the client is innocent, was elsewhere, or that the confession is false, and never discloses anything said in conference. Understands that challenging admissibility is legitimate even where the confession is accurate, and that what is forbidden is advancing a positive case known to be untrue.Telling the judge this is a false confession by an innocent young man, or foreshadowing an alibi, or revealing the client's admission or the client's request to run a false account, any of which breaches confidentiality or misleads the court.

Examiner notes

The discriminator between a pass and a fail is whether the candidate identifies both routes and, in particular, gets the burden the right way round on the first. Weak candidates argue only section 78, or argue section 76 as though the defence had to prove that the confession was unreliable. The statute puts the burden on the prosecution to the criminal standard once representations are made, and a candidate who says so and then holds the Crown to it is already in pass territory. The second discriminator is the reliability limb's circumstances element. Candidates who list the Code breaches but never connect them to this particular suspect's IQ, suggestibility and compliance have missed the architecture of the test, because the same interview of a robust and experienced adult might not have been objectionable at all. The commonest trap is the ethics point hidden in the conference note. Advocates who have absorbed the note's contents sometimes slip into calling this a false confession by an innocent boy, which they know to be untrue, or, worse, reveal to the judge what the client said in conference. Neither is necessary and both are fatal on the ethics criterion. A confession is excluded because of how it was obtained, so the whole application can and must be made without ever asserting innocence. Candidates should also be marked down for overreaching on the consequence of exclusion; inviting the judge to stop the case today is wrong, since the application before him is admissibility, and the correct submission is that the Crown's case is left with nothing, not that the count is dismissed.

Oral station 3: Application to dismiss a theft charge in the Crown Court on a wholly circumstantial case

Advocacy  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

May it please Your Honour. I appear for Ms Ilunga, my learned friend for the Crown.

This is an application to dismiss the single count of theft. The test is whether it appears to Your Honour that the evidence against the applicant would not be sufficient for her to be properly convicted. I take the prosecution's evidence at its highest. I make no complaint about the honesty of any witness and I do not ask Your Honour to decide any question of fact that would be for a jury.

My submission in one sentence is this. Every single strand of this case establishes that somebody at Fenwick Marine Supplies took cash, or that cash went missing somewhere in the system. Not one strand is capable of isolating Ms Ilunga from the other people who had exactly the same access, and the Crown's own expert says he cannot say when, how, or even whether the cash ever reached the safe.

May I take the strands in turn.

The first strand is access to the safe. The Crown's summary is that the combination was known to four people: my client, Mr Fenwick the owner, Mr Okoye the warehouse supervisor, and Mrs Vaughan, whose combination was never changed after she retired in February 2026. So on the Crown's own case, access does not point at my client. It points at four people.

The second strand is the banking. It is said she prepared the banking sheet. Mr Pask's own note records that Mr Okoye did the banking on at least eleven occasions and Mr Fenwick on at least four. So the banking function was shared.

The third strand is attendance, and this is where the case does not merely fail to isolate her, it points away from her. Of the twenty two shortfall days, she was present on nineteen. Mr Okoye was present on seventeen. That is not a meaningful difference in a workplace where both worked most days. But there is a difference that matters. On three of the twenty two days she was not there at all. Those three days include 4 August 2026, and 4 August carries a shortfall of 1,940 pounds, the largest single shortfall in the entire indictment period. On that day Mr Okoye was present and my client was not.

Your Honour, that is not a point about who is guilty. It is a point about what the evidence is capable of proving. The Crown's theory is a single continuing course of dishonesty by one person. On the Crown's own schedule, the largest single event in that course occurred on a day when the person they have charged was not in the building.

The fourth strand is the CCTV, and there is none. The system has not recorded since February 2026, before the indictment period begins. There is no camera on the safe at all.

The fifth strand is forensic evidence, and there is none. Nothing on the safe. Nothing recovered on search. No cash recovered anywhere.

The sixth strand is the bank deposits. The Crown point to 2,100 pounds of cash deposits over nine months. Two observations, neither of which requires Your Honour to accept a word my client says. First, 2,100 pounds is a little over eleven per cent of the sum charged. Even if every penny of it were stolen money, it does not begin to evidence a theft of 18,450 pounds. Second, the Crown's own material accounts for more than half of it: Mr Sowerby has given a statement to the police confirming that he bought a motorcycle from her for 1,150 pounds in cash in April 2026, and there is a signed receipt. That is prosecution evidence, not defence assertion.

The seventh strand is Ms Hallam. Her statement establishes that everyone knew my client handled the cash, which is not in dispute; she was the office manager and it was her job. Beyond that, she says she never saw anyone take anything and has never seen the safe open. The one line the Crown will want is that she heard my client was struggling for money. She cannot say who told her. She never heard my client say it. It was, in her words, "just something that was going about at work". That is not evidence a properly directed jury could act on, and Your Honour will have in mind that she also says Mr Okoye does the banking sometimes and that she has seen him alone in the back office.

Now, Your Honour said at the outset that circumstantial cases are ordinarily for juries, and I entirely accept it. A circumstantial case is properly left to a jury where the strands, taken together, are capable of closing in on the defendant so that a jury could properly exclude any realistic alternative. This case is the opposite. Every strand is shared. And the Crown's own accountant has cut the ground away beneath the inference in four separate ways in his appended notes.

He says he cannot say when any cash was removed, because the reconciliation compares a day's till reading with a weekly banking, and cash sat in the safe for between one and seven days. He says the banking sheet was prepared by whoever did the banking, and that was not always my client. He says the shortfall is consistent with cash removed from the safe, or with cash removed before it ever reached the safe, or with till operator error over a sustained period, and he expressly declines to say which. And he says the stock system was never reconciled, so he cannot exclude the possibility that goods were sold without being rung through the till at all, in which case no cash would ever have entered the safe and the person who took it need never have had the combination.

Your Honour, if the Crown's own expert cannot exclude the possibility that the money never reached the safe, then safe access, which is the only feature of this case that has anything to do with my client's role, is not even established as the mechanism.

Your Honour asked me on what basis I say Mr Okoye is the likelier culprit. I want to be clear: I do not say it, I make no case against him, and I do not need to. My point is confined to what the Crown have served. Their own material shows another employee with the same code, doing the banking on at least eleven occasions, present on all three of the days when my client was not, including the largest shortfall. That is not an accusation. It is a demonstration that the Crown's evidence cannot do the one thing it must do, which is to exclude everyone else.

Taken at its highest, the Crown's case is that money went missing from a business where four people had the safe code, three did the banking, there was no working CCTV, no forensic evidence, no admission, no recovery, and an expert who cannot say when the money went or whether it ever arrived. A jury properly directed on the criminal standard could not properly convict Ms Ilunga on that.

I invite Your Honour to dismiss the charge and quash the count.

Unless I can assist further, that is my application.

The test the application turns on

Where a defendant has been sent to the Crown Court for trial, he or she may apply to the Crown Court for the charge to be dismissed under paragraph 2 of Schedule 3 to the Crime and Disorder Act 1998. The judge shall dismiss the charge, and quash any count relating to it in any indictment preferred, if it appears to the judge that the evidence against the applicant would not be sufficient for the applicant to be properly convicted. The test is in substance the same as the second limb of the familiar approach to a submission of no case to answer: the court takes the prosecution evidence at its highest and asks whether a jury, properly directed, could properly convict on it. The judge does not resolve conflicts of fact, does not choose between competing accounts and does not assess the credibility of witnesses whose evidence is capable of belief; but where the prosecution evidence is so weak or so tenuous, or where its strength depends on inferences that cannot properly be drawn, the case must be stopped. In a wholly circumstantial case the question is whether the evidence is capable of supporting the inference of guilt to the criminal standard, which requires that a jury could properly exclude any realistic alternative explanation; where the same evidence points equally at several people with the same opportunity, the inference against one of them is not one a properly directed jury could properly draw.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client has instructed the firm to tell the court that a colleague, Mr Dean Okoye, is the thief, and that he has money problems and gambles. Two distinct professional problems arise and both must be handled without a word of either reaching the judge. First, conflict and confidentiality: the firm previously acted for Mr Okoye and holds confidential financial information about him which is material to the current matter, and his interests are plainly adverse to the client's. The duty of confidentiality to a former client survives the end of the retainer and takes precedence over the duty to disclose material information to the current client; the firm may not use or refer to that information, and where it holds confidential information which is material and the interests are adverse, it may not act for the current client unless effective measures or the required consents are in place, which is why the matter has been escalated to the COLP and why the firm may have to cease acting. Second, and independently, an advocate may only make assertions and put forward submissions which are properly arguable, and must not put an allegation of dishonesty against a named third party without a proper evidential basis. The competent candidate therefore makes the application solely on the sufficiency of the prosecution's own served evidence, relies on Mr Okoye's access, banking role and attendance only because the Crown itself has served that material, says nothing whatever about his finances, gambling or motive, and does not mention the previous retainer or the conflict to the court. The candidate should also recognise, for the file rather than for the hearing, that the client must be advised that no positive case can be run against a named colleague without a proper basis, and that if the firm cannot continue to act she must be given the opportunity to instruct another firm, without being told the reason.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsCorrect address for a Circuit Judge, no complaint about the honesty of any prosecution witness, and a measured refusal of the judge's invitation to accuse a third party. Makes clear at the outset that no question of fact is being asked of the court, which sets the right tone for the whole application.Emotive assertions of the client's innocence, describing the prosecution as a disgrace or the investigation as lazy, or arguing with the judge when told that she is not trying the case.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsStates the test, states the submission in one sentence, then takes the strands of the circumstantial case one by one, then deploys the accountant's own qualifications, then answers the deposits and the hearsay point, then concludes with the relief sought.No visible structure, so the judge hears an unordered mixture of complaints about the evidence and assertions about the defence account, with the test itself never stated or stated only at the end.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsTurns the Crown's own expert into the strongest defence material, and uses the 4 August shortfall as a demonstration rather than an accusation. Accepts the judge's proposition that circumstantial cases are usually for juries and then distinguishes it rather than resisting it.A list of things the prosecution does not have, with no explanation of why the absence of each matters to the inference the jury would have to draw, so that the submission sounds like a complaint about the investigation rather than an argument about sufficiency.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsAnswers the test question at once and accurately, and declines the invitation at question three courteously and without hesitation, restating the limited purpose of the point about Mr Okoye. Recovers the structure after each intervention.Taking the judge's bait and constructing a case against Mr Okoye, or answering the question about the test with a description of the facts, or arguing back after being told the court is not trying the case.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsDeploys four people with the safe code including a retired manager whose code was never changed, banking shared with at least eleven occasions by Mr Okoye and four by Mr Fenwick, presence on nineteen of twenty two days against seventeen, the three absent days including the 1,940 pound shortfall on 4 August, no CCTV since February 2026, no forensic evidence, no recovery, deposits of 2,100 pounds against 18,450 pounds charged, the buyer's confirmation of the 1,150 pound cash sale, and the unattributed hearsay in Ms Hallam's statement.Missing the 4 August point entirely, or missing the accountant's appended notes, particularly the possibility that goods were never rung through the till so that no cash ever reached the safe.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the statutory test on an application to dismiss accurately, identifies that it corresponds to the second limb of the approach to a submission of no case, and applies it by taking the prosecution evidence at its highest without resolving factual disputes.Applying a test of whether the defendant is guilty, or whether the prosecution is likely to succeed, or inviting the judge to prefer the defence account, all of which are the wrong question and will be corrected from the bench.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawExplains what a circumstantial case must be capable of doing, namely supporting the inference of guilt to the criminal standard so that a properly directed jury could exclude realistic alternatives, and applies that to every strand rather than to one. Deals with the hearsay quality of the struggling for money evidence and with the arithmetic of the deposits.Arguing only that there is no direct evidence, without engaging with how a jury could or could not draw the inference, or leaving the deposits and the hearsay wholly unanswered so that the Crown's two best points stand untouched.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawConfines itself to the Crown's own served material about Mr Okoye's access, banking role and attendance, says expressly that no positive case is advanced against him, and says nothing about his finances, gambling or motive. Does not mention the previous retainer, the conflict or the COLP referral to the court, and understands that the former client's confidentiality survives the retainer and cannot be overridden by the current client's wishes.Suggesting that Mr Okoye had money problems or gambled, or that he had a motive, from any source; or telling the judge about the firm's previous retainer or the conflict, which breaches the former client's confidentiality and is irrelevant to sufficiency.

Examiner notes

This station separates candidates on discipline more than on knowledge. The test is a narrow one and the commonest failure is to argue the trial: candidates start telling the judge that the client is honest, that her partner really is a hairdresser who is paid in tips, and that the motorcycle sale really happened. Judge Vandeleur will stop them, and a candidate who cannot then reorient to sufficiency will lose both the structure criterion and the application of law criteria. The correct approach is to take the prosecution case at its highest and show that each strand is shared, using the Crown's own accountant against the Crown; the appended notes in the schedule are the single richest source in the bundle and a candidate who ignores them has not read the papers properly. The 4 August point, the largest shortfall occurring on a day the defendant was not present, is the strongest fact in the case and should be deployed prominently. The ethics trap is the invitation at question three. The client's instruction is to accuse Mr Okoye and to say he has money problems and gambles, and the firm holds confidential financial information about him from a former retainer which it may not use. A candidate who says anything about his finances, gambling or motive, whatever the source, fails the ethics criterion; so does a candidate who tells the judge about the conflict or the previous retainer, which is confidential to the former client and irrelevant to the application. The right answer is the disciplined one: no positive case against anyone, reliance only on the Crown's own served material, and a clear statement to the judge that the defence is not saying Mr Okoye did it. Candidates should also avoid the overreach of inviting the judge to prefer one suspect over another, which concedes that this is a jury question and destroys the submission.

Oral station 4: Resisting an interim injunction to enforce post termination restrictions

Advocacy  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

My Lady, I appear for the defendant, Miss Northcombe. This is the return date of the order made without notice by Mr Justice Ebbisham on 26 February 2027, and I invite your Ladyship to discharge it.

My Lady, before I turn to the covenants there is something I must put before the court, because my client's served evidence is not complete. At paragraph 8 of her statement she says she has not contacted Harbourline Freight Limited. That was drafted before she told her solicitors that on 3 March 2027 she sent a personal email to a contact at Harbourline saying that she had moved to Caltowe and that the contact should telephone her in a few months. She signed the statement on 6 March without that having been corrected. My instructions are to correct it now, and I have a short corrective statement which can be signed and served today. I make no attempt to minimise it. Your Ladyship will want to weigh it, and I will address its effect when I come to the non dealing covenant.

Turning to the substance, I make four submissions. First, the non compete covenant at clause 11.2 is unenforceable and the claimant has no real prospect of establishing otherwise at trial. Second, on the non dealing covenant there is no serious issue as to breach. Third, damages are plainly an adequate remedy for the claimant and are plainly not an adequate remedy for my client, whose position is being destroyed while the order stands. Fourth, the balance of convenience, delay, and the fact that this order will decide the case, all point to discharge.

First, clause 11.2. Your Ladyship approaches a post termination restraint on the footing that it is void unless the claimant shows a legitimate interest and shows that the clause goes no further than is reasonably necessary to protect it. Clause 11.6, in which the parties recite that the restrictions are reasonable, does not bind the court. So what is the interest? The claimant's evidence identifies two, trade connection and confidential renewal information. Take trade connection. My client dealt with 34 clients out of about 420, producing £96,000 of brokerage out of £2.4 million, so four per cent of the book. Clause 11.2 does not stop her approaching those 34. It stops her being engaged in any capacity in any competing business anywhere in England and Wales for a year. It would prevent her working in a back office in Newcastle for a broker she had never heard of. A covenant of that width is not directed at protecting the connection with 34 clients, and the existence of the narrower covenants at 11.3 and 11.4 shows that the claimant knew how to protect that connection properly. As to confidential information, clause 11.5 protects it directly and my client offers an undertaking in those terms. Where the narrower covenant will do, the wider one is not reasonably necessary.

Second, clause 11.4, the non dealing covenant. I accept that a non dealing covenant limited to clients with whom the employee had material dealings can in principle be enforceable. My submission is that on this evidence there is no serious issue as to breach, and no case for the intrusive relief presently in force. The claimant identifies one client, Harbourline. Mr Vantree's paragraph 11 says in terms that he cannot prove that my client approached them, and that Harbourline did not say where it was going. My client's evidence, which is unchallenged, is that Harbourline approached Caltowe through a comparison service in January. The email I have disclosed is dated 3 March, six weeks after that. It is a discourteous email and my client should not have sent it. It is not dealing with a client and it is not accepting business. Nothing has followed from it. And my client works in cargo and logistics, a line in which the claimant on its own evidence does very little.

Third, adequacy of damages. For the claimant, this is a broking business measuring its loss in lost brokerage on identified accounts. If a client leaves, the claimant knows which client, when, and what the account was worth. That is the paradigm of a loss which damages compensate. For my client the position is the reverse. She is suspended without pay. She has a mortgage of £1,180 a month. Her employer has told her that the offer will be withdrawn at the end of March. If the order continues she loses a £47,500 job in a small market where reputation travels, and she will not readily quantify what that costs her over a career. And the protection she is offered is a cross undertaking from a company whose net assets of £212,000 are represented as to £180,000 by a freehold charged to secure £160,000 of borrowing. The real cushion is a fraction of the figure the claimant puts forward.

Fourth, the balance of convenience and the wider picture. Three matters. One, this order decides the case. My client resigned on 30 November 2026 on one month's notice and worked it in full, so the Termination Date is 31 December 2026 and the restricted period under clause 11.1 runs to 31 December 2027. There will be no trial before then. Where the interim decision is in practice the final decision, your Ladyship is entitled to look at the relative strength of the cases, and on the width of clause 11.2 the claimant's case is weak. Two, delay. Mr Vantree knew where my client had gone on 14 January. He applied on 26 February, six weeks later, and he applied without notice against a defendant whose address he had. Urgency of that kind is difficult to reconcile with delay of that kind. Three, the status quo. My client has been at Caltowe since 5 January. The status quo before the order was that she was working there.

My Lady, I invite you to discharge the order. So that the claimant is not without protection, my client offers to the court an undertaking in the terms of clause 11.5 not to use or disclose confidential information, and an undertaking not to deal with or accept business from the 34 clients on her former portfolio pending trial or further order, on terms that the claimant's cross undertaking continues. I ask for a speedy trial with directions today, and I ask for the costs of the return date, which have been thrown away by an application that was too wide when it was made.

Unless I can help further, those are my submissions.

The test the application turns on

Section 37(1) of the Senior Courts Act 1981 and CPR Part 25. The court asks whether there is a serious issue to be tried, whether damages would be an adequate remedy for the claimant, whether the cross undertaking in damages would adequately compensate the defendant, and where the balance of convenience lies, other things being equal preserving the status quo. Where the interim decision will in practice dispose of the action, because the restricted period will expire before trial, the court also takes into account its assessment of the relative strength of each party's case. A post termination restraint is void as a restraint of trade unless the covenantee shows that it protects a legitimate business interest, being trade connection, confidential information or workforce stability, and that it is no wider in duration, scope and geographical extent than is reasonably necessary to protect that interest, judged as at the date of the contract. A recital that the parties agree the restrictions are reasonable does not bind the court. Delay, and the duty of full and frank disclosure owed on a without notice application, are also relevant.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client's served witness statement, verified by a statement of truth, says at paragraph 8 that she has not contacted Harbourline Freight Limited. The file note records that she emailed Harbourline on 3 March 2027, three days before she signed the statement, and that she does not want the court told because the claimant will never find out. Continuing to rely on that paragraph would put false evidence before the court and would mislead the judge on the very issue of breach that she is being asked to decide. The candidate must not rely on the statement in its present form. A competent candidate advises the client that the statement has to be corrected, obtains instructions to do so, and then discloses the position to the judge at the outset of the submission, offering a short corrective statement to be signed and served, and dealing with the email openly as part of the argument rather than hoping it is not mentioned. If the client refuses to allow the correction, the candidate cannot advance the application on that evidence and the firm must consider ceasing to act, taking care not to reveal privileged information in doing so.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsAddresses the High Court judge as My Lady consistently, opens by identifying appearance and the nature of the return date, and deals with the client's admitted lie and the corrective evidence in measured professional language without either dramatising or excusing it.Uses Judge or Your Honour to a High Court judge, or becomes defensive and evasive when the judge raises the client's admitted untruth.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsSignposts four submissions at the outset, deals with the correction first because it affects the evidence the court is reading, then takes each covenant separately, then adequacy of damages, then balance of convenience, delay and relief.Runs clause 11.2 and clause 11.4 together as a single complaint that the covenants are unreasonable, and never separates adequacy of damages from balance of convenience.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsTurns the claimant's own figures against it, four per cent of the book against a national year long ban, and £180,000 of a £212,000 net asset figure locked in charged property, and offers undertakings so that discharge looks safe rather than reckless.Asserts that the covenant is 'clearly unreasonable' without identifying the interest it is said to protect, and offers the court nothing between the present order and no protection at all.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsAnswers the judge's challenge on the client's credibility immediately and without flinching, accepts the point where it is good, and returns to the structure. Deals with the invitation to concede the non dealing covenant by conceding the principle but not the relief.Answers the credibility question by attacking the claimant instead, or accepts the judge's proposition about clause 11.4 so completely that the submission collapses into agreeing that the order should continue in part with no argument.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsUses the 34 clients out of 420, the £96,000 out of £2.4 million, the geographical width of clause 11.2, the return of the laptop and telephone, the cargo team, the comparison service, the two month delay, the suspension without pay and the charged freehold.Omits the delay between 14 January and 26 February, or ignores the client's financial position and so has nothing to say on the inadequacy of the cross undertaking.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the American Cyanamid stages accurately in order, applies the restraint of trade principle correctly including that the burden is on the covenantee and that reasonableness is judged at the date of the contract, and correctly invokes the strength of the case because the injunction will dispose of the action.Applies American Cyanamid mechanically without recognising that the expiry of the restricted period before trial changes the approach, or asserts that clause 11.6 settles reasonableness.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers serious issue, adequacy both ways, balance of convenience, status quo, strength of case, delay, the without notice duty of full and frank disclosure, the undertakings offered, a speedy trial and costs.Argues only that the covenants are too wide and never addresses adequacy of damages, the cross undertaking, delay or what should happen between discharge and trial.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies the false paragraph 8 without being prompted, refuses the client's request to stay silent, corrects the evidence to the court at the start, offers a corrective statement, and explains the consequences to the client of a false statement of truth.Relies on paragraph 8 as it stands, or says nothing about the 3 March email while submitting that there is no evidence of any contact with Harbourline.

Examiner notes

This station separates candidates on courage. The client has instructed the candidate to say nothing about an email that contradicts her own signed statement of truth on the central factual issue. Advancing paragraph 8 unchanged is placing false evidence before a High Court judge and is a clear fail on the ethics criterion, and it also destroys the advocacy, because a candidate who has to steer around the email cannot argue the breach point properly. The trap is that the file note frames the email as trivial and the client's reasoning sounds plausible. On the law, the recurring error is running American Cyanamid by rote. The defendant resigned on 30 November 2026 on one month's notice and worked it in full, so the Termination Date is 31 December 2026 and the restricted period expires on 31 December 2027; no trial can happen first, so the interim decision is the real decision and the court will look at the merits. A candidate who never makes that point will not persuade the judge to discharge. The second error is treating both covenants alike. Clause 11.2 is vulnerable on width. Clause 11.4 is not, and has to be met on the evidence of breach instead. Candidates who attack both the same way lose credibility on the stronger point. Finally, a candidate who simply asks for discharge and offers nothing will find the judge continuing part of the order; the marks are in the constructive package of undertakings, a speedy trial and costs.

Oral station 5: Striking out a negligence claim brought by a non client against a surveyor

Advocacy  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

Master, I appear for the defendant, Pargate Structural Consultants LLP. This is the defendant's application dated 28 April 2027 to strike out the Particulars of Claim under rule 3.4(2)(a), alternatively for summary judgment under Part 24.

Master, there is a matter I must deal with before I open the application, because it affects how I can put my first ground. The application notice and the evidence in support proceed on the basis that my client had no contact of any kind with the claimant. That is not accurate. My client has confirmed that on 12 June 2026, at the seller's request, he sent a covering letter with a further copy of the report direct to the claimant. The letter says that the scope was limited to the front elevation and offers to quote for the rear elevation if she wanted it looked at. The document was on my client's own file and has not until now been provided. It will be disclosed today. I cannot therefore invite the Master to proceed on the footing that there was no contact, and I do not do so. I put my case differently, and in my submission the difference does not save this claim, for the reason that the letter itself told the claimant that the rear elevation was outside the scope.

Master, I make three submissions. First, on the claimant's own pleaded case there was no assumption of responsibility to her, and so no duty of care. Second, and independently, the alleged breach concerns a part of the building the report never covered, so no amendment can help. Third, if I am wrong on strike out, this is a proper case for summary judgment, and at the least the loss pleading cannot stand as drawn.

Before that, may I state the test, because it governs how the Master approaches the first ground. Under rule 3.4(2)(a) the court assumes the facts pleaded to be true and asks whether the claim, on those facts, is one the law recognises. The court does not weigh evidence, and it should not strike out in a developing area of law where the facts require investigation. I accept that a strike out ends the claim, and I accept that where a defect is curable by amendment the court gives the claimant that opportunity. My submission is that this defect is not curable, because it lies in the transaction itself and not in the drafting.

First, duty. For a negligent statement causing purely economic loss the claimant must show that the defendant assumed responsibility to her, that her reliance was reasonable, and that the defendant knew of the transaction and of the class of person who would rely. Take the claimant's own paragraphs 3 and 4. My client was instructed by the seller, Mr Nevern. The claimant obtained the report from the seller's estate agents. Paragraph 5 pleads the duty on the basis only that my client knew or ought to have known that the report "would or might be shown to a prospective purchaser". Master, foreseeability that a document may be passed on is not an assumption of responsibility. If it were, every professional report would carry liability to the world. The report says at paragraph 8.1 that it is prepared solely for the named party, at 8.2 that no duty is assumed to any third party, and at 8.3 that it is not a survey, is not a substitute for one, and that any prospective purchaser should obtain their own independent advice. And the letter I have disclosed told this claimant, in terms, that the scope was limited to the front elevation. No reasonable purchaser reading those documents could think that responsibility was being assumed to her.

I anticipate the Master will say that a disclaimer engages the reasonableness requirement under the 1977 Act, or fairness under the 2015 Act, and that those questions need evidence. If that were the whole of my argument, I would accept that I could not succeed today. But it is not. The words at paragraph 1.1 and 1.2 do not exclude liability for work done. They define what work was done. A limitation of scope is not an exclusion clause, and there is nothing unreasonable in an engineer confining an appraisal to the front elevation because that is what his client asked him to look at.

That takes me to my second submission, which is the short one. Paragraph 6 alleges a failure to identify movement affecting the rear elevation. Paragraph 1.2 of the report says the rear elevation was not inspected. The claimant does not plead that it should have been. She cannot, because my client was never asked to look at it and told her so directly on 12 June. A claim that a professional negligently failed to report a defect in a part of a building he was never instructed to examine, and expressly said he had not examined, discloses no reasonable grounds however it is redrawn.

Third, and in the alternative, Part 24. The two applications sit together because rule 3.4(2)(a) tests the pleading on assumed facts whereas Part 24 lets the Master look at the documents and ask whether there is a real prospect of success. Here the documents are the report and the covering letter, and they are not in dispute. On the strength of my second submission in particular there is no real prospect, and no other compelling reason for a trial.

Finally the loss pleading. The particulars claim £186,000 for underpinning and, in addition, £95,000 for diminution in value of the same property, which on the face of it is double recovery, and £15,000 for distress and inconvenience in what is a claim for economic loss on a commercial footing. There is no calculation and no basis given for any figure. I accept that this, standing alone, is a matter capable of cure and I do not ask the Master to strike out on that ground alone. I raise it because if any part of this claim survives today it should not go forward in that form.

Master, I invite you to strike out the Particulars of Claim under rule 3.4(2)(a), alternatively to give summary judgment for the defendant. If you are against me on both, I ask for an order that the claimant serve amended particulars properly pleading the assumption of responsibility relied upon, and full particulars of loss, within 21 days. I ask for the costs of the application in any event, summarily assessed, and I have served a schedule.

Unless I can assist further, those are my submissions.

The test the application turns on

CPR 3.4(2)(a), that the statement of case discloses no reasonable grounds for bringing the claim, with an alternative application for summary judgment under Part 24. On a strike out under rule 3.4(2)(a) the court assumes the pleaded facts to be true and asks whether the claim is legally recognisable; it will not strike out in a developing area of law requiring factual investigation, and where the defect is curable by amendment the court will normally allow amendment instead. Substantively the claim depends on liability in tort for a negligent statement causing pure economic loss, which requires an assumption of responsibility by the defendant towards this claimant, reasonable reliance by her, and knowledge of the transaction and of the class of person who would rely. A disclaimer or restriction on reliance is relevant to whether responsibility was assumed, and separately, if it operates to exclude or restrict liability for negligence, is subject to the requirement of reasonableness under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 or, for a consumer, to the fairness regime under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. A term which defines the scope of the work undertaken is not the same as a term excluding liability for work done.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The partner's file note records that the client sent a covering letter with the report direct to the claimant on 12 June 2026, that the letter is on the client's own file, that it has never been provided to the claimant's solicitors, and that the client and the insurers would prefer the application to be run on the basis that there were no dealings with the claimant at all. Submitting to the Master that the defendant had no contact with the claimant, when the solicitor knows a letter was sent to her, would mislead the court, and suppressing a document that undermines the client's own case also cuts across the duty of disclosure once the claim is proceeding. A competent candidate refuses to run the application on that footing, tells the client before the hearing that the letter must be disclosed and that the submission cannot be made, and obtains his instructions; with those instructions the candidate opens the hearing by correcting the position and disclosing the letter, before showing that the letter in fact assists on scope because it told the claimant the rear elevation was excluded. If the client refuses to allow the letter to be disclosed, the candidate cannot make the application, must give the court no reason for that, and the firm must consider whether it can continue to act. Insurer instructions do not displace the solicitor's duties to the court, and the client, not the insurer, is the person to whom the advice on this must be given.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsAddresses the Master correctly as Master, adopts the quieter register appropriate to a procedural hearing in chambers, and makes the disclosure of the 12 June letter matter of factly without theatrics or excuses for the client.Addresses the Master as Your Honour or My Lord, or adopts a jury style delivery which is out of place at a Master's appointment.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsDeals with the correction first, then states the rule 3.4(2)(a) test before applying it, then takes duty, then scope, then Part 24, then loss, then the order sought, and keeps the alternative grounds clearly separated.Runs strike out and summary judgment together as if they were the same application, and never explains what the court is being asked to assume.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsTurns the disclosed letter into a strength by using it on scope, concedes the loss pleading point rather than over arguing it, and reserves the strongest submission, that the rear elevation was never inspected, so that it lands clearly.Asserts that the claim is 'plainly hopeless' without engaging with the assumption of responsibility analysis, or fights every point equally so that the good one is lost among the weak ones.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsMeets the Master's caution about ending a claim head on, answers the reasonableness challenge with a real distinction rather than a bare denial, and gives a clear answer on the difference between rule 3.4(2)(a) and Part 24.Responds to the invitation to allow an amendment by simply repeating that the claim is bad, without distinguishing curable drafting from an incurable claim.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsUses paragraphs 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the Particulars, paragraphs 1.1, 1.2, 8.1, 8.2 and 8.3 of the report, the estate agents as the route by which the report reached the claimant, the covering letter of 12 June 2026 and the overlap between the underpinning cost and the diminution figure.Never identifies that the report expressly excluded the rear elevation, which is the part of the building the claim is about, and so misses the decisive fact.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the rule 3.4(2)(a) approach accurately, states the requirements for liability for a negligent statement causing economic loss accurately, and correctly distinguishes a scope limitation from an exclusion clause subject to the statutory reasonableness test.Asserts that a disclaimer is conclusive, or treats foreseeability that the report might be passed on as sufficient to found a duty and then argues only about the disclaimer.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers duty, scope, the disclaimer and the statutory control of it, the Part 24 alternative, the loss pleading, the possibility of amendment, the form of order including a fallback, and costs.Argues the duty point only, ignores the Part 24 alternative and the loss pleading, and offers no fallback order if the strike out is refused.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies the suppressed covering letter, declines to advance the no contact submission, obtains the client's instructions and then discloses the letter to the court and the other side, advises the client rather than the insurer, and explains why the letter does not sink the application.Submits that the defendant had no dealings whatever with the claimant, or mentions the letter only in passing without disclosing it or correcting the evidence in support.

Examiner notes

The ethics point is designed to look like a commercial judgment call. The insurer asks a reasonable sounding question, the client says the letter does not matter, and the disclaimer in the report appears to make the letter irrelevant. It is not irrelevant, because the whole of the first ground as drafted rests on the assertion that there was no contact with the claimant. A candidate who makes that submission misleads the Master and fails the ethics criterion, and the better candidates realise that disclosing the letter actually improves the application, because it told the claimant in writing that the rear elevation was outside the scope. The main legal trap is running the case as a disclaimer case. If the whole argument is that clause 8.2 excludes liability, the Master is right that reasonableness under the 1977 Act, or fairness for a consumer under the 2015 Act, needs evidence and cannot be decided today, and the application fails. The winning point is scope: the report never covered the rear elevation, and no amendment can cure a complaint about a part of the building the engineer was never asked to inspect. The second trap is over reaching on the loss pleading. It is a drafting defect, it is curable, and a candidate who presses it as a free standing strike out ground looks as though they do not know the difference.

Oral station 6: First time buyer, restrictive covenant and shared driveway at 12 Harlow Rise

Client interview and attendance note/legal analysis  |  Property Practice  |  10 min reading, 25 min interview, 25 min attendance note

Model attendance note and legal analysis

ATTENDANCE NOTE

Client: Nia Whitcombe. Purchase of 12 Harlow Rise, Kettleby, freehold, LT449021. File WHI/2026/1188.

Trainee, in person, 14.9.26, 11.00 to 11.25, 25 mins.

1. INSTRUCTIONS

1.1 Price 248k. Brayford BS offer 2.9.26, 198,400 over 32 yrs. Not exchanged. Sellers want completion end Oct 26.

1.2 Deposit: 29,600 own savings (Halewood) plus 20,000 from father Huw (motorbike sale). Application recorded the 20,000 as savings. Father: no interest, not on title.

1.3 Timber studio approx 4m x 5m, rear garden. Supplier deposit paid, delivery Nov 26.

1.4 Use: dog grooming business. Sole trader, c.11k turnover, 4 days/wk, 6 to 8 dogs/day, clients drive to the house.

1.5 Mortgage application says own residence, silent on business. Asked me not to tell Brayford, see 5. No instructions given today.

1.6 Driveway: registered right of way on foot and with vehicles over strip hatched blue serving 12 and 14, subject to fair proportion of repair and maintenance. No 14 keeps touring caravan on it. She assumes 2 cars plus client turning.

1.7 No planning contact. Agent said covenants old and unenforced.

2. ANALYSIS

2.1 1971 transfer covenants on charges register: (a) single private dwellinghouse only; (b) no trade or business, no nuisance or annoyance; (c) no building without transferor's written consent, not unreasonably withheld. Burden runs with freehold land in equity and is protected on the register, so she takes subject to all three.

2.2 Benefit given to Kettleby Meadows Estate and each part, so estate owners may enforce. Dissolution of Kettleby Estates Ltd does not extinguish; retained land may be bona vacantia. Check Companies House and filed transfer and plan.

2.3 6 to 8 dogs, 4 days/wk, client visits = trade or business, and use other than a single private dwelling: breaches (a) and (b). Studio itself engages (c) whatever the use.

2.4 Remedies: injunction, incl. removal, or damages. Risk depends on who holds the benefit and proximity.

2.5 Options: indemnity insurance (covers consequences, does not permit the breach, no approach to any beneficiary); Upper Tribunal application to discharge or modify (slow, uncertain); express consent if a giver can be identified; or change the plan.

2.6 Planning permission and building regs are separate hurdles; one does not answer another.

2.7 Right of way = pass and repass. No right to park, none for customers. Maintenance contribution ongoing. Caravan may substantially interfere: enquiries of sellers.

2.8 Brayford conditions 7 (residence only), 12 (correct application incl. source of deposit), 19 (report anything affecting security incl. covenant breach). Use and gift both engage these.

3. ADVICE GIVEN, PRELIMINARY

Plan not dead but not safe; commit to nothing. No installation and no exchange before written advice. Do not approach neighbours, it kills insurance. Three separate hurdles. Firm acts for Brayford and cannot withhold this.

4. NEXT STEPS

Firm: Companies House search; filed 1971 transfer and plan; enquiries re driveway, caravan, maintenance, consents, complaints; indicative insurance quote with no approach; source of funds for her and father plus gift declaration; her written instructions on disclosure to Brayford; report on title in 10 working days; no exchange meanwhile.

Client: defer delivery with supplier; speak to duty planning officer; send bank statements, hers and father's; decide on disclosure to Brayford.

5. ETHICS

5.1 Joint retainer with Brayford. Intended use likely breaches covenants and breaches condition 7; condition 19 requires a report. Gift recorded as savings; condition 12 requires correction.

5.2 Duty of confidence to her against duty to disclose to Brayford. Did not agree to withhold. Explained: if she refuses consent, firm ceases acting for Brayford and in practice for her; she instructs another firm and tells Brayford herself.

5.3 Nothing misleading to Brayford. No report and no exchange until instructions. Will decline any report omitting these matters.

5.4 Partner told today.

Signed: trainee, 14.9.26.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The firm acts for the buyer and for Brayford Building Society. The client asks the solicitor to say nothing to the lender about the intended dog grooming business, and it also emerges that the £20,000 gifted deposit was declared to the lender as savings. This creates a direct conflict between the duty of confidentiality owed to the client and the duty to disclose material information to the lender, and the firm cannot allow the lender to rely on information it knows to be incomplete or inaccurate. A competent candidate says so at the meeting rather than nodding it through, does not promise to keep the confidence, seeks the client's consent to disclosure, and records that if consent is refused the firm must cease to act for the lender and in practice for the client too. Nothing may be sent to the lender that is misleading by omission, and the matter must not be exchanged in the meantime.

Interview marking grid (skills only)

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Listen to the client and use questioning effectively to enable the client to tell the solicitor what is important to them.SkillsOpens with a broad question and lets Nia describe the purchase and the garden plan in her own words without interrupting. Then narrows down: what the studio is for, how many dogs, how often, whether clients attend, what the mortgage application said, where the deposit came from. Picks up the throwaway line about the caravan and comes back to it. Summarises what she has said before moving on and checks she has nothing else to add.Working through a mental conveyancing checklist and never asking what the garden studio is actually for, so the whole business use point is missed. Alternatively, hearing 'grooming' and immediately lecturing about covenants without ever establishing scale, frequency or what Brayford was told.
Communicate and explain in a way that is suitable for the client to understand.SkillsExplains a restrictive covenant as a promise attached to the land that binds later owners, explains that a right of way is a right to travel over land and not automatically a right to park, and explains that planning permission and covenants are separate hurdles. Uses short sentences, checks understanding, and gives no jargon without an immediate plain English translation.Using 'burden runs with the land', 'annexation', 'derogation from grant' or 'section 84' without translation, or reading the register wording aloud at her. Equally weak is oversimplifying to the point of inaccuracy, for example telling her covenants are unenforceable if the company is dissolved.
Conduct themselves in a professional manner and treat the client with courtesy, respect and politeness including respecting diversity where relevant.SkillsIntroduces themselves and the firm, explains the purpose and length of the meeting, that a note will be taken and that the advice today is preliminary. Handles the request to say nothing to Brayford calmly and without moralising, treating her as somebody who has not understood the position rather than as a wrongdoer.Becoming accusatory once the mortgage application point emerges, or the opposite, becoming embarrassed and letting the request pass without comment. Interrupting her, or taking the meeting straight into a monologue with no introduction.
Demonstrate client focus in their approach to the client and the issues.SkillsRecognises that the business is the point of the purchase for her and that she has already spent money on the studio. Addresses her real worries: timing before the end of October, cost, and whether the plan can still work. Offers routes forward, such as seeking Brayford's consent, insurance, or an application to modify the covenant, and explains the trade offs.Treating the file as a standard purchase and giving generic conveyancing information about searches and exchange, while never engaging with the thing she came in about. Or simply telling her the plan is impossible, with no options and no timescale.
Establish and maintain an effective relationship with the client so as to build trust and confidence.SkillsBuilds enough rapport early that she volunteers the mortgage application point, then keeps the relationship intact through the difficult message by being clear about what the firm can and cannot do, and why, and by ending with an agreed plan and a date for the next contact.Losing her at the disclosure point by delivering it as a threat, so she stops talking and the gifted deposit is never explored. The mirror image failure is buying her goodwill by hinting the firm can be discreet, which destroys trust the moment the true position emerges.

Attendance note marking grid
