The competent candidate sees the client before the case is called, explains that the instruction cannot be followed if the bench ask directly, and advises that voluntary disclosure by the defence usually reads better than a later discovery, particularly where a conditional discharge for a low value theft carries limited weight anyway. If the client consents, the matter is put before the bench. If she refuses, the advocate frames the mitigation so that no false impression is created, and if the bench ask the direct question and the client still refuses to permit a truthful answer, the advocate must decline to answer in misleading terms, seek an adjournment and, if the position cannot be resolved, withdraw without giving the reason.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsAddresses a lay bench correctly and speaks to them, not past them, translating guideline language into plain English without ever sounding condescending. Concedes the aggravating features openly at the start, which sets a tone of candour that carries the rest of the mitigation.Talking in guideline shorthand about category ranges, starting points and category harm without explaining any of it, or addressing the bench as though they were a judge, or becoming defensive when the chairman signals that the bench has custody in mind.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsFollows the sequence the bench will follow: seriousness and the aggravating features conceded, then mitigation, then credit for plea, then the custody threshold, then suspension in the alternative, then the proposed order and compensation. Each stage is announced so the bench always knows where it is.An undifferentiated list of good things about the client with no visible sentencing structure, so the bench never hears the custody threshold addressed as a discrete question and never hears an alternative position on suspension.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsArgues in the alternative without weakening the primary position, and uses the practical consequences as an argument rather than as sympathy: immediate custody ends the repayment, ends the employment and triggers an emergency care assessment, so it makes every outcome the bench wants less likely.Pure sympathy with no legal argument, or the opposite error of conceding the custody threshold too early and arguing only for suspension, which surrenders the case the report itself supports.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsAnswers each of the bench's questions directly, adapts the remaining submission to what has been dealt with, and if a short adjournment is needed asks for it courteously and uses it properly. Handles the silent conferring between magistrates without losing composure.Reciting a prepared speech regardless of what the bench has said, repeating points already accepted, or reacting to the antecedents question with visible panic and a long silence rather than a professional request for time.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsDeploys the facts that carry weight: no service user harmed, immediate admissions at the investigatory meeting before any police involvement, 1,500 pounds already repaid at 500 pounds a month out of 1,140 pounds net, hours cut from thirty to eighteen in December 2025, employment obtained and the prosecution disclosed to that employer, debt advice engaged voluntarily, the mother's Parkinson's and the documented gap in care, and the plea at the first stage.Missing the voluntary repayment or the self referral to debt advice, or failing to use the adult social care evidence about the gap in cover, which is the strongest single point against immediate custody.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the custody threshold accurately in its statutory terms and applies it, rather than asserting that custody would be harsh. Applies the correct credit of one third for a plea indicated at the first stage. Deals with compensation as something the court must consider where loss has been caused.Misstating the credit, for example offering ten or twenty five per cent when the plea was indicated at the first stage, or treating the custody threshold as a matter of the bench's discretion rather than a statutory test, or forgetting compensation altogether.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawWorks the full sequence: culpability and harm, aggravating and mitigating factors named by reference to the guideline categories, plea credit, custody threshold, shortest commensurate term, suspension with the listed factors applied one by one, and ancillary orders. Argues the primary and the alternative case without confusing them.Stopping at the community order proposal with no fallback, so that a bench which crosses the threshold has heard nothing at all on suspension, or conversely never engaging with the fraud guideline's culpability and harm structure.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises before standing up that the missing Wrexham conviction cannot be concealed if the bench ask, and that mitigation cannot be built on good character. Ideally has taken instructions at court and discloses the matter voluntarily. If the client refuses consent, declines to confirm the list, invites the bench to raise it with the prosecution and asks for time, without breaching confidentiality or asserting anything untrue.Confirming to the bench that the list is complete, or describing the client as of good character or of effectively good character, or ignoring the attendance note entirely. Equally a fail is blurting out to the bench that the client instructed the advocate to conceal the conviction, which breaches confidentiality.

Examiner notes

Two things separate a pass from a fail. The first is the antecedents question. The candidate must never tell the bench that the list is complete and must never use the phrase good character or effectively good character, because the attendance note makes plain that a further conviction exists. Candidates who prepared the mitigation around good character before reading the last document in the bundle will have written themselves into the trap and will often say the words out of habit even after the direct question. The best candidates go and see the client at 09:30 as instructed, obtain consent to disclose, and hand the bench the Wrexham matter themselves, which costs almost nothing because a conditional discharge for a 60 pound shop theft carries little weight, and buys credibility for everything else they say. The second discriminator is whether the candidate treats the custody threshold as a legal test with a defined wording or merely asks the bench to be merciful. A lay bench needs the law explained in plain language, and the criterion on appropriate language is failed by candidates who talk about category ranges and starting points without translating them. The commonest trap beyond the ethics point is the medium likelihood of reoffending in the report: weak candidates ignore it and hope the bench will not notice, whereas the report itself explains that it is debt driven and reducing, which converts an apparent negative into the argument for a rehabilitation activity requirement.

Oral station 2: Application to vary bail conditions after a change of circumstances on a charge of criminal damage

Advocacy  |  Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

Madam, sir, madam. I appear for Mr Braithwaite. My friend Mr Trelease appears for the Crown and opposes this application.

This is an application under the Bail Act to vary conditions. I want to be clear at the outset about what I am and am not asking for, because I think it will shorten matters.

I am not asking the bench to remove the curfew. I am asking the bench to reshape it, so that it still confines him for every hour that is not accounted for.

I am not asking the bench to touch the exclusion zone from Cobbett Street. I am not asking the bench to touch the condition of non contact with Mr Rahmani or Ms Croome. Those conditions protect the two people the court was concerned about in December and my client's instructions are that he does not seek their variation and does not need to go anywhere near Cobbett Street.

What I ask for is three things: a change of address, a reshaping of the curfew hours, and a small adjustment to reporting.

May I start with the principle, because it governs all three. A condition may only be imposed where it is necessary for a statutory purpose, and where it is necessary it must go no further than is needed to meet the risk. The purposes recorded in the bail record are the prevention of further offences and the prevention of interference with witnesses. So the question for this bench on each condition is a narrow one: what risk does it address, and is the version I propose enough to address it.

The address first, because it is the simplest. Mr Braithwaite currently sleeps at 4 Whitmore Terrace, his uncle's home. His uncle is moving to Swansea and that tenancy ends on 28 February. From 1 March he has nowhere. That is a change of circumstances and it is not one of his making.

His sister, Miss Rhian Braithwaite, has written to the court. She is the sole tenant of 18 Pentre Fields, a two bedroom house where she lives with her four year old son. She is willing for her brother to live there, she has obtained written confirmation from the landlord that there is no objection, and she is willing for a tag to be fitted and for the monitoring company to attend. She is in court this morning and the bench can hear from her if that would assist. The Crown do not object in principle, subject to confirmation from the monitoring provider, and I invite the bench to make any order conditional on that confirmation, which is a sensible course and one I adopt.

The curfew second, and this is the heart of it. The bench asked me why a curfew covering the hours of this alleged offence should be relaxed. It should not be relaxed, and that is not my application. My application is that it should be made to fit a man who is at work.

Mr Braithwaite has been offered a permanent position as an assistant baker at Aldworth Bakery, 35 hours a week at 12.60 pounds an hour, Tuesday to Saturday, 22:00 to 06:00, starting 1 March. The production manager's letter answers the obvious question before it is asked. She says that all production runs overnight and there is no day shift, so there is no alternative pattern available. And she says she cannot hold the position beyond 28 February.

Two things about that letter deserve the bench's attention. He told her at interview, unprompted, that he is awaiting Crown Court trial and is subject to a curfew. He did not conceal it and he was offered the job anyway. And this is not casual work. It is a permanent contract for a 23 year old with no previous convictions, and one youth caution in 2019 whose trial is not until 19 April, so on the current conditions he faces two months of enforced idleness.

What I propose is this. The curfew remains, electronically monitored, from 20:00 to 07:00 daily, save that on Tuesday to Saturday it is suspended between 21:15 and 06:45 for the purposes of attending that employment and travelling directly to and from it. That is 45 minutes either side, and the bakery is on Tregaron Trade Park, about twenty minutes' walk. On Sunday and Monday nights, when he does not work, the curfew stands in full. If the bench wish, the order can require him to produce evidence of continuing employment on request, and the employer's contact details can be endorsed on the order.

The bench may think that is a stronger position than the one that exists today, not a weaker one. Today he is at an address between eight in the evening and seven in the morning, with nothing to occupy him. Under my proposal he is either tagged at home or he is in a bakery in front of a production manager. A man in work at night is accounted for in a way a curfew never achieves on its own.

Third, reporting. He reports Mondays and Thursdays. He has enrolled on a college day release class which falls on Thursdays. I ask that reporting be on Mondays only, or, if the bench prefer to keep it twice weekly, that the second day be moved to Wednesday. That is a small point and I do not press it hard. If the bench are against me on it I will not trouble them further.

The Crown make one further point I should answer. They say he elected trial on indictment, so the length of time on bail is his own choosing. With respect, a defendant is entitled to elect trial by jury and cannot be made to pay for exercising that right with conditions that are more restrictive than necessary. The question remains necessity and proportionality, and the length of the wait, whatever its cause, is a reason to look harder at whether conditions are proportionate, not to ignore them.

Madam, sir, madam, the risks the court identified in December are met. The witnesses are protected by conditions I do not seek to touch. The night hours are covered, in part by a tag and in part by a workplace. The address is confirmed, offered by a responsible tenant with her landlord's consent, and can be made conditional on the monitoring provider's confirmation. And a young man with no convictions and a single youth caution gets a permanent job instead of two months at home.

Unless I can assist further, that is my application.

The test the application turns on

Under section 3(6) of the Bail Act 1976 a court may impose conditions on bail only where it appears necessary to do so for one of the statutory purposes, in particular to secure that the defendant surrenders to custody, does not commit an offence while on bail, and does not interfere with witnesses or otherwise obstruct the course of justice, or for his own protection or welfare or to enable enquiries or a report to be made. It follows that a condition which is not necessary for such a purpose cannot be imposed, and that a condition must go no further than is required to meet the risk it addresses; necessity and proportionality are the two questions on any application to vary. Under section 3(8) the court may, on application by the defendant or the prosecution, vary or impose conditions of bail. Where the application is in substance a renewed application for bail rather than a variation, Part IIA of Schedule 1 to the Bail Act 1976 is relevant: at the first hearing after bail has been refused the defendant may support an application with any argument as to fact or law whether or not it has been advanced before, and thereafter the court need not hear arguments as to fact or law which it has heard previously, which is why a genuine change of circumstances matters. Here bail has been granted, so the application proceeds as a variation, and the change of circumstances is the offer of permanent employment and the ending of the tenancy at the current bail address.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client has told the firm that he broke the curfew twice, once for about four hours, that the tag did not alert, and that the advocate should tell the bench that his compliance has been perfect and that the tag was faulty. To say either of those things would be to mislead the court and to make an assertion that is not properly arguable, and it would also mean being complicit in the client's own deception, which the SRA Principles and Code forbid regardless of whether anyone could prove otherwise. The competent candidate sees the client at 11:15 as instructed and explains, first, that the assertion cannot be made, and second, that it is unnecessary to the application, which turns on necessity and proportionality and not on a compliance record. The candidate then either obtains consent to be candid, which is the stronger course because a bench that hears the difficulty acknowledged is more likely to accept the reshaped curfew as workable, or, if consent is refused, confines the positive submission to necessity and proportionality and says nothing at all about the compliance record, so that no false impression is created. If the bench then ask the direct question, the advocate must not answer it obliquely with the absence of breach proceedings, which would convey what the advocate knows to be false; the advocate must say that he or she cannot assist on that question and seek a short adjournment to take instructions. The confidentiality of the instruction is preserved; the candidate does not tell the bench what the client asked them to do. If the client insists on the false assertion and the bench ask a direct question, the candidate cannot answer in misleading terms, should seek a short adjournment, and if the impasse cannot be resolved must withdraw without giving reasons.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsAddresses a lay bench properly and in plain English, refers to the prosecutor courteously, and concedes the points that should be conceded without grudging. Tone is practical rather than pleading, which suits a bench concerned with whether an arrangement will actually work.Legal shorthand a lay bench cannot follow, irritation at the Crown's refusal to agree, or an emotive appeal about a young man's future in place of an argument about necessity.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsOpens by defining the scope of the application, including what is expressly not sought, then states the governing principle, then takes address, curfew and reporting in turn, then answers the Crown's points, then concludes. The bench knows from the first minute how far the application goes.Running the three variations together, or beginning with the client's personal circumstances so that the bench hears several minutes of background before learning what is actually being asked for.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsReframes the curfew request as a reshaping that leaves every unaccounted hour covered, and argues that employment at night is a stronger safeguard than an empty house. Concedes the exclusion zone, the non contact condition and, if needed, the reporting point, which buys credibility for the one request that matters.Asking for everything, so the bench is invited to remove the single condition that most directly addresses the risk with nothing offered in its place, and having no fallback position when told that is a large ask.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsAnswers each question directly, offers the sister as a witness if the bench wish to hear from her, and accepts sensible qualifications such as making the address change conditional on the monitoring provider's confirmation. Adjusts the remaining submission after each intervention.Failing to notice that the sister is at court and available, or resisting a qualification the bench plainly wants to impose, or answering the compliance question with a long silence rather than a professional request for time.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsUses the ending of the tenancy on 28 February, the employer's statement that there is no day shift and the position cannot be held past 28 February, the disclosure of the proceedings and curfew at interview, the landlord's written consent, the sister's willingness to have a tag fitted and to attend, the absence of previous convictions, the trial date of 19 April, and the Thursday day release clash.Missing the employer's express statement that no day shift exists, which is the complete answer to the bench's obvious question, or missing that the client disclosed his bail conditions to the employer voluntarily.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates accurately that conditions may only be imposed where necessary for a statutory purpose and must be no more than is needed, identifies the two purposes actually recorded on the bail record, and applies each proposed variation to those purposes. Identifies the power to vary on application by either party.Arguing that the conditions are unfair or harsh without reference to necessity or purpose, or treating the application as a fresh bail application and arguing the exceptions to the right to bail, which are not in issue because bail has been granted.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawDeals with each condition separately against the purpose it serves, explains why the change of circumstances matters, and answers the Crown's points including the election for trial on indictment, correctly submitting that exercising a right of election cannot justify disproportionate conditions.Addressing only the curfew and leaving the address and reporting requests unargued, or ignoring the Crown's email entirely so that its points go unanswered.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises before court that the instruction to claim perfect compliance and a faulty tag cannot be followed, takes instructions at 11:15, and either obtains consent to be candid about the two occasions or confines the submission to what is true and verifiable without inviting a false inference. Preserves confidentiality and does not tell the bench what the client asked for.Telling the bench his compliance has been perfect, or advancing the faulty tag explanation, or answering the compliance question in terms designed to create the impression of an unblemished record. Equally a fail is disclosing to the bench that the client asked the advocate to lie.

Examiner notes

The station rewards restraint. The client asks for the curfew to be removed and for reporting to be halved; the papers show that the offence is alleged to have been committed at 01:50 and that the Crown's real objection is the curfew. Candidates who simply relay the client's shopping list, and in particular who ask for the curfew to go, will be told by the bench that it is a large ask and will usually have nothing to fall back on. The pass mark is earned by a candidate who reshapes rather than removes, who volunteers that the exclusion zone and non contact conditions should stand, and who ties every request to necessity and proportionality. The ethics trap is the compliance question. The attendance note records two breaches, an instruction to assert perfect compliance and an instruction to say the tag was faulty. Neither can be said. Candidates fail this criterion by claiming perfect compliance, by advancing the faulty tag explanation, or by staying silent about the note in a way that shows they never read it. The best candidates use their 11:15 conference to obtain consent to be candid and then turn candour into an argument, that a curfew which a man can actually live with is more likely to be complied with than one which is at war with his working life. A secondary trap is the Crown's point about election for jury trial; a candidate who accepts it, or ignores it, misses the chance to make the straightforward answer that exercising a right of election cannot be a reason for disproportionate conditions.

Oral station 3: Summary judgment on a contract debt met by an alleged oral variation

Advocacy  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

May it please you, Judge. I appear for the claimant, Halvern Timber Supplies Limited. My learned friend, if there is one, appears for the defendant. This is the claimant's application dated 16 December 2026 for summary judgment under Part 24.

Judge, before I open the application there is a matter I must raise, because it affects the figure I ask you to enter. The Particulars of Claim plead £84,600. Since they were drawn, my client has confirmed that a credit note for £5,400 was issued to the defendant on 30 October 2026 in respect of the April delivery and has never been reversed. The defendant has not taken the point. It is right that I take it. The sum properly due is therefore £79,200, and that is the figure for which I ask for judgment. I will file an amended schedule today.

May I set out the shape of my submission. First, the claim and what is admitted. Second, the test under rule 24.3. Third, why the pleaded defence has no real prospect of success. Fourth, the counterclaim. Fifth, the order I invite you to make.

First, the claim. There is a written supply agreement dated 2 February 2026, signed by a director of each company. Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Defence admit the agreement. Paragraph 2 admits delivery of every load invoiced. So the contract is admitted, delivery is admitted, and the price is fixed by clause 3.1 by reference to the price list. Clause 3.2 makes payment due in 30 days and makes time of the essence. Nothing in the defence disputes the arithmetic of the account.

Second, the test. Under rule 24.3 you may give summary judgment against a defendant if it has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim, and there is no other compelling reason for a trial. Real means better than merely arguable. I accept at once that this is not the occasion for a mini trial and that you will not resolve a genuine conflict of oral evidence today. But the court is not obliged to accept an assertion simply because it has been written into a statement of case. Where the assertion is contradicted by the respondent's own contemporaneous documents, and where it faces an insuperable contractual obstacle, it does not cross the threshold.

Third, the defence. It has two limbs, an oral variation and an estoppel.

The oral variation is at paragraph 3. It faces three difficulties. The first is clause 14.2. No variation is effective unless in writing and signed by a director of each party. There is no such document. Nothing is said to have been signed at all. The parties chose that protection and the court gives effect to it. The second is the pleading itself. The defendant cannot say what date the call took place, only "the second week of May". A halving of price on every future delivery is a very substantial commercial concession, and a company which had obtained it would have said so in writing, checked its invoices against it, or at the very least queried the invoices when they arrived at the full price. It did none of those things. The third difficulty, and in my submission the decisive one, is the letter of 4 September 2026, in the bundle. May I read the second paragraph. "I make it £84,600 on the account as at the end of August, which agrees with your statement." That is the defendant's own director, writing four months after the alleged halving of the price, agreeing the full account, asking for time to pay it, and offering three instalments. If the price had been halved in May there would have been no such account to agree. The defence is contradicted by the defendant's own document.

The estoppel at paragraph 4 adds nothing. It is not enough simply to attach the label. The defendant must identify a clear and unequivocal representation that the strict terms of the contract would not be enforced, and reliance on it which makes it inequitable to go back. The only representation pleaded is the oral agreement which clause 14.2 renders ineffective, so the estoppel is being used to smuggle in what the contract excludes. The pleaded reliance is that the defendant continued to order rather than go elsewhere. There is no evidence of any alternative supplier, of any price obtainable, or of any detriment. And the letter of September is inconsistent with any belief that the strict terms had been abandoned.

Fourth, the counterclaim, and the request for a stay which I anticipate. Clause 7.1 required written notice of any defect within five working days of delivery, failing which the goods are deemed accepted. The delivery was on 28 April 2026. There is no written notice at all. The defendant's own letter says that he telephoned and that the matter was never got to the bottom of, which is confirmation that nothing was ever put in writing. Beyond that, the counterclaim is unsupported by a single document. There is no copy of the Marden Row contract, no correspondence terminating it, and no calculation of the £30,000. And clause 3.3 provides that the buyer shall not withhold, set off or deduct any sum for any reason whatsoever. That clause was freely agreed between two commercial parties of comparable standing and it is directed precisely at this situation. If, contrary to my primary submission, the counterclaim is to survive today, it should not be permitted to hold up payment of an admitted account.

Fifth, the order. I invite you to give judgment for the claimant for £79,200. I invite you to award interest under clause 18.1 at 4 per cent above base, which on my calculation to today is £3,148, and I have the schedule if it assists. I invite you to order payment within 14 days. As to the counterclaim, my primary position is that it too has no real prospect and should be dismissed for want of any notice under clause 7.1 and any evidence of loss. If you are not with me on that, I ask that it be allocated and case managed separately with no stay of execution on the judgment. Finally I ask for the costs of the application, summarily assessed, and I have served an N260 in the sum of £3,940.

Unless I can assist further, those are my submissions.

The test the application turns on

CPR Part 24. The court may give summary judgment against a defendant on the whole of a claim or on a particular issue if (a) the defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim or issue and (b) there is no other compelling reason why the case or issue should be disposed of at a trial. A real prospect means one that is better than merely arguable and more than fanciful. The court does not conduct a mini trial, but it need not accept an assertion which is contradicted by contemporaneous documents or is inherently implausible, and it may take account of evidence reasonably expected to be available at trial. Substantively the application turns on the effect of a no oral variation clause requiring writing signed by a director of each party, on whether an estoppel is properly pleaded and evidenced, and on the effect of a no set off clause on any stay of execution.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The partner's file note records a credit note for £5,400 which the client has never reversed and which the pleaded sum of £84,600 does not reflect, together with the client's request to say nothing about it because the defendant has not spotted it. Asking the court to enter judgment for a sum the solicitor knows to be overstated would mislead the court, and a solicitor must not mislead the court or allow the court to be misled, whether by act or omission. The candidate cannot simply follow the client's instruction, and cannot resolve it by disclosing the client's confidential position to the judge on the candidate's own initiative either. A competent candidate speaks to the client before the hearing, explains that the application cannot be pursued for a sum the firm knows to be overstated, and obtains instructions to correct it; with those instructions the candidate corrects the figure openly at the start of the submission, asks for judgment in the reduced sum of £79,200, offers to file an amended schedule, and does not attempt to bury the correction. If the client had refused to allow the correction, the candidate would have had to decline to make the application and consider whether the firm could continue to act.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsAddresses the District Judge correctly as Judge throughout, opens by announcing appearance and the application, uses restrained courteous language, does not argue with the bench, and adjusts tone when interrupted.Calls the District Judge 'Your Honour' or 'My Lord', reads long passages the judge has already said they have read, or becomes combative when the judge presses on the oral variation point.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsSignposts the structure at the outset, takes the credit note point first because it affects the relief, then deals with the claim, the test, each limb of the defence, the counterclaim and the order, in that order, and keeps to time.Launches straight into the facts with no roadmap, deals with the estoppel and the variation in a single undifferentiated passage, and reaches the counterclaim and the form of order only when the judge prompts.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsBuilds the argument on the documents rather than assertion, uses the letter of 4 September 2026 as the centrepiece, and confronts the mini trial objection head on instead of ignoring it.Simply asserts that the defence is 'hopeless' or 'a sham' without demonstrating why, and offers no answer when the judge suggests that a conflict of evidence must go to trial.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsAnswers each judicial question directly and immediately, concedes the mini trial principle before qualifying it, and returns to the thread of the submission after the interruption without losing the structure.Talks over the judge, answers a different question from the one asked, or abandons the prepared argument entirely after the first interruption.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsDeploys the admissions in paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Defence, clause 14.2, clause 7.1, clause 3.3, clause 18.1, the September letter, the absence of any date for the alleged call and the absence of any Marden Row documents.Omits the September letter or the admissions in the Defence, or overlooks the no set off clause and therefore has nothing to say when the judge raises a stay.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the rule 24.3 test accurately in both limbs, applies the correct standard of a real as opposed to fanciful prospect, and states the effect of a no oral variation clause and the requirements of an estoppel accurately.States the test as whether the defence is 'bound to fail', omits the second limb about no other compelling reason, or asserts that a no oral variation clause defeats an estoppel automatically.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers the claim, the variation defence, the estoppel, the counterclaim, the set off and stay question, interest and costs, and produces a complete draft order.Deals only with the oral variation, leaves the estoppel and the counterclaim untouched, and has no submission on interest, costs or the terms of the order.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawRecognises unprompted that judgment cannot be sought for £84,600, obtains the client's instructions to correct the figure before the hearing, and then raises the £5,400 credit note at the start, explains its effect on the sum claimed, asks for judgment in the corrected figure and offers an amended schedule, without disclosing privileged advice given to the client.Says nothing about the credit note and invites judgment for £84,600, or mentions it only after the judge has asked what sum is sought. Equally a fail is disclosing the credit note, or the client's request that nothing be said about it, to the judge without having gone back to the client for instructions first.

Examiner notes

The pass or fail line is the credit note. A candidate who invites the District Judge to enter judgment for £84,600, knowing the account has been credited with £5,400, has misled the court and will fail the ethics criterion however polished the advocacy. The trap is that the point is buried in a file note that reads like helpful background, and the client's request sounds like ordinary commercial pragmatism. On the law, the common trap is over claiming. Weak candidates tell the judge that the oral variation defence is a lie and invite a finding of fact. Strong candidates concede that the court will not try a conflict of evidence today, then show that the assertion cannot survive contact with clause 14.2 and the defendant's own letter of 4 September 2026 agreeing the full account. The second trap is stopping at the claim: the counterclaim, the no set off clause and the question of a stay are where the marks for comprehensiveness sit, and many candidates never reach them because they have overrun on the variation point.

Oral station 4: Relief from sanctions after breach of an unless order in a personal injury claim

Advocacy  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

Your Honour, I appear for the claimant, Mr Grady. This is his application dated 25 February 2027 for relief from the sanction in paragraph 1 of the order of 21 January 2027.

Your Honour, I must begin with a correction, and I am sorry to have to make it. Paragraph 6 of the witness statement in support says that the signed statements were sent to the claimant on 11 February and came back late because of difficulties with the post. That is not right. Nothing was sent to the claimant on 11 February. There was no problem with the post. The truth is that the unless order was not entered into the firm's diary system, the fee earner with conduct was on annual leave from 9 to 16 February, and the file was not looked at until 17 February, by which time the deadline had gone. The claimant signed his statement in the firm's office on 20 February. The statement in support was signed on information which was itself wrong, and the position came to light on a file review after the fee earner left the firm. I have a short corrective statement from the partner which can be signed and filed today, and I ask your Honour to proceed on the corrected basis. It does my client's application no good at all, but your Honour must have the true position.

Your Honour, the court takes three stages. I will take them in turn and then deal with the terms on which I ask for relief.

Stage one, the seriousness and significance of the breach. The obligation carrying the sanction was to file and serve by 4pm on 15 February. Service took place on 21 February. The breach is six days. In my submission it is significant, and I do not invite your Honour to find otherwise, because any breach of an unless order is significant. But your Honour is measuring what this breach did to the litigation, and the answer is nothing. The defendant's own statements were not due until 1 March, so the sequence was undisturbed. No hearing was lost. The trial window opening on 24 May 2027 is intact and my client is ready for it. This is not a case where the breach has imperilled a trial date or caused any hearing to be vacated. I anticipate your Honour will say that my client had already missed the 12 December date. That is right, and I will come to it, but the earlier default is a matter for stage three; it does not make the six day breach itself more serious than it is.

Stage two, why the default occurred. There is no good reason. I do not advance one. This was oversight by the claimant's solicitors, and my client, who is a plasterer and has done nothing wrong, had no part in it. What I do say is that the absence of a good reason is not determinative. It takes your Honour to stage three, where the balance is struck.

Stage three, all the circumstances, with particular weight on the need for litigation to be conducted efficiently and at proportionate cost and the need to enforce compliance.

I begin with what is against me, because your Honour will have it in mind in any event. There have been two defaults, not one. The order of 6 November was breached by over two months and led to the defendant incurring the costs of an application. The £860 ordered on 21 January was payable by 4 February and has not been paid. That is a poor record and I do not seek to dress it up.

Against that I ask your Honour to weigh five matters. First, the consequence. This sanction does not exclude a piece of evidence or shift a date. It ends a £38,000 claim for a self employed man who has not worked since 4 May 2026, on a liability issue which has never been tried. Second, proportionality. The breach caused no disruption at all and the defendant has identified none in its letter of 1 March. Third, promptness. My client applied on 25 February, four days after service and ten days after the deadline, which is prompt. Fourth, my client's own conduct. He signed his statement the day he was asked to. The failures are those of his solicitors. Your Honour is entitled to take that into account without treating it as a complete answer. Fifth, the defendant's position. The defendant has its statements, has had them since 21 February, and can be compensated in costs for every consequence of the default.

Your Honour asked, or may ask, why the claim against the solicitors is not a complete answer. It is not, for three reasons. It would be a second action, in which my client would still have to prove the road traffic claim he is ready to prove now. It would take years. And a man with no income since May 2026 would fund it in the meantime. The existence of a professional negligence claim is a consequence of refusing relief, not a reason for refusing it.

Your Honour, I ask for relief on terms, so that the need to enforce compliance is met by the order rather than by the destruction of the claim. I invite your Honour to grant relief conditionally on the following. One, the claimant pays the £860 ordered on 21 January 2027 and the costs of this application within 14 days, and unless he does so the claim stands struck out. Two, the witness statements served on 21 February 2027 stand as served. Three, the defendant has an extension for its own statements to a date your Honour thinks fit. Four, the trial window of 24 May 2027 is preserved. As to costs, I accept that my client must pay the costs of this application in any event. I resist indemnity basis costs, because the failure was administrative and the default was not conduct out of the norm directed at the defendant, but I recognise your Honour may take a different view, and if the assessment is on the standard basis I ask that the figure be summarily assessed today.

Unless I can assist further, those are my submissions.

The test the application turns on

CPR 3.8 and 3.9. Where a sanction has taken effect, the defaulting party must apply for relief, supported by evidence. On such an application the court considers all the circumstances so as to deal justly with the application, including the need for litigation to be conducted efficiently and at proportionate cost and the need to enforce compliance with rules, practice directions and orders. The court applies the three stage approach in Denton: first, identify and assess the seriousness and significance of the breach of the obligation carrying the sanction; second, consider why the default occurred; third, evaluate all the circumstances, giving particular weight to the two factors in rule 3.9(1)(a) and (b). Earlier and other breaches are weighed at the third stage rather than at the first. Promptness of the application is relevant. The court may grant relief on conditions, including as to payment of outstanding costs.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Paragraph 6 of the partner's witness statement in support, verified by a statement of truth, blames postal difficulties and says the statements were sent to the client on 11 February 2027. The handover note shows that nothing was sent on 11 February, that there was no postal problem, and that the true cause was a failure to diarise the unless order and the fee earner's annual leave. Inviting the Circuit Judge to find a good reason on the basis of paragraph 6 would mislead the court, and the sympathetic pull of the client's position makes the temptation real. A competent candidate corrects the position at the very start, states plainly that there is no good reason for the default, offers a corrective witness statement, and reframes the argument around stage three, where the merits of relief actually lie. The candidate should also recognise that the client's own interests are now in tension with the firm's, because the claimant may have a claim against the firm, and that he should be advised to take independent advice and told that the firm should notify its insurers.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsAddresses the Circuit Judge as Your Honour throughout, opens with the correction in plain unvarnished language, accepts criticism of the firm without defensiveness and without disparaging the departed fee earner.Uses Judge or My Lord to a Circuit Judge, or responds to the judge's displeasure about the witness statement by arguing that it was substantially accurate.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsAnnounces the three stage structure and follows it, taking the correction first, then seriousness, then reason, then all the circumstances, then the terms of the order and costs, and keeps the concessions in the right stage.Mixes the earlier December default into stage one, or presents an undifferentiated plea for sympathy with no recognisable stage structure at all.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsConcedes what must be conceded early so that the remaining points carry weight, then argues from the concrete consequences: no hearing lost, trial window intact, a £38,000 claim by a man with no income since May 2026, and offers conditions that meet the judge's concern about enforcement.Asks the court to excuse the breach as trivial, or relies on the client's sympathetic circumstances alone with no engagement with the need to enforce compliance.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsAnswers the question about the unpaid £860 without evasion and converts it into an offer of a condition, and answers the professional negligence question with three concrete reasons rather than a bare assertion.Says they have no instructions on the unpaid costs and moves on, or is visibly thrown by the suggestion that the claim against the solicitors is a complete answer.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsUses the exact dates, the six day breach, the 1 March date for the defendant's statements, the 24 May trial window, the 25 February application date, the December default, the unpaid £860, the client's self employment and loss of earnings since 4 May 2026.Cannot say how long the breach actually was, or overlooks that the defendant's statements were not due until 1 March and so cannot show the absence of disruption.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates rule 3.9 and the three stages accurately, correctly places earlier breaches at stage three, correctly treats the absence of a good reason as not determinative, and correctly identifies the court's power to grant relief on conditions.Treats the absence of a good reason as automatically fatal, or argues that a six day breach is neither serious nor significant so that relief follows without more.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers all three stages, promptness, the effect on the trial window, prejudice to the defendant, the client's own blamelessness, the professional negligence point, the conditions sought, the basis of costs and the form of order.Argues seriousness and reason only, and offers no submission on the terms of relief, the outstanding costs order or the basis of assessment.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawCorrects paragraph 6 unprompted, states there is no good reason, offers a corrective statement, and separately recognises the conflict between the client's interests and the firm's, advising independent advice and notification of insurers.Repeats or develops the postal explanation, or stays silent about paragraph 6 while inviting the court to find that the delay was outside the firm's control.

Examiner notes

The trap here is that the false explanation is helpful. Paragraph 6 supplies exactly what stage two of Denton needs, and a candidate who does not read the handover note carefully, or who reads it and decides the point is too damaging to raise, will simply run the postal story. That is misleading the court and fails the ethics criterion outright. The candidate who corrects it loses the good reason argument and gains everything else, because a Circuit Judge who has been told the truth will listen to stage three. The second discriminator is structure. Relief from sanctions is one of the few applications where the analytical framework is fixed, and candidates who blur the stages, particularly by dragging the December default into stage one, show they do not understand it. The third is realism about the order. This judge is minded to refuse. A candidate who simply asks for relief will lose. A candidate who offers conditions, payment of the outstanding £860, costs in any event, preservation of the trial window, gives the judge a way to grant relief while still enforcing compliance, and that is what a competent newly qualified solicitor would do.

Oral station 5: Interim payment in a workplace injury claim where liability has been determined

Advocacy  |  Dispute Resolution  |  45 min preparation, 15 min submission

Model submission

Judge, I appear for the claimant, Mr Blayne. This is his application dated 5 June 2027 for an interim payment. You made the consent order in March, so you have the background.

Judge, I must begin by putting two corrections before you, both of which reduce the sum I ask for.

The first you have already seen. The insurers say in their letter of 15 June that they made a voluntary interim payment of £8,000 on 20 January 2027. That is right. The schedule should have recorded it and did not. Credit is given for it and the sum I ask you to order today is a sum over and above it.

The second you have not seen, and I am sorry that it comes to you this way. The schedule claims a continuing loss of earnings. My client told his solicitors on Saturday that since 4 May 2027 he has been working from home for a family business, taking bookings and doing paperwork, and receiving £310 per week. That is not reflected in the schedule and I cannot invite you to award anything on the footing that his loss of earnings is total. An amended schedule will be served this week giving credit for those earnings from 4 May, and my client has been advised as to his obligations to declare the income elsewhere. It reduces my past loss figure and it reduces the sum I seek. I therefore no longer ask for the £45,000 in the application notice. I ask for £26,000, in addition to the £8,000 already paid.

Judge, may I take it in four stages. The gateway. The conservative valuation. The reasonable proportion. And the form of the order.

First, the gateway. Two of the three grounds are satisfied on the face of the file. Liability was admitted in the protocol response, and by the order of 3 March 2027 my client obtained judgment for damages to be assessed. The insurers say in terms at paragraph 1 of their letter that they do not seek to go behind that order. There is no contributory negligence, no set off and no counterclaim. So the only real question is quantum, and specifically what a reasonable proportion of the likely final judgment is.

Second, the conservative valuation. I accept at once that the final award cannot be assessed today and that Mr Kettering defers his final opinion until six months after the October procedure. But you are not being asked to assess the final award. You are being asked to be satisfied of a floor. I invite you to approach it in this way.

General damages. The schedule puts the bracket at £46,000 to £58,000. For today I take the bottom of it and go below it. Take £40,000. That is a degloving injury to the dominant right forearm, a compound fracture of both bones, internal fixation, two debridements, a skin graft, fixed flexion at the wrist and grip strength at 42 per cent of the other side, with further surgery to come in October and a 15 to 20 per cent risk that it will not restore useful grip. £40,000 is a figure no trial judge could conceivably go below.

Past losses. The schedule claims £23,272. From that I must deduct the earnings since 4 May 2027. That is about seven weeks to today at £310, so roughly £2,170, and the loss of earnings claim continues at a reduced rate rather than the full rate from that date. Taking a deliberately cautious view I put past losses today at £19,000 rather than £23,272. The care claim is modest and is supported. The travel and equipment items are vouched.

So on general damages and past losses alone, without touching a penny of the future loss claim, the conservative floor is £59,000. That is before any award at all for future loss of earnings, for future loss of earning capacity, or for future treatment, each of which is likely to be substantial given a 34 year old right handed man who on the surgeon's evidence will not return to heavy manual work.

Third, the reasonable proportion. You must not order more than a reasonable proportion of the likely amount of the final judgment. £26,000 is 44 per cent of the conservative floor of £59,000, and taken with the £8,000 already paid the total of £34,000 is 58 per cent of that floor. Measured against the likely final judgment, which will include the future losses, the proportion is very considerably lower. In my submission that is comfortably within a reasonable proportion, and it is a long way from the £20,000 the insurers offer, which is less than half the conservative floor for past losses and general damages alone.

Judge, you asked, or may ask, whether an award of this size restricts the trial judge. In my submission it does not, and I have deliberately built the figure so that it does not. Every pound of it is referable to general damages and past losses, which are heads the trial judge will award as a lump sum in any event. Nothing in it is drawn from future care or future loss of earnings, which are the heads a trial judge might wish to structure. If it assists, I invite you to express the order as a payment on account of general damages and past losses, which puts the point beyond argument.

Fourth, the order and my client's position. He is 34, he has a partner and two children, and until 4 May he had no income at all since October. He is in arrears on his rent and his car finance. Need is not decisive, but it is relevant, and it is why the payment should be made now rather than at the costs and case management conference in September. I ask for £26,000 to be paid within 14 days, and I ask for the costs of the application, summarily assessed. If the defendant says 14 days is short for an insurer, I will not resist 21 days.

Unless I can assist further, those are my submissions.

The test the application turns on

CPR Part 25, interim payments. The court may make an order for an interim payment only if one of the specified grounds is made out, relevantly that the defendant has admitted liability to pay damages, or that the claimant has obtained judgment for damages to be assessed, or that the court is satisfied that if the claim went to trial the claimant would obtain judgment for a substantial amount of money. The court must not order an interim payment of more than a reasonable proportion of the likely amount of the final judgment, taking into account contributory negligence and any relevant set off or counterclaim. In practice the court values the likely final judgment conservatively and then awards no more than a reasonable proportion of it. Sums already paid voluntarily by the defendant are taken into account. Where the final award may be structured, for example by a periodical payments order or by awards for future care or accommodation, the court should avoid an interim award of a size which would restrict the trial judge's freedom to structure the final award. The claimant's need is relevant but not decisive. Payment may be ordered in one sum or by instalments.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The attendance note records that the claimant has been working since 4 May 2027 for £310 per week in cash, that the preliminary schedule claims a continuing loss of earnings which takes no account of it, and that the client does not want it mentioned because the defendant does not know. Asking the District Judge to award an interim payment calculated on a total and continuing loss of earnings would put a figure before the court which the solicitor knows to be false, and it would also mean relying on a schedule verified by a statement of truth which is now inaccurate. The client's separate failure to declare the income to the benefits office is his own affair, but the solicitor cannot become the means by which the court is misled. A competent candidate advises the client that the schedule must be corrected and that the earnings must be given credit for, obtains instructions, tells the court at the outset, serves an amended schedule, and reduces the sum sought accordingly. Advising the client to take his own advice about the undeclared cash, and warning him about the consequences of a false statement of truth, are proper parts of the advice. If the client refused to allow the correction, the candidate could not pursue the application on the existing schedule.

Marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Use appropriate language and behaviour.SkillsAddresses the District Judge as Judge, makes both corrections plainly and without dressing them up, and speaks about the client's undeclared earnings in neutral factual terms without volunteering privileged advice or condemning the client.Uses Your Honour to a District Judge, or handles the disclosure of the cash earnings either evasively or with unnecessary editorialising about the client's conduct.
Adopt a clear and logical structure.SkillsOpens with the two corrections and the revised figure, then takes the gateway, the conservative valuation, the reasonable proportion and the form of order in that sequence, so that the arithmetic arrives in an order the judge can follow.Begins with the client's hardship and never separates the gateway question from the quantum question, so the judge has to construct the analysis for the candidate.
Present a persuasive argument.SkillsArgues in numbers rather than adjectives, builds a floor the judge can adopt, expresses the sum sought as a stated percentage of that floor, and pre empts the restriction on the trial judge by constructing the figure out of general damages and past losses only.Relies on the claimant's financial distress as the main argument, or asks for a round figure with no explanation of how it was reached.
Interact with and engage the court appropriately.SkillsGives the judge an arithmetical answer the first time it is asked for, deals with the £8,000 credit immediately, and adapts the sum sought openly rather than clinging to the £45,000 in the application notice.Answers the request for arithmetic with generalities about the seriousness of the injury, or has to be asked three times for a figure.
Include all key relevant facts.SkillsUses the consent order and the admission, the claimant's age and dominance of the injured arm, grip at 42 per cent, the graft, the October 2027 procedure, the 15 to 20 per cent risk, the surgeon's view on heavy manual work, the £8,000 payment and the earnings from 4 May 2027.Overlooks that the claimant is right hand dominant and that the surgeon has already ruled out a return to heavy manual work, and so cannot demonstrate that the final award will be substantial.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawStates the gateway grounds accurately and identifies which apply, states the reasonable proportion limit accurately, applies the conservative valuation approach correctly and correctly gives credit for the voluntary payment.Treats the application as though the only question is the claimant's need, or asks the court to award a proportion of the full pleaded value of the claim including unquantified future losses.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers gateway, conservative valuation of each head, credit for the £8,000, the effect of the newly disclosed earnings, the reasonable proportion, the risk of restricting the trial judge, the form and timing of payment, instalments and costs.Deals with valuation only, and offers nothing on the credit, on the risk of fettering the trial judge, or on the terms of the order.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawDiscloses the earnings from 4 May 2027 unprompted, reduces the sum sought, undertakes to serve an amended schedule, confirms credit for the £8,000, and records that the client has been advised about the statement of truth and about his own position on the undeclared income.Advances the schedule as it stands and invites an award based on a continuing total loss of earnings, or mentions the earnings only after the judge has asked about the figures.

Examiner notes

Two corrections are buried here, and they behave differently. The £8,000 voluntary payment is in the insurers' letter, so the District Judge already knows about it and a candidate who ignores it merely looks careless. The cash earnings from 4 May 2027 are known only to the candidate, and a candidate who stays silent while asking the court to award an interim payment built on a total and continuing loss of earnings is misleading the court. That is the fail. The client's reasoning, that the schedule is only preliminary and the defendant does not know, is the sort of argument candidates find it easy to accept under time pressure. The legal trap is treating this as a hardship application. Need is relevant but it is not the test, and a candidate who spends ten minutes on rent arrears and two on valuation will not get the order. The court wants a conservative floor and a percentage of it. The second trap is asking for too much from the wrong heads. A candidate who justifies the figure out of future loss of earning capacity invites the objection that the trial judge's hands are being tied; a candidate who builds the whole figure out of general damages and past losses removes that objection before it is made, and that is what distinguishes a grade A performance.

Oral station 6: Buying together with unequal contributions, joint tenants or tenants in common

Client interview and attendance note/legal analysis  |  Property Practice  |  10 min reading, 25 min interview, 25 min attendance note

Model attendance note and legal analysis

ATTENDANCE NOTE

Clients: Yasmin Croft (YC) and Marcus Deller (MD), joint retainer. Purchase of 9 Saltmarsh Road, Wivenham, freehold; sale of 3 Ferrers Court. File CRO/2027/0214.

Trainee, in person. Present: YC only; MD offshore to mid March. 3.2.27, 2.00 to 2.25, 25 mins.

1. INSTRUCTIONS

1.1 Price 430k. Joint Colnebridge offer 215k over 25 yrs, both borrowers. Completion target 27.3.27 to match her sale.

1.2 Contributions per YC: YC 150k from 3 Ferrers Court; 45k from her mother Gillian Croft; MD 30k savings.

1.3 The 45k is disputed. Mother treats it as a loan to YC personally, repayable on a sale, nothing in writing. MD told it is a gift to both. YC asked me not to tell him, see 5.

1.4 MD to fund kitchen and loft, c.40k, when contract ends. Mortgage to be shared equally though MD earns c.2x YC.

1.5 YC has a daughter, Amara, 9, from a previous relationship. MD no children. Unmarried, no civil partnership. No wills.

1.6 YC wants her money to go to Amara, not MD. Assumed automatic.

1.7 Shares and separation never discussed. She assumes she gets her 150k back first, never said so to MD.

1.8 Offered to instruct and sign for MD. Asked for correspondence to her personal email only.

2. ANALYSIS

2.1 Legal estate always held by both as joint tenants on trust, cannot be severed. The choice is beneficial only.

2.2 Beneficial joint tenancy: no distinct shares; survivorship on death, operating outside a will and not defeasible by one. Here MD would take the whole incl. her 150k, Amara nothing: opposite of her wish.

2.3 Beneficial tenancy in common: defined, possibly unequal shares; no survivorship; share passes by will or intestacy; Form A restriction, so a survivor cannot sell alone without a second trustee.

2.4 Express declaration of trust signed by both is conclusive between them. Cover: the three contributions; whether the 45k is a loan to YC or a gift and to whom; the 215k advance and monthly payments; credit for the 40k works; order of repayment on sale; sale if only one wants it.

2.5 Separation: unmarried, so no matrimonial regime and no redistribution. Without a declaration she must prove her interest from conduct and intention: uncertain, expensive.

2.6 Death: no wills. If YC died intestate as tenant in common, MD takes nothing as unmarried; her share to Amara on the statutory trusts until 18, no chosen trustee or guardian. Both need wills either way.

2.7 Joint mortgage: joint and several liability for the whole debt, not half each. Shares and liability separate; equal payments do not by themselves create equal shares.

2.8 Cannot take one joint client's instructions for the other; MD not bound by her signature. Offshore no obstacle: video call, execution and witnessing where he is.

3. ADVICE GIVEN, PRELIMINARY

Joint tenancy very unlikely suitable on these contributions and defeats her wish for Amara. Provisional recommendation, subject to MD's instructions: tenancy in common in unequal shares with a declaration of trust. Panel 10 TR1 not completed until both agree. Both need wills. The 45k must be settled openly as it changes the shares. She cannot instruct or sign for MD.

4. NEXT STEPS

Firm: video call with MD within 7 days for his own instructions; letter to both confirming the joint retainer, information sharing and today's advice; written confirmation from Mrs Croft, gift or loan and to whom, plus source of funds; draft declaration of trust once agreed, to both; hold panel 10; refer both to private client for wills; progress sale to 27.3.27; report to partner today on 5.

Clients: both to agree the 45k and the shares before the call, and tell me if they cannot; MD to send ID and source of his 30k; both to confirm credit for the works.

5. ETHICS

5.1 Joint retainer. YC asked me to keep the loan point from MD. Did not agree.

5.2 Explained that acting for both means information about the matter is shared, and this goes to the size of each share, not private background. Offered to help her raise it or to put both versions neutrally.

5.3 If she instructs me not to tell him, conflict of interest: firm must stop acting for one or both, each instructing separate solicitors, delay and cost.

5.4 Declined her offer to instruct and sign for MD. Nothing submitted for him without his own instructions.

5.5 Correspondence cannot be arranged to keep one client uninformed; written advice to both.

5.6 Possible further conflict from the unequal contributions, under review at the call.

Signed: trainee, 3.2.27.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The firm acts for both buyers on a joint retainer. Two issues arise unflagged. First, Yasmin offers to give instructions and sign for Marcus, which cannot be accepted; each joint client must instruct personally, and being offshore is no answer. Second, she asks the solicitor to keep from Marcus that her mother's £45,000 is a loan rather than a gift, which is not private background but the fact that determines the shares. A solicitor acting for both cannot keep material information about the matter from one of them. A competent candidate explains the terms of the joint retainer before advice is given, refuses to accept the confidence, offers to help her raise it with Marcus or to put both versions neutrally, and records that if she refuses there is a conflict of interest requiring the firm to cease acting for one or both, with each instructing separate solicitors. The candidate also keeps the possibility of a conflict arising from the unequal contributions under review.

Interview marking grid (skills only)

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Listen to the client and use questioning effectively to enable the client to tell the solicitor what is important to them.SkillsEstablishes the full funding breakdown figure by figure, then probes the character of the £45,000 rather than accepting 'from my mother'. Asks open questions about what she wants to happen on death and on separation, and hears that Amara is the real driver even though Yasmin never says so directly. Summarises the numbers back and checks them.Accepting 'just the normal way, jointly' as an instruction and moving on to the completion date. Never asking whether the mother's money is a gift or a loan, which is the fact the whole share calculation turns on.
Communicate and explain in a way that is suitable for the client to understand.SkillsExplains survivorship in one plain sentence and gives the concrete consequence: if you die holding as joint tenants, Marcus gets the lot and Amara gets nothing, and your will cannot change it. Explains that ownership shares and mortgage liability are different things. Checks understanding after each point rather than at the end.Reciting the technical difference between the two forms of co-ownership without translating it into what happens to Amara, or drowning her in terms such as severance, equitable interest and Form A restriction with no explanation.
Conduct themselves in a professional manner and treat the client with courtesy, respect and politeness including respecting diversity where relevant.SkillsExplains at the outset that the firm acts for both buyers and what that means for information sharing, before any confidence is offered. Handles the request for secrecy without judgment and without embarrassment, and does not take sides between the couple.Failing to explain joint retainer terms until after she has confided, then telling her the confidence cannot be kept, which feels like a trap. Or being drawn into treating her as the real client and Marcus as an absentee.
Demonstrate client focus in their approach to the client and the issues.SkillsConnects the legal structure to what she actually cares about: Amara's future, getting her flat money back, and completing on 26 March. Offers a practical route that keeps the timetable, such as a video call with Marcus this week and a draft declaration of trust circulated to both. Raises wills because it follows from her own stated wish.Giving a neutral menu of two options and asking her to pick, with no advice, or making the timetable the centre of the meeting and treating co-ownership as a box to tick on the TR1.
Establish and maintain an effective relationship with the client so as to build trust and confidence.SkillsKeeps her onside while delivering two unwelcome messages, that she cannot instruct for Marcus and that the loan point cannot be kept from him, by explaining the reason and offering help to raise it with him. Closes with a clear plan and agreed dates so she leaves feeling in control.Either capitulating on the confidentiality point to keep her happy, or delivering the joint retainer rules so bluntly that she stops volunteering information and the separation and death issues are never explored.

Attendance note marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Record all relevant information.SkillsRecords the price, the mortgage, the exact contributions of £150,000, £45,000 and £30,000 and their sources, the dispute in characterisation of the £45,000, Marcus's absence and his planned £40,000 of works, the intended equal mortgage payments against unequal incomes, Amara's position, the absence of wills, and the client's request for secrecy and for correspondence to her personal email only.Recording the headline figures but not that the £45,000 is treated differently by each of them, which is the fact that generates both the conflict and the trust drafting.
Identify appropriate next steps.SkillsSeparate instructions to be taken from Marcus by video call before any TR1 is completed; confirm with both whether the £45,000 is a gift or a loan and obtain written confirmation from the mother; prepare a draft declaration of trust for both to consider; do not complete panel 10 of the TR1 until both have agreed; refer both to the private client team for wills; consider whether separate advice is required; confirm the position on the sale of the flat so the chain matches 26 March 2027.Next steps addressed only to Yasmin, with the TR1 to be completed on her instruction alone, or no step at all to resolve the £45,000 question before the trust is drafted.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsAdvice states plainly that on these contributions joint tenancy would be unsuitable, explains the survivorship consequence for Amara, recommends tenants in common with a declaration of trust dealing with initial contributions, the £45,000, future capital works, mortgage payments and what happens on separation, and states that wills are needed in either case.Setting out the law and leaving the choice entirely to the clients, or recommending tenants in common in equal shares, which ignores the contributions entirely and would leave Yasmin worse off than the default.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly states that the legal estate is always held on a joint tenancy on trust for the co-owners and cannot be severed, that the choice is about the beneficial interest, that survivorship applies to a beneficial joint tenancy and overrides any will, that tenants in common may hold unequal shares which pass under a will or the intestacy rules, that an express declaration of trust is conclusive as between the parties, and that unmarried cohabitants have no matrimonial remedy on separation.Saying the clients can hold the legal title as tenants in common, confusing legal and beneficial ownership, or saying that a will can override survivorship. Assuming the couple are treated like spouses on separation.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers the Form A restriction on the register where they hold as tenants in common, severance of a joint tenancy by written notice as a fallback, the content the declaration of trust needs, joint and several liability under the joint mortgage, the effect of Marcus's proposed £40,000 of works on shares, the consequence of intestacy for an unmarried partner and for a minor beneficiary, and the need for both to make wills.Advising on the two forms of co-ownership and stopping there, with nothing on the mortgage liability, nothing on the Form A restriction, and nothing on what happens to Amara's inheritance because she is a minor.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies that the firm acts for both buyers, that instructions cannot be taken from one for the other, and that a confidence about the £45,000 cannot be kept from Marcus while acting for both. Records that this was explained before advice was given, that Yasmin was invited to raise it with Marcus with the firm's help, and that if she refuses there is a conflict of interest and the firm must cease to act for one or both, with each then instructing separate solicitors. Notes that correspondence cannot be structured to keep one client uninformed.Agreeing to keep the loan point confidential, or continuing to take instructions from Yasmin alone on the basis that Marcus is offshore, or spotting the conflict but recording no resolution beyond 'to be discussed with the partner'.

Examiner notes

The station looks like a routine co-ownership advice exercise and is not. Pass depends on asking one question that most candidates never ask: is your mother's £45,000 a gift or a loan, and does Marcus know. Everything else follows from the answer, including the conflict, the trust drafting and the share calculation. The commonest trap is accepting the opening instruction, 'just the normal way, jointly', and spending the interview on the completion date. A candidate who advises on joint tenancy without extracting the contributions and the wish to benefit Amara will fail the application of law criteria even if the recitation of survivorship is technically correct, because the advice is wrong for this client. The second trap is the offer to sign for Marcus, which sounds helpful and is often accepted with a nod. The third is a technical one: candidates regularly say the clients can hold the legal title as tenants in common. They cannot; the legal estate is always a joint tenancy on trust and only the beneficial interest can be held in common. Strong candidates also notice that equal monthly mortgage payments from unequal incomes, and Marcus's promised £40,000 of works, will generate a dispute later unless the declaration of trust deals with them now, and they raise wills without being prompted because the client herself has said she wants Amara to benefit.

Oral station 7: Business tenant served with a hostile section 25 notice, and negotiating relocation terms

Client interview and attendance note/legal analysis  |  Property Practice  |  10 min reading, 25 min interview, 25 min attendance note  |  involves negotiation

Model attendance note and legal analysis

ATTENDANCE NOTE

Kemp and Ivory Ltd (Mrs R Kemp, MD). Unit 4, Sanderling Yard: s.25 notice and Unit 9 offer. 22.2.27.

1. INFORMATION

1.1 Lease 26.5.17, 10 yrs from 1.6.17, expiry 31.5.27, rent £34,800 pa, user bakery and cafe, NOT contracted out. The Ivory Loaf here since 1.6.17, no predecessor.

1.2 S.25 notice 12.1.27, termination 31.8.27, opposing renewal on ground (f) only. No redevelopment activity.

1.3 Built in ovens: move c.£60,000 plus c.6 weeks lost trade.

1.4 Objectives in order: stay in Unit 4; else Unit 9 with a landlord contribution to ovens and fit out; else leave for a six figure payment. Ceiling £40,000 pa.

1.5 Unit 9 offer (5.2.27): 7 yrs contracted out, £46,000 pa, 3 months rent free, tenant fit out, landlord only break yr 4, open to 31.3.27, conditional on vacating.

1.6 Mezzanine sublet to Two Rivers Coffee since 2023, £400 pm, no consent. Rent late twice in 2024, caught up.

1.7 Client wants the misdirected email used (para 5).

2. LAW APPLIED

2.1 Business occupation, not contracted out: protected, Pt II LTA 1954; no end by effluxion on 31.5.27. Notice valid on its face (6 to 12 months' notice; termination not before contractual expiry); a hostile notice need not propose terms; no counter notice.

2.2 DEADLINE: court application before 31.8.27 or the renewal right is lost. Extension only by written agreement made before expiry, repeatable.

2.3 Ground (f): firm and settled intention at the hearing date to demolish, reconstruct or substantially construct, and inability to do so without possession. No planning, funding, contract or board resolution apparent.
