2.4 Interim rent, s.24A: at £34,800 passing against £46,000 sought an application would raise the rent, so we do not apply. Landlord may.

2.5 Compensation, s.37 (no fault): RV £28,500 x multiplier 1, occupation under 14 yrs, so £28,500. As the notice specifies ground (f) alone, it is payable not only if the landlord succeeds but also if she gives up possession without applying, or applies and withdraws.

2.6 Sublet breaches cl.14 (absolute bar on parting with possession of part): forfeiture risk and damages. No new ground of opposition (landlord confined to its stated ground). Renewal is of the holding; the mezzanine may be excluded.

3. ADVICE AND NEGOTIATING POSITION

No need to leave in August; only 31.8.27 cannot slip. £28,500 is a floor, not a solution. Unit 9 as offered: contracted out means no renewal right, the landlord only break makes 7 yrs really 4, and £46,000 exceeds her ceiling before the ovens. Opening, subject to instructions: Unit 4 renewal at a surveyor's rent; or Unit 9 at £38,000 pa, 9 months rent free, £85,000 contribution, tenant only break yr 4, not contracted out. Reserve, NOT to be disclosed: max £40,000 pa, 6 months rent free, contribution not below £60,000. All negotiation through this firm; no figures to the agent.

4. NEXT STEPS

Today: letter to Vantree Loxley (para 5); diarise 31.8.27 (reminders 30.4, 31.5, 30.6.27) and 31.3.27. Within 7 days: open letter demanding the ground (f) evidence; written advice on the sublet; surveyor on Unit 4 and 9 rents; claim prepared ready to issue; reply to Halbrook Ryde once para 3 approved.

5. ETHICS

Vantree Loxley's email of 21.2.27 (4.52pm, strictly internal) was plainly sent in error and is confidential to the landlord. Partner stopped reading on realising; attachment not opened, and will not be. Notifying them today that it came in error, was not read further, attachment unopened; we will delete or return as directed. Contents not to be used or disclosed. Client asked that it be used and pressed; refused, explaining that the court can restrain a firm from acting where such material is misused, leaving her without solicitors near a hard deadline; we would cease acting if she insisted. Legitimate alternative: demand the ground (f) evidence openly. No misleading statement in negotiation, including as to the mezzanine. Partner informed; email quarantined.

Trainee solicitor.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The firm has received an email from the landlord's solicitors which was obviously sent in error and which is confidential to the landlord, disclosing that funding for the redevelopment has been refused and that no planning application has been submitted. The client has heard about it and demands that it be used. A solicitor who receives material sent by mistake must stop reading it as soon as the error is apparent, not open the attachment, notify the sender immediately and deal with the material as the sender directs, and must not use or disclose the contents. A competent candidate refuses the client's request explicitly, explains that the court can restrain a firm from acting where such material is misused, records the refusal and the reason, and offers the legitimate alternative of demanding the landlord's ground (f) evidence in open correspondence. There is a linked point: in negotiating the Unit 9 terms the firm must not make any misleading statement about occupation of the mezzanine, which is sublet in breach of covenant.

Interview marking grid (skills only)

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Listen to the client and use questioning effectively to enable the client to tell the solicitor what is important to them.SkillsLets her vent briefly then structures the interview around three questions: what has happened, what she wants, and what she can afford. Extracts her priorities in order, her £40,000 rent ceiling, the £60,000 oven cost and the absence of any visible redevelopment activity. Asks directly whether the company occupies the whole unit, which is the only way the mezzanine sublet emerges.Spending the interview explaining the 1954 Act and never establishing her objectives or her limits, so the note contains no negotiating position. Never asking about occupation of the whole, so the sublet is missed entirely.
Communicate and explain in a way that is suitable for the client to understand.SkillsExplains security of tenure, the effect of the notice and the court deadline in commercial language she can act on, and states the single date that matters more than once. Explains that a contracted out lease means no renewal right at the end, and what a landlord only break really means in practice, using the numbers from the offer.Speaking in statutory shorthand about section 25, section 26, section 30(1)(f), section 37 and section 38A without saying what any of it means for her business, or failing to make the 31 August 2027 deadline unmissable.
Conduct themselves in a professional manner and treat the client with courtesy, respect and politeness including respecting diversity where relevant.SkillsStays calm and courteous under commercial pressure, does not match her hostility to the landlord, and refuses the request to use the misdirected email firmly and without lecturing. Explains the professional obligation as a practical protection for her, not as an inconvenience.Joining in the criticism of the landlord and adopting an adversarial tone that then colours the negotiating advice, or delivering the refusal on the email as a rebuke, so she disengages.
Demonstrate client focus in their approach to the client and the issues.SkillsTreats continuity of trading, the staff and the ovens as the objectives and the law as the means. Frames the deadline, the request for evidence of ground (f) and the Unit 9 offer as one commercial strategy, and identifies what she must decide and by when. Warns her not to agree anything with the agent on the telephone.Advising on the 1954 Act accurately and ignoring the Unit 9 offer, or advising her to accept the offer because it removes the uncertainty, without testing the terms against her stated ceiling and her moving costs.
Establish and maintain an effective relationship with the client so as to build trust and confidence.SkillsHolds the line on the misdirected email while keeping her confidence, by immediately offering the legitimate alternative of demanding the landlord's evidence on the record. Ends with a clear plan, the key date and who does what, so she leaves feeling she has a strategy rather than a problem.Buying her approval with 'let me see what I can do with that email', which is a serious professional failure disguised as good client service. The opposite failure is a flat refusal with no alternative, which leaves her believing her solicitor is unwilling to fight.

Attendance note marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Record all relevant information.SkillsRecords the lease dates and rent, that the lease is not contracted out, the notice date, the specified termination date of 31 August 2027 and the ground relied on, the client's objectives in order, the £40,000 rent ceiling, the £60,000 oven cost and six weeks of lost trade, the absence of visible redevelopment activity, the mezzanine sublet since 2023 without consent, the two late rent payments in 2024, the terms of the Unit 9 offer and its 31 March 2027 expiry, and the client's request that the misdirected email be used.Recording the notice and the offer but omitting the client's commercial limits, which makes the negotiating advice unusable, or omitting the sublet because it seemed embarrassing rather than relevant.
Identify appropriate next steps.SkillsDiarise 31 August 2027 with reminders, and diarise 31 March 2027 for the offer. Write to Vantree Loxley about the misdirected email today. Write separately requesting evidence of the landlord's intention, that is planning position, funding, building contract and board resolution. Prepare the tenant's application for a new tenancy and issue it in good time unless an extension is agreed in writing. Advise the client in writing on the sublet and consider whether to seek retrospective consent or end it. Prepare a negotiating brief on Unit 9 with target and reserve positions. Instruct a surveyor on rental value for Unit 4 and Unit 9.Recording that an application must be made 'in due course' without a date or an owner, or leaving the deadline to be dealt with by agreement with the landlord without noting that any extension must be in writing and made before the deadline expires.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsAdvice states plainly that she does not have to leave in August, that the deadline is the one thing that cannot slip, that the compensation figure of £28,500 is well short of her moving costs and therefore is a floor not a solution, and that Unit 9 should be negotiated as a package with named targets on rent, rent free, capital contribution, the break and contracting out.An accurate statement of the statutory scheme with no commercial recommendation, or advice to accept Unit 9 without any analysis of the contracting out point or the landlord only break.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly states that the tenancy is protected because the company occupies for the purposes of its business and the lease was not contracted out; that the section 25 notice appears valid because it was given between 6 and 12 months before a termination date that is not earlier than contractual expiry; that ground (f) requires a firm and settled intention at the date of the hearing and an inability reasonably to carry out the works without possession; that the tenant must apply to court before 31 August 2027 unless extended in writing; and that compensation on ground (f) is £28,500 on these figures because occupation is under 14 years.Saying the notice is invalid because it does not propose new terms, when a hostile notice does not have to; calculating compensation at double the rateable value; assuming the tenancy simply ends on the contractual expiry date of 31 May 2027; or advising that a counter notice must be served, which has not been required since 2004.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAlso deals with the effect of the mezzanine sublet: it breaches the absolute prohibition on parting with possession of part, exposes the company to forfeiture and to a claim in damages, and means the mezzanine may fall outside the holding on any renewal. Credit a candidate who adds that it gives this landlord no further ground of opposition, because a landlord may rely only on the ground stated in its section 25 notice and this notice states ground (f) alone. Deals with the terms of any new tenancy, with interim rent under section 24A and the fact that on these figures an interim rent would work against the tenant, with the consequences of a contracted out lease of Unit 9, the landlord only break, and the practical evidence needed to test ground (f).Advising fully on ground (f) and the deadline but ignoring the sublet, which is both a live risk to the client and a weakness in her position that any competent negotiator must know about before opening.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies that the email of 21 February 2027 was plainly sent in error and is confidential to the landlord; records that it was not read beyond what was necessary to realise the mistake, that the attachment was not opened, that Vantree Loxley will be notified immediately and the material dealt with as they direct, and that the contents will not be used or disclosed. Records that the client asked for it to be used, that this was refused, and that she was told the firm would have to cease acting if she insisted. Adds that the firm cannot make any statement in the negotiation that misleads the landlord, including about the sublet.Treating the email as a lucky break, referring to its contents in the analysis or in the proposed negotiating strategy, or recording the client's request without recording a refusal. Also failing to see the linked point that the negotiation must not involve any misleading statement about occupation of the mezzanine.

Examiner notes

Three things separate pass from fail. First, the date. The candidate must identify 31 August 2027 as the deadline for the tenant's court application and say so unmistakably to the client, noting that any extension must be agreed in writing before the deadline expires. A candidate who tells the client the tenancy ends on 31 May 2027, or who advises serving a counter notice, has misunderstood the scheme; counter notices were abolished in 2004. Second, the misdirected email. Weak candidates say something accommodating like 'let me consider how we might deploy that', which reads as agreement and is a serious failure on the ethics criterion. Strong candidates refuse, explain the consequence of misuse, and immediately substitute the legitimate route of demanding the landlord's evidence of intention on the record, which gets the client the same commercial benefit. Third, the negotiation. This is the negotiation station, and the note must contain a usable position: objectives in priority order, an opening position, a reserve position that is not to be disclosed, and the client's authority limits. A note that analyses the 1954 Act beautifully and says nothing about rent, rent free, capital contribution, the break and contracting out has missed the point of the instruction. The commonest single trap is failing to ask whether the company occupies the whole of Unit 4. The mezzanine sublet is both a breach of an absolute covenant and a limit on the holding for any renewal, and it changes the negotiating balance. Candidates who never ask will negotiate from a position they do not understand, and their note will be comprehensive on the statute and incomplete on the client.

A note on the model answer. The model attendance note is a full reference answer showing every available point and runs to over 1,700 words, which no candidate can produce in the 25 minute write up. A note of 600 to 900 words takes the top of the range provided it records the lease and notice dates, the client's objectives in priority order with her £40,000 ceiling and her £60,000 oven cost, the mezzanine sublet, the terms of the Unit 9 offer, the 31 August 2027 deadline and the requirement that any extension be agreed in writing before it expires, the compensation figure of £28,500 and that it is payable whether or not the company litigates, an opening and a reserve negotiating position, and the handling of the misdirected email. Candidates should write in short numbered paragraphs and spend the time on those points.

Oral station 8: New will for a blended family: second spouse against children of the first marriage

Client interview and attendance note/legal analysis  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  10 min reading, 25 min interview, 25 min attendance note

Model attendance note and legal analysis

ATTENDANCE NOTE AND LEGAL ANALYSIS

Client: Marion Elizabeth Kestrel, b. 4.3.65, Willow Rise. File PC/6612.

Trainee, in person, alone, 14.9.26, 25 mins. Figures approx.

1. INSTRUCTIONS

1.1 Health good, knee op Nov 26. Capacity fine, no pressure.

1.2 1st husband P Alvery d.2013. Children Rachel 38 (Bristol, daughter Iris 6), Thomas 34 (Perth, Aus). M. Douglas Kestrel 68, 14.4.24, Wellsbourne Reg Office. DK's son Peter 41. DK no will, says all to Peter.

1.3 Will 9.6.16 as M E Alvery: revokes earlier wills, Rachel and Thomas executors, estate to them equally. Not met DK then, no marriage contemplated, will silent on it. Original at home.

1.4 Assets: Willow Rise SOLE 465k unmortgaged, from parents' money 2015; Flat 2 Ardley Court JOINT with DK 190k, mortgage 41k, co-ownership form UNKNOWN; Mendip Mutual SOLE 78k; joint a/c 4k; premium bonds SOLE 12k; chattels incl. jewellery 15k; Cardern Life 60k NOT in trust, payable to estate.

1.5 Gift 20k to Rachel 2023, nothing else. DK: pension c.11k pa plus state pension, savings 9k, no property, cannot rehouse.

1.6 Aims: DK never put out; Willow Rise ultimately to Rachel and Thomas, not Peter Kestrel; no fight after death. Content for DK to move smaller if money stays tied for children. Rachel distant, asks if house "safe".

1.7 Asked us to do DK's will too and hide the gift over: see 4.

2. ANALYSIS AND ADVICE GIVEN

2.1 Marriage revokes an earlier will unless made in expectation of it. Not met DK in 2016, will silent: exception cannot apply, will revoked 14.4.24. Told her: no valid will now, new will urgent before Nov op.

2.2 Intestacy today: DK takes chattels, statutory legacy with interest and half residue absolutely, children the rest on statutory trusts; legacy figure to confirm in writing. So DK takes a large absolute share incl. Willow Rise value, passable to Peter: opposite of her wishes. No executors: letters of administration.

2.3 Flat: joint tenancy = to DK by survivorship, outside will; tenancy in common = into estate. Check register: until then cannot say what her will reaches. Severance by written notice, which DK receives.

2.4 Policy not in trust: 60k into estate, exposed to creditors and 1975 Act claim. Advise writing in trust.

2.5 Recommended: life interest in Willow Rise to DK, remainder Rachel and Thomas equally, meeting both aims. Settle determining events (remarriage, cohabitation, ceasing to occupy), outgoings, repairs, power to sell and rehouse him, capital legacy. Rachel not sole trustee, conflict.

2.6 1975 Act: DK a surviving spouse, so higher standard, reasonable provision whether or not needed for maintenance. Modest means, no home: cutting him out high risk, life interest plus legacy far safer. Signed statement of reasons kept with will, listing resources. Rachel low risk (adult child, no need).

2.7 IHT: spouse life interest on death is an immediate post-death interest: spouse exemption now, tax on his death; figures, RNRB and 2023 gift to advise in writing.

2.8 Executors: Rachel and Thomas jointly unattractive (Thomas abroad, Rachel conflicted over trust asset). Discuss professional executor, cost.

3. NEXT STEPS

Firm: official copies both properties, flat co-ownership report, 5 wd; letters confirming revocation, intestacy, legacy figure, IHT, costs, and that we act for her alone, DK to instruct another firm; instructions on life interest terms, legacy, trustees and executors; draft will and statement of reasons; interim will now; diarise before Nov op.

Client: original 2016 will and policy schedule; confirm we may refer DK elsewhere.

4. ETHICS

4.1 Asked us to act for DK too and withhold the gift over. Cannot do both.

4.2 Acting for both, we would owe DK disclosure of material information, and the remainder gift is plainly material to him. Direct conflict over Willow Rise, not curable by consent.

4.3 Resolved: act for Mrs Kestrel alone; DK to take independent advice elsewhere; nothing she told us passed to him. Explained, accepted, confirm in writing. Partner told.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

The client asks the firm to act for her husband as well, and separately asks that he not be told that the house passes to her children after his life interest. Acting for both spouses on those terms is impossible: the firm would owe Mr Kestrel a duty to disclose material information and could not honour a promise of concealment given to Mrs Kestrel, and there is a direct conflict between their interests in Willow Rise. The candidate must spot this without prompting, tell the client plainly that the firm cannot do it, act for Mrs Kestrel alone, recommend independent advice for Mr Kestrel, and confirm all of that in writing. Simply recording a 'possible conflict for later review' is not a resolution.

Interview marking grid (skills only)

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Listen to the client and use questioning effectively to enable the client to tell the solicitor what is important to them.SkillsOpens with an open question, lets Mrs Kestrel set out the whole family picture before probing, then uses focused follow up to pin down how each asset is held, whether the 2016 will was made in expectation of marriage, and what Douglas has of his own. Picks up the unspoken tension between Douglas and Rachel and asks about it directly but tactfully.Jumps straight to a checklist of assets, never asks whether the will contemplated a marriage, and never establishes how the Wellsbourne flat is held, so the whole analysis of what passes under a will is built on air.
Communicate and explain in a way that is suitable for the client to understand.SkillsExplains revocation by marriage in one clean sentence with no Latin and no section numbers, checks she has followed it, then explains a life interest trust using the house itself as the example: Douglas lives there, the children own it in the end. Uses a short summary at the end of each topic.Says 'your will was revoked by operation of law under section 18' and moves on. Uses 'life interest', 'remainderman' and 'severance' without ever explaining them, and does not check understanding once.
Conduct themselves in a professional manner and treat the client with courtesy, respect and politeness including respecting diversity where relevant.SkillsPunctual, introduces themselves and the firm, explains the purpose and length of the meeting, takes the news about the revoked will seriously without alarming her, and treats her wish to protect both her husband and her children as reasonable rather than as a problem.Talks over her, appears irritated by her list, or implies she has been foolish not to have checked her will after remarrying.
Demonstrate client focus in their approach to the client and the issues.SkillsKeeps returning to her two stated goals and tests every option against both of them. Asks whether she would let Douglas move to a smaller property, which she has not considered, and raises cost and executor choice because she has said cost matters.Delivers a generic will interview. Never tests any proposal against the aim of keeping Willow Rise for Rachel and Tom, and never asks what she wants to happen if Douglas cannot manage the stairs.
Establish and maintain an effective relationship with the client so as to build trust and confidence.SkillsAcknowledges the awkwardness of the request to act for Douglas without embarrassing her, explains the limit honestly, and offers a workable alternative so she leaves feeling helped rather than refused. Confirms next steps and who will do what by when.Either agrees to keep the remainder gift from Douglas in order to please her, or refuses flatly with no explanation and no alternative, so she leaves the meeting resentful and no further forward.

Attendance note marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Record all relevant information.SkillsRecords the full family tree with dates, the date and terms of the 2016 will, the date of the marriage, and every asset with its ownership basis clearly flagged as sole, joint or unknown. Records the 2023 gift of 20,000 pounds to Rachel, the unwritten life policy, and that Douglas has no will.Records a list of assets with no ownership basis, omits the date of the marriage or the date of the will, and loses the 20,000 pound gift and the life policy entirely.
Identify appropriate next steps.SkillsLists next steps in order with owners: obtain office copy entries for both properties, confirm whether the flat is held as joint tenants, obtain the original 2016 will, take instructions on trustees and on the terms of the life interest, prepare a draft will and a statement of reasons, advise on writing the life policy in trust, and write to Mrs Kestrel confirming that the firm cannot also act for Mr Kestrel.Ends with 'draft the will' and nothing else. No land registry check, no severance point, no letter to the client on the conflict.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsAdvice is written for Mrs Kestrel and is anchored to her two goals. States plainly that she is currently to be treated as intestate, what that would produce, and why the life interest route delivers both of the things she wants. Flags the risk from Rachel as well as from Douglas.Sets out the law of revocation and life interests correctly but never says what Mrs Kestrel should actually do, or writes as though the reader were another solicitor.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly states that the 2016 will was revoked by the April 2024 marriage, that the expectation of marriage exception cannot apply on these facts, and that the intestacy rules therefore currently govern. Correctly identifies the surviving spouse's entitlement in outline, correctly identifies that a beneficial joint tenancy in the flat would pass by survivorship outside the will, and correctly states the spouse standard under the 1975 Act.States that the will is merely 'partly out of date' or that the marriage has no effect. Treats the jointly owned flat as passing under the will without checking the form of co ownership. Applies the maintenance standard to a surviving spouse.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawCovers revocation, intestacy, severance, the life interest trust and its terms, the 1975 Act exposure from both the spouse and potentially from a child, the effect of the unwritten life policy falling into the estate, executor selection given the conflict between Rachel and Douglas, and flags that inheritance tax consequences of a spousal life interest must be advised on in writing.Deals only with revocation and stops. Says nothing about the 1975 Act, nothing about the joint flat, nothing about the life policy and nothing about who should be executor.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies unprompted that acting for both spouses creates a conflict of interest and, more sharply, that the client has asked the solicitor to withhold material information from a prospective second client. Records that this cannot be done, that the firm should act for Mrs Kestrel alone, that Mr Kestrel should be advised to instruct another firm, and that the advice given to Mrs Kestrel in the meeting is confirmed in writing.Ignores the request entirely, or notes it as a 'possible conflict' to be reviewed later without deciding anything, or agrees to act for both on the basis that the client has consented.

Examiner notes

PASS: the candidate establishes early that the 2024 marriage revoked the 2016 will, explains that consequence to the client in plain words and checks she has followed it, asks how each asset is held rather than assuming, proposes a life interest trust tested against both of her stated aims, raises the 1975 Act risk from her husband, and deals honestly with the request to act for Mr Kestrel. FAIL: the candidate takes the 2016 will at face value and spends the interview redrafting it. The commonest trap is treating the will as valid but 'in need of updating'. Everything else then goes wrong, because the client is advised on variations to a document that has no legal effect and is never told she is currently intestate. The second commonest trap is agreeing, or failing to respond at all, to the request to keep the remainder gift from Mr Kestrel. A third trap is assuming the Wellsbourne flat passes under the will; a candidate who never asks how it is held cannot advise correctly on what the will can reach.

A note on the model answer. The model attendance note is a full reference answer showing every available point and runs to over 1,850 words, which no candidate can produce in the 25 minute write up. A note of 600 to 900 words takes the top of the range provided it records the family tree with dates, the date and terms of the 2016 will and the date of the marriage, every asset with its ownership basis and the flat marked as form of co ownership unknown, the 2023 gift and the unwritten life policy, the plain statement that she is currently intestate and what that would produce for Mr Kestrel, the life interest structure tested against both of her aims, the 1975 Act exposure, and the refusal to act for Mr Kestrel on the terms proposed. Candidates should write in short numbered paragraphs and spend the time on those points.

Oral station 9: Doubtful capacity and a relative in the room: the golden rule and undue influence

Client interview and attendance note/legal analysis  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  10 min reading, 25 min interview, 25 min attendance note

Model attendance note and legal analysis

ATTENDANCE NOTE AND ANALYSIS

PC/7530 Rowsby, Alfred George, 87. Trainee, 21.4.27, 25 mins. Nephew Gareth Rowsby (GR) present for part. Quotes verbatim.

1. THE MEETING

GR stayed and resisted leaving: "I'd rather stay, he gets muddled and I can help." He answered 3 questions for his uncle ("the house is to come to me") and prompted him ("The house, Alf. Remember what we said in the car"). He then left; client seen alone for 12 mins. Hearing aid off at first.

2. HIS OWN WORDS

2.1 "I've come to change my will. The house is to go to Gareth." Consistent.

2.2 Why: "He comes every week. The girls don't come."

2.3 Present will: "I don't rightly remember. Something for the girls, I should think." No recall of the £2,000 legacy or of the house to his daughters.

2.4 Daughters if the house goes to GR? "They'd still get the house, wouldn't they? They'd get their share." Explained they would then share only the money and shares. "Oh. Well, that doesn't seem right." "But Gareth's the one that comes." Asked again: "I'd have to think about that."

2.5 Property: house, post office money, "some shares"; bonds only on prompting; no values.

2.6 Fence anecdote twice, same words, 12 mins apart ("Did I?"); "Now what was it you asked me?"

2.7 GR: £15,000 to him Jan 27 for an extension, driving him to the bank. Client silent; "Did I?"

2.8 GP letter 14.4.27 via GR: mixed dementia, moderate, declining since Oct 26.

2.9 GR booked and chased (4 calls), supplied GP letter and asset schedule, offered to pay. Jean Hollis rang 20.4.27; nothing confirmed.

2.10 Assets unverified: house £340k, PO £26k, shares £8k, bonds £5k; house c.90%.

3. ANALYSIS

3.1 Test: nature and effect of the act; extent of property; claims he ought to consider; no disorder perverting his sense of right. Capacity presumed and decision specific.

3.2 Applied: nature and effect probably met; extent doubtful (bonds forgotten, no values, house c.90%); claims seriously doubtful per 2.4. Neither capacity nor its absence established.

3.3 Golden rule: an aged or ill testator's will approved and witnessed by a doctor recording his findings on capacity. Ignoring it leaves nothing for a court.

3.4 Knowledge and approval must be proved affirmatively where circumstances excite suspicion, as here.

3.5 Undue influence in wills means actual coercion, proved by the challenger; no presumption from trust.

3.6 Lifetime gifts differ: trust plus a transaction calling for explanation raises a rebuttable presumption; the Jan 27 gift may qualify.

3.7 If capacity is absent, no will by us: only the Court of Protection may authorise a statutory will.

3.8 2018 will stands meanwhile. Likely attack a probate claim, not a 1975 Act claim by adult daughters.

4. ADVICE GIVEN

Him, alone: no will today; the 2018 will stands; a further meeting alone and a doctor first, protecting him and GR. Both told the medical step is what makes a gift hold.

5. NEXT STEPS

No will drafted, sent or executed. Authority to write to Dr Anwuli; instruct a practitioner on testamentary capacity, letter giving the test, both wills' terms and the Jan 27 transfer, and asking whether he understands the gift excludes his daughters. 5 wd. Second attendance alone, 2018 will read to him. Letter to his own address, not via GR. Fee arrangement in writing with him. If capacity confirmed: fresh instructions alone, draft, execute before the doctor, statement of reasons. If not: no will.

6. ETHICS

Client is Mr Rowsby alone: GR and daughters get no advice or information, nothing confirmed to Mrs Hollis. GR's answering and prompting recorded as evidence; his acts innocuous singly, together the classic pattern of a will later set aside, so a repeated instruction is not taken at face value. Paying makes GR no client; his payment needs the client's written consent. Resolution: no will today, independent assessment, further meeting alone, all recorded.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

There is no single flagged issue, there is a cluster that the candidate must assemble. Instructions were being given in the presence of, and partly by, the person who takes the whole benefit; the beneficiary arranged the appointment, supplied both the medical evidence and the asset schedule, and offered to pay the firm's fees; the client's daughter has telephoned trying to find out what is happening; and the firm holds the earlier will that the daughters benefit from. The resolution required is to insist on seeing the client alone, to decline to prepare any will today, to arrange an independent medical assessment following the golden rule, to make clear that the uncle alone is the client and that a paying third party acquires no rights or information, to maintain confidentiality against the daughter, and to record the client's own words in full because the attendance note is the firm's evidence if the will is later challenged. Recording 'possible capacity concerns' and drafting the will anyway is the failure.

Interview marking grid (skills only)

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Listen to the client and use questioning effectively to enable the client to tell the solicitor what is important to them.SkillsDirects every question to Mr Rowsby, not to Gareth. Redirects politely each time Gareth answers for him. Uses open questions, tolerates long pauses, and then uses precise closed questions to test understanding: what does your present will say, what would your daughters get, what else do you own. Notices the repeated fence anecdote and the repeated question and records both.Allows Gareth to answer for his uncle and takes those answers down as instructions. Asks only leading questions such as 'so you want the house to go to Gareth, is that right?', which tests nothing at all.
Communicate and explain in a way that is suitable for the client to understand.SkillsSpeaks to Mr Rowsby normally, faces him, checks he has heard, and adjusts once the hearing aid point emerges. Explains in short concrete sentences using his own assets as the example. Explains why no will is being prepared today in terms that do not sound like a refusal, and explains to Gareth why he must step out in terms that make it his interest too.Shouts, speaks slowly and loudly as though to a child, or uses 'testamentary capacity', 'the golden rule' and 'the residuary estate' to an 87 year old man with a hearing aid. Or tells the client 'I can't do this' with no explanation.
Conduct themselves in a professional manner and treat the client with courtesy, respect and politeness including respecting diversity where relevant.SkillsTreats Mr Rowsby as the client and as a competent adult throughout. Asks Gareth to leave firmly, courteously and without accusing him of anything. Handles the diagnosis with dignity and does not discuss it across the client as though he were not there. Does not display suspicion of Gareth openly.Talks about Mr Rowsby in the third person while he is in the room. Or treats Gareth as the enemy, becomes confrontational, and makes the client distressed and defensive of his nephew.
Demonstrate client focus in their approach to the client and the issues.SkillsRecognises that the client's real concern is that Gareth is recognised for what he does, and explores whether there is a way to achieve that which the client is comfortable with. Picks up his obvious unease when he understands his daughters would lose the house and does not push him past it. Adapts the plan for the meeting when it becomes clear no instructions can safely be taken.Presses on to a completed set of instructions because that is what the email asked for, ignoring that the client has said he would have to think about it. Treats the interview as an exercise in producing a will rather than as an exercise in finding out what this client actually understands and wants.
Establish and maintain an effective relationship with the client so as to build trust and confidence.SkillsEstablishes an individual relationship with the client, particularly after Gareth leaves the room, so that he speaks more freely. Leaves him with a clear, kind account of what happens next and when. Leaves Gareth without a grievance by explaining the reasoning rather than asserting authority.Never sees the client alone, so no independent relationship is established at all and every instruction on the file is contaminated. Or antagonises Gareth so completely that the client will not come back.

Attendance note marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Record all relevant information.SkillsRecords the client's key answers verbatim as the partner asked, especially 'They'd still get the house, wouldn't they? They'd get their share', 'Oh. Well, that doesn't seem right', 'But Gareth's the one that comes' and 'I'd have to think about that'. Records the repeated anecdote and repeated question with timings, the inability to describe the existing will or to value any asset, Gareth's three interruptions and his resistance to leaving, the January 2027 transfer of 15,000 pounds, the daughter's telephone call, and whether and when the client was seen alone.Records a conclusion, 'client appeared confused', with no evidence. Paraphrases the critical answer instead of quoting it, so the file cannot later show what he actually said. Omits the 15,000 pound lifetime transfer entirely.
Identify appropriate next steps.SkillsNext steps are decisive and correctly ordered: no will to be prepared or sent out at this stage; arrange a capacity assessment by a medical practitioner with a proper letter of instruction setting out the test and the terms of both the old and the proposed will; obtain consent to write to the GP; re attend the client alone; retrieve and read the 2018 will to him; write to the client at his own address confirming the position; establish the fee arrangement in writing with the client, not with Gareth.Next step is 'draft the will and send for approval', or 'ask Gareth to confirm instructions'. Or the note identifies the problem correctly and then proposes nothing at all, leaving the file with a diagnosis and no plan.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsAdvice is directed at the client's interests, not at completing the transaction. Explains why proceeding today would put at risk the very gift the client says he wants, so that the client and the nephew both have a reason to accept the delay. Notes that the 2018 will stands in the meantime and that the client is not left unprotected.Advice reads as a defensive memo about protecting the firm. No advice to the client at all, or advice that simply records a refusal to act with no route forward.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawApplies the correct test: whether the testator understands the nature of the act and its effects, the extent of the property being disposed of, and the claims to which he ought to give effect, and is not suffering from a disorder of mind that perverts his sense of right. Applies it to the actual evidence and concludes correctly that the second and third limbs are in genuine doubt while the first may be satisfied. Correctly states the presumption of capacity and that capacity is decision specific, so a dementia diagnosis is not itself decisive. Correctly identifies the golden rule and that undue influence in a will requires proof of actual coercion, with no presumption arising from the relationship.States that the client 'lacks capacity because he has dementia'. Or applies the Mental Capacity Act functional test as though it displaced the testamentary test. Or asserts a presumption of undue influence from the fact that Gareth arranged the appointment, which is wrong for wills, however suspicious the circumstances.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAlso addresses knowledge and approval and the suspicious circumstances that here require it to be affirmatively proved; the risk of a 1975 Act claim by the daughters and their evidential position; the January 2027 lifetime transfer of 15,000 pounds, where a presumption of undue influence may arise on very different principles from wills; the need for a full attendance note as the firm's primary evidence in any later probate claim; that the 2018 will remains in force; and what happens if the medical assessment concludes he lacks capacity, including that only the Court of Protection can then authorise a statutory will.Deals with capacity alone. Says nothing about knowledge and approval, nothing about the lifetime gift, nothing about the 1975 Act, and nothing about what to do if the assessment goes the other way.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawHandles the two matters the partner has asked about, taking instructions from the client alone and recording his own words, and identifies unprompted the rest of the cluster: the person who benefits arranged the appointment, supplied the medical letter, supplied the asset schedule and proposed to pay the bill; the client is Mr Rowsby alone and no information may be given to Gareth or to the daughters; a third party paying the fee does not become the client and this must be confirmed in writing to Mr Rowsby; and the firm holds the 2018 will, which the daughters may later ask about. Resolves it by declining to prepare a will today, arranging an independent medical assessment and a further attendance alone, and recording everything.Notes that 'there may be a capacity issue' and stops. Or accepts Gareth's payment and his presence without comment. Or discloses something to the daughter who telephoned. Or, worst, prepares the will on the footing that the client said he wanted it and that a note of concern on the file is protection enough.

Examiner notes

PASS: the candidate asks the nephew to leave, holds that position courteously when it is resisted, and explains why in terms that make it the nephew's interest too. The candidate then actually tests capacity rather than assuming it either way, by asking what the existing will says, what the client owns and, decisively, what the daughters would receive under the proposed change. The candidate hears the answer 'They'd still get the house, wouldn't they', explains the position, does not press for a decision when the client says he must think, and concludes that no will can be prepared today. FAIL: two opposite errors both fail. The first is proceeding: taking the instruction at face value because the client said the words, letting the nephew answer, and promising to send a draft. The second, and the one candidates rarely expect to be marked down for, is over correcting: announcing that the client 'lacks capacity because he has dementia', treating him as incapable in front of his nephew, and refusing to act. Capacity is presumed and is decision specific; the correct answer is that it is genuinely in doubt and must be resolved by a medical assessment, not by a trainee in 25 minutes. The commonest single trap is asking only leading questions, 'so you want the house to go to Gareth, is that right', which produces a confident yes and tests nothing. The second commonest is missing the January 2027 transfer of 15,000 pounds, which engages an entirely different set of principles from the will and which the nephew will volunteer if he is simply asked.

Oral station 10: Lifetime giving to reduce inheritance tax, a legacy offered to the solicitor, and a request to backdate

Client interview and attendance note/legal analysis  |  Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)  |  10 min reading, 25 min interview, 25 min attendance note

Model attendance note and legal analysis

ATTENDANCE NOTE

Priya Naismith, PC/7811. Seen alone, 3.3.27.

1. INFORMATION

1.1 Widow, 66. Roger died 6.4.24, all to her, so his NRB and RNRB are unused.

1.2 Cardiac procedure 2 yrs ago, on medication; says she is well.

1.3 Serena (husband Duncan Holt bankrupt c.2016, pressing for the barn); Marcus buying into a vet practice, nothing signed; Freya marries Sept 2027.

1.4 House £890,000; Old Dairy £310,000 let, rent £14,400; portfolio £640,000, income £19,000; cash £95,000; ISAs £180,000; chattels £120,000; pension £200,000, unnominated.

1.5 Income c.£59,400, spending c.£40,000; the barn is a quarter of it.

1.6 No prior gifts of substance; £250 to Freya each Christmas; no annual exemptions used.

1.7 Will 19.11.24: Serena executor; paintings to Marcus; £10,000 to the appeal; residue equally.

1.8 Proposals: barn to Serena; £150,000 to Marcus; house to both children while living there; £60,000 to Freya on marriage; a charity gift.

1.9 Also: £50,000 legacies to the supervising partner and to me, and a request to backdate the gift documents.

2. LAW

2.1 PETs: exempt after 7 yrs, otherwise chargeable, using the NRB before the estate. Taper cuts the tax, not the value. Do not bet on 7 yrs.

2.2 Barn: a PET if no benefit or rent is kept, but it loses £14,400 pa and brings CGT now at market value, being a connected person disposal. Outright it is exposed to Duncan's insolvency; a trust protects it and at £310,000 is within the £325,000 NRB, so no immediate charge.

2.3 Marcus £150,000: a PET, but the buy in is not agreed.

2.4 House: a gift with reservation, staying in her estate however long she survives. Cured only by a full market rent paid; pre owned assets tax may bite. Worst, it risks the RNRB twice, hers and Roger's, both needing a residence closely inherited. Advise against.

2.5 Freya, a grandchild: marriage exemption £2,500, not £5,000, and must precede the wedding, in consideration of it. The balance is a PET; the £250 Christmas gifts are small gifts, not combinable with it.

2.6 Charity is exempt without limit; £10,000 is far short of the 10% baseline cutting 40% to 36%.

2.7 Annual exemption £3,000, carried forward one year only and after the current year's: one earlier year at most, not two.

2.8 Best of all: normal expenditure out of income; on a c.£20,000 surplus such gifts are exempt at once, with records.

2.9 Roger's estate was spouse exempt, so 100% of his NRB and RNRB is claimable if the house is closely inherited. RNRB tapers £1 per £2 above £2,000,000; at c.£2,235,000 she is £235,000 into taper, which gifts may recover.

2.10 Will review: the charitable legacy and the 10% test; equal residue once Serena has the barn; sole executor also residuary beneficiary.

3. ADVICE

Do not give the house away. The barn costs income and CGT and is exposed to Duncan; consider a trust. Nothing given away until the cash flow.

4. NEXT STEPS

Cash flow before any gift, 10 days. Expression of wishes to the pension provider. Barn base cost and CGT modelling. Time Freya's gift before the wedding. Review the will. Write confirming the advice and both refusals.

5. ETHICS

(a) The £50,000 legacies to the partner and to me: the firm cannot take that instruction. She must take independent advice from a solicitor with no interest; if she declines we cease to act on the will. It protects her: such a legacy invites challenge for undue influence or want of knowledge and approval. Refer to a non beneficiary partner; confirm in writing.

(b) Backdating refused outright: a document dated to a date on which it was not executed is false and, used with HMRC, a false statement for a tax advantage, breaching honesty and integrity. Her insistence is irrelevant; see 2.7.

(c) No capacity or pressure concerns. Conflict to be reviewed if a child instructs us on the barn.

Trainee solicitor.

The conduct issue hidden in this station

Two unflagged issues in one meeting. First, the client instructs that her will include legacies of 50,000 pounds each to the supervising partner and to the fee earner conducting the interview. The firm cannot take that instruction; she must be advised to obtain independent legal advice from a solicitor with no interest in the gift, and if she declines the firm must cease to act on the will. The reason must be given to her in terms of her own protection, since such a legacy is an obvious target for a later challenge, and the point must be referred to a partner who is not herself a proposed beneficiary. Second, she asks that the gift documents be dated back to April so that earlier annual exemptions are not lost. That is the creation of a false document and, if relied on with HMRC, a false statement made for a tax advantage. It must be refused outright, whatever the client's insistence, and the correct position on carry forward explained instead. Recording either request as something to raise with a partner later, without a decision, is not a resolution.

Interview marking grid (skills only)

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Listen to the client and use questioning effectively to enable the client to tell the solicitor what is important to them.SkillsLets her set out her whole plan before taking it apart, then works through it item by item. Asks what income she would be left with, which she has not considered, and asks about her health, Serena's husband and whether the practice purchase is agreed. Uses her own reaction to the rent point to open up the wider conversation about what she needs to keep.Answers each of her six proposals in turn as posed and never asks what she would live on, never asks about her health despite the seven year rule, and never asks whether the vet practice purchase is real.
Communicate and explain in a way that is suitable for the client to understand.SkillsExplains gifts with reservation using her own house as the example and in words she can repeat to her children. Explains the seven year rule and taper relief accurately, including that taper reduces the tax and not the value, which clients routinely get wrong. Refuses the backdating request in plain words without being priggish.Says 'that would be a GROB' and moves on. Tells her taper relief reduces the value of the gift, which is wrong and would mislead her. Or refuses the backdating with an unexplained 'we can't do that'.
Conduct themselves in a professional manner and treat the client with courtesy, respect and politeness including respecting diversity where relevant.SkillsHandles the offer of a legacy with warmth and without embarrassment, so that a generous client is not made to feel foolish. Declines it clearly all the same. Treats her intelligence with respect, gives direct answers and says what things depend on rather than hedging.Is visibly awkward about the legacy and either accepts it to avoid the awkwardness or refuses it in a way that implies she has done something improper. Or patronises an evidently capable client.
Demonstrate client focus in their approach to the client and the issues.SkillsReorders her plan around what she actually wants, which is to see her children benefit without losing control or running short. Warns her about the outright gift to Serena given Duncan's bankruptcy history, and about giving Marcus money for a purchase that is not agreed. Raises the pension nomination, which she has never made and which is free to fix.Delivers a technically accurate tax lecture that never engages with her circumstances. Misses the pension nomination entirely. Never mentions that an outright gift to a married daughter is exposed if her husband's business fails again.
Establish and maintain an effective relationship with the client so as to build trust and confidence.SkillsTurns the two refusals into reasons to trust the firm, by explaining that both protect her and her family. Builds real confidence with the income point, which is the moment she realises the candidate is thinking about her and not about the tax. Ends with a clear summary of what is agreed, what is being checked and when she will hear.Says yes to the legacy and to the backdating in order to keep a warm client warm, which is the exact failure this station is built to detect. Or refuses both so bluntly that she leaves offended and takes the file elsewhere.

Attendance note marking grid

CriterionTypeWhat a grade A looks likeWhat drops you to D or below
Record all relevant information.SkillsRecords every asset with value and ownership, her income of about 45,000 pounds a year against spending of about 40,000 pounds, all six of her proposals as she framed them, the death of her husband on 6 April 2024 with the whole estate passing to her and neither allowance used, her cardiac history and medication, Duncan's bankruptcy, the unagreed practice purchase, the 250 pound Christmas gifts, the absence of any pension nomination, the wedding date, and both of her improper requests in her own words.Records the assets and the six proposals and nothing about her income, her health, the pension nomination or the family circumstances, so nothing in the note supports the advice given.
Identify appropriate next steps.SkillsNext steps are specific and prioritised: prepare a cash flow of her income and needs before any gift is made; obtain the pension provider's expression of wishes form; check the barn's base cost and the capital gains position; confirm the marriage exemption limits and the timing against the September wedding; review the will, including the charitable gift and the residence nil rate band position; write to her confirming the advice, the refusal of the backdating and the requirement for independent advice on any legacy to the firm.Ends with 'advise on lifetime gifts'. No cash flow, no pension nomination, no capital gains point on the barn, and no written confirmation of either refusal.
Provide client focused advice.SkillsAdvice reorders her plan into what she should do, what she should not do and what needs checking, and says so in that order. Tells her plainly that the house gift does not work and offers the alternatives with their real drawbacks. Tells her to keep enough to live on and shows her the arithmetic.Answers her six proposals in her order without ever forming a view, or gives advice on tax without ever telling her to retain what she needs, which is the advice she most needs and did not ask for.
Apply the law correctly to the client's situation.Application of lawCorrectly applies: outright gifts as potentially exempt transfers, exempt after seven years, chargeable if death is within seven years and using the nil rate band ahead of the estate; taper relief reducing the tax on the gift rather than its value; gifts with reservation, so that the house gift gives no inheritance tax benefit while she continues to occupy without paying full market rent; the annual exemption at 3,000 pounds with one year carry forward usable only after the current year's; the marriage exemption at the parent rate for a child and the lower grandparent rate here, since Freya is a grandchild; the small gifts exemption and that it cannot be combined with the annual exemption for the same person; normal expenditure out of income; the transferable nil rate band and residence nil rate band from her husband; and the reduced 36 per cent rate where at least 10 per cent of the baseline amount goes to charity.Says the house gift works provided she survives seven years, which is the central error. Or applies the parent rate of marriage exemption to a grandchild. Or states that taper relief reduces the value of the gift. Or asserts a figure for the nil rate band different from the sheet provided.
Apply the law comprehensively to the client's situation.Application of lawAlso covers: the residence nil rate band, its taper above a net estate of 2,000,000 pounds and the risk that giving the house away in her lifetime forfeits an allowance she would otherwise have on two counts; the pre owned assets income tax charge as a further obstacle to the house scheme; the capital gains position on the barn, which is not her main residence, and that inheritance tax planning may create a capital gains cost; the pension drawdown fund and the missing expression of wishes; the asset protection risk of an outright gift to a daughter whose husband has been bankrupt, and the alternative of a trust; the risk of giving Marcus 150,000 pounds for a purchase that is not agreed; whether the will still fits, including the charitable legacy and whether the 10 per cent test is met; and that a full cash flow must precede any gift.Deals only with the six proposals as tax questions. Nothing on the residence nil rate band, nothing on capital gains, nothing on the pension, nothing on asset protection, and no advice on whether the existing will still works.
Identify any ethical and professional conduct issues and exercise judgment to resolve them honestly and with integrity.Application of lawIdentifies both unflagged issues and resolves both. On the legacy: a client wishing to make a gift of significant value to the solicitor or the firm must be advised to take independent legal advice, and if she declines the firm must cease to act on it; the note records that this was explained in the meeting and will be confirmed in writing, and that the client's own interest is served because such a gift is a target for challenge. On the backdating: the note states without qualification that the firm will not date any document to a date on which it was not executed, that to do so would be dishonest and, if used in a return, a false statement to HMRC, that it would breach the duty not to mislead and the obligations of honesty and integrity, and that a client's insistence makes no difference. Records that the client accepted both.Records the legacy as 'to be discussed with the partner' with no decision. Or treats the backdating as a technical point about carry forward and never says it is dishonest. Or, worst, says the annual exemption issue can be 'dealt with by dating the documents appropriately'.

Examiner notes

PASS: the candidate tells the client clearly that giving away the house while continuing to live in it produces no inheritance tax saving because of the reservation of benefit rules, and holds that line when she pushes back. The candidate asks what income she would be left with, spots that the barn is a quarter of it, identifies the transferable allowances from her late husband, raises normal expenditure out of income as the exemption she is actually best placed to use, and deals decisively with both the offered legacy and the backdating request. FAIL: the commonest trap is advising that the house gift works provided she survives seven years. That is the error the whole station is built around, and a candidate who makes it has given advice that would cost the family a great deal while also stripping the client of her home. The second trap is applying the parent rate of marriage exemption to a gift to a granddaughter. The third is the backdating request: candidates who treat it as a technical question about carry forward, and answer only that two years cannot be carried forward, have missed that they were asked to create a false document and will lose the ethics criterion even though their tax answer was right. The fourth is accepting the legacy, or thanking the client and saying it will be raised with the partner, without appreciating that the partner named is herself a beneficiary. A candidate who refuses both requests but does so coldly may still lose interview marks; the skill being tested is refusing a generous client without damaging the relationship.

Part 4: Supplementary questions, with answers

SQE2 contains no multiple choice questions. These are revision self-tests on the underlying law, not a model of the assessment. All 500 questions are here, in full, with their answer and explanation directly beneath each one -- none of them are printed in the book itself.

Criminal Law and Practice (Criminal Litigation)

1. Your client tells you that he will give evidence that he was at work, which he accepts to you is untrue, and that a friend will support him. He refuses to reconsider. You withdraw. What do you tell the court about your reasons?

A. That the client proposes to give evidence you know to be untrue.

B. That professional embarrassment has arisen from the alibi he now proposes.

C. That the client has withdrawn his instructions and wishes to represent himself.

D. Nothing about the reasons, because confidentiality survives the retainer's end.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Nothing about the reasons, because confidentiality survives the retainer's end): a solicitor who withdraws because the client will not be dissuaded from giving false evidence must not reveal why, since confidentiality continues after the retainer ends. Option B is the closest wrong answer, because professional embarrassment is the conventional phrase used when coming off the record, but even that formula must not be elaborated into anything that discloses the reason. Telling the court the client intends to lie would breach confidentiality outright.

2. Your client tells you he did take the money but wants to plead not guilty and let the prosecution try to prove it. He does not want to give evidence. He asks whether you can still act for him. What is the position?

A. You may act and put the prosecution to proof, but advance no positive case.

B. You must withdraw at once, because he has admitted the offence to you.

C. You may act and may suggest to the jury that another person took it.

D. You may act only if he agrees to change his plea to guilty.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (You may act and put the prosecution to proof, but advance no positive case): a client who admits guilt but pleads not guilty may still be represented, and you may test the evidence and submit that it falls short of the criminal standard. Option B is the closest wrong answer, because withdrawal becomes necessary only if he insists on a course you cannot properly take. What you may not do is advance a positive case inconsistent with the admission, which is why option C is wrong.

3. Your client snatched a handbag from a woman's shoulder. The strap held and he pulled hard twice before it broke, causing her to stumble. He then ran off with the bag. He says he never intended to hurt her. Is this robbery?

A. No, because force must be used before the theft rather than during it.

B. Yes, because force was used on a person in order to steal.

C. No, because an intention to injure the victim has to be proved.

D. Yes, but only if she was put in fear of immediate force.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Yes, because force was used on a person in order to steal): robbery is theft plus force used on a person immediately before or at the time of the theft and in order to steal, and repeated pulling on a strap that moves the victim is force on the person. Option D is the closest wrong answer, because putting a person in fear is an alternative route to the offence, but it is not required where force is actually used. No intention to injure has to be proved, only the intention to steal.

4. Your client set fire to a wheelie bin standing against the wall of an occupied block of flats at midnight. The fire spread to a door. He is charged with aggravated criminal damage. What must the prosecution prove beyond the basic offence?

A. Intention or recklessness as to endangering life by the damage itself.

B. That life was in fact endangered by the fire he had started.

C. That he intended to cause serious harm to an occupant of the flats.

D. That the property damaged belonged to another and was of high value.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Intention or recklessness as to endangering life by the damage itself): the aggravated form requires intention or recklessness as to whether life is endangered, and the danger must arise from the damage rather than from anything else the defendant did. Option B is the closest wrong answer, because actual danger to life is very likely on these facts, but the offence turns on the defendant's state of mind rather than on the outcome. Value of the property is irrelevant to the aggravated form.

5. You act for a defendant in a burglary. A former client of your firm, unconnected with this case, told you in confidence something that would help your current client's defence. He will not consent to its use. Which duty prevails?

A. The duty of disclosure, because the current client's liberty is at stake.

B. The duty of disclosure, because the former retainer has already ended.

C. Confidentiality, which is owed to former clients and prevails over disclosure.

D. Neither, because the court will decide the question on an application.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Confidentiality, which is owed to former clients and prevails over disclosure): confidentiality is owed to every client including former clients, and where it conflicts with the duty to make a current client aware of material information, confidentiality prevails. Option B is the closest wrong answer, because the end of a retainer feels as though it should release the information, but the duty survives it. The practical consequence may be that you cannot properly act for the current client at all.

6. You are called to advise a 16 year old arrested for robbery. His mother attends as appropriate adult. Before interview she asks you, in front of the client, whether she can tell the officers what her son told her in the cell about where he was. How do you advise her?

A. What she was told is privileged, so she may not be asked about it.

B. What she was told is not privileged, so she could be asked about it.

C. She may pass it on only with the custody officer's written authority.

D. She may pass it on because she is acting as the client's legal representative.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (What she was told is not privileged, so she could be asked about it): the appropriate adult gives no legal advice and nothing said to her attracts legal professional privilege. Her role is to support the detainee and to see that the interview is conducted properly and fairly. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because families assume a parent stands in the solicitor's shoes, but privilege attaches to the lawyer and client relationship. The practical step is to warn both of them before the client says anything sensitive in her presence.

7. The custody officer accepts there is not yet enough evidence to charge your client with fraud. Your client has already been at the station for four hours. You ask on what basis he is being kept. Which of the following is a proper basis for authorising detention without charge?

A. That the client has declined to answer questions put to him.

B. That the officer in the case is not yet available to interview.

C. That the client has previous convictions for offences of dishonesty.

D. That detention is necessary to obtain evidence by questioning him.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (That detention is necessary to obtain evidence by questioning him): where there is insufficient evidence to charge, detention may be authorised only if it is necessary to secure or preserve evidence relating to the offence, or to obtain evidence by questioning the suspect. Option B is the closest wrong answer, because an interview is indeed contemplated, but the availability of a particular officer is administrative convenience rather than a statutory ground. Previous convictions and the exercise of the right to silence are not grounds at all.

8. Your client threatened a shopkeeper with a screwdriver and demanded the till. The shopkeeper pressed an alarm and your client ran out empty handed before touching any money. The whole incident lasted about twenty seconds. He is charged with robbery. What is the correct analysis?

A. Robbery is made out, because the threat itself completes the offence.

B. Robbery is made out, because he intended permanently to deprive the shop.

C. Robbery fails, because the prosecution cannot prove a completed theft.

D. Robbery fails, because a screwdriver is not a weapon of offence.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Robbery fails, because the prosecution cannot prove a completed theft): robbery requires a complete theft, so where nothing is appropriated the offence is not made out and the proper charge is attempted robbery. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because the threat looks like the essence of the offence, but the force or threat is an addition to a theft rather than a substitute for one. The nature of the item used goes to seriousness rather than to whether robbery is available.

9. Your client, attacked from behind, turned and struck his attacker twice with a torch he was holding. He accepts that on reflection one blow would have been enough. He is charged with wounding. How will the court judge the force used?

A. By asking whether the minimum necessary force was in fact used.

B. By asking whether he honestly believed the force used was reasonable.

C. By comparing the injury caused with the injury he was threatened with.

D. Objectively, allowing that he could not weigh matters to a nicety.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Objectively, allowing that he could not weigh matters to a nicety): reasonableness of the response is judged objectively on the facts as the defendant believed them, but the law makes allowance for a person acting in the heat of the moment who cannot measure his response exactly. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because it sounds like the same idea but sets a counsel of perfection the law does not impose. His honest view of his own reasonableness is not the test, which is why option B is wrong.

10. Your client's detention was authorised at 09:00. You attend at 20:00 and read the custody record. It records a review by an inspector at 10:00 and nothing since. The client complains that nobody has looked at his case all afternoon. What do you say about the reviews?

A. The first review was late, since it had to occur within three hours.

B. Reviews may be conducted by the custody officer who authorised the detention.

C. No further review is needed until the 24 hour period has expired.

D. The first review was in time, but a further review is now overdue.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The first review was in time, but a further review is now overdue): the first review must take place within six hours of authorisation, so 10:00 was in time, and later reviews must follow at intervals of no more than nine hours, which expired at 19:00. Option C is the closest wrong answer, because the 24 hour figure is the detention limit rather than the review interval, and the two are separate timetables. Reviews must be carried out by an inspector unconnected with the investigation, not by the authorising custody officer.

11. Your client asked for a solicitor on arrival. The police interviewed him before you arrived and he said nothing. He now relies at trial on a fact he did not mention in that interview. The prosecution seeks an adverse inference from that interview. What is the position?

A. No inference may be drawn, as he had no chance to consult a solicitor.

B. An inference may be drawn, since he was cautioned before being questioned.

C. An inference may be drawn, but he cannot be convicted on it alone.

D. No inference may be drawn, because he later gave evidence at his trial.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No inference may be drawn, as he had no chance to consult a solicitor): no inference from silence may be drawn where the suspect was not allowed an opportunity to consult a solicitor before being questioned. Option C is the closest wrong answer, because the second half of it states a real rule, that nobody may be convicted solely on an inference, but the first half is wrong on these facts. Giving evidence at trial does not remove an inference either; it is the denial of legal advice that does.

12. Your client faces sentence for a burglary of a garden shed. He is working and has no recent convictions. The bench indicates that it has custody in mind. You want to keep him out of prison. What two points does the custody threshold give you?

A. That custody is unavailable for an offence tried in the magistrates' court.

B. That custody requires a previous conviction for a similar offence.

C. That a community order must be attempted before custody is considered.

D. That custody needs the offence to be so serious, and may be suspended.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (That custody needs the offence to be so serious, and may be suspended): a custodial sentence may be passed only where the offence is so serious that neither a fine nor a community sentence can be justified, and even then the court must go on to consider suspension. Option C is the closest wrong answer, because the court must consider whether a community sentence can be justified, but there is no rule requiring a community order to have been tried first. The magistrates plainly can impose custody, so option A is wrong.

13. Your client cut through a neighbour's fence panel to reach a burst pipe that was flooding his own garage. The neighbour was away. He acted quickly and used no more force than needed. He is charged with criminal damage. Which lawful excuse is available and how is it judged?

A. Acting to protect other property, judged on the facts as he believed them.

B. Acting to protect other property, judged on what a reasonable person believed.

C. Necessity, provided the damage caused was less than the damage avoided.

D. Belief in consent, judged objectively by reference to the neighbour's wishes.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Acting to protect other property, judged on the facts as he believed them): the statutory lawful excuse of acting to protect other property is assessed on the facts as the defendant honestly believed them to be, so his belief in the flooding and the need to act quickly is what matters. Option B is the closest wrong answer, because it identifies the right excuse but applies an objective test to the belief, which is not how the statutory excuses work. Belief in consent is a separate excuse, and it too is judged subjectively rather than objectively.

14. Your client used a credit card he knew was cancelled to buy fuel at an unmanned pump, entering the PIN at the terminal. He intended to keep the fuel without paying for it. He says he made no statement to anyone at all. How does the law treat that?

A. A representation may be implied and may be made to a machine.

B. A representation must be express and made to a human being.

C. The conduct is theft of the fuel but cannot amount to fraud.

D. No representation arises where a card is presented without any words.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (A representation may be implied and may be made to a machine): presenting a card carries an implied representation that the user is entitled to use it, and the offence expressly contemplates a representation made to a machine or system. Option C is the closest wrong answer, because theft of the fuel may well also be charged, but the two are not alternatives and the fraud is complete when the card is used. His silence at the pump does not prevent a representation from being made by conduct.

15. Your client has a diagnosed learning disability which the report links to his offending, plays a lesser role than his co-defendant and has begun a course addressing his behaviour. He is being sentenced in the magistrates' court for theft. Which statement about these matters is correct?

A. They go only to whether the custody threshold has been crossed.

B. They must be raised before plea or they are treated as waived.

C. All three are recognised mitigating factors that the court weighs.

D. Only the subordinate role counts, the others being matters for probation.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (All three are recognised mitigating factors that the court weighs): each of these matters counts in the client's favour, though at different stages of the guideline. His lesser role is a culpability factor taken into account at the categorisation step, so it lowers the category itself, while a mental disorder or learning disability linked to the offending and steps taken to address behaviour are recognised mitigating factors applied when adjusting from the category starting point. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because these matters certainly bear on whether custody is justified or can be suspended, but their effect is not confined to that question. Mitigation is advanced at the sentencing hearing, so there is no question of waiver by not raising it earlier.

16. Your client is 34 and has a diagnosed mental health condition. He follows questions with difficulty. The inspector says the interview must start now because a further offence may be committed tonight, and no appropriate adult is available. Which statement is correct?

A. An appropriate adult is required only for detainees who are under 18.

B. The solicitor may act as the appropriate adult for the same client.

C. A vulnerable adult should not be interviewed without one, save in urgent situations.

D. The inspector cannot start the interview until an appropriate adult attends.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (A vulnerable adult should not be interviewed without one, save in urgent situations): adults who are vulnerable because of a mental health condition or mental disorder need an appropriate adult, and the exception for genuinely urgent situations is narrow. Option D is the closest wrong answer, because it states the ordinary rule but leaves no room for the urgency exception the inspector is trying to rely on. Your task is to test whether the urgency is genuine and to have the position recorded either way.

17. Your client's case has been sent to the Crown Court and he is arraigned at the plea and trial preparation hearing, pleading not guilty. He is anxious not to reveal his case. He asks whether he has to set out his defence in advance. What is correct?

A. A defence statement is voluntary in the Crown Court but usually advisable.

B. A defence statement is required only where an alibi is to be relied on.

C. A defence statement is required only after specific disclosure is refused.

D. A defence statement is compulsory in the Crown Court and must be served.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (A defence statement is compulsory in the Crown Court and must be served): service of a defence statement is compulsory on indictment, and it is voluntary only in the magistrates' court. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because it correctly identifies that a statement is usually a good idea but reverses the position on compulsion, which is the point being tested.
