C. No, because the garage had a proprietary interest in the car.

D. No, because taking property at night is itself an aggravating element.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (No, because the garage had a proprietary interest in the car): property belongs to another where another has any proprietary right or interest in it, which is how a defendant can steal goods he owns. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because ownership did remain with the client, but possession had passed to the garage and its lien is a proprietary interest. The remaining questions are dishonesty and intention permanently to deprive, and a genuine belief in a right to take the car would answer the first.

91. Your client threw a glass across a bar to frighten a man, expecting it to miss. It struck him and fractured his cheekbone. He is charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm. He says he never intended serious injury. What must the prosecution prove?

A. Intention or recklessness as to some harm, not serious harm.

B. Intention or recklessness as to grievous bodily harm being caused.

C. Intention to cause some harm, recklessness being insufficient here.

D. Foresight that the glass would probably strike and injure the man.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Intention or recklessness as to some harm, not serious harm): for unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting grievous bodily harm the mental element is intention or recklessness as to some harm, so his denial of any intention to cause serious injury does not answer the charge. Option B is the closest wrong answer, because it matches the seriousness of the injury and feels proportionate, but that higher state of mind belongs to the offence of causing grievous bodily harm with intent. Recklessness suffices, so option C is wrong.

92. Before interview the officer tells you only that your client is suspected of an assault in Cardiff city centre in June and declines to say more. Your client says he cannot remember where he was in June. The officer says disclosure is entirely a matter for him. What is the position?

A. The police must serve all witness statements before any interview under caution.

B. There is no duty to serve evidence, but sufficient information must be given.

C. The police must disclose any material capable of undermining their own case.

D. Disclosure is at the officer's discretion and cannot be challenged before interview.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (There is no duty to serve evidence, but sufficient information must be given): at the police station stage there is no statutory duty to hand over the evidence, but the Codes require enough information for the suspect to understand the nature of the offence and why he is suspected of it. Option D is the closest wrong answer, because disclosure is indeed largely for the officer, but it is not unconstrained and thin disclosure can be pressed and then recorded. A date range of a whole month is a proper basis for arguing you cannot advise on facts he might later rely on.

93. You are on your feet in a plea in mitigation and have dealt with the offence and the offender. A pre sentence report proposing unpaid work has been read. Counsel opposite has sat down. The bench looks at you expectantly. What must you not omit before sitting down?

A. Name the sentence you seek and how the court can properly reach it.

B. Invite the court to adjourn for a further report on his health.

C. Remind the court that the burden of proof rests on the prosecution.

D. Reserve your position on sentence until the court indicates its view.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Name the sentence you seek and how the court can properly reach it): the third part of a plea in mitigation deals with the sentence, and you should never sit down without naming the outcome you want and the route to it. Option D is the closest wrong answer, because it may feel safer to wait and see, but a bench with no proposal in front of it will fall back on its own starting point. The burden of proof has no part to play once the defendant has been convicted.

94. Your client is to be tried summarily for criminal damage. You want the prosecution to review its unused material because you believe there is CCTV showing a third party. He asks whether a defence statement is required. What is the position?

A. It is voluntary, but serving one triggers a review of unused material.

B. It is compulsory in all cases where unused material is in issue.

C. It is voluntary, and serving one has no effect on the prosecutor's duty.

D. It is compulsory once the not guilty plea has been entered summarily.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (It is voluntary, but serving one triggers a review of unused material): in the magistrates' court a defence statement is optional, but serving one brings the prosecutor under a duty to review unused material against the issues identified and opens the way to an application for specific disclosure. Option C is the closest wrong answer, because it correctly identifies the statement as voluntary but wrongly treats it as pointless, which is exactly why it should be served here. Compulsion applies in the Crown Court, not summarily.

95. Disclosure is complete, the CCTV is clear, and your client accepts to you that he took the phone. He asks whether there is anything to be gained from admitting it now rather than fighting on. What is the best advice?

A. Admitting now removes the court's power to impose a custodial sentence.

B. An early admission and plea attract the maximum reduction available for plea.

C. Admitting now guarantees a caution rather than a charge for the offence.

D. Admissions in interview carry no weight because credit runs from the trial.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (An early admission and plea attract the maximum reduction available for plea): where disclosure is full and the case strong, an early account or early guilty plea may serve the client best, and the maximum reduction is available for an indication at the first stage before sliding downwards. Option C is the closest wrong answer, because an admission may open the way to an out of court disposal in a suitable case, but nothing guarantees it. Credit for plea is also separate from remorse, and it does not remove any sentencing power from the court.

96. Your client was cornered by a man who raised what your client honestly believed was a knife. It was a mobile phone. Your client hit him once and ran. He is charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm. How is self defence assessed?

A. The belief must be both honest and reasonable before it can be relied on.

B. The belief is judged subjectively, the response objectively on those facts.

C. Both the belief and the force used are judged entirely subjectively.

D. The mistake defeats the defence, since no knife was in fact present.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The belief is judged subjectively, the response objectively on those facts): a defendant may use force that is reasonable in the circumstances as he honestly believed them to be, so the honesty of the belief is enough even if the belief is mistaken. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because reasonableness does have a part to play, but it attaches to the level of force rather than to the belief about the danger. A single blow against a perceived knife attack will be hard to call unreasonable.

97. The custody officer offers you a consultation with your client in the charge area, within hearing of two officers, saying there are no free rooms. The client wants to tell you what happened. How should you deal with the offer?

A. Decline it and insist on the right to consult privately with the client.

B. Accept it, but ask the client to write his account down instead.

C. Accept it, since privilege attaches wherever the consultation takes place.

D. Decline it and advise the client to answer no comment in interview.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Decline it and insist on the right to consult privately with the client): the right is to consult a solicitor privately, and a consultation in earshot of investigating officers is not private. Option C is the closest wrong answer, because privilege does attach to the advice, but privilege is no protection once officers have simply overheard what was said. Ask for a consultation room, and ask for the request and any refusal to be entered on the custody record.

98. Your client indicates a not guilty plea to an either way offence. He has two recent convictions for similar offences. The prosecution addresses the court and the bench considers whether its powers are adequate. Which statement correctly describes what happens at allocation?

A. Previous convictions are withheld from the bench until after conviction.

B. The defendant elects his venue before the court decides on jurisdiction.

C. The prosecution informs the court of previous convictions before it decides.

D. The Allocation Guideline applies only where the defendant is unrepresented.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The prosecution informs the court of previous convictions before it decides): at allocation the court hears the prosecution, which tells it of previous convictions, then hears the defence and applies the Allocation Guideline before deciding whether its sentencing powers are adequate. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because previous convictions are ordinarily kept from the tribunal of fact, but allocation is a decision about venue and sentencing exposure where they are relevant. Election arises only after the court has accepted jurisdiction.

99. Your client is charged with an imprisonable either way offence. He has settled work, a family home and no history of breaching bail, but the prosecution objects to bail on the basis that the evidence is strong. The bench asks you what the objection has to establish. What do you say?

A. That there is a real prospect of a custodial sentence being imposed.

B. That there are substantial grounds for believing he would fail to surrender.

C. That the strength of the evidence makes a conviction more likely than not.

D. That the court has insufficient information to reach a decision on bail.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (That there are substantial grounds for believing he would fail to surrender): for an imprisonable either way offence the prosecution must establish an exception, and the main exceptions are substantial grounds for believing the defendant would fail to surrender, commit further offences or interfere with witnesses. Option C is the closest wrong answer, because the strength of the evidence is a statutory factor the court weighs when deciding whether a ground is made out, but it is not itself a ground. The distinction between factors and grounds is the point to press in the application.

100. Your client is sentenced for a theft committed while he was on bail for another matter, in company with two others, against an elderly victim. You want to identify what the court will treat as aggravation. Which list is correct?

A. Offending on bail only, as the other matters go to categorisation.

B. Group offending only, as victim characteristics go to harm alone.

C. Offending on bail, offending in a group, and the victim's vulnerability.

D. None of them, since aggravation is confined to previous convictions.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Offending on bail, offending in a group, and the victim's vulnerability): each of these is a commonly listed aggravating factor, along with previous convictions, hostility based on a protected characteristic and being under the influence. Option A is the closest wrong answer, because offending on bail is undoubtedly aggravating, but so are the other two, and excluding them understates the case the court will be considering. Knowing which factors are aggravating lets you anticipate them and answer them in mitigation.

Dispute Resolution

101. Your client has filed a defence to a breach of contract claim and asks what happens next before any trial date is fixed. She wants to know who decides which track the case will be managed on, and when that decision is taken. What do you advise?

A. The court provisionally allocates and sends directions questionnaires after defences are filed.

B. The claimant selects the track when the claim form is first issued.

C. Allocation happens only at a case management conference shortly before trial.

D. The parties agree the track between themselves without involving the court.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The court provisionally allocates and sends directions questionnaires after defences are filed): once the statements of case are closed the court forms a provisional view on track and sends out directions questionnaires so the parties can comment. Option D is the closest wrong answer because the parties' views are sought and carry weight, but allocation is a judicial decision and cannot be settled by agreement between them. The claimant states a value on the claim form, which informs but does not fix the track. A case management conference happens after allocation in a multi track case, not instead of it.

102. You are drafting an offer for your client, a defendant, and want the full costs protection of the regime rather than the weaker protection of an ordinary settlement letter. Your trainee asks what the offer document itself must say. Which requirement must the offer satisfy?

A. It must be open, so that the trial judge can see it during the trial.

B. It must remain open for acceptance for at least three months from service.

C. It must be accepted within seven days of service or it lapses automatically.

D. It must state that it is made under Part 36 and specify a relevant period.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It must state that it is made under Part 36 and specify a relevant period): a compliant offer identifies itself as a Part 36 offer, specifies a relevant period of not less than 21 days, and states whether it relates to the whole claim or part and whether any counterclaim is taken into account. Option B is the closest wrong answer because the offer does remain capable of acceptance after the relevant period expires, but the period itself is a minimum of 21 days rather than three months. A Part 36 offer is not open. It does not lapse after seven days.

103. Your client's finance director wants to hand a privileged advice note to the other side's solicitors to demonstrate good faith in settlement discussions. The client, a company, has not been consulted through its board. Your trainee asks who may waive privilege in that note. What is the position?

A. The solicitor may waive privilege where doing so is in the client's interests.

B. Privilege belongs to the client, and only the client can waive it.

C. Privilege is waived automatically once proceedings are issued in the claim.

D. The court may waive privilege where the document is important evidence.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Privilege belongs to the client, and only the client can waive it): privilege is the client's right, so the decision to give it up is the client's alone and must be taken with informed instructions. Option A is the closest wrong answer because a solicitor advises on waiver and may effect it on instructions, but has no independent power to give away the client's right. Issuing proceedings does not waive anything. The court cannot override a valid claim to privilege simply because the document would be useful evidence.

104. A claim form was issued on 4 May 2026, comfortably inside the limitation period. Your client is still gathering evidence and asks how long the claim form remains valid for service on a defendant within the jurisdiction. Which statement correctly states the position on validity?

A. The claim form must be served within six months of issue within the jurisdiction.

B. The claim form may be served at any time before the limitation period expires.

C. The claim form must be served within four months of the date of issue.

D. The claim form must be served within fourteen days of the date of issue.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The claim form must be served within four months of the date of issue): a claim form is valid for service for four months within the jurisdiction, and six months where it is to be served out of the jurisdiction. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it states the out of jurisdiction period and applies it to domestic service. Validity is a separate question from limitation, so a claim form can expire for service while the limitation period still has time to run. Diarise the expiry date, because an extension after expiry is very difficult to obtain.

105. Your opponent beat its own Part 36 offer at trial but its offer had been made in a form that concealed a significant document from your client until after the relevant period expired. Your client asks whether the enhanced consequences are inevitable. What is the position?

A. The consequences follow unless the court considers it unjust to make them.

B. The consequences are automatic and the court retains no discretion at all.

C. The consequences apply only where the offer was made before proceedings began.

D. The consequences apply only where the offer was repeated after allocation.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The consequences follow unless the court considers it unjust to make them): the Part 36 consequences are the normal order, but the court will not make them where it would be unjust to do so, and conduct such as withholding material bearing on the offer is capable of engaging that exception. Option B is the closest wrong answer because the consequences are indeed the strong default, but describing them as automatic removes the express safety valve. Offers can be made before or after proceedings begin. There is no requirement to repeat an offer after allocation.

106. Your client's modest saloon was written off by the defendant's driver. She hired a large prestige car for eleven weeks at 400 pounds a week, when an equivalent saloon was available locally at 120 pounds a week. The defendant challenges the hire claim. What do you advise?

A. Full hire charges are recoverable, since the defendant caused the need to hire.

B. No hire charges are recoverable, since hire is not a foreseeable head of loss.

C. Only the reasonable cost of an equivalent replacement vehicle is recoverable.

D. Hire charges are recoverable in full if the claimant acted in good faith throughout.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Only the reasonable cost of an equivalent replacement vehicle is recoverable): the duty to mitigate means the claimant cannot recover expenditure she could reasonably have avoided, so recovery is measured by the cost of a comparable vehicle rather than the one she chose. Option A is the closest wrong answer because causation is satisfied, but establishing that the defendant caused the need to hire does not make every sum spent recoverable. Hire is plainly a foreseeable head of loss. Good faith does not answer a failure to act reasonably.

107. Your client's accountant negligently filed a return late. The evidence shows the tax penalty would have been imposed anyway because the underlying figures were wrong for separate reasons unconnected with the delay. The defendant disputes causation. Advise on the position.

A. Causation is established, because the defendant's conduct fell below the standard.

B. Causation fails, because the same loss would have occurred in any event.

C. Causation is established, because the breach materially increased the anxiety suffered.

D. Causation fails, because the claimant cannot prove the precise financial figure.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Causation fails, because the same loss would have occurred in any event): the but for test asks whether the loss would have happened without the breach, and here it would, so factual causation is not made out. Option A is the closest wrong answer because breach and causation are separate elements, and proving that conduct fell below the standard does nothing to show that it caused the loss. Distress that is not an actionable head of loss cannot supply causation. Difficulty in quantifying loss is a question of assessment, not of causation.

108. Your client wants you to sign a statement of truth on a defence containing an account of a meeting that he has privately told you did not happen as pleaded. He asks what could follow if the defence were verified anyway. What is the consequence?

A. The signatory risks contempt proceedings for a false statement of truth.

B. The statement of case becomes void and must simply be re served immediately.

C. The consequence is limited to an adverse costs order made at the trial.

D. The solicitor rather than the client bears responsibility for the false statement.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The signatory risks contempt proceedings for a false statement of truth): verifying a statement of case without an honest belief in its truth exposes the signatory to proceedings for contempt of court. Option C is the closest wrong answer because a costs sanction is a realistic additional consequence but is not the limit of the exposure. The document is not automatically void, and re service would not cure a knowingly false pleading. Separately, you may not advance a case you know to be false, so the answer is to correct the pleading or, if the client insists, to cease acting.

109. You act for a defendant against a litigant in person. Your letter has led her to believe, wrongly, that she cannot recover interest at all, and she is about to accept an offer far below the value of her claim for that reason. Your client tells you to say nothing.

A. Say nothing further, since a solicitor owes duties to her own client alone.

B. Advise the litigant in person on the merits of accepting the settlement offer.

C. Withdraw the offer and report the litigant in person to the court instead.

D. Correct the false impression, since you must not take unfair advantage.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Correct the false impression, since you must not take unfair advantage): you must not take unfair advantage of another party, particularly an unrepresented one, and you must not mislead by an act or omission that creates a false impression. Option A is the closest wrong answer because duties to the client are real but do not override the duties owed to third parties and to the court. Advising the opponent on the merits would go too far the other way and risks a conflict. Reporting her to the court answers nothing.

110. After you filed a witness statement asserting that your client posted a notice on 4 May, he tells you privately that he did not post it at all. He instructs you to say nothing and to run the case as pleaded. What is the correct course?

A. Continue acting, since the client's admission is covered by legal professional privilege.

B. Inform the court of the client's admission at once, whatever the client says.

C. Correct the misleading statement, and cease to act if the client refuses.

D. Continue acting, provided you do not repeat the statement in oral submissions.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Correct the misleading statement, and cease to act if the client refuses): you must not mislead the court, you must correct a misleading statement you have made, and if the client will not permit the correction you must cease to act rather than run a case you know to be false. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it identifies the right instinct but the wrong route, since the privileged admission itself may not be disclosed without consent. Privilege does not entitle you to leave a false statement standing. Staying silent in submissions does not cure the filed document.

111. Your client's supplier repudiated a contract. An identical substitute was available the same week at a slightly higher price, but your client waited four months and paid far more. The defendant says the extra cost should not be recoverable. Advise on the mitigation position.

A. The claimant must prove that it took every possible step to mitigate its loss.

B. Mitigation applies to contract claims only and has no application in tort.

C. The claimant may recover losses which it could have avoided by reasonable steps.

D. The claimant cannot recover avoidable loss, and the defendant proves the failure.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The claimant cannot recover avoidable loss, and the defendant proves the failure): a claimant cannot recover loss it could reasonably have avoided, but the burden of establishing a failure to mitigate rests on the defendant. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it correctly senses that reasonable steps matter but puts the burden on the wrong party and sets the standard too high, since only reasonable steps are required. Mitigation applies in tort as well as contract. Avoidable loss is precisely what cannot be recovered.

112. Your client worries that the judge will think less of her claim if she learns that a Part 36 offer was made and refused. She asks when the trial judge will be told about the offers exchanged between the parties. What do you advise?

A. It is not put before the trial judge until all issues except costs are decided.

B. It is disclosed to the trial judge at the very start of the trial itself.

C. It is included in the trial bundle, on the basis that the judge disregards it.

D. It is put before the judge when the claimant opens its case on quantum.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (It is not put before the trial judge until all issues except costs are decided): a Part 36 offer is made without prejudice except as to costs, so it is withheld from the trial judge until liability and quantum have been determined. Option C is the closest wrong answer because it produces the right formal outcome on paper but exposes the judge to the material, which is exactly what the rule prevents. Disclosure at the start of the trial would risk the judgment being influenced by the offer. Opening on quantum is no different in principle.

113. Your client signed a plant hire agreement at the depot counter without reading it. Clause 14 on the reverse excludes liability for consequential loss. The machine failed and your client lost a week of production. He says he never saw clause 14. What is the position on incorporation?

A. The clause is incorporated by signature, whether or not it was read.

B. The clause is not incorporated, as it was not specifically drawn to his attention.

C. The clause is not incorporated, because it appeared on the reverse of the document.

D. The clause is incorporated only where a prior course of dealing existed.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The clause is incorporated by signature, whether or not it was read): a party who signs a contractual document is bound by its terms, and failure to read them is not an answer. Option B is the closest wrong answer because the requirement to give reasonable notice of an onerous term applies where incorporation depends on notice, typically an unsigned ticket or sign, rather than where the document has been signed. Placing a term on the reverse of a signed document does not exclude it. A course of dealing is a separate route to incorporation, not a precondition.

114. Your client is a defendant facing a claim in which one pleaded head of loss, a claim for lost management time, is hopeless on any view, although the rest of the claim is properly arguable. Your client asks whether summary judgment is open to a defendant. What do you advise?

A. Only a claimant may apply, and only once the defence has been filed.

B. Only a defendant may apply, and only before allocation to a track.

C. Either party may apply, on the whole claim or on a particular issue.

D. Either party may apply, but only with the permission of the trial judge.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Either party may apply, on the whole claim or on a particular issue): summary judgment is available to either party and can be sought on the claim, on a defence or on a discrete issue, which fits a hopeless head of loss inside an otherwise arguable claim. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it correctly identifies that a claimant may apply after a defence, but wrongly makes the remedy one sided. There is no restriction tying a defendant's application to the period before allocation. Permission from the trial judge is not required to make the application.

115. Your client is nervous about mediating a partnership dispute and asks what the mediator will actually do, and whether she could be forced into a settlement she dislikes on the day of the mediation. Which statement best describes the nature of the process?

A. The mediator cannot impose an outcome; any settlement is the parties' own.

B. The mediator gives a binding evaluation which the parties must then follow.

C. The mediator's view of the merits is admissible at trial if talks fail.

D. The mediator decides the dispute on the documents, like an expert determination.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The mediator cannot impose an outcome; any settlement is the parties' own): mediation is voluntary in outcome, and the mediator facilitates rather than adjudicates, so the client cannot be compelled to accept terms. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it describes a determinative process such as arbitration or expert determination, where a third party does decide. The process is confidential and conducted without prejudice, so what is said cannot be deployed at trial on the substantive issues. Being ordered to attend a mediation is not the same as being obliged to settle at one.

116. A claim for damages has a value slightly above the fast track ceiling. There are four parties, the realistic trial estimate is five days, and each party wants two experts giving oral evidence. Your client asks which track the court is likely to choose. What do you advise?

A. It must go to the intermediate track, since its value falls in that bracket.

B. It must go to the fast track, because value alone determines the track.

C. It goes to the small claims track, because the parties agree that is cheapest.

D. It goes to the multi track, since trial length and parties exceed intermediate limits.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It goes to the multi track, since trial length and parties exceed intermediate limits): the intermediate track has conditions beyond value, namely a trial of no more than three days and no more than three parties, and a five day trial between four parties fails both. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it treats value as decisive when value is only the starting point. The fast track is plainly unsuitable on any view of these facts. Allocation cannot be agreed by the parties, and a case of this weight is nowhere near the small claims track.

117. Your supervising partner asks you to explain, for the advocacy station, the difference between an application to strike out a defence and an application for summary judgment against the defendant. Which statement most accurately captures the distinction between the two applications?

A. Strike out examines the evidence, while summary judgment examines the pleading.

B. Strike out requires the respondent to have no real prospect of success.

C. Strike out looks at the statement of case, summary judgment at the evidence.

D. Strike out is available only where a court order has been breached.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Strike out looks at the statement of case, summary judgment at the evidence): strike out is directed at the pleading as it stands, while summary judgment asks whether, on the material available, the respondent has any real prospect of success. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it states the correct distinction with the two applications the wrong way round. The real prospect test belongs to summary judgment, not strike out. Breach of a rule, practice direction or order is one strike out ground among several, so it is not the only route.

118. Your client has a strong looking breach of contract claim worth about 120,000 pounds, but the defendant company has filed abbreviated accounts showing minimal assets and there is no insurance. Your client asks whether she should issue proceedings. What should your advice cover?

A. Advise her to issue immediately, since liability appears strong on the papers.

B. Advise on the evidential gaps, the litigation risk, likely recovery and irrecoverable costs.

C. Advise that the merits alone determine whether the proceedings should be issued.

D. Advise her to await the defendant's response before forming any view at all.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Advise on the evidential gaps, the litigation risk, likely recovery and irrecoverable costs): a candid merits assessment weighs the strength of the case against what can realistically be recovered and the costs that will never be recovered even on a win. Option C is the closest wrong answer because the merits are central to the advice, but a judgment against a company with no assets is worth little, so enforceability has to be part of the picture. Issuing at once ignores that risk. Waiting passively for the defendant abdicates the advice the client is paying for.

119. Your client was injured by a driver on her third driving lesson, who panicked at a junction and accelerated into your client's car. The driver says she was doing her best as a beginner and should not be judged harshly. Advise on the standard of care.

A. The standard is that of the reasonably competent driver, not of a learner.

B. The standard is adjusted downwards to reflect the driver's limited experience.

C. The standard is that of the most careful and skilful driver on the road.

D. No duty is owed at all, because the driver had not yet passed a test.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The standard is that of the reasonably competent driver, not of a learner): breach is measured objectively against the reasonable person doing that activity, so a learner is held to the standard of the competent driver. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it reflects an understandable intuition about fairness to beginners, but the standard in negligence is not tailored to the individual defendant's experience. Nothing requires the driver to reach the standard of the very best. A learner driver plainly owes a duty to other road users.

120. On your summary judgment application the defendant serves a witness statement giving a detailed account of a site meeting which flatly contradicts your client's account. Both accounts are internally plausible and there is no contemporaneous note. How is the court likely to deal with the application?

A. The court will resolve the conflict of credibility on the written evidence.

B. The court will refuse where the case turns on disputed oral evidence.

C. The court will grant judgment because the respondent has served no expert report.

D. The court will adjourn the application to trial only if a counterclaim is pleaded.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The court will refuse where the case turns on disputed oral evidence): the court conducts no mini trial on a summary judgment application, so a genuine conflict of oral evidence that can only be resolved by cross examination defeats the application. Option A is the closest wrong answer because the court does read the written evidence, but reading it is not the same as choosing between two credible accounts on paper. The absence of expert evidence is beside the point on a factual dispute of this kind. Whether a counterclaim is pleaded has no bearing on the test.

121. The parties exchanged several letters headed without prejudice in which your opponent came close to conceding liability. Your client wants those letters put in the trial bundle so the judge can see the concession when deciding liability. What do you advise your client?

A. Without prejudice material cannot be put before the court on the substantive issues.

B. Without prejudice material becomes admissible once the offer within it is rejected.

C. Labelling a letter without prejudice makes any threat contained within it privileged.

D. Without prejudice material may be shown to the judge before judgment on liability.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Without prejudice material cannot be put before the court on the substantive issues): genuine settlement correspondence is privileged so that parties can negotiate freely, and it cannot be deployed on liability or quantum. Option D is the closest wrong answer because it is the mirror image of the rule; the whole purpose of the protection is to keep such material away from the judge deciding the substantive issues. Rejection of an offer does not lift the protection. The label does not protect an open threat, because substance governs rather than the heading used.

122. You are advising on a commercial claim which is worth more than the fast track ceiling. There are two parties, the trial estimate is two days, and each side wants one expert. Your client asks what the intermediate track involves. Which statement correctly describes it?

A. It takes claims above the fast track ceiling however long the trial lasts.

B. It applies only to personal injury claims of moderate value and complexity.

C. It runs on assessed rather than fixed costs, with costs budgeting applying.

D. Trial of no more than three days, with no more than three parties.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Trial of no more than three days, with no more than three parties): the intermediate track was introduced in October 2023 for claims above the fast track ceiling where the trial will last no more than three days, there are no more than three parties, and oral expert evidence is limited to two experts per party. Option A is the closest wrong answer because value alone does not put a claim on the intermediate track; the trial length and party limits are separate conditions. It is not restricted to personal injury. Costs on this track are fixed recoverable costs by complexity band, not assessed.

123. Your client won at trial on the main issue but lost on two of the four heads of loss it pursued, and the judge criticised the way the claim had been exaggerated in the schedule. Your client asks what costs order to expect. What is the correct starting point?

A. The successful party is entitled to its costs and the court has no discretion.

B. Costs are shared equally wherever both parties succeeded on some of the issues.

C. Costs follow the event as a general rule, subject to the court's broad discretion.

D. Costs are determined solely by reference to the amount of damages recovered.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Costs follow the event as a general rule, subject to the court's broad discretion): the unsuccessful party ordinarily pays the successful party's costs, but the court weighs conduct, exaggeration, partial success and any Part 36 offer and may make a different order. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it states the general rule correctly but strips out the discretion that decides cases like this one. Equal sharing is not a rule that follows from mixed success. The sum recovered is one relevant factor rather than the determinant.

124. Your client wants to instruct a structural engineer, a surveyor and an accountant in a claim about defective foundations. He has already commissioned two of the reports and asks whether he can simply serve them and call all three at the trial. What do you advise?

A. A party may call any expert it chooses, provided the report is disclosed.

B. Expert evidence becomes admissible once the expert has signed a statement of truth.

C. Permission is needed only where the parties cannot agree a single joint expert.

D. Permission is required, and evidence is restricted to what is reasonably required.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Permission is required, and evidence is restricted to what is reasonably required): expert evidence may not be adduced without the court's permission, and it is confined to what is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings. Option A is the closest wrong answer because disclosure of a report is a condition of relying on it, but disclosure is not a substitute for permission. A statement of truth is a formal requirement of the report and does not make the evidence admissible. Permission is needed whether or not a single joint expert is proposed, so money spent before permission is at risk.

125. You resist a summary judgment application for your client. The key emails sit on a server belonging to a third party contractor, and a court order for their production has been made with compliance due next month. The judge asks why she should not decide the issue now. What is your best point?

A. Refuse the application, because further documents are reasonably expected to become available.

B. Grant the application, because the respondent has not yet given standard disclosure.

C. Refuse the application, because summary judgment is available only against a defendant.

D. Grant the application, because the burden lies on the respondent to prove its case.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Refuse the application, because further documents are reasonably expected to become available): the court will not give summary judgment where material which may affect the outcome can reasonably be expected to become available before trial. Option B is the closest wrong answer because the absence of disclosure so far is exactly the reason to wait, not a reason to decide the issue against the respondent now. Summary judgment is available to either party, so the identity of the respondent is irrelevant. The burden on the application lies on the applicant to show no real prospect.

126. Your client was hurt when scaffolding erected by a contractor collapsed onto the pavement. You are settling particulars of claim in negligence and your trainee asks what has to be pleaded and proved. Which statement correctly identifies the elements of the tort?

A. Duty, breach and loss, with causation presumed once breach has been proved.

B. Duty, breach and causation, remoteness being irrelevant in a negligence claim.

C. Breach, causation and loss, duty being presumed as between all road users.

D. Duty of care, breach, causation, and loss which is not too remote.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Duty of care, breach, causation, and loss which is not too remote): a claimant must establish a duty of care, breach of that duty, causation in fact and in law, and damage of a kind that is not too remote. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it lists three of the elements correctly but discards remoteness, which limits recovery even where causation is proved. Causation is never presumed from breach. Duty is not presumed, although in an established category such as this it will rarely be contested.

127. At the third stage of the Denton analysis the judge asks what she should be giving particular weight to when deciding whether to grant your client relief from the sanction for late service of witness statements. What is the correct answer to that question?

A. Particular weight is given to the strength of the applicant's underlying case.

B. Particular weight is given to efficient conduct and to enforcing compliance.

C. Particular weight is given to whether the opponent suffered any actual prejudice.

D. Particular weight is given to the level of costs already incurred in the claim.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Particular weight is given to efficient conduct and to enforcing compliance): the third stage requires all the circumstances to be evaluated, with particular weight on the need for litigation to be conducted efficiently and at proportionate cost and on the need to enforce compliance with rules, practice directions and orders. Option C is the closest wrong answer because prejudice to the opponent is plainly a relevant circumstance, but it is not one of the two factors singled out for particular weight. The merits of the underlying claim carry little weight at this stage. Costs already incurred are not the focus.

128. Your client's claim concerns a complex commercial supply agreement, a shareholder dispute and allegations of misuse of confidential information. Value and complexity plainly justify the High Court. The client asks which part of the High Court would ordinarily deal with a claim of this character. What do you advise?

A. The King's Bench Division alone hears all commercial and contractual disputes.

B. The Family Division would hear a claim between the shareholders of a company.

C. The Business and Property Courts hear commercial and business claims of this kind.

D. The County Court retains exclusive jurisdiction over every contractual money claim.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The Business and Property Courts hear commercial and business claims of this kind): the High Court has three divisions, the King's Bench Division, the Chancery Division and the Family Division, and the Business and Property Courts are the umbrella under which the specialist business, commercial and property work of the Chancery Division and of the King's Bench Division is issued and managed, which makes them the natural home for a commercial supply, shareholder and confidential information claim. Option A is the closest wrong answer because the King's Bench Division does hear contractual claims, but it is not the only home for them and it is not the obvious court for a shareholder and confidence dispute. The Family Division has no role in a company dispute. The County Court has wide but not exclusive jurisdiction over contract claims.

129. Your client was knocked off his bicycle by a negligent driver and suffered a broken wrist. Two days later, on his own account, he removed the cast to play football and shattered the joint. The defendant denies liability for the later injury. Advise on the position.

A. The chain is broken whenever a third party contributes to the eventual damage.

B. The chain is unbroken, because factual causation has already been established.

C. The chain may be broken where an intervening act becomes the true cause.

D. The chain is broken only where the claimant himself acted with deliberate intent.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The chain may be broken where an intervening act becomes the true cause): causation in law asks whether an intervening act was so unreasonable that it becomes the effective cause of the further damage, which is arguable on these facts. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it correctly notes that the but for test is satisfied, but factual causation is only the first stage and does not answer the legal question. A third party's contribution does not automatically break the chain. The claimant's act need not be deliberate, only unreasonable.

130. Your client seeks an interim injunction to stop a former sales manager approaching twelve named customers. The account values are documented, the manager is employed by a well resourced competitor, and any diverted profit could be calculated precisely. How is the court likely to approach the application?

A. Grant it, because the balance of convenience favours preserving the restrictive covenant.

B. Refuse it, if damages would adequately compensate the applicant for its loss.

C. Grant it, because a serious issue to be tried has plainly been shown.

D. Refuse it, because interim injunctions are not available in employment disputes.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Refuse it, if damages would adequately compensate the applicant for its loss): after a serious issue is shown the court asks whether damages are an adequate remedy, and quantifiable losses against a solvent defendant usually mean they are. Option C is the closest wrong answer because a serious issue to be tried is necessary but not sufficient; it merely takes the applicant past the first limb. The balance of convenience is only reached if the damages questions do not decide the application. Injunctions are certainly available in employment disputes, so that option misstates the law.

131. A negligently secured drum of solvent fell and injured your client's foot. Because of a rare circulatory condition the injury developed into a far more serious and costly disability than anyone could have expected. The defendant says the loss is too remote. What is the position?

A. Recoverable if the kind of damage was foreseeable, though its extent was not.

B. Recoverable only if the precise extent of the damage was itself foreseeable.

C. Irrecoverable, because personal injury damage differs from the property damage risked.

D. Recoverable, because remoteness has no application to claims founded in tort.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Recoverable if the kind of damage was foreseeable, though its extent was not): remoteness in tort turns on the reasonable foreseeability of the kind of damage, and a defendant takes the claimant as found, so an unforeseeable extent does not defeat recovery. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it applies the foreseeability test at the wrong level of detail, which would deprive most seriously injured claimants of recovery. Physical injury was plainly the kind of harm risked here. Remoteness applies in tort just as it does in contract.

132. Your client is anxious about giving evidence and asks what will actually happen at trial after her exchanged witness statement has been served. She expects to be taken through her whole account again from the beginning by your advocate. What is the usual position?

A. The statement stands as the witness's evidence in chief at the trial itself.

B. The statement is read, but the witness then gives her oral evidence afresh.

C. The statement is used only to cross examine the opposing party's own witnesses.

D. The statement is admissible only where the maker is unavailable to attend court.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The statement stands as the witness's evidence in chief at the trial itself): the exchanged statement takes the place of oral examination in chief, so the witness confirms it and then moves to cross examination. Option B is the closest wrong answer because a witness may be allowed to amplify the statement or deal with matters arising since it was made, but that is a limited exception rather than a fresh account. Cross examination of opposing witnesses is a separate exercise. A statement is not confined to cases where the maker cannot attend.

133. You act for a defendant. The particulars of claim are incoherent, plead no recognisable cause of action, and the claimant has also ignored an order to serve a properly pleaded document. You intend to apply to strike out. On what grounds may a statement of case be struck out?

A. Strike out is unavailable once a defence has already been filed and served.

B. Strike out requires proof that the claim was brought dishonestly by the claimant.

C. Strike out lies only where the claim has no real prospect of success.

D. No reasonable grounds, abuse of process, or breach of a rule or order.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (No reasonable grounds, abuse of process, or breach of a rule or order): those are the three broad grounds, the second of which also covers a statement of case likely to obstruct the just disposal of the proceedings. Option C is the closest wrong answer because it borrows the summary judgment test, which looks at the prospects on the evidence rather than at the adequacy of the pleading. Dishonesty is not required, although it may support an abuse argument. Nothing about having filed a defence prevents the application being made.

134. Your client was injured when a warehouse racking system collapsed. The defendant's insurer has admitted liability in correspondence but disputes quantum, and trial is a year away. Your client cannot work and needs funds now. On what basis can the court order an interim payment?

A. Liability is admitted, or judgment obtained, or a substantial sum would be recovered.

B. The claimant is in financial hardship and needs money before the trial.

C. The defendant is insured and the insurer has reserved its position on quantum.

D. The claim has been allocated to the multi track and a budget approved.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Liability is admitted, or judgment obtained, or a substantial sum would be recovered): the court must be satisfied of one of those gateways, and an admission of liability by the defendant is the clearest of them. Option B is the closest wrong answer because hardship is a powerful reason to make the application and may influence the exercise of discretion, but it is not itself a gateway condition. The existence of insurance is relevant to whether the defendant can pay, not to the test. Allocation and budgeting have nothing to do with the entitlement.

135. Your client relied on a survey that failed to identify obvious rot in the roof timbers. The surveyor says he had only recently qualified and did his honest best on a difficult inspection. Your client asks by what standard the surveyor's conduct will be judged.

A. The standard is that of the most experienced surveyor practising in the region.

B. The standard is that of a reasonable person with no professional training.

C. The standard is whatever the individual surveyor honestly believed was adequate.

D. The standard is that of a reasonably competent member of that profession.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The standard is that of a reasonably competent member of that profession): a professional is judged against the standard of a reasonably competent member of the relevant profession, and inexperience does not lower it. Option B is the closest wrong answer because the reasonable person is the general standard in negligence, but where the activity requires professional skill the standard is that of the skilled practitioner. Nothing requires the surveyor to match the very best in the field. An honest personal belief about adequacy is not the measure.

136. Your client engaged a roofing contractor who completed the work in March 2019. The roof was defective from the outset but the client only discovered water ingress in February 2026 and now wants to sue for breach of contract. Advise on the limitation position for that contractual claim.

A. Time runs from the date the client discovered the defective workmanship.

B. Time runs from the date the client first incurred remedial repair costs.

C. Time runs from the breach itself, so the contract claim is stale.

D. Time runs from the date the contractor's final invoice was paid.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Time runs from the breach itself, so the contract claim is stale): a contract claim accrues on breach, which here was the defective installation in March 2019, so the ordinary six year period expired in March 2025. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it imports a discoverability rule that contract law does not have; discovery of the loss is irrelevant to accrual in contract. The date of payment and the date the client incurred repair costs are equally irrelevant, because neither is the breach. The client should be advised candidly that the contractual route is time barred.

137. You issued a claim form on 2 June 2026 without particulars of claim, intending to plead fully once counsel had settled the document. Your trainee asks when the particulars of claim must be served on the defendant. What is the correct position?

A. Particulars may be served up to four months after the claim form is served.

B. Particulars must follow within fourteen days, and within the claim form's validity.

C. Particulars can only be served at the same time as the claim form itself.

D. Particulars may be served at any time before the defence becomes due.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Particulars must follow within fourteen days, and within the claim form's validity): particulars are served with the claim form or within fourteen days after service of it, and in any event within the period for serving the claim form. Option C is the closest wrong answer because serving together is permitted but is not the only route, so it wrongly removes the fourteen day option. There is no free standing four month period for particulars, and the defence deadline runs from service of the particulars rather than fixing it. Both limbs matter, because the fourteen days cannot extend beyond the claim form's validity.

138. Your client repaired a neighbour's storm damaged fence without being asked. A fortnight later the neighbour, grateful, wrote promising to pay 500 pounds for the work already completed. He has now refused to pay. Your client asks whether the promise can be enforced.

A. The promise is unenforceable, because the consideration for it is past.

B. The promise is enforceable, because the work conferred a real practical benefit.

C. The promise is enforceable, because it was made in a commercial context.

D. The promise is unenforceable, because there was no intention to create relations.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The promise is unenforceable, because the consideration for it is past): consideration must be given in return for the promise, and work already completed before the promise was made cannot support it. Option B is the closest wrong answer because a benefit was undoubtedly conferred, but benefit alone is not consideration if it was not given in exchange for the promise. The context was not commercial, and even if it had been, that would go to intention rather than consideration. The absence of a request before the work was done is the decisive feature.

139. Your client spent 85,000 pounds fitting out premises for a new visitor attraction before the landlord repudiated the lease agreement. The venture had no trading history, so projected profits cannot be established with any confidence. Your client asks how its damages might be framed.

A. No damages are recoverable, since the lost profits cannot be proved at all.

B. Reliance loss may be claimed where expectation loss is too speculative to prove.

C. Damages are assessed at the contract price already paid over, and nothing further.

D. The court will estimate lost profits by reference to the defendant's own turnover.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Reliance loss may be claimed where expectation loss is too speculative to prove): where the expectation measure cannot be established the claimant may instead recover wasted expenditure incurred in reliance on the contract. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it correctly recognises the evidential problem with lost profits but wrongly concludes that no damages follow, when the reliance measure exists for exactly this situation. Recovery is not confined to sums paid to the defendant. The defendant's own turnover is not the yardstick for the claimant's loss.

140. The judge indicates that she is minded to grant your client the interim injunction sought, but asks what protection the respondent will have if the claim ultimately fails at trial. Your client asks you what she is being required to give. What is a cross undertaking in damages?

A. A cross undertaking is required only where the respondent is a trading company.

B. A cross undertaking is given by the respondent to protect the applicant's position.

C. A cross undertaking is unnecessary where the applicant has a strong case.

D. The applicant undertakes to compensate the respondent if the injunction was wrongly granted.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The applicant undertakes to compensate the respondent if the injunction was wrongly granted): the cross undertaking is the price of interim relief, and it is the applicant who gives it, promising to pay for loss the respondent suffers if the injunction turns out to have been wrongly obtained. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it identifies the right mechanism but reverses who gives it. Strength of the case affects the merits limb and the balance of convenience, not the requirement for an undertaking. It is required whether the respondent is a company or an individual.

141. Your client has been served with an English claim form but says the contract contains an exclusive jurisdiction clause in favour of the courts of Ireland, so the English court should not hear the claim at all. Advise on the correct procedural step to challenge jurisdiction.

A. File an acknowledgment, then apply to dispute jurisdiction within fourteen days.

B. File a defence pleading the jurisdiction point as a preliminary issue for trial.

C. Write to the court objecting and take no further step in the proceedings.

D. Apply to strike out the claim form for want of jurisdiction instead.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (File an acknowledgment, then apply to dispute jurisdiction within fourteen days): an acknowledgment of service is the route by which jurisdiction is challenged, with the application to be made within fourteen days of filing it. Option B is the closest wrong answer because filing a defence engages with the merits and risks being treated as a submission to the jurisdiction, which loses the point altogether. Writing to the court without filing anything leaves the client exposed to default judgment. Strike out is aimed at a defective statement of case, not at the court's power to hear the claim.

142. Your client's distributor has told him plainly that it will not perform the remaining two years of the agreement. Your client would rather keep the contract alive for now while he looks for a replacement. He asks what options are open to him. What do you advise?

A. The innocent party may affirm the contract, or accept the repudiation and terminate.

B. The contract terminates automatically as soon as the repudiatory breach occurs.

C. The innocent party must terminate before it can claim any damages at all.

D. The innocent party may terminate only with the agreement of the party in breach.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The innocent party may affirm the contract, or accept the repudiation and terminate): a repudiation gives the innocent party an election, and until it is exercised the contract continues, with damages available in either case. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it assumes the breach itself ends the contract, when the law leaves the choice to the innocent party. Damages do not depend on terminating first. The agreement of the party in breach is irrelevant to the innocent party's right to elect. Advise your client that delay may itself be treated as affirmation.

143. You sent a detailed letter of claim to a haulage company six months ago. It has never replied, and your client has now issued proceedings and succeeded at trial. You are asked to advise on the costs consequences of the defendant's failure to respond. What may the court do?

A. Nothing, since responding to a letter of claim is an optional courtesy.

B. Enter judgment in default before any proceedings have been issued at all.

C. Allow the claimant to recover the costs of the letter as damages.

D. Order indemnity costs and enhanced interest against the unresponsive defendant.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Order indemnity costs and enhanced interest against the unresponsive defendant): a defendant who ignores a compliant letter of claim risks an assessment on the indemnity basis and an award of enhanced interest, because the failure deprived the parties of the chance to settle or narrow issues. Option A is the closest wrong answer because the protocol response is expected, not optional, and silence is precisely the conduct the costs sanction targets. Default judgment cannot be entered before a claim exists. Pre action costs are recovered as costs in the proceedings, not pleaded as damages.

144. Your client has a substantial money claim arising out of a failed distribution agreement, and it is not a personal injury claim. The client, who wants the case taken seriously, asks whether the claim should simply be issued in the High Court. What is the correct approach to venue?

A. Any money claim may be started in the High Court at the claimant's choice.

B. Personal injury claims and commercial claims must both start in the High Court.

C. Start in the County Court unless value, complexity or importance justifies otherwise.

D. The Chancery Division must be used for every substantial contractual money claim.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Start in the County Court unless value, complexity or importance justifies otherwise): money claims must generally be commenced in the County Court, and the High Court is appropriate only where the value exceeds the relevant threshold and the value, complexity, importance or public interest justifies it. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it treats venue as a matter of pure client preference, when starting in the wrong court risks transfer and a costs sanction. There is no rule forcing commercial claims into the High Court. The Chancery Division is a division of the High Court and does not govern County Court commencement.

145. Your client has won and the judge is considering whether to assess costs on the standard or the indemnity basis. Your client asks what practical difference the choice makes to what she will actually recover from the defendant. Which statement correctly explains the difference?

A. On the standard basis any doubt is resolved in favour of the receiving party.

B. On the standard basis costs must be proportionate, with doubt favouring the payer.

C. On the indemnity basis proportionality applies but reasonableness does not apply.

D. On the indemnity basis the receiving party recovers every penny it was billed.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (On the standard basis costs must be proportionate, with doubt favouring the payer): standard basis assessment allows only costs that are proportionate and reasonably incurred and resolves any doubt in favour of the paying party. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it identifies the correct concept of doubt but applies the indemnity basis rule to the standard basis. On the indemnity basis proportionality drops away and doubt favours the receiving party, so option C reverses the position. Even on the indemnity basis costs must still be reasonable, so full recovery is not guaranteed.

146. Your client's substantial professional negligence claim involves three experts, a six day trial estimate and disputed causation. It has been allocated to the multi track. The client asks how the case will be managed and how costs will be controlled. Which statement is correct?

A. Directions are tailored to the case and costs are budgeted rather than fixed.

B. Standard directions are given and costs recovery is tightly restricted throughout.

C. Fixed recoverable costs apply by complexity band and by the stage reached.

D. The trial is limited to three days and to three parties in total.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Directions are tailored to the case and costs are budgeted rather than fixed): multi track cases receive bespoke directions, often at a case management conference, and in most of them the parties file and exchange costs budgets which the court approves. Option C is the closest wrong answer because fixed recoverable costs by band are the fast track and intermediate track regime, and they do not apply here. Standard directions and restricted costs describe the small claims track. Trial length and party limits are intermediate track conditions, not multi track ones.

147. You invited the defendant's solicitors to mediate a commercial dispute three months before trial. They did not reply at all and the matter went to trial, where your client won. You want to raise their conduct on costs. How is the failure to respond likely to be viewed?

A. Silence is neutral, because a party need not explain its settlement position.

B. Silence is acceptable where that party privately considered mediation unsuitable.

C. Silence in response to an invitation is generally unreasonable in itself.

D. Silence matters only if the claim later settles on broadly similar terms.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Silence in response to an invitation is generally unreasonable in itself): a party invited to engage in ADR is expected to answer, and simply ignoring the invitation is treated as unreasonable without more. Option B is the closest wrong answer because reasons for declining must be given at the time and in writing, so a privately held view that mediation would fail is worth nothing on the costs argument. The court weighs matters such as the merits, proportionality and the prospects of settlement, but it can only weigh reasons that were actually communicated. Always answer an ADR invitation in writing and keep the correspondence open.

148. You are settling a defence. Paragraph 7 of the particulars alleges that your client received the goods on 3 March and did not reject them. You have no instructions on that paragraph and are tempted to say nothing about it. What is the risk of silence?

A. A general denial of the whole particulars would be a sufficient answer.

B. Allegations not answered are treated as not admitted by operation of the rules.

C. A defence may lawfully reserve the defendant's position until witness statements.

D. An allegation the defence does not deal with may be taken as admitted.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (An allegation the defence does not deal with may be taken as admitted): a defence must answer each allegation by admitting it, denying it with reasons and the defendant's own version, or not admitting it for want of knowledge. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it reverses the default; silence does not operate as a non admission, which is why a non admission has to be pleaded expressly. A bare general denial does not comply, because it fails to tell the claimant the case it must meet. Take instructions on paragraph 7 before the defence is verified.

149. You are taking a statement from your client's warehouse supervisor. He recalls the delivery himself, but also repeats what a colleague told him about the driver's conduct. Your trainee asks how the statement should be prepared. Which statement correctly describes the requirements?

A. The statement should be drafted throughout in the solicitor's professional language.

B. The statement may include the witness's opinion on the defendant's general credibility.

C. The statement should summarise the documents and argue the client's case on liability.

D. The witness's own words, facts within knowledge, and sources of belief identified.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The witness's own words, facts within knowledge, and sources of belief identified): a statement must be in the witness's own words, confined to facts within that witness's knowledge, and must identify anything given from information or belief together with its source. Option A is the closest wrong answer because solicitors do draft statements in practice, but rewriting the account in lawyers' language breaches the own words requirement and damages the witness in cross examination. Opinion evidence is for experts. Argument belongs in submissions, not in a statement of fact.

150. Your client has an unsatisfied judgment against an individual who rents his flat, owns nothing of value, has no bank balance worth pursuing, but has been in steady salaried employment with the same employer for nine years. Which enforcement route is most likely to work?

A. A third party debt order against the employer's future monthly wage payments.

B. A charging order over the rented flat in which the judgment debtor lives.

C. A winding up petition, given that the judgment debt is undisputed and unpaid.

D. An attachment of earnings order directed at the judgment debtor's employer.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (An attachment of earnings order directed at the judgment debtor's employer): an attachment of earnings order requires the employer to deduct sums from the debtor's wages and pay them to the creditor, which is the route designed for an employed debtor without assets. Option A is the closest wrong answer because a third party debt order attaches a debt already accrued and due, so it cannot capture wages that have not yet been earned. A tenant has no interest in the flat capable of being charged. Winding up applies to companies, not to individuals.

151. On an interim injunction application the judge says that damages would be an inadequate remedy for both sides, and that the competing inconveniences appear to her to be finely balanced. She asks how she should resolve the application. What is the correct approach?

A. Where the balance of convenience is even, preserve the existing status quo.

B. Where the balance is even, the applicant's application must accordingly be refused.

C. Where the balance is even, the court decides the merits of the claim summarily.

D. Where the balance is even, the court orders a speedy trial and nothing more.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Where the balance of convenience is even, preserve the existing status quo): American Cyanamid treats preservation of the status quo as the tie breaker once the balance of convenience gives no clear answer. Option D is the closest wrong answer because ordering a speedy trial is a sensible case management step and often accompanies interim relief, but it does not answer the question of what to do about the injunction in the meantime. Refusal is not the automatic result of an even balance. The court does not decide the merits summarily on an interim application.

152. Your client has a modest claim for a defective laptop and has been allocated to the small claims track. She has been quoted a substantial fee for representation and asks what she could recover from the seller by way of costs if she wins. What do you advise?

A. Costs recovery is very restricted, broadly fees and limited witness expenses.

B. Costs follow the event and are assessed on the standard basis afterwards.

C. Fixed recoverable costs apply by complexity band and by the stage reached.

D. Costs budgeting applies, so the approved budget sets the recoverable figure.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Costs recovery is very restricted, broadly fees and limited witness expenses): the small claims track restricts recovery to matters such as court fees, fixed commencement costs and limited witness expenses, so solicitors' charges are generally irrecoverable. Option B is the closest wrong answer because costs do follow the event as a general rule in civil litigation, but the small claims regime is the deliberate exception to it. Fixed recoverable costs by band belong to the fast and intermediate tracks. Budgeting is a multi track feature. Advise the client on proportionality before she incurs the fee.

153. You act for a claimant and want to serve the claim form on the defendant's solicitors by email. The solicitors have confirmed in an open letter that they are instructed to accept service, but have said nothing about email in particular. Is email service effective?

A. Email service is valid, because the solicitors' email address appears on their letterhead.

B. Email service is valid once the recipient acknowledges receipt of the sent email.

C. Email service needs prior written confirmation that the recipient will accept it.

D. Email service is valid where the parties corresponded by email before action.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Email service needs prior written confirmation that the recipient will accept it): electronic service is only a permitted method where the recipient has confirmed in writing that it will accept service by that means, and confirmation of authority to accept service generally is not enough. Option A is the closest wrong answer because an email address on a letterhead is contact information, not an indication of willingness to be served electronically. Later acknowledgement of receipt does not cure a method that was impermissible when used. Ask the question expressly and get the answer in writing before serving.

154. Your client was injured when a van pulled out without looking. He was not wearing a seatbelt, and the medical evidence suggests his injuries would have been materially less severe if he had been. The defendant relies on that failure. Advise your client.

A. The claim fails entirely where the claimant contributed to his own injury.

B. Damages are reduced by a just and equitable proportion for the claimant's fault.

C. Damages are reduced by exactly half wherever both parties were partly at fault.

D. Contributory negligence is a defence to contract claims but not to negligence.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Damages are reduced by a just and equitable proportion for the claimant's fault): contributory negligence is a partial defence, reducing the award by the proportion the court considers just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it treats a partial defence as a complete one, which has not been the law since apportionment was introduced. There is no fixed fraction such as one half. The defence applies squarely to negligence claims, which is where it is most often deployed.

155. Your client wants to sue a supplier that trades as Harlow Kitchen Supplies but is registered at Companies House as Harlow HKS Limited. The invoices carry the trading style only. The client asks who should be named as defendant on the claim form. What do you advise?

A. Name the managing director personally, as he signed the supply agreement.

B. Name the company by its registered name and its company number.

C. Name the trading style used on the invoices and on the website.

D. Name the parent company, because it controls the trading subsidiary.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Name the company by its registered name and its company number): the correct legal person must be identified, and for a company that is the registered name, with the number included to put identity beyond doubt. Option C is the closest wrong answer because a trading style is not a legal person and cannot sue or be sued, however prominently it appears on the paperwork. A director who contracted as agent for the company is not personally liable, and the parent is a separate legal person that was not the contracting party. Getting the party wrong risks a defective claim form close to limitation.

156. Your client was injured in June 2023 when a delivery driver reversed into her. She did not appreciate until March 2026 that her continuing shoulder pain was attributable to that accident. She asks how long she has to bring her personal injury claim. Which statement is correct?

A. Three years from the injury or the later date of knowledge, extendable.

B. Six years from the date of the accident, with no discretion to extend.

C. Three years from the injury alone, with no discretion available to extend.

D. Six years from the date of knowledge of the significant shoulder injury.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Three years from the injury or the later date of knowledge, extendable): personal injury claims carry a three year period running from the injury or from the claimant's date of knowledge if later, and the court retains a discretion to extend. Option C is the closest wrong answer because it correctly identifies the three year period but wrongly denies both the knowledge alternative and the discretion.
