The six year period stated in the other options is the ordinary contract and tort period and does not apply to personal injury. Advise on the knowledge date and on the risk of relying on a discretion.

157. A trainee asks you to explain the difference between disclosure and inspection, having assumed that the two words describe the same step. Your client's disclosure list has just been served on the other side. Which statement correctly describes what disclosure itself is?

A. Disclosure is the physical delivery of copy documents to the other party.

B. Disclosure is the statement that a document exists or has existed.

C. Disclosure is the right to inspect the documents held by another party.

D. Disclosure is the process of certifying that the search was proportionate.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Disclosure is the statement that a document exists or has existed): a party discloses a document by stating its existence, which is why documents no longer held must still appear on the list. Option C is the closest wrong answer because inspection is the separate step that follows disclosure, and it is subject to any claim to privilege. Delivering copies is how inspection is usually given in practice, not what disclosure means. The disclosure statement certifying the search is part of the process but does not define disclosure itself.

158. Your client needs an injunction tonight, before the respondent can move assets, so the application will be made without notice. Your client asks whether he must mention a text message in which he appears to waive the very restriction he seeks to enforce. What is your advice?

A. The applicant need only present the evidence which supports its own case.

B. The applicant must disclose fully and frankly, including the points against it.

C. The applicant must serve the respondent at least three days before the hearing.

D. The applicant may withhold material which is commercially confidential to it.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The applicant must disclose fully and frankly, including the points against it): on a without notice application the respondent is absent, so the applicant owes a duty of full and frank disclosure and must put the damaging material before the judge. Option A is the closest wrong answer because that is the ordinary position on an inter partes application, where the other side can present its own case. Notice requirements are the very thing dispensed with here. Confidentiality can be protected by other means, but it is not a reason to keep material from the judge. Breach risks the order being discharged.

159. You have received your opponent's expert report. It gives a confident conclusion, says nothing about the questions the expert was asked, and does not acknowledge that other respectable views exist on the same issue. Your client asks what a compliant report must contain. What do you advise?

A. The report must state the expert's fees and the terms of the retainer.

B. The report must state the substance of instructions and the range of opinion.

C. The report must be limited to the conclusion favourable to the instructing party.

D. The report must exhibit every document the expert considered when preparing it.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The report must state the substance of instructions and the range of opinion): a report must set out the substance of the instructions given, summarise the range of opinion on the issues and give reasons for the expert's own view, and it must carry a statement of truth. Option D is the closest wrong answer because the materials relied on must be identified, but there is no requirement to exhibit every document considered. Fees and retainer terms are not part of the required content. A report confined to helpful conclusions would breach the duty to the court.

160. The defendant offered 80,000 pounds under Part 36 fifteen months before trial. Your client rejected it, fought on, and has now recovered a judgment of 62,000 pounds. She asks what the costs consequences of that outcome are likely to be. What do you advise?

A. The claimant recovers its costs throughout, since it succeeded at the trial.

B. The claimant normally pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period.

C. The claimant loses its damages for the period after the offer expired unaccepted.

D. The claimant pays the defendant's costs of the entire action on the indemnity basis.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The claimant normally pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period): a claimant who fails to obtain a judgment more advantageous than the defendant's offer normally pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, with interest on those costs. Option D is the closest wrong answer because the costs shift is real but it runs from the end of the relevant period, not from the beginning of the action, and it is on the standard basis unless the court orders otherwise. Winning at trial does not preserve costs after that date. Damages themselves are unaffected.

161. Your client has a judgment for 90,000 pounds against an individual who owns a house with substantial equity but has little income and few goods. Your client asks what a charging order would achieve and whether it would produce payment immediately. What do you advise?

A. A charging order transfers the debtor's interest in the land to the creditor.

B. A charging order permits immediate seizure and sale of the debtor's home.

C. A charging order is available only where the debt exceeds the existing mortgage.

D. A charging order secures the debt over the land, with sale sought separately.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (A charging order secures the debt over the land, with sale sought separately): the order gives the creditor security over the debtor's interest, and realisation requires a further application for an order for sale, which the court may or may not grant. Option B is the closest wrong answer because sale is indeed the eventual objective, but it is a separate discretionary step rather than something the charging order itself permits. No transfer of ownership occurs. There is no rule confining charging orders to debts larger than the mortgage.

162. Your client has a judgment against a small manufacturing partnership which owns valuable machinery at its workshop but has no realisable land. Your client asks about seizing and selling those assets, and which court's officers would carry it out. What do you advise?

A. Taking control of goods, by a County Court warrant or by a High Court writ.

B. Taking control of goods, which is available only after a charging order is made.

C. Taking control of goods, which permits entry to any third party's premises.

D. Taking control of goods, which requires a fresh claim against the partners to be issued.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Taking control of goods, by a County Court warrant or by a High Court writ): enforcement against goods proceeds by a warrant of control issued in the County Court or a writ of control enforced by High Court enforcement officers, depending on the court and the sum involved. Option B is the closest wrong answer because a creditor may pursue more than one method, but there is no requirement to obtain a charging order first. The power is directed at the debtor's own goods and does not license entry to unconnected premises. No fresh claim is needed to enforce an existing judgment.

163. You act against Kelmarsh Fabrications Limited, which has a registered office in Leicester and a busy factory in Corby. You wish to serve the claim form by post rather than personally. Your trainee asks whether posting to the registered office is a valid method. What is the position?

A. Service must be effected personally on a director of the defendant company.

B. First class post to the company's registered office is a permitted method.

C. Service on a company is valid only at its principal place of trading.

D. Service by document exchange is not a permitted method on a limited company.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (First class post to the company's registered office is a permitted method): the permitted methods include first class post or document exchange to a company's registered office, and personal service is an option rather than a requirement. Option C is the closest wrong answer because the principal place of business can be an appropriate address in some circumstances, but it is not the only valid one and does not displace the registered office. Document exchange is expressly permitted and is not excluded for companies. Whichever method is used, the deemed date of service must then be calculated.

164. Your client refused two reasonable invitations to mediate a construction dispute, insisting the claim was unanswerable, and then won at trial. The defendant now says the refusal should sound in costs. Advise your client on the most likely costs consequence of an unreasonable refusal to engage.

A. A successful party may be deprived of some or all of its costs.

B. A successful party will be ordered to pay indemnity costs of the whole action.

C. The refusal is irrelevant once that party has succeeded at trial on the merits.

D. The refusal reduces the damages awarded rather than affecting the costs order.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (A successful party may be deprived of some or all of its costs): the usual sanction for an unreasonable refusal to engage is that the winner loses part or all of the costs it would otherwise have recovered. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it overstates the sanction; being made to pay the loser's costs on the indemnity basis is possible in an extreme case but is not the normal consequence. Success on the merits does not insulate a party from a conduct based costs order, because costs are always discretionary. Damages are unaffected, since the refusal goes to conduct and not to quantum.

165. Your client is out of patience and instructs you to issue a breach of contract claim immediately, without sending a letter of claim under the Practice Direction on Pre Action Conduct and Protocols. She asks what the consequence of doing so would be. What is the likely outcome?

A. The claim will be struck out for want of a proper letter of claim.

B. The court cannot consider pre action conduct until the trial has concluded.

C. The court may deprive the claimant of costs or interest for non compliance.

D. Proceedings are automatically stayed until the protocol steps have been completed.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The court may deprive the claimant of costs or interest for non compliance): non compliance rarely bars a claimant from issuing, but it is conduct the court takes into account, and the usual sanction bites on costs and interest. Option D is the closest wrong answer because a stay is a discretionary case management option the court may impose, not an automatic consequence of issuing early. Strike out is directed at a defective statement of case, not at a failure to write a letter first. Advise the client that a short delay to comply is usually cheaper than the costs risk.

166. Your client contracted to buy machinery for 40,000 pounds which was never delivered. An equivalent machine now costs 52,000 pounds, and your client has already spent 3,000 pounds preparing its factory floor. Your client asks what principle governs the measure of its damages. What do you advise?

A. Damages restore the claimant to the position it occupied before contracting.

B. Damages are limited to the sums the claimant actually paid the defendant.

C. Damages place the claimant in the position had the contract been performed.

D. Damages are calculated by reference to the defendant's profit from the breach.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Damages place the claimant in the position had the contract been performed): the ordinary contractual measure is expectation loss, which here points to the additional cost of obtaining an equivalent machine. Option A is the closest wrong answer because that describes reliance loss, which is the fallback where expectation loss is too speculative to prove, and it is not the starting point. Recovery is not capped at sums paid over. Contract damages compensate the claimant's loss rather than stripping the defendant of its gain.

167. The parties to a boundary and nuisance dispute are entrenched, and the defendant says it will not mediate under any circumstances. Your client asks whether the court itself can require the defendant to take part in a non court dispute resolution process. What is the position?

A. The court may encourage a non court process but cannot order participation.

B. The court may order such a process only where both parties have consented.

C. The court may order engagement if proportionate and a fair trial is preserved.

D. The court may order such a process only after directions questionnaires are filed.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The court may order engagement if proportionate and a fair trial is preserved): following Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council and the October 2024 rule amendments, the court can order the parties into a non court dispute resolution process, provided the order is proportionate and does not impair the essence of the right to a fair trial. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it states the older position that the court could only encourage. Consent is not required, which is the whole point of the change. There is no rule confining such an order to the period after directions questionnaires.

168. Your firm filed a costs budget four days late and the sanction has bitten. You must apply for relief from sanctions and want to structure the submission around the correct framework. Which statement sets out the three stages the court will work through in Denton?

A. Seriousness of the breach, prejudice to the respondent, then the overriding objective.

B. Seriousness and significance, why the default occurred, then all the circumstances.

C. Merits of the underlying claim, promptness, then the applicant's ability to pay costs.

D. Whether the sanction was proportionate, whether it was breached, then the delay.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Seriousness and significance, why the default occurred, then all the circumstances): the court assesses the seriousness and significance of the breach, considers the reason for it, and then evaluates all the circumstances so as to deal justly with the application. Option A is the closest wrong answer because prejudice to the other side is a factor at the third stage rather than a stage in its own right, and the overriding objective informs the whole exercise. The merits of the underlying claim are not the framework. The proportionality of the sanction itself is not one of the three stages.

169. Particulars of claim were served on your client, the defendant, on 8 September 2026. You need more time to take instructions and to obtain documents from the client's former accountant. Your client asks what filing an acknowledgment of service will achieve. What is its effect?

A. Filing an acknowledgment gives a further fourteen days from the date of filing.

B. Filing an acknowledgment gives the defendant three months to file a defence.

C. Filing an acknowledgment extends the defence to twenty eight days from particulars.

D. Filing an acknowledgment has no effect at all on the defence deadline.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Filing an acknowledgment extends the defence to twenty eight days from particulars): the defence is otherwise due fourteen days after service of the particulars, and filing an acknowledgment in that period extends the deadline to twenty eight days from service of the particulars. Option A is the closest wrong answer because the extension is measured from service of the particulars, not from the date the acknowledgment happens to be filed, so filing late in the period buys less time than it suggests. Three months is not a period the rules recognise here. Further time beyond that requires agreement or an application.

170. A trainee has drafted particulars of claim running to thirty pages, setting out what each witness will say and arguing at length why the defendant's anticipated defence must fail. You are asked to explain what particulars of claim should actually contain. Which statement is correct?

A. Particulars should set out the witness evidence supporting each pleaded allegation.

B. Particulars set out a concise statement of the facts relied upon.

C. Particulars should argue the law and cite the authorities relied upon.

D. Particulars should exhibit the key documents disclosed before proceedings began.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Particulars set out a concise statement of the facts relied upon): the function of a statement of case is to define the issues so that each party knows the case it must meet, which calls for the material facts and not the evidence or the argument. Option A is the closest wrong answer because the evidence for those facts belongs in witness statements exchanged later, not in the pleading. Legal argument is for skeleton arguments and submissions. Documents are dealt with through disclosure and inspection rather than by exhibiting them to particulars.

171. You act for a claimant on an unpaid invoice. The defence asserts an oral variation of the payment terms, but the contract contains a clause requiring variations in writing and there is no such document. You are preparing an application for summary judgment. What is the test you must satisfy?

A. The applicant must show the respondent's case is bound to fail at trial.

B. The applicant must show a serious issue to be tried on the pleadings.

C. The applicant must show the statement of case discloses no reasonable grounds.

D. No real prospect of success and no other compelling reason for a trial.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (No real prospect of success and no other compelling reason for a trial): summary judgment requires the respondent to have no real prospect of succeeding on the claim, defence or issue, and the court must also be satisfied there is no other compelling reason for a trial. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it sets the bar too high; real means more than fanciful, and the applicant does not have to show the case is certain to fail. Serious issue to be tried is the interim injunction threshold. No reasonable grounds is the strike out ground.

172. You act for a claimant. The defence consists of a bare denial of every paragraph with no facts, no alternative version and no reasons given. The defendant has served no evidence at all. You must choose the right application for the advocacy station. What should you apply for?

A. Summary judgment, because the defence pleading is defective on its face.

B. Strike out, because the defendant's witness statement contradicts its pleaded case.

C. Strike out, because the pleading itself discloses no reasonable grounds for defending.

D. Neither, because a bare denial is a permissible form of defence to a claim.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Strike out, because the pleading itself discloses no reasonable grounds for defending): the complaint here is about the document, since a defence must say which allegations are denied, why, and what the defendant's own version is. Option A is the closest wrong answer because summary judgment is aimed at the evidence and its prospects, and it is the natural application once evidence exists, but the vice on these facts is the pleading. There is no witness statement to contradict anything. A bare denial does not comply with the requirements for a defence.

173. Exchange of witness statements was ordered for 12 October 2026. Your opponent served nothing that day and produced a statement from its finance director three weeks later, without any application. It now proposes to rely on that statement at trial. What is the position?

A. A statement served late may be relied on if the trial date still holds.

B. A statement served late becomes admissible once the other side has replied to it.

C. A statement served late cannot be relied on without relief from sanctions.

D. A statement served late may be read by the trial judge at her discretion.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (A statement served late cannot be relied on without relief from sanctions): failure to serve a witness statement in time carries a sanction, so the defaulting party must apply for relief and satisfy the Denton stages before the evidence can be used. Option A is the closest wrong answer because the trial date holding is a relevant circumstance at the third stage, but it does not by itself restore the right to rely on the statement. Responding to the statement does not cure the default. The trial judge's discretion is exercised through the relief application, not instead of it.

174. Your client holds an unpaid judgment against a company. Investigations show the company has no useful goods, but its bank statements reveal a healthy credit balance at a branch in Cardiff. Your client asks which enforcement route best fits those facts. What do you advise?

A. Apply for a charging order over the account, then seek an order for sale.

B. Apply for an attachment of earnings order directed at the company's bank.

C. Apply for a third party debt order attaching the credit balance held.

D. Apply for a warrant of control against the money standing in the account.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Apply for a third party debt order attaching the credit balance held): a third party debt order attaches a debt owed to the judgment debtor, and a bank holding a credit balance is a debtor of its customer, so this is the natural route to money in an account. Option A is the closest wrong answer because charging orders are a real enforcement method, but they attach to land or securities rather than to a current account balance. Attachment of earnings applies to an individual's wages, not to a company. Taking control of goods reaches chattels rather than money in a bank.

175. The defendant made a Part 36 offer of 80,000 pounds with a relevant period of 21 days. After taking your advice your client accepts it on day 15. She asks what will happen about the costs she has already incurred in the proceedings. What do you advise?

A. The claimant recovers its costs up to the date of acceptance of the offer.

B. The claimant pays the defendant's costs from the date the offer was made.

C. Each party bears its own costs of the claim up to the date of acceptance.

D. The claimant recovers indemnity costs for the whole of the proceedings brought.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The claimant recovers its costs up to the date of acceptance of the offer): a claimant who accepts a defendant's Part 36 offer within the relevant period is entitled to its costs of the proceedings down to the date of acceptance. Option C is the closest wrong answer because bearing your own costs is what a negotiated settlement often provides, but the Part 36 code fixes the position and it is more favourable than that. There is no costs shift against a claimant who accepts in time. Indemnity costs are not the consequence of acceptance in time.

176. Your multi track claim has an approved costs budget. Disclosure proved far heavier than expected and your firm has spent 40,000 pounds more on that phase than the budget allowed, without applying to vary it. The client asks what will happen on assessment. What do you advise?

A. The approved budget normally sets the figure allowed on any later assessment.

B. The budget is indicative only and does not bind the judge on assessment.

C. Budgets are filed in fast track claims but are not used in multi track claims.

D. An overspend beyond the approved budget is recoverable on the indemnity basis.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The approved budget normally sets the figure allowed on any later assessment): in most multi track cases the budget as agreed or approved fixes what the court will allow, so an unapproved overspend is usually irrecoverable from the paying party. Option B is the closest wrong answer because a budget is a forecast, but once approved it ceases to be merely indicative and constrains the assessment. Budgeting is a multi track feature; fast track claims run on fixed recoverable costs. Nothing about an overspend converts it into indemnity basis costs. Apply to vary the budget as soon as the extra work is foreseen.

177. Your client's supply agreement required deliveries to be accompanied by a signed docket. Two of forty deliveries arrived without one, causing a minor administrative inconvenience. The term is not classified in the contract. Your client wants to terminate and buy elsewhere. What do you advise?

A. Terminate, because any breach of a delivery obligation permits termination.

B. Terminate, because the term is properly classified as a condition of the contract.

C. Claim damages only, because breach of an innominate term never permits termination.

D. Claim damages only, since the breach did not deprive it of substantially the whole benefit.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Claim damages only, since the breach did not deprive it of substantially the whole benefit): where a term is innominate the right to terminate depends on the consequences of the breach, and a minor administrative inconvenience falls well short of that test. Option C is the closest wrong answer because it reaches the right result on these facts but for a wrong reason, since a sufficiently serious breach of an innominate term does permit termination. Nothing marks this documentation requirement out as a condition. Wrongful termination would itself be a repudiatory breach.

178. You posted the claim form by first class post to the defendant's last known residence on a Monday. The defendant says he was away and only opened the envelope ten days later. Your trainee asks when service took effect for the purposes of the rules. What is the position?

A. Service takes effect on the day the defendant actually reads the documents.

B. Service takes effect on the very day the documents were posted first class.

C. Service is deemed on a date set by the method used, not actual receipt.

D. Service takes effect when the defendant files his acknowledgment of service.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Service is deemed on a date set by the method used, not actual receipt): the rules fix a deemed date of service by reference to the method chosen, so the date must be calculated rather than assumed from what the defendant says happened. Option A is the closest wrong answer because actual receipt is exactly what the deemed service rules displace; if receipt governed, response periods could never be calculated with certainty. Posting is the act that starts the calculation but is not itself the deemed date. Filing an acknowledgment is a response to service, not the moment service occurs.

179. Your client, a defendant, denies the claim and says the claimant in fact owes it 60,000 pounds for separate unpaid work carried out last year. It wants that raised in the same proceedings. Your trainee asks how a counterclaim is treated procedurally. What is the position?

A. A counterclaim is merely part of the defence and attracts no separate fee.

B. A counterclaim must be issued as entirely fresh proceedings against the claimant.

C. A counterclaim cannot exceed the value of the claim which it answers.

D. A counterclaim is a claim in its own right, with its own fee.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (A counterclaim is a claim in its own right, with its own fee): a counterclaim is a claim, not a defensive plea, so it carries its own court fee and its own statement of truth and survives even if the original claim is discontinued. Option A is the closest wrong answer because the counterclaim is served with the defence and looks like part of the same document, but that presentation does not change its character or remove the fee. Fresh proceedings are unnecessary where the counterclaim can be brought in the existing action. Its value is not capped by the value of the claim.

180. A surveyor negligently reported on a house in April 2019. Cracking caused by undetected subsidence first appeared in September 2023. The buyer, who also had a contract with the surveyor, asks whether a claim in negligence gives more time than the contractual claim. What is the position?

A. The tortious period also runs from the date the report was delivered.

B. The tortious claim is barred because the parallel contract claim is barred.

C. The client must elect the contract measure where both routes are available.

D. The tortious period runs from the damage, which may fall later.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The tortious period runs from the damage, which may fall later): negligence is not actionable without damage, so time runs from when the damage occurred rather than from the negligent act. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it applies the contractual accrual rule to tort; in contract time runs from the breach, which is why the two periods can differ on the same facts. The tortious claim is a separate cause of action and is not extinguished merely because the contractual one is. Identifying which route gives the longer period is part of analysing the claim before issue.

181. A claim for defective building work has been allocated to the fast track. Your client wants to call two engineers and a quantity surveyor, and estimates that the trial will occupy three days. She asks whether the case fits the track. Which statement describes the fast track?

A. Trial lasting up to three days, with two experts per party permitted.

B. Trial lasting no more than one day, with one expert per party in two fields.

C. Trial of any length, with directions tailored at a case management conference.

D. Trial lasting no more than one day, with expert evidence entirely excluded.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Trial lasting no more than one day, with one expert per party in two fields): the fast track is designed for a one day trial with expert evidence limited to one expert per party in no more than two fields. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it describes the intermediate track, which allows a longer trial and more oral expert evidence. Expert evidence is limited on the fast track, not excluded. Tailored directions and an unlimited trial estimate point to the multi track, so this case may well need reallocation.

182. Your client offered to supply 500 steel frames at 90 pounds each for delivery in March. The buyer replied accepting but stating that delivery must be in two instalments in January and February. Your client did nothing further and the buyer now sues. Was a contract formed?

A. A contract was formed, because the parties clearly intended to be bound.

B. No contract, because the response was a counter offer rejecting the original.

C. A contract formed on the original terms, the delivery point being a mere inquiry.

D. No contract, because consideration was absent from this exchange of letters.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (No contract, because the response was a counter offer rejecting the original): a purported acceptance which introduces new terms is a counter offer, and it destroys the original offer so that it can no longer be accepted. Option C is the closest wrong answer because a genuine request for information leaves the offer alive, but a stipulation that delivery must happen on different dates changes a term rather than asking about one. Intention to be bound cannot supply an agreement that was never concluded. Consideration was plainly present in the promised price and goods.

183. Your client paid a garage to service her van. The mechanic failed to tighten a wheel and the van was damaged when the wheel came loose. The written agreement says nothing about the quality of the work. Your client asks on what basis the garage is liable.

A. The garage is liable only if the contract expressly promised competent work.

B. A term of reasonable care and skill is implied into the services contract.

C. The garage warrants that the van will be free from any defect afterwards.

D. No term is implied, because the customer inspected the van on collection.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (A term of reasonable care and skill is implied into the services contract): a contract for the supply of a service carries a statutory implied term that the supplier will carry out the service with reasonable care and skill, so no express promise is needed. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it assumes that liability can only arise from an express term, which ignores terms implied by statute. The implied term is one of care and skill rather than a guarantee of a perfect result. Inspection on collection does not displace a term implied by statute.

184. You act for a claimant suing for an unpaid invoice of 42,000 pounds. The defendant has filed neither an acknowledgment of service nor a defence, and the time for responding has expired. Your client asks how judgment can be obtained without a hearing. What is the position?

A. A hearing is required before judgment can be entered for a specified sum.

B. Default judgment may only be entered with the court's prior written permission.

C. The claimant must first apply for summary judgment on the whole claim.

D. Judgment for a specified sum may be entered administratively on request.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Judgment for a specified sum may be entered administratively on request): where the claim is for a specified sum and nothing has been filed in time, default judgment is entered as an administrative act on the claimant's request. Option A is the closest wrong answer because it describes what happens with an unspecified sum, where liability is entered in default and damages are then assessed at a hearing. Permission is not required for a straightforward request in default. Summary judgment is a different application, aimed at a defence that exists but has no real prospect of success.

185. Your client is compiling its disclosure list and asks which of its documents attract legal advice privilege. It has letters from you advising on the merits, board minutes debating commercial options, and a report from an external consultant. Which description correctly identifies legal advice privilege?

A. Confidential lawyer and client communications for the purpose of legal advice.

B. Any document sent to a solicitor, whether or not advice was actually sought.

C. Communications with third parties once litigation is reasonably in contemplation.

D. Internal board minutes discussing the commercial merits of the pending dispute.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Confidential lawyer and client communications for the purpose of legal advice): legal advice privilege covers confidential communications between lawyer and client for the purpose of giving or receiving legal advice, and it applies whether or not litigation is contemplated. Option C is the closest wrong answer because it describes litigation privilege, which is a separate head with its own conditions including the dominant purpose test. Sending a document to a solicitor does not clothe it in privilege if it was not created for that purpose. Board minutes on commercial strategy are not privileged merely because a dispute exists.

186. After a warehouse accident your client's safety manager produced an internal report. Its stated aims were to improve procedures and to inform the insurers, who by then anticipated a claim. The claimant now seeks inspection of the report. Advise on whether it is privileged.

A. Privileged, because litigation was in reasonable contemplation when it was made.

B. Privileged only if that litigation was the dominant purpose of its creation.

C. Privileged, because the report was later sent to the company's own solicitors.

D. Not privileged, since a report prepared by an employee falls outside privilege.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Privileged only if that litigation was the dominant purpose of its creation): litigation privilege requires that litigation was in reasonable contemplation and that the dominant purpose of the communication was that litigation, so a genuinely dual purpose report is vulnerable. Option A is the closest wrong answer because contemplation of litigation is necessary but not sufficient; without the dominant purpose limb the report is disclosable. Sending it on to solicitors afterwards cannot retrospectively change the purpose for which it was created. There is no rule excluding documents produced by employees.

187. Your client holds around 800,000 archived emails on legacy backup tapes. Restoring and reviewing them would cost about 200,000 pounds, and the claim is worth 150,000 pounds. The other side insists every tape be restored. Advise your client on the extent of the search obligation.

A. Every backup tape must be restored, whatever the cost of doing so.

B. The client may decline to search any electronic documents at all here.

C. The search obligation is discharged by disclosing only the paper documents held.

D. The search must be reasonable and proportionate, so restoration may be excessive.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The search must be reasonable and proportionate, so restoration may be excessive): standard disclosure follows a reasonable and proportionate search, and a cost exceeding the value of the claim is a powerful argument that restoring the tapes goes beyond what is required. Option A is the closest wrong answer because backup tapes are certainly within the scope of documents in principle, but scope and proportionality are different questions. Electronic documents cannot be ignored simply because they are electronic. Limiting the search to paper would not be a reasonable search at all.

188. A carrier delivered your client's replacement press three weeks late. Your client had a uniquely lucrative subcontract, worth ten times its normal monthly turnover, which was lost as a result. The carrier was never told about that subcontract. Is the lost profit on it recoverable?

A. Recoverable, because the loss was caused directly by the defendant's own breach.

B. Recoverable, because the defendant knew the claimant was a commercial business.

C. Irrecoverable, because damages in contract are limited to the price paid.

D. Irrecoverable, since the special loss was outside the parties' reasonable contemplation.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Irrecoverable, since the special loss was outside the parties' reasonable contemplation): losses recoverable in contract must arise naturally from the breach or have been within the reasonable contemplation of the parties when they contracted, and an exceptional subcontract never communicated satisfies neither limb. Option B is the closest wrong answer because general knowledge that the customer trades commercially supports ordinary lost profits, but it does not put an extraordinary contract within contemplation. Factual causation is not the test for remoteness. Damages are not capped at the price paid.

189. A surveyor negligently valued your client's investment property in March 2018 under a written retainer. The loss only became apparent in 2024, and your client consults you in 2027. The contractual claim is now time barred. Your client asks whether that is the end of the matter. What do you advise about the routes available?

A. Advise that the claim is barred, since both routes accrue at the same moment.

B. Advise that the tortious route may survive, since accrual and measure can differ.

C. Advise that the client must sue in contract, since a contract exists between them.

D. Advise that the tortious route gives a larger award in every professional case.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Advise that the tortious route may survive, since accrual and measure can differ): where a client has both a contractual and a tortious route the limitation period and the measure of damages may differ, and a tort claim accrues on damage rather than on breach. Option A is the closest wrong answer because the two claims often arise out of the same conduct, but they do not accrue at the same moment, which is the whole reason for considering both. A concurrent contract does not force the client into the contractual route. Neither route is inherently more generous.

190. Your client has been ordered to give standard disclosure in a multi track contract claim. He has found an internal email conceding that the goods were late and asks whether he is obliged to list a document that plainly damages his own case. What do you advise?

A. Only the documents on which the disclosing party positively relies at trial.

B. Every document which has ever existed relating to the subject matter.

C. Documents relied on, those adverse to any case, and those supporting another's.

D. Only documents the other side specifically requests in a written disclosure notice.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Documents relied on, those adverse to any case, and those supporting another's): standard disclosure requires a party to disclose the documents it relies on, documents adversely affecting its own or another party's case, documents supporting another party's case, and anything a practice direction requires. Option A is the closest wrong answer because reliance documents are only the first category, and confining disclosure to them would remove the whole point of the exercise. There is no requirement to disclose every document ever created, because the search need only be reasonable and proportionate. The obligation does not depend on a request.

191. Your client has read the draft report of the expert it instructed and is unhappy with a paragraph accepting that the design was defective. It asks you to tell the expert to delete that paragraph before the report is finalised and served. What do you advise your client?

A. The expert may amend the report, because the client is paying the fee.

B. The expert must amend the report if the instructing solicitors so direct.

C. The expert's duty to the court overrides any duty to the instructing party.

D. The expert may omit the passage provided the range of opinion is stated.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The expert's duty to the court overrides any duty to the instructing party): an expert owes an overriding duty to the court, so a genuinely held opinion cannot be removed because it is unwelcome to the party paying for it. Option D is the closest wrong answer because stating the range of opinion is a real requirement of a report, but it is not a device for suppressing the expert's own conclusion. Neither the client nor the solicitor can direct the substance of the opinion. Pressing the point would also risk misleading the court.

192. Your client agreed to buy a nineteenth century painting, the only known work of its artist, for 60,000 pounds. The seller now refuses to complete and says your client should take damages instead. Your client wants the painting itself. What do you advise on the remedy?

A. Specific performance may be granted where damages are an inadequate remedy.

B. Specific performance is available as of right in every contract of sale.

C. Specific performance is unavailable where the subject matter is a chattel.

D. Specific performance is granted where the claimant would otherwise become insolvent.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Specific performance may be granted where damages are an inadequate remedy): the remedy is discretionary and is reserved for cases where damages will not do justice, which a genuinely unique item satisfies. Option B is the closest wrong answer because specific performance is indeed available in a contract of sale, but never as of right, since it is an equitable remedy subject to the court's discretion. Chattels are not excluded, and uniqueness is exactly the feature that attracts the remedy. The claimant's own solvency is not the test.

193. A prospective client asks you to sue a small company in which you personally hold a significant shareholding and to which you have been giving informal commercial guidance. You believe you could still act fairly and would tell the client about the holding. What is the correct position?

A. Act for both sides, provided each of them gives informed consent in writing.

B. Act, because the conflict here concerns commercial rather than legal interests.

C. Do not act, because there is an own interest conflict with the prospective client.

D. Act for the client and refer the company to counsel for independent advice.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Do not act, because there is an own interest conflict with the prospective client): where your own interests conflict with those of a client you cannot act at all, and no exception rescues the position. Option A is the closest wrong answer because informed consent can permit acting for two clients in a narrow set of circumstances, but it has no application to an own interest conflict. The nature of the interest as commercial does not remove the conflict. Referring the other side elsewhere does nothing about your own shareholding.

194. Your client, the claimant, offered to settle for 100,000 pounds under Part 36 a year before trial. The defendant refused, and the judge has awarded your client 128,000 pounds. Your client asks what she can now seek beyond her ordinary costs. What is the usual outcome?

A. The defendant pays standard basis costs and interest at the ordinary judgment rate.

B. The claimant receives an additional amount but no change to the basis of costs.

C. The claimant receives enhanced interest but recovers no costs after the judgment.

D. Enhanced interest, indemnity costs, interest on those costs and an additional amount.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Enhanced interest, indemnity costs, interest on those costs and an additional amount): where a defendant fails to beat a claimant's own Part 36 offer the court will normally order interest on the sum awarded at up to ten per cent above base rate, indemnity costs from the end of the relevant period with interest on them at the same enhanced rate, and an additional amount calculated as a percentage of the award, subject to a cap. Option B is the closest wrong answer because the additional amount is only one of the four consequences. Ordinary standard basis costs understate the effect. Costs are not lost.

195. Your client seeks an interim injunction restraining a former supplier from disclosing confidential formulations to a rival manufacturer. You are preparing the submission for the advocacy station tomorrow morning. In what order should the American Cyanamid questions be addressed before the judge?

A. The applicant must show it will probably succeed at the eventual trial.

B. A serious issue to be tried, then adequacy of damages, then the balance of convenience.

C. The balance of convenience is considered before any question of the merits arises.

D. The applicant must show irreparable harm and a strong prima facie case.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (A serious issue to be tried, then adequacy of damages, then the balance of convenience): the court asks whether there is a serious issue, then whether damages would adequately compensate either side, and only if those do not decide it does it weigh the balance of convenience. Option D is the closest wrong answer because irreparable harm is a way of describing the damages limb, but requiring a strong prima facie case restores the merits threshold that American Cyanamid deliberately lowered. Probable success is not the test. Convenience is the fallback question, not the opening one.

196. Your client missed a filing deadline by three weeks. The breach was remedied promptly once noticed, but the application for relief from sanctions was not issued until four months afterwards, because the file was passed between fee earners. The opponent points to the delay. How does it bear on relief?

A. Delay in applying is irrelevant once the underlying breach has itself been remedied.

B. The delay in applying weighs against relief at the third stage of Denton.

C. The application fails automatically, because a three week breach is a serious one.

D. Relief follows, because the opponent has suffered no identifiable prejudice from it.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The delay in applying weighs against relief at the third stage of Denton): promptness in applying is one of the circumstances the court evaluates, and an unexplained four month delay tells against a party asking the court for indulgence. Option D is the closest wrong answer because absence of prejudice is a genuine point in the applicant's favour, but it does not guarantee relief when the third stage also weighs efficiency and compliance. Remedying the breach helps but does not make the delay irrelevant. No breach causes automatic refusal; each stage must be worked through.

197. Default judgment was entered against your new client for an unspecified sum. She says she was abroad, never received the particulars of claim, and also has a genuine defence on the merits. She asks whether the judgment can be removed. What is the correct position?

A. Setting aside is mandatory whenever the defendant applies within fourteen days.

B. Setting aside is discretionary even where the judgment was wrongly entered.

C. Setting aside is mandatory if wrongly entered, otherwise discretionary on the merits.

D. Setting aside requires the defendant first to pay the judgment sum into court.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Setting aside is mandatory if wrongly entered, otherwise discretionary on the merits): judgment entered when the conditions for it were not met must be set aside, and otherwise the court may set it aside where there is a real prospect of successfully defending or some other good reason. Option B is the closest wrong answer because it wrongly makes the mandatory ground discretionary, when a judgment that should never have been entered cannot stand. There is no fourteen day rule of right, although promptness weighs heavily in the discretion. Payment into court is not a precondition, though it can be a condition the court imposes.

198. A wealthy client instructs you to send weekly letters threatening ruinous costs to an individual blogger who has published a well sourced piece about the client's business practices. The client says the aim is to make her stop writing rather than to obtain a remedy. What should you do?

A. Send the letters, marking each of them confidential and without prejudice as instructed.

B. Send the letters, but advise the client that the costs risk is significant.

C. Decline the instruction, record the advice given, and explain you cannot act so.

D. Send the letters after obtaining counsel's opinion on the merits of the claim.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Decline the instruction, record the advice given, and explain you cannot act so): this has the hallmarks of a strategic lawsuit against public participation, namely a weak claim against an individual publishing on a matter of public interest, aggressive correspondence and the deliberate running up of costs to exhaust the other side. Option B is the closest wrong answer because advising on costs risk is sound as far as it goes, but it does not address the fact that you must not pursue the claim in that way at all. Labelling letters confidential to deter publication is itself a warning sign. Counsel's opinion cannot cure an abusive purpose.

199. You are settling a letter making a realistic settlement proposal outside the Part 36 regime. Your client wants to be able to show the letter to the judge on the costs argument if the offer is refused and the claim then does no better. How should the letter be marked?

A. Mark it without prejudice, so that it can be deployed on the costs argument.

B. Mark it open, so that its contents remain confidential until after the trial.

C. Mark it without prejudice and disclose it in the trial bundle in any event.

D. Mark it without prejudice save as to costs, to rely on it on costs.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Mark it without prejudice save as to costs, to rely on it on costs): that formula keeps the offer out of the substantive trial but preserves the right to show it to the judge once liability and quantum have been decided, which is the basis on which Part 36 operates. Option A is the closest wrong answer because an unqualified without prejudice label protects the negotiation but also prevents the letter being used on costs. An open letter is not confidential at all. Putting privileged material in the trial bundle would defeat the protection entirely.

200. The gateway for an interim payment is satisfied on your client's personal injury claim. The full claim is pleaded at 300,000 pounds, though contributory negligence is in issue and the medical evidence is incomplete. The judge asks what sum should be ordered. What is the governing principle?

A. The court awards the full sum claimed, leaving quantum entirely to the trial.

B. The court awards half of the sum claimed as a matter of settled practice.

C. The court awards only the claimant's proven out of pocket expenditure to date.

D. The court awards a reasonable proportion of the likely final judgment sum.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The court awards a reasonable proportion of the likely final judgment sum): the order must be for a reasonable proportion of the damages the claimant is likely to recover, which requires a conservative view of the irreducible minimum after contributory negligence. Option C is the closest wrong answer because past expenditure will often form part of the calculation but does not cap it, since future losses can also be taken into account. There is no fixed fraction such as half. Awarding the full pleaded sum would pre empt the trial and is not permitted.

Property Practice

201. A solicitor is giving client care and costs information at the outset of a purchase in Manchester. The client asks what she will have to pay through the firm in addition to the firm's own professional charges. Which answer best identifies the likely disbursements?

A. The estate agent's commission and the seller's own legal costs

B. Search fees, Land Registry fees and the tax on the purchase

C. The lender's arrangement fee and the buyer's building insurance premium

D. The removal costs and the cost of the seller's energy performance certificate

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Search fees, Land Registry fees and the tax on the purchase): the likely disbursements a buyer pays through the firm are the search fees, the Land Registry fees and the tax on the land transaction, and the client care information should identify them in plain English. Option A is wrong because the agent's commission and the seller's costs are the seller's liabilities and do not pass through the buyer's file at all. Arrangement fees, insurance and removal costs are paid by the client directly to other providers.

202. A buyer completes her purchase and then discovers a long running boundary dispute with the neighbour. The seller's property information form stated that there were no disputes, which the seller knew to be untrue. The buyer's solicitor raised no separate enquiry about disputes. What is the buyer's position?

A. The buyer has no remedy, because caveat emptor governs a sale of land

B. The buyer may rescind the transfer as of right and recover the price

C. The seller may be liable in misrepresentation for the untrue answer given

D. The local authority is liable because its search did not disclose the dispute

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The seller may be liable in misrepresentation for the untrue answer given): caveat emptor means the buyer must investigate and ask, but a seller who answers a pre contract enquiry dishonestly may be liable in misrepresentation for that answer. Option A is wrong because caveat emptor bites where the buyer never asked, and here the enquiry was in fact answered untruthfully. Rescission after completion is not available as of right, and a neighbour dispute is not a matter the local search is designed to reveal.

203. A client tells his solicitor, in a private meeting about his purchase, how he intends to use the completion money to disguise the proceeds of an unlawful business. The client later insists that the conversation was privileged and cannot be reported. What is the correct analysis of that claim?

A. Privilege does not protect a communication made to further a criminal purpose

B. Privilege applies, so the solicitor may not report the substance of the conversation

C. Privilege applies unless the client agrees in writing that it may be waived

D. Privilege applies only to litigation, so no property communication is protected

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Privilege does not protect a communication made to further a criminal purpose): privilege does not extend to a communication made in furtherance of a criminal purpose, so the client cannot use it to shield an account of how he intends to launder money. Option B is wrong because it would allow privilege to be used as a cloak for crime, which the law does not permit. Option D is wrong because legal advice privilege applies well beyond litigation, including to conveyancing advice.

204. A solicitor acts for the buyer of a tenanted office building in Birmingham. The residential protocol does not apply and the seller is a property investment company. She must select the appropriate set of standard pre contract enquiries and identify what else the buyer needs to investigate. Which answer is correct?

A. The property information form, and the seller's own buildings insurance policy

B. The leasehold information form, and the buyer's own proposed fit out works

C. The Commercial Property Standard Enquiries, and the occupational leases granted

D. The fittings and contents form, and the seller's business rates account history

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The Commercial Property Standard Enquiries, and the occupational leases granted): a commercial acquisition uses the Commercial Property Standard Enquiries rather than the residential protocol forms, and title investigation is heavier because the building is tenanted, so the buyer must investigate the occupational leases as well as the freehold title. Option A is wrong because the property information form belongs to the residential protocol and is not designed for an investment purchase. The remaining options address peripheral matters rather than the leases that produce the income being bought.

205. Completion of a sale was contractually due on 5 May 2027. The buyer has not completed and gives no explanation, and the seller has a related purchase depending on the money. The Standard Conditions of Sale are incorporated. What is the correct first step for the seller's solicitor, and what is its effect?

A. Issue proceedings for specific performance, which makes time of the essence

B. Rescind the contract immediately and forfeit the deposit already being held

C. Serve a notice to complete, which makes time of the essence

D. Serve a section 25 notice, which sets a fresh completion date

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Serve a notice to complete, which makes time of the essence): time is not initially of the essence in a contract for the sale of land, so the innocent party serves a notice to complete, which makes time of the essence and gives a fixed further period with compensation at the contract rate. Option B is wrong because rescission is premature while the buyer still has the further period the notice must give. A section 25 notice belongs to business tenancy renewal and has no place here.

206. A client produces a bank statement showing a balance sufficient to complete his purchase. The statement shows the account holding only a small balance until a single credit of 600,000 pounds arrived three weeks ago from a name the client does not recognise when asked. What is the correct analysis?

A. The statement satisfies both source of funds and source of wealth requirements

B. The statement is inadequate because it is not certified by the client's bank

C. The statement satisfies source of wealth but not source of funds requirements

D. The statement shows funds without wealth, and further explanation is required

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The statement shows funds without wealth, and further explanation is required): a client producing a statement showing a large recent unexplained credit has shown where the money currently sits but has not explained how he came by it, so funds have been shown without wealth and that is not enough. Option A is wrong because the statement leaves the origin of the credit entirely unexplained, which is the very thing source of wealth is meant to answer. Certification of the document is not the difficulty here.

207. A commercial tenant has fallen badly behind with the rent. The lease contains a forfeiture clause. The tenant's premises are charged to a bank, which has lent against the leasehold interest. The bank's solicitor is reviewing the lease before completion of the loan. What will the bank require the lease to contain?

A. A covenant that the landlord will not forfeit the lease for rent arrears

B. A covenant by the tenant to pay the rent by direct debit monthly

C. An obligation on the landlord to accept rent tendered by any third party

D. An obligation on the landlord to notify the lender before forfeiture proceedings

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (An obligation on the landlord to notify the lender before forfeiture proceedings): forfeiture is the landlord's remedy for breach and destroys the lease, and therefore the lender's security, so a lender will insist on notice before forfeiture proceedings are begun so that it can intervene. Option A is wrong because a landlord will not give up the forfeiture remedy altogether, and no lender expects that. Payment mechanics and the acceptance of third party rent do not protect the lender's security if the lease is forfeited.

208. A solicitor acting for buyer and lender notices that the price in the contract is 20,000 pounds lower than the price stated in the mortgage offer, and that the seller has agreed to pay the buyer's deposit directly. She is preparing her report to the lender. Which statement is correct?

A. Neither matter needs reporting, because the lender's valuation covers the price

B. Both matters are reportable, being a price difference and a direct payment

C. Only the price difference is reportable, since deposits are a private arrangement

D. Only the direct payment is reportable, since the price is a commercial matter

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Both matters are reportable, being a price difference and a direct payment): reportable matters under lenders' handbook instructions include a price differing from that in the mortgage offer and a direct payment between seller and buyer, and both facts here go directly to the value of the lender's security. Option A is wrong because the lender's valuation is carried out on assumed facts and does not relieve the solicitor of the duty to report what she actually knows. Splitting the two and reporting only one leaves the lender misled.

209. A firm is opening a file for the purchase of a house in Coventry by a new client. The supervising partner asks the trainee to set out what customer due diligence actually requires on this retainer, beyond taking a copy of the client's passport. Which answer is correct?

A. Obtaining two forms of photographic identity and a recent utility bill

B. Obtaining a bank reference and a written statement of the client's income

C. Identifying and verifying the client, and understanding the transaction's purpose

D. Searching the register of overseas entities and the insolvency register online

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Identifying and verifying the client, and understanding the transaction's purpose): customer due diligence means identifying the client, verifying that identity from a reliable independent source, identifying any beneficial owner where the client is a company or trust, and understanding the purpose and intended nature of the transaction. Option A is wrong because collecting documents is only the verification element and misses the requirement to understand what the transaction is for. Bank references and register searches may be useful evidence but they do not define what due diligence requires.

210. At a first interview a client asks her solicitor exactly how much tax she will pay on her purchase of a house in Bristol for 480,000 pounds. The solicitor does not have the rate table in front of her and cannot yet say whether any relief applies. What is the best response?

A. Give a figure from memory now and correct it later if wrong

B. Tell the client that the tax is payable by the seller, not her

C. Say that tax is a matter for her accountant rather than the firm

D. Explain the amount depends on price and reliefs, and confirm in writing

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Explain the amount depends on price and reliefs, and confirm in writing): a solicitor should never quote a rate from memory, and the proper course is to explain that the figure turns on the price and on whether a relief applies, then calculate it and confirm it in writing. Option A is wrong because a guessed figure the client relies on is a real risk of negligence and a poor standard of client care. The tax on a purchase is payable by the buyer, and calculating and reporting it is part of the conveyancing retainer, not the accountant's job.

211. A firm has made a report about its buyer client's funding. The seller's solicitor and the estate agent are both telephoning daily about the completion date, and the agent asks outright whether there is a problem with the buyer's money. What is the correct approach to those enquiries?

A. Explain the position fully to the seller's solicitor, who owes a duty of confidence

B. Tell the agent that the buyer's funds are under review by the firm's compliance team

C. Say nothing prejudicial to either, and give no explanation of the delay

D. Refer both of them directly to the National Crime Agency for an explanation

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Say nothing prejudicial to either, and give no explanation of the delay): the prohibition on disclosure is not limited to the client, so nothing prejudicial may be said to the other side's solicitor or to the estate agent, and no hint may be given about the reason for the delay. Option A is wrong because a professional duty of confidence owed by the recipient does not make the disclosure lawful. Referring third parties to the agency would itself reveal that a report exists.

212. The proprietorship register of a title being bought states that the title is qualified. The register excepts from the effect of registration any interest arising under a deed of settlement dated 1968. The buyer asks her solicitor what a qualified title means. What is the correct explanation?

A. The title is guaranteed but the boundaries have not yet been determined

B. The title is guaranteed only while the current proprietor remains in occupation

C. Registration takes effect subject to the specified defect identified on the register

D. Registration is provisional until the settlement trustees confirm they have no claim

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Registration takes effect subject to the specified defect identified on the register): qualified title is registered subject to an identified defect, here the interests arising under the 1968 settlement, so the state guarantee does not extend to that specific matter. Option A is wrong because boundaries are shown as general boundaries on every title plan and have nothing to do with the class of title. Qualified title is not dependent on occupation and does not become absolute merely because trustees give a confirmation.

213. Two friends buy a house together in equal shares of the purchase price and declare that they hold the equitable interest as beneficial joint tenants. One of them later makes a will leaving everything to her brother, and then dies. The brother claims a half share of the house. Is he entitled to it?

A. No, because survivorship applies and the survivor takes the whole equitable interest

B. Yes, because the will disposes of her share, which passes into her estate

C. Yes, because equal contributions to the price produce a tenancy in common

D. No, because a half share can only pass by a written deed of gift

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No, because survivorship applies and the survivor takes the whole equitable interest): beneficial joint tenants own the whole together and survivorship applies, so on death the survivor takes automatically whatever the deceased's will may say. Option B is wrong because a joint tenant has no distinct share to leave by will, which is exactly why the distinction must be explained to co buyers at the interview. Equal contributions are consistent with a joint tenancy and do not by themselves create a tenancy in common where an express declaration has been made.

214. Two sisters held a house as tenants in common in equity. One has now died and the surviving sister has contracted to sell the whole property to a buyer. The proprietorship register carries a form A restriction. What must happen so that the buyer takes free of the deceased sister's equitable share?

A. The survivor must obtain a grant of probate before completing the sale

B. The restriction must be removed by lodging the death certificate alone

C. A second trustee must be appointed to join in the transfer deed

D. The deceased's beneficiaries must each sign a release of their interests

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (A second trustee must be appointed to join in the transfer deed): a form A restriction signals a tenancy in common in equity, so a sole surviving trustee cannot give a good receipt for capital money and a second trustee must be appointed so that the equitable interests are overreached. Option B is wrong because lodging a death certificate is the route where the survivor was a beneficial joint tenant, which is precisely what the form A restriction shows is not the case. Probate deals with the deceased's estate and does not by itself cure the receipt problem on the sale.

215. A solicitor in a firm's residential department has formed a genuine suspicion that the money funding her client's purchase is the proceeds of crime. She is unsure how strong her suspicion needs to be. What is the correct step, and to whom is it taken in the first instance?

A. A report to the National Crime Agency, made directly by the fee earner

B. An internal report to the firm's money laundering reporting officer

C. A report to the Solicitors Regulation Authority, made by her supervising partner

D. A note on the file, to be reviewed if any further concern later arises

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (An internal report to the firm's money laundering reporting officer): where a fee earner suspects, or has reasonable grounds to suspect, that property is criminal property, the step is an internal report to the money laundering reporting officer, also called the nominated officer. Option A is wrong because the decision whether to report externally to the National Crime Agency is one for the reporting officer, not the individual fee earner. Recording the concern on the file without reporting it leaves the suspicion unreported, which is itself an offence.

216. A firm is instructed on the purchase of a commercial unit in Sheffield by a company incorporated last month. The two directors are the only people the firm has met. The company is wholly owned by a second company registered abroad. What does due diligence require the firm to do about ownership?

A. Verify the identity of the two directors, who control the buying company

B. Identify the beneficial owner behind the corporate structure and verify that identity

C. Obtain a certificate of good standing for the overseas holding company only

D. Rely on the company's own confirmation that it has no beneficial owner

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Identify the beneficial owner behind the corporate structure and verify that identity): where the client is a company or a trust, due diligence includes identifying any beneficial owner and verifying that identity, which means looking behind the immediate corporate client. Option A is wrong because directors control the company's management but are not necessarily the beneficial owners, and stopping at the directors is exactly how a structure conceals the person behind it. A client's own assertion that no beneficial owner exists is not verification from a reliable independent source.

217. A buyer completes the purchase of an unregistered freehold house in Leicester on 4 March 2027, and the transaction triggers compulsory first registration. The buyer's solicitor is diarising her post completion deadlines. Within what period must the application for first registration be made, and what follows if it is missed?

A. One month, after which the seller may rescind the completed transfer

B. Twenty one days, after which the buyer must apply to the court

C. Two months, after which the legal estate reverts and is held on trust

D. Six months, after which a fresh transfer deed must be executed

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Two months, after which the legal estate reverts and is held on trust): where a transaction triggers compulsory first registration the application must be made within two months of completion, and failure means the legal estate reverts to the seller, who then holds it on trust for the buyer. Option B is wrong because twenty one days is the deadline for registering a company charge at Companies House, which is a different obligation with a different consequence. A missed registration deadline does not entitle the seller to rescind or require a new transfer deed.

218. A solicitor acts on the purchase of unregistered land in rural Norfolk. The seller has supplied an epitome of title with copies of the supporting documents. The solicitor must check that the chain of ownership begins properly. What is required of the document offered as the root of title?

A. It must be a conveyance executed by the current seller personally

B. It must be registered at HM Land Registry before completion takes place

C. It must be at least thirty years old and deal with the whole

D. It must be a good root of title at least fifteen years old

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It must be a good root of title at least fifteen years old): on unregistered land title is deduced from an epitome beginning with a good root at least fifteen years old, and the chain is then checked down to the seller. Option C is wrong because thirty years is the older, superseded period and is a common trap. A root document need not have been executed by the current seller, and unregistered land is by definition not yet registered before the purchase completes.

219. A buyer wants to build a large rear extension immediately after completion. The charges register contains a covenant not to erect any building on the land without the written consent of the original vendor or its successors in title. The buyer asks whether he can simply proceed. What is the best advice?

A. The covenant is unenforceable because the original vendor no longer owns land

B. The covenant binds only the original buyer and not a later owner

C. Consent or restrictive covenant indemnity insurance should be obtained before exchange

D. Planning permission for the extension will override the private covenant

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Consent or restrictive covenant indemnity insurance should be obtained before exchange): every entry in the charges register must be read and advised on, and a covenant against building without consent is fundamental to a buyer who intends to extend, so consent or indemnity insurance should be dealt with before the buyer is committed. Option D is wrong because planning permission is a public law permission and does not release a private covenant. Whether the benefit is still enforceable is a question of fact that a buyer should not simply assume in his own favour.

220. Contracts are exchanged on the sale of a house in Reading and the deposit is paid to the seller's solicitor. The Standard Conditions of Sale are incorporated without relevant amendment. The seller asks his solicitor to release the deposit to him now, so that he can fund the deposit on his own onward purchase. What is the position?

A. The deposit may be released, because the contract is now binding on both

B. The deposit may be released to the seller if the buyer's lender consents

C. The deposit is held as stakeholder and cannot be released before completion

D. The deposit belongs to the seller absolutely once the contracts have been exchanged

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The deposit is held as stakeholder and cannot be released before completion): under the standard conditions the deposit is held by the seller's solicitor as stakeholder, so it cannot be paid over to the seller for his own free use before completion. The standard conditions do allow the seller to use the deposit as the deposit on a related purchase of a property in England and Wales for his own residence, but only where it continues to be held as stakeholder in that transaction, so it is still not released to him. Option A is wrong because the contract becoming binding is precisely the point at which the stakeholder obligation starts, not the point at which it ends. The buyer's lender has no power to authorise a release, and the deposit does not become the seller's absolutely until completion.

221. A landlord owns a small industrial unit let on a protected business tenancy which is nearing the end of its contractual term. He wishes to bring the tenancy to an end and has taken advice on the statutory route. He asks how much notice a section 25 notice must give. What is the correct advice?

A. Between six and twelve months' notice must be given by the section 25 notice

B. Exactly three months' notice must be given, running from the date of service

C. Between one and three months' notice, depending on the length of the term

D. No minimum period applies, provided the contractual term has already expired

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Between six and twelve months' notice must be given by the section 25 notice): a landlord ends or renews a protected business tenancy by serving a section 25 notice giving between six and twelve months' notice, and stating whether renewal is opposed and on which statutory ground. Option D is wrong because a protected tenancy does not simply stop at the end of the contractual term; it continues until it is ended in a statutory way. Shorter fixed periods of one to three months form no part of the section 25 regime.

222. A prospective client wants a firm to act on an urgent cash purchase. He refuses to attend the office, refuses to provide any identity documents, and offers to pay double the firm's usual fee if the firm proceeds on the strength of his instructions alone. What must the firm do?

A. Act, provided the fee earner records the client's refusal fully on the file
