D. The covenants fail to dovetail, so part of the building is unrepaired

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The covenants fail to dovetail, so part of the building is unrepaired): a buyer's solicitor must check that the tenant's and the landlord's repairing covenants dovetail, so that no part of the building is left unrepaired by anyone, and a gap of this kind is a defect that must be reported and if possible cured. Option A is wrong because liability follows the wording of the lease and cannot simply be assumed from location. A service charge recovers the cost of works the landlord is actually obliged to do.

290. A personal representative is selling a house which formed part of the deceased's estate. She never lived at the property and knows almost nothing about its history. The draft contract sent to the buyer offers limited title guarantee. The buyer asks why full title guarantee is not offered. What is the correct explanation?

A. Limited guarantee is usual where the seller has limited knowledge of the property

B. Limited guarantee is required whenever land is registered with absolute freehold title

C. Limited guarantee applies automatically to every sale made by a corporate seller

D. Limited guarantee is given whenever the buyer is obtaining a mortgage advance

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Limited guarantee is usual where the seller has limited knowledge of the property): a seller sells with either full or limited title guarantee, and limited guarantee is the usual choice where the seller has limited knowledge of the property, the classic example being a personal representative or a trustee. Option B is wrong because the class of title on the register is a separate matter and absolute title does not dictate the guarantee offered. The guarantee turns on the seller's knowledge, not on corporate status or on the buyer's funding.

291. A solicitor acts for a buyer and for her lender on a standard residential mortgage. The buyer tells the solicitor in confidence that her uncle is providing a quarter of the price and expects a share of the house, and asks that the lender not be told. What must the solicitor do?

A. Complete the purchase, and report the uncle's interest to the lender afterwards

B. Keep the information confidential, because it was given in confidence by the client

C. Register the uncle as a joint proprietor, which removes the need to report

D. Explain that the matter must be reported, and cease to act if consent is refused

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Explain that the matter must be reported, and cease to act if consent is refused): an occupier or contributor who is not a borrower is a reportable matter under the lender's instructions, and the duty of disclosure owed to each client pulls in opposite directions, so the solicitor must explain that the point has to be reported and cease acting for one or both if the client refuses consent. Option B is wrong because confidentiality owed to the buyer cannot be used to keep material information from the other client. Reporting after completion comes far too late.

292. A notice to complete served by a seller on a defaulting buyer has now expired without completion taking place. The seller wants to know what remedies are open to him and whether he must wait for the court. The Standard Conditions of Sale are incorporated without relevant amendment. Which answer best states his remedies?

A. He must sue for the price and may not resell the property to anyone

B. He may rescind, forfeit the deposit, resell the property and claim damages

C. He may only claim compensation at the contract rate until completion occurs

D. He must apply to the court for an order permitting him to rescind

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (He may rescind, forfeit the deposit, resell the property and claim damages): once a notice to complete has expired and the buyer remains in default, the seller may rescind, forfeit the deposit, resell the property and claim damages for any shortfall and expense. Option C is wrong because compensation at the contract rate runs during the notice period and does not remain the seller's only remedy once the notice has expired. No court order is needed before the contractual right to rescind can be exercised.

293. A firm has reported a suspicion and cannot proceed with a client's purchase. The client is entitled to be kept informed and is asking direct questions about the delay. The fee earner must say something. What may the fee earner properly say to the client?

A. That the delay is caused by an outstanding search result from the local authority

B. That the firm has reported the matter and is awaiting a response from the agency

C. That the client should instruct another firm, which will be able to complete promptly

D. That the firm is not able to proceed at present, said neutrally and without detail

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (That the firm is not able to proceed at present, said neutrally and without detail): a firm may tell the client neutrally that it cannot proceed at present, and holding that line against the duty to keep the client informed is exactly the judgment required. Option A is wrong because inventing a false reason misleads the client and can itself hint at what is really happening if it later unravels. Confirming the report, or steering the client to another firm so the transaction proceeds elsewhere, both risk prejudicing the investigation.

294. A buyer's solicitor is reading the official copies of a registered title. She wants to identify a right of way over neighbouring land which benefits the property being bought, and to confirm that the estate being sold is freehold rather than leasehold. Which part of the register records both of those matters?

A. The charges register, which lists the burdens affecting the registered land

B. The property register, which describes the land and the rights benefiting it

C. The proprietorship register, which names the proprietor and gives the class

D. The title plan, which shows the general boundaries of the registered land

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The property register, which describes the land and the rights benefiting it): the property register describes the land, states whether the estate is freehold or leasehold, refers to the title plan and records rights that benefit the land, such as a right of way. Option A is wrong because the charges register records burdens on the land, including an easement granted over it rather than one enjoyed by it. The proprietorship register deals with ownership, class of title and restrictions, and the title plan shows extent rather than the estate held.

295. At a first interview a client says she must complete her purchase in Swansea by 30 April 2027 because her own buyer is pushing her hard. She has said nothing about how the purchase is being funded and has volunteered no bank details. Which line of questioning matters most?

A. Whether the seller has already booked a removal firm for that date

B. Where each part of the money comes from and who is contributing

C. Whether the client prefers a written or a telephone progress report

D. Whether the client would like the firm to recommend a local surveyor

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Where each part of the money comes from and who is contributing): at instructions the solicitor must establish the funding, where every part of the money comes from, whether anyone else is contributing and whether anyone else will occupy, because that goes to both the money laundering position and any hidden equitable interest. Option C is wrong because reporting preferences are ordinary client care detail that does not affect the legal analysis. The seller's removal arrangements and a surveyor recommendation are peripheral to the risks the facts raise.

296. Completion of a registered freehold purchase with a mortgage advance is fixed for the Friday. On the Wednesday the buyer's solicitor prepares the final pre completion steps, and needs to protect the lender's position as well as the buyer's. Which searches should she make at this stage?

A. An official search of the whole title with priority, and a bankruptcy search

B. A local authority search and a drainage and water enquiry of the seller

C. An environmental search and a chancel repair liability screening search

D. A company search against the seller and an index map search

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (An official search of the whole title with priority, and a bankruptcy search): immediately before completion the buyer's solicitor makes an official search of the whole title, which confers a priority period for the registration application, and a bankruptcy search against the buyer for the lender. Option B is wrong because the local search and the drainage and water enquiries belong to the pre contract stage, when the buyer is still deciding whether to commit. An environmental search is also a pre contract matter and neither of the remaining options protects the priority of the registration.

297. A buyer tells his solicitor that he can only raise five per cent of the price as a deposit on exchange, because the remainder of his money is tied up until his own sale completes. The Standard Conditions of Sale are incorporated in the draft contract without amendment. What must the solicitor do before exchange?

A. Nothing, because the standard conditions permit any deposit the buyer can raise

B. Obtain the lender's consent, because the deposit forms part of the mortgage advance

C. Advise the buyer that a reduced deposit is prohibited by the standard conditions

D. Agree a special condition with the seller reducing the customary ten per cent

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Agree a special condition with the seller reducing the customary ten per cent): the deposit is customarily ten per cent under the standard conditions, so a smaller deposit must be agreed with the seller and recorded as a special condition amending the standard form. Option C is wrong because a reduced deposit is not prohibited; it is simply a departure from the standard position which the seller must accept and which reduces the seller's security. The deposit is the buyer's own money and is not part of the mortgage advance.

298. A firm verified a client's identity thoroughly when it opened his file eight months ago. Halfway through the transaction the client asks that the property be bought instead in the name of a company he says he has just set up abroad. The fee earner assumes due diligence is complete. Is he right?

A. Yes, because the client's identity was properly verified when the file opened

B. Yes, because a change of buying entity is a commercial decision for the client

C. No, because a company purchase requires the firm to re verify the individual client

D. No, because due diligence is ongoing and this change alters the transaction's nature

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (No, because due diligence is ongoing and this change alters the transaction's nature): due diligence is ongoing rather than a box ticked once at the start, and a sudden change of buying entity to an overseas company changes the purpose and intended nature of the transaction and calls for fresh scrutiny. Option A is wrong because it treats verification at the outset as the whole obligation, which is exactly the mistake the ongoing requirement is designed to prevent. The point is not merely re verifying the individual but reassessing the transaction itself.

299. A fee earner in a conveyancing department realises after completion that the funding of a purchase she handled carried obvious warning signs that she noticed at the time but never reported to anyone in the firm. She asks what her exposure is. What is the correct advice?

A. Failing to report a suspicion arising in the regulated sector is itself an offence

B. No liability arises, because the transaction has already completed successfully

C. Her only exposure is to a negligence claim brought by her disappointed client

D. The firm alone is liable, because reporting obligations attach to the firm's officers

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Failing to report a suspicion arising in the regulated sector is itself an offence): failing to report a suspicion which arises in the course of business in the regulated sector is an offence in its own right, quite apart from any involvement in the underlying laundering. Option B is wrong because completion of the transaction does not extinguish an obligation that arose when the suspicion formed. The duty attaches to the individual who forms the suspicion as well as to the firm and its reporting officer.

300. A buyer is purchasing a house in Leeds which has a recently built conservatory and which fronts onto a lane that may never have been adopted. His solicitor needs to know whether the conservatory had building regulation approval and whether the lane is maintained at public expense. Which search answers both questions?

A. The drainage and water enquiries addressed to the statutory water undertaker

B. The local authority search, which reveals matters recorded by the council

C. The environmental search, which assesses contaminated land and flood risk

D. An official search of the whole register with priority at the registry

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The local authority search, which reveals matters recorded by the council): the local search reveals matters recorded by the local authority, including planning permissions and refusals, building regulation approvals, enforcement notices, tree preservation orders and whether the road is adopted. Option A is wrong because the drainage and water enquiries answer a different question, namely connection to mains water and the public sewer. An environmental search deals with contamination and flooding, and an official search with priority is a pre completion step at the Land Registry.

Wills and the Administration of Estates (Wills and Intestacy, Probate Administration and Practice)

301. A home made will dated 2026 is produced after death. It bears the testator's signature and two witness signatures, but it contains no attestation clause at all. The probate registry raises a query about how the will was executed. Which statement best describes the effect of the missing clause?

A. No presumption of due execution arises, so evidence of execution will be required.

B. The will is void, because an attestation clause is required by statute.

C. The will is valid and no further evidence of execution can be sought.

D. The witnesses must re-sign the will in the presence of the executors.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No presumption of due execution arises, so evidence of execution will be required): an attestation clause reciting compliance with section 9 raises a presumption of due execution, which is why one is always included. Without it the registry will want affidavit evidence from a witness. Option B is wrong because section 9 requires no attestation clause, only signature and attestation.

302. A client of ample means wishes to give her daughter a regular monthly sum out of her salary, which she can comfortably afford without reducing her own standard of living. She asks whether those gifts will be caught if she dies within seven years. What applies here?

A. The gifts are potentially exempt, so only the seven year rule applies.

B. The gifts are exempt only up to the annual exemption in each year.

C. Normal expenditure out of income is exempt, so the gifts fall outside.

D. The gifts are chargeable, because a regular pattern makes them a settlement.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Normal expenditure out of income is exempt, so the gifts fall outside): regular gifts made out of income which leave the donor able to maintain her usual standard of living are exempt, so the seven year rule never engages. Option B applies the annual exemption, which is a separate and much smaller allowance.

303. The same trustees show that they took proper advice, acted openly throughout, and made a decision which turned out badly rather than a careless one. They ask whether the court has any power to excuse them from liability. On what basis might relief be given?

A. Relief is given where the beneficiaries have suffered no financial loss.

B. Relief where they acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused.

C. Relief where the breach was approved by a majority of the beneficiaries.

D. Relief where the trust deed contains an express exemption from liability.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Relief where they acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused): section 61 of the Trustee Act 1925 lets the court relieve a trustee who acted honestly and reasonably and who ought fairly to be excused for the breach. Option D describes a clause in the deed, which is a separate matter from the court's statutory discretion.

304. The same trustees say that neither of them knows anything about investment, so they simply chose a company that one of them had heard of. They took no outside guidance of any kind. Beyond the investment criteria, which further duty did they fail to observe?

A. The duty to appoint a professional trustee where the trustees lack expertise.

B. The duty to obtain and consider proper advice before investing the fund.

C. The duty to distribute the fund where they cannot manage it themselves.

D. The duty to insure the trust property against a fall in its value.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The duty to obtain and consider proper advice before investing the fund): trustees must obtain and consider proper advice on the exercise of the power of investment, and then keep the investments under review. Option A is not a duty; trustees who lack expertise must take advice rather than replace themselves.

305. A son wishes to claim reasonable financial provision from his late mother's estate. The grant of probate issued on 1 March 2027. He first consults you in December 2027, having spent the intervening months trying to negotiate with the executors. What is the position on time?

A. He is out of time, and needs the court's permission to proceed.

B. He is in time, as the period runs six months from the death.

C. He is in time, because the period runs twelve months from the grant.

D. He is out of time, and the court has no power to extend it.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (He is out of time, and needs the court's permission to proceed): a claim must be brought within six months of the grant, and that period may be extended only with the court's permission. Option D is wrong because the deadline is not absolute, though permission cannot be assumed and the date belongs in the attendance note.

306. A will made in 2024 gives a fund to such of the testator's grandchildren as are living at the date of that will. In 2026 the testator executed a codicil changing the executors only. Two further grandchildren were born between those dates. What is the effect of the codicil on the class?

A. None at all, because the codicil dealt only with the appointment of executors.

B. The class gift now fails for uncertainty once the codicil has been executed.

C. The will is republished at the codicil's date, so the later grandchildren qualify.

D. The class closes at the testator's death, so all grandchildren then living qualify.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The will is republished at the codicil's date, so the later grandchildren qualify): a codicil republishes the will as at the codicil's own date, so a reference to the date of the will is read as the date of the codicil. Option A overlooks republication, which operates whatever the codicil actually changes.

307. A testator had full capacity when he signed his will in 2026. By 2027 he had lost capacity, and he died later that year without making any further will or codicil. A relative argues that the will cannot stand because of the later loss of capacity. What is the position?

A. The will fails, because capacity must continue until the date of death.

B. The will fails unless a codicil was executed while capacity still remained.

C. The will stands, because capacity is judged at the time of execution.

D. The will stands only if a doctor certified capacity on the signing day.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The will stands, because capacity is judged at the time of execution): testamentary capacity is assessed when the will is executed, so a later decline has no effect on a will already validly made. Option A would make every will vulnerable to the testator's later health, which is not the law.

308. A will gives 5,000 pounds to the testator's nephew, to be paid out of the testator's account at the Marchford Building Society. That account held 2,000 pounds at the death, and the residuary estate is ample. Which classification best describes that gift?

A. A demonstrative legacy, money directed to be paid from a named fund.

B. A specific legacy of the account, which adeems to the extent unfunded.

C. A general legacy, since a sum of money is not a particular asset.

D. A residuary gift, because the shortfall must come out of the residue.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (A demonstrative legacy, money directed to be paid from a named fund): a demonstrative legacy is a money gift directed to be paid out of a named fund, and it does not adeem simply because the fund is insufficient. Option B is wrong because the gift is of a sum of money, not of the account itself.

309. After a family argument Terence takes his will, writes the word revoked across the front page in large letters, and puts it back in the drawer. He tears nothing and burns nothing. He died in 2027 and the will was found in that state. What is the effect?

A. The will is revoked, since his intention to revoke it is clear.

B. The will is revoked, because writing across it is an act of destruction.

C. The will stands, as symbolic destruction is not enough to revoke it.

D. The will stands only if the words were seen by two witnesses.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The will stands, as symbolic destruction is not enough to revoke it): revocation by destruction requires burning, tearing or otherwise destroying the will with intent to revoke, and a symbolic act such as writing across it will not do. Option A is wrong because intention alone achieves nothing without one of the four recognised methods of revocation.

310. A man died intestate. His widow has not yet obtained letters of administration, but she has already agreed to sell his car to a neighbour and has taken a deposit for it. The neighbour asks whether she was entitled to do that. What is the position on her authority?

A. She had no authority, since an administrator's powers begin at the grant.

B. She had authority, because entitlement to the grant confers it from death.

C. She had authority, provided she accounts for the proceeds after the grant.

D. She had no authority, unless the car was worth less than the deposit.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (She had no authority, since an administrator's powers begin at the grant): an administrator, unlike an executor, has no authority until letters of administration issue, so dealings before the grant are not made on behalf of the estate. Option B applies the executor rule to an intestacy, which is the distinction the question turns on.

311. A will contains a manuscript amendment to the figure in a legacy. The attestation clause states that the will was signed with that amendment already made, and both witnesses confirm it. A beneficiary argues the amendment is ineffective because it was never separately initialled. What is the position?

A. The amendment is ineffective, since each alteration must be separately initialled.

B. The amendment is ineffective, and the original wording underneath takes effect.

C. The amendment stands only if the original wording cannot now be read.

D. The amendment stands, because the evidence shows it preceded the execution.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The amendment stands, because the evidence shows it preceded the execution): the rule is that an unattested alteration is presumed to have been made after execution, and that presumption can be displaced by evidence, here the attestation clause and the witnesses. Option A treats initialling as a statutory requirement, which it is not; it is simply the usual way of proving the point.

312. Gwen gave clear instructions for her will in March 2026 while she plainly had capacity. By the time the engrossment was brought to her in May 2026 her understanding had declined, but she knew she was signing the will she had asked for. She died shortly afterwards. Is the will valid?

A. Yes, she had capacity at instructions and understood she was signing them.

B. No, capacity is judged at execution and she lacked it then.

C. Yes, because a solicitor prepared the will and read it to her.

D. No, unless a medical practitioner had witnessed the will being signed.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Yes, she had capacity at instructions and understood she was signing them): under Parker v Felgate a will stands where the testator had capacity when giving instructions and, at execution, understood that she was signing a will prepared to those instructions. Option B states the general rule but ignores that recognised exception, which is exactly what these facts are built around.

313. A widower transferred his house to his daughter in 2021 but has continued to live there rent free ever since, paying nothing to her. He died in 2027. His daughter assumes the house is outside his estate because more than five years have passed. What is the difficulty?

A. He reserved a benefit in the house, so it is treated as his.

B. The gift is chargeable, since he did not survive it by seven years.

C. The gift is exempt, but the daughter must pay the tax on it.

D. The house is outside the estate, as he survived more than three years.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (He reserved a benefit in the house, so it is treated as his): giving away the house while continuing to live in it rent free is the classic reservation of benefit, so the property remains within the estate whatever the passage of time. Option B misses the point, because the seven year rule does not save a gift with a reservation.

314. A sole administrator of an intestate estate died part way through the administration, leaving assets still to be collected. She herself had made no will. A beneficiary asks whether her own personal representatives can simply carry on with the first estate. What is the position?

A. No, administrators have no chain, so a grant de bonis non is needed.

B. Yes, her own personal representatives continue that administration automatically.

C. Yes, provided the beneficiaries all consent to them continuing to act.

D. No, the remaining assets pass to the Crown as bona vacantia.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No, administrators have no chain, so a grant de bonis non is needed): the chain of representation applies to proving executors only, so on an administrator's death a fresh grant must be taken out for the unadministered estate. Option B applies the chain to administrators, which is exactly the error the rule is designed to catch.

315. A fund is held on trust for Ben absolutely. Ben is 24, of full capacity, and solely entitled to the fund. The trustees would prefer to keep the fund invested until he is 30, which is what the settlor had hoped for. Ben demands the fund now. What is the position?

A. The trustees may retain the fund, since the settlor's wishes bind them.

B. Ben may call for the fund, being absolutely entitled under a bare trust.

C. Ben must wait, because a beneficiary cannot terminate an existing trust.

D. The trustees may retain the fund unless the court orders them otherwise.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Ben may call for the fund, being absolutely entitled under a bare trust): an adult of full capacity who is absolutely entitled can call for the trust property under Saunders v Vautier. Option A treats the settlor's hopes as binding, but once the trust is constituted the settlor's later preferences do not control the trustees.

316. A will gives several pecuniary legacies and a specific gift of the testator's shares, but the residuary clause was omitted from the engrossment in error and the will was executed in that form. The estate is worth considerably more than the legacies. What happens to the balance?

A. It is divided rateably among the pecuniary legatees named in the will.

B. It passes to the specific legatee, as the only gift of an actual asset.

C. It is held by the personal representatives until the court directs otherwise.

D. It passes under the intestacy rules as a partial intestacy.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It passes under the intestacy rules as a partial intestacy): every will must dispose of residue, and any part left undisposed of passes to those entitled on intestacy. Option A is wrong because a pecuniary legatee takes the stated sum and has no claim to share what the will fails to dispose of.

317. Ingrid, who is unwell, asks her friend to burn her will. The friend takes the will home and burns it there. Ingrid died a month later. A copy of the will is found among her papers, and the executor named in it seeks to prove that copy. What is the position on revocation?

A. The will was revoked, because Ingrid clearly intended it to be destroyed.

B. The will was revoked, because a friend may act on the testator's request.

C. The will stands, because a copy of it survived the friend's destruction.

D. The will stands, as destruction must occur in the testator's presence.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The will stands, as destruction must occur in the testator's presence): destruction by another person revokes a will only where it is done in the testator's presence and by the testator's direction, with intent to revoke. Burning it elsewhere fails that requirement. Option A is wrong because intention without a valid act of destruction does not revoke.

318. A will gives the testator's shares in a named company to a son, 15,000 pounds to a daughter, and the residue to a grandson. The daughter asks which category her gift falls into, and how it ranks if the estate turns out to be short of cash. How is her gift classified?

A. A specific legacy, because the sum is identified precisely in the will.

B. A pecuniary legacy, payable out of the estate before residue is ascertained.

C. A demonstrative legacy, payable out of whichever fund holds enough cash.

D. A residuary gift, since cash forms part of the residue by default.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (A pecuniary legacy, payable out of the estate before residue is ascertained): a pecuniary legacy is a gift of money not tied to any particular fund, and residue is what remains after debts, expenses, tax and legacies. Option C is wrong because no fund is named as the source of payment, which is what makes a legacy demonstrative.

319. An administration is nearing its end. The debts and the legacies have been paid and receipts obtained from the legatees. The residuary beneficiaries ask what they should expect from the personal representatives before the balance is paid over. What should the personal representatives prepare?

A. A schedule of the assets sold and the prices actually obtained.

B. Estate accounts of capital, income and distribution for their approval.

C. A copy of the inheritance tax account delivered to the revenue.

D. A statement of truth confirming that the administration has been completed.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Estate accounts of capital, income and distribution for their approval): the final step of an administration is to prepare estate accounts for the residuary beneficiaries to approve before the balance is paid over. Option A gives only part of the picture, since a sales schedule says nothing about income or distribution.

320. A daughter tells you her father cannot make a will because a deputy manages his investments, and because he wishes to leave more to one child than to the other. Your own discussion with him suggests he understands a simple will perfectly well. How should you approach the question of capacity?

A. Treat the deputyship as conclusive evidence that he lacks testamentary capacity.

B. Refuse instructions until the Court of Protection confirms that he has capacity.

C. Treat capacity as decision specific; an unwise choice is not incapacity.

D. Treat the unequal gift as a strong indication that he is being influenced.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Treat capacity as decision specific; an unwise choice is not incapacity): a client may lack capacity to manage a portfolio and still have capacity to make a simple will, and the Mental Capacity Act 2005 provides that an unwise decision is not itself evidence of incapacity. Option A treats an inability in one area as decisive across all decisions, which the framework does not support.

321. A will gives a fund to such of the testator's grandchildren as reach 18. At the testator's death two grandchildren are already over 18 and a third is aged four. A fourth grandchild is born two years after the death. Who is included in the class?

A. All four grandchildren, since the class closes only when all reach 18.

B. The three living at death, as the class closed on a vested interest.

C. Only the two grandchildren who had already reached 18 at the death.

D. All four grandchildren, because the will names no cut off date.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The three living at death, as the class closed on a vested interest): under the class closing rules the class closes once a member takes a vested interest, so grandchildren born afterwards are excluded. Option C is wrong because the four year old is already a member of the closed class and takes on reaching 18.

322. You are gathering the information needed for an inheritance tax account on an estate. The family have provided date of death valuations of the house, the bank accounts, the policies and the pension. What further category of information must you obtain before the account can be completed?

A. The beneficiaries' own resources and any provision they already receive.

B. The dates on which each of the assets was originally acquired.

C. The identity of creditors who have responded to the statutory advertisement.

D. Any lifetime gifts made by the deceased in the previous seven years.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Any lifetime gifts made by the deceased in the previous seven years): the account requires the lifetime transfers in the seven years before death as well as the date of death values of the assets and liabilities. Option C concerns protection on distribution, which comes much later in the administration and does not feed the account.

323. The court is considering a claim by an adult son. The estate is small, another applicant has substantial needs, and the son has a good income of his own. He argues that only his own financial position is relevant to the decision. Which best describes the court's approach?

A. It considers the applicant's needs alone, other beneficiaries being irrelevant.

B. It considers only the estate's size and the applicant's own income.

C. It considers the deceased's wishes, which are conclusive on the question.

D. It weighs all applicants and beneficiaries, the estate, obligations and conduct.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It weighs all applicants and beneficiaries, the estate, obligations and conduct): section 3 requires the court to look at the resources and needs of the applicant, of other applicants and of beneficiaries, the obligations of the deceased, the size and nature of the estate, disability and any other relevant matter. Option A takes one factor and treats it as the whole exercise.

324. Rebecca attends your office to give will instructions. Her son drives her, comes into the meeting room, answers two of your questions for her, and produces a handwritten note setting out how he says the will should read. Rebecca herself says very little. What should you do first?

A. Take the instructions from the note and confirm them with the son.

B. Ask the son to wait outside and see Rebecca on her own.

C. Refuse the instructions and advise Rebecca to instruct a different firm.

D. Proceed on the note but record that the son was present throughout.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Ask the son to wait outside and see Rebecca on her own): a will must record the testator's own decisions, so you see the client alone for part of every appointment. That protects against undue influence and lets you take instructions in Rebecca's own words. Option D is wrong because a file note of the son's presence does not cure the problem of never having heard Rebecca on her own.

325. Hugh, aged 84, gives instructions for a will leaving everything to a neighbour. He knows he is making a will and knows what he owns, but he cannot recall that he has two adult daughters and dismisses any suggestion that he does. Which element of testamentary capacity is in doubt?

A. Understanding the nature of the act of making a will.

B. Understanding the extent of the property being disposed of.

C. Understanding the effect of appointing an executor to act.

D. Appreciating the claims of those he ought to consider.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Appreciating the claims of those he ought to consider): Banks v Goodfellow requires the testator to comprehend and appreciate the claims to which he ought to give effect. Hugh cannot bring his daughters to mind at all, so that limb is in question. Option B is wrong because the stem tells you he does know the extent of his property.

326. Your client is 91, has had two episodes of confusion in hospital this year, and wishes to change her will substantially. Having spoken to her at length you are satisfied she understands what she is doing. What does the golden rule suggest you do, and what follows if you do not?

A. Have a doctor assess and record capacity; omission does not invalidate the will.

B. Have a doctor assess and record capacity; omission renders the will void.

C. Decline instructions until the Court of Protection authorises a statutory will.

D. Ask two independent witnesses to confirm in writing that she understood.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Have a doctor assess and record capacity; omission does not invalidate the will): the golden rule is prudent practice, not law. A medical practitioner should satisfy themselves of capacity and record the reasoning rather than simply signing. Option B overstates the position, because failure to follow the rule invites a dispute but does not of itself make the will void.

327. Alan was the sole proving executor of his mother's estate, which he had not finished administering when he died in 2027. Alan's own will appointed his wife as his executor, and probate of Alan's will has now been granted to her. Who may complete the administration of the mother's estate?

A. Nobody, until a grant de bonis non is obtained for the mother's estate.

B. The mother's residuary beneficiaries, who must apply for a fresh grant.

C. Alan's wife, but only once the court has specially confirmed her appointment.

D. Alan's wife, who becomes executor of the mother's estate by the chain.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Alan's wife, who becomes executor of the mother's estate by the chain): where a sole or last surviving proving executor dies, that executor's own executor becomes executor of the original estate automatically once probate of the second will is granted. Option A would be right only if the chain had been broken, for example by an intestacy or a failure to prove.

328. Elaine died intestate in 2027. She had no spouse and no issue, and both her parents had already died. She is survived by a half brother, two grandparents, and an aunt of the whole blood. The estate is a modest sum in savings. Who is entitled to it?

A. The grandparents, since they take before collateral relatives of any degree.

B. The half brother, as siblings rank ahead of grandparents and aunts.

C. The aunt of the whole blood, who ranks ahead of half blood relatives.

D. The half brother and the grandparents share the estate equally between them.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The half brother, as siblings rank ahead of grandparents and aunts): the statutory order runs issue, parents, whole blood siblings, half blood siblings, grandparents, whole blood uncles and aunts, then half blood uncles and aunts. The estate passes to the first category producing a living taker. Option C is wrong because whole blood only outranks half blood within the same category, not across categories.

329. The same personal representatives are told that the deceased's estranged daughter may bring a claim for reasonable financial provision. The grant issued last month. The sole residuary beneficiary is pressing hard for immediate payment of the whole estate. What is the prudent course?

A. Distribute now, since a claim can only be made against the beneficiaries.

B. Distribute now, provided the daughter is told the estate has been paid.

C. Apply at once for the court's authority to distribute the whole estate.

D. Wait out the six month period for a claim under the 1975 Act.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Wait out the six month period for a claim under the 1975 Act): personal representatives who distribute within six months of the grant risk personal liability if an order is later made, so the standard practice is to hold back until the period has run. Option A misstates the position, because it is the personal representatives who are exposed.

330. Ken died intestate in March 2027, survived by his wife and two adult children. His wife died 12 days after him. Ken's estate is worth more than the statutory legacy, the figure for which will be supplied. What is the effect of the wife's death on her entitlement under Ken's intestacy?

A. She takes her full entitlement, which then passes into her own estate.

B. She takes the chattels and statutory legacy but not the residue share.

C. She takes nothing, as a spouse must survive by 28 days.

D. She takes nothing, because the elder is presumed to have died first.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (She takes nothing, as a spouse must survive by 28 days): the intestacy rules require the surviving spouse or civil partner to survive the deceased by 28 days in order to take, and she survived only 12. The estate therefore passes as though she had not survived. Option D confuses this rule with the commorientes presumption, which has nothing to do with these facts.

331. A trustee of a family trust arranges for the trust to buy a property from a company that he himself controls, at a price he considers to be fair. He mentions his interest to the other trustee but takes no further step. A beneficiary objects to the purchase. What is the difficulty?

A. A trustee must not profit from the trust or act where conflicted.

B. A trustee may not purchase property without a valuation from a surveyor.

C. A trustee may not deal with a company unless it is wholly unconnected.

D. A trustee must obtain the court's approval for every purchase of land.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (A trustee must not profit from the trust or act where conflicted): the no profit and no conflict rules apply whether or not the price is fair, and mentioning the interest to a co trustee does not cure the position. Option B raises a valuation point that would not save the transaction even if it were obtained.

332. A testator's will leaves his house to his brother and the residue of his estate to his two children. His executors ask whether the residence nil rate band is available in respect of the house. The relevant figures will be supplied to them. Which condition causes the difficulty?

A. The house must have been the testator's only residence during his lifetime.

B. The residence must be closely inherited by his lineal descendants.

C. The residence must pass free of any mortgage secured over it.

D. The residence must have been owned for at least seven years.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The residence must be closely inherited by his lineal descendants): the residence nil rate band requires a qualifying residential interest to be closely inherited by lineal descendants, and a brother is not a lineal descendant. Option A invents an only residence test, when what matters is who inherits the property.

333. A will gives 5,000 pounds to the testator's friend Beatrice, with no substitution clause and no contrary intention expressed. Beatrice died in 2026, a year before the testator, leaving two adult children of her own who survived him. Who takes the 5,000 pounds?

A. Beatrice's children take the legacy in equal shares by substitution.

B. The legacy lapses and falls into the testator's residuary estate.

C. The legacy passes to Beatrice's estate for her executors to administer.

D. The legacy passes on a partial intestacy to the testator's own relatives.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The legacy lapses and falls into the testator's residuary estate): a gift lapses where the beneficiary predeceases the testator, and the lapsed gift falls into residue. Option A is wrong because section 33 substitutes only the issue of the testator's own children or remoter issue, and a friend is outside it.

334. A husband and wife died within two days of each other following a road accident. Each will left everything to the other, with a gift over to the same charity. Neither will contained a survivorship clause. A client asks what such a clause would have achieved. What is its purpose?

A. It prevents the two wills being read together as one single instrument.

B. It postpones the grant until the order of the two deaths is settled.

C. It requires survival for a stated period, so an estate does not pass twice.

D. It reverses the presumption that the elder of the two died first.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (It requires survival for a stated period, so an estate does not pass twice): a survivorship clause, commonly 28 or 30 days, stops an estate passing through a spouse who dies days later and then being administered a second time. Option D confuses the clause with section 184 of the Law of Property Act 1925, which is a separate rule.

335. A client wants her brother to take a legacy, and if he dies before her, his children to take it instead in equal shares. You have advised her that section 33 will not assist her on those facts. What drafting should you use to achieve what she wants?

A. A direction that the legacy is to be paid to the brother's estate.

B. A recital that section 33 is to apply to the gift to him.

C. A direction that the legacy is to lapse into residue if he predeceases.

D. An express substitution clause naming his surviving children in equal shares.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (An express substitution clause naming his surviving children in equal shares): where section 33 does not apply, the only reliable route is an express clause providing that if the beneficiary predeceases, his children who survive the testator take. Option B is wrong because a recital cannot extend a statutory substitution beyond the class the section covers.

336. At a first will appointment your client lists her house, her savings and a small business. She mentions in passing that she has supported her partner's adult son financially for several years, although they have never lived in the same household. Which follow up matters most for the will you draft?

A. Whether the business qualifies for a reduced rate of tax on death.

B. Whether the partner's son would prefer a lifetime gift of cash instead.

C. Whether the savings are held jointly or in her sole name.

D. Whether that maintenance could support a claim against her estate.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Whether that maintenance could support a claim against her estate): a person maintained wholly or partly by the deceased immediately before death may apply under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, so the maintenance history shapes both the advice and the drafting. Option C matters for what passes under the will, but it raises no claim against the estate.

337. Peter died intestate in 2027. He and his wife were judicially separated in 2024 and the separation remained in force at his death. They were never divorced. Peter left two adult children. His wife now claims her entitlement on the intestacy. What is the position?

A. She takes the chattels and statutory legacy, but not the residue share.

B. She takes nothing on the intestacy, so the children take the estate.

C. She takes her full spousal entitlement, since the marriage still subsisted.

D. She takes half the estate, and the children share the other half.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (She takes nothing on the intestacy, so the children take the estate): a judicially separated spouse, like a former spouse, takes nothing under the intestacy rules. Option C fixes on the marriage still subsisting, but judicial separation removes the entitlement even though the marriage has not been dissolved.

338. An executor named in a valid will sells perishable stock from the deceased's shop three weeks after the death, before the grant of probate has issued. A residuary beneficiary questions whether the sale binds the estate. What is the position on the executor's authority?

A. The sale is void, because authority begins only when probate issues.

B. The sale is voidable at the option of the residuary beneficiaries.

C. The sale is valid only if the court later confirms his appointment.

D. The sale is valid, as an executor's authority derives from the will.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The sale is valid, as an executor's authority derives from the will): an executor's authority runs from the death, so acts before the grant are valid and probate merely confirms the title. Option A describes the position of an administrator, who has no authority at all until letters of administration issue.

339. Colin died intestate in 2027 leaving no spouse. He had two children. One child, Amy, is aged 15. The other, Barry, died before Colin, leaving a son aged 20 who survived Colin. How do the statutory trusts apply to Colin's estate?

A. Amy takes the whole estate absolutely, since Barry predeceased his father Colin.

B. Amy and Barry's son each take one half absolutely and immediately on death.

C. Amy takes one half now, and Barry's son must reach 25 to take.

D. Amy takes half contingently on reaching 18; Barry's son takes his father's half.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Amy takes half contingently on reaching 18; Barry's son takes his father's half): under the statutory trusts beneficiaries take in equal shares contingently on reaching 18 or marrying or forming a civil partnership earlier, and the issue of a predeceased member take that member's share per stirpes. Option B ignores the contingency, which matters because Amy is still 15.

340. Your elderly client wishes to leave nothing to one of her three children, explaining a long estrangement. She has capacity and you have seen her alone. You think the will is likely to be challenged after her death. Which single step most improves the position if it is disputed?

A. A contemporaneous attendance note recording her reasons in her own words.

B. A clause in the will reciting that the omitted child is excluded.

C. A letter now to the omitted child explaining the client's decision.

D. A second appointment at which the client repeats her instructions again.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (A contemporaneous attendance note recording her reasons in her own words): the file note of who was present, what the client said and why she wishes to benefit as she does is the solicitor's real protection in a later dispute over capacity, knowledge and approval or influence. Option B adds a recital but records nothing about how the decision was reached.

341. A widow is entitled on her husband's intestacy to the personal chattels, the statutory legacy and half the residue. The main asset is the family home, which was in his sole name and which she wishes to keep. Her total entitlement exceeds its value. What can she require?

A. That the personal representatives sell the home and pay her the proceeds.

B. That the children's share be postponed until she no longer needs it.

C. That the home be appropriated towards her entitlement in the estate.

D. That the court transfer the home to her under the 1975 Act.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (That the home be appropriated towards her entitlement in the estate): the Intestates' Estates Act 1952 lets the surviving spouse require the matrimonial home to be appropriated towards her entitlement, so she keeps the house rather than a cash sum. Option D is unnecessary, since she does not need a court order to achieve what the statute already gives her.

342. You are taking will instructions from a man in his sixties who says simply that he wants everything to go to his wife, and if she does not survive him, to his children. This is his second marriage. Which question most directly affects who may later claim against his estate?

A. Whether he wishes to appoint a professional executor alongside his wife.

B. Whether he has children from his first marriage or any stepchildren.

C. Whether his wife has already made a will in similar mirror terms.

D. Whether the family home is held as joint tenants or tenants in common.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Whether he has children from his first marriage or any stepchildren): children of the deceased and persons treated as a child of the family are among the categories who may apply under the 1975 Act, so a second marriage makes that enquiry essential. Option D affects what passes under the will, but survivorship on a joint tenancy creates no claim against the estate.

343. Harold died in 2027 without a will. He is survived by his wife Joan. He had no children and no other issue. Both his parents are alive and he has one brother. The estate consists of a house and savings. Who is entitled on the intestacy?

A. Joan takes half, and his parents take the other half equally.

B. Joan takes the personal chattels and half, his parents the balance.

C. Joan takes the whole estate, since Harold left no issue.

D. Joan takes the house, and the savings pass to his brother.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Joan takes the whole estate, since Harold left no issue): a surviving spouse or civil partner where the deceased left no issue takes the entire estate, and the remaining categories of relative never come into play. Option A applies a division that only arises where there is issue, and parents rank below a spouse in any event.

344. A client cannot hold a pen. She asks her solicitor to sign the will for her. The solicitor writes her name at the foot of the will in her presence and at her direction, while two witnesses watch together, and the witnesses then sign in her presence. Is the signature requirement met?

A. No, only the testator personally may sign a will under section 9.

B. Yes, another may sign in her presence and by her direction.

C. No, unless the solicitor signs his own name and states his authority.

D. Yes, provided the client confirms the signature in writing shortly afterwards.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Yes, another may sign in her presence and by her direction): section 9 allows the will to be signed by the testator or by another person in the testator's presence and by her direction, with the intention of giving effect to the will. Option A states the ordinary case but overlooks the express statutory alternative.

345. A settlor's signed letter directs his trustee to hold the bulk of his shareholding on trust for his niece. The letter does not say how many shares that is, or how they are to be identified from the rest of his holding. Which certainty is lacking?

A. Certainty of intention, since the letter is precatory rather than imperative.

B. Certainty of objects, since the niece is not sufficiently identified here.

C. No certainty is lacking; the trustee may select a reasonable number.

D. Certainty of subject matter, since the trust property is not identified.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Certainty of subject matter, since the trust property is not identified): the bulk of a shareholding gives no way of knowing which or how many shares are held on trust, so the subject matter is uncertain and no trust arises. Option A fails because the letter directs rather than merely wishes, so the imperative language supplies certainty of intention. Option B fails because the niece is a single identified person, so the objects are certain. Option C fails because a trustee cannot cure uncertain subject matter by choosing an amount for the settlor.

346. A client made an outright gift to his son in 2022 and is now told that if he dies within seven years the gift will become chargeable. He asks what practical difference it makes whether he survives four years rather than two. What is the effect of taper relief?

A. It reduces the value transferred once he has survived three years.

B. It reduces the tax payable once he has survived at least three years.

C. It reduces the tax only where the gift exceeds the nil rate band.

D. It removes the charge entirely once he has survived four full years.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (It reduces the tax payable once he has survived at least three years): taper operates on a sliding scale once the donor has survived three years, and it reduces the tax rather than the value transferred. Option A gets the direction of the relief wrong, which matters because the value stays fixed at the date of the gift.

347. Margaret died intestate in 2027 leaving no spouse, no issue, no surviving parents, no brothers or sisters, and no grandparents. Both of her aunts of the whole blood died before her, each leaving one child. Those two first cousins have come forward. Who is entitled to her estate?

A. The two cousins take, substituted on the statutory trusts for their late mothers

B. The Crown takes as bona vacantia, cousins falling outside the statutory order

C. The estate is divided equally among every blood relative who comes forward

D. The estate passes to the cousins' own children rather than to the cousins

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The two cousins take, substituted on the statutory trusts for their late mothers): uncles and aunts of the whole blood take on the statutory trusts, and the statutory trusts substitute the issue of a class member who died before the intestate, so a first cousin inherits in place of a parent who predeceased. Option B is the common error of reading the list of classes as the end of the family tree; the Crown takes only where no class produces a taker, whether directly or by substitution. Option C ignores that entitlement runs class by class rather than by nearness of blood, and option D reverses the substitution, which reaches the next generation down only where the cousin has also died.

348. Trustees invest the whole fund in a way that the trust deed plainly does not permit, and the fund falls sharply in value as a result. The beneficiaries want to know what the trustees can be required to do. There is no suggestion of dishonesty. What is the ordinary consequence?

A. The trustees must resign and hand the fund to replacement trustees.

B. The trustees must account for any profit they made from the investment.

C. The trustees are personally liable to restore the loss to the fund.

D. The trustees are liable only for the fees they charged the trust.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The trustees are personally liable to restore the loss to the fund): a breach of trust makes the trustee personally liable to restore the loss caused, whether or not there was any dishonesty. Option B addresses unauthorised profit, which is a different head of liability and produces nothing where the investment lost money.

349. Colin signs his will at his kitchen table. His neighbour Ruth is present and sees him sign. A second neighbour, Tom, arrives ten minutes later, and Colin acknowledges his signature to Tom alone. Both neighbours then sign as witnesses in Colin's presence. Is section 9 of the Wills Act 1837 satisfied?

A. Yes, because each witness saw or acknowledged the signature in turn.

B. Yes, provided the will contains a properly drafted attestation clause.

C. No, because the witnesses did not sign in each other's presence.

D. No, because both witnesses were not together at signature or acknowledgement.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (No, because both witnesses were not together at signature or acknowledgement): section 9 requires the signature to be made or acknowledged in the presence of two or more witnesses present at the same time. Colin dealt with each separately, so the requirement fails. Option C states a rule that does not exist, since the witnesses need not sign in each other's presence.

350. Frank made a will in 2025 giving his cottage to his nephew and the residue to a charity. In 2026 he made a second will dealing only with the cottage, which he gave to his niece. The second will contains no revocation clause. Frank died in 2027. Who takes what?

A. The niece takes the cottage; the charity still takes the residue.

B. The nephew takes the cottage, since the later will lacks a revocation clause.

C. The niece takes the cottage; the residue passes on a partial intestacy.

D. The niece takes both the cottage and the residue under the later will.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The niece takes the cottage; the charity still takes the residue): a later will revokes an earlier one expressly or by inconsistency, and here the inconsistency reaches only the cottage. The earlier residuary gift is untouched and continues to operate. Option C is wrong because the 2025 residuary gift was never revoked, so no partial intestacy arises.

351. A will appoints Deborah as executor and leaves her nothing at all. Deborah acted as one of the two attesting witnesses, the other being a neighbour with no interest in the estate. After the death a beneficiary suggests Deborah's appointment fails because she witnessed the will. What is the position?

A. Her appointment fails, since an attesting witness cannot take any benefit.

B. Her appointment fails, but the rest of the will remains fully effective.

C. Her appointment stands only if a substitute executor is also named.

D. Her appointment stands, because section 15 voids gifts, not appointments.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Her appointment stands, because section 15 voids gifts, not appointments): section 15 strikes down a gift to an attesting witness or the witness's spouse, and Deborah takes no gift. An executor who is not a beneficiary may safely witness the will. Option A treats an office as a benefit, which section 15 does not do.

352. A will leaves the estate on trust for the testator's children contingently on reaching 18, and two of them are still minors. Six adult beneficiaries all wish to be appointed as administrators with the will annexed. What limits apply to the number of personal representatives?

A. No more than three may take a grant where minors are beneficiaries.

B. No more than four may take, and at least two will be required.

C. Any number may take, provided each signs the statement of truth.

D. Only one may take, so all the others must renounce their entitlement.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (No more than four may take, and at least two will be required): no grant may issue to more than four personal representatives, and where a minority or a life interest arises at least two administrators or a trust corporation will normally be required. Option A states the wrong maximum and adds a rule that does not exist.

353. A valid will appoints a sole executor, who died before the testator, and no substitute executor was named. The will leaves the residue to the testator's daughter, who wishes to administer the estate. The will is otherwise unimpeachable. Which grant should be applied for?

A. A grant of probate, since a valid will disposes of the whole estate.

B. Simple letters of administration, since no executor is able to act.

C. Letters of administration with the will annexed, under rule 20.

D. A grant de bonis non, since the appointed executor has died.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Letters of administration with the will annexed, under rule 20): this grant issues where there is a valid will but no executor able and willing to act, entitlement following rule 20 of the Non Contentious Probate Rules 1987. Option B is wrong because simple letters of administration are for an intestacy, and here there is a valid will.

354. A trust has two trustees. One is the settlor's neighbour, who has no relevant expertise at all. The other is a professional trust manager who advertises specialist investment knowledge. A beneficiary asks whether the same standard of care applies to each of them. What is the position?

A. The standard is higher for the trustee holding out special knowledge.

B. The same standard applies to both, since they hold the same office.

C. The professional is liable only under the terms of any engagement letter.

D. The lay trustee is judged by the standard of the professional trustee.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The standard is higher for the trustee holding out special knowledge): section 1 of the Trustee Act 2000 requires such care and skill as is reasonable in the circumstances, judged higher where a trustee holds themselves out as having special knowledge or acts in the course of a business. Option B ignores that the statutory standard is expressly variable.

355. Ravi made a will in 2026 which recited that it was made in expectation of his forthcoming marriage to Ellen, and that it was not to be revoked by that marriage. They married later that year. Ravi died in 2027. Ellen argues the marriage revoked the will. Is she right?

A. Yes, marriage revokes any earlier will whatever that will may say.

B. No, a will expressly made in expectation of that marriage survives it.

C. Yes, unless Ellen was named as the sole beneficiary of the will.

D. No, because the will was made in the same year as the marriage.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (No, a will expressly made in expectation of that marriage survives it): the general rule that marriage revokes an earlier will is subject to the exception for a will expressly made in expectation of the particular marriage, which is precisely what Ravi's will recites. Option D is wrong because the timing of the will is irrelevant; what matters is the express expectation.

356. A widower changes his will in favour of the daughter who cooks for him and visits daily. She often reminds him of everything she does for him and says she hopes he will remember her. He had capacity and reached the decision himself. Does this amount to undue influence?

A. Yes, because a relationship of dependency raises a presumption of influence.

B. Yes, because repeated reminders of care amount to improper pressure.

C. No, persuasion and appeals to affection fall short of coercion.

D. No, unless the daughter also arranged the appointment with the solicitor.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (No, persuasion and appeals to affection fall short of coercion): undue influence in the making of a will means coercion, so a testator who is persuaded but still exercises his own judgment has not been unduly influenced. Option A is wrong because there is no presumption of undue influence in wills, unlike the lifetime doctrine.

357. A will gives 10,000 pounds to the testator's nephew Simon. Simon died before the testator, leaving two children who survived the testator. The will contains no express substitution clause. Simon's children claim the legacy under section 33 of the Wills Act 1837. Are they entitled to it?

A. Yes, section 33 substitutes the issue of any predeceasing named beneficiary.

B. Yes, provided the testator left no children of his own surviving him.

C. No, section 33 applies to the testator's own children and remoter issue.

D. No, unless the nephew's children were financially dependent on the testator.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (No, section 33 applies to the testator's own children and remoter issue): the section does not reach nephews, nieces, siblings or friends, so the legacy simply lapses into residue. Option A states the section far too widely, and that overstatement is the trap these facts are built on.

358. A man died intestate in 2027. He is survived by his wife, one adult son, and his mother. The wife does not wish to act and is willing to renounce. The son wishes to apply for a grant. Who is entitled to apply, and in what order, under the probate rules?

A. The wife, then the son, then the mother, tracking the intestacy order.

B. The mother first, as the nearest relative in the ascending line.

C. The son first, since the wife has already declined to act.

D. Any of the three, since the rules impose no order of entitlement.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The wife, then the son, then the mother, tracking the intestacy order): entitlement to simple letters of administration follows the rule 22 order, which mirrors the intestacy order of spouse or civil partner, then children, then parents, then siblings and onwards. Option C is wrong because the son's entitlement arises from the order itself once the wife renounces, not from her decision.

359. Ana lived with Gerald in his house as if they were married, in the same household, for the four years immediately before his death in 2027. His will leaves everything to his sister. Ana wishes to apply for reasonable financial provision. On what basis does she qualify to apply?

A. As a person treated by Gerald as a child of the family.

B. As a former spouse of the deceased who has not remarried.

C. She does not qualify, as only spouses and children may apply.

D. As a cohabitant living with him for two years before the death.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (As a cohabitant living with him for two years before the death): a person who lived with the deceased as spouse or civil partner in the same household throughout the two years ending with the death is a qualifying applicant, and Ana comfortably exceeds that period. Option C ignores the cohabitant and dependant categories the Act expressly creates.

360. A will is professionally drafted, read over to the testator clause by clause, and executed with an attestation clause reciting that. The testator had capacity, and the main beneficiary took no part in arranging the will. A disappointed relative alleges the testator did not know the contents. What is the position?

A. Knowledge and approval must be proved afresh by the executors in any event.

B. Knowledge and approval is presumed, and nothing here excites suspicion.

C. Knowledge and approval is presumed only where a medical report exists.

D. Knowledge and approval fails, because reading over is not evidence of understanding.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Knowledge and approval is presumed, and nothing here excites suspicion): the presumption arises on due execution by a testator with capacity, and it is displaced only where the circumstances excite suspicion, typically a substantial gift to whoever arranged the will. Option A ignores the presumption altogether and would put the executors to proof in every case.

361. In another will, the name of a residuary beneficiary has been so heavily obliterated that it cannot be read by any ordinary means. The obliteration is not initialled and not attested. The remaining gifts in the will are unaffected. What is the effect on that residuary gift?

A. The gift takes effect, since an unattested alteration is presumed ineffective.

B. The gift fails, because the original wording is no longer apparent.

C. The gift takes effect once the registry recovers the name by examination.

D. The gift fails, and the whole will is treated as having been revoked.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The gift fails, because the original wording is no longer apparent): an unattested alteration is ineffective unless the original wording is no longer apparent, in which case the obliterated words cannot take effect. Option A applies the general presumption without noticing that this exception is exactly what the facts describe.

362. A will gives the testator's car, identified by its registration number, to his niece. The testator sold that car early in 2027 and bought a different one, which he still owned when he died later that year. The niece claims the replacement car. What is the position?

A. She takes the replacement car, since the gift refers to a class of asset.

B. She takes the value of the original car out of the residuary estate.

C. The gift adeems, because the identified asset was disposed of before death.

D. The gift takes effect, because a will speaks from the date of death.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The gift adeems, because the identified asset was disposed of before death): a specific gift of an identified item adeems where the asset has ceased to exist or been disposed of before death. Option A would be right had the will said any car I own at my death, which is how such a gift should be drafted.

363. Personal representatives are about to distribute an estate. They have identified the known creditors, but they are concerned that an unknown creditor may emerge later and sue them personally. What step protects them against claims by creditors of whom they had no notice?

A. Obtaining an indemnity from each residuary beneficiary before making payment.

B. Waiting six months from the grant before distributing anything at all.

C. Advertising under section 27 of the Trustee Act 1925 for claimants.

D. Applying to the court for directions before the distribution is made.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Advertising under section 27 of the Trustee Act 1925 for claimants): a statutory advertisement protects personal representatives who distribute afterwards against claims by creditors of whom they had no notice. Option B addresses a different risk, since the six month period relates to claims under the 1975 Act rather than to creditors.

364. A will gives the residue to the testator's son Adrian. Adrian died before the testator, leaving a daughter who survived the testator. The will contains no substitution clause and shows no contrary intention. The testator died in 2027. Who takes the residue?

A. Adrian's daughter takes it, because section 33 substitutes his issue.

B. It lapses and passes under the intestacy rules to the next relatives.

C. It passes to Adrian's estate, since a residuary gift cannot lapse.

D. It is divided between Adrian's daughter and the testator's other children.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Adrian's daughter takes it, because section 33 substitutes his issue): section 33 of the Wills Act 1837 substitutes the issue of the testator's children or remoter issue who predecease leaving issue alive at the death, unless the will shows a contrary intention. Option B ignores the statutory substitution, which prevents the gift lapsing here.

365. A will leaves a fixed sum to a registered charity and the residue to the testator's nephew. The executors ask about the tax treatment of the charitable gift, and whether the estate itself can benefit further from it. The rates will be given to them. What is the position?

A. The charitable gift is taxable, but the charity may reclaim the tax paid.

B. The charitable gift is exempt only if it exceeds the nil rate band.

C. The gift is exempt, and a large enough share reduces the death rate.

D. The gift is exempt, and the residue is then exempt to the same extent.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The gift is exempt, and a large enough share reduces the death rate): gifts to charity are exempt, and where a stated proportion of the net estate passes to charity a reduced death rate applies to the rest. Option D is wrong because the exemption attaches to the charitable gift alone and does not extend to residue.

366. You are asked to take will instructions from a client who, on your assessment and on the medical evidence, does not have testamentary capacity. He has no existing will, and the intestacy rules would produce a result his family dislike. They press you to prepare a will. What can you properly advise?

A. That a will signed by his attorney under a lasting power will suffice.

B. That instructions may be taken if two doctors confirm that he understands.

C. That the family may sign a deed of variation after his death instead.

D. That an application may be made to the court for a statutory will.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (That an application may be made to the court for a statutory will): where a client lacks testamentary capacity you cannot take will instructions from him, but the Court of Protection can authorise a statutory will on an application. Option A is wrong because an attorney under a lasting power has no authority to make a will for the donor.

367. Two sisters, aged 70 and 66, died in the same incident and it cannot be established which of them died first. Each had a will leaving her estate to the other, with no substitution and no survivorship clause. How is the order of the deaths dealt with?

A. The elder is presumed to have died first under section 184.

B. Both are presumed to have died at exactly the same moment.

C. The court decides the order on the balance of the medical evidence.

D. The younger is presumed to have died first, so her estate passes.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The elder is presumed to have died first under section 184): where the order of deaths is uncertain, section 184 of the Law of Property Act 1925 presumes the elder died first, subject to the modification that applies to spouses on intestacy. Option B is wrong because the section supplies a presumed order rather than simultaneous deaths.

368. A client wants to add a small legacy to her existing will and asks whether she can simply write and sign a note to that effect, keeping it with the will. She does not want the expense of a fresh will. What must a codicil satisfy in order to be effective?

A. It must be signed by the testator and one independent adult witness.

B. It must be executed with the same formalities as a will.

C. It must be physically attached to the original will before execution.

D. It must be approved in writing by the executors named in the will.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (It must be executed with the same formalities as a will): a codicil must comply with section 9 in the same way as a will, so a signed note kept with the will achieves nothing. Option A is wrong because one witness is never sufficient; section 9 requires two present at the same time.

369. A will gives a gold pocket watch to the testator's godson, without identifying any particular watch. The testator owned no watch of any kind at his death, but the residuary estate is substantial. The godson asks what he receives. How should the personal representatives treat this gift?

A. It adeems, since the testator held no such item at his death.

B. It fails for uncertainty, because no particular watch was ever identified.

C. It is satisfied by paying the godson the watch's value in cash.
