D. It is a general legacy, so they must purchase a watch for him.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It is a general legacy, so they must purchase a watch for him): a general legacy is not tied to a particular asset, so if the estate does not hold the item the personal representatives buy it in. Option A is wrong because ademption defeats a specific gift of an identified item, and no particular watch was identified here.

370. Alison made a will in 2024 leaving everything to her sister. In 2026 she married Paul. The will said nothing about any intended marriage. Alison died in 2027 without making another will. Her sister now produces the 2024 will to the executors. What is the position?

A. The marriage revoked the will, so Alison died wholly intestate.

B. The will stands, since marriage affects only gifts to a former spouse.

C. The will stands, but Paul takes a statutory share of the estate.

D. The marriage revoked only the gift to the sister, not the will.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The marriage revoked the will, so Alison died wholly intestate): marriage or the formation of a civil partnership revokes an earlier will unless the will was expressly made in expectation of that marriage. Nothing here brings the exception into play. Option B describes the effect of divorce under section 18A, which is a different rule altogether.

371. A client is considering settling 200,000 pounds on a discretionary trust for her grandchildren during her lifetime. She assumes it will be treated in the same way as an outright gift to them would be. She asks about the immediate tax position. What should you tell her?

A. It is a potentially exempt transfer, and drops out after seven years.

B. It is exempt, because the beneficiaries are her own lineal descendants.

C. Gifts into most trusts are immediately chargeable, not potentially exempt.

D. It is chargeable only if she does not survive it by three years.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Gifts into most trusts are immediately chargeable, not potentially exempt): a gift into most trusts is a chargeable lifetime transfer with an immediate charge, unlike an outright gift to an individual. Option A treats the settlement as a potentially exempt transfer, which is exactly the assumption the client has made and which is wrong.

372. A will is attested by three witnesses. One of them is a nephew who takes a legacy under the will. The other two witnesses take nothing under it and were both present together when the testator signed. The nephew's legacy is challenged after the death. What is the position on his legacy?

A. It is void, because he attested the will and section 15 applies strictly.

B. It is valid, because two other witnesses can support due execution.

C. It is valid only if the nephew renounces his role as a witness.

D. It is void, but he may claim an equivalent sum from the residue.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (It is valid, because two other witnesses can support due execution): where the will is validly attested by two witnesses who take no benefit, a beneficiary witness may be disregarded and section 15 does not defeat the gift. Option A applies the section without asking whether the will can stand on the other two attestations, which on these facts it can.

373. A widow died in 2027. Her husband died in 2019 leaving his whole estate to her, so none of his nil rate band was used on his death. Her executors ask whether her estate can benefit from his unused band. The figures will be supplied. What is the position?

A. The unused proportion is transferable to her estate on a claim.

B. It is transferable automatically, with no claim needed by her executors.

C. It lapsed on his death, since it was never actually applied.

D. It is transferable only where the second death occurs within seven years.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The unused proportion is transferable to her estate on a claim): any unused proportion of a deceased spouse's nil rate band, and of the residence nil rate band, is transferable to the survivor, but only if a claim is made. Option B is wrong on that last point, and a missed claim is a real risk on an administration.

374. Priya's will leaves a legacy of 20,000 pounds to her friend Owen and the residue to a registered charity. Owen's wife acted as one of the two attesting witnesses. The will was otherwise properly executed. Priya has now died. What is the effect on Owen's legacy and on the will?

A. The whole will fails, and Priya's estate passes on a full intestacy.

B. Owen takes the legacy, since only a witness personally is caught.

C. The legacy is void and falls into residue; the will itself stands.

D. The legacy is halved between Owen and the residuary charity beneficiary.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The legacy is void and falls into residue; the will itself stands): section 15 of the Wills Act 1837 voids a gift to an attesting witness or to the spouse or civil partner of one. Only the gift fails, and it drops into residue. Option B is wrong because section 15 expressly extends to the spouse of a witness, which is the trap on these facts.

375. Marcus arranged his aunt's will, gave all the instructions to the solicitor by telephone, and takes the residue under it. His aunt had capacity and the will was properly executed with an attestation clause. His cousins now challenge the will. What is the effect on the usual presumption of knowledge and approval?

A. It is unaffected, since due execution by a capable testator is enough.

B. It is reversed, so Marcus must disprove undue influence by his aunt.

C. It falls away, so those propounding the will must prove approval.

D. It applies only if the solicitor read the will aloud to her.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (It falls away, so those propounding the will must prove approval): knowledge and approval is presumed on due execution by a capable testator, but the presumption goes where the circumstances excite suspicion. A substantial gift to the person who arranged the will and gave the instructions is the classic example. Option A ignores that suspicion displaces the presumption.

376. A settlor transfers a fund to trustees to distribute among such of his old friends as the trustees may select, in whatever shares they think fit. The trustees say they cannot tell who falls within that description. Which certainty is in question here, and on what test is it judged?

A. Intention, tested by whether the settlor used mandatory rather than precatory words.

B. Subject matter, tested by whether the fund itself is sufficiently identified.

C. Objects, tested by whether any given person can be said to qualify.

D. Objects, tested by whether a complete list of the class can be compiled.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Objects, tested by whether any given person can be said to qualify): a discretionary trust requires certainty of objects, judged by whether it can be said of any given person that they are or are not within the class, and old friends is too vague to apply. Option D applies the complete list test, which belongs to a fixed trust rather than a discretionary one.

377. Alice died in 2027. Her will leaves her whole estate to her husband, who is long term UK resident. Her personal representatives ask what inheritance tax arises on the estate. The rates and thresholds will be supplied to them in due course. Which principle governs the position?

A. Transfers between spouses and civil partners are exempt from inheritance tax entirely.

B. The estate is taxed at the death rate above the nil rate band.

C. The estate is exempt only up to the value of the nil rate band.

D. The estate qualifies for relief only if a claim is made within two years.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Transfers between spouses and civil partners are exempt from inheritance tax entirely): the spouse exemption applies to the whole transfer where the transferee is long term UK resident, so no charge arises on Alice's estate. Option C is wrong because the exemption operates independently of the nil rate band, which is not needed at all on these facts.

378. A discretionary trust is held for a class of the settlor's relatives. One member of the class has received nothing for several years and asserts that she is entitled to a share of the fund. The trustees have made no appointment in her favour at all. What is her position?

A. She is entitled to an equal share with the other members of the class.

B. She is entitled to income, though the capital remains at the trustees' discretion.

C. She has no more than a hope until an appointment is made for her.

D. She may compel an appointment where the trustees have long ignored her.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (She has no more than a hope until an appointment is made for her): under a discretionary trust the trustees select among the class, so no member has a proprietary interest before an appointment. Option A treats a discretionary class as though the fund were held in fixed equal shares, which it is not.

379. Sunita died intestate in 2027 leaving her husband and two adult children. Her estate comprises personal chattels, a house and cash. You are told that the statutory legacy is 322,000 pounds and that the estate is worth considerably more than that. How is the estate distributed?

A. The husband takes the chattels and the whole of the residue absolutely.

B. Chattels and the statutory legacy to him, then residue halved with the children.

C. The husband takes the statutory legacy only, and the children take the rest.

D. Chattels and a life interest in half the residue pass to the husband.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Chattels and the statutory legacy to him, then residue halved with the children): where a spouse survives with issue, the spouse takes the personal chattels absolutely, the statutory legacy free of tax and costs with interest, and half the balance of residue absolutely, the other half going to the issue on the statutory trusts. Option D describes the position before the current rules, as a spouse now takes the half share absolutely.

380. A client wants to transfer a sum of money to his brother, to be held by the brother for the client's own children. He asks what the law requires before an express trust of that money will be recognised as validly created. What must be established?

A. Certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter and certainty of objects.

B. A written declaration, delivery of the fund and acceptance by the trustee.

C. Registration of the trust and the appointment of at least two trustees.

D. Consideration from the beneficiaries and a signed deed of settlement.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter and certainty of objects): the three certainties from Knight v Knight are the foundation of any express trust. Option B lists steps that may well happen in practice but which are not what the law requires for the trust to exist.

381. A trust gives Marion the income for life, with the capital passing to her nephew on her death. Marion asks the trustees to move the whole fund into high yielding investments which are expected to erode the capital over time. What duty governs the trustees' response to her request?

A. They must follow the life tenant's directions on the income producing assets.

B. They must maximise income, since the remainderman takes only what is left.

C. They must obtain the remainderman's consent to every investment decision made.

D. They must hold an even hand between the life tenant and remainderman.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (They must hold an even hand between the life tenant and remainderman): where a life interest is followed by a capital entitlement the trustees must balance income for the life tenant against preservation of capital for the remainderman. Option B favours one beneficiary at the expense of the other, which is the breach the even hand duty exists to prevent.

382. A will is signed by the testator in front of two witnesses who are present together. The testator then covers the text so neither witness can read a word of it. Each witness signs in the testator's presence, but one leaves before the other signs. A beneficiary questions validity. What is the position?

A. Invalid, because each witness must sign in the presence of the other.

B. Valid, since witnesses need not read the will nor watch each other sign.

C. Invalid, because the witnesses could not confirm what they were attesting.

D. Valid only if the testator later acknowledges the will to both witnesses.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Valid, since witnesses need not read the will nor watch each other sign): section 9 requires both witnesses to be present together when the testator signs or acknowledges, which happened here. Each must then attest in the testator's presence, but not in the presence of the other, and neither needs to know the contents. Option A invents a requirement that section 9 does not contain.

383. Nathan lived with his partner Ruth for 19 years in her house, which she owned in her sole name. They never married and never formed a civil partnership. Ruth died in 2027 without a will, leaving a brother as her only relative. What does Nathan take on the intestacy?

A. Nothing, because a cohabitant has no entitlement on an intestacy.

B. A half share, since the relationship lasted more than two years.

C. The personal chattels and a life interest in the house.

D. The whole estate, in priority to a sibling of the deceased.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Nothing, because a cohabitant has no entitlement on an intestacy): cohabitants take nothing under the intestacy rules however long the relationship lasted, which is often the most useful thing a client hears at a first interview. Option B confuses the intestacy rules with the two year qualifying period for a cohabitant's claim under the 1975 Act.

384. A widow applies under the 1975 Act. Her late husband's will left her a modest legacy and gave the residue to his children by an earlier marriage. She is financially comfortable and does not need any more for her own maintenance. On what standard is her claim judged?

A. The maintenance standard, as it applies to every category of applicant.

B. The maintenance standard, unless the estate is unusually large in value.

C. Provision reasonable in all the circumstances, whether or not for maintenance.

D. Provision equivalent to what she would have received on a divorce.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Provision reasonable in all the circumstances, whether or not for maintenance): a surviving spouse or civil partner is judged on the higher standard, so a claim does not fail merely because she is comfortable. Option A applies the maintenance standard, which governs every other category of applicant but not a surviving spouse.

385. For the last three years of her life an elderly woman paid the rent and household bills of a family friend who was unable to work. They lived at separate addresses. She died in 2027 leaving everything to a charity. The friend wishes to claim. Which category applies?

A. A person treated by the deceased as a child of the family.

B. A person maintained by the deceased immediately before the death.

C. A cohabitant of the deceased for the two years before the death.

D. No category applies, since the friend is not a blood relative.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (A person maintained by the deceased immediately before the death): any person maintained wholly or partly by the deceased immediately before the death may apply, and paying rent and bills is plainly maintenance. Option C fails on the facts, because the two lived at separate addresses and so were never in the same household.

386. Nadia's estate passes entirely to the carer who lived with her for the last two years of her life. Nadia's brother says the relationship was one of complete dependency and that the carer must justify the gift. He alleges undue influence in the making of the will. What must he show?

A. That the carer cannot explain a gift arising from a relationship of trust.

B. That Nadia was persuaded by appeals to affection and to loyalty.

C. That Nadia's own will was overborne by coercion, which he must prove.

D. That the carer took no steps to obtain independent advice for Nadia.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (That Nadia's own will was overborne by coercion, which he must prove): there is no presumption of undue influence in wills, so the person alleging it carries the burden and must establish coercion rather than influence. Frailty and dependency make coercion easier to establish but do not shift the burden. Option A imports the lifetime presumption, which does not apply here.

387. Trustees of a modest fund have placed the whole of it in the shares of a single trading company recommended by one of them. Nothing in the trust deed requires that holding and the fund has no special purpose. A beneficiary complains. Which requirement have they most obviously overlooked?

A. The requirement to obtain the beneficiaries' consent before investing the fund.

B. The requirement to invest only in investments authorised by the trust deed.

C. The requirement to review the trust investments at least once each year.

D. The standard investment criteria of suitability and diversification of investments.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The standard investment criteria of suitability and diversification of investments): trustees exercising the general power of investment must have regard to the suitability of the investment and to the need for diversification, and a single holding fails the second limb. Option C names a real duty to review, but the breach here is in the original selection.

388. Diane died intestate in 2027 with no surviving spouse. She had one biological daughter, one child she adopted as a baby, and one stepson, the child of her late husband, whom she never adopted but who lived with her from the age of six. Who takes her estate?

A. The biological daughter and the adopted child equally; the stepson takes nothing.

B. All three children take the estate in equal shares under the statutory trusts.

C. The biological daughter alone, since adoption ends inheritance from the adopters.

D. The biological daughter and stepson equally; the adopted child takes nothing.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The biological daughter and the adopted child equally; the stepson takes nothing): an adopted child counts as a child of the adopters for intestacy, while a stepchild does not unless adopted. Option B is wrong on the stepson, although his upbringing may support a claim under the 1975 Act as a person treated as a child of the family.

389. A client holds shares in a company whose only activity is holding a portfolio of let residential properties and collecting the rents. He has held the shares for many years. He asks whether business relief will apply to those shares on his death. What is the position?

A. Relief applies, since the company carries on an established commercial activity.

B. Relief applies at the lower rate, because the underlying assets are land.

C. Relief applies once the shares have been held for the qualifying period.

D. Relief is not available for a business wholly or mainly holding investments.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Relief is not available for a business wholly or mainly holding investments): business relief excludes a business consisting wholly or mainly of dealing in or holding investments, and a property letting portfolio falls squarely within that exclusion. Option C answers only the ownership condition and overlooks the nature of the business itself.

390. A client owns a trading company which she acquired eight months ago. She asks whether business relief would reduce the value transferred if she were to die shortly. The relief rates and any capped allowance will be supplied to you. Which condition is most obviously in doubt?

A. Whether the company is incorporated in England and Wales.

B. Whether she has owned the property for the minimum qualifying period.

C. Whether the shares are quoted on a recognised investment exchange.

D. Whether she claimed the relief within two years of acquiring the shares.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Whether she has owned the property for the minimum qualifying period): business relief is subject to a minimum ownership period, and eight months is plainly short of it. Option A raises a place of incorporation test that forms no part of the relief conditions, which turn on the nature and ownership of the property.

391. A will is produced after death. The figure in a pecuniary legacy has been crossed through in ink and a larger figure written above it. The original figure can still be read underneath without difficulty. Nobody has initialled or attested the change. What is the effect of the alteration?

A. It is ineffective, and the original legacy figure takes effect instead.

B. It is effective, because the testator's intention to increase it is clear.

C. It is ineffective, and the whole pecuniary legacy therefore fails entirely.

D. It is effective, provided the executors can prove when it was made.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (It is ineffective, and the original legacy figure takes effect instead): an unattested alteration is presumed to have been made after execution and is ineffective, so the will operates as originally written where the original wording is still apparent. Option C is wrong because the gift itself survives; only the attempted change fails.

392. A long standing client of modest means tells you she wishes to leave you personally a legacy of 50,000 pounds in her new will. She says she has thought about it for years and is quite clear. She asks you to draft it. What is the correct course before acting on that instruction?

A. Take the instruction and record your surprise in a full file note.

B. Refuse to act unless she takes independent legal advice on the gift.

C. Take the instruction, but have another partner in the firm approve it.

D. Refuse the instruction outright, since a solicitor cannot receive client gifts.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Refuse to act unless she takes independent legal advice on the gift): where a client wishes to leave the solicitor a gift of significant value, judged against this client's own estate, you must not act unless the client takes independent advice, and you record the advice given and her decision. Option D goes too far, because the gift is not prohibited once independent advice has been taken.

393. Miriam's will left her residue to her husband Daniel and appointed him her sole executor. Their marriage was dissolved by a final order in 2026. Miriam died in 2027 without changing the will. Daniel now claims the residue and the right to prove the will. What is the effect of the dissolution?

A. The dissolution revoked the whole will, so Miriam died wholly intestate.

B. The dissolution has no effect, so Daniel takes residue and proves the will.

C. Daniel keeps the residue, but his appointment as executor no longer takes effect.

D. Daniel is treated as having died then, so gift and appointment both fail.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Daniel is treated as having died then, so gift and appointment both fail): under section 18A the former spouse or civil partner is treated as having died on the date the order was made final, so the gift lapses and the executor appointment fails, while the rest of the will stands. Option A is wrong because divorce does not revoke a will at all.

394. You are instructed to prepare mirror wills for a married couple. During a short separate discussion the husband tells you he has a child from an earlier relationship whom his wife knows nothing about, and asks you to keep this from her. What is the correct approach?

A. Explain you cannot keep it from her and may have to stop acting.

B. Prepare the wills as instructed and keep the disclosure on his file.

C. Tell the wife immediately, since joint instructions waive all client confidentiality.

D. Prepare his will only, and postpone hers until the position changes.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Explain you cannot keep it from her and may have to stop acting): where you act for both, you cannot hold one client's material information secret from the other, and that should be explained at the outset. If the conflict stands you may have to cease acting for one or both. Option C is wrong because you disclose nothing without his agreement; you withdraw instead.

395. Yusuf wishes to revoke his will but does not want to make a new one just yet. He proposes to sign a short letter stating that his existing will is revoked, and to keep it with his papers. He asks what formality the letter needs. What should you tell him?

A. A signed letter suffices, as no particular formality applies to revocation.

B. The letter must be sent to the executors named in the existing will.

C. It must be executed with the same formalities as a will.

D. It must be signed before a solicitor who certifies his intention to revoke.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (It must be executed with the same formalities as a will): a written declaration of revocation is one of the four methods, but only if it is executed with the section 9 formalities, so it must be signed and witnessed like a will. Option A is wrong because a bare signed letter satisfies none of the four recognised methods of revocation.

396. In June 2020 Ronald gave 100,000 pounds outright to his daughter and kept no benefit in it. He made no other lifetime gifts. He died in July 2027, more than seven years later. His executors ask how that gift affects the inheritance tax on his estate. What is the position?

A. It is added back to the estate, since lifetime gifts are always counted.

B. It is added back, but the tax on it is reduced by taper.

C. It remains chargeable, because the seven years run from the tax year end.

D. It drops out of account entirely, as he survived it by seven years.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It drops out of account entirely, as he survived it by seven years): an outright lifetime gift to an individual is a potentially exempt transfer and falls out of account completely once the donor survives seven years. Option B applies taper, which only arises where the donor dies within the seven year period.

397. A client asks that you and your firm be appointed as her executors, and that the will contain a charging clause. She has an adult son who is both willing and capable of acting as her executor. What must you do before including that appointment and clause in her will?

A. Obtain the son's written consent to the firm acting in his place.

B. Include the charging clause and explain the firm's rates after the grant.

C. Decline, because appointing your own firm is a conflict of interest.

D. Explain the alternatives and set out the charging basis in writing.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Explain the alternatives and set out the charging basis in writing): the client must understand that a lay executor may act and instruct solicitors when needed, and must be told in writing how the firm will charge under any charging clause. Option C is wrong because a professional appointment is permissible provided the client makes an informed choice.

398. A testator made a will in 2024 giving a legacy to a friend. In 2025 he made a second will revoking the first entirely. In 2026 he executed a codicil expressed to be supplemental to the 2024 will and confirming it. The friend asks what effect the codicil has. What is the position?

A. The codicil is void, because the will it supplements had been revoked.

B. The codicil takes effect, but only as to the appointment of executors.

C. The codicil revokes the 2025 will and leaves the estate undisposed of.

D. A codicil may revive a revoked will, so the legacy can take effect.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (A codicil may revive a revoked will, so the legacy can take effect): a codicil republishes the will it confirms as at the codicil's own date, and a codicil showing an intention to revive a revoked will can restore it. Option A assumes revocation is final, which overlooks revival by codicil.

399. You ask the general practitioner of a seriously ill client to assess her capacity and to witness the will. The practitioner declines to become involved at all. The client still wishes to proceed, and appears to you to understand fully what she is doing. What should you do?

A. Record the refusal on file and proceed with a full note of your assessment.

B. Refuse to prepare the will until another medical practitioner agrees to act.

C. Prepare the will and ask the client to obtain a medical report afterwards.

D. Prepare the will and have it witnessed by two nurses at the hospital.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Record the refusal on file and proceed with a full note of your assessment): the golden rule is good practice, not a precondition of validity, so a doctor's refusal does not prevent the will being made. You record the refusal and your own reasoning. Option B would leave a seriously ill client without a will for a reason the law does not require.

400. A client sold her large family home in 2024, moved into a small rented flat, and gave much of the sale proceeds to her children. She asks whether her estate can still benefit from the residence nil rate band. The figures will be supplied to you. What is the position?

A. It is lost, because she no longer owns a qualifying residential interest.

B. It is available in full, since she owned a home at some point.

C. A downsizing addition may be available where a home was sold or downsized.

D. It is available only if the flat itself passes to her lineal descendants.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (A downsizing addition may be available where a home was sold or downsized): the residence nil rate band carries a downsizing addition precisely so that selling or moving to a smaller home does not defeat it. Option A applies the ordinary condition without noticing the addition designed for these facts.

Business Law and Practice, including organisations, rules and procedures

401. A client currently trades as a sole trader and is considering incorporating her business. She asks her solicitor to explain, without reference to any rates or thresholds, who is taxed on the trading profits after incorporation and under which tax. Which answer states the correct principle?

A. The company pays corporation tax; a sole trader pays income tax personally.

B. Both pay corporation tax, but the sole trader also accounts for national insurance.

C. The company pays income tax on profits it distributes to directors as salary.

D. A sole trader pays corporation tax once turnover passes the registration threshold.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The company pays corporation tax; a sole trader pays income tax personally): a company is a separate taxable person charged to corporation tax on its taxable total profits, while an unincorporated trader is charged to income tax on trading profits with national insurance. Option B is wrong because corporation tax applies only to companies and similar bodies, never to an individual trading in her own name.

402. A company wants to allot shares for cash to a new investor without offering them to the existing members first. The board asks how the statutory pre emption rights can properly be set aside for that particular allotment. Which answer is correct?

A. By an ordinary resolution of the members disapplying the statutory pre emption rights.

B. By a board resolution recording that the allotment is in the company's best interests.

C. By a special resolution of the members disapplying the statutory pre emption rights.

D. By the written consent of the investor to whom the new shares are to be allotted.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (By a special resolution of the members disapplying the statutory pre emption rights): disapplication requires the seventy five per cent threshold, because the members are giving up a protection the statute gives them. Option A applies the ordinary resolution threshold, which would let a bare majority strip the minority of the very right that protects it against dilution.

403. A member of a company believes a director has diverted a contract to a business of his own, causing the company loss. She wants the wrong put right and asks whether she can sue in the company's name. Which statement correctly describes a derivative claim?

A. She sues in her own name and any damages recovered belong to her personally.

B. She may sue only if she already held her shares when the wrong was committed.

C. She may bring the claim without any permission, provided the company remains solvent.

D. She sues on the company's behalf with permission, and any remedy is the company's.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (She sues on the company's behalf with permission, and any remedy is the company's): a derivative claim is brought by a member in respect of a wrong done to the company, the court's permission to continue is required, and any recovery belongs to the company rather than the claimant. Option A confuses a derivative claim with a personal claim, and is the distinction that decides which route a minority client should take.

404. An administrator is appointed over a manufacturing company. She concludes that the company itself cannot be rescued as a going concern, but that selling the business as a whole would give the creditors more than an immediate winding up would. What should she now do?

A. Wind the company up at once, the rescue objective having proved impossible.

B. Realise the assets for the secured creditors, that being the next objective.

C. Pursue the better result for the creditors as a whole than on a winding up.

D. Apply to the court for directions, because the first statutory objective has failed.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Pursue the better result for the creditors as a whole than on a winding up): the administrator must work through the statutory objectives in order, and where rescuing the company is not reasonably practicable the second objective applies. Option B jumps to the third objective, which is available only where neither of the first two can be achieved.

405. A company's relevant accounts show accumulated realised profits of two hundred thousand pounds and accumulated realised losses of one hundred and eighty thousand pounds. The board wishes to pay a dividend of fifty thousand pounds to its shareholders this month. What is the correct advice to the board?

A. The dividend is lawful, because realised profits comfortably exceed fifty thousand pounds.

B. The dividend is unlawful, because profits available for distribution are only twenty thousand.

C. The dividend is lawful, provided the members first approve it by special resolution.

D. The dividend is unlawful, because a dividend cannot exceed the current year's trading profit.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The dividend is unlawful, because profits available for distribution are only twenty thousand): profits available for distribution are accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses, so the fund here is twenty thousand pounds and a fifty thousand pound dividend exceeds it. Option A looks only at the profits side of the calculation and ignores the accumulated losses that must be deducted.

406. A director entered into a transaction in breach of his general duties. He holds fifty five per cent of the shares and proposes to have the members ratify the breach by ordinary resolution, voting his own shares in favour of it. The minority shareholders object. What is the position?

A. Ratification is effective, because he is entitled to vote his shares as he wishes.

B. Ratification fails, because the votes of the director in breach are left out of account.

C. Ratification requires a special resolution, so his holding is in any event insufficient.

D. Ratification is impossible, since a breach of a general duty may not be ratified.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Ratification fails, because the votes of the director in breach are left out of account): members may ratify a director's breach by ordinary resolution, but the votes of the director concerned and of any person connected with him are disregarded, so his fifty five per cent cannot carry the resolution. Option A is wrong because it applies the ordinary rule that a shareholder votes in his own interest, which is displaced on a ratification vote.

407. A client is buying a business for two million pounds. He explains that the money is coming from an account in his own name at a London bank. The fee earner then asks him how he came by that wealth in the first place. Why is that second question asked?

A. Source of wealth is a different question from source of funds and must be asked.

B. It is asked only where the client is a politically exposed person or a close associate.

C. It replaces the source of funds enquiry once a bank account has been identified.

D. It is asked so that the firm can advise the client properly on his tax position.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Source of wealth is a different question from source of funds and must be asked): source of funds asks where this particular money comes from and by what route, while source of wealth asks how the client came to have the wealth from which it is drawn, and both must be understood. Option C is wrong because identifying an account answers only the narrower question.

408. A firm has made a disclosure and, on the reporting officer's advice, decides to stop acting for the corporate client. The client writes asking for a full explanation of why the retainer is being brought to an end. What should the firm say in its closing letter?

A. Set out the suspicion in full, because the client is owed a candid explanation.

B. State plainly that the firm suspects the transaction involves the proceeds of crime.

C. Cease to act and give no reason, so as not to prejudice any investigation.

D. Explain that a report has been made but that the firm can say nothing more.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Cease to act and give no reason, so as not to prejudice any investigation): where a firm withdraws after a disclosure it should give no reason, because any explanation risks tipping off. Option D is wrong because telling the client that a report exists is itself the disclosure the tipping off offence is designed to prevent, even if no detail is given.

409. A partner in a firm of estate agents orders sixty laptops from a supplier, intending to resell them privately for his own benefit. The supplier knows nothing of that plan and the order looks like an ordinary office purchase. The firm now refuses to pay. Is the firm bound?

A. No, because the partner acted for his own benefit rather than for the firm.

B. Yes, because the act was done in the usual way of the firm's business.

C. No, because a partner binds the firm only with the consent of all partners.

D. Yes, because each partner guarantees the contracts made by every other partner.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Yes, because the act was done in the usual way of the firm's business): every partner is an agent of the firm, and the firm is bound by an act carried on in the usual way of its business unless the partner had no authority and the third party knew that. Option A is wrong because the partner's private motive is invisible to the supplier and does not affect the firm's liability.

410. At a general meeting of a private company, the members vote on an ordinary resolution to approve a transaction with a director. Holders of exactly fifty per cent of the votes cast vote in favour and the remainder vote against. The chair asks whether the resolution has been passed. What is the answer?

A. It has passed, because an ordinary resolution needs fifty per cent of the votes cast.

B. It has passed, because a resolution is carried unless a majority votes against it.

C. It has not passed, because approval of this transaction needs seventy five per cent.

D. It has not passed, because an ordinary resolution needs more than fifty per cent.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It has not passed, because an ordinary resolution needs more than fifty per cent): an ordinary resolution is passed by a simple majority, meaning more than half of the votes cast, so an exact tie fails. Option A is the classic slip: fifty per cent is not more than fifty per cent, and the resolution therefore falls.

411. Eighteen months before it went into liquidation, and at a time when it could not pay its debts, a company transferred a freehold unit worth four hundred thousand pounds to the managing director's wife for one hundred thousand pounds. The liquidator asks how to characterise it. What is the answer?

A. A preference, because a connected person received company property before the liquidation.

B. A lawful sale, because the company received real consideration for the property.

C. Wrongful trading, because the directors carried on trading while the company was insolvent.

D. A transaction at an undervalue, made within two years of the onset of insolvency.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (A transaction at an undervalue, made within two years of the onset of insolvency): the company received consideration significantly less in value than it gave, within the two year period, at a time when it was unable to pay its debts, so the court may restore the position. Option A is wrong because a preference concerns improving the position of an existing creditor, which the director's wife was not.

412. A firm has acted for a corporate client for six years. In that time the ownership of the client has changed twice and the business has moved into an entirely new sector. The fee earner says that the original identity checks are still on the file. What does the regime require now?

A. Ongoing monitoring, so the due diligence must be kept up to date.

B. Nothing, because identity was verified when the relationship was first established.

C. A fresh report to the reporting officer whenever the ownership of a client changes.

D. Enhanced due diligence, which applies to any client of six years' standing.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Ongoing monitoring, so the due diligence must be kept up to date): customer due diligence includes monitoring the relationship throughout its life, which means keeping documents and information current and reviewing them when the ownership or the nature of the business changes. Option B treats due diligence as a one off exercise at the outset, which is the very error the monitoring obligation addresses.

413. A solicitor who is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority advises a client on the merits of buying shares in a quoted company, and then arranges the purchase through a broker. She asks about her own position. What does section 19 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 provide?

A. The prohibition applies only to firms holding client money in the course of business.

B. The prohibition is a civil matter only, so the agreement remains fully enforceable.

C. No person may carry on a regulated activity unless that person is authorised or exempt.

D. Solicitors fall outside the regime entirely, because they are regulated by the SRA.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (No person may carry on a regulated activity unless that person is authorised or exempt): the general prohibition in section 19 applies to any person carrying on a regulated activity in the United Kingdom, or purporting to do so. Option D is wrong because SRA regulation does not displace the general prohibition; a firm must instead find an exclusion or rely on the exemption for professional firms.

414. The members of a private company wish to deal with three matters quickly by written resolution: adopting new articles, approving a loan to a director, and removing a director from office. The solicitor advises that one of the three cannot be done in that way. Which is it?

A. Adopting the new articles, because a constitutional change requires a general meeting.

B. Approving the loan, because the memorandum must be laid before a general meeting.

C. Removing the director, because removal must be dealt with at a general meeting.

D. None of them, because a private company may pass any resolution in writing.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Removing the director, because removal must be dealt with at a general meeting): removal of a director and removal of an auditor are the two matters excluded from the written resolution procedure, because the officer concerned has a right to make representations and be heard. Option A is wrong because new articles may be adopted by written special resolution without any meeting.

415. A director of a construction company learns of a development opportunity while visiting a client on company business. He takes the opportunity personally through his own company and makes a large profit. The company itself was not in a position to fund the project. What is the position?

A. He keeps the profit, because the company could not have funded the project anyway.

B. He keeps the profit, provided he told the client that he was acting personally.

C. He must account for the profit, having failed to avoid a conflict of interest.

D. He must pay damages measured by the loss the company can prove it suffered.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (He must account for the profit, having failed to avoid a conflict of interest): the duty to avoid a situation in which a director has an interest conflicting with the company's applies in particular to the exploitation of property, information or opportunity, and it applies whether or not the company could have taken the opportunity itself. Option D is wrong because the remedy is an account of the gain, not compensation for a proved loss.

416. Members holding sixty per cent of the votes in a private company want a director removed at once. To save time they propose to circulate a written resolution rather than call a meeting. The company secretary asks the solicitor whether that will work. What is the correct advice?

A. No, removal needs a general meeting and special notice of twenty eight days.

B. Yes, a written resolution may remove a director if holders of fifty per cent agree.

C. Yes, provided the director is given seven days in which to make written representations.

D. No, removal of a director requires a special resolution passed at a general meeting.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No, removal needs a general meeting and special notice of twenty eight days): removal under section 168 of the Companies Act 2006 is one of the two matters that cannot be dealt with by written resolution, and special notice must be given so that the director can make representations and be heard. Option D gets the meeting right but the threshold wrong, because the resolution to remove is an ordinary one.

417. A company's articles provide that a named member shall be the company's solicitor for life. The company later instructs a different firm. The member sues on the articles, relying on the statutory contract between the company and its members. What is the likely outcome of that claim?

A. He succeeds, because the articles bind the company and each member contractually.

B. He succeeds, because the relevant article was validly adopted by special resolution.

C. He fails, because the articles may only ever be enforced by the company itself.

D. He fails, because the statutory contract covers rights held in the capacity of member.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (He fails, because the statutory contract covers rights held in the capacity of member): the articles bind the company and its members as if each had signed them, but only in respect of membership rights. A right to be retained as the company's solicitor is an outsider right and is not enforceable through the articles. Option A states the general rule accurately but ignores the limit on the capacity in which the right is held.

418. A director has been found to have carried on the company's business with intent to defraud its creditors. The liquidator asks what consequences may follow beyond an order that he personally contribute to the company's assets in the liquidation. Which answer is correct?

A. He may be fined but cannot be prevented from acting as a director again.

B. He may be disqualified from acting as a director for up to fifteen years.

C. He may be disqualified for at most five years, running from the date of liquidation.

D. He must be made bankrupt before any disqualification order can be considered.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (He may be disqualified from acting as a director for up to fifteen years): both wrongful and fraudulent trading may lead to a disqualification order, and fifteen years is the maximum period. Option C understates the maximum, and the length matters because disqualification, not the contribution order, is often the more serious practical consequence for the individual.

419. A firm is instructed by a company on a share sale. Its shares are held as to sixty per cent by a holding company, thirty per cent by an individual and ten per cent by an employee trust. The trainee asks who must be identified as a beneficial owner. What is the test?

A. Every registered shareholder must be identified, whatever the size of the holding.

B. Only the individual, because a corporate shareholder cannot be a beneficial owner.

C. Individuals who ultimately own or control more than twenty five per cent, or otherwise control.

D. Only the directors, because they control the company's affairs from day to day.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Individuals who ultimately own or control more than twenty five per cent, or otherwise control): the firm must look through corporate shareholders to the individuals who ultimately own or control the client, or who otherwise exercise control over it, and check the register of people with significant control. Option B is wrong because a corporate holding is not the end of the enquiry but the reason to keep going up the chain.

420. A private company circulates a written ordinary resolution to its five members, who between them hold all the voting rights in equal shares. Two members sign and return the resolution in favour. Two vote against it. The fifth does not reply at all. Has the written resolution been passed?

A. No, because the threshold is measured against the total eligible voting rights.

B. Yes, because the threshold is measured against the members who actually replied.

C. Yes, because a written resolution passes once a majority of the members sign it.

D. No, because a written resolution must be signed by every eligible member of the company.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No, because the threshold is measured against the total eligible voting rights): a written resolution is passed when the required majority of the total voting rights of eligible members has signified agreement, so silence counts against the resolution. Two of five is only forty per cent. Option B is wrong because a written resolution is not counted like a poll at a meeting, where only votes cast matter.

421. A lender holds a qualifying floating charge over the whole of a company's business. The company is failing and the lender wants an administrator appointed quickly, without the delay and cost of a court hearing. Can it achieve that, and if so how?

A. No, an administrator may only be appointed by an order of the court.

B. No, only the company or its directors may appoint an administrator out of court.

C. Yes, but only with the written consent of the company's unsecured creditors.

D. Yes, a qualifying floating charge holder may appoint an administrator out of court.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Yes, a qualifying floating charge holder may appoint an administrator out of court): appointment may be made by court order or, out of court, by the company, its directors or the holder of a qualifying floating charge. Option B is wrong because it leaves out the charge holder, whose out of court route is the quickest of the three.

422. A private company wishes to hold a general meeting in six days' time to pass a special resolution. Its two members hold the voting shares as to ninety five per cent and five per cent, and both are willing to attend on that date. What must the company obtain?

A. Nothing, because fourteen days' notice is required only for an annual general meeting.

B. The written consent of the holder of five per cent of the voting shares.

C. An order of the court permitting the meeting to be held on shorter notice.

D. Consent to short notice from a majority in number holding ninety per cent of shares.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Consent to short notice from a majority in number holding ninety per cent of shares): the default notice period for a general meeting of a private company is fourteen clear days, and a meeting may be held on shorter notice only with the agreement of a majority in number of the members holding at least ninety per cent of the voting shares. Option B is wrong because consent must come from a majority in number as well as the required percentage of shares.

423. A private company's articles give the directors a discretion to refuse to register a transfer of shares. A member transfers her shares to her brother and the directors decline to register him. The brother says the transfer is complete because the stock transfer form was properly executed. What is the position?

A. The transfer is complete, because execution and delivery pass the full title to him.

B. The transfer is complete, because directors may not refuse a transfer to a family member.

C. He is not a member, because the company is bound only on registration of the transfer.

D. He is a member, but has no right to vote until the register has been updated.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (He is not a member, because the company is bound only on registration of the transfer): membership depends on entry in the register of members, so a refusal to register under a power in the articles leaves the transferee holding an equitable interest only. Option A is wrong because executing and delivering the form transfers the beneficial interest but does not make the transferee a member.

424. The directors of a private company that has only one class of ordinary shares wish to allot further shares of that same class. The articles say nothing at all about allotment. The company secretary asks whether a members' resolution is needed before the board may allot. What is the position?

A. An ordinary resolution granting authority is required before the directors may allot shares.

B. The directors may allot without further authority, the articles not restricting them.

C. A special resolution is required, because an allotment alters the company's share capital.

D. The directors may allot only after offering the shares to the company's secured creditors.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The directors may allot without further authority, the articles not restricting them): where a private company has only one class of shares, the directors may exercise the power to allot shares of that class unless the articles say otherwise. Option A states the position for a company with more than one class, or where the articles impose a restriction, which is not this company.

425. A company must this month remove a director, approve a loan to another director, adopt new articles, and place itself into members' voluntary liquidation. The trainee asks which of those four matters require a special resolution rather than an ordinary resolution. What is the answer?

A. Removal of the director and adoption of the new articles only.

B. Approval of the loan and the members' voluntary liquidation only.

C. Adoption of the new articles only, the other three requiring ordinary resolutions.

D. Adoption of the new articles and the members' voluntary liquidation only.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Adoption of the new articles and the members' voluntary liquidation only): altering the articles and resolving on a voluntary winding up both need seventy five per cent, while removing a director and approving a loan to a director need only an ordinary resolution. Option A is wrong because removal under section 168 is an ordinary resolution, although it must be taken at a meeting after special notice.

426. A private company appoints a new director by board resolution, as its articles expressly permit. The finance manager asks whether anything further must be done once the appointment takes effect, and whether the members must also vote on the appointment. Which answer is correct?

A. The members must confirm the appointment by ordinary resolution within fourteen days.

B. The appointment must be notified to Companies House and entered in the company register.

C. Nothing further is needed, because a board appointment takes effect on the day made.

D. The appointment must be advertised in the London Gazette before it can take effect.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The appointment must be notified to Companies House and entered in the company register): where the articles allow the board to appoint, no member resolution is needed, but every appointment and termination must be entered in the register of directors and notified to the Registrar. Option C is wrong because it overlooks the filing and register requirements that follow a valid appointment.

427. A board is deciding whether to close a loss making depot. One director argues that the return on capital to shareholders governs the decision. Another says the board must weigh the workforce and the longer term consequences. Which statement reflects the general duty in section 172?

A. The duty is owed to shareholders, so return on their capital governs the decision.

B. The board must give the interests of the employees priority over those of members.

C. The board must promote the company's success, having regard to the listed factors.

D. The duty is owed to employees and creditors in the same way as to members.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The board must promote the company's success, having regard to the listed factors): section 172 requires a director to act in the way he considers, in good faith, most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of the members as a whole, having regard to matters including the long term, employees and business relationships. Option A is wrong because it treats those listed factors as irrelevant when the section requires the board to have regard to them.

428. A firm relying on the professional firms exemption is asked to manage a client's investment portfolio on a discretionary basis, deciding for the client what to buy and what to sell. The compliance officer is uneasy about accepting the instruction. What should the firm do?

A. Accept the work, because managing investments is incidental to the firm's legal services.

B. Decline and refer the client to an authorised person, this falling outside the exemption.

C. Accept the work, provided the firm accounts to the client for any commission received.

D. Accept the work and notify the SRA once the first transactions have been carried out.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Decline and refer the client to an authorised person, this falling outside the exemption): discretionary portfolio management is mainstream investment business rather than an activity incidental to legal services, and the exemption cannot be used for a prohibited activity. Option C is wrong because accounting for commission is only one of several conditions and cannot cure work the exemption does not reach.

429. A company enters administration. A supplier with an unpaid invoice wants to issue proceedings against it, and a lessor wants to repossess equipment held under a lease. Both are told that they cannot simply go ahead as they had planned. What is the reason they are given?

A. Their claims have been extinguished by the appointment of the administrator.

B. A moratorium halts enforcement action against the company during the administration.

C. They must first obtain the consent of the company's directors before proceeding.

D. Administration converts every unsecured claim into a secured claim over the assets.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (A moratorium halts enforcement action against the company during the administration): the statutory moratorium stops proceedings and enforcement, including repossession of goods, without the administrator's consent or the permission of the court, which is what gives the rescue a chance to work. Option A is wrong because the claims survive; only their enforcement is suspended.

430. A director realised eight months ago that there was no reasonable prospect of the company avoiding insolvent liquidation. He carried on ordering stock on credit and took no advice at all. The company is now in liquidation with a much larger deficiency. What claim does the liquidator have?

A. Wrongful trading, so the court may order him to contribute to the company's assets.

B. Fraudulent trading, because trading on while insolvent is dishonest conduct in itself.

C. No claim, because a director owes duties to the members rather than the creditors.

D. A preference claim, because the later suppliers were paid ahead of the earlier ones.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Wrongful trading, so the court may order him to contribute to the company's assets): wrongful trading arises where a director knew or ought to have concluded that insolvent liquidation could not be avoided and did not take every step to minimise the loss to creditors. Option B is wrong because fraudulent trading needs dishonesty, and continuing to trade over optimistically is not by itself dishonest.

431. An investor asks whether he should subscribe for newly issued shares or instead buy shares from an existing member. He wants the route that puts fresh money into the company itself rather than into another shareholder's pocket. Which answer correctly explains the difference?

A. A transfer, because the consideration passes to the company on registration of the buyer.

B. An allotment, because the subscription money is paid to the company itself.

C. Both, because the company receives the price and then accounts to the seller for it.

D. Neither, because consideration for shares is held on trust for the members generally.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (An allotment, because the subscription money is paid to the company itself): on an allotment the company creates and issues new shares and receives the subscription monies, whereas on a transfer an existing share simply changes hands and the price goes to the seller. Option A reverses the two, and the distinction decides whether the transaction raises capital or merely changes the ownership of the company.

432. A client is selling her business. The buyer has offered either to buy the trade and assets, or instead to buy her shares in the company. She asks why her solicitor keeps raising financial services on one route but says nothing about it on the other. What is the explanation?

A. An asset sale involves a specified investment, because goodwill is a form of security.

B. Shares are a specified investment, while the goodwill and assets of a business are not.

C. Both routes involve specified investments, but only the share sale is by way of business.

D. Neither route involves a specified investment, so the point is one of caution only.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Shares are a specified investment, while the goodwill and assets of a business are not): that difference is why an asset sale usually raises no financial services issue at all, while a share sale must be worked through the exclusions and, if necessary, the professional firms exemption. Option A is wrong because goodwill is simply a business asset and appears nowhere in the list of specified investments.

433. A solicitor tells a client that shares in a particular company look a poor buy at the price offered and that she should not proceed with the purchase. He gives no other advice and makes no arrangements. The trainee asks whether that is a specified activity. What is the analysis?

A. No, because advising a client not to buy cannot amount to advising on the merits.

B. No, because advice is a specified activity only where the solicitor also arranges the deal.

C. Yes, advising on the merits of buying or selling a particular investment is specified.

D. Yes, but only because the advice was given to a client for a fee.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Yes, advising on the merits of buying or selling a particular investment is specified): advice on the merits covers advice to sell or not to buy just as much as advice to buy, provided it relates to a particular investment rather than to investments in general. Option A draws a distinction the definition does not make, and generic advice about types of investment would be a better answer to the general prohibition.

434. A company can meet each debt as it falls due, but it has given a guarantee which will almost certainly be called, and once that is taken into account its liabilities exceed its assets. The finance director says contingent liabilities are ignored. What is the correct position?

A. He is right, because only present liabilities count towards the balance sheet test.

B. The balance sheet test takes account of contingent and prospective liabilities too.

C. He is right, because a guarantee is not a liability until a demand has been made.

D. The company is solvent, because it can pay each of its debts as they fall due.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The balance sheet test takes account of contingent and prospective liabilities too): the value of a company's assets is compared with its liabilities including those that are contingent and prospective, so a guarantee likely to be called cannot be left out. Option D is wrong because satisfying the cash flow test does not save a company which fails the balance sheet test.

435. One partner in a two partner firm works full time in the business while the other takes no active part in it at all. There is no written partnership agreement. The working partner claims a salary for her work before the profits are divided. Is she entitled to one?

A. No, because the default rules give a partner no salary for acting in the business.

B. Yes, because a partner working full time is entitled to reasonable remuneration first.

C. Yes, but only where the other partner takes no active part in the business.

D. No, unless she first gives written notice of her claim to the other partner.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No, because the default rules give a partner no salary for acting in the business): under the Partnership Act 1890 no partner is entitled to remuneration for acting in the partnership business, so the working partner's only reward is her equal profit share. Option B assumes a fairness the Act does not supply, which is precisely why an agreement should provide for a salary.

436. A solicitor advises the board of a company which is close to insolvency but still trading. The directors ask what to do about a pressing creditor threatening proceedings, and about a warehouse which they could sell cheaply to a company owned by one of them. What is the best advice?

A. Pay the pressing creditor first and sell the warehouse in order to raise cash quickly.

B. Continue trading as normal, since the company has not entered any formal procedure.

C. Take insolvency advice at once, prefer no creditor and do not sell assets cheaply.

D. Resign from the board immediately, which brings any personal exposure to an end.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Take insolvency advice at once, prefer no creditor and do not sell assets cheaply): as insolvency approaches the directors must shift their focus to the creditors as a whole, and paying one creditor ahead of others or selling to a connected party at a low price invites preference and undervalue claims. Option D is wrong because resignation does not undo exposure for the period in which the director acted.

437. A company wishes to disapply the statutory pre emption rights on a proposed allotment of shares for cash to a new investor. The finance director asks what level of member approval is needed before those rights can be set aside. Which answer is correct?

A. An ordinary resolution, needing more than fifty per cent of the votes cast.

B. A special resolution, needing not less than seventy five per cent of votes cast.

C. A board resolution, because the allotment of shares is a matter for the directors.

D. Unanimous consent of the existing members, because their holdings will be diluted.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (A special resolution, needing not less than seventy five per cent of votes cast): disapplying statutory pre emption rights is one of the matters the Companies Act 2006 reserves to a special resolution, alongside altering the articles, and a special resolution is also what the Insolvency Act 1986 requires for a members' voluntary winding up. Option A applies the ordinary resolution threshold, which governs matters such as appointing directors, not the removal of a statutory protection.

438. A director inherits a shareholding in a key supplier three months after the company entered into a five year supply contract with that supplier. She made no declaration when the contract was made, because she had no interest at that date. What does the Companies Act 2006 now require of her?

A. She must declare her interest in the existing transaction to the other directors.

B. She need do nothing, because no declaration is required once contracts are made.

C. She must obtain member approval by ordinary resolution for the existing supply contract.

D. She must transfer the inherited shares away before the next board meeting is held.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (She must declare her interest in the existing transaction to the other directors): section 182 requires a declaration where a director is interested in a transaction the company has already entered into, which is the counterpart of the section 177 duty for proposed transactions. Option B is wrong because it would leave a gap allowing an interest acquired after contracting to go undisclosed.

439. A director concluded that insolvent liquidation could not be avoided. He immediately took insolvency advice, stopped taking customer deposits, minuted the board's reasoning and cut costs in order to preserve assets. The company nonetheless failed. How does the court approach his position on a wrongful trading claim?

A. He is liable, because the company went into insolvent liquidation despite the steps taken.

B. He is liable, because only resigning from the board can protect a director here.

C. He escapes liability, because he acted honestly throughout the whole of that period.

D. He escapes liability if he took every step to minimise the loss to creditors.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (He escapes liability if he took every step to minimise the loss to creditors): the statutory defence turns on whether the director took every step with a view to minimising the potential loss to creditors, judged by the standard of a reasonably diligent person. Option C is wrong because honesty alone is no answer; the question is what steps were actually taken once the position was clear.

440. A fee earner acting on a company acquisition begins to suspect that the purchase money is the proceeds of crime. She wants to know what she should do next, and whether she should first put her concerns to the client to see what he says. What is the correct course?

A. Raise the concern with the client first, and report only if his answer is unsatisfactory.

B. Report to the firm's money laundering reporting officer as soon as is practicable.

C. Report directly to the police, because an internal report would only delay disclosure.

D. Take no action unless she has actual knowledge rather than a mere suspicion.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Report to the firm's money laundering reporting officer as soon as is practicable): every firm within the regulations appoints an officer to receive internal reports, and a fee earner who knows or suspects, or has reasonable grounds to suspect, must report to that officer. Option A is dangerous, because putting the suspicion to the client risks the separate offence of tipping off.

441. A client will take twenty per cent of the shares in a new company. She wants a genuine veto over the issue of further shares, one which the majority cannot later strip from her. Her adviser must decide where to place that protection. What is the better advice?

A. Place it in the articles, which bind all present and future members alike.

B. Place it in the articles, because they can be altered only by unanimous consent.

C. Place it in a shareholders' agreement, which can be varied only with her consent.

D. Place it in her service contract, which the majority cannot lawfully bring to an end.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Place it in a shareholders' agreement, which can be varied only with her consent): the agreement is a contract between its parties and is altered only by their unanimous agreement, so a minority veto in it is real. Option A is the trap: articles can be amended by special resolution, so a holder of twenty per cent cannot block a change and the very majority the veto exists to control could vote it away.

442. A firm is instructed on a company purchase by a client who is a serving government minister in another country, and part of the funding will come from a company in a high risk third country. The fee earner asks what level of due diligence applies. What is required?

A. Standard due diligence, since the client is well known and easily identified.

B. Simplified due diligence, because a public official's position is a matter of record.

C. Standard due diligence, together with a note of the funding route on the file.

D. Enhanced due diligence, the client being a politically exposed person.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Enhanced due diligence, the client being a politically exposed person): enhanced measures are required where the risk is high, including a politically exposed person or their family or close associates, and a party in a high risk third country, so both features here point the same way. Option B is wrong because a politically exposed person attracts more scrutiny, not less.

443. A trainee is asked to set out the order in which the financial services questions should be worked through before her firm advises a client on a contract of insurance. She drafts a short checklist for the file. Which sequence is correct?

A. Specified investment, specified activity, by way of business, exclusion, then the exemption.

B. Exemption first, then exclusion, then whether the client is an individual or a company.

C. Whether a fee is charged, then whether the firm is authorised, then the client's status.

D. Whether the SRA has been notified, then whether the transaction exceeds any threshold.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Specified investment, specified activity, by way of business, exclusion, then the exemption): the analysis asks first whether the activity is caught at all, then whether an exclusion takes it out, and only then whether the professional firms exemption can be relied upon, failing which the client must be referred to an authorised person. Option B reverses the last two steps, and the exemption is the fallback rather than the starting point.

444. Miriam runs a bakery in Cardiff as a sole trader. The business borrows to buy an oven and then fails, leaving trade debts of eighty thousand pounds. Her accountant asks how those debts, and the profits the bakery made in earlier years, are treated. Which statement is correct?

A. She is personally liable for the business debts and pays income tax on profits.

B. Her liability is limited to the capital she introduced into the bakery business.

C. The bakery is a separate legal person and it alone owes the trade debts.

D. She pays corporation tax on profits and is liable only for unpaid share capital.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (She is personally liable for the business debts and pays income tax on profits): a sole trader is not a separate legal person, so the business assets and liabilities are hers, and the profits are taxed on her as trading income with national insurance. Option B is wrong because limited liability is a consequence of incorporation and has no application to a sole trader, however the business is described to customers.

445. A supplier is owed thirty thousand pounds by a firm of three partners for goods sold to the firm. Two of the partners have no money at all. The supplier asks whether it can recover the whole sum from the third partner, who is wealthy. What is the position?

A. It may recover only one third of the debt from her, that being her share.

B. It may recover nothing from her personally, because the debt is owed by the firm.

C. It may recover the whole sum, but only once the firm's own assets are exhausted.

D. Partners are liable jointly for firm debts, so she may be sued for the whole.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Partners are liable jointly for firm debts, so she may be sued for the whole): every partner is liable jointly with the others for all debts of the firm incurred while she is a partner, and a creditor may enforce the whole debt against any solvent partner, leaving her to seek contribution. Option A confuses the sharing of losses between partners with liability to an outside creditor.

446. A growing engineering business needs two hundred thousand pounds of outside investment. The investor will not lend. She wants an equity stake carrying a right to dividends and a share of any future sale proceeds. The business currently trades as a general partnership. Which point should the adviser make?

A. A partnership may issue shares to the investor if the partners agree unanimously.

B. Only a company can issue shares, so incorporation would suit the investor's aim.

C. A partnership may grant the investor a floating charge over its share capital.

D. The investor must lend, because equity investment is confined to listed companies.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Only a company can issue shares, so incorporation would suit the investor's aim): raising money by issuing shares is a feature of the corporate medium, and it is a real advantage over a partnership, which can offer only a share of profits or a loan. Option A is wrong because a partnership has no share capital to issue, whatever the partners agree between themselves.

447. A private company proposes to allot new ordinary shares for cash to an outside investor. The existing shareholders have not been offered any of the new shares and no resolution has been passed about pre emption. One of them objects to the allotment. What is the correct analysis?

A. Pre emption rights apply only where shares are allotted for a non cash asset.

B. Pre emption rights bind the company only if they are written into its articles.

C. The shareholder's remedy is a petition alleging unfair prejudice rather than pre emption.
