D. Equity securities allotted for cash must first be offered to the existing shareholders.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Equity securities allotted for cash must first be offered to the existing shareholders): the statutory right of pre emption requires equity securities allotted for cash to be offered to existing holders in proportion to their existing holdings unless the right is disapplied. Option B is wrong because the right arises under the Companies Act 2006 itself and applies whether or not the articles mention it.

448. A partnership agreement forbids any partner to borrow more than ten thousand pounds without the consent of the others. A partner borrows fifty thousand pounds from a lender who has read the agreement and knows of the restriction. The firm refuses to repay the loan. What is the position?

A. The firm is bound, because an internal restriction cannot affect an outside lender.

B. The firm is bound, because borrowing falls within the usual course of most businesses.

C. The firm is not bound, because a loan of that size falls outside ordinary business.

D. The firm is not bound, because the lender knew that the partner lacked authority.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The firm is not bound, because the lender knew that the partner lacked authority): the firm is bound by acts done in the usual way of its business only where the partner either had authority or the outsider did not know of the restriction. Option A states the usual protection for a third party, but it is lost once the lender has actual knowledge of the limit.

449. Three shareholders sign a shareholders' agreement restricting the issue of new shares without unanimous consent. One of them later sells her shares to a buyer who never signs that agreement. The remaining two now claim the buyer is bound by the restriction. Is that claim correct?

A. No, the agreement is a contract and binds only the parties to it.

B. Yes, because a shareholders' agreement runs with the shares on any transfer of them.

C. Yes, because the agreement takes effect as part of the company's registered constitution.

D. No, unless the company itself was also named as a party to the agreement.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No, the agreement is a contract and binds only the parties to it): privity means an incoming shareholder takes free of a shareholders' agreement he has not signed, which is why such agreements require a deed of adherence on any transfer. Option B is wrong because obligations of this kind do not attach to the shares themselves, unlike provisions written into the articles.

450. A petition under section 994 succeeds. The petitioner holds a minority stake in a small private company and no longer wishes to be involved in the business at all. The court is now considering what order it should make on the petition. What is the usual remedy?

A. An order winding the company up and distributing any surplus among the members.

B. An order that the company pay the petitioner damages for her lost dividends.

C. An order that the majority buy the petitioner's shares at a proper valuation.

D. An order removing the offending directors and appointing an independent board instead.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (An order that the majority buy the petitioner's shares at a proper valuation): the court has a wide discretion, but the standard outcome is a share purchase order, which releases the minority from a company she can no longer work in. Option A is available in principle on a separate just and equitable winding up petition, but it destroys the business and is treated as a remedy of last resort.

451. A fee earner suspects that the funds for a corporate transaction are criminal property and has reported the matter internally. The reporting officer proposes to make an authorised disclosure and to await a response before the transaction goes ahead. Why does the timing of that disclosure matter?

A. It matters only for the firm's regulatory record and not for any criminal liability.

B. It matters because a disclosure made after completion attracts a higher penalty.

C. It matters because the client must be told once the disclosure has been made.

D. An authorised disclosure with consent may give a defence to a principal offence.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (An authorised disclosure with consent may give a defence to a principal offence): making the disclosure and obtaining consent before the transaction proceeds protects the firm against liability for the principal money laundering offences, which is why the transaction is held up. Option C is wrong and dangerous, because telling the client would risk the separate offence of tipping off.

452. A client wants to start a delivery business. She is anxious that competitors should not be able to read her accounts or discover who owns the business. She also wants to limit her exposure to trade creditors. Her adviser explains the trade off. Which statement is accurate?

A. A company keeps its accounts and its ownership private once it is incorporated.

B. Limited liability comes at the price of public filing of accounts and ownership.

C. A general partnership must file accounts but keeps its membership entirely private.

D. A sole trader must file annual accounts but maintains no register of ownership.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Limited liability comes at the price of public filing of accounts and ownership): a company obtains separate personality and limited liability, but its affairs become public through the register of members, the register of people with significant control and filed accounts. Option A is wrong because incorporation increases publicity rather than reducing it, so the client cannot have limited liability and privacy together.

453. A founder wants the terms regulating dividends and the appointment of directors to stay out of the public domain, but she also wants them to bind every future shareholder automatically. Her solicitor explains that she cannot have both features in one document. Which explanation is accurate?

A. The articles are private, so both of her aims can be met by amending them.

B. A shareholders' agreement is filed publicly but binds all future members automatically.

C. Both documents are filed at Companies House and both bind future members equally.

D. The articles are public but bind future members; the agreement is private but does not.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The articles are public but bind future members; the agreement is private but does not): the constitution is filed and binds members present and future, while a shareholders' agreement stays confidential and binds only its signatories. The founder must choose which feature matters more. Option A is wrong because the articles are a public document available for inspection at Companies House.

454. Three friends set up a company, each taking a third of the shares on the understanding that each would be a director and would share in the management. Two of them later remove the third from the board by ordinary resolution and stop paying dividends. What is her best remedy?

A. A derivative claim, because the removal was a wrong done to the company itself.

B. A claim on the articles, because removal by ordinary resolution is itself unlawful.

C. A petition alleging unfair prejudice, seeking an order that they buy her shares.

D. A claim for wrongful dismissal, which would restore her to the board of directors.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (A petition alleging unfair prejudice, seeking an order that they buy her shares): where members associate on the understanding that each will participate in management, exclusion from the board combined with the withholding of dividends is the classic unfair prejudice case, and a buy out order is the usual result. Option A fails because the wrong complained of is done to her as a member, not to the company.

455. After a disclosure has been made about a corporate client, the client telephones and asks why completion has stalled. The fee earner is tempted to explain that a report has been made, so that the client understands the reason for the delay. What is the correct course?

A. Explain the report, because the client is entitled to know why the matter has stopped.

B. Explain in general terms that a regulator has been contacted, without naming any offence.

C. Say nothing but confirm in writing that the firm suspects money laundering has occurred.

D. Say nothing about the report, since telling the client risks the offence of tipping off.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Say nothing about the report, since telling the client risks the offence of tipping off): once a disclosure has been made it is an offence to tell the client or anyone else of the report or of a contemplated investigation where that is likely to prejudice it. Option B is no safer, because a general indication that a report has gone in can prejudice an investigation just as effectively.

456. A partner retires from a firm of printers. Two months later a supplier sues the firm for goods it delivered before her retirement. She says her retirement brought her liability to an end. No release was ever agreed with the supplier. What is her position on that debt?

A. She remains liable, because retirement alone does not release her from existing debts.

B. She is free of liability, because the continuing partners have taken over the business.

C. She remains liable only if she failed to notify Companies House of her retirement.

D. She is free of liability, because the debt is owed by the firm alone.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (She remains liable, because retirement alone does not release her from existing debts): a retiring partner stays liable for debts and obligations incurred while she was a partner unless the creditor releases her, usually by a novation agreement between the creditor, the outgoing partner and the continuing partners. Option B is wrong because an arrangement between the partners cannot bind a creditor who is not a party to it.

457. A firm advises a client on the purchase of a freehold shop, and separately on the purchase of the entire issued share capital of the company which owns a rival shop. The trainee asks which of the two subject matters is a specified investment. What is the answer?

A. Both, because each transaction involves the acquisition of a valuable business asset.

B. Neither, because commercial property transactions fall outside the regulated regime.

C. The freehold shop, because land is a specified investment of the traditional kind.

D. The shares, because land is not a specified investment but shares are.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (The shares, because land is not a specified investment but shares are): the list of specified investments includes shares, debentures, government securities, insurance contracts and regulated mortgage contracts, but land itself is not on it. Option C reverses the position, and getting the point the right way round is what tells a fee earner which of two similar looking deals raises a financial services issue.

458. The members of a solvent company wish to wind it up and distribute the surplus among themselves. The directors are willing to swear to its solvency, and the company can pay all of its debts in full within twelve months. Which procedure applies to that winding up?

A. A members' voluntary liquidation, supported by a statutory declaration of solvency.

B. A creditors' voluntary liquidation, because every liquidation involves the creditors.

C. A compulsory liquidation, following a petition presented by the company itself.

D. An administration, because the company's business must first be offered for sale.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (A members' voluntary liquidation, supported by a statutory declaration of solvency): a solvent company is wound up by its members once the directors make the statutory declaration that the debts can be paid in full within the stated period. Option B applies where no such declaration can be made, so the creditors take control of the liquidation instead.

459. Four partners share a consultancy business on the Partnership Act 1890 defaults. Three of them wish to admit a fifth partner who would bring new clients with him. The fourth partner refuses. The three say that a three quarters majority is enough to carry the point. Who is right?

A. The three are right, because admitting a partner is an ordinary management decision.

B. The three are right, because a three quarters majority mirrors a special resolution.

C. The fourth is right, because a new partner may not be admitted without unanimous consent.

D. The fourth is right, but only if she shows the newcomer would harm the firm.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The fourth is right, because a new partner may not be admitted without unanimous consent): the Act provides that no person may be introduced as a partner without the consent of all existing partners, because partnership rests on mutual trust and each partner becomes liable for the acts of the others. Option A is wrong because admitting a partner is not an ordinary matter connected with the business.

460. A company adopted bespoke articles on incorporation dealing with directors' meetings and share transfers, but saying nothing at all about dividends. A dispute now arises about how a dividend is properly declared. The company argues that, because its own articles are silent, no rule governs the point. Is that right?

A. Yes, because bespoke articles displace the Model Articles entirely once they are adopted.

B. No, the Model Articles apply so far as they are not excluded or modified.

C. No, because dividends are governed only by any shareholders' agreement then in force.

D. Yes, so the board may declare a dividend on whatever terms it thinks fit.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (No, the Model Articles apply so far as they are not excluded or modified): the Model Articles for private companies limited by shares are the default constitution and fill any gap that bespoke articles leave. The dividend provisions therefore apply. Option A is wrong because bespoke articles displace the model only to the extent of the inconsistency, not wholesale.

461. A board proposes an interim dividend in October. The last annual accounts showed large distributable profits, but the management accounts for the current year show heavy realised losses which have wiped those profits out. The board says the annual accounts govern the question. What is the correct advice?

A. The annual accounts govern, because they are the accounts filed at Companies House.

B. Interim accounts are needed, because the dividend must be justified by the present position.

C. No accounts are needed at all, because an interim dividend is a matter for the board.

D. The dividend is lawful, because realised losses are left out of account until the year end.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Interim accounts are needed, because the dividend must be justified by the present position): a distribution must be justified by reference to relevant accounts, and where the last annual accounts no longer show the true position the directors must prepare interim accounts. Option A is wrong because relying on stale figures would let a company distribute profits that its accumulated realised losses have already consumed.

462. A minority shareholder holding six per cent of the voting capital of a private company wants a general meeting called to consider the removal of a director. The board refuses to call one, saying that only the directors may convene a general meeting. What is the correct position?

A. Members holding five per cent of the voting capital may require a meeting to be called.

B. Only the board may call a general meeting of a private company limited by shares.

C. The shareholder must first obtain permission from the court before convening a meeting.

D. The shareholder must hold ten per cent of the voting capital to require a meeting.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Members holding five per cent of the voting capital may require a meeting to be called): the Companies Act 2006 lets members with at least five per cent of the paid up voting capital require the directors to call a general meeting, and this matters because a director can be removed only at a meeting. Option B would leave the members with no route to remove a director whom the board supports.

463. A fee earner in the regulated sector has reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering on a corporate matter, but decides to say nothing because she cannot prove anything and does not want to lose a valuable client. What is the consequence of that decision?

A. Failing to disclose in the regulated sector is itself a criminal offence.

B. There is no consequence, because a suspicion which cannot be proved need not be reported.

C. The consequence is a regulatory finding by the SRA, but no criminal liability arises.

D. She commits an offence only if the transaction is later shown to have been criminal.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Failing to disclose in the regulated sector is itself a criminal offence): the duty is triggered by knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds for suspicion, so proof is not needed and silence is an offence in its own right. Option D is wrong because liability turns on what she knew or suspected at the time, not on the outcome of any later investigation.

464. A company pays a dividend at a time when it has no distributable profits. One recipient is a non executive director who had seen the management accounts and knew the position. Another is a passive investor who received nothing beyond the payment advice. What is the position on repayment?

A. Both must repay, because an unlawful dividend is recoverable from every recipient.

B. Neither must repay, because the fault lies with the directors who authorised the payment.

C. The recipient who knew the position must repay; the passive investor need not.

D. Both may keep the dividend, but the directors must make good the company's loss.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The recipient who knew the position must repay; the passive investor need not): a member is liable to repay an unlawful distribution where he knew, or had reasonable grounds to believe, that it was unlawful, so knowledge is the test. Option A ignores that requirement, and the directors who authorised the payment may separately be liable to make good the loss.

465. A firm carries on a regulated activity without authorisation and without any exclusion or exemption applying to it. The client later regrets the transaction and asks about the consequences of the breach, both for the firm and for the agreement itself. Which answer is correct?

A. The breach is a disciplinary matter for the SRA and carries no other consequence.

B. The agreement stands, but the firm must refund the fees charged for the work.

C. The breach makes the agreement void from the outset and exposes the client to prosecution.

D. It is a criminal offence, and the agreement may be unenforceable against the client.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It is a criminal offence, and the agreement may be unenforceable against the client): breaching the general prohibition is an offence, and an agreement made in the course of the unauthorised activity is generally unenforceable against the other party, who may also recover money paid. Option C is wrong because it is the firm in breach, not the client, who faces prosecution.

466. Three partners run a surveying firm. One partner, acting in the ordinary course of the firm's work, negligently prepares a valuation report and the client suffers loss. The client sues. The other two partners say the negligent partner alone should pay. How does the law allocate liability to the client?

A. Only the negligent partner is liable, because the wrong was committed by her.

B. The partners are liable jointly only, so the client must sue all three together.

C. Liability falls on the firm's assets first and on no partner personally at all.

D. All the partners are liable jointly and severally for the wrongful act.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (All the partners are liable jointly and severally for the wrongful act): under the Partnership Act 1890 partners are liable jointly for the firm's debts and obligations, and jointly and severally for wrongful acts and omissions in the ordinary course of business. The client may therefore recover the whole loss from any one of them. Option A is wrong because the very point of partnership is that the firm's business exposes every partner to the acts of the others.

467. A firm introduces a client to a stockbroker and passes on the client's instructions so that a share purchase can be completed. The firm gives no advice on the merits of the investment at all. The trainee asks whether the firm has carried on a specified activity. What is the position?

A. Arranging deals in investments is itself a specified activity, whatever advice was given.

B. No specified activity arises, because only advice on the merits is a specified activity.

C. No specified activity arises, because the broker rather than the firm made the arrangements.

D. A specified activity arises only where the firm receives a commission from the broker.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Arranging deals in investments is itself a specified activity, whatever advice was given): the specified activities include dealing as agent, arranging deals, managing investments and advising on the merits, so a firm can be caught without ever expressing a view on the investment. Option B is wrong because it treats advising as the only specified activity, which would leave introductions and arrangements unregulated.

468. A company wishes to lend sixty thousand pounds to its finance director to help him buy a house. The parties accept that the loan falls within no statutory exception. The company secretary asks what the members must be given as part of the approval process. What does the Act require?

A. A special resolution of the members supported by a directors' statement of solvency.

B. An ordinary resolution alone, because a loan to a director needs no further formality.

C. An ordinary resolution, with a memorandum of the loan's nature, amount and purpose.

D. Board approval alone, provided the loan is made on ordinary commercial terms.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (An ordinary resolution, with a memorandum of the loan's nature, amount and purpose): member approval of a loan to a director must be preceded by a memorandum setting out those matters, made available to members before the resolution is passed. Option B is wrong because it omits the memorandum, which is the safeguard that makes the members' approval an informed one.

469. The board of a private company wishes to pay a dividend at the half year, without waiting for the annual accounts or for a members' meeting. The finance director asks whether the members must vote on the payment before it can be made. What is the correct advice?

A. An interim dividend may be paid by the board without any members' resolution.

B. Any dividend requires an ordinary resolution of the members before it may be paid.

C. An interim dividend requires a special resolution because the annual accounts are unavailable.

D. The board may pay an interim dividend only if the articles are first amended.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (An interim dividend may be paid by the board without any members' resolution): a final dividend is declared by the members by ordinary resolution on the board's recommendation, but an interim dividend is decided on by the directors alone. The payment must still come out of profits available for distribution. Option B states the rule for final dividends and applies it too widely.

470. A company allots shares to a supplier in exchange for machinery rather than for cash. An existing shareholder complains that the shares were not offered to him first, and claims that his statutory pre emption rights have been breached. Is that complaint well founded?

A. Yes, because pre emption rights apply to any allotment of equity securities made.

B. Yes, unless the articles expressly exclude pre emption on allotments for a non cash asset.

C. No, because the statutory rights apply only where the allottee is not already a member.

D. No, because the statutory rights apply to equity securities allotted for cash.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (No, because the statutory rights apply to equity securities allotted for cash): the statutory pre emption regime is confined to allotments for cash consideration, so an allotment for machinery falls outside it. Option A overstates the reach of the right by ignoring the cash requirement, which is the limit that makes a non cash allotment a common way of introducing a new shareholder.

471. A company proposes to sell a warehouse to one of its directors. The parties accept that the value of the warehouse exceeds the statutory threshold, so the sale is a substantial property transaction. The board asks what member approval is needed before the sale proceeds. What is required?

A. An ordinary resolution of the members approving the substantial property transaction.

B. A special resolution of the members, with the director abstaining from the vote.

C. Nothing further, because the board may approve any disposal of the company's assets.

D. Written confirmation from the company's auditors that the agreed price is a fair value.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (An ordinary resolution of the members approving the substantial property transaction): a substantial property transaction between a company and a director or a person connected with a director requires member approval by ordinary resolution, and without it the arrangement is voidable and the director must account for any gain. Option B applies the wrong threshold, since a special resolution is required for constitutional matters, not for this approval.

472. A firm cannot bring its work within any exclusion and is considering relying on the exemption for members of a designated professional body. The compliance officer asks what conditions must be satisfied before the firm can rely on it. Which answer states them correctly?

A. The work must be charged at cost and be carried out by a qualified solicitor.

B. The client must be a corporate client and must give informed consent in writing.

C. The activity must be incidental to professional services, with commission accounted for.

D. The firm must notify the Financial Conduct Authority of each individual transaction.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The activity must be incidental to professional services, with commission accounted for): the Part 20 exemption requires the regulated activity to be incidental to the professional services provided, the firm to account to the client for any commission, the activity not to be a prohibited one, and compliance with the SRA Financial Services Scope Rules. Option A invents a costs condition which forms no part of the regime.

473. A trainee is asked to work out whether a piece of advice her firm gave amounts to a regulated activity. She asks what must be established before the general prohibition in section 19 can bite on the firm's work. Which answer sets out the correct elements?

A. A specified activity, carried on by way of business, relating to a specified investment.

B. A specified investment, held by the client, and a fee charged for the work.

C. Advice given in writing, relating to land, and given to a private individual.

D. An activity carried on for profit, in the United Kingdom, by an incorporated body.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (A specified activity, carried on by way of business, relating to a specified investment): all three limbs must be present, and the absence of any one of them takes the work outside the regime before any exclusion is even considered. Option B is wrong because charging a fee is not one of the limbs, although it may be evidence that the activity is carried on by way of business.

474. A company has assets worth four million pounds and liabilities of three million pounds, but its cash has run out and it cannot pay a supplier's invoice which fell due last month. A director says the company cannot be insolvent because its assets exceed its liabilities. Is he right?

A. No, a company is insolvent if it cannot pay its debts as they fall due.

B. Yes, because insolvency depends on whether assets exceed liabilities in the accounts.

C. Yes, provided that the shortfall in available cash is expected to be temporary.

D. No, because a single unpaid invoice is conclusive proof that a company is insolvent.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (No, a company is insolvent if it cannot pay its debts as they fall due): the cash flow test and the balance sheet test are alternatives, and failing either one makes the company insolvent. Option B treats the balance sheet test as the only test, which would let a company with valuable but unsaleable assets carry on incurring credit it cannot meet.

475. A partner retires from a firm of caterers. He wants to be sure that he cannot be fixed with liability for debts which the firm runs up after he has gone. His solicitor advises him on the notices he should give in order to protect himself. Which advice is correct?

A. Notice in the London Gazette alone will protect him against every category of person.

B. Actual notice to the firm's existing customers alone is enough to protect him.

C. Give actual notice to existing customers and publish notice in the London Gazette.

D. No notice is needed, because liability for later debts falls on the continuing partners.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Give actual notice to existing customers and publish notice in the London Gazette): a retired partner remains liable for later debts to anyone who dealt with the firm before and has not had notice of the retirement, so actual notice is needed for existing customers and a Gazette notice covers everyone else. Option A leaves him exposed to established customers, who are entitled to actual notice.

476. Two accountants agree in conversation to practise together as a limited liability partnership. They open a bank account in the chosen name and begin taking on clients. Nothing has been filed with the Registrar. A client now sues them over bad advice. What is the position of the two accountants?

A. They are liable personally, because an LLP exists only once it has been incorporated.

B. They are protected, because they agreed to trade as a limited liability partnership.

C. They are protected, because the chosen name put the client on notice of the entity.

D. They are liable personally, because the members of an LLP have unlimited liability.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (They are liable personally, because an LLP exists only once it has been incorporated): unlike a general partnership, an LLP requires incorporation under the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000, so until registration the two are simply partners with unlimited liability. Option B is wrong because limited liability comes from incorporation and never from the parties' own agreement.

477. A solicitor is choosing between a section 994 petition and a derivative claim for a minority client. The client wants a clean exit from the company with money in her own hand, rather than a recovery that stays inside the company. Which route fits her aim?

A. A section 994 petition, whose usual outcome is a purchase of her shares.

B. A derivative claim, because any sum recovered is paid directly to the claimant.

C. A derivative claim, because the court may order the majority to buy her out.

D. Either route, because both of them produce a payment made personally to the member.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (A section 994 petition, whose usual outcome is a purchase of her shares): the petition is a personal remedy and the standard order is that the majority buy the petitioner out, giving her the exit she wants. Option B is wrong because the whole nature of a derivative claim is that the company, not the member, receives the remedy.

478. A firm is instructed by a new corporate client on an urgent acquisition. The client says the identity documents will follow next week and asks the firm to press on with the drafting and with exchange in the meantime. What is the correct approach for the firm to take?

A. Press on with the drafting, provided the documents arrive before completion takes place.

B. Carry out due diligence before establishing the business relationship with the client.

C. Press on, because due diligence is required only where a transaction looks unusual.

D. Ask the client's own bank to confirm identity, which removes the need for documents.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Carry out due diligence before establishing the business relationship with the client): customer due diligence must be applied before a business relationship is established or an occasional transaction is carried out, and commercial urgency is no answer. Option A postpones the checks to completion, which leaves the firm acting on a matter it has not yet been able to assess for risk.

479. A buyer offers eight hundred thousand pounds for a business whose accounts suggest it is worth two hundred thousand pounds, asks at the last minute for the purchaser to become an unfamiliar overseas company, and will not give ownership information. What should the fee earner conclude?

A. Nothing turns on the price, because parties are free to agree whatever they wish.

B. The change of purchaser is routine, and only the price is a matter of any concern.

C. These are recognised red flags and the position must be considered before proceeding.

D. The transaction is acceptable, because the funds will pass through a regulated bank.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (These are recognised red flags and the position must be considered before proceeding): a price that does not match the value of the business, a late change to the purchaser or the structure, and reluctance to give ownership information are all recognised warning signs, and together they call for the reporting officer's involvement. Option D is wrong because the use of a regulated bank does not show that the money is clean.

480. A new corporate client is owned through two offshore companies, and the client is reluctant to disclose their own ownership. The fee earner has verified the client company's existence and constitution at Companies House and has gone no further. What further step does the regime require?

A. Nothing further, because the client company's existence has already been verified.

B. Take reasonable measures to identify and verify the individuals behind the structure.

C. Report the matter to the Financial Conduct Authority before continuing to act.

D. Obtain a written statement from the offshore companies confirming their own ownership.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Take reasonable measures to identify and verify the individuals behind the structure): customer due diligence requires the beneficial owner to be identified and reasonable measures taken to verify identity, and ownership layered through offshore vehicles is a recognised warning sign rather than an excuse to stop. Option D is wrong because a self serving statement from the very companies in question is not verification from a reliable independent source.

481. A private company calls a general meeting to consider an ordinary resolution. The company secretary asks how much notice must be given to the members, on the footing that nobody has been asked to agree to short notice. Which period does the Companies Act 2006 require?

A. Fourteen clear days' notice to every member entitled to receive notice of it.

B. Twenty one clear days' notice, being the period required for a company's annual meeting.

C. Seven clear days' notice, because the resolution to be proposed is an ordinary one.

D. Twenty eight clear days' notice, matching the special notice period for removing a director.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (Fourteen clear days' notice to every member entitled to receive notice of it): the default period for a general meeting of a private company is fourteen clear days, and it does not vary with the type of resolution proposed. Option C is wrong because the notice period is not shortened simply because the resolution is an ordinary one rather than a special one.

482. A director of a company proposes that the company buy machinery from a business owned by his wife. The board is about to consider the proposal at its next meeting. The director says he need do nothing about his position until after the contract has been signed. What should he do?

A. Nothing, because the interest belongs to his wife and not to him personally.

B. Declare the nature and extent of his interest before the company enters the contract.

C. Resign from the board and rejoin it once the machinery has been delivered.

D. Obtain a special resolution of the members approving the proposed purchase of machinery.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Declare the nature and extent of his interest before the company enters the contract): section 177 of the Companies Act 2006 requires a director interested in a proposed transaction to declare that interest to the other directors before the company commits itself. His wife's ownership is plainly an indirect interest of his. Option A is wrong because the duty catches indirect interests, which is exactly how a connected person's business is treated.

483. Four partners run a bookshop and have no written agreement, so the Partnership Act 1890 defaults apply. Three of them wish to convert half the premises into a licensed bar. The fourth objects. The three say that a majority of partners decides the question. Who is right?

A. The three are right, because ordinary management decisions are taken by majority.

B. The three are right, provided they compensate the objector for her profit share.

C. The objector is right, because a change in the business needs unanimous consent.

D. The objector is right, because each partner has a veto on all management matters.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (The objector is right, because a change in the business needs unanimous consent): the default rules allow ordinary matters connected with the business to be decided by majority, but no change may be made to the nature of the partnership business without the consent of all existing partners. Option A is wrong because converting half a bookshop into a bar changes the nature of the business rather than managing the existing one.

484. Three partners contribute capital of ninety thousand, sixty thousand and thirty thousand pounds to their new business. They have no written agreement. At the year end the largest contributor claims a share of the profits in proportion to capital. The other two disagree. How are the profits shared?

A. In proportion to the capital contributed, because that reflects each partner's investment.

B. Equally between the three partners, whatever capital each of them contributed.

C. Equally, after paying the largest contributor interest on her capital at a commercial rate.

D. In proportion to the hours which each partner has worked in the business that year.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Equally between the three partners, whatever capital each of them contributed): the Partnership Act 1890 default is that partners share equally in the capital and profits, and contribute equally to losses, regardless of what each put in. Option C adds interest on capital, which is another default the Act denies, and both points show why unequal contributors need a written agreement.

485. A solicitor acting as an executor of an estate sells a holding of quoted shares in order to raise money to pay a legacy. She does so in the ordinary course of administering the estate. She asks whether she needs authorisation for that sale. What is the position?

A. An exclusion covers activities carried on in the course of administering an estate.

B. Authorisation is needed, because dealing in quoted shares is a regulated activity.

C. Authorisation is needed unless all of the beneficiaries consent to the sale in writing.

D. No exclusion applies, but a personal representative is exempt from the general prohibition.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (An exclusion covers activities carried on in the course of administering an estate): activities carried out by a personal representative or trustee in the administration of an estate or trust are excluded, so the executor may realise investments to pay legacies. Option B ignores the exclusion and would make routine estate administration impossible without authorisation.

486. A firm arranges a share purchase for a client entirely through an authorised stockbroker, who deals with the client directly on the merits and on the price. The firm asks whether any exclusion is available to it on those facts. Which answer is correct?

A. No exclusion applies, because the firm still made arrangements for the transaction.

B. An exclusion applies only where the client is an experienced professional investor.

C. No exclusion applies, but the firm may rely on its authorisation from the SRA.

D. An exclusion covers arrangements made with or through an authorised person.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (An exclusion covers arrangements made with or through an authorised person): where the transaction is entered into through an authorised person who deals with the client directly, the arranging activity is taken outside the regime. Option C is wrong because SRA regulation is not authorisation under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000.

487. A company was incorporated last year. A creditor now discovers that one of the incorporation documents contained an error about the address of the registered office. He argues that the company never came into existence and that the subscribers are personally liable on the contract. What is the position?

A. The certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the company exists.

B. The company is void from the outset because the delivered documents were defective.

C. The subscribers are personally liable until the register at Companies House is corrected.

D. The company exists only once the Registrar has issued a corrected certificate of incorporation.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The certificate of incorporation is conclusive evidence that the company exists): once the Registrar issues the certificate, the company is validly incorporated and the certificate cannot be gone behind, which protects those dealing with it. The registered office details can simply be corrected by filing. Option B is wrong because a defect in the delivered documents does not retrospectively unmake a company that has been registered.

488. A client is buying the whole of the issued share capital of a trading company and will run the business himself once the acquisition has completed. His solicitor advises on the share purchase agreement and on the price. Which exclusion is most likely to apply to that work?

A. The trustee exclusion, because the buyer will hold the shares for the company's benefit.

B. The takeover exclusion, since the object is day to day control of the company.

C. The professional firms exemption, because the work is incidental to legal services.

D. No exclusion applies, because shares are a specified investment in every case.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (The takeover exclusion, since the object is day to day control of the company): the exclusion covers an acquisition of shares carrying a specified proportion of the voting power where the object is to obtain day to day control, which is why buying an entire company often falls outside the regime. Option C is not an exclusion at all but the separate Part 20 exemption, which is only reached once every exclusion has failed.

489. Two members of a limited liability partnership fall out. One of them negligently advises a client, who sues for the loss. The other member says he must personally meet half of any award, because the two of them are in partnership together. Is that correct?

A. Yes, because members of a limited liability partnership are liable jointly and severally.

B. No, because the limited liability partnership itself owes the liability to the client.

C. Yes, because each member is the agent of every other member of the entity.

D. No, because the negligent member alone is liable and the entity has no liability.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (No, because the limited liability partnership itself owes the liability to the client): an LLP is a body corporate, so its members are agents of the entity and not of each other, and the entity owes the debts. Option A applies the general partnership rule to a body corporate, which is exactly the difference that makes the LLP attractive to professional firms.

490. Two partners have carried on a garage business for eleven years with no written agreement and no fixed term. One of them now writes to the other saying that she is bringing the partnership to an end with immediate effect. The other objects. What is the effect of that letter?

A. It has no effect, because a partnership of that length ends only by court order.

B. It has no effect, because dissolution requires the consent of all of the partners.

C. It dissolves the partnership only once six months of reasonable notice have expired.

D. It dissolves the partnership, because a partnership at will ends on notice.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (It dissolves the partnership, because a partnership at will ends on notice): where no fixed term has been agreed, any partner may determine the partnership by giving notice to the others, and the length of the relationship makes no difference. Option C invents a notice period the Act does not require, and the risk that a partner can end the business by letter is the strongest argument for a written agreement.

491. Four architects wish to practise together. They want the entity itself to contract with clients and to owe its own debts, but they also want to continue being taxed individually on their share of the profits rather than at entity level. Which business medium best meets both aims?

A. A private company limited by shares, taxed on its own trading profits.

B. A general partnership under the Partnership Act 1890 with a written agreement.

C. A sole trader business with three of the architects engaged as employees.

D. A limited liability partnership, a body corporate whose members are taxed transparently.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (A limited liability partnership, a body corporate whose members are taxed transparently): an LLP incorporated under the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 has its own legal personality and contracts in its own name, yet its members are taxed as partners on their profit shares. That combination is why professional firms use it. Option A fails the second aim, because a company is itself charged to corporation tax on its profits.

492. A shareholder signs a stock transfer form and hands it, with her share certificate, to a buyer who pays the agreed price. The buyer has not yet been entered in the register of members. The company then declares a dividend. Who is entitled to be paid that dividend by the company?

A. The seller, because legal title passes only on registration in the register of members.

B. The buyer, because he holds the signed stock transfer form and the share certificate.

C. The buyer, because legal and beneficial ownership both pass on delivery of the form.

D. Neither of them, because the dividend must be held back until the register is updated.

Answer: A

The correct answer is A (The seller, because legal title passes only on registration in the register of members): a transfer binds the company only once the buyer is registered, so until then the seller remains the member the company must pay, holding the benefit for the buyer. Option C is wrong because delivery of the executed form passes the beneficial interest but not the legal title the company recognises.

493. Ravi and Sadia sell handmade furniture together from a workshop in Leeds. They share the profits equally, both take orders and both buy timber. They have signed nothing and registered nothing at Companies House. A supplier now sues over an unpaid timber invoice. What is the legal position of their business?

A. They are a limited liability partnership because they share the profits equally.

B. They are a company, because they trade under a single joint business name.

C. They are a general partnership, formed without any formality or registration.

D. They are a sole trader business run by whichever of them took the order.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (They are a general partnership, formed without any formality or registration): a partnership arises under the Partnership Act 1890 wherever two or more persons carry on a business in common with a view of profit, and no writing, filing or registration is needed. Ravi and Sadia meet that test, so each is liable for the timber debt. Option A is wrong because a limited liability partnership is a body corporate that comes into existence only on incorporation under the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000.

494. A shareholder in a family company complains that she dislikes the board's cautious dividend policy. The policy follows the articles and applies in exactly the same way to every shareholder, including the majority. She wants to petition on the ground of unfair prejudice. What is the main difficulty?

A. A petition may only be brought by a member holding at least ten per cent.

B. She must show both unfairness and prejudice, judged against the members' bargain.

C. A petition may only be presented once the company has already entered liquidation.

D. The only remedy sought must be damages, which the court has no power to award.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (She must show both unfairness and prejudice, judged against the members' bargain): a section 994 petition requires conduct that is both unfair and prejudicial to the petitioner's interests as a member, measured against the terms on which the members agreed to associate. A policy applied evenly and in accordance with the articles is unlikely to qualify. Option A is wrong because there is no minimum shareholding for a petition.

495. A director with no financial training signs off accounts he does not understand, relying entirely on a colleague. He says he did his honest best given his limited experience. The company later suffers loss as a result. How is his conduct judged under section 174?

A. By his own actual knowledge and experience alone, given his lack of any training.

B. By the standard to be expected of a professional accountant in the same position.

C. By whether he acted honestly, because good faith answers a claim of this kind.

D. By an objective standard, raised by any greater knowledge or experience he actually has.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (By an objective standard, raised by any greater knowledge or experience he actually has): section 174 sets a minimum standard of the care, skill and diligence of a reasonably diligent person carrying out that director's functions, which is then raised, but never lowered, by the individual's own knowledge and experience. Option A is wrong because it treats the subjective element as a floor when it operates only to increase the standard.

496. The board of a private company wishes to amend its articles to introduce a compulsory transfer provision applying when an employee shareholder leaves the business. The board asks the solicitor what member approval is required before the amended articles are filed at Companies House. Which answer is correct?

A. An ordinary resolution of the members, passed on a simple majority of votes cast.

B. A special resolution of the members, needing not less than seventy five per cent.

C. A board resolution alone, since the articles regulate the company's internal management.

D. Unanimous written consent of every member, because the change affects share transfers.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (A special resolution of the members, needing not less than seventy five per cent): the articles are altered by special resolution under the Companies Act 2006, and a copy of the amended articles is then filed. Option A applies the wrong threshold: an ordinary resolution of more than fifty per cent is enough to appoint or remove a director, but not to change the constitution.

497. A client compares a limited liability partnership with a private company limited by shares. She asks which features the two share and which they do not. Her adviser explains the position on legal personality, on filing accounts and on the taxation of profits. Which statement is accurate?

A. Both have separate personality, both file accounts, and both pay corporation tax.

B. Neither has separate personality, but both file accounts and are taxed transparently.

C. Both have separate personality and file accounts, but LLP members are taxed transparently.

D. Both are taxed transparently, but only the company has separate legal personality.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (Both have separate personality and file accounts, but LLP members are taxed transparently): an LLP and a company are each a body corporate with public filing obligations, and the difference lies in the tax treatment, since LLP members are taxed on their profit shares while a company pays tax on its own profits. Option A gets the tax point wrong, and that point is usually what decides the choice.

498. A liquidator wants to allege fraudulent trading against a director rather than wrongful trading, because the stigma attached to it is greater. The evidence shows that the director was over optimistic and badly informed, but not dishonest. What is the difficulty with the fraudulent trading allegation?

A. Fraudulent trading may be alleged by the Secretary of State and not by a liquidator.

B. Fraudulent trading requires an intent to defraud creditors, and so requires dishonesty.

C. Fraudulent trading applies only to a company which has entered compulsory liquidation.

D. Fraudulent trading carries no financial remedy, so the allegation would achieve nothing.

Answer: B

The correct answer is B (Fraudulent trading requires an intent to defraud creditors, and so requires dishonesty): the claim depends on the business having been carried on with intent to defraud creditors or for a fraudulent purpose, which sets a far higher bar than wrongful trading. Option D is wrong because the court may order a contribution to the assets on either claim, so the remedy is not the difficulty.

499. A private company wants to buy back the shares of a departing shareholder. It has substantial distributable profits and does not wish to raise any new money for the purpose. The board asks which funds may lawfully be used for the purchase. Which answer is correct?

A. Only the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose.

B. Any of the company's cash, because a buyback is an ordinary trading payment.

C. Only capital, and then only if the strict statutory procedure has been followed.

D. Its distributable profits, the ordinary source for a purchase of its own shares.

Answer: D

The correct answer is D (Its distributable profits, the ordinary source for a purchase of its own shares): a company may buy its own shares out of distributable profits or the proceeds of a fresh issue made for the purpose, and a private company may in addition use capital under a strict procedure. Option C treats the exceptional capital route as the only one available, when the company already has the profits to fund the purchase.

500. Four months before liquidation, an insolvent company repaid in full an unsecured loan owed to the finance director's brother, while leaving its trade creditors unpaid. The liquidator wants that payment set aside. What must be shown, and what assists the liquidator on these facts?

A. Only that the creditor was paid in full, which settles the matter against a connected person.

B. That the company was solvent at the time, which the director's brother must disprove.

C. A desire to prefer, which is presumed where the creditor is a connected person.

D. That the payment was made within six months, a period that cannot be extended.

Answer: C

The correct answer is C (A desire to prefer, which is presumed where the creditor is a connected person): a preference requires that the company was influenced by a desire to put the creditor in a better position than on a liquidation, and that desire is presumed for a connected person, who also has a two year relevant period rather than six months. Option D applies the shorter period, which is reserved for unconnected creditors.
